profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-17T20:38:50.346+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: In the eleventh month,
Gāozǔ dispatched Dù Sēngmíng and Hú Yǐng with two thousand men to station themselves on the ridge.
At the same time, he extensively formed alliances with the magnates and heroes of Shǐxīng to conspire for a righteous uprising.
Hóu Āndū, Zhāng Sī, and others, leading over a thousand men, came to join him.
Xiāo Bó, hearing of this,
sent Zhōng Xiūyuè to persuade Gāozǔ, saying:
“Hóu Jǐng is a fierce hero,
unmatched in the world.
Previously, our relief army of ten myriad men,
with strong and elite soldiers and horses,
yet no one dared to stand against his vanguard,
thus allowing the Jie bandit to achieve his ambition.
With your paltry numbers,
where will you go?
I hear that the princes and marquises north of the ridge are all in an uproar again.
Hédōng and Guìyáng have been successively ravaged,
Shàolíng and Kāijiàn have soon faced warfare.
Lǐ Qiānshì, entrusting himself to Dāngyáng,
immediately seized their horses and weapons.
Given your remote and isolated position,
how can you secretly seek refuge?
It is better to stay in Shǐxīng for now,
projecting your influence from afar,
to hold this great mountain,
and seek your own good fortune.”
Gāozǔ wept and said to Xiūyuè:
“I, your servant, am originally humble and insignificant,
yet I received the nation’s grace and fostering.
When I heard Hóu Jǐng crossed the Jiāng,
I immediately wished to go to his aid,
but I encountered Yuán and Lán,
who blocked my path midway.
Now the capital has fallen,
and the emperor is in distress.
When the ruler is disgraced, the minister dies;
who dares to cherish their life!
Your esteemed lord, being of royal lineage,
bears the heavy responsibility of a regional commander,
yet cannot break through ten thousand *lǐ* to
avenge this injustice and pain.
Even dispatching a single army
would be better than nothing,
but instead, you deliver a belated decree,
which makes one sigh with regret.
My plan is decided;
please convey this on my behalf.”
He then sent an envoy via a secluded path to Jiānglíng
to receive instructions for military operations and dispositions.
At that time, Cài Lùyǎng raised an army and occupied Nánkāng.
Bó dispatched his confidant Tán Shìyuǎn to be the magistrate of Qújiāng,
who allied with Lùyǎng
to jointly obstruct the righteous army.
In the first month of the first year of Dàbǎo,
Gāozǔ set out from Shǐxīng
and reached Dàyǔlǐng.
Lùyǎng led his army out and stationed them at Nányě,
establishing four fortified cities relying on the mountains and rivers to resist Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ engaged them in battle
and thoroughly defeated them.
Lùyǎng escaped and fled.
Gāozǔ advanced and stationed his troops at Nánkāng.
Xiāngdōng Wáng, acting as regent, conferred upon Gāozǔ the titles of Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì, Chíjié, Míngwēi Jiāngjūn, and Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ,
and re-enfeoffed him as Nányě Xiàn Bó.
In the sixth month,
Gāozǔ repaired the ancient city of Qítóu
and moved his residence there.
Lǐ Qiānshì, the Cìshǐ of Gāozhōu, occupied Dàgāo,
and dispatched his commander Dù Pínglǔ with a thousand men to enter Gǎnxí and Yúliáng.
Gāozǔ ordered Zhōu Wényù to lead troops to attack and drive them away.
Qiānshì fled to Níngdū.
Acting as regent, he conferred upon Gāozǔ the titles of Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, Shǐ Chíjié, Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn, and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
while also holding the post of Yùzhāng Nèishǐ,
and re-enfeoffed him as Chángchéng Xiàn Hóu.
Soon after, he was granted the titles of Sànqí Chángshì, Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū Liù Jùn Zhū Jūnshì, Jūnshī Jiāngjūn, and Nánjiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the rest remaining as before.
At that time, Liú Ài and others from Níngdū provided Qiānshì with boats, ships, weapons, and armaments,
intending to attack Nánkāng.
Gāozǔ dispatched Dù Sēngmíng and others with twenty thousand men to occupy Báikǒu,
building a city to defend against them.
Qiānshì also erected a city to confront them.
In the third month of the second year,
Sēngmíng and others attacked and captured their city,
taking Qiānshì alive and sending him to Nánkāng.
Gāozǔ beheaded him.
Acting as regent, he ordered Gāozǔ to advance his troops to pacify Jiāngzhōu,
and then conferred upon him the title of Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the rest remaining as before.
In the sixth month,
Gāo Zǔ departed from Nán Kāng.
Nán Kāng’s Gǎn Shí previously had twenty-four shoals.
The shoals had many large rocks,
which travelers considered difficult.
When Gāo Zǔ departed,
the water suddenly rose several *zhàng*,
and all the large rocks within a three hundred *lǐ* radius were submerged.
The army advanced and encamped at Xī Chāng.
A dragon was seen by the water's edge,
about five *zhàng* tall,
its five colors shining brightly.
Tens of thousands of soldiers and civilians observed it.
At this time, acting under imperial authorization, he dispatched the General Who Conquers the East, Wáng Sēngbiàn, to lead the various armies to attack Hóu Jǐng.
In the eighth month,
Sēngbiàn’s army reached Pén Chéng.
Gāo Zǔ led Dù Sēngmíng and other generals with their armies, as well as the local chieftains from Nán Chuān, totaling thirty thousand men, to meet there.
At this time, the Western Army lacked food.
Gāo Zǔ had previously stored five hundred thousand *dàn* of military provisions;
he now distributed three hundred thousand *dàn* to supply them.
He then encamped at Bā Qiū.
Meanwhile, Hóu Jǐng deposed Emperor Jiǎnwén
and enthroned Dòng, the heir-prince of Yù Zhāng.
Gāo Zǔ sent the Acting Chief Scribe, Shěn Gǔn, to present a memorial at Jiāng Líng, urging an imperial ascension.
In the eleventh month,

acting under imperial authorization, Gāo Zǔ was granted the titles of Bearer of Credentials, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of the Five Commanderies of Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Xīn'ān, Línhǎi, and Yǒngjiā, General Who Pacifies the East, and Governor of Dōngyáng Zhōu,
concurrently serving as Administrator of Kuàijī and Internal Scribe of Yù Zhāng.
All other posts remained as before.
In the first month of the third year,
Gāo Zǔ led thirty thousand armored soldiers, five thousand strong crossbows, and two thousand ships,
departing from Yù Zhāng.
In the second month,
he arrived at Sāngluò Zhōu.
He dispatched the Chief Scribe of the Central Secretariat, Jiāng Yuánlǐ, to present a memorial detailing the situation to Jiāng Líng.
Acting under imperial authorization, Gāo Zǔ was granted an additional set of drums and pipes.
At this time, Sēngbiàn had already departed from Pén Chéng
and met Gāo Zǔ at Báimáo Wān.
They then disembarked and built an altar,
sacrificed animals, and swore an oath.
They advanced and encamped at Wúhú.
The commander of Hóu Jǐng’s city, Zhāng Hēi, abandoned the city and fled.
In the third month,
Gāo Zǔ and the various armies advanced and captured Gū Shú,
then encamped at Cài Zhōu.
Hóu Jǐng ascended Shítóu Chéng to observe the situation.
He was very displeased,
and said to his attendants:
“This army has a purple aura above it;
it will not be easy to contend with.”
He then used boats filled with stones to block the mouth of the Huái River,
and built a city along the Huái.
From Shítóu to Qīng Xī, over ten *lǐ*,
watchtowers and battlements were continuous.
The generals had not yet made a decision.
Sēngbiàn sent Dù Zé to ask Gāo Zǔ for a plan.
Gāo Zǔ said:
“Previously, Liǔ Zhònglǐ’s hundreds of thousands of troops sat across the water,
and Wéi Càn, when at Qīng Xī,
never crossed the shore.
The bandits then ascended to a high vantage point to observe them,
their courage completely gone,
and perpetrated their atrocities,
overwhelming our royal army.
Now, in besieging Shítóu,
we must cross to the north bank.
If the various generals cannot withstand the vanguard,
I request to go first and establish palisades.”
Gāo Zǔ immediately built palisades at Hénglǒng, west of Shítóu Chéng.
The various armies then consecutively built eight fortresses,
extending directly to the northeast.
The bandits, fearing their western route would be cut off,
also built five fortresses in the fruit orchards to the northeast to block the main road.
Jǐng led over ten thousand men and more than eight hundred iron cavalry,
forming a battle array and advancing.
Gāo Zǔ said:
“The military treatises state that
those skilled in warfare
are like the snake of Cháng Shān,
head and tail responding to each other.
Now our army is numerous,
while the bandit horde is very few.
We should divide the bandit’s forces,
to control the strong with the weak.
Why gather their sharp vanguard,
allowing them to die certainly by our hands?”
He then ordered the various generals to deploy their troops separately.
The bandits directly charged Wáng Sēngzhì.
Sēngzhì retreated slightly.
Gāo Zǔ sent Xú Dù to lead two thousand crossbowmen to cut off their rear.
The bandits then withdrew.
Gāo Zǔ, with Wáng Lín and Dù Kān, vigorously pressed them with iron cavalry.
The bandits retreated to their palisades.
Jǐng’s ceremonial aide, Lú Huīlüè, opened the north gate of Shítóu and surrendered.
Battalion commanders Dài Miǎn and Cáo Xuān attacked and captured one fortress in the fruit orchards.
The various armies then captured the other four fortresses.
The bandits returned again,
fighting desperately,
and retook all the captured fortresses and palisades.
Gāo Zǔ was furious
and personally led the attack.
The soldiers scaled the palisades and entered.
The bandits scattered and fled again.
Jǐng, with over a hundred cavalry, abandoned their spears and wielded sabers,
charging the lines left and right.
The lines held firm.
Jǐng’s forces completely collapsed,
and were pursued to Xīmíng Mén.
Jǐng reached the palace gate
but dared not enter the palace.
He sent his trusted aides to retrieve his two sons and then fled.
Gāo Zǔ led his forces out of Guǎnglíng to receive them.
Meanwhile, Jǐng’s general Guō Yuánjiàn fled to Qí.
〔一０〕Gāo Zǔ accepted his three thousand troops and returned.
Sēngbiàn memorialized for Gāo Zǔ to garrison Jīngkǒu.
In the fifth month,
Qí sent Xīn Shù to besiege Yán Chāodá in Qín Jùn.
Gāo Zǔ ordered Xú Dù to lead troops to help defend.
Qí had seventy thousand troops,
filling the area,
building earthen mounds,
and digging tunnels,
attacking very fiercely.
Gāo Zǔ then personally led ten thousand men to relieve the siege,
sending troops to attack the Qí army from all four sides.
Bows and crossbows fired indiscriminately.
Qí’s Prince Píngqín died from a stray arrow.
Hundreds of heads were taken.
The Qí people withdrew their troops and retreated.
Gāo Zǔ led his triumphant army back south.
He sent the Scribe of the Secretariat, Liú Běnrén, to present the victory report to Jiāng Líng.
In the seventh month,
the expatriates of Guǎnglíng, Zhū Shèng and Zhāng Xiàng, secretly raised troops to attack the Qí Governor Wēn Zhòngyōng.
They sent envoys to report,
and Gāo Zǔ led his forces to cross the Jiāng to respond.
Meanwhile, the Qí people came to offer tribute,
requesting to cede the land of Guǎnglíng.
Wáng Sēngbiàn agreed
and reported to Gāo Zǔ.
Gāo Zǔ then withdrew his army back to Nán Xú Zhōu.
More than ten thousand people from north of the Jiāng followed the army south.

Acting under imperial authorization, Gāo Zǔ was granted the titles of Bearer of Credentials, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of Nán Xú Zhōu, Great General Who Conquers the North, Minister of Works with the Powers of the Three Ducal Ministers, and Governor of Nán Xú Zhōu.
All other posts remained as before.
When Wáng Sēngbiàn led his forces to attack Lù Nà in Xiāng Zhōu,
Gāo Zǔ was ordered to take his place in garrisoning Yáng Zhōu.
In the eleventh month,
Prince Xiāngdōng ascended the throne in Jiāng Líng,
changing the third year of Dà Bǎo to the first year of Chéngshèng.
When Xiāng Zhōu was pacified,
〔一一〕Gāo Zǔ returned to garrison Jīngkǒu.
In the third month of the third year,
Gāo Zǔ was promoted to the position of Minister of Works.
〔一二〕All other posts remained as before.
In the eleventh month,
Western Wèi attacked and captured Jiānglíng.
Gāozǔ, Wáng Sēngbiàn, and others presented a memorial to Jiāngzhōu,
requesting Jìn'ān Wáng to assume the position of Tàizǎi and act on behalf of the emperor.
They also dispatched their Chief Clerk Xiè Zhé to present a letter of persuasion to ascend the throne.
In the twelfth month,
Jìn'ān Wáng arrived from Xúnyáng,
entered and resided in the Imperial Hall,
and granted Gāozǔ twenty guards with swords.
In the fifth month of the fourth year,
Qí sent Zhēnyáng Hóu Shēnmíng back to rule the altars of earth and grain.
Wáng Sēngbiàn accepted him, and he was enthroned,
changing the era name to Tiānchéng.
Jìn'ān Wáng was made the Crown Prince.
Initially,
when Qí requested to install Zhēnyáng,
Gāozǔ believed it was unacceptable,
and sent envoys to Sēngbiàn to strongly argue against it.
They went back and forth several times,
but Sēngbiàn ultimately did not comply.
Gāozǔ often sighed with indignation,
and secretly said to his close associates:
"Although Emperor Wǔ established a stable foundation,
extending his influence throughout the four seas,
when it came to avenging humiliation
and overcoming difficulties,
only Xiàoyuán could do it.
His accomplishments were so splendid
that they were unprecedented in previous generations.
Wáng Gōng and I both received important trusts.
Before his words had faded,
his voice was still in our ears.
How could we expect that one day there would be a different plan?
The successor is the grandson of Gāozǔ,
and the son of Yuánhuáng.
The whole country looks to him,
and all under heaven place their trust in him.
What crime did he commit
to be deposed,
seeking barbarians from afar,
and falsely establishing someone out of proper order?
Observing this situation,
one can easily understand."
Thereupon, he secretly prepared thousands of robes,
along with brocade, silk, gold, and silver,
to use as rewards.
On the day Rén'yín in the ninth month,
Gāozǔ summoned Xú Dù, Hóu Āndū, Zhōu Wényù, and others to strategize.
He then arrayed his generals and soldiers,
distributed gold and silk as rewards,
and advanced both by land and water.
That night, he set out from Nánxúzhōu to attack Wáng Sēngbiàn.
On the day Jiǎchén,
Gāozǔ's infantry reached the front of Shítóu.
He dispatched brave soldiers to climb over the city wall from the north.
At that time, Sēngbiàn was attending to official business,
when a report came from outside that there were soldiers.
Soon, soldiers appeared from within.
Sēngbiàn hastily fled,
and encountered his third son Wěi.
They both exited the private chamber,
still accompanied by dozens of guards,
and fought fiercely.
Gāozǔ's main army soon arrived.
Sēngbiàn's forces were outnumbered and outmatched.
He fled to the gate tower of the south city wall.
Gāozǔ used the wind to set fire,
and Sēngbiàn, desperate,
was captured.
That night, Sēngbiàn and Wěi were strangled.
On the day Jǐngwǔ,
and all officials presented a memorial to Jìn'ān Wáng, urging him to ascend the throne.
On the day Jǐyǒu in the tenth month,
Jìn'ān Wáng was enthroned,
and changed the fourth year of Chéngshèng to the first year of Shàotài.
On the day Rénzǐ,
an imperial edict appointed Gāozǔ as Shìzhōng, Dà Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnshì, Chējì Jiāngjūn, and Cìshǐ of Yáng and Nánxú two Prefectures,
with the credentials of Chíjié, Sīkōng, the privilege of armed guards, and drum and fife band, all remaining as before.
Another edict granted Gāozǔ a hundred armored guards
for entry and exit from the palace.
The Cìshǐ of Zhènzhōu, Dù Kān, occupied Wúxīng,
and together with the Tàishǒu of Yìxīng, Wéi Zài, raised an army in rebellion.
Gāozǔ ordered Zhōu Wényù to lead troops to attack Zài in Yìxīng.
Kān sent his cousin Běisǒu to lead troops to resist,
but Běisǒu was defeated and returned to Yìxīng.
On the day Xīnwèi,
Gāozǔ submitted a memorial to campaign in the east,
leaving Hóu Āndū, Cìshǐ of Gāozhōu, and Dù Léng, Cìshǐ of Shízhōu, to guard the imperial palace.
On the day Jiǎxū,
the army reached Yìxīng.
On the day Jǐngzǐ,
they captured its water stockade.
Xú Sìhuī, Cìshǐ of Qínzhōu, occupied his city and surrendered to Qí,
and also called upon Rèn Yuē, Cìshǐ of Nányùzhōu, to raise an army in support of Kān and Zài.
The Qí people supplied them with troops and provisions.
Sìhuī and others, seeing the capital empty,
led five thousand elite soldiers and suddenly arrived at the palace gates.
Hóu Āndū led five hundred brave soldiers out to battle,
and Sìhuī and others retreated and occupied Shítóu.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Zài and Běisǒu surrendered,
and Gāozǔ pacified and released them.
Due to Sìhuī's encroachment,
he returned to the capital with his armor,
and ordered Zhōu Wényù to continue campaigning against Dù Kān.
On the day Jǐmǎo in the eleventh month,
Qí sent five thousand soldiers to cross the river and occupy Gūshú.
Gāozǔ ordered Xú Dù, Cìshǐ of Hézhōu, to build a stockade at Yěchéng Temple,
extending south to Huáizhǔ.
Qí also sent Zhái Zǐchóng, Cìshǐ of Ānzhōu, Liú Shìróng, Cìshǐ of Chǔzhōu,
to cross Húshù with thirty thousand *shí* of grain and a thousand horses,
entering Shítóu.
On the day Guǐwèi,
Gāozǔ dispatched Hóu Āndū to lead a naval force to launch a night attack on Húshù,
burning over a thousand Qí ships.
Zhōu Tiěwǔ led a fleet to cut off Qí's transport,
and seizing several thousand *shí* of grain from transport boats.
He then sent Wéi Zài to build a city at Dàháng,
and ordered Dù Léng to defend it.
The Qí people also built two stockades south of Cāngmén water to resist the government army.
On the day Jiǎchén,
Sìhuī and others attacked the Yěchéng stockade.
Gāozǔ led elite armored cavalry,
emerging from Xīmíng Gate to attack them,
and the rebel forces were utterly routed.
Sìhuī left Liǔ Dámó and others to defend the city,
and personally led his relatives and trusted followers
to Cǎishí in Nánzhōu
On the day Guǐchǒu in the twelfth month,
Gāozǔ dispatched Hóu Āndū to lead a naval force
to attack Sìhuī's family at Qínzhōu,
capturing several hundred people.
The government army connected ships to block the Huái estuary,
cutting off the rebels' waterway.
Previously, Táibái (Venus) had not been seen since Jǐngxū in the eleventh month,
but on Yǐmǎo, it appeared in the east.
On the day Jǐngchén,
Gāozǔ ordered all armies to divide their armored soldiers,
set up a pontoon bridge opposite Yěchéng to ferry troops,
and attack the two stockades south of the water.
Liǔ Dámó and others crossed the Huái and arrayed their forces.
Gāozǔ commanded his troops to fight fiercely,
setting fire to the stockades.
Smoke and dust filled the sky,
and the rebels were routed,
scrambling for boats and pushing each other,
with thousands drowning.
At that time, the common people watched the battle along the Huái,
their shouts shaking heaven and earth.
The soldiers, emboldened by their victory,
each fought with the strength of a hundred,
capturing all their ships.
The rebel army was intimidated.
On that day, Sìhuī, Yuē, and others led over ten thousand Qí soldiers, both infantry and navy,
back to occupy Shítóu.
Gāozǔ dispatched troops to Jiāngníng,
occupying strategic strongholds to cut off the rebels' path.
The rebel navy and infantry dared not advance and halted at Jiāngníng Pǔkǒu.
Gāozǔ dispatched Hóu Āndū to lead a naval force to attack and defeat them.
Sìhuī and others escaped in single skiffs,
and all their military supplies and equipment were captured.
On the day Jǐwèi,
the government army attacked the city from four sides.
From Chén (7-9 AM) to Yǒu (5-7 PM),
they captured the small northeastern city.
The fighting continued through the night.
On the day Gēngshēn,
Dámó sent envoys Hóu Zǐqīn, Liú Shìróng, and others to Gāozǔ to request peace.
Gāozǔ agreed,
and then sacrificed animals outside the city gate to make a solemn oath,
stating that no questions would be asked of their generals, soldiers, or private troops,
and they were free to go north or south.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
Gāozǔ exited the south gate of Shítóu,
arrayed tens of thousands of soldiers,
and escorted those Qí people returning north.
On the day Rénxū,
Wūwán Yuǎn, Chángshǐ of Qí's Hézhōu, fled from Nánzhōu back to Lìyáng.
Chén Sì, Ling of Jiāngníng, and Cáo Lǎng, Huángmén Shìláng, rebelled at Gūshú.
Gāozǔ ordered Hóu Āndū, Xú Dù, and others to suppress them,
beheading several thousand people
and piling their heads into a *jīngguān* (mound of heads).
Shítóu, Cǎishí, and Nánzhōu were all pacified,
and countless horses, weapons, ships, and rice were captured.
In this month, Dù Kān surrendered his city.
On the day Guǐwèi in the first month of the second year,
Dù Kān was executed in Wúxīng.
Kān's cousin Běisǒu and Sīmǎ Shěn Xiàodūn were also put to death.
In the second month, on the day Gēngshēn,
Gāozǔ dispatched Hóu Āndū and Zhōu Tiěwǔ to lead a fleet of舸艦 (gějiàn) to guard Jiāngzhōu,
and they encamped at Liángshān to erect fortifications.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
an imperial edict stated that the Sīkōng, whenever there was a military matter,
could ride a horse in and out of the city.
On the day Wùchén,
Wáng Wèi, formerly an Outer Army Staff Officer (外兵參軍) of Níngyuǎn Shíchéng Gōng, found four jade seals along the sandy banks of Shítóu.
Gāozǔ submitted a memorial to send them to the imperial court.
In the third month, on the day Wùxū,

Qí dispatched the Naval Military Commissioner (水軍儀同) Xiāo Guǐ, Kùdí Fúlián, Yáo Nánzōng, Dōngfāng Lǎo, Attendant-in-ordinary (侍中) Péi Yīngqǐ, Governor (刺史) of Dōngguǎngzhōu Dúgū Pì'è, and Governor of Luòzhōu Lǐ Xīguāng,
〔一八〕along with Rèn Yuē and Xú Sìhuī,
leading an army of 100,000 to depart from Zhàkǒu
towards Liángshān.
Huáng Cóng, a Banner Master (帳內盪主), met and attacked them,
defeating them
and burning their vanguard's ships and vessels.
The Qí army then encamped and fortified Wúhú.
Gāozǔ dispatched Shěn Tài, Governor of Dìngzhōu, and Péi Jì, Administrator (太守) of Wújùn, to join Hóu Āndū,
and together they held Liángshān to resist them.
From last winter until this time,
sweet dew frequently fell upon Zhōngshān, Méigǎng, Nánjiàn, and the borders of Jīngkǒu and Jiāngníng County,
sometimes accumulating to three or four sheng,
with drops as large as Go pieces.
Gāozǔ submitted a memorial to present this to the imperial court.
In the fourth month, on the day Dīngsì,
Gāozǔ went to the Liángshān army to inspect and comfort them.
In the fifth month, on the day Jiǎshēn,
the Qí troops set out from Wúhú.
On the day Jǐngshēn,
they reached the old administrative seat of Mòlíng.
Gāozǔ dispatched Zhōu Wényù to garrison Fāngshān,
Xú Dù to encamp at Mǎmù,
and Dù Léng to encamp south of Dàháng.
On the day Jǐhài,
Gāozǔ led the royal princes and marquises and the court officials and generals
to sacrifice animals and make a solemn declaration to Heaven beneath the Báisòujué (白獸闕) outside the Dàsīmǎ Gate,
〔一九〕stating that the Qí people had broken their covenant.
His words were fervent,
and tears streamed down his face.
None of the allies dared to look up,
and the observing soldiers became even more inspired.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
the Qí army built a bridge and palisade across the Huái River at the old Mòlíng county
to transport troops and horses.
That night, they reached Fāngshān.
Hóu Āndū, Zhōu Wényù, Xú Dù, and others all withdrew to the capital.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
the Qí troops advanced from Fāngshān to Értáng,
and their light cavalry reached the imperial court.
Zhōu Wényù and Hóu Āndū encamped at Báitǔgǎng,
with their flags and drums visible to each other,
and the capital was shaken with alarm.
Gāozǔ secretly withdrew three thousand elite soldiers and assigned them to Shěn Tài,
who crossed the river to attack Qí's Mobile Office Supervisor (行臺) Zhào Yánshēn at Guābù,
〔二０〕capturing over a hundred boats and vessels
and ten thousand dan of grain.
On that day, the Son of Heaven commanded the Yǔlín (羽林) imperial guard,
〔二一〕encamping at Chánglè Sì.
In the sixth month, on the day Jiǎchén,
the Qí troops secretly reached Lóngwěi on Zhōngshān.
On the day Dīngwèi,
they advanced to Mòfǔshān.
Gāozǔ dispatched Qián Míng to lead the naval forces out of Jiāngchéng
to intercept the Qí people's grain transport,
capturing all their boats and rice.
The Qí army was then greatly famished,
and they killed horses and donkeys to eat.
On the day Gēngxū,
the Qí army crossed Zhōngshān.
Gāozǔ's various armies divided and encamped east of Lèyóuyuàn and north of Fùzhōushān,
blocking their strategic points.
On the day Rénzǐ,
the Qí army reached the northwest of Xuánwǔhú and south of Mòfǔshān,
intending to occupy the northern suburban altar.
The various armies moved from east of Fùzhōu
and encamped north of the suburban altar,
facing the Qí people.
That night, there was a great rain with thunder and lightning,
and a fierce wind uprooted trees.
The ground was flooded with over ten feet of water.
The Qí army sat and stood in the mud day and night,
hanging pots to cook.
Meanwhile, the area around the imperial court and north of Cháogōu had receded water and dry roads,
allowing the government forces to take turns regularly.
On the day Jiǎyín,
the weather cleared slightly.
Gāozǔ ordered his armies to feed their horses and eat a hasty meal,
and at dawn they would attack.
At dawn on the day Yǐmǎo,
he personally led his personal guards and subordinates out from south of Mòfǔshān.
Wú Míngchè, Shěn Tài, and the other armies advanced simultaneously,
unleashing their troops in a great battle.
Hóu Āndū led his forces from Báixià to outflank their rear.
The Qí forces were utterly routed,
with several thousand killed and captured.
Those who trampled each other to death were countless.
Xú Sìhuī and his younger brother Sìzōng were captured alive,
and executed to warn others.
The pursuit continued to Línyí.
The armies at Jiāngchéng, Shèshān, Zhōngshān, and other locations successively achieved victories,
capturing a total of forty-six generals, including Xiāo Guǐ, Dōngfāng Lǎo, Wáng Jìngbǎo, Lǐ Xīguāng, and Péi Yīngqǐ.
Those soldiers who managed to escape to the river
bound reed rafts to cross,
but drowned in the middle of the river.
Their floating corpses reached Jīngkǒu,
filling the water and covering the banks.
On the day Dīngsì,
the armies came out from Nánzhōu
and burned the enemy's boats and vessels.
On the day Jǐwèi,
Liú Guīyì, Xú Sìyàn, and Fù Yězhū were executed in Jiànkāng market.
〔二二〕On this day, the state of emergency was lifted.
On the day Gēngshēn,
Xiāo Guǐ, Dōngfāng Lǎo, Wáng Jìngbǎo, Lǐ Xīguāng, and Péi Yīngqǐ were all put to death.
Gāozǔ submitted a memorial to resign from Nánxúzhōu and hand it over to Hóu Āndū.
In the seventh month, on the day Jǐngzǐ,
an edict appointed Gāozǔ as Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監), Sītú (司徒), and Governor of Yángzhōu,
advancing his noble rank to Gōng (公),
and increasing his fief to a total of five thousand households,
with his positions as Shìzhōng (侍中), Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn Shì (都督中外諸軍事), Jiāngjūn (將軍), Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令), Bājiàn (班劒), Gǔchuī (鼓吹), and Jiǎzhàng (甲仗) all remaining as before,
and also granting him an oil-canopied, black-wheeled carriage.
In this month, Hóu Tián surrendered Jiāngzhōu.
Hóu Āndū was dispatched to garrison the upper reaches of the river
and pacify the various commanderies in the south-central region.
In the eighth month, on the day Guǐmǎo,
Hé Nài, Taifù Qīng (太府卿), and Huá Zhì, Governor of Xīnzhōu, each presented a jade seal.
Gāozǔ submitted a memorial to send them to the imperial court,
and an edict returned them to Gāozǔ.
On this day, an edict granted Gāozǔ the revenue of Ānjí and Wǔkāng counties,
totaling five thousand households.
In the ninth month, on the day Rén'yín,
the year name was changed to Tàipíng Yuánnián.
Gāozǔ was promoted to the position of Chéngxiàng (丞相), Lù Shàngshū Shì (錄尚書事), and Zhènwèi Dàjiāngjūn (鎮衞大將軍).
The title of Governor (刺史) was changed to Shepherd (牧),
and he was enfeoffed as Yìxīng Jùn Gōng.
His positions as Shìzhōng, Sītú, Dūdū, Bājiàn, Gǔchuī, Jiǎzhàng, and black-wheeled carriage remained as before.
On the day Dīngwèi,
Wáng Péng, Zhōngsàn Dàfū (中散大夫), presented a memorial stating that on the fifth day of this month, at dawn, dragon tracks were seen on the imperial road,
extending from the Grand Altar (大社) to the Elephant Gate (象闕),
for three or four lǐ.
On the day Gēngshēn,
an edict posthumously granted Gāozǔ's father the titles of Shìzhōng and Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫),
with additional golden insignia and purple ribbons,
enfeoffed as Yìxīng Jùn Gōng,
and given the posthumous title Gōng.
In the tenth month, on the day Jiǎxū,
an imperial command stated that from now on, when the Chéngxiàng comes to inquire about the emperor's health,
a separate couch may be placed close to the screen for him to sit.
In the second year, first month, on the day Rén'yín,
the Son of Heaven held court for all nations in the East Hall of Tàijí.
Gāozǔ was granted ten additional Bājiàn,
making a total of thirty,
with other privileges remaining as before.
On the day Dīngwèi,
an edict posthumously granted Gāozǔ's elder brother Dào Tán the titles of Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),〔二三〕Shǐchíjié, Píngběi Jiāngjūn (平北將軍), Governor of Nánxiùzhōu, and Chángchéng Xiàn Gōng,
with the posthumous title Zhāoliè;
and his younger brother Xiū Xiān the titles of Shìzhōng, Shǐchíjié, Piàojì Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍), Governor of Nánxúzhōu, and Wǔkāng Xiàn Hóu,
〔二四〕with the posthumous title Zhōngzhuàng,
each with a revenue fief of two thousand households.
〔二五〕On the day Jiǎyín,
Lù Shàn, acting as Shìzhōng and Yèzhě Púshè (謁者僕射), was dispatched to formally appoint Lady Zhāng of Chángchéng County as Yìxīng Guó Fūrén.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
an edict posthumously granted Gāozǔ's grandfather the titles of Shìzhōng and Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿),
with the posthumous title Xiào.
Gāozǔ's grandmother, Lady Xǔ, was posthumously enfeoffed as Wújùn Jiāxīng Xiàn Jūn,
with the posthumous title Jìng;
and his mother, Lady Zhāng, as Yìxīng Guó Tàifūrén,
with the posthumous title Xuān.
In the second month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
Xiāo Bó raised an army,
crossing the mountains from Guǎngzhōu and encamping at Nánkāng.
He dispatched his generals Ōuyáng Wěi, Fù Tài, and his son Zī as the vanguard,
〔二六〕who reached Yùzhāng
and divided their forces to garrison strategic and dangerous locations.
Yú Xiàokǐng, Governor of Nánjiāngzhōu, raised an army to support Bó.
Gāozǔ ordered Zhōu Wényù and Hóu Āndū to lead their forces to suppress them.
In the eighth month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
Gāozǔ was promoted to the position of Tàifù (太傅),
with the additional honors of holding a yellow battle-axe,
wearing swords and shoes to court,
not needing to rush when entering the imperial court,
and not having his name announced during ceremonies.
He was also granted one set of feathered canopy and drum and pipe music,
while his positions as Shìzhōng, Dūdū, Lù Shàngshū, Zhènwèi Dàjiāngjūn, Yángzhōu Mù, Yìxīng Jùn Gōng, Bājiàn, Jiǎzhàng, and oil-canopied, black-wheeled carriage all remained as before.
On the day Jǐngshēn,
Gāozǔ was granted additional feathered canopy and drum and pipe music for the front and rear sections.
At this time,
Wáng Lín, Governor of Xiāngzhōu, held military power and did not obey the imperial command.
Gāozǔ dispatched Zhōu Wényù and Hóu Āndū to lead their forces to suppress him.
In the ninth month, on the day Xīnchǒu,
an imperial edict stated: "From the beginning, when the primal chaos was separated and divided,
and the Great Simplicity was imbued with vapor,
to establish human emperors,
it was always necessary to rely on a Grand Steward (洪宰).
Therefore, after the wise and sagely,
the regional governors (牧伯) were dispatched to the four directions,
and divine
The ruler of [Wǔ]
widely governed all states.
There was also the unification of [jiǔ hé],
the bounty of [Qúmén] was profound,
encircling [Dài] and warming [Wēn],
the imperial residence's favor was abundant.
When
in peril, therefore steadfast,
when fortune prevailed, therefore glorious and splendid.
This is the way that has been consistent for a thousand years,
and immutable for a hundred kings.
The Grand Tutor, Lord of [Yìxīng],
truly civil and truly martial,
indeed sagely and indeed divine,
naturally endowed by Heaven with virtue,
to bring peace and relief to the common people.
In times past, during a period of tranquility,
he early on received the court's trust.
Far
across the turbulent seas,
he reached [Jiāozhǐ] and [Yuè].
〔二七〕When the imperial fortune was unfavorable,
a time unheard of in written records,
and [Zhōngguó] was on the verge of collapse,
with all manner of military disasters arriving,
the sorrowful survivors,
were like those trapped in a desperate
prison.
The vast heavens,
seemed unable to reach this extremity.
When misfortune ends, prosperity begins;
the Grand Regent emerged in due time,
saving what was about to crumble,
rescuing what was already drowning.
Riding boats and treading carts,
he traversed dangers
and floated over the deep,
planning and managing the situation midway,
ultimately annihilating all the enemies.
When it came to [Shítou] and [Gūshú],
where blood flowed and intestines lay,
in a single morning, with a wave of his hand,
the whole realm became clear and peaceful.
This was to illuminate
and manifest the martial achievements of the present dynasty,
and to assist and brighten the central capital,
to avenge the mighty enemies of the Three Sovereigns,
and to eliminate the great evils of the Three Spirits.
Even [Yáo] with [Yǔ]'s assistance,
could not begin to compare;
the prime minister of [Yīn] and the Grand Tutor of [Zhōu],
indeed
cannot be mentioned alongside him.
Furthermore, when the remaining symbols of [Tún] and [Bō] (in I Ching) appeared,
and [Jīngchǔ] suffered a great collapse,
Heaven and Earth seemed without purpose,
the imperial carriage was abandoned,
the Five Barbarians repeatedly plundered,
vying to seize all of [Xià],
the eight directions
were scattered,
with no one to deliver salvation,
powerful ministers defied commands,
deposing our young emperor,
looking at his reflection with the soul of a suffering child,
willingly enduring the humiliation of [Níng Qīng].
With his topknot undone,
the path for seeking mercy was blocked.
Stealing an axe and fleeing responsibility,
there was no place to hide.
The Duke's divine army arrived suddenly,
clarifying the situation in days,
only by this weak and ignorant one,
did Heaven's
mandate receive a second endorsement.
This is truly grand and immense,
beyond words to describe its virtue.
Moreover, relying on this loyalty and righteousness,
he slaughtered those treacherous rebels,
eliminated the barbarian miasma in [Zhèn] region,
and dispelled evil omens from [Jīshān].
In [Pānyú] and [Lízé],
the northern border and western suburbs,
he annihilated their fierce brigands,
leaving no remnants.
This determined the life and death,
the length and brevity of the myriad people's lives;
the foundation of the entire land,
its rise and fall depended on it.
Thus, criminal law and rites were taught simultaneously,
reforms and innovations had their
rules,
peace was established both internally and externally,
near and far were unified.
Thus, he was able to make the sunlight harmonize with the moon,
and the celestial bodies display their brilliance,
placing the phoenix in the pavilion and the unicorn roaming the courtyard,
embracing benevolence and embodying trustworthiness,
his grand achievements encompassing
the broad earth,
and his great Way reaching the dark heavens.
Since [Xī], [Nóng], [Yán], and [Hào],
the eras of rolling up sleeves and letting clothes hang loose,
no sage in saving the world
has been like this.
Indeed, for completeness of things and classical records,
[Huán] and [Wén] were fitting;
for assisting Yin and Yang,
[Xiāo] and [Cáo] did not yield.
Yet none have had merits higher than [Yǐn] and [Xiàn],
while their rewards were less than [Yī]
and [Zhōu].
All the people,
indeed harbored longings.
This is because the Duke, being modest and self-restrained,
cherished humility in his heart,
making the auspicious opportunity linger,
forever inspiring sighs of admiration.
How can this
noble disposition be prolonged,
and the court's established customs be long neglected?
The Ministry of Merits should be admonished,
and the grand ceremony respectfully advanced.
Furthermore, [Chónghuá], the great sage,
and the worthy men of [Guīruì],
their sacrifices for their profound virtues are never forgotten,
and the gates of [Gōnghóu]
must be restored.
Therefore, [Yīn Jiā Dǎnfǔ]
succeeded [Hòujì]'s office;
[Yáo] appointed [Xī Hé],
to take over [Zhòng Lí]'s position.
How much more so for one whose main branch is established,
who should be sworn by
mountains and rivers?
Promote him to the rank of Grand Chancellor ([Xiàngguó]),
to manage all state affairs,
enfeoff him with ten commanderies as Duke of [Chén],
grant him the nine bestowals,
add the imperial seal and ribbon, the [yuǎnyóu guān] (long-journey cap), and the green [lǚsòu] (ribbon),
his position to be above all princes.
His titles of Grand General Suppressing the Borders and Governor of [Yángzhōu] remain as before.
The imperial edict states: How great is the creative force of [Qián] (Heaven),
using the sun and moon for righteous observation; how ultimate is the receptive force of [Kūn] (Earth),
relying on mountains and rivers to carry all things.
Thus, only Heaven is great,
and those who ascend to match it are reverent and brilliant;
only the king establishes the state,
and those who assist him are equally sagely.
Therefore, the assistants of [Wén] and [Wǔ],
had their jade tablets of [Pánxī] concealed;
the ministers of [Yáo] and [Shùn],
had their golden plates carved on the [Rónghé].
How much more so for one who embodies the majestic demeanor of obtaining unity,
calming the perils of the ninth Yang,
saving those adrift at [Jiéshí],
and extinguishing the prairie fires at [Kūncén],
driving and commanding like [Wéi] and [Péng],
stepping and trampling
over [Qí] and [Jìn]?
His divine deeds are performed without effort,
his sacred Way operates without seeking fame?
Now I shall bestow upon you this imperial edict;
listen respectfully to my command: Recently, the August Heaven was not merciful,
inflicting chaos upon our nation;
the net with holes large enough for a boat to pass,
the powerful barbarians grew arrogant within,
the vast universe,
the timid common people,
square-footed and round-
skulled,
not one in ten thousand survived.
The Great Purity was in decline,
the sorrow of [Qiáoshān] ran deep,
the great treasure was in distress,
and the calamity of [Píngyáng] followed one after another.
The Grand Chancellor embraced the mandate of the times,
bringing peace and saving the myriad
people,
assembling his army south of [Diānchí],
raising his banners north of [Guìlǐng],
hanging the three luminaries that had fallen,
pacifying the four seas from widespread chaos,
slaughtering the [yàyǔ] (monsters) in the central plains,
and cutting down the [jīngní] (whales/monsters) at [Méngsì].
He swept clean and pacified the capital,
gloriously initiating a restoration.
These are the Duke's great contributions to the imperial house.
Soon after, Heaven did not repent of its misfortunes,
and barbarian invaders arrived repeatedly;
[Nánxià] collapsed,
and [Xījīng] was overthrown,
the many barbarians became rampant,
taking advantage of the chaos and opportunity,
pushing and installing branch families,
The usurpers feigned possession of the divine mandate,
the imperial court was corrupted and disordered,
and they colluded with foreign enemies.
Having been demoted at Tónggōng,
they then plotted against the Hàn court.
The imperial fortune was already in peril,
no different from a dangling tassel.
Zhōngguó was shaken,
more than just hanging by a thread.
You, Gōng, indignantly cast aside your sleeve,
to restore and save the dynasty.
You restored the Qí capital, Jǔ,
and pacified the royal domain from the barbarians.
This is why We were able to reclaim the precious
throne,
and re-occupy the imperial residence,
emulating the virtue of Jiànwǔ,
and singing the elegant odes of Xuān Wáng.
This is again Your achievement, Gōng, in restoring the imperial house.
At the beginning of Your service,
You were first appointed to office.
Sānchuān and Wǔlǐng,
none were beyond Your surveillance.
Yíndòng and Zhūgōng,
everywhere was tranquil.
Sūn and Lú instigated trouble,
the Yuèmò became a disaster.
The Fānbù were in extreme danger,
on the verge of collapse and destruction.
Where Your crimson banner pointed,
the demonic strongholds were pierced.
As soon as Your white feathered fan was waved,
the villains were utterly crushed.
Were it not for Your
divine martial prowess,
the Southern Frontier would have long been lost.
This is yet another of Your accomplishments, Gōng.
At the end of Dàtóng,
border governance was not maintained.
Lǐ Bēn, in his madness,
usurped Our Jiāo and Ài.
He dared to claim a great title,
his arrogance and wantonness exceeding that of Wèi Tuó.
He occupied Liánzhōu,
his tyranny fiercer than Liáng Shuò’s.
You, Gōng, with Your heroic calculations,
swept through like lightning and wind.
You rode swift warships,
directly crossing the vast sea.
Xīnchāng and Diǎnchè,
endured all hardships.
Sūlì and Jiāníng,
were all turned into Jingguan (piles of enemy heads).
The barbarian caves of Sānshān,
the aboriginal corners of Bājiǎo,
the distant lands of the aquatic dwellings,
the remote country of volcanic mountains—
places Mǎ Yuán
could not reach,
and Táo Huáng had never heard of—
all feared Our royal might,
and vied to pay homage to the border commanders,
offering treasures to the imperial treasury,
and submitting petitions to the Hónglú.
This is yet another of Your accomplishments, Gōng.
Since the rebels crossed the Jiāng,
the imperial palace was disgraced.
You, Gōng, slept on Your spear and tasted gall,
gripping Your sword and pounding Your heart.
Your spirit surged into the azure sky,
Your divine will soared to the purple court.
But Fānyú Lián
shuài,
being originally of the various barbarians,
found companions in them,
and harbored evil intentions.
You, Gōng, armed with loyalty,
seized the opportunity to suppress and pacify them.
You captured the commander of Pèi and used him to anoint the drum,
and pacified Xīnyě,
taking control.
This is yet another of Your accomplishments, Gōng.
When the world first fell into hardship,
many regions faced difficulties.
Powerful and cunning clans,
stirred up rebellion in Héngyì.
Their forces reached the city walls,
their multitude included both barbarians and savages.
You, Gōng, aware of the national crisis and border alarms,
did everything within Your power.
You sympathized with the allies,
and executed their wicked kind.
None failed to scatter like frightened fish and birds,
or to be captured and beheaded.
The common people of the Southern lands,
once again found peace and respite.
This
is yet another of Your accomplishments, Gōng.
You drove straight to the mountain passes,
dreaming of the capital region.
The local chieftains along the way,
became obstacles in succession.
The local bandits,
fully occupied the major cities.
They gathered fugitives,
and planned
to create chaos.
Hundreds of watchtowers stood undefeated,
never glimpsed by scaling ladders.
Ten thousand crossbows were fully drawn,
unmatched by high siege engines.
You, Gōng, soared like a dragon and strode like a tiger,
[二八]roaring through the winds and
clouds.
Mountains yielded their strongholds,
the plains had no strong formations.
You cleared the demonic miasma from Gànshí,
and extinguished the pestilence in Yúdū.
This is yet another of Your accomplishments, Gōng.
The renegade officials, sinister and malevolent,
were entrenched in Dàgāo.
Their "survivors" resembled Mǎ Téng's army,
and the refugees were numerous like Dù Tāo's multitudes.
They pushed their way, fighting from north to south,
year after year,
delayed
our campaigns of punishment,
truly formidable enemies.
You, Gōng, sat and wielded the Sānlüè (Three Strategies),
remotely controlling the Liùqí (Six Secret Teachings).
The loyal and brave were of one heart,
fierce warriors exerted their strength.
Like thunder and lightning,
valleys were silent and mountains
empty.
The numerous prefectures had no alarm of barking dogs,
and the local shrines were free from fox-spirit bandits.
This is yet another of Your accomplishments, Gōng.
When the royal army attacked the rebels,
it reached Lúnbō.
The army lacked provisions,
and the soldiers showed signs of hunger.
You, Gōng, turned Your banner at Lízé,
and stockpiled grain at Bāqiú.
The songs of abundant harvests
were sung,
and the welcoming crowds with pots of wine were many.
Soldiers and civilians transported supplies,
without the difficulty of a "pillar in the river" (a difficult barrier).
Prows and sterns were visible to each other,
like moving the granaries of Àocāng.
Rhinoceros hide shields and shell armor,
they
scorned thunder and lightning.
High ships and towering vessels,
reached for the heavens.
Thus, the three armies were brave and sharp,
invincible in a hundred battles.
Receiving these provisions,
they ultimately annihilated the villains.
This is yet
another of Your accomplishments, Gōng.
As for Your heroic plans surpassing the ordinary,
and Your righteous troops numerous as clouds,
the suspicion and discord at Péntú,
delayed military strategy.
You, Gōng, with Your sole aim to promote cooperation,
knew that victory in war depended on harmony.
Húsài was not
feared,
Hóngmén was assembled.
Like the Marquess of Jìn swearing by Bái Shuǐ,
like King Xiāo revealing his true heart,
You humbly made alliances,
and everyone was moved and choked with emotion.
Thus You were able to make the naval forces proceed side by
side,
uniting distant and near hearts.
This is yet another of Your accomplishments, Gōng.
Gūshú was a vital strategic point,
like Xiáohán in its defensive strength.
The rebels occupied its passes,
and the great bandits held its fortified gates.
You, Gōng, waved a single banner,
and three heroes surged forth together.
Zuǒ
Xián and Yòu Jiǎo,
collapsed like sand and earth.
Mù Jiǎ perished in the Central Plains,
Qiú Fù drowned in the Jiāng River.
The myriad counts and thousands of groups,
were in disarray.
The narrow pass of Èbǎn was
open,
the path of Yígēng is unobstructed.
This is again Your Grace's achievement.
The righteous army's masses
all gathered in the Imperial Capital,
while the rebellious villains
still garrisoned the Imperial City.
As for that place, marked by mountains and rivers,
a strong and dangerous fortress,
which opened the Longshǒu to
stand against the palace,
and cut down Huàyuè to make a city,
where various barbarians relied,
and strong soldiers remained calm.
Your Grace turned this terrestrial axis,
resisted this heavenly net,
and in less than a morning,
left no one
alive.
The military demeanor was very solemn,
the national administration was being rectified,
people once again saw the splendor of official attire,
and the populace again looked upon rites and music.
The Chǔ people filled the roads,
vying to see Yè Gōng,
while the Hàn elders,
holding back sorrow,
all rejoiced at the Sīlì.
This is again Your Grace's achievement.
When the internal troubles had just quieted,

and the celestial
bow appeared at dawn.
For a long time, the barbarians were like sheep in a pasture,
but now is the time for dragons to emerge from the spring.
Omens of a change in destiny are all manifest,
and symbols of renewal are converging.
Therefore, I respectfully
reverence Xūn and Huá,
and repeatedly examine the celestial observations.
In the past, when the wood virtue was exhausted,
my great ancestor received it.
Now, the calendar departs from the fiery essence,
and the spirit returns to the central pivot.
With reverence for the fire virtue,
I transmit it to your Chén dynasty.
Looking back at previous kings from afar,
and consulting the various lords nearby,
the bright spirits are pleased,
and all within the four seas are of one mind.
Now I dispatch the envoy Wáng Tōng, who holds the imperial staff and concurrently serves as Grand Mentor, Palace Attendant, Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
Left Assistant, and Marquis of Pínglè Tíng,
〔四二〕and Wáng Yáng, who concurrently serves as Grand Commandant, Minister of Works, and Left Chief Clerk, to present the emperor's seal and cords.
The ceremony for receiving the final mandate
shall be entirely in accordance with that of Táng and Yú.
the affairs of Yú.
At that time, the King ascended to the position of supreme ruler,
to nurture and raise the myriad people,
to brilliantly expand great endeavors,
and to receive the auspicious mandate of August Heaven!
On this day, the Liáng Emperor abdicated to a separate palace.
Gāozǔ humbly declined repeatedly,
but the multitude of officials insisted,
so he consented.
"Diǎn Chè"
is also written as
"Qǔ Chè"
in some editions,
and earlier "Diǎn Chè Hú"
is also like this;
both are questionable.)
Collation Note
Annals, Part 2: Under Gāozǔ
In the winter, tenth month, on the Yǐhài day of the first year of Yǒngdìng,
Gāozǔ ascended to the imperial throne at the southern suburb,
and offered a burnt sacrifice to Heaven, saying:
"Your servant, Emperor Bàxiān,
dares to respectfully announce with a black bull to the August and Supreme Emperor: The Liáng dynasty, having been afflicted by successive calamities and ruin,
its allotted fate has reached its limit.
Respectfully following the heavenly response,
the mandate has been given to Bàxiān.
Indeed, from the very beginning of humanity,
rulers were established,
selecting the virtuous and the capable,
not always from the same lineage.
In the eras of Fàngxūn and Chónghuá,
they had no intention of receiving the mandate,
while the rulers of Dāngtú and Diǎn'wǔ,
though they had the intention of yielding,
all held the myriad chariots with their outstanding talents,
and controlled the four seas with their great achievements.
Thus, they were able to greatly protect the common people
and brilliantly dwell in all regions.
At the end of the Liáng dynasty,
calamities repeatedly struck,
the Xūn savages oppressed,
the divine artifact was long usurped.
Chéngshèng was abroad,
unable to maintain the sacrifices of Xià.
Heaven had not yet regretted the disaster,
and again suffered from bandit rebels.
The legitimate heir was deposed,
and collateral branches usurped and defrauded.
Heaven and Earth were overthrown,
and the cosmic order was utterly destroyed.
Bàxiān, at first, rose to action,
greatly rescuing the chaotic masses.
He raised the righteous army again,
and truly quelled many difficulties.
He deposed kings and established emperors,
truly having achieved this merit.
He pacified the state and secured the altars of soil and grain,
exhausting his strength in doing so.
This is called 'minor peace,'
and we look forward to the 'great Way.'
Thereafter, auspicious colors appeared in the clouds and mist,
the sun and moon presented auspicious omens.
The celestial threads gathered in the Eastern Well,
and a dragon appeared in Qiáo.
Doing away with the old and establishing the new,
was already manifest in the heavenly phenomena.
Transferring the affairs from Yú to Xià,
also accorded with songs and praises.
The nine domains and eight wildernesses,
all expressed their sincere feelings,
and the myriad spirits and all sacrifices,
all had earnest desires.
The Liáng Emperor nobly yielded the myriad states,
and conferred the great treasure.
Bàxiān considered himself unworthy,
and declined the virtue and succession,
even to the third time,
but his refusal was not accepted.
All agreed that the common people needed a ruler,
and the myriad affairs of state could not be left vacant.
The imperial spirits favored the mandate,
which could not be humbly refused.
Fearing the majesty of Heaven,
I therefore receive this auspicious fortune.
Thinking of my long-held aspirations,
how can I not be ashamed of my virtue?
Respectfully selecting an auspicious day,
I ascend the altar and accept the abdication,
announcing to the Supreme Emperor,
to respond to the hearts of the people,
and to forever preserve the state of Chén for us.
May the bright spirits partake of this offering!"
Before this, there was mist and fog,
making day and night obscure.
But on this day,
the weather was clear and serene,
and those who understood recognized the heavenly Way in it.
After the ceremony,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace,
and approached the Tàijí Front Hall.
An edict stated:
"The five virtues alternate in their operation; this is how emperors and kings govern Heaven.
The three Zheng succeed each other; this is how the Xià and Yīn ruled the world.
Although the colors divide literary writings
and the times differ in refinement and simplicity,
and yielding and conquering
have ultimately varied,
yet nurturing virtue and uplifting the people
is ultimately one and the same.
I, being ignorant,
belong to a time of hardship and danger.
The nation's path has repeatedly encountered difficulties,
and the pillar of Heaven has been thrice severed.
I have diligently served my predecessors,
rescuing the drowning masses,
relying on the merits of generals and commanders,
and the strength of brave warriors.
Once I rectified the whole world,
and twice rebuilt the black-haired people.
The Liáng dynasty, with its heavenly blessings coming to an eternal end,
the mandate of Heaven now rests here.
Following the canon of selecting the capable,
the great mandate is gathered upon my person.
Considering my humble virtue,
my refusal was not granted.
I shall comply with Heaven's favor
and humbly accord with the people's hearts.
I have received the mandate from the civil ancestors,
and offered sacrifice to the Supreme Emperor,
following in the footsteps of a hundred kings,
and ruling over all lands.
It is as if crossing a river,
unsure where to land.
The imperial enterprise is newly established,
the imperial throne is refreshed.
I wish to extend benevolence and favor,
to cover the myriad people.
A general amnesty for the entire realm is granted.
The second year of Liáng Tàipíng is changed to the first year of Yǒngdìng.
The people are granted two ranks of nobility,
and civil and military officials two grades of promotion.
Widowers, widows, orphans, and the childless,
who cannot support themselves, shall each receive five hú of grain.
Overdue rents and old debts shall all be forgone.
Those who have violated community decency through corruption, defilement, licentiousness, or theft,
shall have their previous records expunged
and be allowed a fresh start.
Long-term prisoners and those in custody
are all specially pardoned.
Officials who have lost their posts or titles,
or have been imprisoned or deprived of their duties,
shall all be restored according to previous regulations."
Another edict stated:
"The rites of Chén and Sòng were established,
the Odes sing of two guests.
The importance of not serving
has been esteemed throughout the ages.
The Liáng dynasty, respectfully following humanity and the divine,
and modeling themselves on antiquity,
sank the jade disc in the river,
nobly withdrawing from the myriad states.
The allotment of land and tax
should follow the old regulations.
Therefore, the commandery of Jiāngyīn is granted to the Liáng ruler as the King of Jiāngyīn.
He shall follow the calendar of Liáng.
His carriages, banners, and attire
shall all conform to previous standards.
His palaces and residences, and provisions
shall be treated with utmost generosity."
Another edict granted the Liáng Empress Dowager the title of Grand Consort of Jiāngyīn State,
and the Empress the title of Consort of Jiāngyīn State.
Another edict ordered all officials
to temporarily hold their positions according to their ranks.
Jǐngzǐ,
the imperial carriage proceeded to Zhōngshān Temple to worship Jiǎng Dì.
Wùyín,
the imperial carriage proceeded to Huálín Yuán,
personally reviewing lawsuits,
and issuing pardons to prisoners.
Jǐmǎo,
envoys were dispatched to declare the emperor's solicitude throughout the four directions,
and a sealed imperial edict was issued to the prefectures and commanderies, stating:
"When the four kings change dynasties,
it is how Shāng and Zhōu responded to Heaven;
when the Five Phases succeed each other,
it is how Xuān and Xī aligned with destiny.
Liáng's virtue was not sufficient,
and chaos accumulated for years,
with the eastern regions collapsing,
and the western capital overthrown.
Xiāo Bó disrupted the principles,
not just Zhào Lún;
Hóu Jǐng's wickedness reached to the heavens,
surpassing Liú Zài.
Zhēnyáng rebelled and usurped,
the rebels allied their forces,
the area east of the river repeatedly fell to the Xiānbēi,
and Jīnlíng for a long time was no longer a state of Liáng.
From the time of primal chaos and obscurity,
before the dragon diagrams and phoenix annals,
at the beginning of the Xī Hàn Xīngpíng era,
and during the chaos of Xī Cháo Yǒngjiā,
though the empire fractured and disintegrated,
none was comparable to the Liáng dynasty.
Though We are of shallow virtue,
We happened to encounter the rising fortune,
since Our ascension,
We first pacified all the Yuè,
the sea harbors of Xú Mén,
none were left unconquered,
crossing seas and climbing mountains,
everywhere We pacified and stabilized.
Braving the dust of battle,
leading Our armies swiftly,
six times We extended the Liáng sacrifices,
ten times We cut down powerful bandits,
how can this be attributed to human strategy?
It is all due to Heaven's guidance.
The Liáng clan, as Heaven's mandate was changed,
and their destined fortune forever ended,
respectfully followed Táng and Yú,
ceding their imperial regalia.
We, repeatedly declining to the east and west,
bowed and presented Our辭,
avoiding Shùn's son on the sunny side of Jī Shān,
seeking Zhī Bó in the wilderness of Cāng Zhōu,
but the dukes and ministers pressed Us,
and the whole land was anxious and in suspense,
Heaven's will is hard to resist,
so We accepted the great fortune.
This month on Yǐhài,
We ascended to perform rites at the Great Altar,
reflecting on the change of Jióng,
We feel only shame for Our virtue.
From the approaching end of the Liáng clan,
for months there was persistent drought,
as the fire element was ending,
autumn rains suddenly fell.
The next day the ceremony was completed,
the round altar was set up overnight,
the dusty clouds cleared in the evening,
and the stars were arrayed at night.
In the morning, the sun's halo appeared,
with dew dripping like oil from Sānwēi,
the morning light showed a double halo,
adorned with five-colored auspicious clouds.
Considering Our inadequacy,
We are all the more ashamed of these blessings,
from dawn, manifesting greatly,
We contemplate achieving good governance.
You, sirs, holding banners in your regional commands,
are entrusted as Our arms and legs,
dividing tallies and serving as celebrated governors,
We rely on you to care for the vulnerable.
As the imperial calendar is renewed,
We think of your joy and celebration,
We expect you to deeply seek out the people's sufferings,
and strive for integrity and fairness,
showing kindness and benevolence to comfort the orphaned and impoverished,
and using awe-inspiring punishments to deter the strong and cunning.
If there are bandits from Huánpú,
or those who violate the market,
or chiefs from mountains and valleys,
who assert their power in secluded and treacherous places,
all shall be pardoned,
and made aware of this.
But if they remain lost,
they shall not be excused.
Now We dispatch envoys to fully proclaim Our intentions,
reflect on good governance,
and fulfill this humble wish."
Gēngchén,
an edict ordered the display of the Buddha's tooth at Dù Mǔ's residence,
assembling the four assemblies for a great unrestricted dharma assembly,
and Gāozǔ personally came out before the palace gate to prostrate.
Initially,
the late Sēngtǒng Fǎxiàn of Qí obtained it in Wūchán Guó,
and it was always kept at Dìnglín Shàng Sì;
at the end of Liáng Tiānjiān era,
it was entrusted to Huìxīng, a Bhikṣu from Shè Shān Qìngyún Sì for safekeeping;
when Huìxīng was about to die,
he entrusted it to his younger brother Huìzhì;
at the end of Chéngshèng era,
Huìzhì secretly sent it to Gāozǔ,
and it was only now brought out.
Xīnsì,
the imperial father was posthumously honored as Jǐng Huángdì,
with the temple name Tàizǔ;
the imperial mother, Lady Dǒng, was posthumously honored as Ān Huánghòu.
The former consort, Lady Qián, was posthumously given the title Zhāo Huánghòu,
and the heir apparent Kè was posthumously honored as Xiàohuái Tàizǐ.
Consort Zhāng was established as Empress.
Guǐwèi,
the mausoleum of Jǐng Dì was honored as Ruì Líng,
and the mausoleum of Zhāo Huánghòu as Jiā Líng,
following the precedents of the imperial gardens and mausoleums from the early Liáng dynasty.
A Shāndìng Láng was established,
to revise the laws and regulations.
Wùzǐ,
the spirit tablet of Jǐng Huángdì was moved to be enshrined in the Tàimiào.
Xīnmǎo,
Wáng Chōng, General of the Central Command, Open-Palace Administrator with the Same Privileges as the Three Dukes, and Administrator of Dānyáng, was appointed Left Guānglù Dàfū.
Guǐsì,
the emperor's elder brother, the late Sànqí Chángshì, General Píngběi, and Administrator of Yǔn Zhōu of Liáng,
Dào Tán, Duke of Chángchéng County, was posthumously granted the titles of Píqí Dàjiāngjūn and Tàiwèi,
and enfeoffed as Prince of Shǐxīng Commandery;
his younger brother, the late Shìzhōng, Píqí Jiāngjūn, and Administrator of Nánxú Zhōu, Marquis of Wǔkāng County of Liáng,
Xiū Xiān, was posthumously granted the titles of Chējí Dàjiāngjūn and Sītú,
and enfeoffed as Prince of Nánkāng Commandery.
This month,
the Western Expeditionary Military Governor Zhōu Wényù and Hóu Āndū suffered a defeat in Yǐng Zhōu,
and were imprisoned by Wáng Lín.
In the eleventh month, Jǐngshēn,
an edict stated:
"Qí Guó of the Eastern Capital,
was righteous and virtuous to his relatives,
Chéngyáng of the Western Hàn,
had both achievements and merits.

Sànqí Chángshì, Bearing the Imperial Tally, Supervisor of Military Affairs for the Ten Commanderies including Kuàijī, Xuānyì Jiāngjūn, and Grand Administrator of Kuàijī, Marquis of Chángchéng County, Qiàn,
is learned and exceptionally refined,
his spirit is steady and upright,
his civil accomplishments align with rites and music,
his military prowess pacifies ominous influences,
his mind and strength, strategies and plans,
are for managing the family and governing the state,
holding the banner as a governor,
he achieved success within a year,
opening up the passes and rivers,
his achievements surpassed Xiāo and Kòu,
the bandits of Huánpú,
spontaneously returned to farming,
the powerful figures of the bamboo thickets,
submitted to his reputation and authority.
We, being of shallow virtue,
happened to encounter the rising fortune,
holding the three-foot sword,
We are respected by the four directions,
the royal enterprise is difficult,
and relies on this son,
it is fitting to elevate him to a high peerage,
commensurate with his foundational merits.
He is to be enfeoffed as Prince of Línchuān Commandery,
with two thousand households.
His elder brother's son, Xù, Liáng Zhōngshū Shìláng, shall inherit the title of Prince of Shǐxīng,
and his younger brother's son, Tán Láng, Liáng Zhōngshū Shìláng, shall inherit the title of Prince of Nánkāng,
their ceremonial status being the same as proper princes."
Jǐhài,
sweet dew descended upon the pine forest of Zhōngshān,
filling the ravines and valleys.
Gēngzǐ,
Bhīkṣu Cǎi Zhī of Kāishàn Sì collected and presented it,
and an imperial edict ordered it distributed to the assembled officials.
Jǐngchén,
Xú Dù, General Zhènxī and Administrator of Nányù Zhōu, was appointed General Zhènyòu and Leader of the Imperial Guards.
Gēngshēn,
a great fire occurred in the capital.
In the twelfth month, Gēngchén,
the Empress paid respects at the Tàimiào.
In the second year, in spring, the first month, on the *yǐwèi* day,
an edict stated:
“The establishment of offices and division of duties
are based on the importance of affairs,
while ceremonial chariots and horses
rise and fall with the times.
The Five Schools of the Jìn [Dynasty]
sounded their *jiā* horns to clear the way,
and the Nine Ministers of the Hàn [Dynasty]
were heralded to walk abreast.
The Yu officials and Xià rites
cannot be said to belong to the same category;
the simplicity of Yīn and the culture of Zhōu
certainly had no constant standard.
I, having received this precious mandate
and taken on this heavenly task,
have kept the official system in mind,
hoping it accords with the will of the times.
During the Tiānjiān era of the Liáng [Dynasty],
the Left and Right Xiāoqí, holding the positions of Zhūyī Zhíhé,
were both granted ceremonial retinues.
Chāng Yìzhī, the Governor of Běixú Zhōu, was the first to hold this position.
〔一０〕After years of chaos and separation,
court customs no longer exist,
and the younger generation
rarely hears of the old regulations.
Now, the Left and Right Xiāoqí [positions]
should be open to both civil and military officials.
Civil officials should be trusted confidants,
and military officials should be meritorious subjects.
Their granted ceremonial retinues
shall be the same as those of the two Guards Commanders of the Crown Prince.
As for all other officials,
the Grand Secretariat shall elaborate on the regulations.”
Hóu Tián, the Chējì Jiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, was promoted to Sīkōng.
Wáng Chōng, the Zhōngquán Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and newly appointed Zuǒguānglù Dàfū, became the Tàizǐ Shǎofù.
Xú Shìpǔ, the Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn, became Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
Wú Míngchè, the Governor of Nányún Zhōu, was promoted to Ānnán Jiāngjūn.
Ōuyáng Wěi, the Governor of Héng Zhōu, was promoted to Zhènnán Jiāngjūn.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
the imperial carriage personally offered sacrifices in the Southern Suburb.
An edict stated:
“I received the mandate to rule,
and for the first time moved the celestial sphere.
In this auspicious month of Mèngzōu,
I performed the complete rites at the Great Altar.
With propitious omens and bright splendor,
heaven and earth rejoice.
I wish to command the myriad people
to all renew themselves.
Moreover, the corrupting influence of past generations
still obstructs us today.
Military affairs have not ceased,
and conscriptions and taxes are all burdensome.
It is unavoidable,
and I have long known the hardships of the people.
When I think of the common folk,
I cannot forget them, whether I am awake or asleep.
Regarding offenses, regardless of their severity,
whether discovered or not discovered,
before dawn this morning,
all shall be pardoned.
As for the western bandits, from Wáng Lín downwards,
all are permitted to return from their delusion;
nothing shall be questioned.
The recently recruited volunteer army,
originally intended for the western bandits,
shall all be disbanded
to return home and to their livelihoods.
Those whose military provisions ordered recently have not yet been delivered shall all be stopped,
and half of the outstanding military grain from the first year shall be forgiven.
All military garrisons in commanderies, prefectures, and counties are forbidden from dispatching envoys to the common people without authorization;
they must strive to treat them kindly and support them.
If there is any infringement or disturbance,
strict laws shall be enforced.”
On the *yǐsì* day,
the imperial carriage personally offered sacrifices in the Northern Suburb.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
Zhāng Lì, the Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Governor of Liáng Zhōu, reported that in the eighth month of the *yǐhài* year,
〔一一〕on the border of Dāntú and Lánlíng counties, beside a遗mountain,
a sandbank suddenly emerged due to surging tides,
expanding
to over a thousand *qǐng* in circumference,
all fertile
and suitable for cultivation.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
the imperial carriage personally offered sacrifices in the Míngtáng.
In the second month, on the *rénshēn* day,
Shěn Tài, the Governor of Nányù Zhōu, fled to Qí.
〔一二〕On the *xīnmǎo* day,
an edict commanded Hóu Tián, the Chējì Jiāngjūn and Sīkōng, to lead all naval and land forces to repel the Qí invaders.
In the third month, on the *jiǎwǔ* day,
an edict stated:
“Punishment not extending to descendants
is an ancient and universal code.
Punishing with leniency in cases of doubt
is recorded in the annals.
Shěn Tài’s perfidy and misconduct
are known far and wide.
In the past, he had minor merits
and was still entrusted by the court,
appointed to prominent commanderies,
and promoted to several frontier regions.
After returning from the campaign at Hànkǒu,
he resided in a great region,
with fertile fields exceeding four hundred *qǐng*,
and retainers no less than three thousand.
Such wealth, nobility, and glory
were precisely what he deserved.
But evil harmed his fullness,
and Heaven took his spirit.
He recklessly and without reason
threw himself to the barbarian savages.
Although knowing men is wisdom,
it is difficult even for the emperor.
Guāngwǔ was misled by Páng Méng,
and Wèiwǔ did not know Yú Jìn.
I only wish that the court does not fail anyone.
His subordinates, wives, and children shall each be allowed to resume their livelihoods.
Anyone, whether local residents or soldiers, who threatens or plunders them,
shall be treated as robbers.
If any men or women are hidden by others,
all are permitted to report their case to the court.
If they wish to follow the Prince of Línchuān or the commanders to render service,
all shall be allowed.”
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Gāozǔ went to the Rear Hall to hear lawsuits.
Returning, he observed the mountains and waters from a bridge,
and composed a poem to show his officials.
This month,
Wáng Lín enthroned Xiāo Zhuāng, the Prince Yǒngjiā of Liáng, in Yǐng Zhōu.
In summer, the fourth month, on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the imperial carriage personally offered sacrifices in the Tàimiào.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
the Prince of Jiāngyīn passed away.
An edict commanded the Tàizǎi to offer condolences and sacrifices,
and the Sīkōng to supervise the funeral arrangements.
Whatever was needed for the funeral rites
was to be prepared accordingly.
Xiāo Jìqīng, son of Xiāo Zī, the Marquis Wǔlín of Liáng, was made successor as Prince of Jiāngyīn.
On the *jǐngyín* day,
the imperial carriage went to Shítóu [City]
to bid farewell to Sīkōng Hóu Tián.
On the *wùchén* day,
purple smoke extended to the sky from the eastern *chīwěi* of the Chóngyún Diàn.
In the fifth month, on the *yǐwèi* day,
there was an earthquake in the capital.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
Zhāng Xiǎnhé, the Commander of Guǎnglíng Nánchéng of Qí, and Zhāng Sēngnà, the Chángshǐ, each led their respective units to defect.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
the imperial carriage went to Dàzhuāngyán Sì to renounce the world.
On the *rénxū* day,
the officials presented a petition requesting the emperor's return to the palace.
In the sixth month, on the *jǐsì* day,
an edict commanded Sīkōng Hóu Tián and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Xú Dù to lead the naval forces as the vanguard
to suppress Wáng Lín.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the *wùxū* day,
the imperial carriage went to Shítóu [City],
personally sending off Tián and others.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Zhōu Dí, the Governor of Jiāng Zhōu, captured Wáng Lín’s generals Lǐ Xiàqīn, Fán Měng, and Yú Xiàqīng at Gōngtáng.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
Xiè Zhé, the Lìbù Shàngshū, was dispatched to admonish Wáng Lín.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
a single stalk of auspicious grain with six branches grew in Wǔchéng.
Previously,
when Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
fire had burned the Tàijí Diàn.
During the Chéngshèng era, there was discussion about rebuilding it,
but it lacked one pillar.
At this time, a camphor tree log, eighteen *wéi* in circumference
and forty-five *chǐ* long,
drifted to the back islet of Táo family.
Zōu Zǐdù, the Jiānjūn, reported this.
An edict commanded Shěn Zhòng, the Zhōngshū Lìng, to concurrently serve as Qǐbù Shàngshū,
and Cài Chóu, the Shǎofù Qīng, to concurrently serve as Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng,
to rebuild the Tàijí Diàn.
In the eighth month, on the *jǐngyín* day,
Guǎngliáng Commandery was renamed Chénliú Commandery.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
an imperial edict commanded Línchuān Wáng Qiàn to campaign in the west.
[一三]With a naval force of 50,000, he departed from the capital.
The imperial carriage proceeded to Yěchéng Temple to personally see him off.
Zhōu Wényù, former *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī* and Governor of Nányù Prefecture,
Hóu Āndū, former General of the Pacified North, Governor of Nánxú Prefecture, and newly appointed *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*, and others who had escaped from Wáng Lín,
impeached themselves before the Imperial Censorate.
They were granted an audience the same day,
and all were pardoned.
On the *wùyín* day,
an imperial edict restored Wényù and the others to their original offices.
On the *réngwǔ* day,
the imperial prince Lì was posthumously enfeoffed as Yùzhāng Wáng,
with the posthumous title Xiàn;
Quán was posthumously enfeoffed as Chángshā Wáng,
with the posthumous title Sī;
the eldest daughter was posthumously enfeoffed as Yǒngshì Gōngzhǔ,
with the posthumous title Yì.
Xiè Zhé returned from his mission,
and Wáng Lín requested to return to his post at Xiāngchuān.
An imperial edict ordered the various armies to slow their attack.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
the western campaign armies arrived from Dàléi.
On the *dīnghài* day,
Zhōu Dí, General of Awe-Inspiring Trust and Governor of Jiāng Prefecture, was appointed *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*,
and advanced to the title General Who Pacifies the South.
Nánlánlíng Commandery, formerly under Nánxú Prefecture, was renamed Dōnghǎi Commandery.
In winter, on the *gēngwǔ* day of the tenth month,
Zhōu Wényù, General Who Quells the South and *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*, was dispatched to command the various armies from Yùzhāng,
to campaign against Yú Xiàomài.
On the *yǐhài* day,
the imperial carriage proceeded to Zhuāngyán Temple,
and initiated the *Jīnguāngmíng Jīng* recitation.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Huáng Fǎmó, General of Awe-Inspiring Benevolence and Governor of Gāo Prefecture, was appointed *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*,
[一四]and advanced to the title General Who Guards the South.
[一五]On the *jiǎyín* day,
Tàijí Hall was completed,
and all artisans were granted a period of tax exemption.
In the twelfth month, on the *gēngshēn* day,
Línchuān Wáng Qiàn, *Shìzhōng* and General Who Pacifies the East, led the hundred officials to the front hall for an audience,
and offered cattle and wine.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the imperial carriage proceeded to Dàzhuāngyán Temple,
where a Grand Wúshé Assembly was held,
and the imperial carriage and Dharma objects were relinquished.
The multitude of officials, fully equipped with the imperial entourage, welcomed him,
and on the same day, the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
On the *jǐngyín* day,
Gāozǔ hosted a banquet for the officials in the eastern hall of Tàijí Hall,
with music played on bells and stone chimes,
to announce the completion of the imperial residence.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Yánguān, Hǎiyán, and Qiánjīng counties were carved out of Wú Commandery to establish Hǎiníng Commandery,
subordinated to Yáng Prefecture.
Guǎngxīng Six Caves, formerly under Ānchéng, was established as Ānlè Commandery.
On the *jǐngxū* day,
Xióng Tánlǎng, General Who Pacifies Afar and Governor of Běijiāng Prefecture, was appointed *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*,
and advanced to the title General Who Pacifies the West.
On the *dīnghài* day,
an imperial edict stated:
“Former officials during the Liáng dynasty,
scattered by chaos and displacement,
are now returning to the court,
many of whom have not yet been assigned positions.
Furthermore, since the raising of troops,
military achievements are numerous.
The Bureau of Selection shall immediately compile a register of civil and military officials, and generals with seals who are eligible for the nine ranks,
and assess their suitable appointments.”
Consequently, over fifty individuals were promoted and employed according to their talents.
In the third year, in the first month, on the *jǐchǒu* day,
a green dragon appeared in the east.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Ōuyáng Wèi, General Who Guards the South and Governor of Guǎng Prefecture, was appointed *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī* with his current title.
That night there was a heavy snowfall,
and by dawn,
dragon tracks were seen in front of Tàijí Hall.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Ōuyáng Wèi, Governor of Guǎng Prefecture, reported that a white dragon was seen on the south bank of the river in the prefecture,
[一六]dozens of *zhàng* long,
and about eight or nine arm-spans in circumference,
which traveled along the western road of the prefectural city and entered Tiānjǐnggāng.
An immortal was seen in the small stone tower of Luófúshān Temple,
about three *zhàng* tall,
completely pure white,
with elegant and beautiful clothing.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
an imperial edict stated:
“The younger sisters of Nánkāng Wáng and Shǐxīng Wáng
have already been enfeoffed and given noble titles,
and according to ritual, they are merely feudal lords.
However, these two kings
are exceptional, differing from ordinary circumstances,
and their ritual treatment should be elevated.
The ceremonial rank of these princesses and their marriages to lords
may all be made equivalent to that of imperial daughters.”
On the *wùshēn* day,
an imperial edict commanded Línchuān Wáng Qiàn to investigate legal disputes in Yáng and Xú prefectures.
In the second month, on the *xīnyǒu* day,
Chúnyú Liàng, General Who Pacifies the West and Governor of Guì Prefecture, was appointed *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*,
and advanced to the title Grand General Who Guards the West.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Sīkōng Hóu Zhèn commanded the various armies to enter Hé Prefecture from the river,
and burned the Qí ships and vessels.
In the third month, on the *jǐngshēn* day,
Hóu Zhèn arrived from Héféi,
and the various armies presented their victories.
In summer, in the intercalary fourth month, on the *gēngyín* day,
an imperial edict stated:
“Opening granaries to relieve the destitute
is a great benevolence in nurturing the people;
touring the regions to care for the distressed
is a fine tradition of former kings.
As I am in this degenerate age,
and have received this popular acclaim,
my virtue as a ruler is not yet deeply trusted,
and the people's suffering is still severe.
Grieved by these numerous hardships,
I feel even more regret at their falling into ravines.
This is truly because the four ears do not reach,
[一七]and a thousand *lǐ* receive no response.
[一八]How could the benevolence of broad charity
be thus impaired?
The path of ruin and decay
has led to this lack of peace.
Wú Prefecture and Jìn Prefecture suffered locusts and drought last year;
though the crops of Yǐng were cursed,
[一九]the channels of Zhèng ultimately ran dry.
There is no hope of filled storerooms,
and families lament at their empty granaries.
If the common people lack sufficiency,
how can the myriad people rely on me?
Recently, I dispatched *Zhōngshū Shèrén* Jiāng Dézǎo with an imperial order to Dōngyáng,
to inquire into the people's hardships with the magistrates and officials of two thousand *dàn* salary,
and to distribute rice from the imperial granaries for relief.
Although my virtue is not such as to fully satisfy,
I hope it can slightly alleviate starvation.”
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
an imperial edict ordered the establishment of Western Palace Academicians, as in previous dynasties,
and that skilled technicians also participate.
