Qīngchē Jiāngjūn (General of Light Chariots) and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jiāngzhōu) Jìnxī Wáng Shúwén (Prince Shúwén of Jìnxī) was appointed Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn (General of Trust and Awe) and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Xiāngzhōu).
Rénwēi Jiāngjūn (General of Benevolence and Awe) and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yángzhōu) Shǐxīng Wáng Shúzhòng (Prince Shúzhòng of Shǐxīng) was appointed Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.

Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn (General of Trust and Martiality), Nánlángyé Péngchéng Èrjùn Tàishǒu (Administrator of the two commanderies of Nánlángyé and Péngchéng) Nánpíng Wáng Yí (Prince Yí of Nánpíng) was appointed Yángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel) Jiāng Zǒng (江總) was appointed Shàngshū Púyè (Director of the Imperial Secretariat).
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the Wùchén day,
Chángshā Wáng Shújiān (Prince Shújiān of Chángshā) was appointed Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and Zhènzuǒ Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the Left).
On the Rénwǔ day,
the Heir Apparent came of age,
and civil and military officials in service were granted silk, each in differing amounts.
Those who were filial and diligent in farming, and were successors to their fathers, were each granted one rank.
Widowers, widows, the old, and the infirm who could not support themselves were each given five *hú* of grain.
In the ninth month, on the Guǐwèi day,
Tàibái (Venus) was seen during the day.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the Jǐyǒu day,
an imperial edict stated:
"When people farm and dig for themselves and are self-sufficient,
it is called a pure custom.
The rise of tributes and taxes,
its origin is ancient.
It is perhaps due to the extreme toil of the people,
that it became unavoidable.
However, laws and regulations multiply,
and there are many instances of villainy and theft.
Customs are becoming increasingly deceitful,
and government lacks sagely guidance.
From dawn till dusk, I pity any single person who has lost their place,
weeping for the innocent and blaming myself,
ashamed that the three thousand (laws) have not been set in place.
It was hoped that the initial regulations would be established,
making powerful patrons and dependents equally accountable.
However, it is heard that the rich and poor are equally burdened,
and the weak and solitary suffer greater hardship.
Is this truly the intention of aiding the poor and fanning the oppressed?
This is but the harsh exploitation by lower officials.
Hence it is said, 'If the people are not sufficient,
how can the ruler be sufficient?'
From the fourteenth year of Tàijiàn, all outstanding rent and taxes that have not been collected
are hereby remitted and cancelled.
All officials in charge of affairs,
when judging and deciding various matters,
must ensure fairness in acceptance and rejection,
and must not take advantage of public office to harm the people,
or seek personal fame and achievement,
thereby disrupting the way of government."
In the eleventh month, on the Jǐngyín day,
a general amnesty for the empire was granted.
On the Rénshēn day,
the state of Pámpán sent envoys to present local products.
On the Wùyín day,
the state of Báijì sent envoys to present local products.
In the third year, in spring, in the first month, on the Wùwǔ day, which was the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
Chángshā Wáng Shújiān (Prince Shújiān of Chángshā), who was Zhènzuǒ Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the Left), was confirmed in his current rank and appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Fán Yì (樊毅), who was Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the West) and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jīngzhōu), was appointed Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (General Protector of the Army).
Lù Qióng (陸瓊), who was Shǒu Lìbù Shàngshū (Acting Minister of Personnel) and Lǐng Zhùzuò (Director of the Imperial Historiography Office), was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū.
Yuán Jìng (袁敬), who was Jīnzǐguānglù Dàfū (Grandee of the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon), was additionally granted Tèjìn (Special Advance).
In the third month, on the Xīnyǒu day,
Zhāng Dàbǎo (章大寶), former Fēngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Fēngzhōu), raised an army in rebellion.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the Gēngxū day,
Chén Jǐngxiáng (陳景詳), leader of the Fēngzhōu Righteous Army, beheaded Dàbǎo
and sent his head to the capital.
In autumn, in the eighth month, on the night of the Wùzǐ day,
the Lǎorén Xīng (Canopus) was seen.
On the Jǐyǒu day,
Xiè Zhòu (謝伷), who was Zuǒmín Shàngshū (Minister of the Left of the People), was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel).
[一一]In the ninth month, on the Jiǎxū day,
Tèjìn (Special Advance) and Jīnzǐguānglù Dàfū (Grandee of the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon) Yuán Jìng (袁敬) passed away.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the Jǐchǒu day,
the state of Dāndān sent envoys to present local products.
In the eleventh month, on the Jǐwèi day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Xuānxī (Confucius), born with supreme wisdom,
embodies ultimate sageliness.
He compiled the canons of ancestral teachings and regulations,
aligning his virtue with heaven and earth.
He rectified the essence of music and odes,
shining brightly with the sun and moon.
He left a model for future generations,
opening the ears and eyes of humankind.
In the late Liáng dynasty, his reverence faded,
and his spiritual dwelling place was forgotten.
It became overgrown with lush grass
for over thirty years.
I look up to him as if he were still present,
and sigh in eternal longing.
Now, the elegant way is flourishing and harmonious,
and the people have found their place.
Broken zithers and old shoes
are scattered and cannot be recovered.
Reading through cases and opening books,
there is no means to follow and restore them.
Therefore, external rituals should be thoroughly examined.
The old temple should be rebuilt.
Orchid chambers and cassia beams
should all be made new.
Fragrant offerings and pure water
should be presented at appropriate times."
On the Xīnsì day,
the imperial carriage proceeded to Chánggān Sì (Chánggān Temple),
and a general amnesty for the empire was granted.
In the twelfth month, on the day *bǐngxū* (丙戌),
the planet Tàibái (太白) was seen in daylight.
On the day *xīnmǎo* (辛卯),
the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ 皇太子) left the Grand Academy (Tàixué 太學)
to lecture on the *Xiàojīng* (孝經).
On the day *wùxū* (戊戌),
the lecture concluded.
On the day *xīnchǒu* (辛丑),
a *shìdiàn* (釋奠) ceremony was held for the Former Teachers (Xiānshī 先師).
After the ceremony,
music of bells and chimes (*jīnshí zhī yuè* 金石之樂) was performed,
and a banquet was held for the kings, dukes, ministers, and gentlemen.
On the day *guǐmǎo* (癸卯),
the Kingdom of Gāolì (高麗) sent envoys to present local products.
In this year,
Xiāo Kuí (蕭巋) died,
and his son, Xiāo Cóng (蕭琮), succeeded him.
In the fourth year, spring, first month, on the day *jiǎyín* (甲寅),
an imperial edict stated:
"Yáo (堯) displayed the drum for remonstrance,
and Yǔ (禹) bowed to righteous words.
Seeking those of exceptional talent
has long been recorded in history.
[一二] Elevating those who have been overlooked
revives ancient practices.
This is a profound principle for governance
and an urgent task for emperors.
As for Us, being ignorant,
We have broadly inherited this great enterprise,
but We have not yet enlightened Our humble self.
From dawn to dusk, Our heart is filled with concern.
The myriad affairs of state are often in disorder,
and the four faculties of hearing do not reach [Us].
[一三] We desire to hear forthright and bold words
and to adopt their strategies and plans.
From the kings and dukes downwards,
each should recommend those they know.
Broadly inquire among the scribes and attendants,
even reaching the common people.
If even one person has ability,
or one word is useful,
We will personally listen and examine it,
awaiting their admonitions."
Zhōngquán Dàjiāngjūn (中權大將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), Pányáng Wáng (鄱陽王) Bóshān (伯山) was promoted to Zhènwèi Jiāngjūn (鎮衞將軍).
Zhōngwèi Dàjiāngjūn (中衞大將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), Yùzhāng Wáng (豫章王) Shúyīng (叔英) was promoted to Piàojí Dàjiāngjūn (驃騎大將軍).
[一四] Zhèn Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (鎮左將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀 同三司), Chángshā Wáng (長沙王) Shújiān (叔堅) was promoted to Zhōngjūn Dàjiāngjūn (中軍大將軍).
Ānnán Jiāngjūn (安南將軍), Jìn'ān Wáng (晉安王) Bógōng (伯恭) was promoted to Zhèn Yòu Jiāngjūn (鎮右將軍).
Yì Yòu Jiāngjūn (翊右將軍), Yídū Wáng (宜都王) Shúmíng (叔明) was promoted to Ān Yòu Jiāngjūn (安右將軍).
In the second month, on the day *jǐngxū* (景戌),
Zhèn Yòu Jiāngjūn (鎮右將軍), Jìn'ān Wáng (晉安王) Bógōng (伯恭) was appointed Tèjìn (特進).
On the day *jǐngshēn* (景申),
the imperial younger brother Shúmó (叔謨) was enfeoffed as Bādōng Wáng (巴東王).
Shúxiǎn (叔顯) was enfeoffed as Línjiāng Wáng (臨江王).
Shútǎn (叔坦) was enfeoffed as Xīnhuì Wáng (新會王).
Shúlóng (叔隆) was enfeoffed as Xīnníng Wáng (新寧王).
Summer, fifth month, on the day *dīngsì* (丁巳),
the imperial son Zhuāng (莊) was enfeoffed as Kuàijī Wáng (會稽王).
Autumn, ninth month, on the day *jiǎwǔ* (甲午),
the imperial carriage went to Xuánwǔ Hú (玄武湖).
Warships were arrayed for a military review,
[一五] and a banquet was held for the assembled officials to compose poems.
On the day *wùxū* (戊戌),
Zhènwèi Jiāngjūn (鎮衞將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開Fǔyítóng Sānsī), Pányáng Wáng (鄱陽王) Bóshān (伯山) was appointed Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ (東揚州刺史).
Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn (智武將軍), Yuèyáng Wáng (岳陽王) Shúshèn (叔慎) was appointed Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹).
On the day *dīngwèi* (丁未),
the Kingdom of Bǎijì (百濟) sent envoys to present local products.
Winter, tenth month, on the day *guǐhài* (癸亥),
Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射) Jiāng Zǒng (江總) was appointed Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令).
Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Xiè Zhóu (謝伷) was appointed Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射).
Eleventh month, on the day *jǐmǎo* (己卯),
an imperial edict stated:
"Punishment exists solely to curb violence,
and virtue perfects all things.
These are the foundations of the three powers (heaven, earth, man),
immutable through a hundred kings.
Yet, there are no clashing horns in the world,
and few who violate taboos in this era.
Though horses startled at Wèiqiáo (渭橋),
no open remonstrance was heard in court;
though cattle escaped into Táolín (桃林),
their purpose was not perceived.
While the fierce and insolent
are rightly to be shackled,
the foolish and silent
should properly be shown compassion and magnanimity.
If governance lacks excellence,
and our enlightenment shames the wise,
how can we hope to achieve a state where punishments are abolished?
How can that be attained?
Therefore, Our heart is troubled in waking and sleeping,
and We sigh heavily behind the throne.
Now, with the reunion of the broken jade (moon)
and the convergence of the scattered pearls (stars),
the *huángzhōng* (黃鍾) has given its pitch,
and harmonious *qì* (和氣) begins to sprout.
Xuányīng (玄英) announces the middle (of winter),
and the long path is under Our rule.
To pardon transgressions according to the season
is indeed appropriate now.
A general amnesty is hereby granted to all under heaven."
Zhēnmíng (禎明) first year, spring, first month, on the day *jǐngzǐ* (景子),
Ānqián Jiāngjūn (安前將軍), Héngyáng Wáng (衡陽王) Bóxìn (伯信) was promoted to Zhènqián Jiāngjūn (鎮前將軍).
Āndōng Jiāngjūn (安東將軍), Wúxīng Tàishǒu (吳興太守), Lúlíng Wáng (廬陵王) Bórén (伯仁) was appointed Tèjìn (特進).
[一六] Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn (智武將軍), Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹), Yuèyáng Wáng (岳陽王) Shúshèn (叔慎) was appointed Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (湘州刺史).
Rénwǔ Jiāngjūn (仁武將軍), Yìyáng Wáng (義陽王) Shúdá (叔達) was appointed Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹).
On the day *wùyín* (戊寅),
an imperial edict stated:
"Bóhuáng (柏皇) and Dàtíng (大庭) spread pure harmony in ancient days,
while the Jī (姬) kings and Yíng (嬴) empresses were affected by the decadent customs of later generations.
With penal laws already cast,
good transformation did not flourish;
with rites and righteousness already astray,
villainy arose.
How can it be that simplicity and honesty do not return,
but superficiality and extravagance compete to spread?
We, residing centrally and governing all things,
are mindful of the pit (for the unrighteous).
We have frequently unfurled the heavenly net,
and repeatedly severed the three frontiers,
yet the myriad common people
ultimately suffer the five punishments.
This is perhaps due to Our meager virtue,
or perhaps because laws and decrees proliferate.
Therefore, We are not pleased on the throne,
and We pity the intent of those who stand in the corner (discontent).
Now, the three cosmic forces are in order,
and the myriad nations offer tribute at dawn.
The auspicious *língzhī* (靈芝) is presented at the beginning of spring,
and sweet dew condenses at the year's end.
Giving commands from spring,
we look up to heaven to spread virtue,
desiring to share with the nine regions
and renew the seven policies.
A general amnesty is hereby granted to all under heaven,
and the fifth year of Zhìdé (至德) is renamed the first year of Zhēnmíng (禎明)."
On the day *yǐwèi* (乙未),
there was an earthquake.
On the day *guǐmǎo* (癸卯),
Zhènqián Jiāngjūn (鎮前將軍), Héngyáng Wáng (衡陽王) Bóxìn (伯信) was appointed Zhènnán Jiāngjūn (鎮南將軍) and Xīhéngzhōu Cìshǐ (西衡州刺史).
Second month, on the day *dīngwèi* (丁未),
Tèjìn (特進), Zhèn Yòu Jiāngjūn (鎮右將軍), Jìn'ān Wáng (晉安王) Bógōng (伯恭) was promoted to Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn (中衞將軍).
Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令), Jiàn'ān Wáng (建安王) Shúqīng (叔卿) was appointed Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監).
On the day *dīngmǎo* (丁卯),
an imperial edict ordered that all outstanding rent and tax arrears from the first year of Zhìdé (至德)
be pardoned.
Autumn, eighth month, on the day *guǐmǎo* (癸卯),
the Old Man Star (Lǎorénxīng 老人星, Canopus) was seen.
On the day *dīngwèi* (丁未),
Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍) Xiāo Móhē (蕭摩訶) was appointed Piàojí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍).
[一七]
Ninth month, on the day *yǐhài* (乙亥),
Piàojí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), Yùzhāng Wáng (豫章王) Shúyīng (叔英) was appointed Piàojí Dàjiāngjūn (驃騎大將軍).
On the day *gēngyín* (庚寅),
Xiāo Yán (蕭巖), who was Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) and Tàifù Ānpíng Wáng (太傅安平王) under Xiāo Cóng (蕭琮),
[一八] and Xiāo Fán (蕭瓛), who was Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (中軍將軍) and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史) Yìxīng Wáng (義興王),
[一九] sent their Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書) Shěn Jūngōng (沈君公)
to Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史) Chén Jì (陳紀) to surrender.
[二０] On the day *xīnmǎo* (辛卯),
Xiāo Yán (蕭巖) and others led over one hundred thousand men and women, military and civilian, across the Jiāng (江, Yangtze River).
On the day *jiǎwǔ* (甲午),
a general amnesty was granted to all under heaven.
Winter, eleventh month, on the day *yǐhài* (乙亥),
Wú Jùn (吳郡) of Yángzhōu (揚州) was partitioned to establish Wúzhōu (吳州).
Qiántáng Xiàn (錢塘縣) was partitioned to form a commandery,
attached to it.
On the day *jǐngzǐ* (景子),
Xiāo Yán (蕭巖) was appointed Píngdōng Jiāngjūn (平東將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), and Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ (東揚州刺史).
Xiāo Fán (蕭瓛) was appointed Āndōng Jiāngjūn (安東將軍) and Wúzhōu Cìshǐ (吳州刺史).
On the day *dīnghài* (丁亥),
Piàojí Dàjiāngjūn (驃騎大將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), Yùzhāng Wáng (豫章王) Shúyīng (叔英) additionally held the post of Sītú (司徒).
Twelfth month, on the day *jǐngchén* (景辰),
former Zhènwèi Jiāngjūn (鎮衞將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ (東揚州刺史), Pányáng Wáng (鄱陽王) Bóshān (伯山) was appointed Zhènwèi Dàjiāngjūn (鎮衞大將軍) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
[二一] Former Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn (中衞將軍), Jìn'ān Wáng (晉安王) Bógōng (伯恭) was appointed Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn (中衞將軍) and Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (右光祿大夫).
Second year, spring, first month, on the day *xīnsì* (辛巳),
the imperial son Quán (恮) was enfeoffed as Dōngyáng Wáng (東陽王).
Tián (恬) was enfeoffed as Qiántáng Wáng (錢塘王).
In this month,
Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) Zhōu Luó (周羅) was dispatched to lead troops to garrison Xiákǒu (峽口).
Summer, fourth month, on the day *wùshēn* (戊申),
countless swarms of rats
entered from the shores of Càizhōu (蔡洲), crossed the Huái River (淮) at Shítóu Dù (石頭渡),
[二二] reaching both banks of Qīngtáng (青塘).
After several days, they died
and drifted out into the Jiāng (江, Yangtze River).
On the day *wùwǔ* (戊午),
Zuǒmín Shàngshū (左民尚書) Cài Zhēng (蔡徵) was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書).
In this month,
the water in Nánpǔ (南浦) of Yǐngzhōu (郢州) turned black like ink.
Fifth month, on the day *rénwǔ* (壬午),
Ānqián Jiāngjūn (安前將軍), Lúlíng Wáng (廬陵王) Bórén (伯仁) was appointed Tèjìn (特進).
On the day *jiǎwǔ* (甲午),
at Dōngyě (東冶) iron foundry,
an object, red and the size of several *dǒu* (斗),
[二三] fell from the sky into the smelting area.
There was a rumbling sound like thunder,
and molten iron flew out over the wall, burning people's homes.
In the sixth month, on the day Wùxū,
the kingdom of Fúnán dispatched envoys to present local products.
On the day Gēngzǐ,
the Crown Prince Yìn was deposed and made the King of Wúxīng.
Shǐ’ān Wáng Shēn, General of the Army and Governor of Yángzhōu, was established as Crown Prince.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
Nánpíng Wáng Yí, General Who Quells the South and Governor of Jiāngzhōu, was promoted to General Who Guards the South.
Yǒngjiā Wáng Yàn, General of Loyal Valor and Governor of Nánxúzhōu, was promoted to General Who Pacifies the North.
Kuàijī Wáng Zhuāng was made General Who Assists the Vanguard and Governor of Yángzhōu.
Jiāng Zǒng, General Who Spreads Favor and Director of the Department of State Affairs, was promoted to General of the Central Command.
Yuán Xiàn, General of Cloud Standards and Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince, was made Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Xiè Zhòu, Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, was made Special Grand Master.
Cài Zhēng, General Who Pacifies Distant Regions and newly appointed Minister of Personnel, was promoted to General Who Pacifies the Right.
On the day Jiǎchén,
Lǔ Guǎngdá, General Who Pacifies the Right, was made Central Leader of the Army.
〔二四〕On the day Dīngsì,
a great wind came from the northwest, churning up the waves and driving water into Shítóuchéng.
The淮渚 (Huáizhǔ) overflowed suddenly,
sweeping away boats and carriages.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Jǐhài,
the Imperial Son Fān was made King of Wújùn.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
Yáo Chá, Minister of the Treasury and concurrently Grand Author, was made Minister of Personnel.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
the imperial carriage proceeded to Mòfǔshān,
where a grand hunt was held.
In the eleventh month, on the day Dīngmǎo,
an imperial edict stated:
“Deliberating on legal cases and lenient punishments
is what sagely kings have set as a model, and
triumphing over cruelty and abolishing killing
is what benevolent individuals hold in their hearts.
Since the cessation of drawing caps (for punishment),
officials who inflict harsh penalties have risen.
Laws have proliferated,
leaving people at a loss.
I rule this land,
at a time of decline.
The statutes concerning severity and leniency
are not yet well-ordered in governance.
Regarding both major and minor affairs,
speaking of them fills me with shame.
Looking at these prisons,
I feel profound sorrow and pity.
It is decreed that a day be set to review legal cases at Dàzhèngdiàn.”
On the day Rénshēn,
Nánpíng Wáng Yí, General Who Guards the South and Governor of Jiāngzhōu, was made General Who Conquers the West and Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
Yǒngjiā Wáng Yàn, General Who Pacifies the North and Governor of Nánxúzhōu, was made General Who Pacifies the South and Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
Nánhǎi Wáng Qián, General of the Army, was made General Who Pacifies the North and Governor of Nánxúzhōu.
〔二五〕On the day Jǐngzǐ,
the Imperial Brother Shúróng was made King of Xīnchāng,
and Shúkuāng was made King of Tàiyuán.
In this month,
the Suí dispatched Jìn Wáng Guǎng with a large army to invade.
From Bā and Shǔ, and from Miǎnhàn downstream to Guǎnglíng,
they entered by dozens of routes simultaneously.
Garrisons along the Jiāng (Yangtze River)
reported their advance one after another.
At this time, Shī Wénqìng, the newly appointed Governor of Xiāngzhōu, and Shěn Kèqīng, Attendant Secretary of the Central Secretariat, who were in charge of confidential matters,
suppressed the reports and did not speak of them,
hence there was no preparation for defense.
In the third year, spring, the first month, on the first day, Yǐchǒu,
fog filled the four quarters.
On this day,
Suí Commander-in-Chief Hèruò Bì crossed the Jīngkǒu from Guǎnglíng via the northern route.
Commander-in-Chief Hán Qínhǔ hastened to Héngjiāng,
〔二六〕crossed at Cǎishí,
and was to meet Bì’s army from the southern route.
On the day Jǐngyín,
Xú Zǐjiàn, the Cǎishí garrison commander, galloped to report the change.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
the Dukes and Ministers were summoned to discuss military matters.
On the day Wùchén,
internal and external areas were put on high alert.
Xiāo Móhē, General of Agile Cavalry,
Fán Měng, Governor of Nányùzhōu, was dispatched to lead a naval force out of Báixià.
Gāo Wénzòu, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, led troops to garrison Nányùzhōu.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Hèruò Bì attacked and captured Nánxúzhōu.
On the day Xīnwèi,
Hán Qínhǔ again captured Nányùzhōu,
and Wénzòu was defeated and returned.
By this time, the Suí armies were advancing simultaneously on both northern and southern routes.
The Last Ruler dispatched Yùzhāng Wáng Shūyīng, Grand General of Agile Cavalry and Minister of Education, to garrison the 朝【堂】 (Cháotáng).
〔二八〕Xiāo Móhē garrisoned Lèyóuyuàn.
Fán Yì garrisoned Qíshé Sì.
Lǔ Guǎngdá garrisoned Báitǔ Gāng.
Kǒng Fàn, General of Loyal Valor, garrisoned Bǎotián Sì.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Rèn Zhōng, Grand General Who Guards the East, entered from Wúxīng to answer the call,
and subsequently garrisoned Zhūquè Mén.
On the day Xīnsì,
Hèruò Bì advanced and occupied Zhōngshān,
and encamped southeast of Báitǔ Gāng.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
the Last Ruler dispatched various armies to engage Bì in battle,
but these armies were utterly defeated.
Bì, capitalizing on his victory, reached Lèyóuyuàn.
Lǔ Guǎngdá still led scattered troops in a desperate fight,
but could not resist.
Bì advanced to attack the palace city,
and burned the Běiyè Mén.
At this time, Hán Qínhǔ led his forces from Xīnlín to Shízǐ Gāng.
Rèn Zhōng surrendered to Qínhǔ,
and then led Qínhǔ via Zhūquè Háng towards the palace city,
entering through the Nányè Mén.
Thereupon, all civil and military officials within the city fled,
only Yuán Xiàn, Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, remained in the main hall.

Jiāng Zǒng, Director of the Department of State Affairs, Yáo Chá, Minister of Personnel, Yuán Quán, Minister of the Treasury, Wáng Yuàn, former Minister of the Treasury, and Wáng Kuān, Palace Attendant, remained in the secretariat.
When the Last Ruler heard that the army had arrived,
he, with more than ten palace women, exited the rear hall’s Jǐngyáng Diàn,
and intended to throw himself into a well.
Yuán Xiàn, attending by his side,
bitterly advised against it, but he would not listen.
Xiàhóu Gōngyùn, Palace Attendant of the Rear Chambers, also used his body to cover the well.
The Last Ruler struggled with them for a long time
before he finally managed to get in.
By night,
he was captured by the Suí army.
On the day Jǐngxū,
Jìn Wáng Guǎng entered and occupied the capital city.
In the third month, on the day Jǐsì,
the Last Ruler, along with the princes, dukes, and all officials, departed from Jiànyè
and entered Cháng’ān.
In the fourth year of Suí Rénshòu, eleventh month, on the day Rénzǐ,
he died in Luòyáng,
at the age of fifty-two.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand General,
ennobled as Duke of Chángchéng County,
and given the posthumous title Yáng.
He was buried on Mángshān in Luòyáng, Hénán.
Historian and Palace Attendant Zhèngguó Gōng Wèi Zhēng said: Gāozǔ rose from humble origins,
possessing a heroic and exceptional bearing.
Initially assisting a lesser domain,
he displayed brilliant and extraordinary strategies.
He pacified the Nánhǎi region,
his duty being to quell disorder.
Raising his banner,
he marched north,
his righteous cause being to serve the emperor.
He swept away Hóu Jǐng after his establishment
and rescued the Liáng dynasty from its collapse.
The imperial net was broken but reconnected,
the state's fortune was in distress but recovered.
The many spirits
had a master,
and the old order was not lost.
The way Wèi Wáng extended the Hàn's imperial legacy,
and Sòng Wǔ returned the Jìn's imperial carriage—
his magnificent achievements and great merits
could not be surpassed.
At that time, internal strife
was not yet settled,
and external neighbors were formidable enemies.
Wáng Lín caused trouble in the upper reaches,
and Zhōu and Qí agitated the Jiāng and Hàn regions.
He was fearful of both front and back,
as if existing and not existing.
Not planning for
this,
he abruptly shifted the heavenly mandate.
Although the imperial spirits were favorable,
how swift it was!
Nevertheless, his ambition and breadth of vision were grand and far-reaching,
his mind open and clear.
He sometimes recruited officials from his enemies,
and sometimes promoted talents
from among exiles.
He overlooked their fault of accepting gold,
and pardoned their crime of criticizing the ruler.
He entrusted them with his innermost confidants and vital military power,
and all were able to exert their utmost effort.
Thus, he made decisive moves and won a hundred battles,
achieving this division of the realm into three.
Compared to the heroes who stood as tripods,
he was certainly not ashamed before Quán and Bèi.
Shìzǔ was naturally intelligent and astute,
with integrity and clarity of mind.
He participated in governance early,
knew the people's suffering,
and considered selecting excellent laws,
hoping for ultimate good governance.
He employed both virtue and punishment,
saving the state from difficulties and dangers.
All villains submitted,
and powerful neighbors were awed.
Although his transformation through loyalty and generosity could not reach far,
his style of reverence and frugality was sufficient to set an example.
If he had not been fond of clear
discernment,
he would have been a good ruler who preserved the established order.
Línchuān was older than Chéngwáng,
and his faults were slighter than Tàijiǎ.
Xuāndì had the close kinship of Zhōugōng,
but not the ambition of Yī Yǐn.
The enlightened sovereign did not return,
and the Tóng Gōng then
Ah,
if one wants to condemn someone,
will they lack a pretext?
When Gāo Zōng 當時 was still in the countryside,
his magnanimity was vast and expansive.
Upon ascending to the throne and wielding supreme power,
the people were drawn to his generosity.
He treated his subordinates with kindness,
〔二九〕and tolerated the masses with broad-mindedness.
His wisdom and courage
both soared;
his military campaigns were justified,
banners waved and divisions were arrayed.
Like wind sweeping and lightning striking,
he expanded his territory by a thousand *lǐ*,
encompassing the Huái and Sì Rivers.
The momentum of his victories in battle and successful conquests
had not
been seen in recent antiquity.
〔三０〕Later, the ruler became extravagant and the people toiled;
the generals grew arrogant and the soldiers slack.
The imperial treasury was depleted,
and the armies suffered setbacks.
At that time, the Qín people were growing strong,
and thus they cast their gaze upon the armies along the
Jiāng River.
Lǐ Kè believed that the premature downfall of Wú
was due to its numerous battles [and numerous victories].
〔三一〕Numerous battles weary the people,
and numerous victories make the ruler arrogant.
To govern
weary people with an arrogant ruler
is to face certain downfall.
How true his words!
Gāo Zōng initially gained people through his magnanimity,
but eventually brought about defeat through his arrogance and extravagance.
The achievements of Wén and Wǔ
〔三二〕
were lost in this era.
Hòu Zhǔ was born in the deep palace,
and raised by women.
When the state was already in a state of exhaustion,
he knew not the hardships of farming.
Initially fearful of impending danger,
he frequently issued
decrees of pity and compassion.
Later, as things gradually settled,
he again fanned the flames of淫chì (licentiousness and extravagance).
He treated high-ranking officials with ceremonial courtesies,
but only indulged his passions in literature and wine.
He drew close to petty individuals,
and entrusted them with the reins
of power.
Wherever his counsel reached,
there were no upright and outspoken officials;
wherever power resided,
there were only corrupt and rapacious officials.
Governance and laws became daily disordered,
and idle officials filled the court.
He indulged in
all-night drinking bouts,
and his favored concubines brought about calamities akin to those caused by seductive wives.
He disregarded peril and destruction,
while superiors and subordinates deceived each other.
With many rebelling and close relatives estranged,
he failed to awaken to the crisis at hand.
He threw himself into a well,
hoping to eke out a meager existence.
To see him seek preservation in this way,
surely the people were truly lowly then!
Looking back at the various rulers,
who succeeded to power and rose to prominence,
they all initially wished to rival the brightness of the sun and moon,
and match the virtue of heaven and earth.
They looked up to the Five Dì,
and aimed to emulate the Three Wáng.
However,
none started without ambition,
but few were able to finish well.
Why was this so?
They all possessed mediocre talent,
and a nature that could be swayed.
Their mouths spoke of benevolence and righteousness,
but their hearts trembled before
desires.
Benevolence and righteousness benefit all beings but their path is distant;
desires fulfill one's nature and are convenient for the self.
Convenience for the self cannot be long denied,
and a distant path is difficult to maintain with firm resolve.
The sycophantic crowd,
observing their expressions and moods,
indulged their preferences
to please and guide them.
It was like a ball rolling down a slope,
or like breaching a dam in a flowing stream.
Unless one is touched by the spirit of the celestial phenomena,
and born with luminous
virtue,
who can forsake what they enjoy
and take the common people to heart?
This is why Chéng, Kāng, Wén, and Jǐng are rarely seen in a thousand years,
while Guǐ, Xīn, Yōu, and Lì
are found in every generation.
Their poison afflicted the imperial altars,
and their persons suffered disgrace and humiliation,
becoming a laughingstock to all under heaven.
How painful this is!
The ancients had a saying:
rulers of fallen states
often possessed talents
and arts.
Examining Liáng, Chén, and Suí confirms
this is no empty claim.
Therefore, if one does not uphold the foundation of instruction and righteousness,
but instead solely values decadent and beautiful literature,
it will only foster a corrupt and deceitful trend,
and provide no
salvation from the calamity of chaos and destruction.
The historian says: Hòu Zhǔ, when he was in the Eastern Palace,
early demonstrated noble virtues.
Upon inheriting the throne and continuing the enterprise,
he truly fulfilled the expectations of both heaven and man.
As for rituals, music, laws, and governance,
he followed all the old precedents,
and moreover, he deeply cultivated the Six Arts
and broadly opened the four gates.
Thus, those awaiting imperial summons
competed to rush to the Jīnmǎ Gate,
and scholars studying antiquity
gathered like clouds at the Shíqú Pavilion.
Furthermore, ascending mountains and sailing seas,
tributaries often arrived annually.
Since the Zhèngshǐ reign of Wèi and the mid-Jìn dynasty,
although high officials sometimes understood governance,
they all associated with each other through literature,
rarely concerning themselves with practical affairs.
Only for grand court ceremonies and important rituals
would they participate in discussions.
Official documents and records
were all entrusted to petty officials.
This gradually became a custom,
persisting until Chén.
Hòu Zhǔ continued this practice,
having no time for reform.
Therefore, individuals like Shī Wénqìng and Shěn Kèqīng
monopolized important military and national affairs.
These cunning and unorthodox individuals
considered exploitation and harshness as achievements.
They sought personal glory
and disregarded national interests.
Consequently, court discipline deteriorated,
and disaster arose from neighboring states.
This was also a cosmic cycle reaching a point of crisis,
where the imperial destiny changed.
It was not merely that human affairs did not flourish,
but also that it was the will of Heaven.
Collation Notes
Biographies, First Volume: Empress Gāo Zǔ Zhāng, Empress Shì Zǔ Shěn, Empress Fèi Dì Wáng, Empress Gāo Zōng Liǔ, Empress Hòu Zhǔ Shěn, (Noble Consort Zhāng).
According to the Zhōu Lǐ,
when a king establishes an empress,
there are six palaces,
three *fūrén*,
nine *pín*,
twenty-seven *shìfù*,
and eighty-one *yùqī*,
to manage the internal affairs of the realm.
However, rulers who received the mandate and succeeded to the throne
were not only assisted by external ministers,
but also aided by internal virtue.
Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
the offices of the six palaces
have been inherited and augmented,
differing across generations.
Gāo Zǔ, taking over in an era of decline and chaos,
gloriously received the heavenly mandate.
He maintained a simple lifestyle,
thus many positions in his imperial harem were vacant.
In the early Tiānjiā reign of Shì Zǔ,
an edict established the number of positions in the imperial harem.
Initially, three positions were created: *guìfēi*, *guìpín*, and *guìjī*,
to correspond to the three *fūrén* of antiquity.
Also, nine positions were created: *shūyuán*, *shūyí*, *shūróng*, *zhāohuá*, *zhāoróng*, *zhāoyí*,
*xiūhuá*, *xiūyí*, and *xiūróng*,
to correspond to the nine *pín* of antiquity.
Furthermore, five positions were created: *jiéyú*, *rónghuá*, *chōnghuá*, *chénghuī*, and *lièróng*,
called the five ranks,
subordinate to the nine *pín*.
Additionally, three positions were created: *měirén*, *cáirén*, and *liángrén*.
These positions had no fixed number of personnel
and were called "unassigned ranks."
Shì Zǔ was by nature humble and frugal,
and many of his imperial concubines' positions were vacant.
Gāo Zōng and Hòu Zhǔ made no changes to the internal offices.
(（令）)【今】The contents appended here
briefly complete this chapter.
Gāozǔ Xuānhòuzhāng Shì,
personal name Yāo'ér,
was a native of Wúxīng Wūchéng.
Her original surname was Niǔ.
Her father, Jǐngmíng, was adopted by the Zhāng clan,
and thus changed his surname.
Jǐngmíng,
during the Liáng dynasty, reached the office of Sànqí Shìláng.
The Empress's mother, Sū,
once encountered a Daoist who gave her a small tortoise,
lustrous with five colors,
saying:
"There will be a sign in three years."
When the time came,
the Empress was born, and a purple light illuminated the room,
and the tortoise's whereabouts were then lost.
She was intelligent in her youth,
with a beautiful appearance,
and her fingernails were five cùn long,
all white and red.
Whenever there was mourning for a relative within a year,
one nail would break first.
Gāozǔ first married a daughter of Qián Zhòngfāng from the same commandery,
who died early;
afterward, he betrothed the Empress.
The Empress was skilled in calligraphy and calculation,
and could recite poetry and the Chǔ Cí.
When Gāozǔ campaigned south from Guǎngzhōu against Jiāozhǐ,
he ordered the Empress and Héngyángwáng Chāng to return to Chángchéng with Shìzǔ via the sea route.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
when Gāozǔ descended to Yùzhāng,
the Empress was imprisoned by Jǐng.
After Jǐng was pacified,
and Gāozǔ became Chángchéng Xiàn Gōng,
the Empress was appointed Fūrén.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
in the first year of Yǒngdìng, she was established as Empress.
Her father Jǐngmíng was posthumously granted the titles of Tèjìn and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
with the addition of a golden seal and purple ribbon,
and her mother Sū was appointed Ānjí Xiànjūn.
In the second year,
Ānjí Jūn died,
and was interred with the Empress's father in Wúxīng.
The following year,
the Empress's father was posthumously enfeoffed as Guǎngdé Xiàn Hóu,
with an estate of five hundred households,
and given the posthumous name Wēn.
When Gāozǔ passed away,
the Empress, together with Zhōngshū Shèrén Cài Jǐnglì, devised a plan
to keep the death a secret,
and summoned Shìzǔ to succeed to the throne.
This matter is recorded in the biographies of Cài Jǐnglì and Hóu Āndū.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he honored the Empress as Huáng Tàihòu,
and her palace was named Cíxùn.
When Fèidì ascended the throne,
he honored her as Tàihuáng Tàihòu.
In the second year of Guāngdà,
the Empress issued an edict deposing Fèidì as Línhǎiwáng,
and ordered Gāozōng to succeed to the throne.
In the first year of Tàijiàn,
she was honored as Huáng Tàihòu.
In the third month, Jǐngshēn day, of the second year,
she passed away at the Zǐjí Diàn,
aged sixty-five.
Her dying wish was that funeral arrangements
should all be frugal and simple,
and that no sacrificial animals
should be used for offerings.
In the fourth month of that year,
the assembled officials presented the posthumous name Xuān Tàihòu,
and she was interred beside Wàn'ānlíng.
None of the Empress's immediate relatives held positions at court;
only her clan elder brother Niǔ Qià reached the office of Zhōngsàn Dàfū.
Shìzǔ's Empress Shěn, personal name Miàoróng,
was a native of Wúxīng Wǔkāng.
Her father, Fǎshēn,
was an Ānqián Zhōng Lùshì Cānjūn during the Liáng dynasty.
When the Empress was over ten years old,
she married Shìzǔ during the Dàtóng era of the Liáng.
When Gāozǔ campaigned against Hóu Jǐng,
Shìzǔ was then in Wúxīng,
and Jǐng sent envoys to seize Shìzǔ and the Empress.
After Jǐng was pacified,
they were able to escape.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
in the first year of Yǒngdìng,
the Empress became Línchuān Wángfēi.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
she became Empress.
Her father Fǎshēn was posthumously granted Guānglù Dàfū,
with the addition of a golden seal and purple ribbon,
enfeoffed as Jiànchéng Xiàn Hóu,
with an estate of five hundred households,
and given the posthumous name Gōng.
Her mother Gāo was posthumously granted Suí'ān Xiànjūn,
with the posthumous name Dìng.
When Fèidì ascended the throne,
he honored her as Huáng Tàihòu,
and her palace was named Āndé.
At that time, Gāozōng, together with Púyè Dào Zhòngjǔ and Shèrén Liú Shīzhī, had all been entrusted with assisting in governance after the emperor's death.
Shīzhī and Zhòngjǔ constantly resided in the forbidden palace to participate in deliberating on all matters,
while Gāozōng was Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and entered and resided in the Shàngshū Shěng with three hundred attendants.
Shīzhī, seeing Gāozōng's growing power,
secretly became wary of him,
and thus falsely issued an edict to Gāozōng saying:
"Now that the four quarters are peaceful,
the Prince may return to Dōngfǔ
to manage the affairs of the province."
When Gāozōng was about to depart,
Zīyì Máo Xǐ stopped him, saying:
"If you leave now,
you will be controlled by others,
like Cáo Shuǎng,
and will not even be able to become a rich old man."
Gāozōng then feigned illness,
summoned Shīzhī to stay and talk with him,
and sent Máo Xǐ to first go in and speak to the Empress.
The Empress said:
"Now Bózōng is young,
and all government affairs are entrusted to my second son [Gāozōng];
this is not my intention."
Xǐ then spoke to Fèidì,
and the Emperor said:
"This is Shīzhī and others' doing;
it is not my intention."
Xǐ came out and reported this to Gāozōng.
Gāozōng then imprisoned Shīzhī,
and personally went in to see the Empress and the Emperor,
and vehemently listed Shīzhī's faults.
He then drafted an edict himself and requested it be signed,
handing Shīzhī over to the Tíngwèi for punishment.
That night,
Shīzhī was granted death in prison.
From then on, all matters, great and small,
fell to Gāozōng.
The Empress was worried and could not think of a solution,
so she secretly bribed the eunuch Jiǎng Yù,
ordering him to entice Zhāng Ānguó from Jiàn'ān,
to have him seize the commandery and rebel,
hoping to use this to plot against Gāozōng.
Ānguó's plot was discovered,
and he was executed by Gāozōng.
At that time, many of the Empress's close attendants were aware of the matter,
and the Empress, fearing they would be implicated,
killed them all.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
he made her Wén Huánghòu.
After Chén fell and she entered Suí,
in the early years of Dàyè,
she returned from Cháng'ān to Jiāngnán,
and after a short while,
she died.
The Empress's elder brother Qīn
followed Shìzǔ in campaigns,
and for his merits reached Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn and Ānzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he inherited the title of Jiànchéng Hóu,
was granted Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, Chíjié, and military command over the nine commanderies including Kuàijī, Míngwēi Jiāngjūn, and Kuàijī Tàishǒu.
He then entered as Shìzhōng, Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn, and Wèiwèi Qīng.
During Guāngdà,
he became Shàngshū Yòu Púyè,
and soon after was promoted to Zuǒ Púyè.
Qīn had always been without special skills,
and merely looked after himself.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
he was sent out as Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn and Yìxīng Tàishǒu,
with a salary of two thousand dàn.
He died in the first year of Tàijiàn,
aged sixty-seven.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng, Tèjìn, and Yìzuǒ Jiāngjūn,
with the posthumous name Chéng.
His son Guān succeeded him,
and was quite learned,
reaching the office of Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Fèidì's Empress Wáng was
the daughter of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū Gù.
In the first year of Tiānjīa,
she became the Crown Prince's Consort.
When Fèidì ascended the throne,
she was established as Empress.
When Fèidì became Línhǎiwáng,
she became Línhǎiwángfēi.
She died during Zhìdé.
The Empress bore Línhǎi Sìwáng Zhìzé.
Zhìzé became the Crown Prince in the first year of Guāngdà.
In the first year of Tàijiàn,
he inherited the title of Línhǎi Sìwáng.
Soon after, he was appointed Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn,
and had his own subordinate officials.
After Chén fell, he entered Cháng'ān.
Gāozōng Liǔ Huánghòu, courtesy name Jìngyán,
was from Xiè in Hédōng.
Her great-grandfather was Shìlóng,
who served as Qí Shìzhōng, Sīkōng, Shàngshūlìng, and Zhēnyáng Zhōngwǔgōng.
Her grandfather, Yùn,
had a great reputation during the Liáng dynasty.
He reached the office of Mìshūjiān,
and was posthumously granted the titles Shìzhōng and Zhōnghùjūn.
Her father, Yǎn,
married Chángchéng Gōngzhǔ, Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's daughter,
and was appointed Fùmǎ Dōuwèi.
During the Dàbǎo reign,
he became Póyáng Tàishǒu,
and died in office.
At that time, the Empress was nine years old,
but managed family affairs
as if an adult.
During the Hóu Jǐng Rebellion,
the Empress and her younger brother, Pàn, went to Jiānglíng to rely on Emperor Yuán of Liáng.
Emperor Yuán, due to Chángchéng Gōngzhǔ,
treated them very generously.
When Gāozōng arrived in Jiānglíng,
Emperor Yuán betrothed the Empress to him.
In the second year of Chéngshèng (553 CE),
the Empress gave birth to Hòuzhǔ in Jiānglíng.
The next year,
Jiānglíng fell,
and Gāozōng was moved to Guān Yòu.
The Empress and Hòuzhǔ both remained in Rángchéng.
In the second year of Tiānjiā (561 CE),
she returned to court with Hòuzhǔ,
and was made Ānchéng Wángfēi.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
she was established as Empress.
The Empress was beautiful,
seven feet two inches tall,
with hands that hung below her knees.
Initially,
when Gāozōng lived in his hometown,
he had first married a daughter of the Qián clan of Wúxīng.
When he ascended the throne,
she was appointed Guìfēi,
and was greatly favored.
The Empress wholeheartedly deferred to her.
Whenever supplies from the Imperial Workshops were presented,
she always pushed the best items to the Guìfēi,
and used the secondary ones herself.
When Gāozōng passed away,
Shǐxīng Wáng Shūlíng rebelled.
Hòuzhǔ was saved and escaped thanks to the Empress and Lè'ān Jūn Wú Shì;
this incident is detailed in the biography of Shūlíng.
When Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
he honored the Empress as Huáng Tàihòu,
and her palace was named Hóngfàn.
At that time,
the land of Huáinán had just been lost,
Suí armies were approaching the Jiāng (Yangtze River),
and the country was mourning a great loss.
Hòuzhǔ was ill with sores and unable to govern.
The execution of Shūlíng, the management of the late emperor's funeral rites, border defense, and all administrative affairs of the various departments,
though issued in Hòuzhǔ's name,
were all decided by the Empress.
When Hòuzhǔ's sores healed,
he then resumed governance.
After Chén fell, she entered Cháng'ān.
In the eleventh year of Dàyè (615 CE), she died in Dōngdū
at the age of eighty-three,
and was buried on Mángshān in Luòyáng.
The Empress was humble and discreet,
never making requests for her relatives,
nor even sharing food or clothing with them.
Her younger brother, Pàn,
married Shìzǔ's daughter Fùyáng Gōngzhǔ during the Tàijiàn reign,
and was appointed Fùmǎ Dōuwèi.
When Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
he was made Sànqí Chángshì as the emperor's maternal uncle.
Pàn was foolish and stubborn,
and given to drinking.
He often rode his horse into the palace gate while drunk,
and was impeached by the appropriate authorities,
resulting in his dismissal from office.
He died at home.
He was posthumously granted the titles Shìzhōng and Zhōnghùjūn.
The Empress's paternal cousin, Zhuāng,
was bright, astute, and discerning.
Towards the end of Tàijiàn,
he served as Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
and was in charge of the Eastern Palace records.
When Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
he gradually rose to Sànqí Chángshì and Wèiwèi Qīng.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng (587 CE),
he was transferred to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
concurrently serving as Zhōngshū Shèrén,
and overseeing Yōngzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng.
After Pàn's death,
Zhuāng was the only close relative of the Empress Dowager's clan.
Moreover, he had always enjoyed a good reputation,
and was thus deeply favored.
Soon after, he was promoted to Dùzhī Shàngshū.
After Chén fell, he entered Suí,
and became Qízhōu Sīmǎ.
Hòuzhǔ Shěn Huánghòu, courtesy name Wùhuá,
was the daughter of Yítóng Sānsī Wàngcài Zhēnxìan Hóu Jūnlǐ.
Her mother was Gāozǔ's daughter Huìjī Mù Gōngzhǔ.
The Princess died young,
and at that time, the Empress was still a child,
but she grieved excessively, emaciated by sorrow.
After the period of mourning ended,
whenever it was the first or fifteenth day of the lunar month,
she would always sit alone weeping,
her grief moving those around her,
and both insiders and outsiders held her in respect and awe.
In the third year of Tàijiàn (571 CE), she was taken as the Crown Prince's consort.
When Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
she was established as Empress.
The Empress was upright and serene,
with few desires.
She was intelligent and had a strong memory,
read widely in the classics and histories,
and was skilled in calligraphy.
Initially,
while Hòuzhǔ was in the Eastern Palace,
her father Jūnlǐ died.
The Empress was in mourning,
residing in a separate hall,
and grieved beyond the prescribed rites.
Hòuzhǔ's treatment of the Empress was already cold,
and Guìfēi Zhāng's favor overshadowed the entire imperial harem.
All administration of the harem was delegated to her.
The Empress remained calm and never showed any jealousy or resentment.
Her living quarters were frugal,
her clothes without brocade or embroidery decorations.
She had only about a hundred attendants.
Her only pursuits were reading books and histories and reciting Buddhist scriptures.
After Chén fell,
she and Hòuzhǔ both entered Cháng'ān.
When Hòuzhǔ passed away,
the Empress personally composed an elegy for him,
the text of which was extremely poignant.
Whenever Emperor Yáng of Suí went on an inspection tour,
he always ordered her to accompany him.
When Emperor Yáng was killed by Yǔwénhuàjí,
the Empress returned to her hometown by crossing the river from Guǎnglíng,
and her ultimate fate is unknown.
The Empress had no sons,
and adopted Sūn Jī's son Yìn as her own.
Many of her clan members held prominent official positions;
their affairs are detailed in the biography of Jūnlǐ.
Her uncle, Jūngōng,
had always been in Jiānglíng after the defeat of Emperor Yuán of Liáng.
During the Zhēnmíng reign,
he, along with Xiāo Huán and Xiāo Yán, led troops in rebellion against Suí and returned to Chén.
Hòuzhǔ promoted him to Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
Jūngōng was erudite, talented in debate,
and skilled in discussion.
Hòuzhǔ deeply esteemed him.
When Chén fell,
Emperor Wén of Suí, considering his rebellion,
ordered him to be executed in Jiànkāng.
Hòuzhǔ Zhāng Guìfēi, personal name Lìhuá,
was the daughter of a military family.
Her family was poor;
her father and brothers made their living by weaving mats.
When Hòuzhǔ was Crown Prince,
she was selected to enter the palace.
At this time, Gōng Guìpín was a Liángdì.
The Guìfēi was ten years old
and served as her attendant.
Hòuzhǔ saw her and was pleased,
thus she gained his favor
and became pregnant,
giving birth to Crown Prince Shēn.
When Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
she was appointed Guìfēi.
She was intelligent and wise,
and greatly favored.
Whenever Hòuzhǔ invited the Guìfēi to feasts and entertainments with guests,
the Guìfēi would recommend other palace women to participate.
All the women in the harem were grateful to her
and competed to praise the Guìfēi's virtues,
which made her love overshadow the entire harem.
She also enjoyed the art of sorcery
and used shamanic practices to bewitch Hòuzhǔ.
She established illicit cults in the palace,
gathering various sorcerers to perform dances.
Through them, she would inquire about external affairs.
If anyone uttered a word or performed an act,
the Consort would know of it first
and report it to Hòuzhǔ.
Because of this, Hòuzhǔ valued her even more,
and many of her internal and external relatives
were employed in official positions.
When the Suí army captured Táichéng,
the Consort and Hòuzhǔ both entered a well.
The Suí army pulled them out,
and Jìn Wáng Guǎng ordered the Guìfēi to be executed
and her head displayed on Qīngxī Zhōngqiáo.
The imperial historian and chamberlain, the Duke of Zhèngguó, Wèi Zhēng, in his examination of records and
consultation with venerable elders,
says that when the Last Emperor (Hòuzhǔ) first ascended the throne,
due to the rebellion of Shǐxīng Wáng Shūlíng,
he was wounded and lay in the Chéngxiānggé.
At that time, none of his concubines were allowed to enter,
only Guìfēi Zhāng (Empress Zhāng) attended him.
Meanwhile, Tàihòu Liǔ (Empress Dowager Liǔ) still resided in the Bóliángdiàn,
which was the empress's main palace.
Hòuzhǔ's Empress Shěn had always been out of favor
and was not allowed to attend to his illness,
residing separately in the Qiúxiándiàn.
In the second year of Zhìdé (582 CE),
the three pavilions Línchūngé, Jiéqǐgé, and Wàngxiāngé were built in front of the Guāngzhàodiàn.
The pavilions were several *zhàng* high,
each with several tens of rooms.
Their windows, wall panels, suspended eaves, and railings,
were all made of agarwood and sandalwood.
They were also decorated with gold and jade,
interspersed with pearls and kingfisher feathers.
Outside hung pearl curtains,
and inside were jeweled beds and canopies.
Their furnishings and ornaments
were magnificent, rare, and beautiful,
unprecedented in recent history.
Whenever a gentle breeze arrived,
the fragrance could be smelled several *lǐ* away.
When the morning sun first shone,
its light illuminated the rear garden.
Below them, stones were piled to form mountains,
water was drawn to create ponds,
and exotic trees were planted,
mixed with flowers and medicinal herbs.
Hòuzhǔ himself resided in the Línchūngé,
Guìfēi Zhāng resided in the Jiéqǐgé,
and the two noble consorts, Gōng Guìpín and Kǒng Guìpín, resided in the Wàngxiāngé.
Covered walkways connected them for mutual access.
There were also the two beauties Wáng Měirén and Lǐ Měirén, the two *shūyuàn* Zhāng Shūyuàn and Xuē Shūyuàn, Yuán Zhāoyí, Hé Jiéyú, and Jiāng Xiūróng, a total of seven people,
all favored,
who took turns enjoying themselves there.
Among the palace women, those with literary talent, such as Yuán Dàshè, were appointed as female scholars.
Whenever Hòuzhǔ invited guests to feast and enjoy themselves with Guìfēi Zhāng and others,
he would have the noble ladies and female scholars compose new poems with his intimate companions,
exchanging verses.
He would select the most beautiful and elegant ones to be set to music,
given new tunes.
Thousands of palace women of beautiful appearance were selected,
taught to sing them,
divided into groups, and brought in turns
to entertain him.
Their songs included "Yùshù Hòutíng Huā" and "Línchūn Yuè," among others.
The general theme
was always to praise the beauty of Guìfēi Zhāng and Kǒng Guìpín.
A brief excerpt says:
"The jade moon is full night after night,
the jade trees are fresh morning after morning."
Guìfēi Zhāng's hair was seven *chǐ* long,
raven black like lacquer,
its luster capable of reflecting an image.
She was exceptionally intelligent
and possessed a radiant spirit.
Her movements were graceful and unhurried,
her countenance beautiful and elegant.
Every time she looked around,
her eyes sparkled with brilliance,
illuminating her surroundings.
She often made herself up in the pavilion,
leaning against the balcony railing.
When viewed from afar within the palace,
she seemed to float like a divine immortal.
She was eloquent, had a strong memory,
and was skilled at discerning the ruler's mood.
At this time,
Hòuzhǔ was negligent in matters of state.
All memorials from officials
were submitted through the eunuchs Cài Tuō'ér and Lǐ Shàndù for his consideration.
Hòuzhǔ would place Guìfēi Zhāng on his lap and decide on them together.
What Lǐ and Cài could not remember,
Guìfēi Zhāng would summarize for him,
omitting nothing.
Because of this, she became even more favored and distinguished,
surpassing all others in the rear palace.
Moreover, the families of those in the inner palace
did not abide by the laws and regulations.
If anyone's conduct was contrary to principle,
they would merely beg for mercy from the noble consort.
The noble consort would then order Lǐ and Cài to first inform the emperor of the matter,
and then she would calmly speak on their behalf.
If there were high officials who did not comply,
she would consequently slander them,
and whatever she said was always listened to.
Thus, the influence of Zhāng Guìfēi and Kǒng Guìpín
spread far and wide.
High officials in power
also yielded to their influence.
Eunuchs and sycophants,
colluding both inside and outside,
mutually promoted each other.
Bribery was rampant,
rewards and punishments were arbitrary,
and the governmental order became confused and chaotic.
The imperial historian says: "The 'Guānjū' ode expresses the virtue of a proper consort,
and the *Yì* sets forth the foundation of Heaven and Earth.
Indeed, the relationship between husband and wife
is the great human moral principle.
If one is to be a partner in heavenly principles
and assist in the transformation of royal governance,
then Tàihòu Xuān possessed such excellence."
Collated Notes
Biographies, Part Two: Dù Sēngmíng; Zhōu Wényù (son Bǎo'ān); Hóu Āndū
Dù Sēngmíng, courtesy name Hóngzhào,
was a native of Línzé, Guǎnglíng.
Though small in stature,
his courage surpassed others; he possessed great strength
and was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
During the Dàtóng era of the Liáng dynasty,
Lú Ānxīng served as the Governor of Nánjiāng, Guǎngzhōu.
Sēngmíng, along with his elder brother Tiānhé and Zhōu Wényù,
were all recommended by Ānxīng,
who requested to take them with him.
They frequently distinguished themselves in campaigns against the Lí and Láo tribes,
serving as assistant defenders for Xīnzhōu.
Tiānhé also had talent and ability,
participating in the campaigns.
After Ānxīng's death,
Sēngmíng again served as assistant to his son, Zǐxióng.
When Lǐ Bēn, a local magnate in Jiāozhōu, rebelled
and drove out the Inspector Xiāo Zī,
Zī fled to Guǎngzhōu.
The court dispatched Zǐxióng and Sūn Jiǒng, the Inspector of Gāozhōu, to suppress Bēn.
At that time, spring grass had already grown,
and miasmas were beginning to rise.
Zǐxióng requested to wait until autumn to campaign,
but Xiāo Yìng, the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu and Marquis of Xīnyú, refused to listen.
Xiāo Zī also urged them on,
so Zǐxióng and others had no choice but
to proceed.
Upon reaching Hépǔ,
sixteen or seventeen out of every ten died.
The troops, all weary of the service, dispersed.
They could not be stopped,
so Zǐxióng led the remaining soldiers to retreat.
Xiāo Zī reported that Zǐxióng and Jiǒng were colluding with the rebels
and deliberately delaying their advance.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng ordered them to be granted death in Guǎngzhōu.
Zǐxióng's nephews Zǐlüè and Zǐliè were both prominent and chivalrous,
with their families residing in Nánjiāng.
Tiānhé deliberated with the crowd, saying:
"Duke Lú and his family have treated us very generously for generations.
Now to see him wronged and dead,
and be unable to avenge him, is not the act of a true man.
My younger brother Sēngmíng is a match for ten thousand men.
If we besiege the provincial capital,
and summon the common people,
who would dare not follow?
After the city falls,
we will execute the two Marquises as a sacrifice to Sūn and Lú.
Then we will await the court envoy,
surrender to the Minister of Justice.
Death is still better than life.
Even if we do not succeed,
there will be no regrets."
The crowd, filled with righteous indignation, said:
"This is our wish,
we only await your command."
Thereupon, he and Zhōu Wényù and others led the masses to form an alliance,
installing Zǐxióng's nephew Zǐlüè as their leader,
and attacked Inspector Xiāo Yìng.
Zǐlüè encamped south of the city,
Tiānhé encamped north of the city,
Sēngmíng and Wényù occupied the east and west respectively.
Officials and commoners all responded,
and within a single day,
their numbers reached several tens of thousands.
Gāozǔ was in Gāoyào at the time.
Hearing of the uprising,
he led his forces to suppress them,
utterly defeating them.
He killed Tiānhé,
captured Sēngmíng and Wényù alive,
and Gāozǔ released them both,
appointing them as his chief commanders.
When Gāozǔ campaigned against Jiāozhǐ and attacked Yuán Jǐngzhòng,
Dù Sēngmíng and Zhōu Wényù both rendered meritorious service.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
they both followed Gāozǔ to relieve the capital.
When Gāozǔ defeated Lán Yù in Shǐxīng,
Dù Sēngmíng was the vanguard,
capturing and beheading Yù.
Also, when fighting Cài Lùyǎng at Nányě,
Dù Sēngmíng's horse was wounded.
Gāozǔ rode to his rescue,
giving his own horse to Dù Sēngmíng.
Dù Sēngmíng, riding the horse, advanced again with dozens of men.
The enemy scattered,
and taking advantage of this,
they thoroughly defeated Lùyǎng.
Lǐ Qiānshì, the Cìshǐ of Gāozhōu, then occupied Dàgāo
and entered Gǎnshí,
thereby pressing Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ sent Zhōu Wényù as the vanguard,
who, with Dù Sēngmíng, attacked and repulsed him.
Qiānshì and Liú Xiàoshàng of Níngdū combined forces to raid Nánkāng.
Gāozǔ again ordered Dù Sēngmíng and Zhōu Wényù to resist them.
They were locked in battle for over a hundred days,
eventually capturing Qiānshì
and sending him to Gāozǔ's army.
When Gāozǔ captured Nánkāng,
he left Dù Sēngmíng stationed at Xīchāng,
to oversee the military affairs of the two commanderies, Ānchéng and Lúlíng.
Yuándì, acting by imperial authority, bestowed upon him the title of Jiǎjié, Qīngyě Jiāngjūn, Cìshǐ of Xīnzhōu,
Viscount of Línjiāng County,
with an estate of three hundred households.
Hóu Jǐng sent Yú Qìng and others to raid Nánjiāng.
Gāozǔ stationed at Yùzhāng,
and ordered Dù Sēngmíng to be the vanguard.
Wherever he went, he achieved victories.
Gāozǔ memorialized to make Dù Sēngmíng a Zhǎngshǐ,
and he continued to follow the eastern campaign.
When the army reached Càizhōu,
Dù Sēngmíng led his subordinates to burn the enemy's water gate and large warships.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
for his merits, he was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì, Míngwēi Jiāngjūn, and Cìshǐ of Nányùnzhōu.
His noble rank was advanced to Hóu,
and his estate, including previous grants, was increased to five hundred households.
He also concurrently held the post of Jìn líng Tàishǒu.
In Chéngshèng 2nd year (553),
he followed Gāozǔ north to besiege Guǎnglíng.
He was promoted to Shǐchíjié
and then to Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì and Píngběi Jiāngjūn,
while other posts remained as before.
When Jīngzhōu fell,
Gāozǔ ordered Dù Sēngmíng to lead Wú Míngchè and others to follow Hóu Tián in the western relief effort.
He died of illness in Jiāngzhōu
at the age of forty-six.
He was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì,
and given the posthumous name Wēi.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
In Tiānjiā 2nd year (561),
he was accorded the privilege of being enshrined in Gāozǔ's ancestral temple.
His son Jìn inherited his title.
Zhōu Wényù, whose courtesy name was Jǐngdé,
was a native of Yángxiàn, Yìxīng.
Orphaned and poor in his youth,
he originally lived in Shòuchāng County, Xīn'ān,
with the surname Xiàng and given name Měnglú.
At eleven years old,
he was able to swim back and forth for several *li* in the water
and jump five or six *chi* high.
When playing with other children,
none could match him.
Zhōu Huì, a man from Yìxīng, who was the戍zhǔ of Pǔkǒu in Shòuchāng,
saw him and was impressed.
He summoned him for a conversation.
Wényù replied:
"My mother is old, my family is poor,
and my elder siblings are grown.
We suffer from taxes and labor duties."
Huì pitied him,
and so he followed Wényù home
and asked his mother to adopt Wényù as his own son.
His mother agreed.
When Huì's term of office was over,
he returned to the capital with Wényù
and met with Zhōu Shě, the Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
He requested Shě to give him a name.
Shě then named him Wényù
with the courtesy name Jǐngdé.
He ordered his nephew Hóngràng to teach him reading and calculation.
Hóngràng was skilled in Lìshū and
copied Cài Yōng's *Quànxué* and ancient poems to give to Wényù.
Wényù paid no attention to them
and said to Hóngràng:
"Who can learn this?
To gain wealth and honor, one only needs a great spear."
Hóngràng admired his spirit
and taught him horsemanship and archery.
Wényù was greatly pleased.
Chén Qìngzhī, the Cìshǐ of Sìzhōu, was from the same commandery as Huì
and they had always been good friends.
He recommended Huì to be the Jūnzhǔ of the vanguard.
Qìngzhī sent Huì to lead five hundred men to Xīncài Xuánhù
to console the Báishuǐ Mán.
The Mán plotted to seize Huì and surrender to Wèi.
When the plot was discovered,
Huì and Wényù resisted them.
At that time, the bandits were very numerous.
They fought dozens of engagements in one day.
Wényù, as the vanguard, broke through the enemy lines
and his bravery surpassed all in the army.
Huì died in battle.
Wényù rode forth to retrieve his body,
and the bandits dared not approach.
By evening,
both sides withdrew.
Wényù suffered nine wounds on his body.
After his wounds healed,
he requested leave to return and bury Huì.
Qìngzhī admired his integrity
and gave him generous funeral gifts before sending him off.
After the burial,
Lú Ānxīng happened to be the Dūhù of Nánjiāng,
and he invited Wényù to join him.
He repeatedly campaigned against the Líliáo,
achieving success wherever he went,
and was appointed Nánhǎi Lìng.
After Ānxīng died,
Wényù and Dù Sēngmíng attacked Guǎngzhōu
but were defeated by Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ pardoned him;
the story is in the biography of Dù Sēngmíng.
Later, the Inspector of the Province, Wáng Mài, appointed Wényù as Zhǎnglìu Lìng
and entrusted him deeply.
When Mài was replaced,
Wényù wanted to go south with Mài.
Upon reaching Dàyǔlǐng,
he visited a diviner.
The diviner said:
"If you go north, you will be no more than a magistrate.
If you enter the south, you will become a Duke or Marquis."
Wényù said:
"If I have enough money, that's fine. Who expects to be a Duke or Marquis?"
The diviner then said:
"You will suddenly acquire two thousand *liǎng* of silver very soon.
If you don't believe me, let this be the proof."
That evening,
he stayed at an inn.
A merchant asked to gamble with Wényù.
Wényù won
and obtained two thousand *liǎng* of silver.
The next day, he took leave of Mài.
Mài asked the reason.
Wényù told him,
and Mài then sent him off.
Gāozǔ was in Gāoyào.
Hearing of his return,
he was greatly pleased,
sent people to welcome him,
gave him generous rewards,
and assigned some of his subordinates to him.
When Gāozǔ attacked Hóu Jǐng,
Wényù and Dù Sēngmíng were the vanguard,
conquering Lán Yù
and relieving Ōuyáng Wěi,
both with merit.
When Gāozǔ defeated Cài Lùyǎng at Nányě,
Wényù was surrounded by Lùyǎng's forces,
several layers deep on all sides.
Arrows and stones rained down.
His horse died.
Wényù fought with his right hand
and unfastened his saddle with his left hand,
breaking out of the encirclement.
He then met up with Dù Sēngmíng and others,
combined forces and advanced again,
thereby thoroughly defeating them.
Gāozǔ then memorialized to appoint Wényù as Fǔ Sīmǎ.
When Lǐ Qiānshì 李遷仕 occupied Dàgāo 大臯,
he sent his general Dù Pínglǔ 杜平虜 to enter Gǎnmù Shíyúliáng 灨石魚梁 and build a city.
Gāozǔ 高祖 ordered Wén Yù 文育 to attack him.
Pínglǔ 平虜 abandoned the city and fled.
Wén Yù 文育 occupied his city.
When Qiānshì 遷仕 heard of Pínglǔ’s 平虜 defeat,
he left the old and weak in Dàgāo 大臯,
personally selected and led all his elite troops
to attack Wén Yù 文育.
Their vanguard was very sharp,
and the soldiers were intimidated.
Wén Yù 文育 engaged in battle,
and Qiānshì 遷仕 gradually retreated.
They remained in a standoff,
until Gāozǔ 高祖 sent Dù Sēngmíng 杜僧明 to reinforce them.
He separately defeated Qiānshì’s 遷仕 water army,
and Qiānshì’s 遷仕 forces collapsed.
He did not dare to pass Dàgāo 大臯,
but fled directly to Xīngàn 新淦.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng 梁元帝 granted Wén Yù 文育 the titles of Jiǎjié 假節, Xióngxìn Jiāngjūn 雄信將軍, and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ 義州刺史.
Qiānshì 遷仕 then conspired with Liú Xiàoshàng 劉孝尚 to resist the righteous army.
Gāozǔ 高祖 sent Wén Yù 文育, along with Hóu Āndū 侯安都, Dù Sēngmíng 杜僧明, Xú Dù 徐度, and Dù Léng 杜稜, to build a city at Báikǒu 白口 to resist them.
Wén Yù 文育 frequently went out to battle,
and subsequently captured Qiānshì 遷仕.
Gāozǔ 高祖 set out from Nánkāng 南康,
and sent Wén Yù 文育 to lead five thousand soldiers
to open up the river route.
Hóu Jǐng’s 侯景 general Wáng Bóchǒu 王伯醜 occupied Yùzhāng 豫章.
Wén Yù 文育 attacked and routed him,
and then occupied his city.
For his accumulated past achievements,
he was appointed Yóuqí Jiāngjūn 遊騎將軍 and Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì 員外散騎常侍,
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngqiān Xiàn 東遷縣侯,
with five hundred households.
When Gāozǔ’s 高祖 army reached Báimáo Wān 白茅灣,
he ordered Wén Yù 文育 and Dù Sēngmíng 杜僧明 to always serve as the army's vanguard,
and to pacify Nánlíng 南陵, Quètóu 鵲頭, and other cities.
Upon reaching Gūshú 姑熟,
they battled Jǐng’s 景 general Hóu Zǐjiàn 侯子鑒,
and defeated him.
After Jǐng 景 was pacified,
he was granted Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì 通直散騎常侍,
re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Nányí Xiàn 南移縣侯,
with one thousand households,
and appointed Tàishǒu 太守 of Xìnyì 信義.
He was successively promoted to Tàishǒu 太守 of Nándānyáng 南丹陽, Lánlíng 蘭陵, and Jìn líng 晉陵, Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn 智武將軍, and Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍.
When Gāozǔ 高祖 executed Wáng Sēngbiàn 王僧辯,
he ordered Wén Yù 文育 to oversee the combined armies and meet Shìzǔ 世祖 in Wúxīng 吳興,
besiege Dù Kān 杜龕,
and conquer him.
He then crossed the Jiāng 江 and attacked the Tàishǒu 太守 of Kuàijī 會稽, Zhāng Biāo 張彪,
and captured his prefectural city.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 was attacked by Biāo 彪,
Wén Yù 文育 was then stationed at Xiāngyán Sì 香巖寺 north of the city.
Shìzǔ 世祖 went to him by night,
and they then jointly erected a stockade.
After a short while,
Biāo 彪 came to attack again.
Wén Yù 文育 fought with all his might in a bitter battle.
Biāo 彪 could not prevail,
and Wén Yù 文育 then defeated and pacified Biāo 彪.
Because Gāozǔ 高祖 considered Hóu Zhèn 侯瑱 to be occupying Jiāngzhōu 江州,
he ordered Wén Yù 文育 to attack him.
He was then appointed Dūdū Nányùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì 都督南豫州諸軍事, Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn 武威將軍, and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ 南豫州刺史,
and led troops to attack Pénhéng 湓城.
Before it was conquered,
Xú Sìhuī 徐嗣徽 led the Qí 齊 invaders across the Jiāng 江 and occupied Wúhú 蕪湖.
An imperial edict recalled Wén Yù 文育 to the capital.
Sìhuī 徐嗣徽 and others arranged their ships at Qīngdūn 青墩,
up to Qī Jī 七磯,
to cut off Wén Yù’s 文育 return route.
At dusk,
Wén Yù 文育 beat drums and shouted as he set off.
Sìhuī 徐嗣徽 and others could not stop him.
At dawn,
he counter-attacked Sìhuī 徐嗣徽.
Sìhuī’s 徐嗣徽 valiant general Bāo Pēng 鮑砰 alone commanded a small ship to cover the rear.
Wén Yù 文育, on a single *zhěngměng* 舴艋 (small boat), engaged him in battle,
leaped onto his ship,
cut down Pēng 砰,
and then towed his ship back.
The bandit forces were greatly alarmed,
and thus abandoned their ships at Wúhú 蕪湖,
and marched on foot from Dānyáng 丹陽.
At this time, Gāozǔ 高祖 was resisting Sìhuī 徐嗣徽 at Báichéng 白城,
and happened to rendezvous with Wén Yù 文育.
As they were about to fight,
the wind was strong.
Gāozǔ 高祖 said:
"Troops should not fight against the wind."
Wén Yù 文育 said:
"The situation is urgent,
we must decide it,
why adhere to ancient methods?"
He drew his spear and mounted his horse,
then charged forward.
The various armies followed him,
and the wind also immediately shifted.
Several hundred people were killed or wounded.
Sìhuī 徐嗣徽 and others moved their camp to Mòfǔ Shān 莫府山.
Wén Yù 文育 shifted his position to confront them.
After frequent battles and achieving the greatest merit,
he was promoted to Píngxī Jiāngjūn 平西將軍,
advanced in noble rank to Duke of Shòuchāng Xiàn 壽昌縣公,
and granted a set of drums and trumpets.
When the Cìshǐ 刺史 of Guǎngzhōu 廣州, Xiāo Bó 蕭勃, raised an army and crossed the mountains,
an edict ordered Wén Yù 文育 to oversee the combined armies and attack him.
At that time, Yú Xiàoqǐng 余孝頃, the *dòngzhǔ* 洞主 of Xīnwú 新吳, raised an army to support Bó 勃.
He sent his younger brother Xiàomài 孝勱 to guard the prefectural city,
while he himself went out to Yùzhāng 豫章,
and occupied Shítou 石頭.
Bó 勃 sent his son Zī 孜 to lead troops to meet Xiàoqǐng 孝頃,
and also sent his separate general Ōuyáng Wěi 歐陽頠 to station troops at Kǔzhútān 苦竹灘,
and Fù Tài 傅泰 to occupy Kuākǒu Chéng 咵口城,
〔一０〕to resist the government forces.
The government forces had few ships.
Xiàoqǐng 孝頃 had three hundred *zhěngměng* 舴艋 and over a hundred ships at Shàngláo 上牢.
〔一一〕Wén Yù 文育 sent his army commanders Jiāo Sēngdù 焦僧度 and Yáng Jiǎn 羊柬 to secretly attack them,
seized them all, and returned.
He then erected a stockade at Yùzhāng 豫章.
At this time, the government forces ran out of food,
and all wanted to retreat.
Wén Yù 文育 would not allow it.
He then secretly sent someone to deliver a letter to Zhōu Dí 周迪,
proposing to become sworn brothers,
and outlining the advantages and disadvantages.
Dí 周迪 was very pleased to receive the letter,
and promised to provide grain and provisions.
Thereupon, Wén Yù 文育 divided his old and young, who embarked on old boats,
and floated downstream together,
burning the stockade they had erected at Yùzhāng Jùn 豫章郡,
feigning a retreat.
Xiàoqǐng 孝頃 observed this,
was greatly pleased,
and thus became unprepared.
Wén Yù 文育 traveled by a secret path,
reaching Qiānsháo 芊韶 overnight.
Upstream from Qiānsháo 芊韶 were Ōuyáng Wěi 歐陽頠 and Xiāo Bó 蕭勃,
and downstream were Fù Tài 傅泰 and Yú Xiàoqǐng 余孝頃.
Wén Yù 文育 occupied the middle ground,
built a city, and feasted his soldiers.
The bandit gangs were greatly alarmed.
Ōuyáng Wěi 歐陽頠 then retreated into Níxī 泥溪,
built a city, and defended himself.
Wén Yù 文育 sent Yánwēi Jiāngjūn 嚴威將軍 Zhōu Tiěwǔ 周鐵武,
〔一二〕along with his Chángshǐ 長史 Lù Shāncái 陸山才, to attack Wěi 頠,
and captured him.
He then grandly displayed his armor and weapons,
and dined with Wěi 頠 on a boat,
cruising below Fù Tài’s 傅泰 city.
He then attacked Tài 泰,
and conquered it.
When Xiāo Bó 蕭勃 in Nánkāng 南康 heard of this,
his entire force trembled with fear,
and none could hold their ground.
His general Tán Shìyuǎn 譚世遠 attempted to kill Bó 勃 and surrender,
but was harmed by others.
Shìyuǎn’s 世遠 army commander Xiàhóu Míngchè 夏侯明徹 held Bó’s 勃 head and surrendered.
Xiāo Zī 蕭孜 and Yú Xiàoqǐng 余孝頃 still occupied Shítou 石頭.
Gāozǔ 高祖 sent Hóu Āndū 侯安都 to assist Wén Yù 文育 in attacking them.
Zī 孜 surrendered to Wén Yù 文育.
Xiàoqǐng 孝頃 retreated to Xīnwú 新吳.
Guǎngzhōu 廣州 was pacified.
Wén Yù 文育 returned and stationed himself at Yùzhāng 豫章.
For his achievements, he was granted Zhènnán Jiāngjūn 鎮南將軍, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī 開府儀同三司, Dūdū Jiāng Guǎng Héng Jiāo Děng Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì 都督江廣衡交等州諸軍事, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ 江州刺史.
Wáng Lín 王琳 occupied the upstream areas.
An imperial edict ordered Hóu Āndū 侯安都 to be the Dūdū 都督 of the western route,
and Wén Yù 文育 to be the Dūdū 都督 of the southern route,
to meet together at Wǔchāng 武昌.
They battled Wáng Lín 王琳 at Dùnkǒu 沌口,
and Wén Yù 文育 was captured by Lín 王琳.
Later, he managed to escape and return.
His story is in the biography of Āndū 安都.
Soon after, he was granted Shǐchíjié 使持節, Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍, Zhènnán Jiāngjūn 鎮南將軍, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī 開府儀同三司,
Duke of Shòuchāng Xiàn 壽昌縣公,
and a set of drums and trumpets.
When Zhōu Dí broke Yú Xiàokǒng,
Xiàokǒng's son, Gōngyáng, and younger brother, Xiàomài, still occupied their old stockades,
agitating the southern territories.
Gāozǔ again dispatched Wén Yù, along with Zhōu Dí, Huáng Fǎqū, and others, to suppress them.
Yùzhāng's Internal Administrator, Xióng Tánlǎng, also led his army to join them,
with a force of nearly ten thousand men.
Wén Yù sent Wú Míngchè as the naval commander,
assigning Zhōu Dí to transport provisions.
He himself led the main army into the Xiàngyá Jiāng,
and fortified Jīnkǒu.
Gōngyáng, with five hundred men, feigned surrender,
plotting to seize Wén Yù.
When the plot was discovered,
Wén Yù imprisoned him
and sent him to the capital,
distributing his troops among the various armies.
Then, abandoning their boats, they became an infantry force,
advancing to occupy Sānpō.
Wáng Lín dispatched his general Cáo Qìng with two thousand soldiers to rescue Xiàomài.
Qìng divided his forces, sending his commander Cháng Zhòng'ài to resist Wén Yù,
while he personally led his troops directly to attack Zhōu Dí's and Wú Míngchè's armies.
Dí and others were defeated,
and Wén Yù retreated to Jīnkǒu.
Xióng Tánlǎng, taking advantage of this defeat,
plotted to assassinate Wén Yù
in collusion with Zhòng'ài.
Wén Yù's army supervisor, Sūn Báixiàng, was somewhat aware of the plot
and advised him to strike first.
Wén Yù said:
"No,
my old soldiers are few,
and the guest troops are many.
If I were to seize Tánlǎng,
everyone would be terrified,
and destruction would come swiftly.
It's better to treat them with sincerity and soothe them."
Initially,
when Zhōu Dí was defeated,
he abandoned his boats and fled,
his whereabouts unknown.
When Wén Yù later received a letter from Dí,
he was pleased,
and immediately showed it to Tánlǎng.
Tánlǎng assassinated him at the meeting,
at the age of fifty-one.
When Gāozǔ heard of it,
he immediately declared mourning.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng and Sīkōng,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngmǐn.
Earlier,
when Wén Yù was occupying Sānpō,
a meteor fell to the ground,
its sound like thunder.
The ground collapsed by one *zhàng* in area,
and inside were several *dǒu* of碎炭.
Also, in the army market, the cries of a child were suddenly heard.
The whole market was startled,
and listening, they found it was coming from beneath the earth.
The soldiers dug up a coffin three *chǐ* long.
Wén Yù considered this an ill omen.
Soon after, Dí was defeated,
and Wén Yù was killed.
In the second year of Tiānjiā,
an imperial edict ordered him to be honored in Gāozǔ's ancestral temple.
His son, Bǎo'ān, succeeded him.
Wén Yù's paternal cousin, Jǐngyào,
was appointed Xīn'ān Tàishǒu due to Wén Yù's influence.
Bǎo'ān's courtesy name was Ānmín.
At around ten years old,
he was already skilled in riding and archery.
As a son of a noble family, he was arrogant, self-indulgent, and fond of leisure.
He enjoyed dogs and horses,
delighted in racing,
and indulged in luxurious clothing and excessive eating.
When Wén Yù served as Jìnlíng's administrator,
being too occupied with military campaigns to manage the prefecture,
he appointed Bǎo'ān to supervise the prefectural affairs.
Bǎo'ān particularly gathered unruly youths,
which troubled Gāozǔ.
When Wén Yù was defeated in his western campaign
and captured by Wáng Lín,
Bǎo'ān then changed his ways and devoted himself to studying,
associating with scholars and gentlemen.
He managed Wén Yù's soldiers and officers,
and commanded great authority and beneficence.
He was appointed Yuánwài Sǎnjì Shìláng.
When Wén Yù returned,
he was again appointed Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn and Wúxīng Tàishǒu.
When Wén Yù was assassinated by Xióng Tánlǎng,
Bǎo'ān was recalled.
He was appointed Měngliè Jiāngjūn,
leading his former troops,
and was again ordered to campaign in the south.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he greatly esteemed him,
entrusting him with his innermost confidence,
and assigned many elite troops and sharp weapons to him.
Upon the pacification of Wáng Lín,
he contributed significantly.
When Zhōu Dí defeated Xióng Tánlǎng,
Bǎo'ān advanced south,
exterminating the remaining rebels.
In the second year of Tiānjiā,
he was again appointed Xióngxìn Jiāngjūn and Wúxīng Tàishǒu,
inheriting the title of Shòuchāng Xiàn Gōng.
In the third year,
he campaigned against Liú Yì,
serving as Hóu Āndū's vanguard.
After Yì was pacified,
he was appointed Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng and Wèiwèi Qīng.
In the fourth year,
he was granted the titles of Chíjié, Dūdū Nánxúzhōu Zhū Jūnjì, Zhēnyì Jiāngjūn, and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was recalled to serve as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
and additionally granted Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn.
Soon after, he concurrently held the position of Wèiwèi Qīng,
and was further promoted to Rénwēi Jiāngjūn.
He died in the first year of Tiānkāng,
at the age of twenty-nine.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
and given the posthumous name Chéng.
His son, Sì, succeeded him.
After Bǎo'ān's death,
Sì also served as a general.
He campaigned against Ōuyáng Hè
and pacified Huáinán,
contributing significantly to both.
He was enfeoffed as Jiāng'ān Xiàn Bó,
with four hundred households.
He successively served as the administrator of Jìnlíng and Dìngyuǎn Commanderies.
He died in the ninth year of Tàijiàn,
at the age of twenty-four,
and was posthumously granted Diànwēi Jiāngjūn.
Hóu Āndū, courtesy name Chéngshī,
was a native of Qǔjiāng, Shǐxīng.
His family had for generations been a prominent clan in the commandery.
His father, Wénhàn,
served in the prefecture and commandery in his youth,
known for his loyalty and diligence.
After Āndū rose to prominence,
he was appointed Guānglù Dàfū and Shǐxīng Nèishǐ,
with a salary of two thousand *dàn* of grain.
Āndū was skilled in clerical script,
could play the *qin*,
read extensively in historical texts,
and composed five-character-line poetry,
which was also quite refined and elegant.
He was also good at riding and archery,
and was a local strongman.
Xiāo Zǐfàn, the Internal Administrator of Shǐxīng during the Liáng dynasty, appointed him as his main clerk.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
he gathered soldiers and weapons, amassing up to three thousand men.
When Gāozǔ entered to aid the capital,
Āndū led his troops to follow Gāozǔ.
He attacked Cài Lùyǎng,
defeated Lǐ Qiānshì,
and vanquished Hóu Jǐng,
all with meritorious service in fierce battles.
Emperor Yuán appointed him Měngliè Jiāngjūn and Tōngzhí Sǎnjì Chángshì,
enfeoffing him as the Count of Fùchuān County,
with three hundred households.
He followed Gāozǔ to garrison Jīngkǒu,
and was appointed Lánlíng Tàishǒu.
When Gāozǔ planned to attack Wáng Sēngbiàn,
none of the other generals knew of it;
only with Āndū did he finalize the plan.
He then sent Āndū to lead a naval force from Jīngkǒu towards Shítóu,
while Gāozǔ himself led the cavalry and infantry from Jiāngchéng Luóluò to meet him.
When Āndū reached the north of Shítóu,
he abandoned his boats and disembarked,
and Sēngbiàn was not aware of it.
Shítóu City's northern side was connected to hills,
and its battlements were not very steep or high.
