Āndū, wearing armor and carrying a long saber,
was hoisted by his soldiers and thrown over the parapet.
His men followed him in,
and advanced to press upon Sēngbiàn's sleeping quarters.
Gāozǔ's main army also arrived,
and fought Sēngbiàn in front of the audience hall.
Āndū emerged from the inner chambers,
attacking them from front and back,
and thus captured Sēngbiàn.
In the first year of Shàotài
for his merit, he was granted the titles of Shǐchíjié (使持節), Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), Dūdū Nánxúzhōu Zhūjūnjì (都督南徐州諸軍事), Rénwēi Jiāngjūn (仁威將軍), and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ (南徐州刺史).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) campaigned east against Dù Kān (杜龕),
Āndū (安都) was left in the capital to guard it.
Xú Sìhuī (徐嗣徽), Rèn Yuē (任約), and others led Qí (齊) invaders to occupy Shítou (石頭),
and their cavalry patrols reached the palace gates.
Āndū closed the city gates and lowered the flags and banners,
showing weakness,
and he ordered the city:
"Those who climb the ramparts to observe the enemy shall be executed."
At dusk,
the bandits withdrew their troops and returned to Shítou.
Āndū secretly ordered his soldiers that night to prepare defenses against the enemy.
At dawn,
the bandit cavalry arrived again.
Āndū led three hundred armored soldiers,
opened the east and west side gates, and engaged them in battle,
defeating them decisively.
The bandits then retreated to Shítou,
no longer daring to press upon Táichéng (臺城).
When Gāozǔ arrived,
he appointed Āndū as commander of the naval forces
to cut off the bandits' supply lines in the middle of the river.
He also attacked Qínjùn (秦郡),
destroyed Sìhuī's palisade,
and captured his family members, horses, donkeys, and baggage.
He obtained Sìhuī's personal Pípá (琵琶) and his pet hawk,
and sent a messenger to him, saying:
"Yesterday I arrived at your dwelling and obtained these;
I now return them to you."
Sìhuī and others were greatly alarmed upon seeing this,
and soon after requested peace.
Gāozǔ allowed them to return north.
When Sìhuī and others crossed the Jiāng (江) [Yangtze River],
the remaining Qí forces still occupied Cǎishí (採石),
with very strict defenses.
Gāozǔ again dispatched Āndū to attack them,
capturing many.
In the spring of the following year,
an imperial edict ordered Āndū to lead troops to garrison Liángshān (梁山)
to guard against Qí.
Xú Sìhuī and others re-entered Dānyáng (丹陽),
Gāozǔ recalled Āndū,
who led his cavalry and infantry to resist them at Gāoqiáo (高橋).
They fought again south of Gēngtán (耕壇).
Āndū led twelve horsemen,
charged into their formation,
and broke it,
capturing the Qí Yítóng (儀同) Qǐfú Wúláo (乞伏無勞) alive.
He also stabbed the Qí general Dōngfāng Lǎo (東方老), who fell from his horse.
At that moment, enemy cavalry arrived
and rescued Lǎo, who thus escaped.
The bandits crossed north of Jiǎngshān (蔣山).
Āndū then fought the Qí general Wáng Jìngbǎo (王敬寶) at Lóngwěi (龍尾).
He ordered his cousin Xiǎo (曉) and army officer Zhāng Zuǎn (張纂) to charge their formation.
Xiǎo was wounded by a spear and fell from his horse;
Zhāng Zuǎn died.
Āndū galloped to rescue Xiǎo,
killing eleven of their cavalrymen.
He then retrieved Zuǎn's body and returned.
The Qí army did not dare to press on.
When Gāozǔ fought the Qí army at Mòfùshān (莫府山),
he ordered Āndū to lead over a thousand infantry and cavalry
to flank their rear from Báixià (白下).
The Qí army was greatly defeated.
capturing countless heads and prisoners.
For his merits, he was advanced in peerage to Hóu (侯),
his stipend was increased by five hundred households,
and he was granted a set of drums and trumpets.
He was further promoted to the title Píngnán Jiāngjūn (平南將軍)
and re-enfeoffed as Xījiāng Xiàngōng (西江縣公).
He then commanded the naval forces to proceed to Yùzhāng (豫章)
to assist the Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (豫州刺史) Zhōu Wényù (周文育) in suppressing Xiāo Bó (蕭勃).
Before Āndū arrived,
Wényù had already beheaded Bó
and captured his generals Ōuyáng Wèi (歐陽頠) and Fù Tài (傅泰) and others.
Only Yú Xiàoqǐng (余孝頃) and Bó's son Zī (孜) still held Shítou (石頭) in Yùzhāng,
having constructed two fortresses.
Xiàoqǐng and Zī each occupied one,
and also deployed numerous ships and vessels,
lining them up along both sides of the water.
Upon Āndū's arrival,
he ordered his troops to hold their bits in their mouths and burn their ships by night.
Wényù led the naval forces,
while Āndū led the infantry and cavalry,
landing on the bank and forming battle arrays.
Xiàoqǐng suddenly cut off their retreat path.
Āndū then ordered his soldiers to cut down many pine trees,
erect palisades,
and advance their camps gradually.
They fought repeatedly and won many victories,
whereupon Zī surrendered.
Xiàoqǐng fled back to Xīnwú (新吳)
and offered his son as hostage,
which was accepted.
Upon their return,
for his merits, he was promoted to the title Zhènběi Jiāngjūn (鎮北將軍),
and given the additional title Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
He then led his troops to assemble at Wǔchāng (武昌)
to campaign west with Zhōu Wényù against Wáng Lín (王琳).
As they were about to depart,
Wáng Gōng (王公) and others saw them off at Xīnlín (新林).
Āndū spurred his horse across the bridge;
both he and his horse fell into the water.
He then sat in the *zī* (嗞) [a type of boat], falling into the bilge of the *lǔjǐng* (櫓井) [oar well].
At the time, this was considered inauspicious.
Upon reaching Wǔchāng,
Lín's general Fán Měng (樊猛) abandoned the city and fled.
Wényù also arrived from Yùzhāng.
At this time, the two generals were both on campaign
and did not command each other,
which led to disputes among their subordinates
and gradually created disharmony.
When the army reached Yǐngzhōu (郢州),
Lín's general Pān Chún (潘純) shot arrows from within the city at the government forces.
and advanced his troops to besiege it,
but could not capture it.
When Wáng Lín reached Yǎnkǒu (弇口),
Āndū abandoned Yǐngzhōu
and led all his troops to Dùnkǒu (沌口) to resist him,
but could not advance due to a storm.
Lín occupied the east bank,
while the government forces occupied the west bank.
They held their ground for several days,
then engaged in battle.
Āndū and others were defeated.
Āndū, Zhōu Wényù, and Xú Jìngchéng (徐敬成) were all captured by Lín.
Lín tied them all together with a long chain,
placed them below the *zī*,
and ordered his trusted eunuch Wáng Zǐjìn (王子晉) to guard them.
When Lín descended to Báishuǐpǔ (白水浦) at Pénchéng (湓城),
Āndū and the others sweetened their words and promised Zǐjìn a large bribe.
Zǐjìn then pretended to fish from a small boat near the *zī*.
At night, he transported Āndū, Wényù, and Jìngchéng ashore,
into the deep grass,
and they walked to the government forces.
Upon returning to the capital, Āndū impeached himself.
An imperial edict pardoned them all
and restored their official titles and ranks.
Soon after, he was appointed Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹),
then transferred out as Dūdū Nányùzhōu Zhūjūnjì (都督南豫州諸軍事), Zhènxī Jiāngjūn (鎮西將軍), and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ (南豫州刺史).
He was ordered to succeed Zhōu Wényù in attacking Yú Xiàomài (余孝勱) and Wáng Lín's generals Cáo Qìng (曹慶) and Cháng Zhòng'ài (常衆愛) and others.
Āndū departed from Gōngtínghú (宮亭湖) and exited at Sōngmén (松門),
following closely behind Zhòng'ài.
Wényù was killed by Xióng Tánlǎng (熊曇朗).
Āndū turned back to seize large warships,
and encountered Lín's generals Zhōu Jiǒng (周炅) and Zhōu Xié (周協) returning south.
He fought them
and defeated them,
capturing Jiǒng and Xié alive.
Xiàomài's brother Xiàoyóu (孝猷) led his four thousand households, intending to join Wáng Lín,
but encountered the defeat of Jiǒng and Xié,
and so surrendered to Āndū.
Āndū then advanced his troops to Qínqízhōu (禽奇洲),
defeated Cáo Qìng and Cháng Zhòng'ài and others,
and burned their ships and vessels.
Zhòng'ài fled to Lúshān (廬山),
where he was killed by villagers.
The rest of the rebels were all pacified.
He returned his army to Nánwǎn (南皖),
where Gāozǔ died.
Āndū followed Shìzǔ (世祖) back to court,
and with the other officials, settled on the plan
to assist Shìzǔ.
At that time, Shìzǔ humbly declined and did not dare to accept.
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) also, due to the Hēngyáng Wáng (衡陽王),
was unwilling to issue an edict.
The officials hesitated and could not decide.
Āndū said:
"Now the four directions are not yet settled;
how can we delay?
The Línchuān Wáng (臨川王) has rendered service to the whole world;
we must jointly enthrone him.
As for today's matter,
those who hesitate shall be executed."
He then drew his sword and ascended the hall,
requesting the Grand Empress Dowager to produce the imperial seal.
He also personally loosened Shìzǔ's hair
and pushed him to the mourning place.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Sīkōng (司空).
He remained Dūdū Nánxúzhōu Zhūjūnjì (都督南徐州諸軍事), Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn (征北將軍), and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ (南徐州刺史),
and was granted *fú* (扶) [a staff of honor].
When Wáng Lín descended to Zhàkǒu (柵口),
the main army set out and encamped at Wúhú (蕪湖).
At this time, Hóu Tián (侯瑱) was the Grand Commander (Dà Dūdū),
but the command and strategy
were mostly from Āndū.
In the first year of Tiānjīa
his stipend was increased by a thousand households.
When Wáng Lín was defeated and fled into Qí territory,
Āndū advanced his troops to Pénchéng (湓城),
suppressing Lín's remaining factions,
and all places he attacked submitted.
Then, a separate imperial edict was
sent to welcome Héngyáng Xiànwáng Chāng.
Initially,
when Chāng was about to enter the capital,
he sent a letter to Shìzǔ,
the language of which was very disrespectful.
Shìzǔ was displeased,
and so he summoned Āndū and said casually,
"The Crown Prince is about to arrive.
We need to find another feudal state for him.
I am getting old."
Āndū replied,
"Since ancient times, how could there be an emperor who was replaced?
Your ignorant servant dares not accept this edict."
Thereupon, he volunteered to welcome Chāng himself,
but Chāng died while crossing the Hàn River.
For his merits, he was promoted to the peerage of Qīngyuǎn Jùngōng,
with an additional four thousand households.
From then on, his prestige and reputation became very great,
and none of the officials surpassed him.
Āndū's father, Wénhàn,
served as the Shǐxīng Nèishǐ,
and died in office.
Shìzǔ summoned Āndū back to the capital
to mourn his father.
Soon after, he was reinstated to his original post,
and his father was posthumously honored as Sànqí Chángshì and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
His mother was granted the title of Qīngyuǎn Guó Tàifūrén.
She was also to be brought back to the capital,
but his mother firmly requested to remain in her hometown.
Thereupon, the Emperor issued an edict
to rename Rǔchéng Xiàn of Guìyáng as Lúyáng Jùn,
〔一七〕and to divide the two commanderies of Shǐxīng and Ānyuǎn from Héngzhōu,
combining the three commanderies to form Dōnghéngzhōu.
Āndū's younger cousin, Xiǎo, was appointed as its Cìshǐ.
Āndū's third son, Mì, was nine years old,
and the Emperor appointed him as Shǐxīng Nèishǐ,
ordering them both to remain in their hometown to attend to their mother.
That same year,
Āndū was re-enfeoffed as Guìyáng Jùngōng.
After Wáng Lín's defeat,
the Zhōu army entered and occupied Bā and Xiāng.
Āndū received an imperial edict to campaign against them in the west.
When Liú Yì then occupied Dōngyáng,
he again received an imperial edict to campaign against him in the east.
Yì originally thought that the imperial army would advance via the Qiántáng Jiāng,
but Āndū marched on foot from Zhūjì in Kuàijī,
emerging at Yǒngkāng.
Yì was greatly alarmed,
and fled to Táozhī Lǐng,
hiding in the valleys of the ridge.
At the mouth of the gorge, he erected a palisade
to resist the imperial army.
Āndū built a continuous fortress to [攻] attack Yì,
〔一八〕and personally engaged in battle.
He was hit by a stray arrow,
and his blood flowed down to his ankles.
Āndū rode in his carriage, directing the army,
his demeanor unchanged.
Utilizing the terrain of the mountain ridges,
he pressed forward and built a dam.
In the summer of Tiānjiā third year,
there was a flood,
and the water rose high.
Āndū led boats into the dam,
and built tower-ships that were as tall as Yì's fortress.
He used catapults to smash their battlements.
Yì and his second son, Zhōngchén, escaped and fled to Jìn'ān.
Āndū captured their wives and children,
and seized all their men, horses, and weapons.
He returned with his victorious army.
For his merits, he was awarded the titles of Shìzhōng and Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn,
with an additional five thousand households, bringing the total to five thousand.
He then returned to his original garrison.
That same year,
the [吏] officials and people came to the palace gate to present a memorial requesting the erection of a stele
〔一九〕to praise Āndū's achievements.
The Emperor issued an edict granting permission.
After Wáng Lín was pacified,
Hóu Ān Dū’s merits and achievements grew increasingly great.
He also, relying on his contributions to secure the state,
gradually became arrogant and presumptuous.
He frequently gathered civil and military men,
some of whom would shoot and ride,
or compose poetry and rhapsodies.
He would rank their quality
and bestow rewards accordingly.
The literati included Chǔ Jiè, Mǎ Shū, Yīn Kēng, Zhāng Zhèng Jiàn, Xú Bó Yáng,
Liú Shān, and Zǔ Sūn Dēng.
The military men included Xiāo Mó Hē and Péi Zǐ Liè,
all of whom became his retainers.
Inside his residence, there were often as many as a thousand people.
Many of his subordinate generals
did not abide by laws and regulations.
When an investigation and arrest were made,
they would flee back to Hóu Ān Dū.
Shì Zǔ was by nature strict and discerning,
and deeply resented this.
Hóu Ān Dū did not change,
becoming daily more arrogant and overbearing.
Whenever he submitted a memorial,
after sealing it,
if there was something he had not finished,
he would open it and write himself,
saying, “Further memorializing such and such a matter.”
When attending banquets and drinking heavily,
he would sometimes sit sprawled out or leaning askew.
Once, when accompanying the emperor at the Lè Yóu purification ceremony and feast,
he said to the emperor,
“How does this compare to when Your Majesty was the Prince of Lín Chuān?”
The emperor did not respond.
Hóu Ān Dū repeated it two or three times.
The emperor said,
“Although this is Heaven’s decree,
it is also due to your efforts, My Lord.”
After the feast,
he again requested to borrow the ceremonial tents and water decorations
to take his wives and concubines to feast at the imperial hall.
Although Shì Zǔ granted his request,
he was very displeased.
The next day,
Hóu Ān Dū sat on the imperial throne,
and his retainers occupied the positions of the various officials,
raising cups to toast his longevity.
Initially,
when the Chóng Yún Hall caught fire,
Hóu Ān Dū led his armed officers and soldiers into the hall.
The emperor greatly disliked this,
and from then on secretly made preparations against him.
When Zhōu Dí rebelled,
the court expected Hóu Ān Dū to suppress him.
Instead, the emperor sent Wú Míng Chè to suppress Zhōu Dí.
He also frequently dispatched court envoys to investigate Hóu Ān Dū’s subordinates,
checking for fugitives and deserters.
Hóu Ān Dū felt uneasy inwardly.
In the winter of the third year,
he sent his Aide, Zhōu Hóng Shí, to ingratiate himself with the Imperial Secretary Cài Jǐng Lì,
and also inquire about matters within the palace.
Cài Jǐng Lì recorded his account and fully reported it,
trying to please the emperor by claiming Hóu Ān Dū was plotting rebellion.
Shì Zǔ, fearing he would not be brought under control,
in the spring of the following year,
appointed Hóu Ān Dū as Grand Administrator of military affairs of Jiāng and Wú Prefectures, General-in-Chief Pacifying the South, and Governor of Jiāng Prefecture.
As he returned to the capital from Jīng Kǒu,
his troops entered Shí Tóu.
Shì Zǔ invited Hóu Ān Dū to a feast in the Jiā Dé Hall,
and also gathered his subordinate generals in the Shang Shu cháo táng (Secretariat-Chancellery).
There, Hóu Ān Dū was arrested,
and imprisoned in the western wing of the Jiā Dé Hall.
His generals were also arrested,
their horses and weapons were all confiscated, and then they were released.
Thereupon, the memorial from Imperial Secretary Cài Jǐng Lì was presented to the court.
Then an imperial edict stated:
"In the past, the Hàn dynasty honored meritorious officials, yet Hán and Péng initiated rebellion.
The Jìn dynasty relied on its vassal princes, yet Dūn and Yuē raised armies.
Entrusting a six-foot orphan to Páng Méng, his wild ambition secretly stirred;
entrusting a trusted minister to Huò Yǔ, his evil plot lay hidden.
Reflecting on past ages,
inciting rebellion has always followed the same pattern;
speaking of ancient times,
troubles and calamities share the same rule.
Hóu Ān Dū has always lacked foresight,
and was fundamentally ashamed of his virtuous conduct.
Fortunately, he joined the rising tide,
and participated in state affairs.
He rose from the ranks,
was given wings,
promoted to a regional commander,
and entrusted with military campaigns.
His position reached the highest ranks,
his responsibility was like the Four Sacred Mountains.
His fame and authority were illustrious,
his courtesies unparalleled.
Yet his ambition was solely self-aggrandizement,
his spirit was overbearing.
He gathered fugitives,
was utterly frivolous and cunning,
unruly and unprincipled,
without fear or respect.
Entrusted with military authority,
he plundered wantonly.
Wherever he was appointed governor,
he extorted without end.
Appointed to Xú Fān,
bordering the Qí territory,
he moved prohibited goods,
sold residents,
ambushed and robbed,
spreading poison throughout the land.
He bore grudges and caused deaths,
disregarding moral principles and laws.
I, considering his initial contributions
and notable achievements,
and his participation in the sagacious plans for the imperial succession,
therefore withheld action from officials,
always hoping he would reform,
cutting off accusations from all ministers,
and daily awaiting his self-renewal.
I
expressed my sincere thoughts in conversation,
and showed utmost sincerity in all dealings.
When he rode his horse to my residence,
the imperial guards were at ease;
when he held banquets in his grand hall,
there were no guards on the imperial steps.
When have I ever harbored a hidden grievance,
departing from Bò Rén without lodging,
or outwardly shown suspicion and caution,
entering Chéng Gāo without staying?
Yet he remained unrepentantly rebellious,
and his arrogance and cruelty grew even greater.
He enticed civil and military men,
secretly harboring rebellious schemes.
Last year, on the eleventh day of the twelfth month,
I received a memorial from Imperial Secretary Cài Jǐng Lì,
stating that Hóu Ān Dū, on the tenth day of last month, sent his Aide Zhōu Hóng Shí to stay privately in Cài Jǐng Lì's residence,
inquiring about matters in the forbidden palace,
and fully outlining a plan for rebellion.
I still tolerated and endured it,
treating him as before.
Since he was moved from the northern gate
and appointed to the southern region,
while awaiting his appointment,
his treacherous plot became even more evident.
Now, he intends to use his initial appointment
to carry out his illegal actions.
If this can be tolerated,
what cannot be endured?
Thanks to the spirits of the altars of soil and grain,
and the sincerity of my close attendants,
his vile intentions have been exposed,
and his rebellious acts clearly revealed.
Externally, the old statutes should be thoroughly examined,
and the punishment quickly applied.
Only those involved in the conspiracy should be questioned,
the rest are not to be interrogated.”
The next day,
he was granted death in the western wing,
at the age of forty-four.
Soon after, an imperial edict was issued,
pardoning his wife, children, and household,
and burying him with the rites of a scholar.
All necessary expenses for the funeral
were to be generously provided.
Earlier,
when Gāo Zǔ was in the capital,
he once feasted with his generals.
Dù Sēng Míng, Zhōu Wén Yù, and Hóu Ān Dū toasted him,
each boasting of their achievements.
Gāo Zǔ said,
“You are all good generals,
yet all have shortcomings.
Dù Gōng has great ambition but dim understanding,
is familiar with subordinates yet arrogant to superiors,
and boasts of his achievements without acknowledging his failures.
Hóu Zhōu associates with people indiscriminately,
and trusts others excessively.
He lives in danger and walks on precipices,
without setting up defenses.
Hóu Láng is arrogant and without restraint,
frivolous and unrestrained in his will.
None of these are ways to preserve oneself.”
In the end, all turned out as he had predicted.
Hóu Ān Dū’s eldest son, Dūn,
at the age of twelve,
served as an Administrator without portfolio, Provisional Palace Attendant.
In the second year of Tiān Jiā, he fell from his horse and died.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Mǐn Shì Zǐ of Guì Yáng Commandery.
In the third year of Tài Jiàn,
Gāo Zōng posthumously enfeoffed Hóu Ān Dū as the Marquis of Chén Jí County,
with an estate of five hundred households.
His son, Dǎn, succeeded him.
Ān Dū's younger cousin, Xiǎo,
repeatedly followed Ān Dū on campaigns and achieved merits.
His official positions reached Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì, Míngwēi Jiāngjūn, and Dōnghéngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was enfeoffed as Huáihuà Xiànhóu,
with an estate of five hundred households.
He died in the third year of Tiānjiā (562 CE),
at the age of forty-one.
The historian comments: Dù Sēngmíng and Zhōu Wényù both established great achievements,
and were successful during the rise of the dynasty.
They can certainly be compared to Pó, Mù, Hán, and Péng.
However, Hóu Āndū's
disposition changed over time,
his power surpassed that of former days.
He used this to invade and commit atrocities,
and added to it with indulgence and recklessness.
If one were to say he was not a rebellious villain,
how could he have escaped destruction?
In ancient times, Emperor Gāo of Hàn gave minced meat as a reward (to those who captured Pēng Yuè),
and Emperor Wǔ of Sòng dragged (Dàn Tàizhī) to his side.
There was certainly a reason for such actions.
Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter Three: Hóu Tián, Ōuyáng Wěi (Zǐhé), Wú Míngchè (Péi Zǐliè)
Hóu Tián, courtesy name Bóyù,
was a native of Chōngguó, Baxī.
His father, Hóngyuǎn,
was for generations a chieftain of Xīshǔ.
When the Shǔ bandit Zhāng Wén'è occupied Báiyá Shān
with a force of ten thousand men,
Xiāo Fàn, the Prince of Póyáng and Governor of Yìzhōu under the Liáng dynasty, ordered Hóngyuǎn to suppress him.
Hóngyuǎn died in battle.
Tián earnestly requested to avenge him,
and in every battle, he would lead the vanguard and break the enemy lines.
He eventually beheaded Wén'è,
and thus became famous.
He then served Fàn.
Fàn entrusted him with the command of generals,
and whenever the mountain valley barbarians and Man tribes were not submissive,
Fàn would dispatch Tián to conquer them.
Through accumulated merits, he was appointed Qīngchē Fǔ Zhōngbīng Cānjūn and Jìnkāng Tàishǒu.
When Fàn became Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
Tián was appointed Chāowǔ Jiāngjūn and Féngyì Tàishǒu.
When Fàn moved his garrison to Héfēi,
Tián again followed him.
When Hóu Jǐng besieged Táichéng,
Fàn dispatched Tián to assist his heir, Sī,
to lead a relief force to the capital.
When the capital fell,
Tián and Sī retreated to Héfēi,
and then followed Fàn as he moved his garrison to Pénchéng.
Soon after, Fàn and Sī both died.
Tián took command of their troops
and relied on Zhuāng Tiě, the Yùzhāng Tàishǒu.
Tiě suspected him.
Tián, fearing for his safety,
feigned inviting Tiě to discuss matters,
then stabbed him with a blade,
and occupied the land of Yùzhāng.
Hóu Jǐng's general Yú Qìng campaigned southwards and reached Yùzhāng.
All cities and towns submitted,
and Tián, in distress,
surrendered to Qìng.
Qìng sent Tián to Jǐng.
Jǐng, sharing the same surname as Tián,
claimed him as a relative,
treated him very generously,
and kept his wife, children, and younger brother as hostages.
He dispatched Tián to follow Qìng in pacifying the southern commanderies of Lí.
When Jǐng was defeated at Bālíng,
Jǐng's generals Sòng Zǐxiān and Rèn Yuē, among others, were captured by the western army.
Tián then executed Jǐng's partisans
to respond to the righteous army.
Jǐng also executed all of Tián's younger brothers and family members.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng appointed Tián Wǔchén Jiāngjūn and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ,
enfeoffed him as Píxiàn Hóu,
with an estate of one thousand households.
He then followed the Grand Supervisor Wáng Sēngbiàn in campaigning against Jǐng,
always serving as the vanguard,
and repelling the enemy in every battle.
After Táichéng was recovered,
Jǐng fled to Wú County.
Sēngbiàn ordered Tián to lead troops to pursue him.
They fought Jǐng at Wúsōng Jiāng,
and greatly defeated Jǐng,
capturing all his military provisions.
They advanced to Qiántáng,
where Jǐng's generals Xiè Dárén and Lǚ Zǐróng, among others, all surrendered.
For his merits, he was appointed Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and garrisoned at Gūshú.
In the second year of Chéngshèng (553 CE),
when Qí dispatched Guō Yuánjiàn from Rúxū,
Sēngbiàn sent Tián to lead three thousand armored soldiers
to build a stronghold at Dōngguān to defend against him,
and greatly defeated Yuánjiàn.
He was appointed Shǐchíjié, Zhènběi Jiāngjūn,
granted a drum and fife ensemble,
and his estate was increased by two thousand households.
When Western Wèi invaded Jīngzhōu,
Wáng Sēngbiàn made Tián his vanguard
to rush to its aid,
but Jīngzhōu fell before he arrived.
Tián went to Jiǔjiāng
and escorted Prince Jìn'ān back to the capital.
By imperial mandate, Tián was made Shìzhōng, Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Jiāng Jìn Wú Qí Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnshì, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was re-enfeoffed as Kānglè Xiàngōng,
with an estate of five thousand households,
and promoted to the title of Chējì Jiāngjūn.
When Sītú Lù Fǎhé occupied Yǐngzhōu
and invited Qí troops to invade,
Tián was ordered to supervise all armies in a western campaign.
Before he arrived,
Fǎhé led his subordinates northwards into Qí territory.
Qí then dispatched Mùróng Shìdé to garrison at Xiàshǒu.
Tián, controlling his forces, returned westwards,
attacking him by water and land.
Shìdé ran out of provisions
and requested peace.
Tián returned to garrison Yùzhāng.
Sēngbiàn ordered his younger brother Sēngyīn to lead troops with Tián to campaign against Xiāo Bó.
When Emperor Gāozǔ executed Sēngbiàn,
Sēngyīn secretly plotted to eliminate Tián and seize his army.
Tián learned of this,
rounded up all of Sēngyīn's partisans,
and Sēngyīn fled to Qí.
In the second year of Shàotài (558 CE),
he was granted the additional title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī with his original designation,
and all other appointments remained as before.
At this time,
Tián occupied the middle reaches of the river,
and his military strength was very formidable.
Also, because he had previously served Wáng Sēngbiàn,
though he outwardly displayed loyalty,
he had no intention of going to court.
Originally,
Yú Xiàokǐng was Yùzhāng Tàishǒu.
When Tián garrisoned Yùzhāng,
Xiàokǐng established a separate fortress in Xīnwú County,
and resisted Tián.
Tián left the wives and children of his soldiers in Yùzhāng,
ordering his younger cousin Yūn to manage the rear affairs,
and led all his troops to attack Xiàokǐng.
From summer to winter,
he could not overcome him.
He then laid a long siege,
and seized all of Xiàokǐng's crops.
Yūn and his subordinate Fāng'ér were not in harmony.
Fāng'ér, angered,
led his subordinates to attack Yūn,
plundered Tián's military camp, concubines, gold, and jade,
and returned to Emperor Gāozǔ.
Having lost his base,
Tián's troops all scattered.
He hastily returned to Yùzhāng,
but the people of Yùzhāng resisted him.
He then hurried to Pénchéng
and sought refuge with his general Jiāo Sēngdù.
Sēngdù advised Tián to surrender to Qí,
but Tián believed that Emperor Gāozǔ was magnanimous
and would surely accept him.
So he went to the palace gate to plead guilty.
Emperor Gāozǔ restored his titles.
In the first year of Yǒngdìng,
he was appointed Shìzhōng and Chējì Jiāngjūn.
In the second year,
he was promoted to Sīkōng.
When Wáng Lín reached Dùnkǒu,
Zhōu Wényù and Hóu Āndū were both lost.
So, Zhèn was made Dūdū of all armies for the Western Expedition.
Zhèn reached Liángshān.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Zhèn was promoted to Tàiwèi,
and his fief was increased by a thousand households.
When Wáng Lín reached Zhàkǒu,
Zhèn was again made Dūdū,
and Hóu Āndū and others were all subordinate to him.
Zhèn and Lín were locked in a standoff for over a hundred days,
without a decisive outcome.
In the second month of the first year of Tiānjiā,
the spring waters in Dōngguān gradually rose,
allowing ships to pass.
Lín led his forces from Héféi and Cháohú,
with sterns and bows following one another as they descended,
their momentum very strong.
Zhèn led his army to advance to Shòukǎn Zhōu.
Lín also sent out his ships and arrayed them along the west bank of the river,
anchoring across the islet.
The next day, they engaged in battle.
Lín's army retreated slightly,
falling back to secure the west bank.
By evening,
a strong northeast wind arose,
blowing their ships.
The ships were all damaged,
sinking in the sand,
and hundreds of people drowned.
The waves were too strong to return to the harbor,
and during the night, a meteor fell into the bandit camp.
By dawn, the wind had quieted.
Lín entered the harbor to repair his ships,
using reed boats to block the harbor entrance,
and also surrounding the bank with deer antlers,
daring not to venture out again.
At this time,
Western Wèi dispatched Grand General Shǐ Níng to press upstream.
Upon hearing this, Zhèn
knew Lín could not hold out for long.
He withdrew his troops and occupied Húpǔ,
awaiting their exhaustion.
When Shǐ Níng arrived
and besieged Yǐngzhōu,
Lín feared his forces would collapse.
He then led his ships downstream,
anchoring ten *lǐ* from Wúhú,
the sound of the drumsticks audible throughout the army.
The next day,
the Qí people sent tens of thousands of troops to assist Lín.
Lín led his forces towards Liángshān,
intending to bypass the government army and garrison a strategic position.
Qí Yítóng Liú Bóqiú led over ten thousand soldiers to assist Lín in the naval battle.
Xíngtái Mùróng Shìdé's son Zǐhuì commanded two thousand armored cavalry,
stationed on the west bank of Wúhú, south of Bówàngshān,
to project their power.
Zhèn ordered his army to cook breakfast and eat in their beds at dawn,
and divided his forces to assault and occupy the tail of Wúhú Zhōu to await them.
As the battle was about to begin,
a light breeze came from the southeast.
All the armies deployed catapults and launched fire attacks.
Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Zhāodá advanced on the central river in a large "Pinglǔ" ship,
and
fired a catapult that hit a bandit ship.
The others, "Màotū" and "Qīnglóng" ships,
each engaged their respective targets.
They also used small "Méngchōng" boats covered with ox-hide
to ram the bandit ships,
and sprinkled molten iron on them.
Lín's army was utterly defeated.
His infantry on the west bank
trampled each other.
The cavalry were all mired in the reeds,
and only two or three tenths of the horses, stripped of their saddles, escaped.
All their ships and equipment were captured,
and Qí generals Liú Bóqiú and Mùróng Zǐhuì were taken prisoner.
The number of other captives and beheaded enemies was in the tens of thousands.
Lín and his confederate Pān Chún and others escaped through the lines in a single small boat to Pénchéng.
He still wished to rally the scattered forces,
but no one joined him.
So, with his wife, concubines, and about ten attendants, he fled into Qí territory.
That year,
an imperial edict appointed Zhèn Dūdū of the military affairs of Xiāng, Bā, Yǐng, Jiāng, and Wú five prefectures,
and stationed him in Pénchéng.
When Zhōu generals Hèrǔo Dūn and Dúgū Shèng and others raided Bā and Xiāng,
Zhèn was again made Dūdū for the Western Expedition.
He fought against Shèng at Xījiāngkǒu,
utterly defeating Shèng's army.
The captured men, horses, and equipment
were innumerable.
For his achievements, he was granted the titles of Shǐchíjié, Dūdū of the military affairs of Xiāng, Guì, Yǐng, Bā, Wǔ, and Yuán six prefectures, and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was re-enfeoffed as Línglíng Jùngōng,
with seven thousand households,
and the rest remained as before.
In the second year,
due to illness, he submitted a memorial requesting to return to court.
In the third month,
he died on the way,
aged fifty-two.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng, Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Dàsīmǎ,
with additional honors of Yǔbǎo, Gǔchuī, and twenty Bānjiàn guards.
He was given Eastern Garden Secret Regalia,
and his posthumous name was Zhuàngsù.
In the ninth month of that year,
he was ritually honored and worshipped in Gāozǔ's ancestral temple.
His son Jìngzàng succeeded him.
Jìngzàng married Shìzǔ's second daughter, Fùyáng Gōngzhǔ.
Because of the princess, he was made Yuánwài Sǎnqí Shìláng.
He died in the third year of Tàijiàn,
and was posthumously granted Sītú Zhǔbù.
Jìngzàng had no sons,
so his younger brother Jiù inherited the title.
Ōuyáng Wèi, courtesy name Jìngshì,
was a native of Línxiāng, Chángshā.
He belonged to a prominent local clan.
His grandfather Jǐngdá
served as Běnzhōu Zhìzhōng during the Liáng dynasty.
His father Sēngbǎo was a Túnojì Xiàowèi.
Wèi was honest and thoughtful in his youth,
and was renowned throughout Lǐngbiǎo for his trustworthy words and deeds.
Upon his father's death, his grief and emaciation were extreme.
He accumulated family property,
but ceded it all to his elder brothers.
Repeated invitations from the prefecture and commandery he declined,
and instead built a hut near Lùshān Sì,
devoting himself to study and mastering his craft,
becoming broadly learned in the Classics and histories.
At the age of thirty,
his elder brothers compelled him to enter officialdom.
He began his career as Xìngwǔ Fǔ Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
and was promoted to Píngxī Shàolíng Wáng Zhōngbīng Cānjūnshì.
When Liáng Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Lán Qīn was young,
he was on good terms with Wèi,
so Wèi often followed Qīn on campaigns.
When Qīn became Héngzhōu Cìshǐ,
Wèi was still appointed Qīngyuǎn Tàishǒu.
Qīn campaigned south against the barbarians (yíláo),
capturing Chén Wénchè,
with countless spoils.
He presented a large bronze drum,
unseen for generations,
and Wèi contributed to this achievement.
Upon his return, he became Zhíhé Jiāngjūn,
and was then appointed Tiānmén Tàishǒu,
achieving merit in suppressing the barbarian *zuǒ*.
Cìshǐ Lúlíng Wáng Xiāo Xù greatly praised him,
and invited him as a guest.
When Qīn campaigned in Jiāozhōu,
he again requested Wèi to accompany him.
Qīn died of illness after crossing the mountain range (Lǐng).
Wèi was appointed Línhè Nèishǐ,
but requested permission to escort Qīn's coffin back to the capital
before taking up his post.
At that time, over fifty caves (villages) on the border of Xiāng and Héng were unsubmissive.
An imperial edict ordered Héngzhōu Cìshǐ Wéi Càn to suppress them.
Càn entrusted Wèi as Dūdū,
and he completely pacified them.
Càn reported to Liángwǔ that
Wèi was truly capable,
and an imperial edict praised and rewarded him,
also adding the title Chāowǔ Jiāngjūn,
for campaigning against mountain bandits in Guǎng and Héng prefectures.
Hóu Jǐng Gòu Nì,
Càn personally freed himself and returned to the capital to campaign against Jǐng.
He appointed Wěi as the Supervisor of Héngzhōu.
After the imperial capital fell,
Lǐngnán mutually annexed territories.
Lán Qīn's younger brother, the former Cìshǐ of Gāozhōu, Yù, attacked Shī Xīng Nèishǐ Xiāo Shàojī,
and seized his commandery.
Yù knew that his elder brother Qīn had an old acquaintance with Wěi,
so he sent someone to recruit him,
but Wěi did not comply.
He then said to the envoy:
"The brothers of Gāozhōu are prosperous and prominent,
all due to national grace.
Now, one should respond to the crisis and aid the capital;
how can one become unruly oneself?"
When Gāozǔ entered to aid Jīngyì,
and was about to reach Shīxīng,
Wěi then deeply allied himself with him.
Yù sent troops to attack Wěi,
Gāozǔ reinforced him,
and Yù was defeated.
Gāozǔ appointed Wáng Huáimíng as the Cìshǐ of Héngzhōu,
and transferred Wěi to be the Nèishǐ of Shīxīng.
When Gāozǔ was campaigning against Cài Lùyǎng and Lǐ Qiānshì,
Wěi led troops across the mountain range
to assist Gāozǔ.
After Lùyǎng and others were pacified,
Wěi had rendered meritorious service.
Liáng Yuándì, acting on Imperial authority, changed Shīxīng Commandery to Dōnghéngzhōu,
and appointed Wěi as Chíjié, Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū of all military affairs of Dōnghéngzhōu, Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn, Cìshǐ of Dōnghéngzhōu,
Bó of Xīnfēng County,
with a stipend of four hundred households.
When Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Yuándì asked all the court officials:
"Now that the realm has just been settled,
we urgently need capable talents.
Each of you should recommend those you know."
The assembled ministers had not yet responded.
The Emperor said:
"I have already found one person."
Shìzhōng Wáng Bāo stepped forward and said:
"May I ask who it is?"
The Emperor said:
"Ōuyáng Wěi is just and possesses the talent to rectify and assist;
I fear that Xiāo Guǎngzhōu will not allow him to come."
He then appointed him as Cìshǐ of Wǔzhōu,
and soon thereafter as Cìshǐ of Yǐngzhōu,
intending to send him out of the mountain range,
but Xiāo Bó kept him,
so he was unable to accept the appointment.
Soon after, he was appointed as Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū of all military affairs of Héngzhōu, Zhōngwǔ Jiāngjūn, Cìshǐ of Héngzhōu,
and promoted to be Hóu of Shīxīng County.
At that time, Xiāo Bó was in Guǎngzhōu,
with strong forces and a heavy position.
Yuándì deeply worried about him,
and sent Wáng Lín to replace him as Cìshǐ.
Lín had already reached Xiǎoguìlǐng.
Bó sent his general Sūn Yáng to supervise the prefecture,
and led all his subordinates to Shīxīng,
to avoid Lín's military edge.
Wěi separately occupied a city,
did not go to pay respects to Bó,
closed the gates, and built high ramparts,
nor did he refuse to fight.
Bó was enraged,
and sent troops to attack Wěi,
seizing all his property, horses, and weapons.
Soon after, he pardoned him,
restored his possessions,
and renewed their alliance.
When Jīngzhōu fell,
Wěi pledged allegiance to Bó.
When Bó crossed the mountain range and advanced to Nánkāng,
he appointed Wěi as Qiánjūn Dūdū,
and stationed him at Kǔzhútān in Yùzhāng.
Zhōu Wényù attacked and defeated them,
captured Wěi and sent him to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ released him,
and treated him with great hospitality.
After Xiāo Bó died,
Lǐngnán was in turmoil.
Wěi had a reputation in the southern lands,
and also had an old acquaintance with Gāozǔ.
He was then appointed as Shǐchíjié, Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū of all military affairs of Héngzhōu, Ānnán Jiāngjūn, Cìshǐ of Héngzhōu,
and Hóu of Shīxīng County.
Before he reached Lǐngnán,
Wěi's son, Hē, had already conquered and pacified Shīxīng.
When Wěi arrived in Lǐngnán,
everyone was awed and submitted,
and he then advanced to Guǎngzhōu,
taking possession of all the Yuè territory.

He was reappointed as Dūdū of the military affairs of Guǎng, Jiāo, Yuè, Chéng, Dìng, Míng, Xīn, Gāo, Hé, Luó, Ài, Jiàndé, Yíhuáng, Lì'ān, Shí, Shuāng, and ten other prefectures, Zhènnán Jiāngjūn, Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiàng, Cìshǐ of Guǎngzhōu,
with his titles of Chíjié, Chángshì, and Hóu remaining as before.
Wáng Lín occupied the middle reaches of the river,
while Wěi maintained uninterrupted diplomatic missions via the sea route and the eastern mountain passes.
In the third year of Yǒngdì,
he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì,
and had the Dūdū of military affairs of Héngzhōu added to his titles,
and established a government with the status of Yí Tóng Sān Sī under his original title.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn,
and re-enfeoffed as the Gōng of Yángshān Commandery,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred households,
and also granted a full set of drum and wind instruments.
Initially,
Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Tánhuǎn secretly entrusted Wěi with five hundred liǎng of gold,
instructing him to return one hundred liǎng to the Taishou of Hépǔ, Gōng Wěi,
and give four hundred liǎng to his son Zhìjǔ,
with no one else knowing.
Wěi was soon after defeated by Xiāo Bó,
and all his property was lost,
only the entrusted gold remained.
Tánhuǎn also died soon after.
At this point, Wěi returned all of it according to the trust,
and everyone at the time was filled with admiration.
Such was his regard for promises.
At that time, Wěi's younger brother Shèng was Cìshǐ of Jiāozhōu,
and his next younger brother Suì was Cìshǐ of Héngzhōu.
His entire family was prominent and noble,
and their fame resonated throughout the southern lands.
He also brought many bronze drums and captives,
and offered rare and exotic treasures,
which accumulated in vast quantities,
greatly assisting the military and the state.
Wěi passed away in the fourth year of Tiānjiā,
at the age of sixty-six.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng, Chējì Dàjiāngjūn, Sīkōng, and Cìshǐ of Guǎngzhōu,
with the posthumous name Mù.
His son Hē succeeded him.
Hē, courtesy name Fèngshèng,
possessed considerable strategy and resourcefulness.
During the Tiānjiā era,
he was appointed Huángmén Shìláng and Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì.
He was successively promoted to Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Héngzhōu.
He inherited the title of Gōng of Yángshān Commandery,
and was Dūdū of the military affairs of Jiāo, Guǎng, and nineteen other prefectures, and Cìshǐ of Guǎngzhōu.
He served in the prefecture for over ten years,
and his prestige and benevolence were renowned among the Bǎiyuè people.
He was promoted to Qīngchē Jiāngjūn.
During the Guāngdà era,
many of the border garrisons in the upper reaches harbored disloyalty.
Gāozōng, knowing that Hē had been in the southern territories for a long time,
was quite suspicious of him.
In the first year of Tàijiàn,
an imperial edict was issued to summon Hē to serve as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
Hē was afraid,
and did not wish to comply with the summons.
Many of his subordinates urged him to rebel,
so he raised an army and attacked Qián Dàojí, the Cìshǐ of Héngzhōu.
Dàojí reported the rebellion,
whereupon Yí Tóng Zhāng Zhāodá was sent to suppress Hē.
After repeated battles, Hē's forces were defeated,
and he was captured and sent to the capital,
where he was executed,
at the age of thirty-three.
His family and property were confiscated.
His son, Xún, was spared due to his youth.
Wú Míngchè, courtesy name Tōngzhāo,
〔一０〕was a native of Qínjùn.
His grandfather, Jǐng'ān, was Qí Nánqiāo Tàishǒu.
His father, Shù, was Liáng Yòujūn Jiāngjūn.
Míngchè was orphaned young,
and was extremely filial by nature.
At fourteen,
he felt that the tomb mound was not yet complete,
and as his family was poor and had no means to provide for it,
he diligently cultivated the land.
At that time, there was a severe drought throughout the land,
and the crops withered.
Míngchè was sorrowful and indignant.
Whenever he went to the fields,
he would cry aloud,
looking up to heaven and pleading.
After several days,
someone returning from the fields
said that the sprouts had regrown.
Míngchè doubted him,
thinking he was deceiving him.
When he went to the fields,
it was indeed as the person had said.
In autumn, he had a great harvest,
sufficient for the funeral expenses.
At that time, there was a Mr. Yī,
who was skilled in geomancy for graves.
He said to Míngchè's elder brother:
"On the day of your burial,
there will surely be someone riding a white horse chasing a deer passing by the tomb.
This is a sign that the youngest filial son will achieve great nobility."
At the appointed time, this indeed occurred,
and Míngchè was precisely Shù's youngest son.
He began his career as an aide to the Crown Prince of Liáng.
When Hóu Jǐng attacked the capital,
the world fell into great chaos.
Míngchè had over three thousand hú of grain and wheat,
and when his neighbors were starving,
he said to his elder brothers:
"Nowadays, there are bandits everywhere,
and people do not plan for the long term.
How can we have this much and not share it with our fellow villagers?"
Thereupon, he divided it equally by household,
sharing their abundance and scarcity.
The various bandits heard of this and avoided them,
and many relied on him to survive.
When Gāozǔ was garrisoned at Jīngkǒu,
he deeply sought to ally with Míngchè.
Míngchè then went to Gāozǔ,
who descended the steps for him,
took his hand, and led him to a seat,
discussing the affairs of the time with him.
Míngchè had also vaguely read through historical records and classical texts,
and studied astronomy, gūxū (solitary emptiness), and dùnjiǎ (hiding Jia) with Zhōu Hóngzhèng of Rǔnán,
largely understanding their subtleties.
He rather fancied himself a hero,
and Gāozǔ deeply admired him for this.
In the third year of Chéngshèng (554 CE),
he was appointed Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn (General Who Manifests Valor) and Ānzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Ān Prefecture).
In the beginning of Shàotài (555 CE),
he followed Zhōu Wényù to suppress Dù Kān and Zhāng Biāo, et al.
After the eastern region was pacified,
he was appointed Shǐ Chíjié (Bearer of Credentials), Sànqí Chángshì (Palace Attendant), Āndōng Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the East), and Nán Yuánzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Nán Yuán Prefecture),
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ānwú County.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
Míngchè was appointed Ānnán Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the South),
and then, with Hóu Āndū and Zhōu Wényù, led troops to attack Wáng Lín.
When the assembled armies were defeated and annihilated,
Míngchè extricated himself and returned to the capital.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
an edict appointed him Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Guard) in addition to his original post.
After Wáng Lín was defeated,
he was appointed Dūdū Wǔ Yuán Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì (Area Commander-in-Chief of Wǔ and Yuán Prefectures), Ānxī Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the West), and Wǔzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Wǔ Prefecture),
with his other posts remaining as before.
The Zhōu dynasty sent Grand General Hèruò Dūn with over ten thousand cavalry and infantry who suddenly arrived at Wǔlíng.
Míngchè's forces were outnumbered and unable to contend,
so he led his army to Bālíng,
and subsequently defeated a separate Zhōu army at Shuānglín.
In the third year of Tiānjiā (562 CE),
he was appointed Ānxī Jiāngjūn.
When Zhōu Dí rebelled in Línchuān,
an edict appointed Míngchè Ānnán Jiāngjūn and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jiāng Prefecture),
also holding the post of Yùzhāng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Yùzhāng),
to command all the armies
for the suppression of Dí.
Míngchè had a naturally firm and upright character,
and his subordinates were not very harmonious with him.
When Shìzǔ heard of this,
he sent Wáng Xū, Prince of Ānchéng, to comfort and enlighten Míngchè,
instructing him to return to court with his original title.
Soon after, he was appointed Zhènqián Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the Front).
In the fifth year (564 CE),
he was promoted to Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the East) and Wúxīng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Wúxīng).
When he was taking leave to go to the commandery,
Shìzǔ said to Míngchè:
"Although Wúxīng is a commandery,
it is important as the Emperor's homeland,
which is why I entrust it to you.
You must exert yourself!"
When Shìzǔ became ill,
Míngchè was summoned and appointed Zhōnglǐngjūn (Commander of the Palace Guard).
When Fèidì (Deposed Emperor) ascended the throne,
Míngchè was appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (Commander of the Palace Guard),
and soon after promoted to Dānyáng Yǐn (Magistrate of Dānyáng),
and an edict further ordered Míngchè to enter and exit the palace with forty armed guards.
When Dào Zhòngjǔ falsely ordered the removal of Gāozōng,
Máo Xǐ knew of the plot.
Gāozōng was suspicious and fearful,
and sent Xǐ to deliberate with Míngchè.
Míngchè said to Xǐ:
"The heir apparent is in mourning,
and many affairs of state are lacking.
There are strong enemies abroad,
and a great funeral within.
Your Highness is truly like Zhōu and Shào,
and your virtue surpasses Yī and Huò.
The state is of utmost importance,
I hope you will deliberate deeply within,
and not harbor doubts."
When Huá Jiǎo, the Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu, secretly harbored disloyal intentions,
an edict appointed Míngchè Shǐ Chíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Xiāng Guì Wǔ Sān Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì (Area Commander-in-Chief of Xiāng, Guì, and Wǔ Prefectures), Ānnán Jiāngjūn, and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
granting him a set of drums and pipes,
and further ordered him, along with Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General Who Conquers the South) Chúnyú Liàng et al., to lead troops to attack Jiǎo.
After Jiǎo was pacified,
Míngchè was appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Grandee with Ceremonial Privileges Equal to the Three Dukes),
and advanced in peerage to Duke.
In the first year of Tàijiàn (569 CE),
he was appointed Zhènnán Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the South).
In the fourth year (572 CE),
he was summoned to serve as Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and Zhènqián Jiāngjūn,
with his other posts remaining as before.
At the time, the court discussed a northern expedition,
and the high officials held differing opinions,
but Míngchè firmly decided and requested to go.
In the fifth year (573 CE),
an edict added the title of Shìzhōng and Dūdū Zhēngtǎo Zhū Jūnshì (Area Commander-in-Chief of All Punitive Expeditions),
and also bestowed a set of female entertainers.
Míngchè commanded a total of over one hundred thousand troops,
setting out from the capital.
The cities and towns along the Yangtze River
successively surrendered.
When the army reached Qín Jùn,
they captured its water stockade.
Qí sent Grand General Wèi Pòhú to lead troops as reinforcement,
but Míngchè defeated and routed him,
with countless enemy casualties and captures.
Qín Jùn then surrendered.
Gāozōng, considering Qín Jùn Míngchè's old hometown,
issued an edict to prepare a grand sacrifice,
ordering him to perform rites at the shrine and visit the graves.
The civil and military officials with their ceremonial guard were very grand,
and the local villagers considered it an honor.
He advanced and conquered Rénzhōu.
He was granted the title of Grand General Who Conquers the North (Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn),
and his peerage was advanced to Duke of Nánpíng Commandery (Nánpíng Jùn Gōng).
His tax households were increased to two thousand five hundred, including those previously granted.
Next, he pacified the two cities of Píngxiá and Shí'àn.
He advanced to besiege Shòuyáng.
Qí dispatched Wáng Lín to lead troops to defend it.
When Lín arrived,
he and the Inspector (Cìshǐ) Wáng Guìxiǎn defended its outer city.
Míngchè, seeing that Lín had just arrived
and the hearts of the multitude had not yet attached themselves to him,
attacked by night.
They were routed in the middle of the night.
The Qí troops retreated and occupied Xiàngguó Chéng and Jīnchéng.
Míngchè ordered the army to improve and repair their siege equipment
(12) and also dammed the Féishuǐ to flood the city.
The people in the city suffered greatly from the dampness,
many had abdominal diseases,
their hands and feet were all swollen,
and sixteen or seventeen out of ten died.
At this time, Qí dispatched Grand General Pí Jǐnghé to lead several tens of thousands of troops to reinforce them.
They stopped thirty *lǐ* from Shòuchūn
and did not advance.
All the generals said:
"The strong city has not yet been taken,
and a large relief force is nearby.
We wonder what plan your excellency will devise?"
Míngchè said:
"Speed is paramount in warfare,
but they have established camp and not advanced,
blunting their own vanguard.
I know they dare not fight, this is clear."
Thereupon, he personally donned his armor and helmet
and launched a swift assault on all four sides.
The city was filled with terror,
and it was taken with a single drum roll.
Wáng Lín, Wáng Guìxiǎn, Fúfēng Wáng Kězhūhún Xiàoyù, Minister Lú Qián, and Left Assistant Lǐ Táotú were captured alive
and sent to the capital.
(13) Jǐnghé fled in panic,
and all their horses and baggage were captured.
When Lín was captured,
many of his former subordinates were in the army.
Lín had always gained the hearts of his soldiers,
and those who saw him all sighed and could not look up.
Míngchè, fearing a mutiny,
ordered his retainers to pursue and kill Lín
and transmit his head.
An imperial edict stated:
"Shòuchūn is an ancient metropolis,
embracing the Huái and Rǔ rivers,
controlling the Hé and Luò rivers.
Those who possess it are secure;
it is known as a vital strategic point.

Attendant Minister (Shìzhōng), Bearer of Imperial Credentials (Shǐchíjié), Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs for the Punitive Expedition (Dūdū Zhēngtǎo Zhū Jūnshì), Grand General Who Conquers the North (Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn), Initiator of the Bureau of a Grand Minister (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), and Founding Duke of Nánpíng Commandery (Nánpíng Jùn Kāiguó Gōng) Míngchè
has achieved a grand strategy,
his great plans surpassing all others.
In the past, when he was stationed at Yí,
he established the imperial enterprise,
covering Héng and Yuè,
thereby clearing away the ominous miasma,
truly swallowing Yúnmèng,
and immediately settling the upper reaches.
Now, he has swept and pacified the area,
restoring our royal strategy.
Like the wind sweeping and lightning striking,
brave warriors contend and race,
(14) moon-shaped formations and cloud ladders,
capturing formidable strongholds,
his prestige overawing foreign customs,
his beneficence permeating the border populace.
With his功 (gōng) and ability,
he is entrusted as the Grand Marshal (Yuánróng).
To elevate his banner and expand his provisions
is fitting for the flourishing tradition.

He is appointed Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs for the six prefectures of Yù, Hé, Jiàn, Guāng, Shuò, and Běixú (Dūdū Yù Hé Jiàn Guāng Shuò Běixú Liùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Dàjiāngjūn), and Inspector of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu Cìshǐ).
His enfeoffment is increased to three thousand five hundred households, including those previously granted.
The rest remains as before."
An imperial edict dispatched the Usher (Yèzhě) Xiāo Chúnfēng
(15) to Shòuyáng to formally invest Míngchè.
An altar was set up south of the city,
with two hundred thousand soldiers
displaying banners, drums, spears, and armor.
Míngchè ascended the altar, bowed to receive the appointment,
completed the ceremony, and withdrew.
All the generals and soldiers were filled with joy.
Initially,
Qín Commandery belonged to Nányǔnzhōu.
Later, it was subordinated to Qiáozhōu.
By this time,
an imperial edict returned the three commanderies of Qín, Xūyí, and Shénnóng of Qiáo to Nányǔnzhōu,
this was due to Míngchè.
In the sixth year,
he returned to court from Shòuyáng.
The imperial carriage visited his residence,
and he was bestowed a set of bells and chimes,
ten thousand *hú* of rice,
and two thousand rolls of silk and cloth.
In the seventh year,
he advanced to attack Péngchéng.
When his army reached Lǚliáng,
Qí dispatched tens of thousands of relief troops, arriving one after another,
and Míngchè again decisively defeated them.
In the eighth year,
he was promoted to Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
with the rest remaining as before.
Another imperial edict stated:
"In ancient times, military affairs involved raising banners
and striking drums when engaging in battle.
In recent days, due to errors and alterations,
many practices deviate from the old regulations,
especially concerning battle formations,
where distinctions are not made.
Now, the Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and Grand Administrator (Dà Dūdū) shall be granted the battle-axe and the dragon banner (fǔyuè lónghuī),
and the ranks of his subordinate generals shall vary accordingly."

Soon after, he was appointed Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs for the five prefectures of Nányǔn, Běiyǔn, Nánqīng, Běiqīng, and Qiáo (Dūdū Nán Běiyǔn Nán Běiqīng Qiáo Wǔzhōu Zhū Jūnshì), and Inspector of Nányǔnzhōu (Nányǔnzhōu Cìshǐ).
At that time, the Zhōu dynasty destroyed Qí,
and Emperor Gāozōng was about to campaign against Xú and Yǔn.
In the ninth year,
an imperial edict ordered Míngchè to advance his army northward.
His eldest son, General of the Róngzhāo (Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn) and Supernumerary Gentleman-in-Waiting (Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng) Huìjué, was ordered to temporarily manage the affairs of the prefecture.
When Míngchè's army reached Lǚliáng,
Liáng Shìyàn, the Zhōu Administrator-General of Xúzhōu (Xúzhōu Zǒngguǎn), led his troops to resist and fight.
Míngchè repeatedly defeated him,
causing him to retreat and defend the city,
no longer daring to sally forth.
Míngchè then dammed the Qīngshuǐ to flood the city,
surrounding the city with a ring of boats and warships below it,
attacking with great urgency.
Zhōu dispatched Grand General (Shàng Dàjiāngjūn) Wáng Guǐ to lead troops to relieve them.
Guǐ traveled lightly from Qīngshuǐ into the Huáikǒu,
blocking the current with horizontally laid wood
and iron chains strung through chariot wheels,
cutting off the boat route.
When the generals heard of this,
they were greatly alarmed
and discussed breaking the dam and withdrawing the army,
transporting the horses by boat.
The stable master Péi Zǐliè proposed (16)
"If we break the dam and send the boats down,
the boats will surely capsize.
How can this be done?
It is better to send the horses out first;
this would be more appropriate for the situation."
Just then, Míngchè was suffering from a severe back ailment.
Knowing that the situation was unsalvageable,
he followed the advice
and dispatched Xiāo Móhē to lead several thousand cavalry back ahead.
Míngchè then personally breached his dam
and used the force of the water to retreat the army,
hoping to succeed.
However, when they reached Qīngkǒu,
the water flow gradually diminished,
and none of the boats and warships could pass.
All the troops were routed,
and Míngchè, cornered and desperate,
was captured.
Soon after, due to worry and indignation, he contracted an illness
and died in Cháng'ān
at the age of sixty-seven.
In the first year of Zhìdé, an imperial edict stated:
“Lǐ Líng’s arrows ran out,
and he could not avoid surrendering;
Yú Jìn’s army was submerged by floods,
yet he was still captured alive.
Thus, it is known that among those who master the highest art of warfare,
few are found in this world.
Therefore, the former Shìzhōng, Sīkōng, and Nánpíng Jùn Gōng Míngchè,
from his initial entry
until he became a grand marshal,
〔一七〕displayed the marvel of a hundred victories in a hundred battles,
and the courage to decide the moment and face death,
which indeed equals that of the ancients.
He then secured the Huái and Féi rivers,
and advanced rapidly towards Péng and Biàn.
He overthrew powerful enemies as easily as lifting a feather,
and swept away elite forces as effortlessly as melting snow with hot water.
His formidable prestige awed foreign peoples,
and his achievements were acknowledged among our own.
Just as he intended to rest his chariots at Yīnshān
and unbridle his horses by the sea,
his army had already grown old,
and his destiny for marvels had ended.
He did not achieve the glory of tying up his topknot (in victory),
nor could he avoid the humiliation of being placed in a prison cart.
It was hoped that sealing Xiáo would be easy,
and pacifying Dí would not be difficult.
Though his ambition was to advance and retreat as appropriate,
he was suddenly struck down by fate.
His resentment was buried in a distant land,
which is truly lamentable.
This matter has passed,
and many general amnesties have been issued.
All offenses and transgressions
have been cleansed,
yet this lone spirit
has not received such leniency,
leaving his noble title and land extinguished,
and his sacrifices without a master.
It is appropriate to record and employ his descendants
at this moment.
He is posthumously enfeoffed as Shàolíng Xiàn Kāiguó Hóu,
with a fiefdom of one thousand households,
and his son Huìjué is made his heir.”
Huìjué successively served as Huángmén Shìláng,
and for his meritorious service in pacifying Dàbǎo,
he was appointed Fēngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Míngchè’s nephew, Chāo,
courtesy name Yìshì.
He was uninhibited in his youth,
and known for his competence.
He accompanied Míngchè on campaigns,
gained military merits,
and rose to the positions of Zhōngyì Jiāngjūn, Sànqí Chángshì, and Guìzhōu Cìshǐ,
and was enfeoffed as Rǔnán Xiàn Hóu,
with a fiefdom of one thousand households.
When he died,
he was posthumously appointed Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the posthumous title Jié.
Péi Zǐliè, courtesy name Dàshì,
was a native of Wénxǐ, Hédōng,
and the son of Liáng Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì Yī.
Zǐliè was orphaned young,
and possessed ambition and spirit.
During the chaos at the end of the Liáng dynasty,
he practiced martial arts
and became known for his bravery and prowess.
He frequently accompanied Míngchè on campaigns,
always being the first to climb walls and break enemy lines.
He rose to the positions of Diànwēi Jiāngjūn, Běiqiáo Tàishǒu, Yuèyáng Nèishǐ,
and Hǎi’ān Xiàn Bó,
with a fiefdom of three hundred households.
〔一八〕He died in the fourth year of Zhìdé.
The historian remarks: Gāozǔ quelled the chaos and established the foundation,
gloriously inaugurating the heavenly mandate.
Hóu Tián and Ōuyáng Wěi both dedicated themselves to the righteous path,
and held esteemed positions as chief ministers.
This was excellent.
Wú Míngchè, in his role as a commander,
initially achieved military successes,
but his defeat at Lǚliáng
was due to miscalculation.
He lacked the valor of Hán Xìn and Bái Qǐ,
and the strategic insight of Sūn Wǔ and Wú Qǐ.
This led to the contraction of territory and loss of troops,
weakening Jīnlíng,
and was indeed the gradual cause of Zhēnmíng’s downfall.
(In the ‘Biography of Hóu Tián’,
“divided and attacked the end of Wúhú Zhōu”,
some versions read
“divided and stationed”,
which is doubtful.
“Wú Míngchè, courtesy name Tōngzhāo”,
some versions read
“Tōngzhào”,
which is doubtful.
) Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter 4: Zhōu Tiěhǔ, Chéng Língxǐ (son Wénjì)
Zhōu Tiěhǔ,
his origin is unknown. He crossed south during the Liáng dynasty.
His accent was heavy and rustic,
his physical strength surpassed others,
and he was skilled with the horse spear.
He served Xiāo Yù, Prince of Hédōng during the Liáng dynasty,
and was known for his bravery and valor.
Yù appointed him Fǔzhōng Bīng Cānjūn.
When Yù became Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ,
he made Tiěhǔ the Magistrate of Xīngníng.
When Yù was transferred to Xiāngzhōu,
he again made him the Magistrate of Línzhēng.
During the Hóu Jǐng Rebellion,
Emperor Yuán, from Jīngzhōu, sent his heir Fāngděng to replace Yù,
and moreover brought troops to confront him.
Yù resisted the attack
and won a great victory;
Fāngděng died,
and Tiěhǔ’s contribution was the greatest.
Yù trusted and valued him greatly.
When Wáng Sēngbiàn attacked Yù,
he captured Tiěhǔ in battle.
Sēngbiàn ordered him to be boiled.
Tiěhǔ cried out:
“Hóu Jǐng is not yet destroyed,
why kill a brave warrior?”
Sēngbiàn was struck by his words,
pardoned him,
and returned him to his command.
When Hóu Jǐng moved west,
Tiěhǔ followed Sēngbiàn in defeating Rèn Yuē
and capturing Sòng Zǐxiān;
he distinguished himself in every battle.
Emperor Yuán, acting under imperial authority, appointed him Rénwēi Jiāngjūn and Tóngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and enfeoffed him as Dùnyáng Xiàn Zǐ,
with a fiefdom of three hundred households.
He then followed Sēngbiàn in conquering and pacifying the capital,
subduing Xiè Dárén,
and pacifying Lù Nà in Xiāngzhōu.
In the second year of Chéngshèng,
for his previous and subsequent military achievements,
he was promoted to Hóu,
and his fiefdom increased to a total of five hundred households.
He also served as Sànqí Chángshì,
and concurrently as Xìnyì Tàishǒu,
with his general rank remaining unchanged.
When Gāozǔ executed Sēngbiàn,
Tiěhǔ led his unit to surrender,
and his original positions were restored.
When Xú Sìhuī led Qí invaders across the river,
Tiěhǔ defeated their navy at Bǎnjiáo Pǔ,
capturing all their armor, weapons, and boats.
He also attacked Lìyáng
and raided the Qí invaders’ infantry camp,
achieving victories in both.
After Sìhuī was pacified,
in the second year of Shàotài,
he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì, Yánwēi Jiāngjūn, and Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ.
Soon after, he accompanied Zhōu Wényù to Nánjiāng to resist Xiāo Bó,
always serving as the vanguard.
Wényù also ordered Tiěhǔ to lead a separate detachment
to raid Bó’s vanguard, Ōuyáng Wěi, at Kǔzhútān.
He also followed Wén Yù west to campaign against Wáng Lín.
They were defeated at Dùnkǒu.
Tiě Hǔ, Wén Yù, and Hóu Āndū were all captured by Lín.
Lín brought in his generals to meet him,
and spoke with them.
Only Tiě Hǔ's words and demeanor were unyielding.
Therefore, Lín pardoned all of Wén Yù's followers,
but Tiě Hǔ alone was harmed.
He was forty-nine years old at the time.
Gāozǔ heard of this,
and issued an edict saying:
"Among the treasures of Heaven and Earth,
life is what is most valued.
Among mortals,
what is most esteemed is one's fate.
To sacrifice one's life to uphold integrity,
and to dedicate one's life to repay kindness,
remembering the distant past and cherishing what has been,
it is truly fitting to grant higher honors.

Tiě Hǔ, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, General of Stern Might, Left Guard Commander of the Crown Prince, Administrator of Tóngzhōu, concurrently Grand Administrator of Xìnyì, and Founding Marquis of Dùnyáng County,
was of profound bearing and steadfast character,
valiant and vigorous in spirit.
In northern expeditions and southern campaigns,
he exerted his utmost loyalty and effort.
He spearheaded the attack at Jiāngxià,
trapping the dangerous rebels.
His divine spirit was even more formidable,
speaking fearlessly without faltering.
How can this be compared to Wēn Xù, who was harmed
while merely trimming his beard,
or Páng Dé, who, facing peril,
could still glare angrily?
Such loyalty and integrity
fill us with profound sorrow.
He is hereby posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant, General Protecting the Army, and Administrator of Qīng and Jì Provinces.
His fief is increased by one thousand households,
and he is granted a drum and fife band.
His marquessate remains as before."
In the fifth year of Tiānjiā (566),
Shìzǔ again issued an edict saying:
"The meritorious ministers of the Hàn dynasty
had their images painted in palaces and temples;
the brave generals of the Wèi court
had their names associated with ancestral temples.
Thus, their achievements endure forever,
and their generations are thereby immortal.
The late Palace Attendant, General Protecting the Army, Administrator of Qīng and Jì Provinces, and Founding Marquis of Dùnyáng County, Tiě Hǔ,
was truly upright and resolute,
heroic and bold in his actions.
At the dawn of the imperial enterprise,
he accumulated many merits.
Though fallen in the enemy's camp,
he maintained a righteous demeanor before the rebel court.
His posthumous achievements are those of ancient heroes,
admired by all discerning people.
He perished unyielding.
Though his honors are great,
his valorous spirit is easily forgotten in the distance,
and we speak now to recall and cherish him.
It is fitting that he should attend at the imperial ancestral temple
and respectfully receive offerings.
He shall be given sacrifice in Gāozǔ's ancestral temple."
His son Yú succeeded him.
At that time, there was Mǎ Míng from Xūyí,
whose courtesy name was Shìlǎng.
During the Liáng dynasty, he served Xiāo Fàn, the Prince of Póyáng by succession.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
he occupied the eastern border of Lújiāng,
resisting the rebels by holding city walls and stockades.
Yuándì appointed him Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, General Pacifying the North, and Administrator of the Northern Yù Province,
concurrently Grand Administrator of Lújiāng.
When Jīngzhōu fell,
he submitted to Gāozǔ.
During Shàotài,
his official positions were restored,
and he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīhuá County,
with a fief of two thousand households.
He also followed Wén Yù west to campaign against Wáng Lín.
His army was defeated at Dùnkǒu,
and Míng fought bravely and died.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Bearer of Credentials, General Punishing the West, and Administrator of Yǐngzhōu.
Chéng Língxǐ, whose courtesy name was Xuándí,
was a native of Hǎiníng, Xīn'ān.
From a young age, he was known for his courage and strength.
He could walk over two hundred *lǐ* a day,
was skilled at horsemanship, and adept at swimming.
At the end of the Liáng dynasty,
Hǎiníng, Yī, Shè, and other counties, as well as the borders of Póyáng and Xuānchéng Commanderies, were plagued by many bandits.
The nearby counties suffered greatly.
Língxǐ had long been respected and feared by his local community.
Successive magistrates frequently enlisted him to recruit young men
to pursue and capture robbers.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Língxǐ gathered followers and occupied Yī and Shè to resist Jǐng.
Jǐng's army occupied Xīn'ān.
Xiāo Yǐn, the Marquis of Xiāngxī Village and Grand Administrator of Xīn'ān, fled and relied on Língxǐ.
Língxǐ honored him as their leader.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng, acting by imperial prerogative in Jīngzhōu,
also sent an envoy with a memorial via a secret path.
Liú Shénmào rose in righteousness from Dōngyáng to resist the rebels.
Língxǐ attacked and captured Xīn'ān,
and linked up with Shénmào.

Emperor Yuán conferred upon him the titles of Bearer of Credentials, Palace Attendant Straightening the Back, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for Xīn'ān Commandery, General of Cloud Cavalry, and Administrator of Qiáozhōu,
concurrently Grand Administrator of Xīn'ān,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Bāqiū County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
Shénmào was defeated by Jǐng.
Jǐng's subordinate general Lǚ Zǐróng advanced to attack Xīn'ān.
Língxǐ retreated to defend Yī and Shè.
When Jǐng was defeated,
Zǐróng retreated.
Língxǐ reoccupied Xīn'ān.
He then advanced his army to Jiàndé,
capturing the rebel leader Zhào Sānggān.
For his merits, he was appointed Bearer of Credentials, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for Qīng and Jì Provinces, and Administrator of Qīngzhōu.
His fief was increased to a total of one thousand households,
and his general and grand administrator positions remained as before.
Língxǐ was then ordered to lead his subordinate troops to Yángzhōu,
to assist Wáng Sēngbiàn in defense.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Wúxìng.
Before he could take up the post,
Sēngbiàn ordered Língxǐ to accompany Hóu Zhèn west to reinforce Jīngzhōu.
When Jīngzhōu fell,
he returned to the capital.
When Gāozǔ executed Sēngbiàn,
Língxǐ led his troops to provide assistance.
His followers fought fiercely at the west gate of Shítóu,
but the army suffered a disadvantage.
Envoys were sent to persuade him,
and after some time, he surrendered.
Gāozǔ greatly appreciated his loyalty.
In the first year of Shàotài (555),
he was appointed Bearer of Credentials, General of Martial Trust, and Grand Administrator of Lánlíng.
His position as Cavalier Attendant remained as before,
and he assisted in defending Jīngkǒu.
After Xú Sìhuī was pacified,
Língxǐ rendered meritorious service,
and was appointed Grand Administrator of Nándānyáng,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Suí'ān County,
with his fief increased to a total of one thousand five hundred households.
He then garrisoned Cǎishí.
He followed Zhōu Wényù west to campaign against Wáng Lín,
and was defeated at Dùnkǒu,
where he was detained by Lín.
The following year,
he escaped and returned with Hóu Āndū and others.
He was concurrently appointed Magistrate of Dānyáng,
and then appointed Grand Administrator of Gāotáng and Tàiyuán Commanderies,
continuing to garrison Nánlíng.
He was promoted to Left Guard Commander of the Crown Prince.
When Gāozǔ died,
Wáng Lín's vanguard advanced eastward.
Língxǐ defeated them at Nánlíng,
capturing their soldiers,
and also seizing more than ten "Azure Dragon" chariots.

For his merits, he was appointed Bearer of Credentials, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for Nányù Province along the Yangtze River, General of Martial Trust, and Administrator of Nányù Province.
Hóu Zhèn and others defeated Wáng Lín at Shàkǒu.
Língxǐ pursued the fleeing enemy,
and occupied Lǔshān.
He was recalled to serve as Left Guard General,
with his other positions remaining as before.
In the fourth year of Tiānjiā (563),
Zhōu Dí again raided Línchuān.
Língxǐ was appointed Commander-in-Chief,
and attacked him from Póyáng via a different route.
Dí again fled into the mountains and valleys.
In the fifth year (564),
he was promoted to Central Protecting Army General,
with his position as Cavalier Attendant remaining as before.
He was sent out to serve as Bearer of Credentials, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for Yǐng, Bā, and Wǔ Provinces, General of Firm Might, and Administrator of Yǐngzhōu.
When the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he was promoted to the title of General of Cloud Cavalry.
When Huá Jiǎo rebelled,
he sent an envoy to entice Língxǐ.
Língxǐ executed Jiǎo's envoy,
and reported the situation.
The imperial court deeply commended his loyalty,
increased his defenses,
and granted him a drum and fife band.
Thereupon, they treated him with utmost trust,
sending his son Wénjì to lead a naval force to assist in defense.
At this time, the Zhōu dynasty sent its general, Cháng Húgōng Tuòbá Dìng, to lead twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to assist Jiǎo in besieging Língxǐ.
Língxǐ defended the city resolutely.
When Jiǎo retreated,
Língxǐ launched his army to pursue Dìng.
Dìng was unable to cross the river,
and surrendered with his troops.
He then advanced to attack Zhōu's Miǎnzhōu,
capturing it,
and apprehending its Administrator Péi Kuān.
For his merits, he was promoted to the title of General Pacifying the West,
and re-enfeoffed as Duke of Chóng'ān County,
with his fief increased to a total of two thousand households.
Chéng Língxǐ's nature was severe and urgent,
and he was very harsh with his subordinates.
If soldiers committed even a minor offense,
he would execute them according to military law.
In an instant,
he would apply flogging.
However, his orders were clear,
and he shared hardships with his soldiers.
Because of this, the multitude also became attached to him.
He was fond of sowing and planting,
personally toiling in farming and cultivation.
As for what was suitable for land or water,
and the timing of harvesting,
even old farmers could not surpass him.
His concubines and maids had no idle hands,
and he supervised them all in spinning and weaving.
As for spending money,
he was not frugal or stingy.
In the second year of Guāngdà,
he died in his prefecture
at the age of fifty-five.
He was posthumously granted the title of Zhènxī Jiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
with the posthumous name Zhōngzhuàng.
In the fourth year of Tàijiàn,
an imperial edict ordered him to be honored in the temple of Gāozǔ.
His son, Chéng Wénjì, succeeded him.
Chéng Wénjì's courtesy name was Shàoqīng.
As a child, he practiced riding and archery,
possessed much strategic ability,
and was decisive, having his father's demeanor.
In his youth, he accompanied Língxǐ on campaigns,
always being the first to climb and breach enemy lines.
When Língxǐ, along with Zhōu Wényù, Hóu Āndū, and others, were defeated at Dùnkǒu,
and captured by Wáng Lín,
Gāozǔ summoned the sons and younger brothers of the generals captured by the enemy and treated them generously.
Wénjì was the most courteous and proper,
and was deeply admired by Gāozǔ.
During the Yǒngdìng era,
he was successively promoted to Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng and Jùróng Lìng.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Xuānhuì Shǐxīng Wángfǔ Xiànnèi Zhōngzhíbīng Cānjūn.
At that time, the Prince was the Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoned at Yěchéng,
and all military affairs within the commandery
were entrusted to Wénjì.
In the second year of Tiānjiā,
he was appointed Zhēnyì Jiāngjūn and Xīn'ān Tàishǒu,
and then followed Hóu Āndū eastward to attack Liú Yì.
Yì's partisan Xiàng Wénzhèng occupied Xīn'ān.
Wénjì led three hundred elite armored soldiers
and lightly advanced to attack him.
Wénzhèng sent his nephew Zàn to resist.
Wénjì fought with him,
severely defeating Zàn's army,
whereupon Wénzhèng surrendered.
In the third year,
when Shǐxīng Wáng Bómào was sent out to garrison Dōngzhōu,
Wénjì was again appointed Zhèndōng Fǔzhōngbīng Cānjūn,
concurrently serving as Shàn Lìng.
In the fourth year,
Chén Bǎo Yìng allied with Liú Yì,
and also sent troops with Zhōu Dí to again emerge from Línchuān.
Shìzǔ dispatched Xìnyì Tàishǒu Yú Xiàoqǐng to attack Jìn'ān by sea.
Wénjì served as the vanguard,
achieving victories wherever he went.
After Chén Bǎo Yìng was pacified,
Wénjì's military achievements were numerous.
Upon his return,
he was transferred to Fǔ Zīyì Cānjūn,
leading Zhōngzhíbīng.
He was sent out as Línhǎi Tàishǒu.
Soon after, he rode a golden-winged boat to assist his father in garrisoning Yǐngchéng.
When Huá Jiǎo was pacified,
Língxǐ and Wénjì both had merits in defense and resistance.
When Língxǐ died,
Wénjì took full command of his forces,
was appointed Chāowǔ Jiāngjūn,
and continued to assist in defending Yǐngzhōu.
Wénjì was extremely filial by nature;
although military campaigns took precedence over mourning rites,
his emaciation was severe.
In the second year of Tàijiàn,
he was appointed Yùzhāng Nèishǐ,
retaining his general rank.
After his mourning period ended,
he inherited the title of Chóng'ān Xiàn Gōng.
He followed Dūdū Zhāng Zhāodá, leading troops to Jīngzhōu to campaign against Xiāo Kuí.
Kuí and the Zhōu army had built many boats and ships,
placing them in the Qīngní River.
At that time, the water was high and swift, so
Zhāodá dispatched Wénjì together with Qián Dàojí to launch a surprise attack with light boats,
burning all their boats and ships.
Taking advantage of the slight slackening of Xiāo Kuí's forces,
Zhāodá again sent Wénjì to enter their outer city at night,
killing and wounding many.
Soon after, the Zhōu army launched a major attack;
Bālíng Nèishǐ Léi Dàoqín fought and died in resistance,
and Wénjì barely escaped with his life.
For his merits, he was promoted to Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì and Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn,
with an increase of five hundred households in his fief.
In the fifth year,
Dūdū Wú Míngchè campaigned north to Qínjùn.
In front of Qínjùn, the Jiāngpǔ channel led to the Tū River.
The Qí people had sunk large pillars as stakes,
forming a barrier in the water.
Míngchè first sent Wénjì to lead his elite to remove this barrier.
Míngchè then led the main army to arrive from behind,
attacking and capturing Qínjùn.
He also separately dispatched Wénjì to besiege Jìngzhōu,
sacking its city,
and then advanced to attack Xūyí,
capturing it.
He then followed Míngchè to besiege Shòuyáng.
Wénjì was cautious and swift in handling affairs,
and his command over his subordinates was strict and orderly.
In all the cities and fortresses he captured,
he generally built dikes by intercepting water.
Earth and timber works
often exceeded tens of thousands.
Whenever he deployed troops or engaged in labor,
Wénjì would always lead his generals,
rising early at night
and not resting until dusk.
No one in the army failed to admire his diligence and competence.
In every battle, he always served as the vanguard.
The Qí army deeply feared him,
calling him "Chéng Shòu" (Chéng the Beast).
For his merits, he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì and Míngwēi Jiāngjūn,
with an increase of five hundred households in his fief.
He also concurrently served as Xīn'ān Nèishǐ,
and was promoted to the title Wǔyì Jiāngjūn.
In the eighth year,
he was appointed Chíjǐe, Dūdū Qiáozhōu Zhū Jūnjì, Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn, and Qiáozhōu Cìshǐ.
That same year,
he was also Dūdū Běixú Rénzhōu Zhū Jūnjì and Běixúzhōu Cìshǐ,
with other appointments remaining as before.
In the ninth year,
