he again followed Míngchè on a northern campaign,
building a dike at Lǚliáng.
Details can be found in Míngchè's biography.
In the spring of the tenth year,
he suffered a defeat
and was captured by the Zhōu,
who then granted him Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
In the eleventh year,
he escaped from Zhōu,
but upon reaching Wōyáng,
he was captured by border officials
and sent back to Cháng'ān,
where he died in prison.
Hòuzhǔ, having already broken ties with Zhōu at that time,
was unaware of this.
In the first year of Zhìdé,
Hòuzhǔ first learned of it
and posthumously granted him Sànqí Chángshì.
Soon after, an imperial edict stated:
"The late Sànqí Chángshì, former Chóng'ān Xiàn Kāiguó Gōng Wénjì,
inherited the family legacy
and was able to uphold the family name.
He went to war at an early age;
though not the commander-in-chief,
he was the foremost in initiating action,
and his achievements were well-known.
However, having suffered a defeat on the battlefield,
it was fitting to reduce his rank.
But Língxǐ's establishment of meritorious defense and resistance
has long been remembered,
and Wénjì's burial in a foreign land
is indeed pitiable.
Remembering his past labors,
I am saddened by this abandonment.
It is proper to preserve his temple offerings,
so he does not starve.
He shall be demoted to Chóng'ān Xiàn Hóu,
with a fief of one thousand households,
and his son Xiǎng shall inherit the title."
The historian said: Chéng Língxǐ and his son both governed their subordinates with severity and harshness,
and commanded their troops with strict discipline.
However, they shared hardships with the multitude
and did not privatize wealth or profit,
so many soldiers relied on them.
Therefore, they were able to achieve victory in battle.
校勘記
列傳第五 黃法☴ 淳于量 章昭達
Huáng Fǎchǔ, courtesy name Zhòngzhāo,
was a native of Xīnjiàn, Bāshān.
In his youth, he was strong, agile, and courageous,
able to walk three hundred *lǐ* a day
and leap three *zhàng*.
He was quite proficient in writing official documents
and skilled in managing registers and accounts.
Coming and going in the commandery,
he was feared by his fellow villagers.
During Hóu Jǐng's Rebellion,
he gathered followers in his hometown.
When the Grand Administrator Hè Xǔ went down to Jiāngzhōu,
Fǎchǔ oversaw the affairs of the commandery.
When Gāozǔ was about to cross the mountains to come to the aid of Jiànyè,
Lǐ Qiānshì obstructed his path.
Gāozǔ ordered Zhōu Wényù to garrison at Xīchāng,
and Fǎchǔ dispatched troops to assist Wényù.
At that time, Fǎchǔ was stationed at Xīngàn County.
Hóu Jǐng sent his *xíngtái* Yú Qìng to Yùzhāng.
Yú Qìng divided his troops and came to attack Xīngàn.
Fǎchǔ resisted the attack
and defeated him.
Gāozǔ also sent Wényù to advance and attack Yú Qìng.
Wényù, suspecting that Yú Qìng's forces were strong,
did not dare to advance.
Fǎchǔ led his troops to join him,
then advanced and captured Shēngtún,
taking many prisoners.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng, acting by imperial authority, granted him the title of Chāoměng Jiāngjūn and the資 of Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ,
also holding the post of Xīngàn Xiànlìng,
and enfeoffed him as a Viscount of Bāshān County,
with three hundred households.
In the third year of Chéngshèng (554 CE),
he was appointed Míngwēi Jiāngjūn and Yóuqí Jiāngjūn,
and his noble rank was advanced to Marquis,
with five hundred households.
When the Marquis of Zhēnyáng usurped the throne,
he was appointed Zuǒxiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
Upon Emperor Jìng's ascension,
he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīnjiàn County,
with the same number of households as before.
In the first year of Tàipíng (556 CE),
four commanderies of Jiāngzhōu were separated to establish Gāozhōu.
Fǎchǔ was appointed Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Gāozhōu Zhūjūnjì, Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Gāozhōu Cìshǐ,
and garrisoned at Bāshān.
Xiāo Bó sent Ōuyáng Wěi to attack Fǎchǔ.
Fǎchǔ engaged him in battle
and defeated him.
In the second year of Yǒngdìng (558 CE),
Wáng Lín sent Lǐ Xiàoqīn, Fán Měng, and Yú Xiàoqǐng to attack Zhōu Dí,
and also planned to capture Fǎchǔ.
Fǎchǔ led his troops to reinforce Zhōu Dí
and captured Xiàoqǐng and two other generals.
He was promoted to the title of Xuānyì Jiāngjūn,
and his enfeoffment was increased to a total of one thousand households,
and he was granted one set of drums and pipes.
Also, for his merit in resisting Wáng Lín,
he was appointed Píngnán Jiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
When Xióng Tánlǎng rebelled at Jīnkǒu
and killed Zhōu Wényù,
Fǎchǔ and Zhōu Dí jointly attacked and pacified him.
The account is in the biography of Tánlǎng.
Upon Emperor Shìzǔ's succession,
he was promoted to the title of Ānnán Jiāngjūn.
In the second year of Tiānjia (561 CE),
Zhōu Dí rebelled.
Fǎchǔ led his troops to join the Grand Supervisor Wú Míngchè
and attacked Zhōu Dí at Gōngtáng.
After Zhōu Dí was pacified,
Fǎchǔ's merit was the greatest.
He was summoned to be Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Nánxúzhōu Zhūjūnjì, Zhènběi Dàjiāngjūn, and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the *yítóng* and drums and pipes remaining as before.
Before he could be formally installed,
he was again reassigned as Dūdū Jiāngwú Èrzhōu Zhūjūnjì, Zhènnán Dàjiāngjūn, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the sixth year (565 CE),
he was summoned to be Zhōngwèi Dàjiāngjūn.
Upon the abdicated emperor's accession,
he was promoted to the rank of Duke
and granted the privilege of imperial escort.
In the first year of Guāngdà (567 CE),
he was sent out as Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Nánxúzhōu Zhūjūnjì, Zhènběi Jiāngjūn, and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the second year (568 CE),
he was transferred to be Dūdū Yǐngbāwǔ Sānzhōu Zhūjūnjì, Zhènxī Jiāngjūn, and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the *chíjié* privilege remaining as before.
In the first year of Tàijiàn (569 CE),
he was promoted to the title of Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn.
In the second year (570 CE),
he was summoned to be Shìzhōng and Zhōngquán Dàjiāngjūn.
In the fourth year (572 CE),
he was sent out as Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Nányùzhōu Zhūjūnjì, Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn, and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the fifth year (573 CE),
a large-scale northern expedition was launched.
The Grand Supervisor Wú Míngchè marched out from Qínjùn,
and Fǎchǔ was appointed Grand Supervisor
to march out from Lìyáng.
The Qí dispatched their King of Lìyáng with fifty thousand cavalry and infantry to reinforce,
building a city at Xiǎoxiàn.
Fǎchǔ sent the General of the Left Guard Fán Yì to divide his forces and defend at Dàxiàn,
greatly defeating the Qí army
and capturing all their men, horses, and equipment.
Then, battering rams and pontoon bridges were constructed,
and the rams were deployed to press Lìyáng.
The people of Lìyáng, in distress, sought surrender.
Fǎchǔ delayed them,
whereupon they again held firm.
Fǎchǔ, angered,
personally led his soldiers to assault the city,
applying battering rams to its towers and battlements.
At that time, there was also heavy rain,
and the city walls collapsed.
He captured it
and executed all the garrisoned soldiers.
He advanced his troops to Héféi,
and they surrendered at the sight of his banner.
Fǎchǔ did not allow his soldiers to plunder,
personally comforted and rewarded them,
and made a treaty with them,
then sent them all back north.
For his merit, he was granted the additional title of Shìzhōng,
re-enfeoffed as Duke of Yìyáng Commandery,
with two thousand households.
In the same year,
he was promoted to Dūdū Héhuò Èrzhōu Zhūjūnjì, Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn, and Hézhōu Cìshǐ,
and his enfeoffment was increased by five hundred households.
In the seventh year (575 CE),
he was transferred to Dūdū Yùjiànguāngshuòhéběixú Liùzhōu Zhūjūnjì and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoned at Shòuyáng,
with Shìzhōng, Sànqí Chángshì, *chíjié*, general, *yítóng*, drums and pipes, and imperial escort all remaining as before.
In the tenth month of the eighth year (576 CE),
he passed away
at the age of fifty-nine.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng, Zhōngquán Dàjiāngjūn, and Sīkōng,
and given the posthumous name Wēi.
His son Wán succeeded him.
Chúnyú Liáng, courtesy name Sīmíng.
His ancestors were from Jìběi,
and his family had resided in the capital for generations.
His father, Wénchéng,
served Liáng as a general,
reaching the official positions of Guāngliè Jiāngjūn and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Liáng was skilled in self-management from a young age,
possessed a magnificent appearance,
had talent and strategy,
and was proficient in archery and horsemanship.
When Emperor Yuán of Liáng was the Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu,
Wénchéng allocated troops and horses to Liáng
and ordered him to serve there.
He began his career as Chángshì of the Kingdom of Xiāngdōng,
also serving concurrently as Zhōngbīng Cānjūn of the Xīzhōngláng government.
He was successively promoted to various governmental assistant positions, often concurrently holding the posts of Zhōngbīng and Zhíbīng for over ten years,
and his armed forces and soldiers
were numerous within the government.
At the border of Jīng and Yǒng,
the barbarians frequently rebelled,
and the mountain chieftain Wén Dàoqí accumulated into a border threat.
The *zhōngbīng* Wáng Sēngbiàn campaigned against him
but frequently suffered disadvantages in battle.
He sent Liáng to assist him.
When Liáng arrived,
he joined forces with Sēngbiàn
and greatly defeated Dàoqí,
executing his chieftains
and capturing tens of thousands of prisoners.
For his merit, he was enfeoffed as a Baron of Guǎngjìn County,
with three hundred households,
and appointed Fúlíng Tàishǒu.
He successively served as Grand Administrator of Xīnxīng and Wǔníng commanderies.
During Hóu Jǐng's Rebellion,
Emperor Yuán of Liáng sent a total of five armies to aid the capital,
and Liáng was part of one of them.
When Táichéng fell,
Liáng returned to Jīngzhōu.
Emperor Yuán, acting by imperial authority, appointed Liáng as Jiǎjié, Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Bāzhōu Zhūjūnjì, Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn, and Bāzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Hóu Jǐng marched west to attack Bāzhōu,
Emperor Yuán sent the Grand Supervisor Wáng Sēngbiàn to occupy Bālíng.
Liáng and Sēngbiàn jointly resisted Hóu Jǐng
and greatly defeated Hóu Jǐng's army,
capturing his general Rèn Yuē.
They then attacked Yǐngzhōu
and captured Sòng Zǐxiān.
Afterward, he followed Sēngbiàn to defeat and pacify Hóu Jǐng.
In the first year of Chéngshèng (552 CE),
for his merit, he was appointed Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Xièmù County,
with five hundred households.
Soon after, he was sent out as Chíjié, Dūdū Guìdìng Dōngxīníngděng Sìzhōu Zhūjūnjì, Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn, Ānyuǎn Hùjūn, and Guìzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Jīngzhōu fell,
Liáng protected and garrisoned Guìzhōu.
Wáng Lín held and divided Xiāng and Yǐng,
repeatedly sending for Liáng.
Outwardly, Liáng had dealings with Lín,
but secretly dispatched envoys through a hidden path to return to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ received the abdication,
and bestowed upon him the titles of Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, and Píngxī Dàjiāngjūn,
granting him one set of drums and pipes.
His positions as Dūdū and Cìshǐ remained as before.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zhènnán Jiāngjūn.
Then he was appointed Dūdū, Zhènxī Dàjiāngjūn, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
When Shìzǔ succeeded to the throne,
he was promoted to Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn.
After Wáng Lín was pacified,
he frequently requested to enter the court.
In the fifth year of Tiānjiā,
he was summoned as Zhōngfǔ Dàjiāngjūn;
his positions as Chángshì, Yítóng, and his drums and pipes remained as before.
Many of the generals and commanders under Liáng
were fond of their homelands,
and all wished to flee into the mountains and valleys,
unwilling to enter the court.
Shìzǔ sent Huá Jiǎo, the Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu, to campaign against the Huángdòng in the border area of Héngzhōu,
and also to bring troops to welcome Liáng.
In the first year of Tiānkāng,
he arrived at the capital.
Because of his delay on the journey,
he was impeached by the appropriate authorities,
and stripped of his Yítóng title,
while the rest remained as before.
In the first year of Guāngdà,
he was granted one set of drums and pipes.
When Huá Jiǎo instigated a rebellion,
Liáng was appointed Shǐchíjié, Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn, and Xītǎo Dàdūdū,
to lead a large fleet,
and from Fánpǔ in Yǐngzhōu, resist him.
After Jiǎo was pacified,
he also captured the Zhōu generals Chánghúgōng Tuòbá Dìng and others.
For his achievements, he was appointed Shìzhōng, Zhōngjūn Dàjiāngjūn, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
further enfeoffed as the Duke of Lǐlíng County,
with an increase of one thousand households to his fief.
Before he could accept the appointment,
he was dispatched as Shǐchíjié, Dūdū of all military affairs of Nánsúzhōu, Zhènběi Jiāngjūn, and Cìshǐ of Nánsúzhōu.
His positions as Shìzhōng, Yítóng, and his drums and pipes remained as before.
In the first year of Tàijiàn,
he was promoted to Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn,
and granted the privilege of Fú.
In the third year,
he was impeached for buying trees from Xiāo Jìqīng, Prince of Jiāngyīn, in the mausoleum of the Liáng dynasty.
Jìqīng was dismissed,
and Liáng was stripped of his Shìzhōng title.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Shìzhōng.
In the fifth year,
he was summoned as Zhōnghù Dàjiāngjūn;
his positions as Shìzhōng, Yítóng, his drums and pipes, and Fú remained as before.
When Wú Míngchè campaigned westward,
Liáng supported the endeavor,
sending his sixth son, Cén, to lead his subordinates and join the army.
After Huáinán was conquered and pacified,
Liáng was re-enfeoffed as the Duke of Shǐ'ān Commandery,
with an increase of one thousand five hundred households to his fief.
In the sixth year,
he was dispatched as Shǐchíjié, Dūdū of all military affairs of Yǐng, Bā, Nánsī, and Dìng four prefectures, Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn, and Cìshǐ of Yǐngzhōu.
His positions as Shìzhōng, Yítóng, his drums and pipes, and Fú remained as before.
In the seventh year,
he was summoned as Zhōngjūn Dàjiāngjūn and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the ninth year,
he was stripped of his Shìzhōng title due to public affairs.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Shìzhōng.
In the tenth year,
when Wú Míngchè was captured and fell,
Liáng was granted the additional title of Shǐchíjié, Dūdū of all land and naval military affairs,
and then appointed Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū of all military affairs of Nánxǔn, Qíao, and Sān prefectures, Chēqí Jiāngjūn, and Cìshǐ of Nánxǔnzhōu.
The rest remained as before.
In the thirteenth year,
he was granted the additional title of Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū,
with an increase of five hundred households to his fief.
The rest remained as before.
In the fourth month of the fourteenth year, he died,
at the age of seventy-two.
He was posthumously granted the title of Sīkōng.
Zhāng Zhāodá, courtesy name Bótōng,
was a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
His grandfather, Dàogài,
was the Prefect of Guǎngpíng during the Qí dynasty.
His father, Fǎshàng,
was the Yìcáo Cóngshì of Yángzhōu during the Liáng dynasty.
Zhāodá was uninhibited by nature,
lightly regarding wealth and valuing spirit.
When he was young,
he once met a physiognomist
who told Zhāodá:
"Your appearance is very good,
but it needs a slight imperfection,
then you will attain wealth and nobility."
During the Dàtóng era of the Liáng dynasty,
Zhāodá was a Zhíhòu of the Eastern Palace.
He fell from his horse while drunk,
sustaining a minor injury to his temples.
Zhāodá was pleased by this,
but the physiognomist said,
"Not yet."
When the Hóu Jǐng rebellion broke out,
Zhāodá led recruited villagers to assist Tái Chéng.
He was struck by a stray arrow,
losing sight in one eye.
When the physiognomist saw this,
he said,
"Your physiognomy is now excellent;
you will soon be noble."
When the capital fell,
Zhāodá returned to his hometown.
He befriended Shìzǔ,
thereby establishing the bond between sovereign and subject.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Shìzǔ became the Prefect of Wúxīng.
Zhāodá came to pay his respects to Shìzǔ with a staff.
Shìzǔ was greatly pleased to see him,
and entrusted him with military command.
His favor and grace were abundant,
surpassing his peers.
When Gāozǔ campaigned against Wáng Sēngbiàn,
he ordered Shìzǔ to return to Chángchéng to gather troops,
to prepare against Dù Kǎn.
He frequently sent Zhāodá to Jīngkǒu
to receive plans.
After Sēngbiàn was executed,
Kǎn sent his general Dù Tài to attack Chángchéng.
Shìzǔ resisted him,
and ordered Zhāodá to oversee all military affairs within the city.
After Dù Tài retreated,
he followed Shìzǔ eastward,
stationing his army in Wúxīng,
to campaign against Dù Kǎn.
After Kǎn was pacified,
he again followed Shìzǔ eastward to campaign against Zhāng Biāo in Kuàijī,
and conquered him.
For his accumulated merits, he was appointed Míngwēi Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Dìngzhōu.
At this time, Liú Yì held and occupied Dōngyáng,
privately appointing officials.
Gāozǔ was troubled by this,
so he appointed Zhāodá as the Magistrate of Chángshān County,
placing him at the heart of the matter.
In the second year of Yǒngdìng,
he was appointed Magistrate of Wǔkāng.
When Shìzǔ succeeded to the throne,
he was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì.
In the first year of Tiānjiā,
commemorating his achievements at Chángchéng,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xīnlè County,
with a fief of one thousand households.
Soon after, he followed Hóu Āndū and others to resist Wáng Lín at Zhákǒu,
and fought at Wúhú.
Zhāodá rode a Pínglǔ grand warship,
advancing in the middle of the river.
His vanguard launched catapults which struck the enemy ships.
After Wáng Lín was pacified,
Zhāodá was ranked first in merit.
In the second year,
he was appointed Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū of all military affairs of Yǐng, Bā, Wǔ, and Yuán four prefectures, Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Cìshǐ of Yǐngzhōu,
with an increase of one thousand five hundred households to his fief, including the previous amount.
Soon after, he was promoted to Píngxī Jiāngjūn.
Zhōu Dí (周迪) fortified Línchuān (臨川) and rebelled.
An imperial edict ordered Zhāo Dá (昭達) to proceed directly to suppress him.
After Dí (迪) was defeated and fled,
Zhāo Dá (昭達) was appointed Protector-General (護軍將軍),
granted a full complement of drums and pipes (鼓吹一部),
re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Shàowǔ County (邵武縣侯),
with an additional five hundred households, totaling two thousand households including the previous grant,
and retained his position as Palace Attendant (常侍).
In the fourth year,
Chén Bǎo’yīng (陳寶應) gave refuge to Zhōu Dí (周迪),
and together they again attacked Línchuān (臨川).
Zhāo Dá (昭達) was again appointed Grand Controller (都督) to suppress Dí (迪).
Upon reaching Dōngxīng Ridge (東興嶺),
Dí (迪) again retreated.
Zhāo Dá (昭達) then crossed the ridge,
encamping at Jiàn’ān (建安),
to campaign against Chén Bǎo’yīng (陳寶應).
Bǎo’yīng (寶應) held the border between Jiàn’ān (建安) and Jìn’ān (晉安) commanderies,
erecting stockades by water and land
to resist the imperial army.
Zhāo Dá (昭達) fought a battle but was unsuccessful.
He then occupied the upper reaches of the river,
ordering his soldiers to cut down trees with branches and leaves to make rafts,
placing boards on top of them,
and connecting them with large ropes,
arraying camps one after another,
along both banks.
Bǎo’yīng (寶應) challenged him to battle several times,
but Zhāo Dá (昭達) kept his troops still.
Soon, there was a heavy rain,
and the river water rose greatly.
Zhāo Dá (昭達) released the rafts to crash into Bǎo’yīng’s (寶應) water stockade,
completely destroying it.
He then sent out troops to attack Bǎo’yīng’s (寶應) infantry.
As a great battle was about to take place,
coincidentally Shìzǔ (世祖) dispatched Yú Xiàoqǐng (余孝頃) by sea.
They arrived just then,
and joining forces, they attacked.
Bǎo’yīng’s (寶應) forces suffered a great defeat,
and thus Mǐnzhōng (閩中) was pacified,
and Líu Yì (留異), Bǎo’yīng (寶應), and others were all captured.

For his accomplishments, he was granted the title of General Who Guards the Front (鎮前將軍) and given the privilege of establishing an administration with the same ranking as the Three Ducal Ministers (開府儀同三司).
Previously,
Shìzǔ (世祖) had once dreamed of Zhāo Dá (昭達) ascending to the pinnacle of power,
and at dawn,
he told Zhāo Dá (昭達) of the dream.
Now, at a banquet,
Shìzǔ (世祖) looked at Zhāo Dá (昭達) and said:
"Do you remember the dream?
How will you repay the dream?"
Zhāo Dá (昭達) replied:
"I shall serve with the utmost diligence,
fulfilling my duties as a subject.
Beyond this, I have nothing to offer in return."

Soon after, he was again appointed Bearer of Credential, Grand Controller of Military Affairs of Jiāng (江), Yǐng (郢), and Wú (吳) Three Prefectures (使持節、都督江郢吳三州諸軍事), General Who Guards the South (鎮南將軍), and Governor of Jiāng Prefecture (江州刺史),
with his positions as Palace Attendant (常侍), Counselor-in-chief (儀同), and the drum and pipe ensemble (鼓吹) remaining as before.
When Fèidì (廢帝) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Palace Attendant (侍中) and General Who Suppresses the South (征南將軍),
and re-enfeoffed as Duke of Shàolíng Commandery (邵陵郡公).
When Huá Jiǎo (華皎) rebelled,
his letters and manifestos
all falsely claimed to act in Zhāo Dá’s (昭達) name.
He also repeatedly sent envoys to entice him.
Zhāo Dá (昭達) captured all of these envoys
and sent them to the capital.
After Jiǎo (皎) was pacified,
Zhāo Dá (昭達) was promoted to Grand General Who Suppresses the South (征南大將軍),
and his fief was increased by two thousand five hundred households, including the previous grant.
After his term of office,
he was summoned to be Grand General of Middle Pacification (中撫大將軍),
with his positions as Palace Attendant (侍中), Counselor-in-chief (儀同), and the drum and pipe ensemble (鼓吹) remaining as before.
When Gāozōng (高宗) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry (車騎大將軍).
Because he was slow in returning to court,
he was impeached by the appropriate officials,
and his title was demoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry (車騎將軍).
When Ōuyáng Hé (歐陽紇) rebelled in Língnán (嶺南),
an imperial edict commanded Zhāo Dá (昭達) to be the Grand Controller of all armies to suppress him.
Zhāo Dá (昭達) marched day and night with double speed,
reaching Shǐxīng (始興).
When Hé (紇) heard that Zhāo Dá (昭達) had arrived suddenly,
he was terrified and did not know what to do.
So he moved his camp to Kuāngkǒu (洭口),
gathering a large quantity of sand and stones,
filling them in bamboo cages,
and placing them outside his water stockade,
to block boats and ships.
Zhāo Dá (昭達) positioned his forces upstream,
constructing battering rams and assault rafts,
to attack the enemy stockade.
He also ordered his soldiers to hold knives in their mouths
and dive underwater
to cut the bamboo cages.
The bamboo strips of the cages all broke apart.
He then unleashed large ships to charge downstream,
and the enemy forces were utterly defeated.
He consequently captured Hé (紇)
and sent him to the capital,
and Guǎngzhōu (廣州) was pacified.
For his accomplishments, he was promoted to Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry (車騎大將軍),
and transferred to Minister of Works (司空),
with all other positions remaining as before.
In the second year of Tàijiàn (太建) (570 CE),
he led an army to attack Xiāo Kuí (蕭巋) at Jiānglíng (江陵).
At that time, Xiāo Kuí (蕭巋) and the Zhōu (周) army had amassed a large number of boats and ships in Qīngní (青泥).
Zhāo Dá (昭達) dispatched his subordinate generals Qián Dàojí (錢道戢) and Chéng Wénjì (程文季) and others,
to attack them with light boats,
burning their boats and ships.
The Zhōu (周) army also built a fortified camp on the south bank below the gorges,
named Ānshǔ City (安蜀城),
and stretched a large rope across the river,
weaving rafts to form a bridge,
to transport military provisions.
Zhāo Dá (昭達) then ordered his soldiers to make long poles (長 ),
placing them on top of tower ships,
and cutting the rope from below.
The rope broke, cutting off their provisions.
He then unleashed his troops to attack the city,
and it surrendered.
In the third year (571 CE),
he fell ill
and died,
at the age of fifty-four.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand General (大將軍),
his fief was increased by five hundred households,
and twenty ceremonial sword-bearers were provided.
Zhāo Dá (昭達) was strict and severe by nature.
Whenever he was ordered to go on campaign,
he would always double his marching speed day and night.
However, whenever he achieved victory,
he would always attribute the success to his generals and commanders.
His meals and drinks
were always the same as those of his subordinates,
and the officers and soldiers were therefore attached to him.
At every banquet,
he would always provide elaborate performances by female musicians and various entertainments,
fully showcasing the music of Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) peoples,
with their melodies and beauty
being the finest of their time.
Even when facing the enemy,
with banners and drums visible to each other,
he would not forgo these performances.
In the fourth year (572 CE),
he was granted the honor of being enshrined in Shìzǔ’s (世祖) ancestral temple.
His son, Dàbǎo (大寶),
inherited the title of Duke of Shàolíng Commandery (邵陵郡公),
and successively held offices up to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (散騎常侍) and Protector-General (護軍).
He was appointed Governor of Fēng Prefecture (豐州).
While in the prefecture, he was greedy and indulgent,
and the common people deeply resented him.
The Later Lord (後主) replaced him with the Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud (太僕卿) Lǐ Yūn (李暈).
In the fourth month of the third year of Zhìdé (至德) (585 CE),
when Yūn (暈) was about to arrive at the prefecture,
Dàbǎo (大寶) ambushed and killed Yūn (暈),
raising an army in rebellion.
He sent his general Yáng Tōng (楊通) to attack Jiàn’ān (建安).
Wú Huìjué (吳慧覺), the Internal Scribe of Jiàn’ān (建安), defended the commandery city,
and Tōng (通) attacked repeatedly but could not conquer it.
As the imperial army gradually approached,
popular sentiment became divided.
Dàbǎo (大寶), at his wit's end,
fled with Tōng (通).
The palace army commander Chén Jǐngxiáng (陳景詳) led troops to pursue Dàbǎo (大寶).
After Dàbǎo (大寶) entered the mountains,
the mountain paths were steep and dangerous,
and he could no longer proceed.
Tōng (通) carried him on his back,
moving forward slowly.
Soon, they were overtaken by the pursuing soldiers,
captured alive and sent to the capital.
Dàbǎo (大寶) died on the way,
and his head was sent and displayed at the Zhuquè Bridge (朱雀航).
His entire clan was exterminated.
The court historian said: Huáng Fǎlì (黃法☴) and Chúnyú Liàng (淳于量) lived in the chaotic period at the end of the Liáng (梁) dynasty.
At a time when Lúi (劉) and Xiàng (項) had not yet decisively distinguished themselves,
few were able to clearly discern right from wrong.
These two dukes understood the principles of allegiance and defection,
and rose to the position of the Three Ducal Ministers (鼎司).
This was their wisdom.
Zhāo Dá (昭達) and Shìzǔ (世祖) were from the same locality and were old friends,
their righteousness was like that of Dèng (鄧) and Xiāo (蕭).
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he entrusted Zhāo Dá (昭達) with heavy responsibilities.
As for his victories in battle and successful conquests,
repeatedly pacifying rebellious difficulties,
he was indeed a good minister and a good general,
the Wú (吳) and Gěng (耿) of his generation.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 6: Hú Yǐng (胡穎), Xú Dù (徐度) (son Jìngchéng (敬成)), Dù Léng (杜稜), Shěn Kè (沈恪).
Hú Yǐng, courtesy name Fāngxiù,
was a native of Dōngqiān in Wúxīng.
His ancestors sojourned in Wúxīng,
and were settled as commoners.
Yǐng had a magnificent appearance,
and was broad-minded and generous by nature.
During the Liáng dynasty, he served as Attendant-in-ordinary of Wǔlíng Commandery,
and Guard of the Eastern Palace.
He went out to Pānyú
to suppress the Lǐ caves.
When Gāozǔ was the Grand Protector of the Western River in Guǎngzhōu,
Yǐng then personally befriended Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ, being from the same commandery as him,
treated him with great respect.
When the southern expedition to Jiāozhǐ took place,
Yǐng followed in the campaign,
and all other generals and commanders were inferior to him.
When Lǐ Bēn was pacified,
Gāozǔ returned with his army.
Yǐng was attached to the Western River command,
and was often left in charge when troops were dispatched.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Gāozǔ defeated Yuán Jǐngzhòng,
then crossed the mountain range to relieve Tái,
and pacified Cài Lùyǎng and Lǐ Qiānshì.
Yǐng had accomplishments in all of these.
He successively served as Magistrate of Pínggù and Suìxīng counties.
When Gāozǔ advanced his army to Dùn Xīchāng,
he appointed Yǐng as Magistrate of Bāqiū County,
stationed at Dàgāo,
to supervise grain transport.
When they advanced to Yùzhāng,
he appointed Yǐng as Supervisor of Yùzhāng Commandery.
Gāozǔ led his forces to meet Wáng Sēngbiàn at Báimáo Wān,
to jointly suppress Hóu Jǐng,
and appointed Yǐng to manage the affairs of the remaining headquarters.
In the early Chéngshèng reign of Liáng,
Emperor Yuán conferred upon Yǐng the titles of Jiǎjié, Iron Cavalry General, and Governor of Luózhōu,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Hànyáng County,
with an estate of five hundred households.
Soon after, he was appointed Internal Historian of Yùzhāng,
and followed Gāozǔ to guard Jīngkǒu.
When Qí sent Guō Yuánjiàn out of the pass,
Grand Commander Hóu Zhèn led his army to resist him.
Gāozǔ selected three thousand brave and fierce men from his headquarters to be assigned to Yǐng,
ordering him to follow Zhèn,
and they decisively defeated (Yuánjiàn) him at Dōngguān.
In the third year,
Gāozǔ besieged Guǎnglíng.
Dōngfāng Guāng of Qí, who was holding Sùyù, requested to surrender.
Yǐng was appointed Grand Protector of Wǔyuán,
and followed Dù Sēngmíng to relieve Guāng,
but was unsuccessful,
and returned.
He was then appointed Magistrate of Qǔ'ā.
Soon after, he took command of the cavalry,
and followed Gāozǔ to attack Wáng Sēngbiàn.
He then followed Zhōu Wényù to Wúxīng to suppress Dù Kān.
In the first year of Shàotài,
he was appointed Jiǎjié, Grand Commander of Military Affairs of Nányùzhōu, Light Chariot General, and Governor of Nányùzhōu.
In the first year of Tàipíng,
he was appointed Chíjié, Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary, and Rénwēi General.
Soon after, he concurrently served as Governor of Dānyáng.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he concurrently served as Left Guard General,
with other appointments remaining as before.
In the third year of Yǒngdìng,
he followed Hóu Āndū to campaign against Wáng Lín,
and defeated the bandit leader Cháng Zhòng'ài and others at Gōngtíng.
When Shìzǔ succeeded to the throne,
he was appointed Attendant-in-ordinary, Grand Commander of Military Affairs of Wúzhōu, Xuānhuì General, and Governor of Wúzhōu.
He did not proceed to the post,
but was soon made Grand Protector of Yìxīng,
with his general title remaining as before.
In the first year of Tiānjia,
he was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary and Grand Protector of Wúxīng.
He died in the sixth month of that year,
at the age of fifty-four.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Attendant-in-ordinary and Central Protector General,
and given the posthumous name Zhuàng.
In the second year,
he was honored with a place in Gāozǔ's ancestral temple.
His son Liù Tóng succeeded him.
Yǐng's younger brother, Shuò,
also followed Yǐng as a general.
When Yǐng died,
Shuò took command of his troops.
He successively served as Grand Protector of Dōnghǎi and Yùzhāng commanderies,
and was promoted to Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary.
He followed Zhāng Zhāodá to pacify Ōuyáng Hè in the south,
and became Grand Protector of the Eastern River in Guǎngzhōu.
Upon his return, he participated in the northern expedition,
and was appointed Xióngxìn General and Grand Protector of Lìyáng.
He died in the sixth year of Tàijiàn,
and was posthumously granted the title of Governor of Guìzhōu.
Xú Dù, courtesy name Xiàojié,
was a native of Ānlù.
His family had resided in the capital for generations.
In his youth, he was unrestrained
and did not bother with minor details.
As he grew older,
he had a remarkable and imposing appearance.
He enjoyed wine and gambling,
and always had his servants butcher and sell alcohol.
When Xiāo Jiè, the Internal Historian of Shǐxīng of Liáng, was in his commandery,
Dù followed him,
leading soldiers
to campaign against various mountain tribes,
and became known for his bravery.
When Gāozǔ campaigned against Jiāozhǐ,
he cordially invited him,
and Dù then pledged his allegiance.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Gāozǔ pacified Guǎngzhōu,
subdued Cài Lùyǎng,
and defeated Lǐ Qiānshì.
Many of the plans originated from Dù.
He also commanded the army,
and achieved merits in every battle.
Upon returning to Báimáo Wān,
Emperor Yuán of Liáng conferred upon him the titles of Níngshuò General and Governor of Hézhōu.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
his past and present military achievements were recognized,
and he was promoted to Palace Assistant Remonstrant,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Guǎngdé County,
with an estate of five hundred households.
He was promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary.
When Gāozǔ was stationed at Zhūfāng,
he was appointed Xìnwǔ General and Grand Protector of Lánlíng.
Gāozǔ sent Prince Xiàn of Héngyáng to pacify Jīngzhōu,
and Dù led his subordinates to follow him.
When Jiānglíng fell,
he secretly returned east.
When Gāozǔ pacified Wáng Sēngbiàn,
Dù and Hóu Āndū commanded the naval forces.
In the first year of Shàotài,
when Gāozǔ campaigned east against Dù Kān,
he escorted Emperor Jìng to Jīngkǒu,
and appointed Dù to lead the imperial guards,
and also manage the affairs of the remaining headquarters.
When Xú Sìhuī, Rèn Yuē and others attacked,
Gāozǔ and Emperor Jìng returned to the capital.
At that time, the rebels had already occupied Shítóu City,
and the residents of the city
were all on the southern road,
far from the palace.
Fearing that they would be exploited by the rebels,
Dù was sent to lead troops to guard Yěchéng Temple,
and built fortifications to cut off the rebels.
The rebels attacked with all their forces,
but could not prevail.
Gāozǔ also soon came to relieve them,
and decisively defeated Yuē and others.
The following year,
Sìhuī and others again led Qí invaders across the Jiāng River.
Dù followed the various armies and defeated them at the Northern Suburban Altar.
For his merits, he was appointed Xìnwēi General and Governor of Yǐngzhōu,
concurrently holding the title of Grand Protector of Wúxīng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zhèn Yòu General, Commander of the Imperial Army, Supervisor of various military affairs along the Jiāng River in Xúzhōu,
Zhèn Běi General, and Governor of Nánxúzhōu,
and was granted a set of drums and pipes.
When Zhōu Wényù, Hóu Āndū and others campaigned west against Wáng Lín,
they were defeated
and captured by Lín.
Dù was then appointed Grand Commander of the Vanguard,
stationed at Nánlíng.
When Shìzǔ succeeded to the throne,
he was promoted to Attendant-in-ordinary, Central Pacification General, and Administrator of the Imperial Household with the Three Divisions,
and elevated to the rank of Duke.
Before he was invested,
he was sent out as Envoy with Credentials, Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary, Zhèndōng General, and Grand Protector of Wújùn.
In the first year of Tiānjia,
his estate was increased by a thousand households.
For his merits in pacifying Wáng Lín,
he was restyled Duke of Xiāngdōng Commandery,
with an estate of four thousand households.
Upon the completion of his term,
he became Attendant-in-ordinary and Central Army General.

He was sent out as Envoy with Credentials, Grand Commander of military affairs of Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Línhǎi, Yǒngjiā, Xīn'ān, Xīnníng, Xìn'ān, Jìn'ān, and Jiàn'ān commanderies (nine commanderies), Zhèndōng General, and Grand Protector of Kuàijī.
Before he departed, Grand Preceptor Hóu Zhèn died in Xiāngzhōu.
Dù was then appointed to replace Zhèn as Grand Commander of military affairs of Xiāng, Yuán, Wǔ, Bā, Yǐng, and Guì commanderies (six commanderies), Zhènnán General, and Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
Upon the completion of his term,
he became Attendant-in-ordinary and Grand Central Army General,
with his ceremonial privileges and drums and pipes remaining as before.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) passed away,
Dù Yù (度預) was given a deathbed commission.
He entered the palace with fifty armored guards.
When Fèi Dì (廢帝) ascended the throne,
Dù Yù was promoted to Sīkōng (司空).
Huá Jiǎo (華皎) rebelled, taking command of Xiāngzhōu (湘州),
and led Zhōu (周) troops down to Dùnkǒu (沌口),
where they stood in confrontation with the imperial army.
Dù Yù was then granted the titles of Shǐchíjié (使持節) and Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍),
and made overall commander of the infantry.
He set out from Ānchéng Jùn (安成郡) along the mountain road, emerging east of Xiāng (湘) river,
to attack Xiāngzhōu (湘州).
He captured all the military families left behind there and returned with them.
He passed away in Guāngdà (光大) second year,
at the age of sixty.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi (太尉),
provided with twenty guards bearing ceremonial swords,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngsù (忠肅).
In Tàijiàn (太建) fourth year,
he was enshrined in Gāozǔ’s (高祖) ancestral temple.
His son Jìngchéng (敬成) succeeded him.
Jìngchéng was intelligent in his youth,
fond of reading,
quick-witted in his early years,
skilled in conversation,
and befriended literary scholars.
He became renowned for his discernment.
He began his career as a Zhùzuò Láng (著作郎).
In Yǒngdìng (永定) first year,
he commanded the soldiers of Dù Yù’s (度) former division
and followed Zhōu Wényù (周文育) and Hóu Āndū (侯安都) to campaign against Wáng Lín (王琳).
They were defeated at Dùnkǒu (沌口)
and captured by Wáng Lín.
In the second year,
he returned with Wényù (文育) and Āndū (安都),
and was appointed Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人),
then promoted to Xǐmǎ (洗馬).
(Jìngchéng’s (敬成) father) Dù Yù (度) was Wú Jùn (吳郡) Tàishǒu (太守),
and appointed Jìngchéng (敬成) as Supervisor of the Commandery.
In Tiānjiā (天嘉) second year,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén (太子中舍人),
and granted the title of Hereditary Prince of Xiāngdōng Jùn Gōng (湘東郡公).
In the fourth year,
when Dù Yù (度) returned to court from Xiāngzhōu (湘州)
with his elite cavalry and infantry,
Jìngchéng (敬成) took full command of his troops.
He followed Zhāng Zhāodá (章昭達) to campaign against Chén Bǎoyìng (陳寶應),
pacified Jìn’ān (晉安),
and was appointed Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn (貞威將軍) and Yùzhāng Tàishǒu (豫章太守).
In Guāngdà (光大) first year,
when Huá Jiǎo (華皎) plotted rebellion,
Jìngchéng (敬成) was appointed Jiǎjié (假節), Dūdū Bāzhōu Zhū Jūnfàn (都督巴州諸軍事), Yúnqí Jiāngjūn (雲旗將軍), and Bāzhōu Cìshǐ (巴州刺史).
Soon after, an imperial edict made him commander of the naval forces,
to follow Wú Míngchè (吳明徹) in the campaign against Huá Jiǎo (華皎).
After Jiǎo (皎) was pacified, he returned to his prefecture.
In Tàijiàn (太建) second year,
he resigned from office due to his father's passing.
Soon, he was reinstated as Chíjié (持節), Dūdū Nányùzhōu Zhū Jūnfàn (都督南豫州諸軍事), Zhuàngwǔ Jiāngjūn (壯武將軍), and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ (南豫州刺史).
In the fourth year,
he inherited the title of Xiāngdōng Jùn Gōng (湘東郡公),
and was appointed Tàizǐ Yòuwèishuài (太子右衞率).
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn (貞威將軍) and Wúxīng Tàishǒu (吳興太守).
That same year, he followed Dūdū Wú Míngchè (吳明徹) on a northern expedition,
departing from Qín Jùn (秦郡).
Jìngchéng (敬成) was separately dispatched as Dūdū (都督),
sailing on a 'Golden Wing' from Ōuyáng (歐陽) to ascend the river via the dyke from Guǎnglíng (廣陵).
The Qí (齊) people all remained within their city walls,
not daring to venture out.
He then sailed down the Huái (淮) River from Fánliáng Hú (繁梁湖),
and besieged Huái’yīn Chéng (淮陰城).
He also supervised Běi Yùnzhōu (北運州).
The volunteers from Huái (淮) and Sì (泗) rallied and responded to him,
and within one or two days,
his forces grew to tens of thousands.
He then captured the three commanderies of Huái’yīn (淮陰), Shānyáng (山陽), and Yánchéng (鹽城),
along with the two garrisons of Liánkǒu (連口) and Qúshān (朐山).
He then advanced to attack Yùzhōu (鬱州),
and conquered it.
For his achievements, he was promoted to Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍) and Yúnqí Jiāngjūn (雲旗將軍),
and his enfeoffment was increased by five hundred households.
He was further granted the title of Zhuàngwǔ Jiāngjūn (壯武將軍)
and stationed at Qúshān (朐山).
Due to an arbitrary levy and
the execution of recent surrenderers in the army,
he was dismissed from office.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Chíjié (持節), Dūdū Ān Yuán Tóng Sānzhōu Zhū Jūnfàn (都督安元潼三州諸軍事), and Ānzhōu Cìshǐ (安州刺史),
his general's title remaining as before,
and stationed at Sùyù (宿預).
He died in the seventh year,
at the age of thirty-six.
He was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
and given the posthumous name Sī (思).
His son Chǎng (敞) succeeded him.
Dù Léng (杜稜), courtesy name Xióngshèng (雄盛),
was a native of Qiántáng (錢塘) in Wú Jùn (吳郡).
His family had for generations been a prominent local clan.
Léng (稜) had considerable knowledge of books and historical records,
but in his youth, he was somewhat unrefined
and not recognized by his contemporaries.
He then traveled to Lǐngnán (嶺南),
serving Xiāo Yǐng (蕭暎), the Marquis of Xīnyú (新渝) and Liáng (梁) Governor of Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
After Yǐng (暎) died,
he followed Gāozǔ (高祖)
and consistently managed his secretarial affairs.
During Hóu Jǐng’s (侯景) rebellion,
Léng (稜) was ordered to lead troops
and achieved merit in pacifying Cài Lùyǎng (蔡路養) and Lǐ Qiānshì (李遷仕).
When the army reached Yùzhāng (豫章),
Emperor Yuán (元帝) of Liáng (梁), acting under imperial authority, appointed Léng (稜) as Rénwēi Jiāngjūn (仁威將軍) and Shízhōu Cìshǐ (石州刺史),
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Shàngmò Xiàn (上陌縣),
with eight hundred households.
After Hóu Jǐng (侯景) was suppressed,
Gāozǔ (高祖) was stationed at Zhūfāng (朱方),
and Léng (稜) supervised the two commanderies of Yìxīng (義興) and Lángyé (琅邪).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) decided to execute Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯),
he invited Léng (稜) to discuss the matter with Hóu Āndū (侯安都) and others.
Léng (稜) expressed reservations.
Fearing that Léng (稜) might leak the plan, Gāozǔ (高祖)
strangled Léng (稜) with a hand towel,
causing Léng (稜) to collapse unconscious.
He was then confined to a separate room.
When the army set out,
he was summoned to join them.
After Sēngbiàn (僧辯) was pacified,
Gāozǔ (高祖) campaigned eastward against Dù Kān (杜龕) and others,
leaving Léng (稜) and Āndū (安都) to guard the capital.
Xú Sìhuī (徐嗣徽) and Rèn Yuē (任約) led Qí (齊) invaders across the Yangtze River,
attacking Táichéng (臺城).
Āndū (安都) and Léng (稜) resisted them from all sides.
Léng (稜) patrolled day and night,
pacifying and reassuring the soldiers,
never once taking off his belt.
After the rebels were suppressed,
for his achievements, he was appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍), Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (右衛將軍), and Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹).
In Yǒngdìng (永定) first year,
he was given the additional titles of Shìzhōng (侍中) and Zhōngwǔ Jiāngjūn (忠武將軍).
Soon after, he was promoted to Zhōnglǐngjūn (中領軍) and
Shìzhōng (侍中),
his general's title remaining as before.
In the third year,
Gāozǔ (高祖) passed away,
and Shìzǔ (世祖) was in Nánwǎn (南皖).
At that time, there was no legitimate heir within the court,
and strong enemies threatened from outside.
Hóu Tián (侯瑱), Hóu Āndū (侯安都), Xú Dù (徐度), and others were all with the army.
Among the veteran generals at court,
only Léng (稜) was in the capital,
solely commanding the palace guards.
He then, with Cài Jǐnglì (蔡景歷) and others, secretly concealed the news of the emperor's death
and welcomed Shìzǔ (世祖).
Details are found in Jǐnglì’s (景歷) biography.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
Léng (稜) was promoted to Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍).
In Tiānjiā (天嘉) first year,
for his contributions to the establishment of the new reign,
he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒngchéng Xiàn (永城縣),
with an additional five hundred households.
He was appointed Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn (雲麾將軍)
and Jìnlíng Tàishǒu (晉陵太守),
with his rank increased to Zhōng'èrqiānshí (中二千石).
In the second year,
he was summoned back as Shìzhōng (侍中) and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍).
Soon after, he was promoted to Yìzuǒ Jiāngjūn (翊左將軍) and Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹).
When Fèi Dì (廢帝) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zhènyòu Jiāngjūn (鎮右將軍) and Tèjìn (特進),
his Shìzhōng (侍中) and Yǐn (尹) titles remaining as before.
In Guāngdà (光大) first year,
he was relieved of the Yǐn (尹) duty,
given an appropriate number of assistant officials,
provided with palanquin bearers,
and re-appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍).
In Tàijiàn (太建) first year,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn (鎮東將軍), and Wúxīng Tàishǒu (吳興太守),
with a rank of Zhōng'èrqiānshí (中二千石).
In the second year,
he was summoned back as Shìzhōng (侍中) and Zhènyòu Jiāngjūn (鎮右將jūn).
Soon after, he was additionally granted Tèjìn (特進) and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (護軍將軍).
In the third year,
he was dismissed from Shìzhōng (侍中) and Hùjūn (護軍) due to an official matter.
In the fourth year,
he was reinstated as Shìzhōng (侍zhong) and Yòuguānglù Dàfū (右光祿大夫),
and also provided with a set of drums and pipes,
his general's title, assistant officials, and palanquin bearers all remaining as before.
Léng (稜) served three emperors
and was consistently favored.
In his later years, he was not involved in campaigns,
living comfortably in the capital,
with generous rewards and provisions.
He died in office shortly after,
at the age of seventy.
He was posthumously granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司),
and all necessary expenses for his funeral
were ordered to be covered.
He was given the posthumous name Chéng (成).
That same year, he was enshrined in Gāozǔ’s (高祖) ancestral temple.
His son Ānshì (安世) succeeded him.
Shěn Kè [沈恪], courtesy name Zǐgōng [子恭],
was a native of Wúxīng Wǔkāng [吳興武康].
He was profound and had administrative ability.
When Xiāo Yìng [蕭映], the Marquis of Xīnyú [新渝侯] of Liáng [梁], was the commander of the commandery,
he summoned Kè [恪] to be his zhǔbù [主簿] (chief clerk).
When Yìng [映] moved to Běixúzhōu [北徐州],
Kè [恪] followed Yìng [映] to his post.
When Yìng [映] moved to Guǎngzhōu [廣州],
he appointed Kè [恪] concurrently as his fǔzhōng bīngcānjūn [府中兵參軍] (military advisor of the staff),
and Kè [恪] often led troops to suppress the Lǐ [俚] tribes.
When Lú Zǐlüè [盧子略] rebelled,
Kè [恪] fought bravely and gained merit,
and was appointed zhōngbīng cānjūn [中兵參軍] (military advisor).
Gāozǔ [高祖] (Emperor Wǔ [武] of Chén [陳]) was from the same commandery as Kè [恪],
and their friendship was very close.
After Xiāo Yìng [蕭映] died,
Gāozǔ [高祖] campaigned south against Lǐ Bēn [李賁],
and sent his wife and children to return to their hometown under Kè [恪]'s care.
Soon after, he was appointed Dōnggōng Zhíhòu [東宮直後] (Palace Guard of the Eastern Palace).
For his merits in Lǐngnán [嶺南], he was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng [員外散騎侍郎] (Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant),
and was ordered to recruit his relatives and younger family members.
When Hóu Jǐng [侯景] besieged Táichéng [臺城],
Kè [恪] led his subordinates into the city
and was promoted to Yòujūn Jiàngjūn [右軍將軍] (General of the Right Army) as was customary.
The rebels built two earthen mounds, east and west, to press the city,
and those inside the city also built earthen mounds to counter them.
Kè [恪] was in charge of the eastern earthen mound,
fighting day and night.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngxīng Xiàn [東興縣侯],
with a stipend of five hundred households.
He was promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì [員外散騎常侍] (Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary).
When the capital fell,
Kè [恪] secretly returned to his hometown.
When Gāozǔ [高祖] campaigned against Hóu Jǐng [侯景],
he sent an envoy to inform Kè [恪],
who then raised troops in the east to respond.
After the rebels were pacified,
Kè [恪] met Gāozǔ [高祖] in Jīngkǒu [京口],
and was immediately appointed Dūjūn Fù [都軍副] (Deputy Commander of the Army).
Soon after, he became Fǔ Sīmǎ [府司馬] (Chief Clerk of the Prefecture).
When Gāozǔ [高祖] planned to attack Wáng Sēngbiàn [王僧辯],
Kè [恪] participated in the plan.
At that time, Dù Kān [杜龕], Sēngbiàn [僧辯]'s son-in-law, was garrisoned in Wúxīng [吳興].
Gāozǔ [高祖] then sent Shìzǔ [世祖] (Emperor Wén [文] of Chén [陳]) back to Chángchéng [長城],
to build a palisade to defend against Kān [龕].
He also sent Kè [恪] back to Wǔkāng [武康]
to recruit soldiers.
When Sēngbiàn [僧辯] was executed,
Kān [龕] indeed sent his deputy Dù Tài [杜泰] to lead troops to attack Shìzǔ [世祖] at Chángchéng [長城].
Kè [恪] had already led his soldiers out of the county to punish Kān [龕]'s followers.
Gāozǔ [高祖] soon sent Zhōu Wényù [周文育] to reinforce Chángchéng [長城].
When Wényù [文育] arrived,
Tài [泰] fled.
Shìzǔ [世祖] then advanced with Wényù [文育] out of the commandery.
Kè [恪]'s army also arrived
and camped south of the commandery.
After Kān [龕] was pacified,
Shìzǔ [世祖] attacked Zhāng Biāo [張彪], the Inspector of Dōngyángzhōu [東揚州],
and appointed Kè [恪] to supervise Wúxīng Jùn [吳興郡].
In the first year of Tàipíng [太平] (556),
he was appointed Xuānměng Jiàngjūn [宣猛將軍] (General Who Declares Bravery) and Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ [交州刺史] (Inspector of Jiāozhōu).
In the same year, he was promoted to Yǒngjiā Tàishǒu [永嘉太守] (Administrator of Yǒngjiā).
He did not accept the appointment,
and was again ordered to supervise Wúxīng Jùn [吳興郡].
He traveled from Wúxīng [吳興] to the imperial court.
When Gāozǔ [高祖] accepted the abdication,
he sent Liú Shīzhī [劉師知], the Zhōngshū Shèrén [中書舍人] (Imperial Secretary), to summon Kè [恪],
ordering him to lead his troops to bid farewell,
and then to escort Emperor Jìng [敬] to a separate palace.
Kè [恪] then pushed open the palace gate and met Gāozǔ [高祖],
bowing his head and saying:
“Kè [恪] has personally served the Xiāo [蕭] family.
Today I cannot bear to see this happen.
I accept death,
and will certainly not obey the order.”
Gāozǔ [高祖] commended his intention,
and no longer pressured him,
instead replacing him with Wáng Sēngzhì [王僧志], a Dàngzhǔ [盪主].
When Gāozǔ [高祖] ascended the throne,
he appointed Kè [恪] Wúxīng Tàishǒu [吳興太守] (Administrator of Wúxīng).
In the second year of Yǒngdìng [永定] (558),
he was transferred to supervise Kuàijī Jùn [會稽郡].
When Yú Xiàoqǐng [余孝頃] plotted to assist Wáng Lín [王琳],
and sent troops to Línchuān [臨川] to attack Zhōu Dí [周迪],
Kè [恪] was made Zhuàngwǔ Jiàngjūn [壯武將軍] (General of Martial Valor),
and led troops across the mountains to rescue Dí [迪].
When Yú Xiàoqǐng [余孝頃] heard that Kè [恪] had arrived,
he retreated.
In the third year (559),

he was promoted to Shǐchíjié [使持節] (Bearer of Credentials), Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì [通直散騎常侍] (Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary), Zhìwǔ Jiàngjūn [智武將軍] (General of Wise Martiality), and Wúzhōu Cìshǐ [吳州刺史] (Inspector of Wúzhōu),
and proceeded to Póyáng [鄱陽].
Soon an imperial edict recalled him,
and he administered the affairs of Kuàijī Jùn [會稽郡].
In the same year,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì [散騎常侍] (Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary), Zhōngwǔ Jiàngjūn [忠武將軍] (General of Loyal Martiality), and Kuàijī Tàishǒu [會稽太守] (Administrator of Kuàijī).
When Shìzǔ [世祖] succeeded to the throne,
with his general and administrator titles remaining as before.
In the first year of Tiānjiā [天嘉] (560),
his stipend was increased by five hundred households.
In the second year (561),
he was recalled to serve as Zuǒwèi Jiàngjūn [左衛將軍] (General of the Left Guard).

Soon after, he was sent out as Dūdū Yǐngwǔbādìng Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnjūnshì [都督郢武巴定四州諸軍事] (Area Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of the four prefectures of Yǐng, Wǔ, Bā, and Dìng), Jūnshī Jiàngjūn [軍師將軍] (General of the Military Advisor), and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ [郢州刺史] (Inspector of Yǐngzhōu).
In the sixth year (565),
he was recalled to serve as Zhōnghùjūn [中護軍] (Central Protector of the Army).
Soon after, he was promoted to Hùjūn Jiàngjūn [護軍將軍] (Protector of the Army General).
In the second year of Guāngdà [光大] (568),

he was promoted to Shǐchíjié [使持節] (Bearer of Credentials), Dūdū Jīngwǔyòu Sānzhōu Zhū Jūnjūnshì [都督荊武祐三州諸軍事] (Area Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of the three prefectures of Jīng, Wǔ, and Yòu), Píngxī Jiàngjūn [平西將軍] (General Who Pacifies the West), and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ [荊州刺史] (Inspector of Jīngzhōu).
Before he arrived at his post,
he was changed to Hùjūn Jiàngjūn [護軍將軍] (Protector of the Army General).
When Gāozōng [高宗] (Emperor Xuān [宣] of Chén [陳]) ascended the throne,

he was additionally appointed Sànqí Chángshì [散騎常侍] (Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary), Dūdū Guǎnghéng Dōnghéng Jiāoyuèchéng Dìngxīnhé Luóàidéyíhuáng Lì'ānshí Shuāngděng Shíbāzhōu Zhū Jūnjūnshì [都督廣衡東衡交越成定新合羅愛德宜黃利安石雙等十八州諸軍事] (Area Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of the eighteen prefectures of Guǎng, Héng, Dōnghéng, Jiāo, Yuè, Chéng, Dìng, Xīn, Hé, Luó, Ài, Dé, Yí, Huáng, Lì, Ān, Shí, and Shuāng), Zhènnán Jiàngjūn [鎮南將軍] (General Who Guards the South), Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiàng [平越中郎將] (Gentleman-General Who Pacifies Yuè), and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ [廣州刺史] (Inspector of Guǎngzhōu).
Before Kè [恪] reached the mountains,
the former inspector Ōuyáng Hē [歐陽紇] raised an army to defend the passes,
so Kè [恪] could not advance.
The imperial court sent Sīkōng [司空] (Minister of Works) Zhāng Zhāodá [章昭達] to lead the combined armies to attack Hē [紇].
After Hē [紇] was pacified,
Kè [恪] was able to enter the prefecture.
The prefecture had suffered from war,
and was devastated everywhere.
Kè [恪] pacified and settled the people,
and bestowed favor and kindness upon them.
The Lǐngbiǎo [嶺表] region relied on him.
In the fourth year of Tàijiàn [太建] (572),
he was recalled to serve as Lǐngjūn Jiàngjūn [領軍將軍] (General Who Leads the Army).
When he was replaced and returned,
because the journey was long and he did not arrive on time,
he was impeached by the relevant authorities and dismissed.
In the eleventh year (579),
he was reappointed Sànqí Chángshì [散騎常侍] (Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary) and Wèiwèi Qīng [衞尉卿] (Minister of the Palace Guard).
In the same year, he was appointed Píngběi Jiàngjūn [平北將軍] (General Who Pacifies the North), was granted jiǎjié [假節] (authority to execute),
and supervised Nányùnzhōu [南贇州].
In the twelfth year (580),
he was reappointed Sànqí Chángshì [散騎常侍] (Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary) and Yìyòu Jiàngjūn [翊右將軍] (General Who Assists the Right),
and supervised Nánxúzhōu [南徐州].
He also sent Diànwēi Jiàngjūn [電威將軍] (General of Lightning Might) Péi Zǐliè [裴子烈] to lead five hundred horses
to assist Kè [恪] in defending the river along the banks.
The next year (581),
he entered the court to serve as Wèiwèi Qīng [衞尉卿] (Minister of the Palace Guard),
with his titles of Chángshì [常侍] and Jiàngjūn [將軍] remaining as before.
Soon after, he was additionally appointed Shìzhōng [侍中] (Palace Attendant),
and promoted to Hùjūn Jiàngjūn [護軍將軍] (Protector of the Army General).
When Hòuzhǔ [後主] (the Last Emperor of Chén [陳]) ascended the throne,

due to illness, he was changed to Sànqí Chángshì [散騎常侍] (Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary), Tèjìn [特進] (Special Advanced), and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū [金紫光祿大夫] (Grand Master of Golden Seals and Purple Ribbons).
In the same year, he died
at the age of seventy-four.
He was posthumously granted Yìzuǒ Jiàngjūn [翊左將軍] (General Who Assists the Left),
and an imperial edict provided secret burial artifacts from the Eastern Garden.
Furthermore, an official was sent to mourn,
and all necessities for the funeral
were provided.
His posthumous name was Yuán [元].
His son Fǎxīng [法興] inherited his title.
The historian remarks: Hú Yǐng [胡穎], Xú Dù [徐度], Dù Léng [杜稜], Shěn Kè [沈恪] all rode on swift steeds and soared,
relying on the brilliance of the sun and moon.
Only then did they encounter the talent of a king's assistant,
and only then did they realize the capacity of a Duke and Grand Tutor.
While alive, they enjoyed meat and wealth;
in death, they received sacrifices.
How glorious!
Collations and Notes
Biographies 7: Xú Shìpǔ [徐世譜] Rǔ Xīdá [魯悉達] Zhōu Fū [周敷] Xún Lǎng [荀朗] (Zǐfǎ Shàng [子法尚]) Zhōu Jiǒng [周炅]
Xú Shìpǔ [徐世譜], courtesy name Xīngzōng [興宗],
was a native of Bādōng Yúfù [巴東魚復].
His family had lived in Jīngzhōu [荊州] for generations,
serving as chief commanders,
campaigning against the Mán [蠻] and Yán [蜒] tribes.
By the time of Shìpǔ [世譜], he was particularly brave and strong,
and skilled in naval warfare.
When Emperor Yuán [元] of Liáng [梁] was the Inspector of Jīngzhōu [荊州],
Shìpǔ [世譜] commanded the local people and served him.
During the Hóu Jǐng zhī Luàn,
due to his participation in the campaigns,
he was successively promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì.
He soon took command of the navy
and followed Sītú Lù Fǎhé to attack Jǐng.
They fought Jǐng at Chìtíng Hú.
At that time, Jǐng's army was very strong,
so Shìpǔ additionally built tower-ships, ramming-ships, fire-rafts, and water-vehicles to augment his forces.
Before the battle,
he again sailed a large ship at the front,
utterly defeating Jǐng's army,
and capturing Jǐng's general Rèn Yuē alive.
Jǐng retreated and fled.
Following Wáng Sēngbiàn to attack Yǐngzhōu,
Shìpǔ again sailed a large ship to its warehouse gate.
The rebel general Sòng Zǐxiān surrendered, holding the city.
For his accomplishments, he was appointed Shǐchíjié, Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, Xìnzhōu Cìshǐ,
and ennobled as the Marquis of Yúfù Xiàn,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
He then followed Sēngbiàn eastward
and always served as the vanguard.
He also defeated Jǐng's general Hóu Zǐjiàn at Húshú.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
for his accomplishments, he was appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, Hénzhōu Cìshǐ zī,
【and held the post of】Hédōng Tàishǒu,
and his stipend was increased to a total of one thousand households.
When Western Wèi invaded Jīngzhōu,
Shìpǔ garrisoned Mǎtóu Àn,
occupying Lóngzhōu.
Yuándì appointed him Shìzhōng, Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Jiāngnán Zhūjūnshì, Zhènnán Jiāngjūn, Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
and granted him a set of musical instruments (gǔchuī).
When Jiānglíng fell,
Shìpǔ went east to rely on Hóu Tián.
In Shàotài first year (555 CE),
he was summoned to be Shìzhōng and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
When Gāozǔ resisted Wáng Lín,
all the equipment for naval warfare
was entrusted to Shìpǔ.
Shìpǔ was naturally ingenious
and well-versed in old methods.
The instruments and machines he created
were all modified and improved as needed,
with an extraordinary ingenuity surpassing others.
In Yǒngdìng second year (558 CE),
he was promoted to Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
When Shìzǔ succeeded to the throne,
he was given the additional title Tèjìn,
and advanced to the title Ānyòu Jiāngjūn.
In Tiānjiā first year (560 CE),
his stipend was increased by five hundred households.
In the second year (561 CE),
he was sent out as Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Xuānchéng Jùn Zhūjūnshì, Ānxī Jiāngjūn, Xuānchéng Tàishǒu,
with a salary of two thousand shi.
Upon returning, he was Ānqián Jiāngjūn, Yòuguānglù Dàfū.
He soon lost his sight due to illness,
begged leave on account of his illness, and did not attend court.
He died in the fourth year (563 CE),
at the age of fifty-five.
He was posthumously granted his former office,
and given the posthumous name Huán Hóu.
Shìpǔ's younger paternal cousin, Shìxiū,
followed Shìpǔ from Liáng on campaigns,
and also had military achievements.
His official positions reached Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì, Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn,
Marquis of Zhǐ Xiàn,
with a stipend of eight hundred households.
In Guāngdà second year (568 CE),
he served under Dūdū Chúnyú Liàng in the campaign against Huá Jiǎo.
He died
and was posthumously granted Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
with the posthumous name Zhuàng.
Lǔ Xīdá, courtesy name Zhìtōng,
was a native of Méi, Fúfēng.
His grandfather, Fěi,
was Qí Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Hénzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Marquis of Yángtáng.
His father, Yìzhī,
was Liáng Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn and Tàishǒu of the two commanderies of Xīncài and Yìyáng.
Xīdá was known for his filial piety from a young age,
and began his career as Liáng Nánpíng Sìwáng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
During the Hóu Jǐng zhī Luàn,
Xīdá gathered his fellow villagers,
secured Xīncài,
and diligently farmed and hoarded grain.
At that time, due to warfare and famine,
eight or nine out of ten people in the capital and the upper reaches of the river died of starvation.
Those who survived
all brought their old and young to him.
Xīdá distributed food and provisions,
saving many lives.
He then established a settlement in Xīncài to house them.
He gathered the five commanderies, including Jìnxī,
and took possession of all their lands.
He sent his younger brother, Guǎngdá, to lead troops to follow Wáng Sēngbiàn in attacking Hóu Jǐng.
When Jǐng was pacified,
Liáng Yuándì appointed him Chíjié, Rénwēi Jiāngjūn, Sànqí Chángshì, Běijiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Jìngdì ascended the throne,
Wáng Lín occupied the upper reaches of the river,
while Liú Yì, Yú Xiàoqǐng, Zhōu Dí, and others rose up everywhere.
Xīdá governed and appeased the five commanderies,
gaining great popular support,
and his soldiers were all happy to serve him.
Lín appointed Xīdá Zhènběi Jiāngjūn,
while Gāozǔ also sent Zhào Zhīlǐ to appoint him Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn, Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Both sent musical instruments (gǔchuī) and female musicians.
Xīdá accepted both,
procrastinating and waiting to see,
but did not take office for either.
Gāozǔ sent Ānxī Jiāngjūn Shěn Tài to secretly lead an army to attack him,
but could not defeat him.
Qí sent Xíngtái Mùróng Shàozōng with thirty thousand troops to attack the various garrisons at Yùkǒu.
Their army and weapons were very powerful.
Xīdá fought them
and defeated the Qí army.
Shàozōng barely escaped with his life.
Wáng Lín wanted to move eastward downriver.
He feared Xīdá, who controlled the middle reaches of the river,
would become a threat to him.
He frequently sent envoys to entice him,
but Xīdá ultimately did not comply.
As Lín could not proceed downriver,
he allied with Qí,
jointly submitting memorials.
Qí sent Qīnghé Wáng Gāo Yuè to assist him.
They were in a standoff for over a year.
Coincidentally, his subordinate general Méi Tiānyǎng and others, fearing punishment,
led the Qí army into the city.
Xīdá led several thousand of his subordinates
across the river to return to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ saw him
and was very pleased,
saying:
"Why are you so late in coming?"
Xīdá replied:
"Your servant has been pacifying the upper reaches of the river,
wishing to serve as a protective barrier.
Your Majesty bestowed official titles upon your servant;
your grace was exceedingly generous.
Shěn Tài attacked your servant;
your might was also profound.
However, the reason your servant returned to Your Majesty
is truly because Your Majesty is broad-minded and magnanimous,
matching the character of Hànzǔ."
Gāozǔ sighed and said:
"Your words are correct."
He was appointed Píngnán Jiāngjūn, Sànqí Chángshì, Běijiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and ennobled as the Marquis of Péngzé Xiàn.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was advanced to the title Ānzuǒ Jiāngjūn.
Although Xīdá was courageous and chivalrous,
he did not become arrogant towards others because of wealth and status.
He had a refined fondness for poetry and essays,
and invited and treated talented and virtuous people with courtesy,
meeting with them to appreciate and enjoy.
He was promoted to Ānnán Jiāngjūn, Wúzhōu Cìshǐ.
He suffered the sorrow of his mother's death,
and grieved excessively beyond propriety.
He then contracted an illness and died
at the age of thirty-eight.
He was posthumously granted Ānzuǒ Jiāngjūn, Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the posthumous name Xiàohóu.
His son, Lǎn, succeeded him.
His younger brother, Guǎngdá,
has a separate biography.
Zhōu Fū, courtesy name Zhòngyuǎn,
was a native of Línchuān.
He was a prominent local family.
Fū's physique was small and delicate,
as if he could not bear his clothes,
yet his courage and resolve were strong and firm,
surpassing his contemporaries.
He was chivalrous by nature,
lightly regarded wealth but highly esteemed scholars.
Young people in his hometown who were spirited all gravitated towards him.
During the Hóu Jǐng zhī Luàn,
a fellow villager, Zhōu Xù, gathered a multitude, ostensibly to suppress the rebels.
Liáng Nèishǐ and the Prince of Shǐxīng, Xiāo Yì, yielded the commandery to Xù.
Among Xù's subordinates, there were some who wanted to plunder Yì,
but Fū protected him,
personally leading his followers to defend him,
and escorted him to Yùzhāng.
At that time, Guānníng Hóu Xiāo Yǒng, Chánglè Hóu Xiāo Jī, and Fēngchéng Hóu Xiāo Tài were displaced refugees fleeing disaster.
Hearing of Fū's trustworthiness and integrity,
they all went to rely on him.
Fū pitied their danger and fear,
humbly showed them great respect,
provided them generously with provisions,
and sent them westward upriver.
Soon after, Xù's subordinates and generals competed for power.
They rebelled again,
killed Xù, and surrendered to Zhōu Dí.
Dí, who had always lacked a prominent lineage,
feared losing popular support,
so he relied on Fū's esteemed clan
and eagerly sought to establish ties.
Fū, unable to secure himself,
served Dí with great deference.
Dí relied heavily on him,
and gradually accumulated troops.
Dí occupied Gōngtáng in Línchuān,
while Fū garrisoned the old commandery of Línchuān.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Emperor Yuán of Liáng appointed Fū as Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Níngzhōu, with the titles Shǐchíjié (使持節), Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍), and Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn (信武將軍).
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xīfēng County,
with a thousand households.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) accepted the abdication,
Wáng Lín occupied the upper reaches of the river.
Yú Xiàoqǐng, along with Lín's partisan Lǐ Xiàoqīn (李孝欽) and others, jointly besieged Zhōu Dí.
Fū sent a large force of men and horses to assist Dí.
Dí captured Xiàoqǐng and others,
with Fū's contribution being significant.
When Xióng Tánlǎng killed Zhōu Wényù
and occupied Yùzhāng,
he led over ten thousand soldiers to attack Fū,
arriving directly at the city walls.
Fū engaged him in battle,
severely defeating him.
He pursued the routed army for over fifty lǐ.
Tánlǎng escaped on a single horse,
and all his military provisions were seized.
Tánlǎng fled to Bāshān Commandery,
gathering his remaining partisans.
Fū then advanced with Zhōu Dí and Huáng Fǎlì (黃法𣽾) to besiege Tánlǎng,
and annihilated him.
After Wáng Lín was pacified,
Fū was appointed Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), Píngxī Jiāngjūn (平西將軍), and Yùzhāng Tàishǒu (豫章太守).
At this time, the chieftains of Nánjiāng (南江) were all attached to their old haunts,
privately appointing magistrates,
and refusing to respond to summons.
The court had not yet had time to launch a punitive expedition,
only keeping them loosely bound.
Only Fū was the first to enter the court.
In the second year of Tiānjiā (天嘉),
he went to the palace,
and was promoted to Ānxī Jiāngjūn (安西將軍),
granted a set of drums and pipes,
and bestowed a troupe of female musicians,
then ordered to return to garrison Yùzhāng.
Zhōu Dí, considering Fū to have always been beneath him,
was deeply displeased by his sudden rise to prominence.
He then raised an army in rebellion,
and sent his younger brother Fāngxīng (方興) with troops to attack Fū.
Fū engaged him in battle,
utterly defeating Fāngxīng.
He then led his troops to join Dūdū (都督) Wú Míngchè (吳明徹) in attacking Dí,
defeating him,
and capturing his younger brother Fāngxīng and other chieftains.
An imperial edict appointed Fū as Ānxī Jiāngjūn and Línchuān Tàishǒu (臨川太守),
with other appointments remaining unchanged.
Soon after, he was summoned and appointed Shǐchíjié, Dūdū of the military affairs of the two zhōus of Nányù (南豫) and Běijiāng (北江), Zhènnán Jiāngjūn (鎮南將軍), and Nányùzhōu Cǐshǐ,
with an increase of five hundred households in his fief.
His titles of Chángshì and the drum and pipe troupe remained as before.
In the fifth year,
Dí again gathered his remaining forces
and returned to attack Dōngxīng (東興).
Shìzǔ (世祖) dispatched Dūdū Zhāng Zhāodá (章昭達) to campaign against Dí,
and Fū again joined the army.
Upon reaching Dìngchuān County,
they confronted Dí.
Dí deceived Fū, saying:
"In the past, I and my brother (referring to Fū) worked together with one heart.
Our clan is not hostile to each other.
How could I plan to harm you?
Now I wish to confess my crime and return to court.
Through you, my brother, I wish to reveal my innermost feelings,
and first request that we step forward and make a solemn oath together."
Fū agreed.
As he was ascending the altar,
he was killed by Dí.
He was thirty-five years old at the time.
An imperial edict stated:
"Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū of the military affairs along the river in Nányùzhōu, Zhènnán Jiāngjūn, Nányùzhōu Cǐshǐ, and Founding Marquis of Xīfēng County, Fū,
was entrusted with a distant expedition,
lingered and violated discipline,
empty-heartedly engaged with treacherous cunning,
and thus brought about his own downfall.
However, he had long demonstrated diligence and loyalty,
and frequently toiled in military campaigns.
We are still deeply saddened,
and feel compassion and grief in our hearts.
His revenue from the fief may be preserved,
and a generous funeral gift bestowed.
He shall be buried in the capital."
His posthumous name was Tuò (脫).
His son Zhì'ān (智安) inherited the title.
Fū's elder brother Tuán (彖),
together with Fū, occupied their native place
and was also appointed Línchuān Tàishǒu.
Xún Lǎng (荀朗), courtesy name Shēnmíng (深明),
was from Yǐngyīn (潁陰) in Yǐngchuān (潁川).
His grandfather, Yánzǔ (延祖), was the Liáng Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu.
His father, Bódào (伯道), was Wèiwèi Qīng (衛尉卿).
Lǎng was brave and resolute in his youth,
possessing the grand strategy of a general.
He began his career in the Liáng dynasty as the Xíng Cānjūn (行參軍) of the Prince of Lúlíng (廬陵王).
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Lǎng recruited and led a multitude of followers,
occupying the area around Cháohú (巢湖),
unaffiliated with any faction.
After Táichéng (臺城) fell,
Emperor Jiǎnwén (簡文帝) secretly issued an edict appointing Lǎng as Yùzhōu Cǐshǐ (豫州刺史) with the title Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn (雲麾將軍),
ordering him to join the regional governors in attacking Jǐng.
Jǐng sent Yítóng (儀同) Sòng Zǐxiān (宋子仙) and Rèn Yuē (任約) and others repeatedly to campaign against him.
Lǎng held positions in the mountains, building strongholds to defend himself,
and Zǐxiān was unable to overcome him.
At that time, the capital was severely afflicted by famine,
and the common people all went outside the Jiāng (Yangtze River) for food.
Lǎng further recruited military units,
giving away his clothes and sharing his food
to relieve and provide for them.
His followers reached tens of thousands.
When Hóu Jǐng was defeated at Bālíng (巴陵),
Lǎng emerged from Rúxū (濡須) to intercept Jǐng,
destroying his rear guard.
When Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) marched eastward,
Lǎng sent his general Fàn Bǎoshèng (范寶勝) and his younger brother Xiǎo (曉) with two thousand soldiers to assist him.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Lǎng separately defeated the Qí (齊) general Guō Yuánjiàn (郭元建) at Chíchú Shān (踟躕山).
In the second year of Chéngshèng (承聖) of Liáng,
he led over ten thousand households of his subordinates across the Jiāng,
establishing a temporary camp within the borders of Xuānchéng Commandery.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng appointed Lǎng as Cǐshǐ of Nánwǎn (南皖) Zhōu, with the titles Shǐchíjié, Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, Ānnán Jiāngjūn (安南將軍), and Dūdū of the military affairs of Nánwǎn Zhōu.
Before he could take office, Jīngzhōu (荊州) fell.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) entered to assist in governance,
Qí (齊) sent Xiāo Guǐ (蕭軌), Dōngfāng Lǎo (東方老), and others to invade,
occupying Shítouchéng (石頭城).
Lǎng came from Xuānchéng to aid,
and along with Hóu Āndū (侯安都) and others, utterly defeated the Qí army.
In the first year of Yǒngdìng (永定),
he was granted the title Marquis of Xīngníng County,
with two thousand households.
Lǎng's elder brother Áng (昂) was appointed Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍),
and his younger brother Guǐ (晷) was appointed Tàizǐ Yòuwèilǜ (太子右衞率).
Soon after, Lǎng was sent to follow Shìzǔ to resist Wáng Lín at Nánwǎn.
When Gāozǔ died,
Empress Xuān (宣太后) and Shèrén (舍人) Cài Jǐnglì (蔡景歷) secretly withheld the news of his passing.
Lǎng's younger brother Xiǎo, then in the capital, vaguely learned of it
and conspired to lead his household troops to attack the palace.
The plot was discovered,
and Jǐnglì killed Xiǎo,
then imprisoned his brothers.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he released them all.
He then generously comforted and appeased Lǎng,
ordering him to join Hóu Āndū and others in resisting Wáng Lín.
After Lín was pacified,
Lǎng was promoted to Cǐshǐ of Hézhōu (合州), with the titles Shǐchíjié, Ānběi Jiāngjūn (安北將軍), Sànqí Chángshì, and Dūdū of the military affairs of the three zhōus of Huò (霍), Jìn (晉), and Hé (合).
He died in the sixth year of Tiānjiā,
at the age of forty-eight.
He was posthumously granted the title Nányùzhōu Cǐshǐ,
and his posthumous name was Zhuàng (壯).
His son Fǎshàng (法尚) inherited the title.
Fǎshàng was unrestrained and ambitious in his youth,
possessing both literary and military talent.
He began his career as Jīngníng Lìng (江寧令),
and inherited the title Marquis of Xīngníng County.
In the fifth year of Tàijiàn (太建),
he followed Wú Míngchè in the northern expedition.
Soon after, he was appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng (通直散騎侍郎),
and dismissed to serve as Jīng Lìng (涇令).
He successively served as Tàishǒu of Liáng (梁) and Ānchéng (安城).
In the Zhēnmíng (禎明) era,
he served as Dūdū of the military affairs of the three zhōus of Yǐng (郢), Bā (巴), and Wǔ (武), and Yǐngzhōu Cǐshǐ.
When the Suí army crossed the Jiāng,
Fǎshàng surrendered to Qín Wáng (秦王), the Yuánshuài (元帥) of Hándōng Dào (漢東道).
After entering the Suí dynasty,
he successively served as Cǐshǐ of the four zhōus of Shào (邵), Guàn (觀), Mián (綿), and Fēng (豐),
and Tàishǒu of the two commanderies of Bādōng (巴東) and Dūnhuáng (燉煌).
Zhōu Jiǒng (周炅), courtesy name Wénzhāo (文昭),
was from Ānchéng (安城) in Rǔnán (汝南).
His grandfather, Qiáng (彊), was Qí Tàizǐ Shèrén (齊太子舍人) and Liángzhōu Cǐshǐ.
His father, Língqǐ (靈起), was Liáng Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (梁通直散騎常侍) and Cǐshǐ of the two zhōus of Lú (廬) and Guì (桂),
and Marquis of Bǎochéng County.
Guì (炅) was young, heroic, and impetuous.
He possessed the talent of a general.
In the Dàtóng (大同) era of the Liáng (梁) dynasty, he served as Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng (通直散騎侍郎) and Zhūyī Zhíhé (朱衣直閤).
In the first year of Tàiqīng (太清) (547 CE),
he was sent out to serve as Yìyáng Tàishǒu (弋陽太守).
During the chaos of Hóu Jǐng (侯景),
Yuán Dì (元帝) authorized his reassignment as Xīyáng Tàishǒu (西陽太守),
and he was enfeoffed as Bó (伯) of Xīlíng (西陵) County.
Jǐng (景) sent his nephew Sīmù (思穆) to garrison Qí'ān (齊安).
Guì (炅) led his brave and strong men to attack and defeat Sīmù (思穆),
capturing and executing him.
For this achievement, he was granted the title of Chíjíe (持節) and Gāozhōu Cìshǐ (高州刺史).
At this time, Guì (炅) held Wǔchāng (武昌) and Xīyáng (西陽) two commanderies,
gathering soldiers and followers.
His armed forces were very strong.
Jǐng's (景) general Rèn Yuē (任約) came to garrison Fánshān (樊山).
Guì (炅) and Níngzhōu Chángshǐ (寧州長史) Xú Wénshèng (徐文盛) attacked Yuē (約),
beheading his subordinate generals Chìluó Zǐtōng (叱羅子通) and Zhào Gālóu (趙迦婁) among others.
Seizing the momentum of victory, they pursued him,
frequently achieving victories,
until Yuē's (約) forces were almost entirely wiped out.
In the first year of Chéngshèng (承聖) (552 CE),
he was promoted to Shǐchíjíe (使持節), Dūdū Jiāng Dìng Èrzhōu Zhūjūnjì (都督江定二州諸軍事), Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn (戎昭將軍), and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (江州刺史).
His noble rank was advanced to Hóu (侯),
with an estate of five hundred households.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
Wáng Lín (王琳) occupied the upper reaches of the river,
and Guì (炅), with his prefecture, followed him.
When Wáng Lín (王琳) sent his generals Cáo Qìng (曹慶) and others to attack Zhōu Dí (周迪),
he also ordered Guì (炅) to lead troops to act in concert and advance.
Guì (炅) was defeated by Hóu Āndū (侯安都),
who captured Guì (炅) and sent him to the capital.
Shìzǔ (世祖) released Guì (炅),
appointing him Róngwēi Jiāngjūn (戎威將軍), Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ (定州刺史),
concurrently serving as Tàishǒu (太守) of Xīyáng (西陽) and Wǔchāng (武昌) two commanderies.
In the second year of Tiānjiā (天嘉) (561 CE),
Liú Yì (留異) rebelled, occupying Dōngyáng (東陽).
Shìzǔ (世祖) summoned Guì (炅) back to the capital,
intending to have him suppress Yì (異).
Before he arrived, Yì (異) was pacified,
so Guì (炅) returned to his original post.
In the first year of Tiānkāng (天康) (566 CE),
he participated in the suppression of Huá Jiǎo (華皎)'s rebellion,
and was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍).
In the first year of Tàijiàn (太建) (569 CE),
he was promoted to Chíjíe (持節), Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍), and Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍).
In the fifth year (573 CE),
he was further appointed Shǐchíjíe (使持節), Xīdào Dūdū Ān Qí Jiāng Héng Sī Dìng Liùzhōu Zhūjūnjì (西道都督安蘄江衡司定六州諸軍事), and Ānzhōu Cìshǐ (安州刺史).
He was re-enfeoffed as Hóu (侯) of Lóngyuán (龍源) County,
with an increased estate totaling one thousand households, including the previous ones.
In that year, he followed Dūdū (都督) Wú Míngchè (吳明徹) on a northern expedition.
Wherever they went, they achieved victories,
capturing twelve cities
within a single month.
Qí (齊) sent Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞) Lù Qiān (陸騫) with twenty thousand men from Bā (巴) and Qí (蘄),
where they encountered Guì (炅).
Guì (炅) left the weak and the baggage train,
setting up a feigned force to confront them.
He personally led his elite troops
along a secret path to ambush them from behind,
soundly defeating Qiān's (騫) army.
The captured weapons, equipment, horses, and donkeys
were countless.
He then attacked Bāzhōu (巴州),
taking it.
Thereupon, all cities north of the Jiāng (江) river, and the gentry and commoners of Gǔyáng (穀陽),
executed their leaders and surrendered their cities.
He was promoted to Héjiāng Jiāngjūn (和戎將軍) and Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
with an increased estate totaling one thousand five hundred households, including the previous ones.
An imperial edict then commanded Guì (炅) to return to the court.
Initially,
Xiāo Chá's (蕭詧) Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ (定州刺ǐ) Tián Lóngshēng (田龍升) surrendered his city.
He was appointed Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn (振遠將軍) and Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ (定州刺史),
and enfeoffed as the King of Chìtíng (赤亭).
When Guì (炅) entered the court,
Lóngshēng (龍升), with six prefectures and seven garrisons north of the Jiāng (江) river, rebelled and defected to Qí (齊).
Qí (齊) sent Lìyáng Wáng (歷陽王) Gāo Jǐng'ān (高景安) to lead an army in response.
Thereupon, Guì (炅) was appointed Dà Dūdū (大都督) of the Jiāngběi Dào (江北道),
overseeing all armies,
to attack Lóngshēng (龍升).
Lóngshēng (龍升) had Yìyáng Tàishǒu (弋陽太守) Tián Lóngyǎn (田龍琰) lead twenty thousand men and array them at Tíngchuān (亭川).
Gāo Jǐng'ān (高景安) provided support at Shuǐlíng (水陵) and Yīnshān (陰山).
Lóngshēng (龍升) led his army to set up a separate camp in the mountain valleys.
Guì (炅) then divided his troops, each to confront an enemy army.
He personally led his elite and brave men to first attack Lóngshēng (龍升).
Lóngshēng (龍升) was soundly defeated.
Lóngyǎn (龍琰) fled at the sight of dust
and was pursued and beheaded.
Gāo Jǐng'ān (高景安) fled,
and all the territory north of the Jiāng (江) river was recovered.
For his achievements, his estate was increased to a total of two thousand households, including the previous ones.
He was promoted to Píngběi Jiāngjūn (平北將軍),
Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ (定州刺史),
with the titles of Chíjíe (持節) and Dūdū (都督) remaining as before.
He was also bestowed with a troupe of female entertainers.
In the eighth year of Tàijiàn (太建) (576 CE), he died in office
at the age of sixty-four.
He was posthumously granted the title of Sīzhōu Cìshǐ (司州刺史),
enfeoffed as Duke of Wǔchāng Jùn (武昌郡公),
and given the posthumous name Zhuàng (壯).
His son Fǎsēng (法僧) succeeded him,
and his highest office was Xuānchéng Tàishǒu (宣城太守).
The court historian said: Those several individuals,
some served in previous generations,
others held their native lands.
All recognized the changing times and knew where to return,
seizing opportunities to attach themselves to power.
Their positions rose to provincial governors,
and their noble ranks reached that of marquises.
This is commendable!
Formerly, Zhāng Ěr (張耳) and Chén Yú (陳餘) regarded each other as closest kin.
Zhōu Fū (周敷) and Zhōu Dí (周迪) also swore oaths like intimate relatives.
Yet they pursued each other with blades and slew the remnants.
This is indeed worse than Hú (胡) and Yuè (越)!
How contemptible it is
for animosity to arise from power and profit!
Collation Notes
