Biography 8: Héngyáng Xiànwáng Chāng (衡陽獻王昌) Nánkāng Mǐnwáng Tánlǎng (南康愍王曇朗) (Sons Fāngtài (方泰), Fāngqìng (方慶))
Héngyáng Xiànwáng Chāng (衡陽獻王昌), courtesy name Jìngyè (敬業),
was the sixth son of Gāozǔ (高祖).
In the late Tàiqīng (太清) era of the Liáng (梁) dynasty,
Gāozǔ (高祖) went south to campaign against Lǐ Bēn (李賁).
He ordered Chāng (昌) and Empress Xuān (宣后) to return to Wúxīng (吳興) with Shěn Kè (沈恪).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) campaigned eastward against Hóu Jǐng (侯景),
Chāng (昌), Empress Xuān (宣后), and Shìzǔ (世祖) were all imprisoned by Jǐng (景).
After Jǐng (景) was pacified,
he was appointed Chángchéng Guó Shìzǐ (長城國世子) and Wúxīng Tàishǒu (吳興太守).
He was sixteen years old at the time.
Chāng (昌)'s appearance was magnificent and beautiful,
his demeanor elegant and clear.
His nature was refined, intelligent, and articulate,
and he was proficient in political affairs.
Gāozǔ (高祖) sent Xiè Zhé (謝哲) from Chénjùn (陳郡) and Cài Jǐnglì (蔡景歷) from Jìyáng (濟陽) to assist Chāng (昌) in his administration of the commandery.
He also sent Dù Zhīwěi (杜之偉) from Wújùn (吳郡) to instruct Chāng (昌) in the classics.
Chāng (昌) would read a book once and be able to recite it,
clear in its principles,
analyzing them fluently.
Soon after, he went to Jīngzhōu (荊州) with Gāozōng (高宗).
Liáng Yuán Dì (梁元帝) appointed him Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍).
When Jīngzhōu (荊州) fell,
he and Gāozōng (高宗) were both relocated to Guān Yòu (關右).
The Western Wèi (西魏) dynasty, due to Gāozǔ (高祖)'s former status,
treated him with great respect.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
he repeatedly sent envoys to request the return of Gāozōng (高宗) and Chāng (昌).
The Zhōu (周) people agreed but did not send them.
After Gāozǔ (高祖) died,
they finally sent them.
At this time, Wáng Lín (王琳) blocked the middle reaches of the river,
so Chāng (昌) could not return and resided in Ānlù (安陸).
After Wáng Lín (王琳) was pacified,
in the second month of the first year of Tiānjiā (天嘉) (560 CE),
Chāng (昌) departed from Ānlù (安陸),
crossed the Jiāng (江) river from Lǔshān (魯山).
Bālíng Wáng (巴陵王) Xiāo Yǎn (蕭沇) and others, along with all officials, submitted a memorial, stating: We heard that
feudal lords serve as the bulwarks of the state, a splendid model of the prosperous Zhōu (周) dynasty,
and the establishment of feudal states as defensive screens
was a grand regulation of the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
This is why the dynasty's longevity
relied on Xíng (邢)
and Wèi (衞),
and the imperial mandate's enduring length
truly depended on Hé (河) and Chǔ (楚).
We humbly observe that Your Majesty's divine wisdom is vast and radiant,
your sacred virtue revered and enlightened.
Your Way is higher than the sun and moon,
your virtue matches creation itself.
In the past, when the imperial enterprise was just beginning,
and the path of Heaven was still difficult,
you participated in devising strategies,
upholding righteousness and valor.
Your might and strategies were displayed externally,
and your divine martiality pacified internally.
Therefore, you were able to restore the achievements of Yǔ (禹) a second time,
and greatly shelter the common people.
When
the sagely martial ruler ascended
to the heavens (died),
the royal army was far away,
the imperial heir was distant and isolated,
with no one to succeed the enterprise.
The ancestral temple was in peril,
its precariousness incomparable.
Then, the imperial carriage was said to be returning,
and the high officials settled the succession plan.
You inherited our grand foundation,
illuminating the brilliant destiny.
The hearts of the people were devoted,
and the imperial tombs found peace.
The later generations revived,
this day having arrived.
The sentiments of the people and the will of Heaven are clearly discernible.
Wáng Lín rebelled against orders,
having evaded punishment for many years.
Now, he has allied with barbarians,
taking advantage of the current situation to stir up trouble.
Boats with flags and troops in the field
stretch along the river and cover the land.
The soldiers are weary, the people are exhausted,
looms
are empty,
the realm, both inside and out, is in turmoil,
and the frontier defenses are not secure.
Therefore, [Your Majesty] has eaten late and presided over court,
relying on the current situation to issue commands.
Once the "Azure Rhinoceros" banners are unfurled,
the long-standing problem will be resolved.
The four quarters will be pacified,
and the eight directions cleansed.
Your grand vision will extend far,
and your benevolent renown will spread widely.
Wherever your moral influence reaches,
it will be like the wind blowing and the grass bending.
Thus, your achievements surpass those of the great Yǔ,
and your Way is greater than that of Yáo.
Not only will the state be at peace,
but the common people will also depend on it.
The Sixth Imperial Younger Brother, Chāng,
recently, at a tender age, was sent as a hostage.
He was held in the hands of the enemy,
separated by barriers and borders,
with no way to return immediately.
Your Majesty's fraternal love is already
deep,
and your spirit of humility and self-restraint is always earnest.
We humbly consider that great virtue is impartial,
and utmost fairness exists.
How can one indulge in the common sentiments of an ordinary man,
and forget the grand strategy for the imperial enterprise?
Following
ancient precedents and established practices,
and adhering to the traditional rites,
reverently emulate the Jī and Hàn dynasties,
by appointing worthy relatives.
Xiāngzhōng is a strategically important and beautiful region,
controlling rivers and hills.
The responsibility of defending this city
should not
be entrusted to non-relatives.
It is appropriate to open up the possibility of him taking on this burden,
and at the same time enhance his prestigious decorations.
We, your ministers, have deliberated and agreed,
to appoint Chāng as Grand Master with Imperial Credentials, Attendant-in-ordinary, Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs of Xiāngzhōu,
General of Agile Cavalry, and Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
He shall be enfeoffed as Héngyáng Jùn Wáng,
with a fief of five thousand households,
and be granted a three-wheeled carriage with black wheels,
a rear drum and fife band,
and twenty
guards with ceremonial swords.
We request approval for this to be carried out.
The imperial edict stated:
"Granted."
In the third month, upon entering the territory,
an imperial edict commanded officials of the Secretariat and Palace Attendants to meet him along the way.
On a *jǐngzǐ* day,
while crossing the river,
his boat broke in mid-stream,
and he drowned and died.
On a *gēngyín* day in the fourth month,
his coffin arrived at the Jīngshī.
The Emperor personally came out to mourn.
An imperial edict was then issued, saying:
"Indeed, grand titles are for commending virtue,
and ceremonial honors are for exalting relatives.
These are common rules throughout the ages,
and indeed excellent precedents of previous kings.

The newly appointed Grand Master with Imperial Credentials, Attendant-in-ordinary, Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs of Xiāngzhōu, General of Agile Cavalry, and Governor of Xiāngzhōu, Héngyáng Wáng Chāng,
possessed brilliance and wisdom,
displaying early talent and integrity.
Filial piety and reverence were deeply embedded within him,
and intelligence and sagacity were outwardly manifest.
During the late Liáng dynasty's troubles and anxieties,
the imperial house and state were in decline.
Xījīng was lost,
and he himself fell into the Guānlǒng region.
When our dynasty was first established,
foreign territories rebelled against orders.
Envoys were blocked,
and communication was impossible.
He looked back at the strategic pass,
with his hair turning grey.
Now, with the concerted efforts of all officials,
many difficulties have been cleared.
He was quickly sent into the city,
without needing to feign a route.
The Zhōu court strengthened its friendly relations,
and he returned, accompanied by chariots.
Rejoicing at this morning's news,
we hoped for joy in the evening.
Rewards and reciprocation are mere words;
they never aid benevolence.
As the saying goes, 'when a person dies,'
desolation and sorrow remain.
His sudden demise
doubles our grief and lament.
The lament at the city gate remains in vain,
and the deep sorrow for the constant abode cannot be pursued.
Quietly reflecting on this,
our heart is as if torn.
It is proper to greatly enhance the posthumous rites,
to match his distinguished conduct.

He is to be posthumously granted the titles of Attendant-in-ordinary, Bearer of the Yellow Axe, Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital, Grand Chancellor, and Governor of Yángzhōu.
He shall be provided with secret burial artifacts from the Eastern Garden,
a nine-streamer imperial carriage with bells,
a yellow imperial canopy and a left *dú* banner,
one hundred armored guards with ceremonial swords,
a covered carriage,
and front and rear feather-canopied drum and fife bands.
The funeral arrangements
shall fully follow the precedents of Hàn Dōngpíng Xiàn Wáng and Qí Yùzhāng Wénxiàn Wáng.
Furthermore, the Grand Minister of Works shall be dispatched with imperial credentials to oversee the funeral arrangements,
and the Grand Herald shall assist with his feathered guards.
All necessities for the funeral
shall be provided as needed."
His posthumous name was Xiàn.
He had no son.
Shìzǔ appointed his seventh imperial son, Bóxìn, as his heir.
Nánkāng Mǐn Wáng Tánlǎng,
was the son of Gāozǔ's maternal younger brother, Zhōngzhuàng Wáng Xiūxiān.
Xiūxiān, while young, was chivalrous and had grand aspirations.
When Liáng Jiǎnwén was in the Dōnggōng,
he was greatly appreciated.
During the Tàiqīng era, Hóu Jǐng was received,
and there were affairs in the north.
So, Xiūxiān was sent to recruit over a thousand men,
and was appointed commander-in-chief.
He died shortly thereafter.
When Gāozǔ came to rule the realm,
he often said of Xiūxiān:
"If this brother were alive,
the Héluò region would not be hard to pacify."
When Liáng Jìngdì ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted the titles of Attendant-in-ordinary, Grand Master with Imperial Credentials, General of Agile Cavalry, and Inspector of Nánxúzhōu,
enfeoffed as Wǔkāng Xiàn Gōng,
with a fief of one thousand households.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he was posthumously granted the titles of Attendant-in-ordinary, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Minister of Education,
enfeoffed as Nánkāng Jùn Wáng,
with a fief of two thousand households,
and his posthumous name was Zhōngzhuàng.
Tánlǎng was orphaned young,
and was particularly beloved by Gāozǔ,
his favor surpassing that of Gāozǔ's own sons.
He had courage and strength,
and was good at pacifying and governing.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
he started his career as an Assistant Gentleman of the Secretariat.
When Gāozǔ crossed the Jiāng to the north,
and besieged Guǎnglíng,
Dōngfāng Guāng of Sùyù raised an army in his hometown.
Gāozǔ then sent Tánlǎng and Dù Sēngmíng from the Huái River into the Sì River to respond and assist him.
When a large Qí relief force arrived,
Tánlǎng and Sēngmíng built strongholds to resist.
Soon after, they received orders to return with their troops,
bringing three thousand households of the Sùyù volunteer army across the Jiāng.
When Gāozǔ executed Wáng Sēngbiàn,
he left Tánlǎng to guard Jīngkǒu,
overseeing the affairs of the resident government.
In the first year of Shàotài,
he was appointed Gentleman of the Central Secretariat,
and Administrator of Nánxúzhōu.
In the second year,
Xú Sìhuī 徐嗣徽 and Rèn Yuē 任約 led Qí 齊 invaders to attack and besiege the capital.
Soon after, they sought peace,
requesting a son or nephew of Gāozǔ 高祖 as a hostage.
At that time, many prefectures and commanderies in the four directions had not yet submitted,
and the capital was weak.
The grain supply was disrupted.
The civil and military officials at court all wished to make peace with Qí 齊,
but Gāozǔ 高祖 found it difficult.
However, he was reluctant to go against public opinion,
so he spoke to the court, saying:
"I have mistakenly assisted the royal house,
allowing barbarians to infest Xià 夏,
and I have been unable to quell and destroy them.
How can I escape blame?
Now, all you worthy officials in office
desire to rest your shoulders and cease military action,
making peace with Qí 齊
to bring tranquility to the borders.
If I were to go against your collective opinion,
you would certainly say that I cherish my sons and nephews.
Therefore, I have decided to send Tánlǎng 曇朗
to their court as a hostage.
However, the Qí 齊 people are untrustworthy.
They will not cease their spying and covetousness,
and believing us to be gradually weakening,
they will certainly break the alliance.
If the Qí 齊 invaders return,
all of you must fight with all your might for me!"
Gāozǔ 高祖 feared that Tánlǎng 曇朗 would be afraid to go,
or might flee to the eastern route.
So he personally led infantry and cavalry to Jīngkǒu 京口 to meet him,
brought Tánlǎng 曇朗 back to the capital,
and then sent him to Qí 齊 as a hostage.
Qí 齊 indeed broke the pact,
again sending Xiāo Guǐ 蕭軌 and others to follow Sìhuī 嗣徽 across the river.
Gāozǔ 高祖 fought them
and soundly defeated them,
capturing Xiāo Guǐ 蕭軌, Dōngfāng Lǎo 東方老, and others.
The Qí 齊 people requested to cede territory and offer horses and cattle to ransom them,
but Gāozǔ 高祖 refused.
When Guǐ 軌 and the others were executed,
the Qí 齊 people also killed Tánlǎng 曇朗 in Jìnyáng 晉陽.
He was twenty-eight at the time.
At this time, having already cut ties with Qí 齊,
this was not known.
When Gāozǔ 高祖 ascended the throne,
he still had Tánlǎng 曇朗 inherit the enfeoffment as Prince of Nánkāng Jùn 南康郡,
offering sacrifices to the Zhōngzhuàng Wáng 忠壯王,
with rituals and status identical to a prince.
It was not until the second year of Tiānjiā 天嘉,
when the Qí 齊 people formed a good relationship,
that this was finally known.
Shìzǔ 世祖 issued an edict saying:
"Indeed, cherishing the distant past and being careful with the end
is a teaching heard from ancient admonitions.
Nánkāng Wáng Tánlǎng 南康王曇朗,
intelligent and earnestly devoted to his kin,
belonged to the imperial family.
He entered Qí 齊 as a hostage
to alleviate the difficulties of the time.
Although the imperial destiny had begun to flourish,
he was unable to return.
We constantly think of him with longing,
day and night never forgetting.
When the Qí 齊 envoy first arrived,
the ill tidings suddenly reached us.
His memory brings poignant grief,
more than double normal emotions.
It is fitting to bestow great favor and honor
to illuminate the constant order.
He is to be posthumously granted Shìzhōng 侍中, Āndōng Jiāngjūn 安東將軍, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī 開府儀同三司, and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ 南徐州刺史,
and given the posthumous title Mǐn 愍."
Then, he sent the acting Lángzhōnglìng 郎中令, along with the envoys Jiāng Dézǎo 江德藻 and Liú Shīzhī 劉師知, to welcome Tánlǎng's 曇朗 coffin,
which arrived in the capital in the spring of the third year.
Initially,
before Tánlǎng 曇朗 was taken hostage by Qí 齊,
he had given birth to sons Fāngtài 方泰 and Fāngqìng 方慶.
When he was about to go to Qí 齊,
he took two concubines with him.
In the north, he had two more sons: Fānghuá 方華 and Fāngkuàng 方曠.
They also returned together.
Fāngtài 方泰 was rough and wild in his youth,
associating with groups of bad youths,
indulging in excessive revelry.
Shìzǔ 世祖, for the sake of Nánkāng Wáng 南康王,
especially pardoned him.
In the first year of Tiānjiā 天嘉,
an edict stated:
"Nánkāng Wáng Tánlǎng 南康王曇朗,
was separated from us in the Qí 齊 court,
and his return cannot be ascertained.
As the imperial ancestral temple is being restored,
an inheritor for offerings and sacrifices is needed.
Therefore, his eldest son Fāngtài 方泰 may be made heir to Nánkāng 南康,
to succeed the Prince of Nánkāng."
Later, upon hearing of Tánlǎng's 曇朗 death,
he succeeded to the title as Prince of Nánkāng.
Soon after, he became Rénwēi Jiāngjūn 仁威將軍 and Dānyáng Yǐn 丹陽尹,
and was provided with subordinate officials.
In the fourth year of Tàijiàn 太建,

he was promoted to Shǐchíjié 使持節, Dūdū Guǎnghéngjiāoyuechéngdìngmíngxīnhéluódéyíhuánglìānjiànshíyá Shíjiǔ Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì 都督廣衡交越成定明新合羅德宜黃利安建石崖十九州諸軍事 [Governor-General of the military affairs of nineteen prefectures, including Guǎngzhōu, Héngzhōu, Jiāozhōu, Yuèzhōu, Chéngzhōu, Dìngzhōu, Míngzhōu, Xīnzhōu, Hézhōu, Luózhōu, Dézhōu, Yízhōu, Huángzhōu, Lìzhōu, Ānzhōu, Jiànzhōu, Shízhōu, and Yázhōu],
Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng 平越中郎將, and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ 廣州刺史.
His governance was cruel and violent,
for which he was impeached by the appropriate authorities
and dismissed from office.
Soon after, he was reappointed as Rénwēi Jiāngjūn 仁威將軍,
with subordinate officials provided.
In the sixth year,
he was appointed Chíjié 持節, Dūdū Yùzhāngjùn Zhū Jūnshì 都督豫章郡諸軍事 [Governor-General of the military affairs of Yùzhāng Commandery], and Yùzhāng Nèishǐ 豫章內史.
While in the commandery, he neglected the people's affairs.
At the end of his term,
he repeatedly allowed his troops to engage in robbery,
and also set fires that spread to residential areas,
then took advantage of the situation to plunder,
rounding up wealthy individuals
to extort wealth.
When his replacement arrived,
he further delayed his return.
Upon reaching the capital,
an edict appointed him Zōngzhèng Qīng 宗正卿,
with his general rank and subordinate officials remaining as before.
Before he could take up the post,
he was impeached by Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Zōng Yuánráo 御史中丞宗元饒
and dismissed from office,
returning to his residence as a prince.
In the eleventh year,
he was reinstated as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn 寧遠將軍,
serving in the Diàshěng 殿省.
Soon after, he was granted the additional title Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍,
and a limited number of subordinate officials were provided.
In the eighth month of that year,
Gāozōng 高宗 visited the Dàzhuàng Guān 大壯觀,
and held a grand military review.
He ordered Dūdū Rèn Zhōng 都督任忠 to lead 100,000 infantry and cavalry,
forming ranks at Xuánwǔ Hú 玄武湖.
Dūdū Chén Jǐng 都督陳景 was ordered to lead 500 tower-ships,
emerging from Guābù Jiāng 瓜步江.
Gāozōng 高宗 ascended the Xuánwǔ Mén 玄武門 to observe,
and feasted his officials while watching.
He then visited the Lèyóu Yuàn 樂遊苑,
hosting a music and dance gathering.
He then revisited the Dàzhuàng Guān 大壯觀,
assembling the various armies for a triumphant return.
At this time, Fāngtài 方泰 was supposed to accompany him,
but he reported that his birth mother was ill,
and did not go.
Instead, he and twenty fugitives including Yáng Zhōngqī 楊鍾期,
dressed in plain clothes, went among the common people
and had illicit affairs with others' wives,
for which he was apprehended by the prefecture.
He also led armed men in resistance,
injuring enforcement officers,
for which he was impeached by the appropriate authorities.
The Emperor was greatly angered
and had Fāngtài 方泰 imprisoned.
Initially, Fāngtài 方泰 only admitted to the illicit affairs,
but not to resisting the enforcement officers.
The Emperor said if he did not admit it, then he would be investigated further.
Fāngtài 方泰 then threw himself down and confessed.
Thereupon, the concurrently serving Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Xú Jūnfū 御史中丞徐君敷 presented a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the heart of a king
does not let criminals escape the net or show favoritism,
and the foundation of perfect governance
does not bend the law to extend mercy.
Upon careful examination, although Chén Fāngtài 陳方泰, Prince of Nánkāng, is distantly related to the imperial clan,
he luckily relies on this connection;
impeachments are not effective,
and his contributions to governance are rare.
Your Majesty magnanimously seeks his repentance for past deeds,
allowing him to be appointed and employed.
He has been given important duties in the imperial household,
serving as a palace guard.
How can it be that when the golden gates open at dawn,
and the imperial carriage proceeds at first light,
with a hundred officials rushing forth
and a thousand detachments soaring,
he shirks the effort of accompanying the emperor,
and falsely pleads illness in the morning and evening?
Instead, he appears with an unruly cap by the Qí 淇 river
and gaudy clothes in Sāngzhōng 桑中.
No transgression of a minister or son
is greater than this.
He should be subjected to the severe law
and duly placed in the autumn office [i.e., Ministry of Justice].
Your servants have deliberated
and request, according to the facts of the case,
to strip Fāngtài 方泰 of his current official posts
and refer him to the Zōngzhèng 宗正 to have his title and territory rescinded.
I respectfully present this white memorial."
The Emperor approved his memorial.
Soon after, he was reinstated to his original official position and title.
In the early years of Zhēnmíng 禎明,
he was promoted to Shìzhōng 侍中,
his general rank remaining as before.
Three years later,
the Suí army crossed the Jiāng.
Fāng Tài, together with Zhōngwǔ Jiāngjūn Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ Fán Měng and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Jiǎng Yuánsùn, led the navy at Báixià,
constantly blocking the river passage.
Suí dispatched Xíngjūn Yuánshuài Chángshǐ Gāo Gǐng to lead ships upstream to confront them.
Měng and Yuánsùn both surrendered.
Fāng Tài's subordinate officers and soldiers scattered,
so he abandoned his ship and fled.
When Táichéng fell,
he entered the pass together with the Later Lord.
During the Dàyè era of Suí, he served as Yèlìng.
Fāng Qìng was intelligent and alert in his youth,
and widely read in books and histories.
When he grew up,
he possessed strategic talent.
During the Tiānjiā era,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Línrǔ County.
Soon after, he became Gěishì Zhōng and Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
temporarily holding the concurrent post of Zōngzhèng Qīng,
and serving in the Diànshěng.
In the ninth year of Tàijiàn,
he was appointed Qīngchē Jiāngjūn, Jiǎjié, Dūdū Dìngzhōu Zhū Jūnfù, and Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ.
After his term expired,
he again became Sànqí Chángshì,
concurrently Zōngzhèng Qīng.
In the second year of Zhìdé,
he was promoted to Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn and Wǔzhōu Cìshǐ.
Initially,
Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ Mǎ Jìng had long resided in Lǐngbiǎo,
gaining great popular support.
His soldiers and horses were strong,
and the imperial court was suspicious of him.
Therefore, Fāng Qìng was appointed Rénwēi Jiāngjūn and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and attacked Jìng with his troops.
After Jìng was executed,
Fāng Qìng was promoted to Xuānyì Jiāngjūn.
Fāng Qìng was upright and cautious by nature,
and gained great harmony among the people.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng,
the Suí army crossed the Jiāng.
Dōng Héngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Yǒng dispatched Gāozhōu Cìshǐ Dài Zhìliè with 500 cavalry to meet Fāng Qìng,
intending for him to act under imperial authority and oversee all military affairs of the expedition.
At this time, Suí Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn Wéi Guǎng led troops across the Lǐng.
He proclaimed an imperial edict from Suí Wéndì, saying:
"If Lǐngnán is pacified,
Wáng Yǒng and Fēngzhōu Cìshǐ Zhèng Wànqǐng shall retain their former posts."
When Fāng Qìng heard this,
fearing that Wáng Yǒng would betray him,
he did not comply.
He led his troops to resist Dài Zhìliè.
Zhìliè fought him
and defeated him,
beheading Fāng Qìng in Guǎngzhōu
and capturing his wife and children.
Wáng Yǒng,
during the Tàijiàn era, served as Jìnlíng Tàishǒu,
and was known for his competence in office.
When Fāng Qìng attacked Mǎ Jìng,
the imperial court appointed Wáng Yǒng as Chāowǔ Jiāngjūn and Dōng Héngzhōu Cìshǐ,
concurrently Shǐxīng Nèishǐ,
to support Fāng Qìng's authority.
After Jìng was executed,
Wáng Yǒng was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Lóngyáng County for his meritorious service.
When the Suí army approached the Jiāng,
an imperial edict appointed Wáng Yǒng as Shǐchíjié, Guāngshèng Jiāngjūn, Dūdū Héng, Guǎng, Jiāo, Guì, Wǔ, and other twenty-four prefectures' military affairs, and Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiàng,
and ordered him to come to the aid of the capital.
When the capital fell, Wáng Yǒng then issued a proclamation throughout his jurisdiction,
calling for troops to hold their positions.
He sent his full brother Dèng Gǎo with 5,000 soldiers
to encamp on the Lǐng.
He also sent an envoy to welcome Fāng Qìng,
intending to use him for his prestige,
while personally controlling military power.
When Fāng Qìng was defeated,
Wáng Yǒng captured his wife and children,
seized his property,
and distributed it as rewards to his generals.
He also ordered his generals Wáng Zhòngxuān and Zēng Xiàowǔ to welcome Xīhéngzhōu Cìshǐ Héngyáng Wáng Bóxìn.
Bóxìn was afraid
and fled to Qīngyuǎn Commandery.
Xiàowǔ pursued and killed him.
At this time, Wéi Guǎng's army had already crossed the Lǐng.
Fēngzhōu Cìshǐ Zhèng Wànqǐng held his prefecture and refused Wáng Yǒng's summons,
while the Xǐ clan, women of Gāoliáng, raised troops to respond to the Suí army
and attacked and captured neighboring commanderies.
Wáng Yǒng had no other choice,
so he surrendered with his followers.
When he reached Jīngzhōu,
he fell ill and died on the way.
Suí posthumously honored him as Dàjiāngjūn and Sòngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Duke of Guīrén County.
Zhèng Wànqǐng was
from Xíngyáng,
a clansman of Liáng Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Shào Shú.
His father, Mín,
entered Wèi at the end of Liáng.
Wànqǐng was knowledgeable and capable.
During the reign of Zhōu Wǔdì, he served as Sīchéng Dàfū,
then as Wēnzhōu Cìshǐ.
During the Zhìdé era,
he defected with Sīmǎ Xiāonàn.
Soon after, he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì, Zhāowǔ Jiāngjūn, and Fēngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He governed the prefecture with great beneficence,
and the officials and common people requested to erect a stele,
which was granted by imperial edict.
Initially,
when Wànqǐng was in Zhōu,
he was deeply appreciated by Suí Wéndì.
When Suí Wéndì ascended the throne,
Wànqǐng always thought of returning north.
When Wáng Yǒng killed Fāng Qìng,
Wànqǐng then led the prefectural troops to resist Wáng Yǒng,
and sent an envoy through a secret path to surrender to the Suí army.
He was appointed Shàngyí Tóng
and died soon after.
The historian says: The two princes, Xiàn and Mǐn,
shone brightly in the firmament.
One was cherished as a son,
the other favored as a nephew.
Yet, obstacles arose like bridges,
and their carriages had no way to pass.
They were separated in their prime,
and ultimately met an early demise.
Alas!
Collation Notes
Biographies Volume 9: Zōngshì Chén Nǐ, Chén Xiáng, Chén Huìjì
Chén Nǐ, courtesy name Gōngzhèng,
was a distant relative of Gāozǔ.
He was orphaned and poor in his youth,
and was by nature upright and had a strong memory.
When Gāozǔ marched south to Jiāozhǐ,
Nǐ accompanied him.
When he advanced to attack Hóu Jǐng,
upon reaching Yùzhāng,
Nǐ was appointed Luózhōu Cìshǐ,
and together with Hú Yǐng, managed logistical affairs,
and coordinated the supply of military provisions.
When Gāozǔ garrisoned Zhūfāng,
Nǐ was appointed Bùbīng Xiàowèi and Qǔ'ā Lìng.
In the first year of Shàotài,
he was granted Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn and Yìxīng Tàishǒu.
In the second year,
he entered to manage the affairs of Wèiwèi,
and was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì, Míngwēi Jiāngjūn, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
concurrently overseeing Nánxúzhōu.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he issued an edict saying:
"The Zōngzǐ (princes of the imperial clan) are the walls and ramparts
that truly belonged to the ancient Zhōu dynasty.
They are the firm foundation of close relatives,
thereby exalting the great Hàn dynasty.
Therefore, when forming alliances, those of different surnames became successors;
when allocating land, none but those of the Liú surname could be kings.
This was how the branches and trunk were brought together,
and numerous screens and barriers were erected.
These were the excellent practices of former kings,
and the constant regulations of successive dynasties.
My cousin Chén Nǐ (陳擬), holding the imperial credentials, Attendant Cavalier Regular Staff Member, General of Manifest Might, Inspector of Yōngzhōu, and Overseer of Nánxúzhōu;
Chén Bāo (陳襃), holding the imperial credentials, Attendant Cavalier Gentleman of the Palace, General of Righteous Might, and Inspector of Běixúzhōu;
my cousins Chén Huǎng (陳晃) and Chén Jiǒng (陳炅);
my grand-cousin Chén Diǎo (陳訬), holding the imperial credentials, Attendant Cavalier Regular Staff Member, and General of Manifest Might;
Chén Xuān (陳諠), holding the imperial credentials, General of Trusty Might, Inspector of Běixúzhōu, and Founding Marquis of Jíyáng County;
Chén Shí (陳祏), holding the imperial credentials, Attendant Cavalier Gentleman of the Palace, and General of Trusty Valor;
Chén Xiáng (陳詳), holding the imperial credentials, Attendant Cavalier Gentleman, General of Heroic Trust, Inspector of Qīngzhōu, and Grand Administrator of Guǎngliáng;
Chén Huìjì (陳慧紀), General of Righteous Might and Attendant Cavalier Gentleman of the Palace;
my grand-cousins Chén Jìngyǎ (陳敬雅) and Chén Jìngtài (陳敬泰]—
all are close relatives and kin,
who have toiled for the imperial house.
They should be ranked among the mountains and rivers,
to illuminate the establishment of the state.
Chén Nǐ shall be the Founding Marquis of Yǒngxiū County;
Chén Bāo, Founding Marquis of Zhōnglíng County;
Chén Huǎng, Founding Marquis of Jiànchéng County;
Chén Jiǒng, Founding Marquis of Shàngráo County;
Chén Diǎo, Founding Marquis of Qiánhuà County;
Chén Xuān retains his previous enfeoffment;
Chén Shí, Founding Marquis of Yùzhāng County;
Chén Xiáng, Founding Marquis of Suìxīng County;
Chén Huìjì, Founding Marquis of Yíhuáng County;
Chén Jìngyǎ, Founding Marquis of Níngdū County;
Chén Jìngtài, Founding Marquis of Pínggù County.
Each shall receive an estate of five hundred households."
Chén Nǐ was soon appointed General of Light Chariots,
concurrently Inspector of Nánxúzhōu,
his status as Attendant Staff Member remaining as before.
In that year,
he was granted Attendant Cavalier Regular Staff Member and Central Army Commander.
In the third year,
he was again made Overseer of Nánxúzhōu with his original office.
When Shìzǔ succeeded to the throne,
Chén Nǐ was appointed Governor of Dānyáng,
his status as Attendant Staff Member remaining as before.
Due to an incident,
he was again made to govern the prefecture as a commoner,
but soon after his original post was restored.
He died in the first year of Tiānjiā,
at the age of fifty-eight.
He was posthumously granted General of the Army Commander,
and all necessary funeral expenses
were provided by the government.
His posthumous name was Dìng.
In the second year,
he was enshrined in Gāozǔ's ancestral temple.
His son Chén Dǎng (陳黨) succeeded him.
Chén Xiáng (陳詳), courtesy name Wénjǐ (文幾),
became a Buddhist monk (Sāngmén) in his youth.
He was skilled in writing,
and his discussions were clear and elegant.
When Gāozǔ was campaigning against Hóu Jǐng,
he summoned Chén Xiáng,
ordering him to return to secular life.
He was assigned troops and horses,
and followed Gāozǔ in pacifying the capital.
When Gāozǔ campaigned eastward against Dù Kān,
Chén Xiáng separately captured the three counties of Ānjí, Yuánxiāng, and Gùzhàng.
When Dù Kān was pacified,
Chén Xiáng was awarded Attendant Cavalier Gentleman, holding the imperial credentials, General of Heroic Trust, and Inspector of Qīngzhōu for his achievements.
The territories of Gùzhàng and Guǎngdé were detached to establish Guǎngliáng Commandery,
and Chén Xiáng was made its Grand Administrator.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Guǎngliáng was renamed Chénliú,
and he was again made Grand Administrator of Chénliú.
In the second year of Yǒngdìng,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Suìxīng County,
with an estate of five hundred households.
In that year, he was appointed General of Manifest Might and Attendant Cavalier Regular Staff Member.
In the third year,
he followed Hóu Āndū to defeat Wáng Lín's general Cháng Zhòng'ài at Gōngtíng Lake.
When Shìzǔ succeeded to the throne,
Chén Xiáng was appointed Grand Administrator of Xuānchéng,
his general title remaining as before.
When Wáng Lín advanced to occupy Zhàkǒu,
Chén Xiáng followed Wú Míngchè to attack Pénchéng,
and captured Wáng Lín's family,
but was unsuccessful.
He then entered Nánhú Lake
and returned by foot from Póyáng.
When Wáng Lín was pacified,
Chén Xiáng and Wú Míngchè both received no merit.
In the first year of Tiānjiā,
his estate was increased by the usual decree, totaling one thousand five hundred households.
He was then appointed Attendant Cavalier Regular Staff Member,
concurrently General of the Right Guard.
In the third year,
he was sent out as holding the imperial credentials, Area Commander-in-chief of all military affairs of Wúzhōu, General of Benevolent Might, and Inspector of Wúzhōu.
When Zhōu Dí raised an army and occupied Línchuān,
Chén Xiáng attacked Zhōu Dí's detached camp at Rúchéng from his prefecture by another route,
capturing his wife and children.
Zhōu Dí was defeated and fled,
and Chén Xiáng returned to his original garrison.
In the fifth year,
Zhōu Dí again emerged from Línchuān,
so Chén Xiáng was made Area Commander-in-chief,
leading land and naval forces to suppress Zhōu Dí.
When the army reached Nánchéng,
they encountered the bandits,
were defeated in battle,
and he died,
at the age of forty-two.
Because his command was undisciplined,
he received no posthumous grant or name.
His son Chén Zhènglǐ (陳正理) succeeded him.
Chén Huìjì (陳慧紀), courtesy name Yuánfāng (元方),
was a grand-cousin of Gāozǔ.
He dabbled in books and history,
and possessed talent and spirit.
When Gāozǔ pacified Hóu Jǐng,
Chén Huìjì followed him.
He was soon assigned troops and horses.
When Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
he followed in the campaign against Dù Kān.
He was appointed General of Righteous Might and Attendant Cavalier Regular Staff Member.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yíhuáng County,
with an estate of five hundred households,
and appointed Court Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was sent out as Magistrate of Ānjí County.
He was promoted to Deputy General of Manifest Might.
When Sīkōng Zhāng Zhāodá campaigned against Ānshǔ City,
Chén Huìjì served as Commander of the Naval Forces,
burning the prows of boats at Qīngní in Jīngzhōu.
In the first year of Guāngdà,
for his achievements, he was appointed holding the imperial credentials, Attendant Cavalier Regular Staff Member, General of Far-Reaching Proclamation, and Inspector of Fēngzhōu,
his estate increasing to a total of one thousand households.
In the tenth year of Tàijiàn,
Wú Míngchè's northern campaign suffered a defeat,
so Chén Huìjì was appointed holding the imperial credentials, General of Wise Valor, Area Commander-in-chief along the Jiāng River, and Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
his estate increasing to a total of two thousand households,
with other posts remaining as before.
The Zhōu army, exploiting their victory, occupied Huáinán,
causing unrest south of the Jiāng River.
Chén Huìjì gathered soldiers,
and returned to the capital by sea.

He was soon appointed Bearer of Imperial Credentials, Attendant Cavalier Regular Staff Member, General of Martial Might, Area Commander-in-chief of all military affairs of Yǐng and Bā two prefectures, and Inspector of Yǐngzhōu,
his estate increasing to a total of two thousand five hundred households.
In the second year of Zhìdé,

he was promoted to Bearer of Imperial Credentials, Attendant Cavalier Regular Staff Member, General of Cloud Cavalry, Area Commander-in-chief of all military affairs of Jīng and Xìn two prefectures, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
and was bestowed a troupe of female entertainers,
his estate increasing to a total of three thousand households.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng,
Xiāo Cóng's Left Grandee Secretary Ānpíng Wáng Xiāo Yán (蕭巖) and Jìnxī Wáng [Xiāo] Huán (蕭瓛) and others,
led their retinues of over twenty thousand men and women,
and went to Chén Huìjì to surrender.
Chén Huìjì met them with troops.
In that year,
for his achievement in receiving the surrender,
he was additionally appointed Palace Attendant, Gold and Purple Grandee of Radiant Happiness, Administrator with the Privileges of the Three Dukes, and General Who Conquers the West,
his estate increasing to a total of six thousand households,
with other posts remaining as before.
When the Suí army crossed the Jiāng River,
Marshal Qīnghé Gōng Yáng Sù (楊素) descended from Bāxiá,
Chén Huìjì sent his generals Lǚ Zhōngsù (呂忠肅) and Lù Lún (陸倫) to resist him.
They were defeated in battle,
and Yáng Sù advanced to occupy Mǎtóu.
At this time,
Suí generals Hán Qínhǔ (韓擒虎) and Hè Ruòbì (賀若弼) had already crossed the Jiāng River and occupied Jiǎngshān.
When Chén Huìjì heard this,
he left his Chief Clerk Chén Wénshèng (陳文盛) and others to guard the place,
and personally led thirty thousand officers and soldiers,
and over a thousand樓船 (multi-decked ships),
downstream along the Jiāng River,
intending to head for Táichéng.
When he reached Hànkǒu,
he was blocked by the Qín Wáng's (秦王) army,
and could not advance.
He then, along with Inspector of Xiāngzhōu Jìnxī Wáng Shūwén (晉熙王叔文) and Inspector of Bāzhōu Bì Bǎo (畢寶) and others, requested to surrender.
Upon entering Suí,
he was granted Yítóng Sānsī (privileges of the Three Dukes) according to regulation.
He died shortly after.
His son Chén Zhèngpíng (陳正平)
had considerable literary talent.
The court historian says: The Odes say,
"The Zōngzǐ are the walls and ramparts,
let not the walls be overthrown."
And it also says,
"The gourd spreads its tendrils,
the kudzu vine entwines them."
The Western Capital's prominent figures were all old acquaintances from Fēngpèi,
and the Eastern Capital's distinguished ones were mostly from Nányáng.
There is a reason for this!
Correction Notes
Biographies, Chapter 10: Zhào Zhīlǐ, Cài Jǐnglì, Liú Shīzhī, Xiè Qí
Zhào Zhīlǐ
had the courtesy name Qídàn, and was a native of Tiānshuǐ Lǒngxī.
His father, Xiàomù,
was the Magistrate of Hòuguān during the Liáng dynasty.
Zhīlǐ dabbled in literature and history,
and was skilled in clerical script.
When Gāozǔ was campaigning against Yuán Jǐngzhòng,
someone recommended him,
and he was appointed as Staff Officer for Record-keeping.
Zhīlǐ's writing was comprehensive and swift;
whenever he was assigned to compose military dispatches,
he would put pen to paper and finish immediately,
and they always conformed to the emperor's wishes.
Because of this, he always attended the emperor's side,
was deeply trusted and relied upon,
and at that time, no plans
were made without his involvement.
Zhīlǐ also made many suggestions and recommendations.
When Gāozǔ pacified Hóu Jǐng,
and the army reached Báimáo Wān,
the memorials to Emperor Yuán of Liáng and the discussions of military affairs with Wáng Sēngbiàn
were all composed by Zhīlǐ.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
he was appointed Palace Assistant Secretary,
enfeoffed as a Viscount of Shǐpíng County,
with an estate of three hundred households.
When Gāozǔ became Minister of Works,
he made Zhīlǐ a Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary.
When Gāozǔ entered the court as a regent,
Zhīlǐ was promoted to Palace Attendant,
and concurrently served as Minister of the Imperial Guards.
When Gāozǔ received the Mandate,
he was promoted to Palace Attendant,
and served in the Palace Secretariat.
Soon after, he was promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary,
assumed the post of Minister of the Imperial Treasury,
and temporarily oversaw military affairs.
In the first year of Tiānjiā (560 CE),
his peerage was advanced to Earl,
and his estate was increased to seven hundred households in total.
After Wáng Lín was pacified,
he was appointed Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Wú Prefecture, General of Illustrious Might, and Governor of Wú Prefecture.
Zhīlǐ was calm and resourceful;
whenever there were major military or state affairs,
Shìzǔ would always send an imperial letter to inquire of him.
After his term of office expired,
he served as General of Illustrious Might and Right Leader of the Eastern Palace Guards.
He was promoted to Right General of the Guards,
and concurrently led the Vanguard General.
In the sixth year (565 CE), he died,
at the age of forty-seven.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Palace Attendant,
and his posthumous name was Zhōng.
His son, Yǔngōng, succeeded him.
Cài Jǐnglì,
had the courtesy name Màoshì, and was a native of Jìyáng Kǎochéng.
His grandfather, Diǎn,
was the Left Palace Attendant of the Ministry of Civil Affairs during the Liáng dynasty.
His father, Dàtóng,
was the Staff Officer for Record-keeping to Prince Yuèyáng, the Light-chariot General,
and was in charge of the capital's civil service selection.
Jǐnglì was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
and was filial.
His family was poor but he loved to study,
was skilled in writing letters,
and proficient in cursive and clerical scripts.
He began his career as an assistant in various princely mansions,
and was later dispatched as the Magistrate of Hǎiyáng,
where he gained a reputation for effective governance.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
and Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng was imprisoned by Hóu Jǐng,
Jǐnglì plotted with Xiāo Huìlǐ, the heir to the Prince of Nánkāng,
intending to escort Emperor Jiǎnwén in an escape.
The plot was discovered, and he was captured.
The rebel leader Wáng Wěi protected him,
and he was able to escape.
He then wandered to Jīngkǒu as a guest.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Gāozǔ was stationed at Zhūfāng,
and having long heard of Jǐnglì's reputation,
he invited him by letter.
Jǐnglì dictated a reply to the envoy,
his brush never pausing,
and the text never needing revision.
He said: "Having received your letter,
extending your gracious invitation,
I have repeatedly pondered it with deep joy and elation.
I humbly believe that the world seeks famous steeds,
capable of covering a thousand *lǐ* on land,
and at times prizes
rare gems,
a mere inch of which can illuminate a carriage.
Yet, it is said that all birds sing,
but one stops singing the Bāyú tune,
and when the *cí* tree is carved,
how can one look for the *chūlì*?
I look up to your esteemed General's banner,
where outstanding talent flourishes,
and heroic bearing excels.
The times are arduous,
and your ambition is to restore order amidst great difficulties.
You roused the Héng Mountain and pacified
the Five Ridges,
cleansed the Gǎn River source and clarified the Nine Streams.
With a hundred thousand armored soldiers,
and several thousand powerful crossbows,
you pledged to lead the loyal army,
uniting the strength of righteous men.
The whales and monsters were swiftly cut down,
the campaign
did not exceed its time limit,
the fog and mist were cleared,
and no soldier shed blood.
Although the Hàn dynasty executed Lù and Chǎn,
the entire court relied on Duke of Jiàng,
and the Jìn dynasty suppressed Yuē and Jùn,
both internal and external affairs depended on Táo
Mù;
comparing these events and discussing their merits,
how can they be truly counted?
Moreover, you manifested awe and compelled the Six [Barbarians] to submit,
and official carriages reached the northern gate.
You marshaled banners in Xú Province,
and songs filled the eastern road,
enabling
border watchtowers to keep their drums silent,
travelers to sleep openly on the road,
no lost items to be picked up in alleys,
and no varied prices in markets.
How vast are your merits, virtues, and transformative governance,
unmatched throughout antiquity,
truly not something superficial
can fully describe.
Therefore, people throughout the realm,
drawn by your influence and admiring your righteousness,
follow one another, opening their collars,
arriving in droves.
Some are brilliant and virtuous members of the imperial clan,
nobles of high renown,
outstanding talents from Qí and Chǔ,
and extraordinary individuals from Jīng and Wú.
As for warriors, their fierce spirits surge,
their heroic hearts seize all four directions.
On land, they uproot mountains;
in water, they sever dragons.
Wielding bows of six *jūn*,
they shoot from left and right while galloping.
With swords of ten thousand men,
they engage in close combat.
They attack strongholds like Wén Yāng,
and burn fleets like Huáng Gài.
Victorious in a hundred battles,
they are like a swarm of *píxiū*.
As for literati,
they are learned scholars with extensive knowledge,
brilliant talents and great vessels.
Their ornate writings shine with brilliance,
their expressions are vivid and splendid.
Zǐyún cannot match their brush,
and Yuányú cannot surpass their records.
A single letter
gallops forth and Liáochéng falls;
a clear discussion rouses and the Yíng army retreats.
Furthermore, there are eloquent speakers from Sānhé,
who change sorrow and joy in an instant;
strategists of six stratagems,
who resolve crises in a
flash.
They govern the people like Zǐjiàn,
achieving success wherever they step.
They settle disputes like Zhòngyóu,
and a single word brings reason.
They speak frankly like Máo Suì,
able to enhance their lord's authority.
They serve as envoys like
Xiāngrú,
not disgracing their sovereign's command.
They harbor loyalty and embrace righteousness,
grateful and self-sacrificing.
Their sincerity cuts through gold,
their spirit penetrates the white sun.
Heroic and virtuous men from within the seas,
are gathered and ready.
The Illustrious
General dismounts,
pushes aside his table and stops eating,
promotes them to honor them,
builds mansions to settle them,
values character over wealth,
humbles himself and treats scholars generously.
How magnificent!
How magnificent!"
Alas!
Furthermore, I have heard that
the generals and chancellors of the Warring States period
all widely welcomed guests and retainers;
the provincial governors and prefects of the middle ages
also greatly extended invitations to colleagues and friends.
With a multitude of talented men,
they were able to achieve the
nobility of a general.
Provided that abilities are measured and evaluated,
talents are matched to duties,
and each is allowed to reach their full potential,
everyone will fulfill their proper role.
When entrusted with responsibility and held accountable,
who would not exert their utmost effort?
As for this humble one,
I am merely a rash and mediocre person.
Though I studied in autumn and winter,
I am ultimately ashamed of my specialized learning.
Serving as an official with brush and knife,
I have indeed lacked exceptional qualities.
Living in a humble dwelling with declining reputation,
I have achieved no renown or advancement.
With a meager official salary and light
means,
how could I achieve anything great?
Since the "nine-fold Yang" brought misfortune
and the heavenly path was perilous,
I, like those noble officials,
was submerged by mighty bandits,
often faced mortal danger,
and indeed trod upon thin ice.
Now
the King's Way is revitalized,
with earnest sorrow the new era begins;
to have preserved my humble life
is indeed a great fortune.
I am now enjoying food and drink,
which is called 'coming back to life.'
However, the imperial carriage has not yet returned,
Wǎn and Luò
are desolate and overgrown.
Our four walls are the remnants of three armies,
and in the long summer, we have not half a bean's worth of produce.
Old friends wander about,
seeking temporary loans.
In this happy land,
it is truly beautiful, making one forget to return home.
Secretly admiring your lofty righteousness,
I briefly call upon your gate.
The enlightened general graciously bestowed his countenance,
and a few scholarly friends lent me their remaining discourse.
Though I am but mere grass and rushes,
you invited me to stay with a written note.
You wish to
place chickens and ducks among mandarin ducks and wild geese in the pond,
and to elevate rubble to the value of gold and jade.
In the past, Quē Xí, with a broken rib, traveled to Qín
and suddenly received a favorable glance.
Yán Dēng entered Zhào
and was immediately
detained and honored.
Though I am now a sojourner,
compared to them I am no match.
How can I bear the honor bestowed by Fán Lín?
How can I possibly endure it?
But tiny brambles
rely on tall pines to rise,
and swarming small
gnats
attach themselves to the tail of a team of horses to travel far.
I presume not to measure myself,
but wish to serve as a humble follower,
to be even as the hair on the back and belly,
or perhaps to swell the number of those who bark and crow.
To increase my honor and improve my standing
would be
a great fortune already.
The sea does not disdain depth,
nor does the mountain yield in height.
I dare to lay bare my heart,
hoping the general will consider it.
Gāo Zǔ received the letter
and greatly admired and appreciated it.
He then wrote a reply,
and on that very day appointed Jǐng Lì as the Staff Officer for the Secretariat of the Grand General who Conquers the North's office,
and he continued to oversee the Secretariat.
When the Prince Xiàn of Héngyáng, Chāng, was serving as the Administrator of Wúxīng Commandery,
Chāng was still young.
Wúxīng was the native place of the Prince,
and there were many elders and old acquaintances,
with a clear order of seniority.
Gāo Zǔ feared that Chāng, being young,
might mishandle interactions due to improper etiquette,
so he sent Jǐng Lì to assist him.
During the Chéngshèng reign,
he was appointed Palace Gentleman with Access to the Throne,
and returned to manage the Secretariat of the Prince's office.
When Gāo Zǔ was about to attack Wáng Sēngbiàn,
he consulted only with Hóu Āndū and a few others;
Jǐng Lì was unaware of this.
After the deployment was complete,
he was summoned to draft a proclamation.
Jǐng Lì took up his brush and completed it immediately;
its language was inspiring and its meaning moving,
and everything accorded with Gāo Zǔ's wishes.
After Sēngbiàn was executed,
Gāo Zǔ assumed regency,
and Jǐng Lì was appointed Attendant Aide-de-camp,
managing the Secretariat as before.
In the first year of Shàotài (555 CE),
he was promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
and concurrently managed the Secretariat of the Prime Minister's office.
When Gāo Zǔ received the abdication,
Jǐng Lì was promoted to Supervisor of the Imperial Library,
Palace Aide-de-camp of the Central Secretariat,
and was in charge of imperial edicts.
In the second year of Yǒngdì (558 CE),
he was impeached by Censor-in-chief Shěn Jiǒng
for his wife's younger brother, Liú Yān, having fraudulently received horses as tribute from Zhōu Bǎo'ān.
He was demoted to Gentleman of the Central Secretariat,
but remained Palace Aide-de-camp.
In the third year (559 CE),
Gāo Zǔ passed away.
At that time, there were strong enemies outside,
and Shì Zǔ was stationed in Nánwǎn.
There were no influential ministers in court.
Empress Xuān summoned Jǐng Lì, Jiāng Dàquán, and Dù Léng to decide on a course of action.
They then secretly refrained from announcing the mourning
and swiftly summoned Shì Zǔ.
Jǐng Lì personally, together with eunuchs and palace women,
secretly arranged the burial clothes.
As it was a hot summer,
a coffin needed to be made.
Fearing that the sound of axes and chisels might be heard outside,
they used wax to make secret tools.
Documents and imperial edicts
continued to be issued as usual.
When Shì Zǔ ascended the throne,
Jǐng Lì was reinstated as Supervisor of the Imperial Library,
and remained Palace Aide-de-camp.
For his merit in determining the succession,
he was enfeoffed as Viscount of Xīnfēng County,
with four hundred households.
He was successively promoted to Regular Mounted Attendant.
When Shì Zǔ executed Hóu Āndū,
Jǐng Lì encouraged and helped him achieve it.
In the third year of Tiānjīa (562 CE),
for his merit, he was promoted to Palace Guard Commander of the Heir Apparent,
further ennobled as a Marquis,
and his fief was increased by a hundred households.
He remained Regular Mounted Attendant and Palace Aide-de-camp.
In the sixth year (565 CE),
he was dismissed from office
for his wife's elder brother, Liú Qià, having relied on Jǐng Lì's power and influence
to commit various frauds, and also for receiving a hundred bolts of silk as tribute from Ōuyáng Wǔwēi.
He was dismissed from office.
When the deposed emperor ascended the throne,
he was appointed Advisory Counselor to the Prince of Póyáng who Guards the East,
and concurrently Grand Minister of Shipping.
When Huá Jiǎo rebelled,
Jǐng Lì was appointed General of Martial Might and Army Administrator for Wú Míngchè.
After Jiǎo was pacified,
Míngchè unilaterally executed Yáng Wéntōng, the Grand Administrator of Ānchéng, in the army,
and also dealt with the surrendered men, horses, and weapons in an unclear manner.
Jǐng Lì was also implicated for failing to rectify the situation,
and was arrested and brought to justice.
After a long time,
he was pardoned
and reappointed Advisory Counselor to the Prince of Póyáng who Guards the East.
When Gāo Zōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Chief Clerk to the Prince of Yùzhāng who Proclaims Benevolence,
concurrently serving as Administrator of Kuàijī Commandery,
and acting as the Prefect of Dōngyáng Prefecture.
Upon completing his term,
he was promoted to General of Military Brilliance, Chief Clerk to the Prince of Chángshā who Manifests Valor,
and Grand Administrator of Xúnyáng,
acting as the Prefect of Jiāng Prefecture.
He resigned due to illness,
and consequently did not take up the post.
He entered court as Palace Gentleman with Access to the Throne, Regular Mounted Attendant, and Palace Aide-de-camp of the Central Secretariat,
in charge of imperial edicts,
and his fief was restored.
He was promoted to Palace Guard Commander of the Heir Apparent,
remaining Regular Mounted Attendant and Palace Aide-de-camp.
In the fifth year of Tàijiàn (太建),
Dūdū (都督) Wú Míngchè (吳明徹) launched a northern expedition.
Wherever he went, he achieved victories.
He battled Zhōu (周) general Liáng Shìyàn (梁士彥) at Lǚliáng (呂梁),
and inflicted a great defeat upon him.
He captured and beheaded tens of thousands of enemy soldiers.
He was about to advance and capture Péngchéng (彭城).
At this time, Gāozōng (高宗) was intent on reconquering Hénán (河南),
believing that it could be settled with a mere command.
Jǐnglì (景歷) advised against it, stating that the army was weary and the generals arrogant,
and it was not advisable to pursue distant strategies excessively.
Gāozōng (高宗) detested his attempt to discourage the troops,
and was greatly enraged.
However, considering him an old official of the imperial court,
he did not punish him severely.
He was dismissed and appointed Xuānyuǎn Jiāngjūn (宣遠將軍) and Yùzhāng Nèishǐ (豫章內史).
Before he could depart,
he was impeached by a "flying memorial" (飛章).
It stated that during his time in office,
he had been notorious for corruption.
The Emperor ordered the authorities to investigate him.
Jǐnglì (景歷) admitted to only half of the charges.
Thereupon, Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) Zōng Yuánráo (宗元饒) memorialized, saying:
"Your subject has heard that a gentleman's conduct
is characterized by loyalty in serving his superiors
and integrity in maintaining himself.
Should one deviate from this path,
punishment will be unforgiving.
We respectfully note that Xuānyuǎn Jiāngjūn (宣遠將軍), Yùzhāng Nèishǐ (豫章內史), and Xīnfēng Xiàn Kāiguó Hóu (新豐縣開國侯) Jǐnglì (景歷),
by virtue of great fortune,
had previously served the rising king.
When the imperial fortunes first began,
he considerably participated in the founding.
During the Tiānjiā (天嘉) era,
he was notorious for bribery.
Yet, by imperial grace, he was employed
and granted an opportunity for redemption.
His territorial fief and high rank
were soon restored.
However, he failed to change his ways and exert himself
to repay this extraordinary favor.
Instead, he indulged in greed and corruption,
which became known far and wide.
One instance would have been excessive;
how could there be a second?
He should be subjected to the law
to clarify the autumn ordinances.
We, your subjects, have discussed the matter
and propose that, based on the current evidence, Jǐnglì (景歷) be dismissed from his current offices,
and be sent to the Hónglú (鴻臚) to have his noble titles and land stripped.
We respectfully present this white tablet for your consideration."
The imperial edict said,
"Approved."
Thereupon, he moved to Huìjī (會稽).
When Wú Míngchè (吳明chè) was defeated,
the Emperor recalled Jǐnglì's (景歷) previous words.
He immediately recalled him
and reinstated him as Zhēngnán Póyáng Wáng Cīyì Cānjūn (征南鄱陽王諮議參軍).
A few days later,
he was promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍),
concurrently Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞).
His original noble titles and fiefs were restored,
and he was appointed Dùzhī Shàngshū (度支尚書).
According to old custom, official appointments were made in the afternoon.
On the day Jǐnglì (景歷) was appointed,
the imperial carriage happened to be visiting Xuánwǔ Guàn (玄武觀).
All officials were attending the imperial banquet.
The Emperor, fearing Jǐnglì (景歷) might be displeased,
specifically ordered an early appointment,
showing the extent of his regard.
That year,
he died in office from illness,
aged sixty.
He was posthumously granted Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿)
and given the posthumous name Jìng (敬).
Thirteen years later,
he was reburied,
and posthumously granted Zhōnglǐngjūn (中領軍).
In the first year of Zhēngmíng (禎明),
he was honored with a place in Gāozǔ's (高祖) ancestral temple.
In the second year,
the imperial carriage personally visited his residence.
Jǐnglì (景歷) was posthumously granted Shìzhōng (侍中) and Zhōngfǔ Jiāngjūn (中撫將軍),
given the posthumous name Zhōngjìng (忠敬),
provided with one set of drum and wind instruments (鼓吹),
and a stele was erected at his tomb.
Jǐnglì's (景歷) writings
did not emphasize elaborate elegance,
but excelled in their substance.
He was quick and agile in responding to situations,
and was praised by his contemporaries.
He had a collection of thirty volumes of his writings.
Liú Shīzhī (劉師知)
was a native of Pèiguó Xiàng (沛國相).
His family had been an old established clan for generations.
His grandfather, Xīzhī (奚之),
was Qí Jìn'ān Wáng Cīyì Cānjūn (齊晉安王諮議參軍)
and Huáinán Tàishǒu (淮南太守) during the Qí (齊) dynasty.
He governed ably,
and Qí Wǔdì (齊武帝) frequently praised and rewarded him with imperial edicts written by hand.
His father, Jǐngyàn (景彥),
was Liáng Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (梁尚書左丞) and Sīnóng Qīng (司農卿).
Shīzhī (師知) loved learning
and possessed talent suitable for his era.
He was widely versed in books and history,
skilled in writing,
and adept at etiquette.
He was well-versed in many precedents and regulations of the imperial court.
During the Liáng (梁) dynasty, he served successively as Wángfǔ Cānjūn (王府參軍).
At the beginning of Shàotài (紹泰),
when Gāozǔ (高祖) entered to assist,
he appointed Shīzhī (師知) as Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人),
in charge of imperial edicts.
At that time, after the chaos of war,
many ritual protocols were missing.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) became Prime Minister, was granted the Nine Bestowals, and accepted the abdication,
all the ceremonial procedures were determined by Shīzhī (師知).
After Gāozǔ (高祖) received the mandate,
he remained Shèrén (舍人).
He was naturally informal and straightforward,
and often clashed with others.
Although his official position did not advance,
he was entrusted with heavy responsibilities,
and his suggestions for reform or abolition were all greatly beneficial.
When Gāozǔ passed away,
after six days of putting on mourning attire (chéngfú),

the court officials jointly deliberated on the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the attire worn by those attending the spirit-seat (língzuò) of the great departed Emperor (Dàxíng Huángdì) and the imperial attendants (xiá yù rén).
Doctor Bóshì Shěn Wén'ā argued
that auspicious attire (jí fú) should be worn.
Shī Zhī argued:
“Since it is called 'putting on mourning attire,'
it is fundamentally for preparing the funeral rites.
The clothing and items on the spirit-mat (líng yán)
should all be plain white (gǎosù).
Although there is no official duty for the great departed emperor's imperial attendants (Dàxíng xiá yù guānshì) now,
according to the passing of Liáng Zhāomíng Tàizǐ,
the officials attending (xiáshì) in mourning attire (chéngfú)
all wore coarse mourning clothes (cuī zhǎn),
except for their armor, which was unchanged.
This can be taken as a precedent.
I believe that on the sixth day of putting on mourning attire,
those attending the spirit-seat must wear mourning clothes and headbands (cuī dié).”
Cài Jǐnglì, a scholar of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén), also said:
“Although not entirely in accordance,
according to the auspicious and inauspicious ceremonial guards (yǔ yí) for imperial tombs (shānlíng),
the putting on of mourning attire is only inauspicious, not auspicious.
It is inappropriate for military and civil attendants (wénwǔ xiá yù)
to exclusively wear sable and jade ornaments (míng yù ěr diāo).
Given the conflict between sentiment and ritual,
it is reasonable to wear coarse mourning clothes.”
Jiāng Dézǎo and Xiè Qí, scholars of the Secretariat, and others all agreed with Shī Zhī’s argument.
Wén'ā re-argued:
“According to the ritual records for imperial tombs of the Jìn and Sòng dynasties: ‘When the spirit carriage (líng yú) and coffin (zǐ gōng) descend from the hall,
each attending minister (shì zhōng) plays a musical instrument.’
The ritual for putting on mourning attire also states: ‘The spirit carriage and coffin accommodate attendant officials (xiá yù guān) and fragrant candles.’
Further, the ritual for the movement of the spirit carriage and coffin states: ‘The direct attendants (zhí líng xiá yù) wear auspicious attire,
among the auspicious ceremonial procession (jí lǔbù).’
It also says: ‘The coffin attendants wear mourning attire,
among the inauspicious ceremonial procession (xiōng lǔbù).’
This means there are both auspicious and inauspicious attendants in the hall.”
At that time, since the two arguments differed,
a request was made to Left Assistant (Zuǒ Chéng) Xú Líng for a decision.
Líng said:
“The coffin is interred in the imperial tomb,
and the spirit-mat is placed in the ancestral temple.
There is this distinction,
which proves auspiciousness or inauspiciousness.
According to the auspicious section of the imperial tomb procession,
those who lead, from dukes and ministers downwards,
as well as the brave warriors (wǔbēn), musicians (gǔchuī), umbrella-bearers (zhí gài), and carriage attendants (fèng chē),
all wear auspicious attire.
How can the attendants alone wear mourning clothes?
The decision is obvious.
If it is said that dukes, ministers, clerks, and officials all wear coarse mourning clothes,
what difference would this make from the coffin procession?
If it is said that all cultural relics (wénwù) are auspicious,
but the functionaries are inauspicious,
how can one wear coarse mourning clothes and hold a magnificent canopy,
〔10〕or wear mourning attire and ascend a jade chariot?
I agree with the Doctor's argument.”
Shī Zhī again argued:
“The Left Assistant cited that the coffin is interred in the imperial tomb,
and the spirit-mat is placed in the ancestral temple,
and that there must be auspicious and inauspicious sections.
It is inappropriate for the putting on of mourning attire to be entirely inauspicious,
and the Doctor still adheres to his previous judgment,
which ultimately concerns the rites of the imperial tomb.
If the dragon carriage (lóng jià) initiates the moving of the coffin,
and the imperial chariot (luán yú) is also provided,
the rituals of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness
have always been prepared.
To apply this to the putting on of mourning attire,
I feel it is inappropriate.
The system of mourning rites
applies from the Son of Heaven downwards.
According to the clear record of mourning attire by Wáng Wénxiàn: ‘For officials of the third rank,
there are twenty spirit attendants (shì líng rén).
For officials of the fourth rank,
down to the rites for scholars,
the number of spirit attendants
is ten people.
They all wear white cloth trousers (bái bù kù zhě)
and white silk caps (bái juàn mào).
For inner mourning, the number of female attendants is the same as outside,
but they wear even-hemmed mourning clothes (qí cuī).
Someone asked why the inner and outer spirit attendants are the same,
but their mourning attire suddenly differs?
The answer is,
if according to the rites between ruler and subject,
then the outer attendants wear rough mourning clothes (zhǎn),
and the inner attendants wear even-hemmed mourning clothes.
In recent times, due to many incidents,
the rites have been simplified as circumstances dictated.
For those below feudal lords,
their subjects and officials are perhaps humble,
and as for attendance,
many come out of righteous attachment.
The protocol between ruler and subject is not complete,
and the cost of mourning caps (cuī guān) is indeed lacking,
so they adapt their regular attire,
only changing their caps.
Female attendants
are all humble slaves.
Since the way of ruler and concubine is pure,
their attire is therefore fully prepared.’
The current dynasty's regulations
are still not like this.
From this, it can be inferred
that mourning clothes (zhǎn) should be worn.
If there are spirit attendants,
they are like imperial attendants.
Since they wear white caps,
it is unreasonable for them to wear red attire (tóng fú).
Moreover, the ritual records for Liáng Zhāomíng are still extant today.
These two texts provide clear evidence,
serving as a significant precedent.
Furthermore, ritual originates from human sentiment
and can be adjusted.
When a person experiences a loss,
the tables and chairs are arranged,
the coarse silk curtains and spirit screens
〔11〕change their usual appearance.
The reed mat and straw hut
are for the inauspicious rites.
Inside the hall,
relatives and guests gather,
wearing even-hemmed or rough mourning clothes and hempen mourning clothes,
crying in their respective places.
Black caps are not worn for condolences.
Everyone wears plain clothes (sù fú).
Have you ever seen disciples and former officials
rushing about in fine silk and gauze,
or a concubine on the left and a concubine on the right
mixing red and purple?
Moreover, the four seas are silenced in mourning (è mì),
and the sentiments of the entire land are the same.
The three armies wear plain white,
and the system of mourning attire is unified.
Thus, when a thousand gates open at dawn,
it is not to apply plaster to red gates.
When hundreds of officials arrive,
they change their attire to coarse clothes over their red girdles.
Yet, if gold ornaments gleam in the ranks,
and jade pendants jingle as they walk,
it is certainly not satisfactory
when considering our emotions.
Applying this to the ritual classics,
there is even less precedent for such a thing.
How can the ritual for putting on mourning attire
be compared to the rites of the imperial tomb?
When the burial is completely finished from beginning to end,
there are indeed auspicious and inauspicious rites.
What is called 'putting on mourning attire'
is fundamentally about completing the mourning rites.
All internal and external departments
change their auspicious appearance.
If the imperial attendants alone do not,
what is meant by 'putting on mourning attire'?
If there are no imperial attendants for the spirit, then so be it.
If there are, they must wear mourning attire.”
Xiè Qí argued:
“The spirit-mat is placed in the ancestral temple,
and the coffin is interred in the imperial tomb.
This is indeed as the Left Assistant argued.
However, the imperial tomb procession
is equipped with both auspicious and inauspicious elements.
Those who follow the spirit carriage have unchanged ritual attire,
while those who follow the coffin all wear coarse mourning clothes.
Down to the rites for scholars,
all conform to this system.
This is specifically the ritual for the imperial tomb,
not related to putting on mourning attire.
Now, it is said that the coffin and spirit screen (líng yǐ)
are both on the western steps,
referred to as putting on mourning attire.
There is also no procession.
It is simply that from clerks and officials
up to kings and dukes,
within the four seas,
all must wear mourning clothes and headbands.
The passing of Liáng Zhāomíng Tàizǐ
is broadly an established precedent.
How can it be that all common people
wear heavy mourning,
while the attendants, from ministers to military guards,
who are the closest officials,
instead jingle jade and wear green,
no different from ordinary auspicious times?
Since the Left Assistant relies on matters of the imperial tomb,
I think it may differ from putting on mourning attire.
If so, on that day, the imperial attendants,
civil and military alike, would be no different.
And the spirit attendants,
scribe, announcer, document manager, and imperial edict responder,
should all remain unchanged.”
Cài Jǐnglì again argued:
“The imperial attendants
originally numbered five hundred.
On that day, they would be fully dressed, residing in the mourning hut,
still in their original departments.
When led up to the hall,
how could they change into sable and jade attire?
If other officials were temporarily appointed,
to fill hairpins and earrings,
then on that day there would immediately be someone who is not in mourning attire.
For mountain mausoleums, there are naturally two opinions, auspicious and inauspicious.
As putting on mourning attire is inauspicious and not auspicious,
I still follow the previous opinion,
like Attendant Liu Shèrén.”
Dézǎo further deliberated, saying:
“I believe that for the ancestral burial day,
from start to finish,
when high officials receive posthumous honors,
it is necessary to display their grace and glory.
Having an auspicious imperial procession [lǔbù]
might stem from this meaning,
and private families imitating this [fàngxiào]
then turned it into a custom.
Wearing mourning attire inherently changes auspiciousness to inauspiciousness;
it is logically inappropriate to still wear fine silk.
Attendant Liu Shèrén cited the funeral rites of Wáng Wèijūn and examined the records of Liáng Zhāomíng,
which are clearly established precedents.
The Erudite and Left Assistant Director have each expressed their genuine opinions.
Since no conclusion has been reached,
further detailed inquiry is needed.

It is advisable to consult the Bāzuò, the Jìanshì, the Tàicháng, the Zhōngchéng (Kǒng), and the Zhōngshù, all of whom are well-versed, such as Yuán Shū, Zhāng Zhǒng, Zhōu Hóngzhèng, Hóngràng, Shěn Jiǒng, and Kǒng Huàn
At that time, the Bāzuò and others
all requested:
“Examining the various opinions,
and considering the old rites,
the detailed regulations for the mourning attire rites of Crown Prince Liáng Zhāomíng
are clearly preserved in writing [míngwén jiàncún]
and serve as a sufficient standard.
On the day of putting on mourning attire,
it is logically inappropriate for attending officials to still follow auspicious rites.
The distinction of auspiciousness in burial rites
is solely for the time of the mountain mausoleum [shānlíng zhī shí],
and has nothing to do with the day of putting on mourning attire.
I believe Attendant Liu Shèrén’s opinion is sound in this matter.”
Líng replied heavily:
“Old and sick, barely breathing [shǔkuàng],
I cannot speak much.
Ancient people’s disputes
often led to resentment.
Fù Xuán was criticized in the Jìn Dynasty,
and Wáng Shāng was entrapped in the Hàn Dynasty.
I will be extremely cautious [jǐn zì sānjiān]
and respectfully comply with the high decree.
If by some chance I do not die,
I may still express my views,
perhaps to further discuss and deliberate with the court worthies.”
Wén'ē still held to his view,
and the public discussion could not reach a decision.
So, both opinions were fully recorded and presented to the throne,
adopting Shīzhī’s opinion.
Soon, he was promoted to Hónglú Qīng,
while Attendant remained as before.
In Tiānjiā first year (560),
he was dismissed due to an incident.
Initially,
Shìzǔ ordered Shīzhī to compile the Records of Daily Life [qǐjūzhù].
From Yǒngdìng second year autumn to Tiānjiā first year winter,
it comprised ten scrolls.
He started as Zhōngshū Shèrén
and again took charge of imperial edicts.
In Tiānkāng first year (566),
Shìzǔ was unwell.
Shīzhī, along with Shàngshū Púyè Dào Zhòngjǔ and others, attended to his medicine.
When Shìzǔ passed away,
Shīzhī had already received the dying instructions.
When Gāozōng became Shàngshū Lìng
and entered to assist,
in Guāngdà first year (567),
Shīzhī, Zhòngjǔ, and others dispatched Attendant Yīn Bùnìng to falsely proclaim an edict ordering Gāozōng to return to the Eastern Palace.
When the matter was discovered,
he was granted death in the Northern Prison.
Xiè Qí was
a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His father, Dá,
was an Erudite of the Grand Academy in the Liáng Dynasty.
Qí was astute and quick-witted in his youth,
fond of learning,
and was praised in the Liáng era.
He served as Shàngshū Jīnbù Láng
and Magistrate of Shānyīn.
During the chaos of Hóu Jǐng,
Qí lived as a refugee in Dōngyáng.
When Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
he sought refuge with Zhāng Biāo.
When Biāo was in Wújùn and Kuàijī,
he entrusted all matters to him.
Whenever Biāo went on campaigns,
he always left Qí to supervise the commandery [jiānjùn]
and manage subsequent affairs.
When Biāo was defeated,
Gāozǔ summoned Qí to participate in confidential matters,
and made him concurrently Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
At that time, military campaigns were frequent,
and provisions were often scarce.
Qí managed affairs wherever he was stationed,
and was deeply appreciated and trusted.
In Yǒngdìng first year (557),
he was appointed Jìshì Huángmén Shìláng and Zhōngshū Shèrén,
concurrently holding the post of Yòuchéng as before.
He died in Tiānjiā second year (561),
and was posthumously granted Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì.
Qí’s younger brother, Jiǎo,
was diligent in study [dúxué]
and became a renowned scholar of his time.
The Imperial Historian said: Gāozǔ established his foundation and undertook his enterprise,
resolving chaos and calamities.
His martial prowess indeed achieved his success,
and his literary talent also exerted its strength.
and were thus among the ministers who laid the foundation.
Liú Shīzhī was broadly learned and well-versed,
but was ignorant of adapting to circumstances [jībiàn].
Though he wished to uphold integrity and righteousness,
he ultimately suffered extreme punishment.
This was unwise.
(In the biography of Liú Shīzhī,
“Kǒng Zhōngshù Zhū Tōng”
is doubtful.)

with his staff and area commander titles remaining as before.
Wáng Lín occupied the upper reaches of the river,
and Héngzhōu and Guǎngzhōu were disloyal,
so Mài could not take up his post
and remained at Dàyǔ Lǐng.
In the first year of Tiānjiā,
he was summoned to be Shìzhōng and Dūguān Shàngshū.
Before he could accept,
he was again made Zhōngshū Lìng.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
acting as head of the Eastern Palace,
with the title of Shìzhōng remaining as before.
He was granted the additional title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and concurrently served as Dùzhī Shàngshū.
When Fèi Dì ascended the throne,
he was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
In the first year of Tàijiàn,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Yòu Púyè.
At that time, the eastern border suffered a great flood,
and the common people experienced famine.
Mài was appointed Rénwǔ Jiāngjūn and Jìnlíng Tàishǒu.
He had great prestige and benevolence in the commandery.
The people of the commandery petitioned to erect a stele
to praise Mài's political achievements,
and an imperial edict granted permission.
He was summoned to be Zhōngshū Jiān,
again appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púyè,
and concurrently served as Yòujūn Jiāngjūn.
He died in the fifth month of the fourth year,
at the age of sixty-seven.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng and Zhōngshū Jiān,
with the posthumous title Wēn.
Yuán Jìng, courtesy name Zǐgōng,
was a native of Yángxià, Chén Jùn.
His grandfather, Yǐ,
was Sòng Shìzhōng, Lìbù Shàngshū, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
His father, Áng,
was Liáng Shìzhōng and Sīkōng,
with the posthumous title Mù Gōng.
Jìng was purely filial and had a distinguished character.
He was diligent in his studies from a young age
and showed no weariness even in old age.
He began his career as Mìshū Láng,
and successively rose to Tàizǐ Shèrén, Xǐmǎ, and Zhōngshèrén.
When Jiānglíng fell,
he took refuge in Lǐngbiǎo.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
Jìng was in Guǎngzhōu,
dependent on Ōuyáng Wèi.
When Wèi died,
his son Hè occupied the prefecture
and harbored rebellious intentions.
Jìng repeatedly admonished Hè,
explaining the principles of loyalty and rebellion,
with very sincere words,
but Hè ultimately did not listen.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
he sent Zhāng Zhāodá to lead troops to suppress Hè.
When Hè was about to be defeated,
he regretted not having heeded Jìng's words.
The court recognized his righteousness.
That year, he was summoned to be Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ and Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì.
Shortly after, he was transferred to Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zuǒmín Shàngshū,
then transferred to Dūguān Shàngshū,
and concurrently served as Yùzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng.
He successively rose to Tàicháng Qīng, Sànqí Chángshì, Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and was granted the additional title of Tèjìn.
He died in the third year of Zhìdé,
at the age of seventy-nine.
He was posthumously granted Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū,
with the posthumous title Jìngdé.
His son Yuán Yǒu succeeded him.
His younger brother Bì has his own biography.
His elder brother's son was Shū.
Shū, courtesy name Jiànyán,
was the son of Liáng Wú Jùn Tàishǒu Jūnzhèng.
He had a beautiful appearance,
a calm and quiet nature,
and loved reading,
never letting a book leave his hand.
His family was distinguished and wealthy for generations,
with abundant assets,
yet Shū alone lived a simple life,
had no social interactions,
sat quietly in one room,
and never went out for pleasure unless for public affairs.
His ambition for honor and profit was indifferent.
He began his career as Liáng Mìshū Láng,
and successively held positions such as Tàizǐ Shèrén, Qīngchē Hédōng Wáng Zhǔbù,
and Gōngcáo Shǐ in the two administrations of Ānqián Shàolíng Wáng
and Zhōngjūn Xuānchéng Wáng.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Shū went to Wú Jùn to visit his father,
and consequently observed mourning for his father.
At that time, the four directions were in turmoil,
and people sought to escape calamity.
Shū became known for his extreme filial piety during mourning.
When Wáng Sēngbiàn pacified Hóu Jǐng
and garrisoned the capital,
officials flocked to seek an audience,
but Shū alone kept his door shut and lived in quiet seclusion,
not seeking fame or advancement.
In the first year of Shàotài,
he was summoned to be Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng.
Before he could accept,
he was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì
and concurrently Shìzhōng.
In the second year,
he concurrently served as Lìbù Shàngshū.
That year, he was sent out as Wúxīng Tàishǒu.
In the second year of Yǒngdìng,
he was summoned to be Zuǒmín Shàngshū.
Before he arrived,
he was reassigned as Shìzhōng,
and was in charge of the Grand Selection.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Dūguān Shàngshū,
with his duty of selection remaining as before.
Shū was widely read and had a strong memory,
and was thoroughly familiar with old regulations.
Initially,
Gāozǔ's eldest daughter, Yǒngshì Gōngzhǔ, was first married to Chénliú Tàishǒu Qián Chǎn,
and bore a son, Jié.
Both the princess and Jié died during the Liáng dynasty.
When Gāozǔ received the mandate,
only the princess was posthumously enfeoffed.
When the time came for her burial,
the Shàngshū Zhǔkè requested a detailed discussion,
wishing to bestow the title Fùmǎ Dūwèi upon Chǎn
and posthumously grant an official rank to Jié.
Shū deliberated, saying:
"In ancient times, when a royal princess married,
she would certainly marry a feudal lord.
It is stated in the *Gōngyáng* commentary that those of the same surname were rulers.
The non-conformance of carriages and garments
is evident in the poems of the poets.
When the Hàn dynasty first arose,
marquises married princesses.
From then on,
princesses were married into common families.
The position of Fùmǎ Dūwèi was established by Hàn Wǔdì,
