sometimes bestowed upon meritorious officials,
and sometimes upon imperial relatives.
Therefore, Cáo Zhí of Wèi submitted a memorial stating that Fùmǎ and Fèngchē should be one title.
The *Qí Zhíyí* states
that anyone who marries a princess must be appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
this has been the standard.
This is probably because of the importance of a royal princess
and the low status of a commoner.
If their ranks were not raised,
how could they share a wedding cup?
Therefore, the position of Fùmǎ was granted
to honor the imperial daughter.
Now, the princess died early,
and her marital bond is already broken.
Since there are no ceremonial doubts,
why is the bestowal of Fùmǎ necessary?
Consider Dù Yù, who married Jìn Xuāndì's second daughter, Gāolíng Xuān Gōngzhǔ.
When Jìn Wǔdì ascended the throne,
the princess had already died.
During the Tàishǐ era, the princess was posthumously granted her title,
but Yuán Kǎi no longer had the title of Fùmǎ.
Liáng Wéndì's daughter, Xīn'ān Mù Gōngzhǔ, died early.
In the early Tiānjiān era, there was no posthumous appointment for the Wáng clan.
These two distant and recent examples
are sufficient to clarify the matter.
The princess's son
had not yet reached the age of adulthood,
so there is no need for this bestowal.
It is now appropriate to posthumously grant him the title of Tíng Hóu."
At that time, Shū's opinion was considered superior.
In the first year of Tiānjiā (560),
he held the position of Shàngshū of the Ministry of Personnel.
In the third year,
he became the true holder of the office.
Soon after, he was appointed General of the Right Army,
and then Governor of Dānyáng Commandery,
with his original position remaining unchanged.
In the fifth year,
because of his father's funeral,
he submitted a memorial to resign,
and an imperial edict granted him fifty bolts of silk and cloth,
and one hundred thousand coins,
ordering him to reside at home and oversee commandery affairs after the funeral.
(After) the period of mourning ended,
he returned to his original post.
In that same year, his term of office expired,
and he relinquished the position of Yǐn (Governor).
He was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì,
while his positions as general and Shàngshū remained unchanged.
At this time,
although Púshè Dào Zhòngjǔ was involved in personnel selection,
the selection and promotion of officials
all originated from the Central Secretariat.
Many of those he recommended
were in accord with the emperor's will.
He was cautious and thorough,
and maintained a reputation for integrity.
Among civil and military officials,
few frequented his gate.
When the deposed emperor ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè.
He died in the first year of Guāngdà (567),
at the age of fifty-one.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng and Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū,
and given the posthumous name Jiǎnyì.
His collected works in ten volumes were circulated in the world.
His younger brother Xiàn has his own biography.
The historian says: Wáng Chōng and Wáng Tōng both rose early to prominent positions through their noble lineage,
and yet they observed rites and etiquette,
and served their superiors with sincere devotion.
This is commendable.
Wáng Mài's spirit was serene and detached,
and Yuán Shū's upright conduct was profound.
Though their restrictions and liberations differed,
their superior qualities were the same.
The so-called "famous scholars" of ancient times
were perhaps such men!
Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter 12: Shěn Zhòng, Yuán Bì, Liú Zhòngwēi, Lù Shāncái, Wáng Zhì, Wéi Zài (clan cousin Huì).
Shěn Zhòng, courtesy name Zhòngshī,
was a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
His grandfather, Yuē,
was a Grandee of Liáng.
His father, Xuán, was an Attendant-in-ordinary to the Yellow Gate of Liáng.
Zhòng loved learning and was quite skilled in literary composition.
He began his career as a Judicial Aide to the Prince of Nánpíng, Zhènwèi of Liáng, and a Palace Gentleman of the Heir Apparent.
At this time,
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng composed the 'Thousand-Character Poem,'
and Zhòng provided annotations for it.
He and Xiè Jǐng of Chénjùn were summoned together for an audience at the Wéndé Palace.
The emperor ordered Zhòng to compose a 'Rhapsody on Bamboo.'
When the rhapsody was completed
and presented,
the emperor praised it,
and personally issued an edict in reply, saying:
"Your literary style is elegant and fluid,
it can be said you do not disgrace your ancestors."
When Duke Dāngyáng, Xiāo Dàxīn, was Governor of Yǐngzhōu,
he appointed Zhòng as his Secretary-aide within the specified limits.
Soon after, he was appointed Secretary-aide to the Prince of Xiāngdōng, Zhènnán.
He was promoted to Middle Palace Gentleman of the Heir Apparent,
and concurrently Sànqí Chángshì.
After his mission to Wèi
and return,
he was promoted to Counselor-in-attendance to the Prince of Lúlíng, Piàojì,
with his position as Palace Gentleman remaining unchanged.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Zhòng memorialized Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
stating that his family's generations of retainers and loyal followers
were all in Wúxīng,
and requested to return to recruit them to suppress the rebels.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng granted his request.
When Jǐng besieged Táichéng,
Zhòng led his clan members and five thousand loyal followers,
and entered to aid the capital city,
stationing themselves at Xiǎoháng.
Facing the rebels at Dōngfǔ, he arrayed his troops.
His military formation was very orderly,
and Jǐng greatly feared him.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng remotely appointed Zhòng as Right Guard Commander of the Heir Apparent from within the city.
When the capital fell,
Zhòng surrendered to Jǐng.
After Jǐng was pacified,
he traveled west to Jīngzhōu.
Emperor Yuán appointed him Middle Palace Gentleman of the Heir Apparent and Great Rectifier of his home province.
Soon after, he was promoted to Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works.
When Jiānglíng fell,
he was captured by Western Wèi.
He soon escaped and returned.
Emperor Jìng, by imperial decree,
appointed him Palace Assistant Imperial Censor.
In the first year of Shàotài (555),
he was appointed Shìzhōng,
and promoted to Shàngshū of the Left Ministry of the People.
When Gāozǔ received the mandate,
he was promoted to Central Secretariat Director,
with his position as rectifier remaining unchanged.
Gāozǔ, knowing Zhòng was renowned in his home region,
greatly respected him,
and his rewards and grants were more generous
than those of his contemporaries.
Zhòng was naturally frugal;
he managed his household property,
and his wealth amounted to hundreds of millions,
yet he shared nothing.
His own sustenance was very meager.
Often at court assemblies,
his clothes were torn,
or he would personally carry his cap and shoes.
In the second year of Yǒngdìng (558),
he concurrently served as Shàngshū of the Ministry of Public Works,
supervising the construction of the Tàijí Palace.
He always wore a plain cloth robe and straw sandals,
using a hemp rope as a belt.
He would also carry dried fish and vegetables with rice and eat them alone.
The court officials all criticized his behavior.
Zhòng was by nature irritable and impatient,
and so he became resentful,
and proceeded to denigrate the dukes and ministers,
and criticize the court.
Gāozǔ was greatly angered.
However, because Zhòng had always had a good reputation,
he did not want to execute him openly.
Later, when Zhòng took leave and returned to Wǔkāng,
he was given death in Wúzhōng,
at the age of fifty-six.
Yuán Bì, courtesy name Wényáng,
was the younger brother of Yuán Jìng, the Left Grandee of Radiance.
He was pure, upright, and capable,
with a stately and robust physique,
and his aspirations and conduct were refined and circumspect.
He began his career as an Extra Attendant to the Sànqí,
and served successively as an aide in various princely mansions.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Bì wished to become a general.
At this time, Bì's elder brother, Jūnzhèng, was Governor of Wújùn.
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng appointed Bì as Director of the Eastern Palace,
ordering him to go to Wúzhōng to recruit soldiers.
When Jǐng besieged Táichéng,
Bì led his forces to reinforce it.
When the capital fell,
he retreated and held Dōngyáng.
Jǐng sent troops to pursue him,
so he left from the eastern ridge of Kuàijī and exited at Pénchéng,
seeking refuge with Xiāo Fàn, the Prince of Póyáng.
When Fàn died,
Bì surrendered to Jǐng.
After Jǐng was pacified,
Wáng Sēngbiàn memorialized Bì as Governor of Fùchūn,
and concurrently Governor of Dānyáng.
When the Marquess of Zhēnyáng usurped the throne,
he appointed Bì as Shìzhōng,
and sent him on a mission to Qí.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
Wáng Lín occupied the upper reaches of the river.
Bì traveled from Qí with Xiāo Zhuāng, the Prince of Yǒngjiā of Liáng, to Lín's location.
When Zhuāng usurped the throne,
he appointed Bì as Shìzhōng and Chief Clerk to the Chancellor.
In the second year of Tiānjiā (561),
Bì and Lín assisted Zhuāng to Zàkǒu.
When Lín's army was defeated,
everyone fled and scattered.
Only Bì alone took a small boat and escorted Zhuāng to the northern border,
entrusting Zhuāng to Liú Zhòngwēi, the Palace Assistant Imperial Censor,
and instructing them to enter Qí together.
Only then did he bow and take leave to return,
and proceed to the court to plead guilty.
Emperor Wén greatly admired his righteousness.
Soon after, he was appointed Cānchán for the Fǎcáo of the Níngyuǎn Shǐxīngwáng Mansion.
He was then transferred to Zīyì Cānjūn.
He was appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
concurrently Shìzhōng,
and in charge of Yùzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng.
He was sent as an envoy to Zhōu.
After returning from his mission,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì
and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
His position as Zhōngzhèng remained as before.
When Gāozōng entered the government to assist,
Mì was appointed Yúnqí Jiāngjūn and Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ.
He died in the first year of Guāngdà,
aged fifty-eight.
On his deathbed, he admonished his son Mànhuá, saying:
"I have no achievements at court.
After I close my eyes,
bury me with my hands and feet drawn in,
and do not accept any posthumous honors or titles."
His son conveyed Mì's last wishes
and submitted a memorial requesting this.
The court did not allow it,
and bestowed upon him the title Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
with the posthumous name Zhì.
Liú Zhòngwēi was a native of Nièyáng, Nányáng.
His grandfather, Qiú,
was summoned as Guózǐ Bóshì during the Qí dynasty,
but did not accept.
His father, Zhīlín,
was Jīngzhōu Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ.
Zhòngwēi was ambitious in his youth
and well-versed in literature and history.
During the Chéngshèng reign of Liáng, he served as Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Xiāo Zhuāng falsely appointed him Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
He followed Zhuāng into Qí
and died in Yèzhōng.
Zhòngwēi's younger cousin, Guǎngdé,
was also fond of learning,
talented and spirited.
His father, Zhīhēng,
was Liáng Ānxī Xiāngdōngwáng Chángshǐ and Nánjùn Tàishǒu.
Guǎngdé,
during the Chéngshèng reign, rose through military merits to Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng and Xiāngdōng Tàishǒu.
After Jīngzhōu fell,
he took refuge with Wáng Lín.
When Lín was pacified,
Wéndì appointed Guǎngdé as Níngyuǎn Shǐxīngwáng Fǔ Xiànwài Jìshì Cānjūn,
and he retained his former troops.
Soon after, he became Tàiwèi Hóu Zhèn Xiāngzhōu Fǔ Sīmǎ,
then successively Tàishǒu of Lèshān and Yùzhāng commanderies,
and Xīn'ān Nèishǐ.
During the Guāngdà reign,
he was granted the title Jiǎjié, Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì, Yúnqí Jiāngjūn, and Hédōng Tàishǒu.
He died in his commandery in the first year of Tàijiàn,
aged forty-three,
and was posthumously granted Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
Lù Shāncái, courtesy name Kǒngzhāng,
was a native of Wú, Wújùn.
His grandfather, Wēngbǎo,
was Liáng Shàngshū Shuǐbù Láng.
His father, Fàn,
was Sànqí Chángshì.
Shāncái was unconventional in his youth
and fond of literature and history.
Zhāng Zàn of Fànyáng,
and Zàn's younger brother Wǎn,
both greatly esteemed him.
He began his career as Wángguó Chángshì,
then moved to Wàibīng Cānjūn.
Soon after, due to his father's illness,
he returned east to attend to him.
In the first year of Chéngshèng,
Wáng Sēngbiàn appointed Shāncái Yítóngfǔ Xīcáoyuàn.
When Gāozǔ executed Sēngbiàn,
Shāncái fled to Huìjī and took refuge with Zhāng Biāo.
After Biāo's defeat,
he returned to Gāozǔ.
During the Shàotài reign,
Dūdū Zhōu Wényù was sent to garrison Nányùzhōu.
Being illiterate,
he appointed Shāncái as Chángshǐ,
entrusting all administrative matters to him.
Wényù campaigned south,
defeated Xiāo Bó,
and captured Ōuyáng Wěi;
many of his strategies came from Shāncái.
When Wényù campaigned west against Wáng Lín,
Shāncái was left to oversee Jiāngzhōu affairs,
and also garrisoned Yùzhāng.
Wényù and Hóu Āndū were defeated at Dùnkǒu.
Yú Xiàoqǐng came from Xīnlín to attack Yùzhāng.
Shāncái gathered the remaining troops
and took refuge with Zhōu Dí.
After Yú Xiàoqǐng and Lǐ Xiàoqīn were captured,
Shāncái was sent to escort them from Dōuyáng's Lè'ānlǐng by the eastern road to the capital.
He was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng.
He again proceeded from Lè'ānlǐng to pacify the southern commanderies of Chuān.
When Wényù re-garrisoned Yùzhāng Jīnkǒu,
Shāncái was again appointed Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn, Zhènnán Chángshǐ, and Yùzhāng Tàishǒu.
When Wényù was killed by Xióng Tánlǎng,
Tánlǎng imprisoned Shāncái and others,
and sent them to Wáng Lín.
Before they arrived,
Hóu Āndū defeated Lín's general Cháng Zhòng'ài at Gōngtínghú.
Because of this, Shāncái was able to return,
and was appointed Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn and Xīn'ān Tàishǒu.
As Wáng Lín was not yet pacified,
he was stationed in Fùyáng
to defend the eastern route.
He was recalled to serve as Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì,
and promoted to Xuānhuì Shǐxīngwáng Chángshǐ,
acting as Dōngyángzhōu Shǐ.
When Hóu Āndū campaigned against Liú Yì,
Shāncái led the Mansion's troops to follow him.
After Yì was pacified,
he was appointed Míngwēi Jiāngjūn and Dōngyáng Tàishǒu.
He was recalled to serve as Zhèndōng Shǐxīngwáng Chángshǐ,
concurrently Huìjī Jùnchéng,
acting as Dōngyángzhōu Shǐ.
Before he could take up the post,
he was reappointed Sànqí Chángshì,
concurrently Dùzhī Shàngshū.
After a year, he became a regular appointee.
When Gāozōng campaigned south against Zhōu Dí,
Shāncái was appointed Jūnsī.
After Dí was pacified,
he returned to his former post.
When Yú Xiàoqǐng attacked Jìn'ān by sea,
Shāncái, still holding his office, went to Huìjī
to direct military strategies.
Upon returning to court,
he was impeached by the Censorate
for an inappropriate exchange with Cài Jǐnglì at a banquet,
and dismissed from office.
Soon after, he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
and promoted to Yúnqí Jiāngjūn, Tàishǒu of Xīyáng and Wǔchāng commanderies.
He died in the first year of Tiānkāng,
aged fifty-eight.
He was posthumously granted Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
with the posthumous name Jiǎnzǐ.
Wáng Zhì, courtesy name Zǐzhēn,
was the younger brother of Yòuguānglù Dàfū Tōng.
He was ambitious in his youth
and widely read in books and history.
During the Liáng dynasty, as a nephew of Wǔdì, he was enfeoffed as Jiǎkǒutínghóu,
appointed Guózǐ Zhōuyìshēng,
and achieved high marks in the policy examination.
He began his career as Mìshū Láng, Tàizǐ Shèrén, and Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng.
He grieved over his mother's death,
and was renowned for his filial piety during mourning.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ and Dōnggōng Lǐngzhí.
He was successively promoted to Zhōngshèrén and Shùzǐ.
In the first year of Tàiqīng,
he was appointed Jiǎjié, Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn,
in charge of the Eastern Palace troops,
and followed Zhēnyánghóu on the northern expedition.
When Zhēnyáng was defeated,
Zhì escaped and returned.
When Hóu Jǐng revolted at Shòuyáng,
Zhì again led the navy to resist with the various armies.
When Jǐng's army crossed the Jiāng,
Zhì immediately retreated.
Soon after, he led infantry and cavalry to camp outside Xuānyángmén.
When Jǐng's army reached the capital,
Zhì's forces collapsed without a fight.
He then shaved his head to become a Buddhist monk (Sāngmén)
and hid among the common people.
When Liǔ Zhònglǐ and others assembled to relieve the capital,
and their army occupied the south bank,
Zhì again gathered his remaining troops and joined them.
After the capital fell,
he fled west to Jīngzhōu.
Yuándì, acting by imperial prerogative,
appointed Zhì as Yòuchángshǐ,
concurrently Hédōng Tàishǒu.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shìzhōng.
He was then sent out as Chíjé, Dūdū Wúzhōu Zhū Jūnshì, Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, and Wúzhōu Cìshǐ,
concurrently Póyáng Nèishǐ.
When Jīngzhōu fell,
Hóu Zhèn was stationed at Pénchéng,
and was at odds with Zhì.
He sent his subordinate general Yáng Liàng to replace Zhì,
and also brought troops to threaten him.
Zhì led his subordinates,
crossed Xìn'ānlǐng,
and took refuge with Liú Yì.
When Wéndì garrisoned Huìjī,
he sent troops to assist Zhì,
ordering him to garrison Xìn'ān Xiàn.
In the second year of Yǒngdì,
Gāozǔ ordered Zhì to lead his subordinates across the mountains into Yùzhāng
to follow Dūdū Zhōu Wényù in campaigning against Wáng Lín.
Zhì and Lín had always been on good terms,
and some slandered him, claiming he was secretly communicating with Lín in the army.
Gāozǔ ordered Zhōu Wényù to kill Zhì.
Wényù pleaded to save him,
and he was spared.
Soon after, he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì and Jìnlíng Tàishǒu.
When Wén Dì ēn (文帝) succeeded to the throne,
he was summoned to serve as Shǒuwǔbīng Shàngshū (守五兵尚書).
When Gāozōng (高宗) became Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (揚州刺史),
he appointed Zhì (質) as Rénwēi Jiāngjūn (仁威將軍) and Piàojí Fǔzhǎngshǐ (驃騎府長史).
In the second year of Tiānjiā (天嘉),
he was appointed Jìn'ān Tàishǒu (晉安太守).
When Gāozōng (高宗) assisted in governance,
he made him Sītú Zuǒzhǎngshǐ (司徒左長史),
his generalship remaining as before.
He was dismissed from office due to official misconduct.
Soon after, he became Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍),
then promoted to Tàifǔ Qīng (太府卿) and Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書).
He died in the second year of Tàijiàn (太建),
aged sixty.
He was posthumously granted his original office,
and given the posthumous name Ānzǐ (安子).
Wéi Zài (韋載), courtesy name Déjī (德基),
was a native of Dùlíng (杜陵) in Jīngzhào (京兆).
His grandfather, Ruì (叡),
was Liáng Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (梁開府儀同三司),
Yǒngchāng Yán Gōng (永昌嚴公).
His father, Zhèng (政),
〔一０〕was Liáng Huángmén Shìláng (梁黃門侍郎).
Zài (載) was intelligent and wise in his youth,
and devoted himself to study.
At the age of twelve,
he accompanied his uncle Léng (稜) to visit Liú Xiǎn (劉顯) of Pèiguó (沛國).
Xiǎn (顯) asked ten questions about the Book of Han,
and Zài (載) answered each question,
without any hesitation.
When he grew up,
he was widely read in literature and history,
and was profound, acute, and had a great capacity.
He began his career as Liáng Shàolíngwáng Fǎcáo Cānjūn (梁邵陵王法曹參軍),
then promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人) and Shàngshū Sāngōng Láng (尚書三公郎).
During Hóu Jǐng’s (侯景) rebellion,
Yuán Dì (元帝) appointed him Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎) by imperial prerogative.
Soon after, he became Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍) and Xúnyáng Tàishǒu (尋陽太守),
and followed Dūdū (都督) Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) eastward to campaign against Hóu Jǐng (侯景).
At that time, Sēngbiàn’s (僧辯) army was stationed at Pénchéng (湓城),
while Lǔ Xīdá (魯悉達) and Fán Jùn (樊俊) and others each held troops and defended their territories,
observing the outcome.
Yuán Dì (元帝) appointed Zài (載) as Jiǎjié (假節), Dūdū Tàiyuán Gāotáng Xīncài Sānjùn Zhūjūnjì (都督太原高唐新蔡三郡諸軍事), and Gāotáng Tàishǒu (高唐太守).
He was then ordered to persuade Xīdá (悉達) and others to send troops to attack Jǐng (景).
When the main army advanced eastward,
Zài (載) led the troops of the three commanderies from Jiāohú (焦湖) out through Zháilù (柵口),
and met Sēngbiàn (僧辯) at Liángshān (梁山).
After Jǐng (景) was pacified,
he was appointed Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) and Lángyé Tàishǒu (琅邪太守).
Soon after, he was sent on a mission to Dōngyáng (東陽) and Jìn'ān (晉安),
to recruit and pacify Liú Yì (留異) and Chén Bǎo'yìng (陳寶應) and others.
He was then granted Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn (信武將軍) and Yìxīng Tàishǒu (義興太守).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) executed Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯),
he sent Zhōu Wényù (周文育) with light troops to attack Zài (載).
Before Wényù (文育) arrived, Zài (載) was already aware,
and so he fortified the city and defended himself.
Wényù (文育) attacked very fiercely.
The county soldiers under Zài (載)’s command were all Gāozǔ’s (高祖) former soldiers,
and many were skilled archers.
Zài (載) gathered dozens of them,
tied them with long ropes,
and ordered his close associates to supervise them,
making them shoot at Wényù’s (文育) army.
He stipulated that if they failed to hit twice out of ten shots, they would be executed.
Each shot consistently hit,
and everyone hit was killed.
Wényù’s (文育) army gradually retreated.
They then built a stockade outside the city, relying on the water,
and held out for several tens of days.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) heard that Wényù’s (文育) army was at a disadvantage,
he personally led the campaign,
and conquered their water stockade.
He then sent Zài (載)’s cousin, Huì (翽), with a letter to persuade Zài (載) about the intention of executing Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯),
and also presented an imperial edict from Liáng Jìng Dì (梁敬帝),
【勑】ordering Zài (載) to disband his troops.
〔一一〕Upon receiving the letter, Zài (載)
surrendered his forces to Gāozǔ (高祖).
Gāozǔ (高祖) provided him with generous comfort and reassurance,
and immediately appointed his cousin Huì (翽) to supervise Yìxīng Jùn (義興郡).
The generals and commanders under Zài’s (載) command
were all appointed according to their talents.
Zài (載) was always kept close to Gāozǔ (高祖)’s side,
and consulted with him on important matters.
When Xú Sìhuī (徐嗣徽) and Rèn Yuē (任約) and others led the Qí (齊) army across the Yangtze River,
occupying Shítóu Chéng (石頭城),
Gāozǔ (高祖) asked Zài (載) for advice.
Zài (載) said:
“If the Qí (齊) army were to divide their forces and first occupy the routes to Sānwú (三吳),
and seize territory in the eastern region,
then the situation would be lost.
Now, we must immediately build a city at the former fortress of Hóu Jǐng (侯景) in Huáinán (淮南),
to open up the eastern route for transport.
Separately order light troops to cut off their grain supply,
so that they have nothing to plunder if they advance,
and nothing to rely on if they retreat.
Then the head of the Qí (齊) general
can be obtained within ten days.”
Gāozǔ (高祖) followed his plan.
In the first year of Yǒngdìng (永定),
he was appointed Héróng Jiāngjūn (和戎將軍) and Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍).
In the second year,
he was promoted to the title Qīngchē Jiāngjūn (輕車將軍).
Soon after, he was granted Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài (太子右衛率),
his generalship remaining as before.
In the first year of Tiānjiā (天嘉),
he left office due to illness.
Zài (載) owned over ten qīng (頃) of land,
located in Báishān (白山) in Jiāngchéng Xiàn (江乘縣).
At this point, he built a house there and resided in it,
completely isolating himself from society.
He did not participate in auspicious or inauspicious events, celebrations, or condolences,
and did not go anywhere,
nor did anyone enter his fenced gate for nearly ten years.
He died at home during the Tàijiàn (太建) period,
aged fifty-eight.
Zài (載)’s cousin was Huì (翽).
Huì (翽), courtesy name Zǐyǔ (子羽),
had high aspirations and moral integrity in his youth.
His grandfather, Ài (愛),
was Liáng Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (梁輔國將軍).
His father, Gānxiàng (乾向),
was Rǔyīn Tàishǒu (汝陰太守).
Huì (翽) lost his father when he was just crowned,
and his grief and sorrow were extreme.
He supported his mother and raised his orphaned brothers and nephews,
and was renowned for his benevolence and filial piety.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) was Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ (南徐州刺史),
he summoned Huì (翽) to be Zhēngběi Cānjūn (征北參軍),
and soon after, he supervised Yìxīng Jùn (義興郡).
In the first year of Yǒngdìng (永定),
he was appointed Zhēnyì Jiāngjūn (貞毅將軍) and Bùbīng Xiàowèi (步兵校尉).
He was promoted to Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍),
and concurrently served as Zhūyī Zhíhé (朱衣直閤).
The office of Xiāoqí (驍騎)
traditionally commanded the camp soldiers,
and also supervised the imperial guards.
Since the Liáng (梁) dynasty,
its responsibility had become increasingly heavy.
When going out, he cleared the way with imperial escorts;
when entering, he communicated directly with the two guards;
when attending court, he ascended the hall and stood guard.
Huì (翽) had always been highly regarded,
and on every major occasion, he was always ordered to stand guard by the emperor's side.
People at the time honored him for this,
calling him
“Xiáyù Jiāngjūn” (俠御將軍).
Soon after, he was appointed Xuānchéng Tàishǒu (宣城太守).
In the second year of Tiānjiā (天嘉),
he participated in the pacification of Wáng Lín (王琳),
and was enfeoffed as Qīngyuán Xiàn Hóu (清源縣侯),
with an estate of two hundred households.
He died in office during the Tàijiàn (太建) period,
and was posthumously granted the title of Míng (明), Huò (霍), Luó (羅) Sānzhōu Cìshǐ (三州刺史).
His son, Hóng (宏),
courtesy name Délǐ (德禮),
was learned in literature.
He successively held official positions up to Yǒngjiā Wáng Fǔ Zīyì Cānjūn (永嘉王府諮議參軍).
After the fall of Chén (陳), he entered the Suí (隋) dynasty.
The historian remarks: In ancient times, Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) was founded on literary studies,
Dù Yù (杜預) came from a background of refined scholarship,
yet they eventually achieved military merits,
and their names were renowned in previous generations.
When the Jìn (晉) dynasty suffered chaos and upheaval,
and was forced to relocate to the east of the Yangtze,
figures like Gù Róng (顧榮) and Xī Jiàn (郗鑒),
and those akin to Wēn Jiào (溫嶠) and Xiè Xuán (謝玄),
were all scholarly gentlemen in simple robes,
highly respected literati,
who resisted enemies to protect the state,
and achieved merit to ascend to high office.
From then onwards,
there were such individuals in every generation.
However, as the Liáng (梁) dynasty descended into turmoil,
even weak men found purpose.
Having personally encountered opportune circumstances,
and being relied upon by the ruler of the time,
how admirable!
Proofreading Notes
Biographies Volume 13 Shěn Jiǒng (沈炯), Yú Lì (虞荔) (younger brother Jì (寄)), Mǎ Shū (馬樞)
Shěn Jiǒng (沈炯), courtesy name Lǐmíng (禮明),
was a native of Wǔkāng (武康) in Wúxīng (吳興).
His grandfather, Yǔ (瑀),
was Liáng Xúnyáng Tàishǒu (梁尋陽太守).
His father, Xù (續), was Wángfǔ Jìshì Cānjūn (王府記室參軍).
Jiǒng, in his youth, possessed outstanding talent
and was highly esteemed at the time.
He was appointed as a Chángshì (常侍) of a kingdom upon entering officialdom,
then promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒ Mín Shìláng (尚書左民侍郎),
and later sent out as the magistrate of Wú (吳) county.
During Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) rebellion,
Yuán Jūnzhèng (袁君正), the grand administrator of Wújùn (吳郡), entered the capital to provide aid,
entrusting Jiǒng with supervising the commandery.
When the capital fell,
Sòng Zǐxiān (宋子仙), one of Jǐng's generals, occupied Wúxīng (吳興),
and sent an envoy to summon Jiǒng,
entrusting him with the duty of secretary.
Jiǒng firmly declined, citing illness,
whereupon Zǐxiān grew angry
and ordered him to be executed.
Jiǒng, having removed his clothes and about to face execution,
was obstructed by a mulberry tree in the path,
so he was dragged to another location.
Someone promptly rescued him,
and he barely escaped death.
Zǐxiān, admiring his talent,
ultimately forced him to take charge of the secretarial duties.
When Zǐxiān was defeated by Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯),
Sēngbiàn, who had long heard of Jiǒng's reputation,
purchased him from among the troops,
rewarding the captor with 100,000 iron coins.
From then on, all urgent military dispatches and documents came from Jiǒng.
When Jiǎnwén (簡文) was murdered,
regional governors and magistrates from all four directions submitted memorials from Jiānglíng (江陵) urging the ascension to the throne.
Sēngbiàn ordered Jiǒng to draft the memorial,
and its prose was exceedingly skillful,
unsurpassed by anyone at the time.
Gāozǔ (高祖) went south
and met Sēngbiàn at Báimáo Wān (白茅灣),
where they ascended an altar and swore an oath;
Jiǒng composed the text for this.
When Hóu Jǐng fled east to Wújùn (吳郡),
he captured Jiǒng's wife, Yú shì (虞氏),
and his son, Xíngjiǎn (行簡),
and killed them both.
Jiǒng's younger brother escaped with his mother and was spared.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Liáng Yuándì (梁元帝), pitying that Jiǒng's wife and son had been executed,
specially enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Yuánxiāng Xiàn (原鄉縣),
with an income of 500 households.
When Sēngbiàn became Sītú (司徒),
he appointed Jiǒng as Cóngshì Zhōngláng (從事中郎).
Liáng Yuándì (梁元帝) summoned him to be Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng (給事黃門侍郎),
concurrently serving as Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng (尚書左丞).
When Jīngzhōu (荊州) fell,
he was captured by the Western Wèi (西魏).
The Wèi (魏) people treated him with great courtesy,
bestowing upon Jiǒng the title of Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司).
Jiǒng, whose elderly mother was in the east,
constantly longed to return to his homeland.
Fearing that the Wèi (魏) people, appreciating his literary talent, would retain him,
he kept his doors shut and swept away visitors,
avoiding all social interaction.
When he composed any literary works,
he would immediately destroy them,
not allowing them to circulate.
Once, he traveled alone past Hànwǔ Tōngtiāntái (漢武通天臺)
and presented a memorial,
expressing his desire to return home.
Its words were:
"Your servant has heard that though Mount Qiáo (喬山) is concealed,
the spirit of Dǐnghú (鼎湖) may be worshipped;
though the state of Yǒu Lǔ (有魯) is desolate,
the traces of Dàtíng (大庭) are not obliterated.
I humbly contemplate Your Majesty's descent of virtue to the yīlán (猗蘭) orchid,
inheriting the spiritual essence of Fēnggǔ (豐谷).
As the Hàn (漢) Way ascended,
immortality seemed within reach.
Shooting the Zhīfú (之罘) at the seashore,
and performing rituals at the Rìguān (日觀) to proclaim merits;
crossing the Fén Hé (汾河) midstream,
and pointing to the Báiliáng (柏梁) for grand banquets—
how joyous it was!
Was it not so!
But then fate led to an ascent to the celestial realm,
and the path of life ended with the imperial carriage's departure.
The 'armored' curtains and pearl screens
crumbled in a single morning;
the jade bowl of Máolíng (茂陵)
unexpectedly appeared among mortals.
The old foundation that once touched the clouds
now lies overgrown with fertile fields;
the remaining ruins of the 'separating wind' (biéfēng yúzǐ/biéfēng yǔzhǐ 別風餘趾/別風餘址)
face the mounds in a vast expanse.
As a traveler in captivity,
how can I not shed tears?
In the past, when Chéngmíng (承明) was disliked,
Yán Zhù (嚴助) returned east.
When a four-horse carriage was available,
Chángqīng (長卿) returned west.
Reverently hearing these old stories,
I secretly harbor a foolish wish.
Although millet is not fragrant,
I dare not forget to seek blessings."
After submitting the memorial,
that night Jiǒng dreamed of an imperial palace,
with very strict guards.
Jiǒng then presented his situation and plea,
and heard someone say:
"It's quite alright to let you return.
When can you arrive?"
A few days later,
he, along with Wáng Kè (王克) and others, were granted permission to return east.
In the second year of Shàotài (紹泰) (556 CE), he arrived in the capital,
was appointed Sīnóng Qīng (司農卿),
and then promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) accepted the abdication,
Jiǒng was given the additional title of Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍),
with his position as Zhōngchéng (中丞) remaining unchanged.
Citing his elderly mother, he memorialized to request retirement to care for her,
but the imperial edict did not permit it.
When Emperor Wén (文帝) succeeded to the throne,
[Xú Jǒng (徐炯)] again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant, from infancy, has been unfortunate.
I became an orphan when I was in my weak冠 [age, twenty sui].
My mother and I were isolated and alone;
my brothers raised each other.
I diligently guarded myself to provide for my mother;
I did not choose my official position when serving.
My career prospered during the Liáng (梁) dynasty,
and my life was preserved during a time of chaos.
I braved dangers and trod through perils,
[(self)]【百】times I faced death and lightly regarded my life.
My wife and children were executed;
my brothers perished.
Only my mother and I remained,
able to encounter this flourishing era.
My mother, concubine Liú (劉),
is now eighty-one years old.
My paternal aunt, concubine Qiū (丘),
is seventy-five.
My younger brothers and nephews have long since perished,
and concubine Qiū's children and grandchildren also died out long ago.
Of the two families, for their care and support,
only I remain.
The former emperor knew of my solitude and desolation,
and supported me within the province and locality,
not wishing me to remain in the wilds.
He also pitied my need to keep warm in winter and cool in summer [for my mother],
which is why, within a year,
I was twice or thrice granted休沐 (xiūmù, days off).
That I have repeatedly presented my sincere petitions
and frequently risked disturbing the imperial gaze
is not because I wish to casually disobey the court
and distance myself from the imperial capital.
One reason is that I am nearly sixty,
with a heart burning [with anxiety],
and each time I kneel to read a family letter,
I fear first and then rejoice.
Warming the pillow and fanning the mat [for my mother]—
I am no longer a child who can do these things.
The second reason is that I hold the position of 彝憲 (yíxiàn, a high censor),
the director of justice for the state.
If I myself fail to uphold personal propriety,
how can I question the national laws?
The former virtuous emperor was meticulous [in considering my plea],
and initially allowed my compassionate release.
The palace attendants and close ministers
were mostly aware of this decree.
It was precisely to select the worthy and the capable,
and widely seek out the discerning and wise,
that hesitations and delays occurred,
and my talent was not taken advantage of [for this purpose].
But the Supreme Heaven sent down its wrath,
and suddenly it is today.
His virtuous words are still in my ears,
but the earth on his tomb is already dry.
Oh vast Heaven,
mourn this boundless sorrow.
Furthermore, my private anxieties are burning and pressing,
ever more urgent in these recent times,
so my earnest plea
has made me forget worldly concerns.
I humbly submit that Your Majesty is sagacious and intelligent,
succeeding to the martial [virtue of your predecessors],
setting an example for the four seas,
and promoting this filial governance.
With a small brush, I seek [to reach] Heaven;
I look up to your imperial presence.
If there is feeling, there must be a response;
I truly hope for Your Sagacious Majesty's illumination.
I particularly beg that you generously extend this private rite [of filial piety to me].
Then the virtue of the king
will spread limitlessly,
and as for those who fly or swim,
who will not be nurtured?"
The imperial edict replied:
"I have read your memorial and fully understand your sentiments.
Your reputation has spread throughout Xián (咸) and Luò (雒),
and your feelings are as deep as Wǎn (宛) and Pèi (沛).
Previously, you felt a keen desire to lean against the door [awaiting your mother],
and wished to return to your homeland,
but were again tied by the duties of the time,
thus missing the opportunity to attend to your parent.
Although Zhōu Shēng (周生) desired
repeatedly to relinquish his office,
and the Lǐ (禮) records stated that one could be excused from governance,
the former court, which illuminated the four seas,
toiled over myriad affairs.
Considering your talent to be peerless,
and your office to be a unique and important one,
he deeply entrusted you with responsibilities,
and repeatedly had to infringe upon your filial sentiments.
I have succeeded to this grand foundation,
and wish to promote this great enterprise.
Considering my own inadequacy and weakness,
and furthermore being entangled in sorrow and grief,
I truly rely on worthy and wise individuals
to together achieve harmony and prosperity.
How can I easily release [you from] the court in the south
and remove your sash to return to the eastern road [home]?
At present, Féng Qīn (馮親) moved into his residence,
and Xún Mǔ (荀母) followed her son to his official post.
This allows them to see the honor of the court
without diminishing family rites.
I will immediately order the relevant department
to welcome your revered family [to the capital],
so that you, minister, may find fulfillment in both your public and private duties,
and neither will be neglected."
Initially,
Gāo Zǔ (高祖) once praised Jǒng (炯) as suitable for a king's chief advisor.
Major military and state policies
were often deliberated with his participation.
Emperor Wén (文帝) also highly regarded his talent and ability,
and wished to honor and ennoble him.
At that time, Wáng Lín (王琳) invaded Dàléi (大雷),
and Liú Yì (留異) occupied the eastern border.
The Emperor wished Jǒng (炯) to seize this opportunity to achieve merit,
so he relieved him from his position as Zhōngchéng (中丞),
added the title of Míngwēi Jiāngjūn (明威將軍),
and sent him back to his hometown
to gather followers.
He died of illness in Wúzhōng (吳中),
at the age of fifty-nine.
When Emperor Wén (文帝) heard of it,
he immediately observed mourning,
and dispatched condolences and sacrifices,
posthumously granting him the title of Shìzhōng (侍中),
and the posthumous name Gōngzǐ (恭子).
His collected works in twenty volumes circulated in the world.
Yú Lì (虞荔), courtesy name Shānpī (山披),
was from Yúyáo (餘姚), Kuàijī (會稽).
His grandfather, Quán (權),
was Liáng (梁) Court Steward (廷尉卿) and Administrator of Yǒngjiā (永嘉 Tàishǒu).
His father, Jiǎn (檢),
was the Advisory Counselor (諮議參軍) to the Prince of Shǐxīng (始興王), Píngběi (平北).
Lì (荔) was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
with noble aspirations and integrity.
At nine years old,
he accompanied his elder paternal cousin, Chǎn (闡), to visit the Grand Master of Ceremonies, Lù Chuí (陸倕).
Chuí (倕) asked him ten questions about the Five Classics,
and Lì (荔) answered each question promptly,
without any omissions,
which greatly astonished Chuí (倕).
He also once visited the hermit Hé Yìn (何胤).
At that time, the Administrator of Héngyáng (衡陽), Prince Yì (王亦), also arrived.
Yìn (胤) spoke of him to the Prince,
and the Prince wished to see Lì (荔).
Lì (荔) declined, saying:
"I do not have a formal calling card,
so I cannot present myself in obeisance."
The Prince, seeing Lì (荔)'s lofty aspirations,
greatly respected him.
Upon returning to his commandery,
he immediately appointed him as Chief Clerk (主簿).
Lì (荔) again declined due to his young age and did not accept.
When he grew up,
he was handsome in appearance and demeanor,
widely read in classics,
and skilled in writing.
He began his career in the Liáng (梁) dynasty as an Acting Staff Officer (行參軍) in the Western Department of the Censorate,
and soon was appointed Staff Officer of Legal Affairs and Military Records (法曹外兵參軍),
concurrently serving as the Chief Jailer (詔獄正) of Dānyáng (丹陽).
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng (梁武帝) established the Shìlín Guǎn (士林館) to the west of the city.
Lì (荔) composed a stele inscription
and submitted it.
The Emperor ordered it to be carved into the馆 (guǎn),
and consequently appointed Lì (荔) as a Scholar of the Shìlín Guǎn (士林學士).
He soon became Sīwén Láng (司文郎),
and was promoted to Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng (通直散騎侍郎),
concurrently serving as Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人).
At that time, those in positions around the emperor
often participated in the levers of power,
and managed both internal and external affairs.
Only Lì (荔) and Gù Xié (顧協) were detached and retired quietly,
residing in the western province [of the imperial secretariat],
known only for their literary and historical knowledge.
They were then called 'pure and uncorrupted'.
He soon took charge as Grand Director of Composition (大著作).
During the chaos of Hóu Jǐng (侯景),
Lì (荔) led his relatives into the Palace,
and was appointed Advisory Counselor to the Commander-in-Chief of the West (鎮西諮議參軍),
with his position as Shèrén (舍人) remaining as before.
When the capital city fell,
he fled back to his hometown.
After Hóu Jǐng (侯景) was pacified,
Emperor Yuán (元帝) summoned him to be Zhongshū Shìláng (中書侍郎),
and Zhēnyáng Hóu (貞陽侯),
and conferred upon him the title of Yángzhōu Biéjià (揚州別駕),
but he did not accept any of these.
When Zhāng Biāo 張彪 occupied Kuàijī 會稽,
Yú Lì 虞荔 was there.
When Emperor Wén 文平ed Biāo 彪,
Gāozǔ 高祖 sent Lì 荔 a letter saying:
"Since the chaos and disorder began,
the wise and virtuous have scattered.
Your talent and ability are excellent,
and your reputation is known in Xǔ 許 and Luò 洛.
The imperial court is now renewing itself,
broadly seeking out heroes and brilliant men.
How can you remain idle in the eastern lands,
only looking out for yourself?
I am now sending your elder brother's son to escort you to the capital.
I trust you will certainly live up to the court's earnest expectations."
Emperor Wén 文 also wrote to him, saying:
"Your excellence in the southeast
and your widespread reputation are well-known.
You should soar to the capital, Xǔ 許,
and together address the current ills.
Instead, you have (carved out) [削] effaced your tracks in hills and gardens,
maintaining this self-sufficiency.
How can you allow the hopes of the 'empty valley' to be frustrated?
I earnestly wish you to immediately pack your bags
and make plans to come to the capital.
The only thing I await is our meeting,
which I hope will be today."
Pressured and having no alternative,
he responded to the summons and arrived at the capital.
When Gāozǔ 高祖 passed away,
Emperor Wén 文 succeeded to the throne.
He was appointed Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子 (Central Secretariat Aide to the Crown Prince),
and continued to attend the Crown Prince in his studies.
Soon after, he was also appointed Dà Zhùzuò 大著作 (Grand Historian) and Dōngyáng Yángzhōu Èrzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng 東揚揚州二州大中正 (Grand Moderator for the two provinces of Dōngyáng 東揚 and Yángzhōu 揚州),
while retaining his position as Zhōngshùzǐ 中庶子.
Initially,
Lì's 荔 mother had followed Lì 荔 into the palace.
She died within the palace,
and soon after, the city fell.
He could not perform the proper rituals of mourning,
and for this reason, he ate only vegetables and wore plain clothes for the rest of his life,
and did not listen to music.
Although his official appointments were prestigious and important,
his dwelling was simple and unadorned,
and he was indifferent and without ambition.
Emperor Wén 文 deeply valued him,
often kept him by his side,
and consulted him morning and evening.
Lì 荔 was reserved and thoughtful,
speaking little.
Whatever proposals he made or criticisms he offered,
no one ever saw the beginning or end of them,
so they are not listed here later.
At that time, Lì's 荔 second younger brother was living as a guest in Mǐnzhōng 閩中,
relying on Chén Bǎo'yìng 陳寶應.
Whenever Lì 荔 spoke of him, he would weep.
Emperor Wén 文 felt pity and said to him:
"I also have a younger brother far away;
this feeling is very strong,
which others cannot know."
Thereupon, he ordered Bǎo'yìng 寶應 to seek out his brother.
Bǎo'yìng 寶應 ultimately refused to send him.
Consequently, Lì 荔 fell ill from grief,
and the Emperor frequently visited him.
He ordered Lì 荔 to bring his family into the palace.
Lì 荔, believing that the Forbidden Palace was not a place for private residence,
begged to stay outside the city.
Emperor Wén 文 refused,
and instead ordered him to reside in Lántái 蘭臺.
The imperial carriage visited him two or three times,
and he personally commanded imperial envoys
to constantly check on him along the road.
Moreover, as Lì 荔 had eaten vegetables for a long time,
which was not suitable for his weakened state due to illness,
he issued an edict saying:
"To adhere to plain living is indeed noble.
However, your years are many,
and your strength is gradually declining.
I intend to rely heavily on you,
so you truly need to be robust.
I now provide you with fish and meat;
you must not stubbornly adhere to your principles."
Lì 荔 ultimately did not comply.
He died in Tiānjia 天嘉 second year (561 CE),
at the age of fifty-nine.
Emperor Wén 文 grieved and lamented his passing greatly.
He was posthumously granted the title Shìzhōng 侍中 (Palace Attendant)
and given the posthumous name Dézǐ 德子.
When his coffin was returned to his hometown,
the Emperor personally went out to oversee the farewell,
which was considered a great honor at the time.
His sons, Shìjī 世基 and Shìnán 世南,
were both well-known in their youth.
Yú Jì 虞寄, courtesy name Cì'ān 次安,
was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth.
When he was several years old,
a guest who had come to visit his father
met Jì 寄 at the gate.
The guest then playfully mocked him, saying:
"Young master Yú 虞,
you must certainly be witless."
Jì 寄 immediately replied:
"If one cannot even discern characters (wén zì 文 字),
how can one not be foolish (yú 愚)?"
The guest was greatly ashamed.
He entered and said to Jì's 寄 father:
"This child is no ordinary person;
his retort is no less than that of Wénjǔ 文舉."
When he grew up,
he loved learning
and was skilled at writing.
He was calm and reserved by nature,
with a desire to live in seclusion.
At the age of twenty, he was recommended as Xiùcái 秀才 (Outstanding Talent),
and his policy proposals ranked high.
He began his career as Zuǒ Chángshì 左常侍 (Left Attendant) for Liáng Xuānchéngwáng 梁宣城王 (Prince Xuānchéng of Liáng).
During the Dàtóng 大同 era (535-546 CE),
there was once a heavy rain.
In front of the palace, there were often multi-colored precious pearls.
Liáng Wǔdì 梁武帝 (Emperor Wǔ of Liáng) observed them with great delight.
Jì 寄 then presented a "Song of Auspicious Rain."
The Emperor said to Jì's 寄 elder brother, Lì 荔:
"This song has a refined and outstanding style;
he is the 'dragon among the scholars' of your family.
How should he be promoted and employed?"
When Jì 寄 heard this,
he sighed and said:
"It was merely an expression of the joy of 'beating the clods of earth' to praise the descriptions of great virtue.
How could I be seeking fame and office?"
Thereupon, he closed his doors, claiming illness,
and only entertained himself with books.
When Yuèyángwáng 岳陽王 became the Grand Administrator of Kuàijī 會稽,
he appointed Jì 寄 as Xíng Cānjūn 行參軍 (Acting Staff Officer),
then promoted him to Jìshì Cānjūn 記室參軍 (Secretary to the Staff Officer),
and concurrently Zhǎng Jùn Wǔguān Yuàn 掌郡五官掾 (Director of the Five Bureaus of the Commandery).
He was again transferred to Zhōng Jìshì 中記室 (Central Secretary),
with the Yuàn 掾 position as before.
In office, he simplified tedious matters,
focusing on the broader principles.
Within his bureaus,
it was quiet all day long.
During the chaos of Hóu Jǐng 侯景,
Jì 寄 followed his elder brother Lì 荔 into the palace.
He was appointed Zhènnán Xiāngdōngwáng Zīyì Cānjūn 鎮南湘東王諮議參軍 (Advisor to the Prince of Xiāngdōng, Defender of the South),
and granted the title Zhēn Wēi Jiāngjūn 貞威將軍 (General of Firm Awe).
When the capital city fell,
he fled back to his hometown.
When Zhāng Biāo 張彪 went to Línchuān 臨川,
he forced Jì 寄 to go with him.
Jì 寄 traveled in the same boat as Biāo's 彪 general Zhèng Wěi 鄭瑋.
Wěi 瑋 had once offended Biāo's 彪 sensibilities,
and so he abducted Jì 寄 and fled to Jìn'ān 晉安.
At that time, Chén Bǎo'yìng 陳寶應 occupied Mǐnzhōng 閩中,
and was very pleased to have Jì 寄.
When Gāozǔ 高祖 pacified Hóu Jǐng 侯景,
Jì 寄 advised Bǎo'yìng 寶應 to align himself with the new power.
Bǎo'yìng 寶應 followed his advice
and sent an envoy to pledge allegiance.
In Chéngshèng 承聖 first year (552 CE),
he was appointed Hé Róng Jiāngjūn 和戎將軍 (General for Pacifying Barbarians) and Zhōngshū Shìláng 中書侍郎 (Imperial Secretariat Attendant).
Bǎo'yìng 寶應 cherished his talent
and, citing blocked roads, refused to send him.
Whenever he wanted to appoint Jì 寄 to his staff
and entrust him with literary matters,
Jì 寄 firmly declined
and managed to avoid it.
When Bǎo'yìng 寶應 formed a marriage alliance with Liú Yì 留異
and secretly harbored rebellious intentions,
Jì 寄 subtly became aware of his aims.
During their conversations,
he would repeatedly explain the principles of loyalty and rebellion,
subtly using these to remonstrate.
Bǎo'yìng 寶應 would then change the subject to other matters to evade him.
He also once ordered his attendants to recite the Hàn Shū 漢書 (Book of Han)
while he listened lying down.
When they reached Kuǎi Tōng's 蒯通 speech to Hán Xìn 韓信,
saying: "The signs on your back
indicate an unspeakably noble future,"
Bǎo'yìng 寶應 suddenly rose and said,
"He can be called a wise man."
Jì 寄, with a stern expression, said:
"To overthrow Lìyì 酈食其 and make Hán Xìn 韓信 arrogant is not enough to be called wise.
How can he compare to Bān Biāo 班彪, who recognized the mandate of heaven
and knew where allegiance lay?"
Yú Jì knew Bǎo Yīng could not be swayed,
and fearing calamity would befall himself,
he adopted the attire of a reclusive scholar to refuse him.
He often resided at Dōngshān Temple,
falsely claiming a leg ailment,
and would not rise again.
Bǎo Yīng thought it was a pretense,
and had the house Yú Jì was lying in set on fire.
Yú Jì lay peacefully and did not move.
His close attendants were about to help Yú Jì out,
but Yú Jì said:
"My fate is predetermined.
Where would I go to escape?"
Those who set the fire
soon extinguished it themselves.
Bǎo Yīng only believed him after this.
When Liú Yì raised troops,
Bǎo Yīng provided his forces with supplies.

Yú Jì then used a letter to remonstrate strongly, saying: Yú Jì of Dōngshān respectfully writes this letter to General Míng, Commander of the forces, under your esteemed command: Having drifted through worldly affairs,
Yú Jì has taken up temporary residence in your esteemed region.
The General has treated me with the courtesy due to an honored guest,
and shown
me the kindness due to a national hero.
The sentiments stirred by this
I shall never forget.
However, Yú Jì is deeply ill and lingering,
his time drawing to an end.
I constantly fear that I shall ultimately fill a ditch or gully,
unable to repay
even a drop of dust.
Therefore, I dare to lay bare my innermost feelings,
and presumptuously present my sincere devotion,
wishing that the General would pause for a moment to consider,
and contemplate it briefly.
Then, on the day I close my eyes,
all my aspirations will be fulfilled.
Indeed, the omens of safety and danger,
and the junctures of misfortune and fortune,
are not solely dependent on heaven's timing,
but also on human affairs.
A deviation of a hair's breadth
can lead to an error of a thousand *lǐ*.
Therefore,
wise and discerning individuals
hold high positions without faltering,
and uphold great principles without straying.
How could they be misled by empty words?
The General possesses both civil and military talents,
and his heroic might is peerless.
In the past, due to
many difficulties,
you drew your sword and raised an army,
raised banners and rallied the masses,
projecting your might for a thousand *lǐ*.
Was it not because the four borders were beset by fortresses,
and you sought to collectively protect the royal house,
to rectify the times and repay the sovereign,
to stabilize the nation and shelter
the people?
This is why even five-foot-tall boys
all wished to carry halberds and follow the General.
When Emperor Gāozǔ and Emperor Wǔ first established the foundation in chaotic times,
they initially overcame difficulties.
At that time, the world was in turmoil,
the people had no stable ruler,
wolves and jackals blocked the way,
and great whales attacked wantonly.
The whole country was in trepidation,
not knowing whom to follow.
The General exercised the discernment of
minute movements,
and broke through the arguments of vertical alliances and horizontal confederations.
You pledged your name and committed your service,
entrusting yourself to the imperial clan.
This was the General's brilliant calculation and far-sighted plan,
emanating from sincere devotion.
When the present Emperor succeeded to the throne,
he was revered, enlightened, wise, and sagacious.
He selected the worthy and employed the capable,
and his officials were harmonious.
He bound the General with the heavy responsibility of a protective wall,
and honored the General with a grant of land.
Was this not a grand strategy and
a temple plan,
extending a red heart to all things?
Repeatedly, clear edicts were issued,
sincere and earnest.
The relationship between sovereign and subject was established,
and the affection like flesh and blood was profound.
I did not expect the General to be misled
by perverse theories,
and suddenly conceive a divergent plan.
This is why I feel pain in my head and heart,
and have wept until my tears are exhausted, succeeded by blood.
A strategy for complete safety –
I secretly lament its loss for the General.
Although
Yú Jì is afflicted by illness and senility,
and his words are not worth adopting,
from a thousand deliberations, one thought may be gained.
Please allow me to present my foolish calculations.
I beg the General to briefly curb his thunderous wrath,
and spare me a moment of time,
so that I may fully express my wild
and blind opinions,
and bare my heart and liver in sincerity.
Then, even on the day of my death,
it will be like a year of life.
〔一０〕Since Heaven was weary of the virtue of Liáng,
many difficulties repeatedly arose.
The world disintegrated,
and heroes rose in succession,
too many to count.
Everyone believed they would attain it.
However, to eliminate
the violent and suppress the chaotic,
to rescue the drowning and support the imperiled,
the four seas joyfully acclaimed,
and the three spirits bestowed their mandate.
The one who yielded and resided facing south
is the Chén clan.
Is this not because the sequence of mandates exists,
bestowed
solely by Heaven,
to uphold the jade disc and respond to the times?
This matter is very clear,
the first point.
The present Emperor
〔一一〕succeeded to the foundation,
his brilliant virtue extended far and wide.
Heaven's net was re-extended,
and the earth's axis
re-knotted.
Consider Wáng Lín's strength,
and Hóu Tiàn's power:
advancing, they were sufficient to shake the Central Plains
and contend for supremacy in the world;
retreating, they were sufficient to be unyielding outside the Jiāng River,
and assert dominance
in a corner.
Yet, either a single army was commanded,
or the advice of a single scholar was utilized,
and Wáng Lín disintegrated like thawing ice,
fleeing to foreign lands,
while Hóu Tiàn bowed and prostrated,
submitting his life
at the imperial court.
This was Heaven lending its might,
and removing their troubles.
This matter is very clear,
the second point.
Now, the General, with the importance of a noble relative,
and the multitude of the Southeast,
devotes
his loyalty to serve the Emperor,
and exerts his strength to aid the throne.
Would your merits not surpass Dòu Róng,
and your favor exceed Wú Ruì,
dividing a ceremonial *guī* and partitioning territory,
ruling as a solitary lord in the south?
This matter is very clear,
the third point.
Furthermore, the sagely court overlooks flaws and forgets transgressions,
is generous and wins people over.
Those who reform and make a fresh start
are all promoted and appointed.
As for Yú Xiàoqǐng, Pān Chún, Lǐ Xiàoqīn, Ōuyáng
Wěi, and others,
all were entrusted as confidants,
and appointed as close assistants.
The court's heart is open,
without the slightest trace of resentment.
How much more so for the General, whose misdeed is not like Zhāng Xiù's,
and whose crime differs from Bì Chén's!
Why should
you worry about danger and ruin,
or lose wealth and honor?
This matter, again, is very clear,
the fourth point.
Currently, Zhōu and Qí are in peaceful relations,
there are no worries outside the borders.
Uniting forces in one direction,
it will not be long.
This is not the opportune moment for Liú Bāng and Xiàng Yǔ to compete,
nor the situation for Chǔ and Zhào to form alliances.
How can you leisurely fold your hands,
and idly discuss becoming Xībó?
This matter is very clear,
the fifth point.
Moreover, General Liú Yì, like a wolf looking back from his corner,
has repeatedly suffered defeats and setbacks.
His reputation and strength are diminished,
and his courage and morale are low.
Gāo Xiāng, Xiàng Wénzhèng, Liú Yú, Huáng Zǐ
Yù,
these several individuals
whom Your Excellency knows,
are indecisive and wavering,
acting solely for their own gain.
The rest of your generals and commanders
are also apparent.
Who among them can don armor and grasp sharp weapons,
drive deep into enemy territory,
tie up their horses and bury their wheels,
fight with no regard for their lives,
and lead the soldiers?
This matter is also very clear;
this is the sixth point.
Furthermore, Your Excellency’s strength,
who compares to Hóu Jǐng?
Your Excellency’s army,
who compares to Wáng Lín?
Emperor Wǔ destroyed Hóu Jǐng in the past,
and the current Emperor crushed Wáng Lín recently.
This is the will of Heaven,
not
human effort.
Moreover, after the wars,
the people are all weary of chaos.
Who among them can [⿱𠫓廾] graves,
abandon their wives and children,
and undertake a plan that disregards myriad deaths,
following Your Excellency amidst
sharp blades?
This matter is also very clear;
this is the seventh point.
Looking back through ancient history,
and reflecting on past events,
Zǐyáng and Jìmèng
fell one after another,
and Yúshàn
( (石) ) [right] Qú
likewise met with peril and ruin.
Heaven’s mandate is formidable,
and mountains and rivers cannot be relied upon.
How much more so when Your Excellency wishes to use the land of a few commanderies
to oppose the armies of the realm,
and with the resources of a regional lord
to defy the Emperor’s command?
Can strength and weakness, rebellion and obedience,
be considered equal?
This matter is also very clear;
this is the eighth point.
Furthermore, those who are not of our kind
will surely have different intentions.
If one does not love their own kin,
how can they extend it to others?
Liú Jiāngjūn is personally bound by national titles,
and his son is married to an imperial princess.
Yet he still [⿱𠫓廾] his celestial kin and disregards them,
betraying
an enlightened ruler to stand alone.
In times of crisis,
how could he share your worries and hardships,
and not betray Your Excellency?
When the army is exhausted and its strength depleted,
fearing punishment and coveting rewards,
there will
surely be plots like Hán and Zhì at Jìnyáng,
and situations like Zhāng and Chén at Jǐngxíng.
This matter is also very clear;
this is the ninth point.
Furthermore, the northern army fights from a thousand Lǐ away,
and its vanguard is irresistible.
When Your Excellency fights in your own territory,
many people look to their rear.
Liáng Ān is duplicitous,
Xiū Wù possesses only the strength of a common man.
The many and the few are mismatched,
and the generals and commanders are unequal.
The army
marches out without a righteous cause,
and the action is initiated without opportunity.
To wage war with this,
the benefit is unknown.
Indeed, in the Hàn dynasty, the states of Wú and Chǔ,
and in the Jìn dynasty, Yǐng and Yóng,
with dozens of
cities connected,
and a length of millions,
uprooting the foundation and blocking the source,
plotting for their own families and states,
did any of them succeed?
This matter is also very clear;
this is the tenth point.
For Your Excellency’s sake,
there is no better course than to return without further delay,
sever ties with the Liú family,
send Qín Láng and Kuài Láng
as hostages,
lay down arms,
and completely follow the imperial
edict.
Moreover, the imperial court has promised the pledge of an iron certificate,
and renewed it with the White Horse Pact.
I will not break my word,
I swear this to the imperial ancestral temple.
I have heard that the discerning see what is not yet manifest,
and the wise
do not reconsider.
The outcome of success or failure,
Your Excellency should not doubt.
The critical moment for fortune or misfortune
is a hair's breadth away.
Currently, the imperial domains are still few,
and the imperial princes are young.
All who belong to the imperial clan
receive favor and protection.
How much more so with Your Excellency’s territory,
Your Excellency’s talent,
Your Excellency’s fame,
and Your Excellency’s power,
if you can diligently perform your duties as a vassal,
and face north to declare yourself a subject?
Would you not be spoken of for your accomplishments on par with Liú Zé?
Would your person not be as secure as mountains and rivers,
and your name endure as long as metal and stone?
I beg you to consider
three times,
and ponder it carefully without neglect.
My strength and energy are weak,
my remaining years are few.
Grateful for kindness and mindful of virtue,
I speak wildly without realizing it.
The punishment of axe and hatchet
I would accept like eating water caltrop.
BǎoYīng read the letter and was furious.
Someone said to BǎoYīng,
“Yú Gōng’s illness is worsening,
his words are often mistaken.”
BǎoYīng’s anger then slightly abated.
Also, because Jì had popular support,
he was treated leniently.
When BǎoYīng was defeated and fled,
arriving at Pútián at night,
he looked back and said to his son, Gǎnqín,
“If I had followed Yú Gōng’s advice earlier,
I would not be in this situation today.”
Gǎnqín only wept.
After BǎoYīng was captured,
all guests who had even slight dealings with him
were executed.
Only Jì was spared misfortune due to his foresight.
Originally,
the Buddhist monk Huìbiāo was learned and talented.
When BǎoYīng raised an army,
he wrote a five-character poem to send him off,
saying:
“The departing horses still face the water,
the parting banner slightly draws the wind.
It will be good to see tonight’s moon,
as it enters the Zǐwēi Palace.”
BǎoYīng was very pleased to receive it.
Huìbiāo presented it to Jì,
but Jì merely glanced at it and stopped,
his expression solemn and silent.
Biāo withdrew.
Jì said to his close associates,
“Since Master Biāo began with this,
he will surely end with this.”
Later, he was indeed executed for this.
Emperor Wén (文帝) then immediately ordered the Dūdū Zhāng Zhāodá (都督章昭達) to manage his dispatch,
sending him back to court.
When he arrived,
he was granted an audience that very day.
The Emperor said to Jì (寄):
"Guǎn Níng (管寧) is well."
Such was the extent of his concern and comfort.
After a while,
Emperor Wén (文帝) said to Dào Zhòngjǔ (到仲舉):
"Since the King of Héngyáng (衡陽王) has left the inner chambers,
though he hasn't yet been assigned personal staff,
he still needs someone to be with him day and night,
and also to manage his correspondence.
We should seek out a seasoned scholar of virtuous conduct."
Zhòngjǔ (仲舉) did not know how to respond.
Emperor Wén (文帝) said:
"I will find him myself."
Then he personally issued an order to employ Jì (寄).
When Jì (寄) came to express his gratitude,
Emperor Wén (文帝) said:
"The reason for temporarily appointing you to serve a prince
is not merely to trouble you with literary tasks,
but to have you act as his teacher and model."
Soon after, he was concurrently appointed Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
When he was to be sent on an embassy to Qí (齊),
Jì (寄) declined due to old age and illness
and did not go.
He was then appointed Guózǐ Bóshì (國子博士).
After a while,
he again memorialized to resign his post and return to his hometown.
Emperor Wén (文帝) graciously granted his request
and permitted him to return east.
He was then appointed Dōngyángzhōu Biéjià (東揚州別駕),
but Jì (寄) again declined due to illness.
When Gāozōng (高宗) ascended the throne,
he summoned and appointed him Yángzhōu Zhìzhōng (揚州治中) and Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞),
but he did not accept either post.
Then he was appointed Dōngzhōngláng Jiàn'ān Wáng Zīyì (東中郎建安王諮議),
with the added title of Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn (戎昭將軍).
He again declined due to illness,
stating he was unable to attend daily.
The King (王) therefore specially ordered that his duties in the royal administration be suspended,
and that any questionable matters
should be decided by him on the spot,
with only monthly memorials needing to be submitted.
In the eighth year of Tàijiàn (太建), he was granted the added title of Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫),
his general's title remaining as before.
He died in the eleventh year,
at the age of seventy.
Jì (寄) was diligent in his conduct from a young age,
always acting with benevolence and generosity even in hasty situations.
He never spoke harshly to even servants and stable boys.
However, when facing danger and upholding integrity,
his words and demeanor were stern,
and he did not fear drawn blades.
Since his exile to the southern lands,
he was separated from his elder brother Lì (荔).
He developed an emotional illness,
and whenever he received a letter from Lì (荔),
his illness would worsen,
bringing him close to death several times.
In all the official positions he held,
he never completed his full term,
but after only a year and a few months,
he would resign himself.
He often said:
"Contentment avoids disgrace;
I am content."
When he resigned due to illness and lived in his private residence,
whenever a prince became a provincial governor,
they would, upon arrival, visit his gate to pay respects,
order their whips and boards to be set aside,
and sit by him, attending with a small table and a staff.
He often went out to visit nearby temples,
and word would spread through the villages;
the old and young would line up,
bowing to him by the roadside.
Some would even make vows, saying if they only pointed to Jì (寄), they would not lie;
such was the influence of his utmost virtue.
Most of his written works
were lost during the period of unrest.
Mǎ Shū (馬樞), courtesy name Yàolǐ (要理),
was a native of Méi (郿) in Fúfēng (扶風).
His grandfather, Língqìng (靈慶),
was a Lùshì Cānjūn (錄事參軍) for the King of Jìnglíng (竟陵王) in Qí (齊).
Shū (樞) lost both parents when he was a few years old
and was raised by his aunt.
At six,
he could recite the Xiàojīng (孝經), Lúnyǔ (論語), and Lǎozǐ (老子).
When he grew up,
he extensively studied the classics and histories,
especially excelling in Buddhist scriptures and the commentaries on the Zhōuyì (周易) and Lǎozǐ (老子).
When Liáng Shàolíng Wáng Lún (梁邵陵王綸) was the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州),
having long heard of his reputation,
Lún (綸) himself lectured on the Dàpǐn Jīng (大品經),
he invited him to be a scholar.
starting on the same day.
Two thousand people, both monastics and laypeople, attended.
The King (王) wished to observe their relative merits closely,
so he said to the assembly:
"When debating with Scholar Mǎ (馬),
you must ensure he yields;
no one should simply stand as host or guest."
Thereupon, scholars from several schools rose to ask questions.
Shū (樞) then proceeded to analyze and explain them in order,
clarifying their main points,
and then branching out into various distinctions,
transforming endlessly.
The debaters could only listen in silence.
Lún (綸) greatly praised him
and intended to recommend him to the court.
Soon after, Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) rebellion occurred.
Lún (綸) raised an army to aid Tái (臺)
and left twenty thousand scrolls of books with Shū (樞).
Shū (樞) diligently read through them,
almost completing the entire collection.
Then he sighed and said:
"I have heard that those who value rank and position regard Cháo (巢) and Yóu (由) as shackles,
while those who love mountains and forests regard Yī (伊) and Lǚ (呂) as mere gatekeepers.
Those who adhere to fame and reality consider the words of Zhùxià (柱下) as straw and mustard,
while those who delight in purity and emptiness dismiss the teachings of Xíshàng (席上) as chaff and husks.
Judging by profound discourse,
each follows their own preference.
However, Zhī Fù (支父) had the integrity to decline a throne,
and Yán Zǐ (嚴子) had the ambition to govern an emperor.
These are beautiful tales of a thousand years,
which are not discarded.
In comparison, those who seek aspirations
stop when they see the path.
Is it that Heaven is not benevolent to the noble and exalted,
or why is it that those in mountains and forests are so unheard of?"
He then went into reclusion on Máoshān (茅山),
with the intention of living there permanently.
In the first year of Tiānjīa (天嘉),
Emperor Wén (文帝) summoned him to be Dùzhī Shàngshū (度支尚書),
but he declined to respond to the summons.
At that time, Shū's (樞) relatives and friends all lived in Jīngkǒu (京口).
Every autumn and winter,
he would occasionally visit there.
When the King of Póyáng (鄱陽王) became the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州),
he admired Shū's (樞) noble character
and felt it was beneath him not to be able to attract him.
So, with humble words and generous intentions,
he sent envoys to invite him.
This happened several times,
but Shū (樞) firmly declined due to illness.
One of his disciples or others then said:
"The King of Póyáng (鄱陽王) treats you as a teacher and friend,
not based on rank.
What harm is there in maintaining your tranquility amidst the market and court?"
Shū (樞), having no choice,
then
went.
The King (王) built a separate residence for him,
but Shū (樞) disliked its grandeur
and instead built his own thatched hut in a bamboo grove to live in.
Whenever kings and dukes sent gifts,
he would accept only one tenth if he could not decline.
Shū (樞) experienced many rebellions in his youth,
and wherever he resided,
bandits would not enter.
Those who sought refuge with him often numbered several hundred families.
His eyes were remarkably bright yellow,
and he could see objects in the dark.
There was always a pair of white swallows
nesting in a tree in his courtyard.
They were tame and familiar with the porch,
sometimes gathering on his table.
They came in spring and left in autumn,
for almost thirty years.
He died in the thirteenth year of Tàijiàn (太建),
at the age of sixty.
His work, the Dàojué Lùn (道覺論) in twenty volumes, circulated in the world.
The imperial historian says: Shěn Jiǒng (沈炯) served the Liáng (梁) court.
At the age of knowing his destiny,
he aspired to a minor official position in the secretariat,
and
stopped at the humble post of a district magistrate.
When he took up his brush at the covenant altar,
composing a persuasive memorial,
his intent was stirring and profound.
Indeed, he was a great man of letters!
Yú Lì's (虞荔) contribution of strategies was profound and thorough,
demonstrating his full sincerity.
It can be said that he benefited an enlightened era.
Collation Notes
Biographies Volume 14: Dào Zhòngjǔ (到仲舉), Hán Zǐgāo (韓子高), Huá Jiǎo (華皎)
Dào Zhòngjǔ (到仲舉), courtesy name Déyán (德言),
was a native of Wǔyuán (武原) in Péngchéng (彭城).
His grandfather, Tǎn (坦),
was a Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎) in Qí (齊).
His father, Qià (洽),
was a Shìzhōng (侍中) in Liáng (梁).
Dào Zhòngjǔ had no other skills or accomplishments,
but he conducted himself with integrity and uprightness.
He began his career as a Zhùzuò Zuǒláng, Tàizǐ Shèrén, and Wángfǔ Zhǔbù.
He was then sent out as the Magistrate of Chángchéng
and was known for his honesty and fairness in governance.
When Wéndì was living in the countryside,
he once visited Zhòngjǔ.
At that time, it was cloudy and rainy.
Zhòngjǔ was sitting alone in his study.
He heard the sound of flutes and drums outside the city.
Soon after, Wéndì arrived.
Zhòngjǔ found this unusual
and thus became deeply connected with him.
Wéndì also once stayed overnight in Zhòngjǔ's tent
after a drinking session.
Suddenly, a divine five-colored light shone inside the room.
From then on, Zhòngjǔ served him with even greater reverence.
During the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng,
Zhòngjǔ depended on Wéndì.
When Hóu Jǐng's rebellion was quelled,
Wéndì became the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng Commandery.
He appointed Zhòngjǔ as the Commandery Assistant.
Zhòngjǔ and Yǔ Chí of Yǐngchuān were both Wéndì's retainers.
When Wéndì became Xuānyì Jiāngjūn,
he appointed Zhòngjǔ as his Zhǎngshǐ,
and soon after, he was also given the post of Magistrate of Shānyīn.
When Wéndì succeeded to the throne,
Zhòngjǔ was granted the title of Shìzhōng
and participated in managing electoral affairs.
In the first year of Tiānjiā (560),
he was appointed Shǒudūguān Shàngshū
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Bǎo'ān County,
with an estate of five hundred households.
In the third year (562),
he was appointed Dūguān Shàngshū.
In the same year,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Yòupúshè and Dānyáng Yǐn.
His participation in managing affairs remained as before.
Soon after, he was re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jiànchāng County.
As Zhòngjǔ had no scholarly knowledge,
court regulations were not his forte.
All selections and appointments
came from Yuán Shū.
He was naturally simple and detached,
not interfering in worldly affairs,
and had no close acquaintances among the court officials.
He merely amassed wealth and indulged in drinking.
In the sixth year (565),
his term expired,
and he was relieved of his post as Yǐn.
At this time,
Wéndì had been ill for many years
and did not personally manage the myriad affairs of state.
All matters of the Shàngshū
were decided by Zhòngjǔ.
In the first year of Tiānkāng (566),
he was promoted to Shìzhōng and Shàngshū Púshè,
participating in managing affairs as before.
When Wéndì's illness became severe,
Zhòngjǔ attended to his medicine.
After Wéndì's death,
Gāozōng received the dying imperial edict to be Shàngshū Lìng and assist in governing.
Zhòngjǔ, along with Zuǒchéng Wáng Xiān, Zhōngshū Shèrén Liú Shīzhī, and Yīn Bùnìng,
seeing that the court's hopes rested with Gāozōng,
sent Bùnìng to falsely declare an imperial decree ordering Gāozōng to return to Dōngfǔ.
When the matter was exposed,
Shīzhī was sent to Běiyù and ordered to commit suicide.
Xiān and Bùnìng were both handed over for investigation.
Zhòngjǔ was then appointed Zhēnyì Jiāngjūn and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Previously,
Zhòngjǔ's son, Yù, had married Wéndì's younger sister, Xìnyì Chánggōngzhǔ.
Yù's official position reached Zhōngshū Shìláng.
He was then sent out as the Grand Administrator of Xuānchéng.
Wéndì provided him with soldiers and horses.
In that same year, he was promoted to Nánkāng Nèishǐ.
Due to the national mourning, he had not yet assumed the post.
Zhòngjǔ, now dismissed and residing in his private home,
and Yù both felt uneasy.
At that time, Hán Zǐgāo was in the capital,
and his men and horses were always numerous.
Yù would often ride in a small carriage, disguised in women's clothing, to conspire with Zǐgāo.
Zǐgāo's army commander reported the matter.
Gāozōng arrested Zǐgāo, Zhòngjǔ, and Yù, and handed them all over to the Tíngwèi.
An imperial edict stated:
"Dào Zhòngjǔ, with his mediocre and petty talent,
undeservedly enjoyed high status,
receiving appointments in the previous reign,
with immense favor and prestige.
The father participated in the royal administration,
the son governed a major state.
The ties of marriage were strong,
and their influence equaled that of the imperial relatives.
Yet, he indulged in arrogance and ignorance,
overbearing all officials.
At the very beginning of the mourning period,
he arbitrarily managed state affairs,
ostracized imperial relatives,
and slighted the highest officials.
Hán Zǐgāo, a small and insignificant person,
was elevated from humble beginnings.
He participated in the imperial guards
and was entrusted with confidential matters.
Like a venomous wasp,
he dared to retaliate.
Zhòngjǔ and Zǐgāo
acted in concert,
secretly concocting treacherous schemes,
and clandestinely planning rebellion.
Ānchéng Wáng, my imperial uncle,
is the closest of kin.
He received the mandate to guide and propagate,
and was entrusted with the care
of me, the young and weak ruler,
tasked with protection and support.
The safety of the family and state
rests with the prime ministers.
The importance of Yī Yǐn and Zhōu Gōng
is undisputed by all.
Generals, ministers, and former officials
all revere him.
Yet, they gathered evil followers,
intending to ambush him,
stationed troops in the eastern city,
advanced to pressure Chónglǐ,
planning to install Zhòngjǔ
to seize state power,
and expel the Sītú,
with the intention of monopolizing power.
They secretly formed factions
to endanger the state.
Thanks to the spirits of our ancestors,
their treacherous plot was revealed.
Former Magistrate of Shàngyú, Lù Fāng, and others fully reported the matter,
with corroborating evidence,
stating they had set the seventh day of this month
to unleash their sinister plot.
Língjūn Jiāngjūn Míngchè,
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn and Wèiwèi Qīng Bǎo'ān, and other dukes
were also aware of the matter.
These repeated evil deeds
are clear to the court and the populace.
Their actions are contrary to righteousness and morality,
and are shocking to hear and see.
Now that the great evildoers have been eradicated,
the culprits have been caught.
They are all to be taken to the Tíngwèi
to enforce justice according to the law.
The guilt is limited to Zhòngjǔ, his son, and Zǐgāo, only these three.
As for the rest, they shall all be pardoned
and not questioned."
Zhòngjǔ and Yù were both granted death in prison.
Zhòngjǔ was fifty-one years old at the time.
Yù's sons and daughters were spared because they were the emperor's nephews and nieces.
Hán Zǐgāo
was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His family was originally of humble status.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
he was living in the capital.
When Hóu Jǐng's rebellion was quelled,
Wéndì went out to govern Wúxīng.
Zǐgāo was sixteen years old,
with his hair tied in two knots (a child's hairstyle).
His appearance was beautiful,
resembling a woman.
At the Huái River bank, he joined a group of soldiers, hitching a ride to return to his hometown.
Wéndì saw him and asked,
"Can you serve me?"
Zǐgāo agreed.
Zǐgāo's original name was Mánzǐ.
Wéndì changed his name.
He was respectful and cautious by nature,
diligent in serving,
always carrying Wéndì's personal knife and serving wine and roasted meat.
Wéndì was short-tempered,
but Zǐgāo always anticipated his wishes.
As he grew up,
he gradually learned horsemanship and archery,
and was quite brave and decisive.
He wished to be a general.
After Dù Kān was suppressed,
Zǐgāo was assigned soldiers.
Wéndì greatly favored him
and never let him leave his side.
Wéndì once dreamed of riding a horse up a mountain,
the path was perilous, and he was about to fall.
Zǐgāo pushed and supported him, allowing him to ascend.
When Wén Dì was campaigning against Zhāng Biāo,
Shěn Tài and others surrendered first.
Wén Dì occupied the provincial capital,
and Zhōu Wényù garrisoned Xiāngyán Temple to the north of the city.
Zhāng Biāo returned from Shànxiàn at night to raid the city.
Wén Dì exited through the north gate.
In the sudden darkness of the evening,
the soldiers were in disarray.
Wényù also could not ascertain Wén Dì's whereabouts.
Only Zǐgāo was at his side.
Wén Dì then dispatched Zǐgāo through the confused troops to see Wényù,
returning with messages and responses,
and in the darkness, he again went to comfort the various armies.
Wén Dì's scattered troops gradually reassembled.
Zǐgāo led them into Wényù's camp,
and together they erected a palisade.
The next day,
they fought against Biāo.
Biāo's general Shēn Jìn surrendered again.
Biāo fled to Sōngshān,
and Zhèdōng was pacified.
Wén Dì then allocated a large portion of his troops to Zǐgāo.
Zǐgāo also spent money lightly and treated scholars with respect,
so many flocked to him.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne,
he appointed him Right Army General.
In the first year of Tiānjiā,
he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Wénzhāo County,
with a stipend of three hundred households.
When Wáng Lín reached Zhákǒu,
Zǐgāo was on duty guarding the palace.
When Lín was pacified,
Zǐgāo commanded even more troops.
As for the generals and soldiers who attached themselves to him,
Zǐgāo exerted himself to recommend them,
and Wén Dì employed them all.
In the second year,
he was promoted to Auxiliary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, General Zhuàngwǔ, and Governor of Chéngzhōu.
When Liú Yì was campaigned against,
he followed Hóu Āndū and camped beneath the cliffs of Táozhī Lǐng.
At that time, Zǐgāo's army was elite and well-equipped.
He personally commanded a separate camp,
rode alone into the battle formation,
was wounded on the left side of his neck,
