and half of his topknot fell off.
When Yì was pacified,
he was appointed Acting Governor, General Zhēnyì, and Administrator of Dōngyáng.
In the fifth year,
Zhāng Zhāodá and others campaigned against Jìn'ān from Línchuān.
Zǐgāo rendezvoused with them at Jiàn'ān from Ānquán Lǐng,
and his men and horses were the strongest among all the generals.
When Jìn'ān was pacified,
for his merits, he was promoted to Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary,
advanced in noble rank to Count,
with an increase in stipend, totaling four hundred households.
In the sixth year,
he was summoned to be Right Guard General.
Upon arrival at the capital,
he garrisoned the Lead Army Bureau.
When Wén Dì was unwell,
he entered to attend to his medicine.
When Fèi Dì ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
his position as Right Guard remained as before,
and he moved his camp to Xīn'ān Temple.
When Gāozōng began to assist in governance,
Zǐgāo's military power became too great,
and he felt deeply insecure.
He frequently visited the imperial court and offices to inquire about matters,
and also requested to be sent out as a garrison commander in Héng or Guǎng prefectures.
In the eighth month of the first year of Guāngdà,
Lù Fāng, the former magistrate of Shàngyú County, and Zǐgāo's military commander accused him of plotting rebellion.
Gāozōng was in the Department of State Affairs,
and so he summoned the civil and military officials in office to discuss establishing a crown prince.
Zǐgāo was included in this.
He entered the department at dawn,
was apprehended,
and sent to the Chief Justice.
That evening, he was granted death along with Dào Zhòngjǔ,
at the age of thirty.
His father Yánqìng and his sons and younger brothers were all pardoned.
Yánqìng, due to Zǐgāo's favor,
rose to the office of Attendant-in-Ordinary and Magistrate of Shānyīn.
Huà Jiǎo was
a native of Jìyáng, Jìnlíng.
His family served as minor officials for generations.
Jiǎo,
during the Liáng dynasty, served as a clerk in the Bureau of Accounts, Department of State Affairs.
During the Hóu Jǐng Rebellion,
he served Wáng Wěi, a partisan of Jǐng.
When Gāozǔ marched south,
Wén Dì was imprisoned by Jǐng,
and Jiǎo treated Wén Dì very well.
When Jǐng was pacified,
Wén Dì became Administrator of Wúxīng,
The grain and silk of the military headquarters
were largely entrusted to him.
and appointed Jiǎo as Chief Clerk.
and diligent in managing records.
When Wén Dì pacified Dù Kān,
he was still assigned men, horses, armor, and weapons,
and remained Chief Clerk.
He governed his subordinates clearly
and was good at nurturing them.
At that time, after the ravages of war,
the common people suffered from famine.
Jiǎo would give away his clothes and food,
distributing whatever amount he had fairly.
Thus, he was gradually promoted to be magistrate of Jìyáng and Shānyīn counties.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne,
he was appointed General Kāiyuǎn
and Left Army General.
In the first year of Tiānjiā,
he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Huáirén County,
with a stipend of four hundred households.
When Wáng Lín marched east,
Jiǎo followed Hóu Tián to resist him.
When Lín was pacified,
he garrisoned Péngchéng
and oversaw the affairs of Jiāngzhōu.
At that time, many local magistrates in the southern prefectures were powerful local chieftains
who did not comply with imperial laws.
Wén Dì ordered Jiǎo to control them with the law.
When Wáng Lín's forces scattered,
many of his generals and soldiers attached themselves to Jiǎo.
In the third year,
he was appointed Acting Governor, Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary, General Rénwǔ, and Governor of Xīnzhōu,
and concurrently supervised Jiāngzhōu.
Soon after, he was ordered to supervise all military affairs of Xúnyáng, Tàiyuán, Gāotáng, Nánxīn Cài, and Wǔjùn, and serve as Administrator of Xúnyáng.
His positions as Acting Governor, General, Governor, and Supervisor remained as before.
Zhōu Dí plotted rebellion,
sending his nephew to conceal armored soldiers in boats,
falsely claiming to be merchants,
intending to attack Jiǎo at Péngchéng.
Before they could act,
the plot was discovered.
Jiǎo sent men to intercept and attack them,
capturing all their boats and weapons.
In that year,
Jiǎo followed Commander-in-chief Wú Míngchè to campaign against Dí.
When Dí was pacified,
for his merits, he was awarded Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary, General Píngnán, and Administrator of Línchuān,
advanced in noble rank to Marquis,
with an additional stipend, totaling five hundred households.
Before he was formally invested,
he entered the court.
He was then appointed Imperial Commissioner, Supervisor of all military affairs of Xiāng, Bā, and four other prefectures, and Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
His positions as Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary and General remained as before.
Jiǎo rose from a humble official
and was good at managing industries.
Xiāngchuān produced many resources,
and what he acquired was all submitted to the imperial court.
He transported a large amount of grain, bamboo, and timber.
As for oil, honey, preserved meat, and vegetables,
there was nothing he did not procure.
He also campaigned against the mountain tribes and caves,
obtaining many bronze drums and captives,
all of which he sent to the capital.
When Fèi Dì ascended the throne,
he was advanced to the title of General Ānnán,
and his enfeoffment was changed to Marquis of Zhòng'ān County,
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred households.
Wén Dì, because Xiāngzhōu produced fir wood for boats,
ordered Jiǎo to build over two hundred large ships, such as the "Golden Wings,"
as well as all sorts of equipment for naval warfare,
intending to use them to enter Hàn and the gorges.
After Hán Zǐgāo was executed,
Jiǎo felt insecure.
He repaired armor, gathered followers,
and lavishly rewarded the local magistrates and administrators under his command.
Gāozōng repeatedly ordered Jiǎo to send the large ships like the "Golden Wings,"
but he delayed and did not comply.
In the first year of Guāngdà,
he secretly memorialized requesting Guǎngzhōu,
to gauge the emperor's intentions.
Gāozōng falsely agreed,
but the imperial edict had not yet been issued.
Jiǎo also sent envoys to connect with the Zhōu army
and moreover revered Xiāo Kuī as his lord,
having a very large army.
The imperial edict then appointed Wú Míngchè as Governor of Xiāngzhōu,
actually intending to attack Jiǎo with light troops.
At this time, fearing Jiǎo would strike first,
Míngchè was sent ahead with thirty thousand troops,
riding the "Golden Wings" directly towards Yǐngzhōu.
Grand General Fǔjūn Chúnyú Liáng was also sent with fifty thousand troops,
aboard large ships to follow him.
Furthermore, Imperial Commissioner and General Guānwǔ Yáng Wéntōng was ordered to take a separate infantry route from Ānchéng to Chálíng,
and Administrator of Bāshān Huáng Fǎhuì was ordered to take a separate route from Yíyáng to Lǐlíng,
to launch a surprise attack,
catching him off guard.
They were also to consult with Zhāng Zhāodá, Governor of Jiāngzhōu, Chéng Língxǐ, Governor of Yǐngzhōu, and others to plan the suppression of the rebel.
At this time, Xiāo Kuí (蕭巋) sent a naval force to aid Huá Jiǎo (華皎).
Zhōu Wǔ (周武) also dispatched his younger brother, Wèi Guó Gōng (衛國公) Yǔwén Zhí (宇文直), to lead troops and garrison Lǔshān (魯山),
and sent his Zhùguó (柱國) Cháng Hú Gōng (長胡公) Tuòbá Dìng (拓跋定) with thirty thousand men
to attack and besiege Yǐngzhōu (郢州).
Xiāo Kuí (蕭巋) appointed Huá Jiǎo (華皎) as Sīkōng (司空);
Bāzhōu Cìshǐ (巴州刺史) Dài Sēngshuò (戴僧朔),
Héngyáng Nèishǐ (衡陽內史) Rèn Mánnú (任蠻奴),
Bālíng Nèishǐ (巴陵內史) Pān Zhìqián (潘智虔),
Yuèyáng Tàishǒu (岳陽太守) Zhāng Zhāoyù (章昭裕),
Guìyáng Tàishǒu (桂陽太守) Cáo Xuān (曹宣),
Xiāngdōng Tàishǒu (湘東太守) Qián Míng (錢明),
were all subordinate to Huá Jiǎo (華皎).
Furthermore, Chángshā Tàishǒu (長沙太守) Cáo Qìng (曹慶) and others, originally under Huá Jiǎo (華皎)'s command,
were now employed by him.
The Emperor, fearing that all the provincial governors and administrators in the upper reaches of the river would be incited and misled by Huá Jiǎo (華皎),
issued an edict stating:
"The rebel Huá Jiǎo (華皎) was of humble and lowly origins,
but was specially promoted,
entrusted with a frontier governorship,
and given an important charge.
Yet he betrayed this nurturing,
concocted treasonous schemes,
supported the Xiāo (蕭) clan,
and his alliance was openly revealed.
With venom in his heart,
he aimed to endanger the imperial altars of soil and grain,
inciting and gathering forces in the border regions,
driving and coercing both gentry and commoners.
He gathered like ants in Bā (巴) and Xiāng (湘),
and charged like pigs into Yān (鄢) and Yǐng (郢),
defying Heaven and earth,
provoking the wrath of both men and gods.
Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn (征南將軍) Chúnyú Liàng (淳于量), Ānnán Jiāngjūn (安南將軍) Wú Míngchè (吳明徹), and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ (郢州刺史) Wèi Língxǐ (衞靈洗),
received the mandate to lead the campaign,
and exerted their utmost efforts,
comforting and encouraging the brave and mighty.
Their naval forces advanced together,
displaying righteous valor and striving fiercely.
The wicked rebels were routed and annihilated,
with reports of victories constantly arriving.
The heavy miasma has been dispelled.
Reflecting on those who committed crimes,
we wish for them to renew themselves.
Therefore, a general amnesty is granted for the two prefectures of Xiāng (湘) and Bā (巴): all those who were coerced or controlled by the rebels,
and were part of the rebellious faction,
shall all be pardoned without question;
as for the rebel commanders and generals,
they are all permitted to surrender and receive clemency,
and be treated with equal magnanimity."
Earlier,
an edict also dispatched Sīkōng (司空) Xú Dù (徐度) and Yáng Wéntōng (楊文通) and others to march from Ānchéng (安成) to Xiāngdōng (湘東),
to attack Huá Jiǎo (華皎) from the rear.
At that time, Huá Jiǎo (華皎) was arrayed at Báiluó (白螺) in Bāzhōu (巴州),
with his warships positioned in a stalemate against the imperial army.
Upon hearing that Xú Dù (徐度) was approaching Xiāngzhōu (湘州), he then led his troops from Bā (巴) and Yǐng (郢) and attacked with the advantage of the wind.
Chúnyú Liàng (淳于量), Wú Míngchè (吳明徹) and others recruited small vessels from the army,
offering generous rewards of gold and silver,
ordering them to confront the enemy's large vessels first,
and withstand their catapults.
After the enemy's catapults had expended all their projectiles,
the government army then used their large vessels to attack them with catapults.
The enemy's vessels were all shattered
and sank in the middle of the river.
The enemy also loaded large vessels with firewood,
and, using the wind, set them on fire.
Soon, the wind shifted, and they burned themselves,
causing a great defeat for the rebel army.
Huá Jiǎo (華皎) then fled with Dài Sēngshuò (戴僧朔) in a single boat.
Passing Bālíng (巴陵),
they dared not enter the city,
but went straight to Jiānglíng (江陵).
Tuòbá Dìng (拓跋定) and others had no more boats to cross,
and marched on foot towards Bālíng (巴陵).
Since the city of Bālíng (巴陵) had been occupied by the imperial army,
they headed towards Xiāngzhōu (湘州).
Upon reaching Shuǐkǒu (水口),
they could not cross.
Their provisions were almost exhausted,
so they surrendered to the army.
More than ten thousand people were captured,
and over four thousand horses,
which were sent to the capital.
Huá Jiǎo (華皎)'s partisans Cáo Qìng (曹慶), Qián Míng (錢明), Pān Zhìqián (潘智虔), Lǔ Xián (魯閑), Xí Huìlüè (席慧略) and over forty others were all executed.
Only Rèn Mánnú (任蠻奴), Zhāng Zhāoyù (章昭裕), Cáo Xuān (曹宣), and Liú Guǎngyè (劉廣ye) were spared.
Dài Sēngshuò (戴僧朔)
was a native of Qiántáng (錢塘) in Wú Jùn (吳郡).
He possessed great physical strength,
was brave and skilled in combat.
His elder cousin, Yòu Jiāngjūn (右將軍) Dài Sēngxī (戴僧錫), loved him dearly.
When Dài Sēngxī (戴 Sēngxī) grew old,
he always sent Dài Sēngshuò (戴 Sēngshuò) to lead the troops in campaigns.
He distinguished himself in subduing Wáng Lín (王琳).
When Dài Sēngxī (戴 Sēngxī) died,
he succeeded him as Nándānyáng Tàishǒu (南丹陽太守),
stationed at Cǎishí (採石).
He participated in the campaign against Liú Yì (留異).
When Hóu Āndū (侯安都) sallied forth from the foot of the cliff
and was wounded by the rebels,
Dài Sēngshuò (戴 Sēngshuò) advanced on foot with a single saber to aid him.
For his merits, he was appointed Zhuàngwǔ Jiāngjūn (壯武將軍) and Běijiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (北江州刺史),
concurrently holding the position of Nánlíng Tàishǒu (南陵太守).
He again distinguished himself in the campaign against Zhōu Dí (周迪),
and was promoted to Bāzhōu Cìshǐ (巴州刺史),
with his Jiǎjié (假節) and Jiāngjūn (將軍) titles remaining as before.
At this point, he conspired with Huá Jiǎo (華皎) in rebellion,
and was executed in Jiānglíng (江陵).
Cáo Qìng (曹慶) was originally Wáng Lín (王琳)'s general.
Xiāo Zhuāng (蕭莊) falsely appointed him Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衛將軍) and Wúzhōu Cìshǐ (吳州刺史),
and his command was second only to Pān Chún (潘純).
When Wáng Lín (王琳) was defeated,
Emperor Wén (文帝) assigned him to Huá Jiǎo (華皎).
He rose to the office of Chángshā Tàishǒu (長沙太守).
Qián Míng (錢明)
was originally Gāozǔ (高祖)'s chief commander,
later serving as various prefects in Xiāngzhōu (湘州).
Pān Zhìqián (潘智虔)
was the son of Pān Chún (潘純).
He was ambitious from a young age,
and at twenty, he became Bālíng Nèishǐ (巴陵內史).
Lǔ Xián (魯閑)
was a native of Qiántáng (錢塘) in Wú Jùn (吳郡).
Xí Huìlüè (席慧略)
was from Āndìng (安定).
Lǔ Xián (魯閑) was originally Zhāng Biāo (張彪)'s chief commander,
and Xí Huìlüè (席 Huìlüè) was a subordinate of Wáng Lín (王琳).
Emperor Wén (文帝) assigned both to Huá Jiǎo (華皎).
They rose to the office of Jùnshǒu (郡守).
Both were executed.
Zhāng Zhāoyù (章昭裕)
was the younger brother of Zhāng Zhāodá (章昭達);
Liú Guǎngyè (劉廣業)
was the younger brother of Liú Guǎngdé (劉廣德);
Cáo Xuān (曹宣)
was an old minister of Gāozǔ (高祖);
Rèn Mánnú (任蠻奴) had once secretly reported to the imperial court.
For these reasons, they were all pardoned.
The historian says: "Although Hán Zǐgāo (韓子高) and Huá Jiǎo (華皎) were of humble origins,
from the lowest ranks of society,
Emperor Wén (文帝), learning from ancient examples of employing worthy men,
and addressing the urgent problems of his time,
applied the art of discerning wisdom and clear sight,
and the principle of pacifying the people and harmonizing the masses.
He entrusted them with his innermost confidence,
regardless of their noble lineage.
Huá Jiǎo (華皎) had participated in close affairs early on,
and had experienced difficulties and dangers.
The emperor knew he had nothing to hide,
and rewarded his full efforts.
There was sincere trust in him,
and no grounds for suspicion.
Huá Jiǎo (華皎) held the upper reaches of the river,
and was loyal to Emperor Wén (文帝).
Zhòngjǔ (仲舉) and Zǐgāo (子高) also did not falter in their duties as ministers."
Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter 15: Xiè Zhé (謝哲), Xiāo Gān (蕭乾), Xiè Gǔ (謝嘏), Zhāng Zhǒng (張種), Wáng Gù (王固), Kǒng Huàn (孔奐), Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) (brother Yǐn (引))
Xiè Zhé (謝哲), courtesy name Yǐngyù (穎豫),
was a native of Yángxià (陽夏) in Chén Jùn (陳郡).
His grandfather, Xiè Pèi (謝朏), was Liáng Sītú (梁司徒).
His father, Xiè Jì (謝譓), was Liáng Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (梁右光祿大夫).
Zhé’s (Zhē’s) demeanor was beautiful and elegant,
his bearing graceful and restrained,
yet his disposition was open and unreserved,
and he was highly regarded by gentlemen-scholars.
He began his career as a secretary to the Grand Chancellor of Liáng (Liáng Mìshū Láng).
He was successively promoted to Grand Administrator of Guǎnglíng.
During Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion,
because his mother was old, he settled in Guǎnglíng.
When Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) crossed the Jiāng River from Jīngkǒu to meet Guō Yuánjiàn,
Zhé then pledged his allegiance,
and was deeply respected.
When Gāozǔ became the Inspector of 【Nán】Xúzhōu,
he memorialized to appoint Zhé as Chief Clerk.
When Jīngzhōu fell,
Gāozǔ sent Zhé to present a memorial to Prince Jìn'ān urging his enthronement.
Jìngdì, by imperial authority, summoned him to be a Palace Attendant and Yellow Gate Remonstrance Official,
concurrently holding the position of Commandant of Infantry.
When Zhēnyáng Hóu usurped the throne,
he made Zhé a Gentleman-in-Waiting and Palace Regular Attendant,
serving the Eastern Palace.
When Jìngdì ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Palace Attendant and concurrently held the position of Chief.
When Gāozǔ received the Mandate,
he was promoted to Minister of Personnel, Grand Impartial Judge of Yùzhōu, and Minister of the Bureau of Civil Office.
He was sent out as General Manifesting Martial Might and Grand Administrator of Jìnlíng,
then returned to serve as Director of the Central Secretariat.
When Shìzǔ succeeded to the throne,
he became Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
He was sent out as General Manifesting Martial Might and Inner Administrator of Héngyáng,
with a salary of two thousand shi.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Chángshā,
with his generalship and added rank remaining as before.
He returned and was appointed Palace Regular Attendant and Director of the Central Secretariat.
When Fèidì ascended the throne,
he held his original office and concurrently served as General of the Van.
When Gāozōng became Supervisor of the Masters of Writing,
he appointed him as Palace Attendant, General Manifesting Awe, and Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works.
Before he could take office,
he died in the first year of Guāngdà,
at the age of fifty-nine.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant and Supervisor of the Central Secretariat,
and was posthumously honored with the epithet Kāngzǐ.
Xiāo Gān, courtesy name Sītì,
was a native of Lánlíng.
His grandfather was Yí,
Prince Wénxiàn of Yùzhāng and Grand Chancellor of Qí.
His father was Zǐfàn,
Supervisor of the Central Secretariat of Liáng.
Gān’s deportment was elegant and proper,
his nature quiet and simple.
He excelled at clerical script (lìshū),
inheriting the method of his uncle Zǐyún.
At the age of nine,
he was summoned and appointed as a student of the Yìjīng (Zhōuyì) in the Directorate of Education.
Yuán Áng, the Minister of Works of Liáng at the time, was the Libationer,
and deeply respected him.
At fifteen,
he passed the examination for “understanding the classics” (míngjīng).
He began his official career as an Adjutant in the legal section for Prince Xiāngdōng, the Central Director,
and was promoted to Palace Secretary.
When Marquis Jiàn’ān, Xiāo Zhènglì, was sent to govern Nányùzhōu,
he was again appointed as Adjutant in charge of records.
He was successively promoted to Advisory Adjutant in charge of records for Prince Xuānchéng, the Central Army.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Gāozǔ governed Nánxúzhōu,
and appointed Gān as General Manifesting Integrity and Central Gentleman for Attendance of the Minister of Works.
He was promoted to Central Secretariat Remonstrance Official and Palace Steward of the Crown Prince.
In the first year of Yǒngdìng,
he was appointed Palace Attendant and Yellow Gate Remonstrance Official.
At this time, Xióng Tánlǎng was in Yùzhāng,
Zhōu Dí in Línchuān,
Liú Yì in Dōngyáng,
and Chén Bǎo Yìng in Jiàn and Jìn.
They were all allied with each other.
The powerful chieftains in Mǐnzhōng,
often established strongholds to protect themselves.
Gāozǔ was greatly troubled by this,
so he ordered Gān to go on an envoy mission,
to explain the principles of loyalty and rebellion,
and also to observe their true situation.
As he was about to depart,
Gāozǔ said to Gān:
“Jiàn and Jìn rely on their dangerous terrain,
and are prone to treachery.
Now that the world is just settled,
it is difficult to immediately deploy troops.
In the past, Lù Jiǎ campaigned in the south,
and Zhào Tuó submitted.
Suí Hé went on an envoy mission,
and Qíng Bù came to be a subject.
Remembering their pure conduct,
it seems as if they are right before my eyes.
Moreover, you yourself can stabilize the refined and the unrefined,
your talent surpasses the ancients.
You should strive to achieve glorious deeds,
without the need for further military campaigns.”
After Gān arrived,
he enlightened them with the principles of loyalty and rebellion.
The local chieftains, along with their followers, all opened their strongholds and submitted.
In the same year,
he was appointed General Manifesting Integrity and Grand Administrator of Jiàn’ān.
In the second year of Tiānjiā,
Liú Yì rebelled.
Chén Bǎoyìng led troops to assist him,
and also supplied Zhōu Dí with soldiers and provisions.
They launched an attack on Línchuān,
and then pressured Jiàn’ān.
Gān, alone, went to the commandery.
As he had no soldiers,
he was unable to defend it.
So he abandoned the commandery to avoid Bǎoyìng.
At that time, the administrators and magistrates in Mǐnzhōng
were all coerced by Bǎoyìng,
and accepted his appointments.
Only Gān refused to yield,
moving to the countryside,
and completely cutting off social interaction.
When Bǎoyìng was pacified,
he then went to visit the Regional Commander Zhāng Zhāodá.
Zhāodá reported his situation,
and Shìzǔ greatly praised him,
promoting him exceptionally to Minister of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
He died in the first year of Guāngdà,
and was posthumously honored with the epithet Jìngzǐ.
Xiè Gǔ, courtesy name Hánmào,
was a native of Yángxià, Chénjùn.
His grandfather was Wěi,
Grand Master of Brilliant Light with Gold and Purple Seal and Grand Administrator of Qí.
His father was Jǔ,
General of the Central Guard and Minister with Special Conferment of Liáng.
Gǔ had an elegant and refined demeanor,
and was quite skilled at writing prose.
He began his career as a Secretary of the Grand Chancellor of Liáng,
gradually rising to Central Gentleman for Attendance of the Crown Prince,
overseeing the records of the Eastern Palace,
and then went out to serve as Grand Administrator of Jiàn’ān.
During Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion,
Gǔ went to Guǎngzhōu to rely on Xiāo Bó.
During the Chéngshèng period,
Yuándì summoned him to be Minister of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
but he declined, citing the obstructed roads.
He was then transferred to the position of General Zhìwǔ.
Xiāo Bó appointed him as Chief Clerk of the Protector of the South and Grand Administrator of Nánhǎi.
When Bó was defeated,
he returned to Línchuān,
where he was detained by Zhōu Dí.
After a long time,
he again crossed the mountains to Jìn’ān to rely on Chén Bǎoyìng.
Shìzǔ repeatedly summoned him before and after,
but Gǔ was in a difficult situation among the bandits
and could not extricate himself.
When Bǎoyìng was pacified,
Gǔ then went to the capital.
He was impeached by the Censor-in-Chief Jiāng Dézǎo.
Shìzǔ did not punish him,
and made him Palace Attendant and Yellow Gate Remonstrance Official.
Soon after, he was transferred to Palace Attendant.
In the first year of Tiānkāng,
he was dismissed due to official matters,
but soon restored to his original position.
In the first year of Guāngdà,
he became General Manifesting Awe and Chief Clerk of Prince Shǐxīng of the Central Guard.
He was promoted to Director of the Central Secretariat, Grand Impartial Judge of Yùzhōu, and Minister of Personnel,
concurrently supervising the Feathered Forest Guard,
with his position as Grand Impartial Judge remaining as before.
He died in the first year of Tàijiàn,
and was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant and Director of the Central Secretariat,
and was posthumously honored with the epithet Guāngzǐ.
He had a collection of writings circulating in the world.
He had two sons, Yǎn and Zhòu.
Yǎn served as Palace Regular Attendant, Palace Attendant, Censor-in-Chief, and Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
and was then sent out to supervise Dōngyángzhōu.
He died in Kuàijī in the second year of Zhēnmíng,
and was posthumously granted the title of Protector of the Central Army.
Zhāng Zhǒng, courtesy name Shìmiáo,
was a native of Wújùn.
His grandfather was Biàn,
Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu during the Sòng dynasty.
His father was Lüè,
Central Gentleman for Attendance of the Crown Prince and Grand Administrator of Línhǎi during the Liáng dynasty.
Zhǒng was by nature tranquil,
and his dwelling was refined and proper.
He did not associate rashly,
and there were no uninvited guests around him.
People of the time made a saying about him:
“In Sòng, Fū and Yǎn were esteemed;
in Liáng, Juǎn and Chōng.
For a pure and serene scholarly demeanor,
Zhǒng embodies their style.”
He served in the Liáng royal household as a Fǎcáo,
then was promoted to Wàibīng Cānjūn.
Due to his father’s mourning, he resigned from office.
After the mourning period concluded,
he became Zhōngjūn Xuānchéngwáng Fǔ Zhǔbù.
Zhǒng was then over forty years old.
His family was poor,
so he requested to be Shǐfēng Lìng.
He was appointed Rùchú Zhōngwèi Xīchāng Hóu Fǔ Xīcáo Yuàn.
At that time, Wǔlíng Wáng was the Yìzhōu Cìshǐ,
and he carefully selected his staff.
He appointed Zhǒng as Zhēngxī Dōngcáo Yuàn.
Zhǒng declined, citing his mother’s old age,
and submitted a memorial petitioning to be excused.
He was impeached by the relevant authorities,
and dismissed from office.
During Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion,
Zhǒng fled eastward with his mother,
and after a long time, reached their hometown.
Soon after, his mother died.
Zhǒng was fifty years old at the time,
and his emaciation was excessive.
Moreover, pressed by famine,
he could not bury her promptly.
Although the mourning period was over,
his living and eating habits
remained as if he were still in mourning.
When Jǐng’s rebellion was quelled,
Sītú Wáng Sēngbiàn reported his situation
and appointed him Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn, Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ,
and also arranged a funeral for him.
After the burial,
Zhǒng then resumed normal life.
Sēngbiàn also noted Zhǒng’s advanced age
and lack of an heir,
so he bestowed upon him a concubine
and living essentials.
When Zhēnyáng Hóu usurped the throne,
Zhǒng was appointed Tíngwèi Qīng and Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
Upon Jìng Dì’s ascension,
he became Sànqí Chángshì,
then promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
leading the Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he became Tàifǔ Qīng.
In the first year of Tiānjiā (560 CE),
he was appointed Zuǒmín Shàngshū.
In the second year (561 CE),
he temporarily supervised Wújùn,
then was recalled to his original post.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng,
leading Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
Due to a public matter, he was dismissed,
but served as Báiyī Jiān Tàicháng Qīng,
and soon after was formally appointed.
Upon Fèi Dì’s ascension,
he was additionally appointed Ròujūn Jiāngjūn.
Before he was formally installed,
he was reassigned to lead Hóngshàn Gōng Wèiwèi,
and also led the Dàzhōngzhèng of Yáng and Dōngyáng Prefectures.
Upon Gāozōng’s ascension,
he was reappointed Dūguān Shàngshū,
leading Zuǒxiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
He was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng,
with Xiāoqí and Dàzhōngzhèng remaining as before.
Due to illness, he was granted the title Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Zhǒng was profound and serene,
yet his discernment and capacity were vast.
People of the time all considered him a talent for a prime minister.
Púshè Xú Líng once submitted a memorial yielding his position to Zhǒng, saying:
“Zhǒng possesses a profound and reserved character,
and is abundant in literature and history.
As a noble talent from the southeast,
and a trusted worthy in the imperial court,
he is capable of great strategies,
and should properly occupy the left position (i.e., prime minister).”
Such was the esteem he received at the time.
He died in the fifth year of Tàijiàn (573 CE),
aged seventy.
He was posthumously granted Tèjìn,
and given the posthumous name Yuánzǐ.
Zhǒng was benevolent, tolerant, and had few desires.
Although he held prominent positions,
his family property was often empty,
yet he remained calm all day,
not considering it a hardship.
In the early Tàijiàn period,
his daughter became the princess of Shǐxīng Wáng.
Due to his cramped and humble dwelling,
he was specially granted a residence,
and repeatedly bestowed the rank of Marquis of Wúxī and Jiāxīng Counties.
He once saw a heavy prisoner in jail in Wúxī.
It was cold,
so he called him out to bask in the sun,
and subsequently lost him.
Shìzǔ laughed heartily,
but did not deeply reprimand him.
He had a collection of fourteen volumes.
Zhǒng’s younger brother, Líng,
was also pure, tranquil, and discerning.
His highest office was Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ.
He died in the eleventh year of Tàijiàn (579 CE),
aged seventy.
He was posthumously granted Guānglù Dàfū.
Zhǒng’s clan nephew, Zhìcái,
was the grandson of Qí Hùjūn Chōngzhī.
As a youth, he was independent and had a unique character.
He served as Shàngshū Jīnbù Lángzhōng.
He was promoted to Yòuchéng,
Jiànkāng Lìng, Tàizhōu Qīng,
Yángzhōu Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ,
concurrently Sànqí Chángshì.
He was an envoy to Zhōu,
and upon returning, became Sīnóng and Tíngwèi Qīng.
In all his posts, he was known for his integrity.
Wáng Gù, courtesy name Zǐjiān,
was the younger brother of Zuǒguānglù Dàfū Tōng.
In his youth, he was pure and upright,
and quite versed in literature and history.
As the maternal nephew of Liáng Wǔ Dì, he was enfeoffed as Mòkǒu Tínghóu.
He was recommended as a Xiùcái.
He started his career in Liáng as Mìshū Láng,
promoted to Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
and oversaw the records of the Eastern Palace.
He resigned due to mourning for his birth mother.
After the mourning period concluded,
he was appointed Dānyáng Yǐn Céng.
During Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion,
he fled to Jīngzhōu.
Liáng Yuán Dì, acting as regent, appointed him Xiàngguó Hùcáo Shǔ,
overseeing records.
Soon after, he was invited to Western Wèi.
The Wèi people treated him very generously
because he was a maternal relative of the Liáng imperial family.
In the first year of Chéngshèng (552 CE),
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
then became Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn, Ānnán Zhǎngshǐ, and Xúnyáng Tàishǒu.
When Jīngzhōu fell,
Gù went to Póyáng,
followed his elder brother Zhìdù to Dōnglǐng,
and resided in Xìn’ān County.
In the first year of Shàotài (555 CE),
he was summoned to be Shìzhōng,
but did not accept.
During the Yǒngdìng period,
he moved to Wújùn.
Shìzǔ esteemed Gù for his purity and tranquility,
and also wished to establish a marriage alliance.
In the second year of Tiānjiā (561 CE),
he arrived at the capital and was appointed Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
In the third year (562 CE),
he was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng.
In the fourth year (563 CE),
he again became Sànqí Chángshì and Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
That same year,
Gù’s daughter was made the Imperial Crown Princess,
and he received extremely respectful treatment.
Upon Fèi Dì’s ascension,
he was granted Shìzhōng and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
At that time, Gāozōng was assisting in governance.
As Gù was the maternal relative of Fèi Dì,
his wet nurse often went in and out of the forbidden palace,
quite frequently relaying secret messages.
When the matter was exposed,
he was almost executed.
Gāozōng, considering that Gù originally had no military power
and lived a clean life,
merely dismissed him from his current office
and placed him under house arrest.
In the second year of Tàijiàn (570 CE),
he was appointed, by general rule, Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Xuānhuì Yùzhāngwáng Zīyì Cānjūn.
He was promoted to Tàizhōng Dàfū, Tàicháng Qīng, and Nánxúzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng.
In the seventh year (575 CE),
he died in office,
aged sixty-three.
He was posthumously granted Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
All necessities for his funeral
were provided from the treasury.
In the second year of Zhìdé (584 CE),
he was reburied and given the posthumous name Gōngzǐ.
Gù was pure, tranquil, and had few desires.
During periods of mourning, he was known for his filial piety.
He also deeply believed in Buddhism.
When his birth mother died,
he ate only vegetables for the rest of his life.
At night, he would sit in meditation,
and during the day, he would recite Buddhist sūtras,
also studying the principles of the Chéngshí Lùn.
However, he was not skilled in profound philosophical discourse.
He was once invited to Wèi,
and during a banquet,
he requested that the killing of a sheep be stopped.
The sheep knelt and bowed before Gù.
Another banquet was held at Kūnmíng Chí.
The Wèi people, knowing that southerners enjoyed fish,
set up many fishing nets.
Gù chanted Buddhist incantations over them,
and not a single scale was caught.
His son, Kuān,
rose to the office of Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ and Shìzhōng.
Kǒng Huàn, courtesy name Xiūwén,
was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His great-grandfather, Xiùzhī,
was Qí Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū and Wúxīng Tàishǒu.
His grandfather, Jiàn,
was Tàizǐ Shèrén and Shàngshū Sān Gōng Láng.
His father, Zhìsūn,
was Liáng Níngyuǎn Zhījiāng Gōngzhǔ Zhǔbù and Wúxī Lìng.
Huàn was orphaned at several years old
and raised by his uncle Qiánsūn.
He loved learning
and was good at writing.
He was well-versed
in the classics, histories, and the hundred schools of thought.
Liú Xiǎn of Pèiguó, at the time known as a "library,"
often discussed with Huàn,
and greatly admired him,
taking Huàn's hand and saying:
"In the past, Bójiē's complete collection of writings was given to Zhòngxuān.
I aspire to be like that Lord Cài,
and you are worthy of being a member of the Wáng clan."
His treasured books
were soon given to him.
The province recommended him as Xiùcái,
and he achieved a high rank in the policy examination.
He began his career as Yángzhōu Zhǔbù and Xuānhuì Xiāngdōng Wáng Xíng Cānjūn,
but did not take either position.
He was then appointed Zhènwèi Xiāngdōng Wáng Wàibīng Cānjūn,
and entered the court as Shàngshū Cāngbù Lángzhōng,
then promoted to Yícáo Shìláng.
At that time, Shěn Jiǒng, the Zuǒ Mín Láng, was slandered by anonymous accusations
and was about to face a severe penalty.
The matter implicated high officials,
causing widespread anxiety.
Huàn argued for him in court
and he was eventually cleared.
Hé Jìngróng, the Dānyáng Yǐn, impressed by Huàn's integrity,
requested him for the post of Gōngcáo Shǐ.
He was sent out as Nánchāng Hóu Xiàng,
but during Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
he did not take up the office.
When the capital fell,
all court officials were detained.
Someone recommended Huàn to the bandit leader Hóu Zǐjiàn.
Zǐjiàn ordered his shackles removed,
treated him with great courtesy,
and put him in charge of scribal duties.
At that time, Jǐng's soldiers were unchecked in their brutal power.
Zǐjiàn was Jǐng's confidant,
and his authority was heavy.
Any court officials who saw him
would humble themselves and bow.
Huàn alone remained haughty and composed,
showing no deference.
Someone advised Huàn, saying:
"In these chaotic times,
people seek to merely survive.
These Xūnjié barbarians are ignorant;
how can you resist them with righteousness?"
Huàn replied:
"My life has its fate.
Although I cannot yet die,
how can I curry favor with these villains
to save myself?"
At that time, the bandits plundered women and children
and forced commoners and officials into servitude.
Huàn consistently protected them,
and many were saved.
Soon after, he suffered the loss of his mother,
and his grief and emaciation exceeded the proper rites.
At that time, the world was in chaos and war,
and no one could complete the three-year mourning period.
Only Huàn and Zhāng Zhǒng of Wúguó,
maintained the customary rites amidst the banditry,
and both were known for their filial piety.
When Jǐng was pacified,
Sītú Wáng Sēngbiàn first issued an order of appointment,
inviting Huàn to be Zuǒ Xīcáo Yuàn,
and then made him Dānyáng Yǐn Céng.
When Liáng Yuándì ascended the throne in Jīngzhōu,
he summoned Huàn and Shěn Jiǒng, ordering them to proceed west.
Sēngbiàn repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to retain them.
The Emperor personally dispatched an imperial rescript to Sēngbiàn, saying:
"The two scholars Kǒng and Shěn
are temporarily lent to you, sir."
Such was the esteem in which they were held by the court.
He was then appointed Tàiwèi Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
When Sēngbiàn became Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
Huàn was again appointed Yángzhōu Zhìzhōng Cóngshì Shǐ.
At that time, Hóu Jǐng's rebellion had just been pacified,
and everything was being rebuilt from scratch.
Old regulations and precedents
no longer existed.
Huàn was learned and had a strong memory,
clearly understanding old facts and practices.
There was nothing he didn't know when asked.
The official protocols and forms,
memorials and letters,
all originated from Huàn.
When Gāozǔ became Prime Minister,
Huàn was appointed Sītú Yòu Chángshǐ,
and promoted to Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng.
When Qí sent Dōngfāng Lǎo, Xiāo Guǐ, and others to invade,
their army reached Hòuhú,
causing disturbance in the capital.
Furthermore, the four directions were blocked,
and grain supplies were cut off.
The three armies relied
solely on the capital for provisions.
So Huàn was appointed Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn and Jiànkāng Lìng.
At that time, years of war and famine had occurred,
households were scattered,
and a powerful enemy suddenly arrived.
There was nowhere to conscript or requisition.
Gāozǔ set a date for a decisive battle,
and ordered Huàn to prepare many portions of wheat meal,
wrapped in lotus leaves.
Within one night,
tens of thousands of portions were obtained.
The soldiers ate them in the morning
and carried the rest.
They then engaged in a decisive battle,
and utterly defeated the enemy.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
Huàn was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
In the second year of Yǒngdìng,
he was appointed Jìnlíng Tàishǒu.
Since the Sòng and Qí dynasties, Jìnlíng
had been a major commandery.
Although it had suffered from banditry,
it still remained intact and substantial.
Previous officials of two thousand *shí* often engaged in exploitation and oppression.
Huàn maintained his integrity,
and his wife and children did not accompany him to his post.
He arrived at the commandery alone in a single boat.
The salary he received
he immediately distributed to the orphaned and widowed.
The commandery greatly rejoiced,
calling him
"Divine Lord."
Yīn Yǐ, a wealthy man from Qū'ā,
seeing Huàn's simple living conditions,
sent him a set of clothes
and a felt blanket.
Huàn said:
"As the Taishou, I enjoy a good income;
why would I be unable to acquire these things?
It is just that there are people whose needs are not met,
and I cannot enjoy warmth and satiety alone.
I appreciate your kind intentions,
but please do not trouble yourself further."
Initially,
when Shìzǔ was in Wúzhōng,
he heard of Huàn's good governance.
After he ascended the throne,
he summoned Huàn to be Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and concurrently Dàzhōngzhèng of Yángzhōu.
Huàn's nature was upright and firm,
he was good at upholding principles,
and he impeached many people.
The imperial court held him in great reverence and awe.
He deeply understood the principles of governance,
and every time he presented a memorial,
the emperor never failed to commend it.
All stagnant affairs of the various bureaus
were entrusted to Huàn to resolve.
He was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì,
concurrently leading the Bùbīng Xiàowèi,
Zhōngshū Shèrén,
in charge of imperial edicts,
and Dàzhōngzhèng of Yáng and Dōngyáng prefectures.
In Tiānjiā fourth year (563 CE),
he was again appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and soon after became Wǔbīng Shàngshū,
while his positions as Chángshì and Dàzhōngzhèng remained as before.
At this time, Shìzǔ was unwell,
and all the numerous affairs of the bureaus
were jointly handled by Púyè Dào Zhòngjǔ and Huàn.
When Shìzǔ's illness became critical,
Huàn, along with Gāozōng, Zhòngjǔ, Lìbù Shàngshū Yuán Shū, and Zhōngshū Shèrén Liú Shīzhī, among others, attended to his medicine.
Shìzǔ once said to Huàn and others:
"Now the three regions stand like tripods,
and the common people are not yet settled.
The affairs of the realm are weighty,
and a grown ruler is needed.
I wish to emulate Jìn Chéng in the near future,
and profoundly follow the example of the Yīn dynasty in the distant past.
You must all adhere to this intention."
Huàn then shed tears and sobbed as he replied:
"Your Majesty's health has been compromised,
but recovery will not be long.
The Crown Prince is in the prime of his youth,
and his sage virtues are daily increasing.
The Anchéng Wáng, as an esteemed younger brother,
is sufficient to be a Zhōu Dàn.
As your Àhéng and chief ministers,
if there were any intention of deposing or establishing a ruler,
this humble minister and others,
would not dare to hear such an edict."
Shìzǔ said:
"The integrity of the ancients
is seen again in you."
In Tiānkāng first year (566 CE),
Huàn was appointed Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
with his Dàzhōngzhèng positions for the two prefectures remaining as before.
Upon Shìzǔ's death,
Fèidì ascended the throne, and Huàn was appointed Sànqí Chángshì and Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
In Guāngdà second year (568 CE),
he was sent out as Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, Nánzhōngláng Kānglè Hóu Zhǎngshǐ, and Xúnyáng Tàishǒu,
acting as administrator of Jiāngzhōu.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Rénwēi Jiāngjūn, Yúnhuī Shǐxīng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ,
with all other positions remaining as before.
Huàn was clean and frugal in office,
and offered many corrections and admonitions.
Gāozōng commended him,
bestowed five hundred hú of rice,
and frequently sent imperial edicts inquiring about his well-being and expressing solicitude.
In Tàijiàn third year (571 CE),
he was summoned to be Dùzhī Shàngshū,
and concurrently Yòujūn Jiāngjūn.
In the fifth year (573 CE),
he was reassigned to concurrently lead Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
and with Zuǒpúyè Xú Líng, jointly managed the five departments of the Shàngshū.
In the sixth year (574 CE),
he was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū.
In the seventh year (575 CE),
he was granted the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
In the eighth year (576 CE),
he was further granted the additional title of Shìzhōng.
At that time, there was a northern expedition,
which recovered Huái and Sì,
and the tribal chiefs of Xú and Yù
submitted one after another.
Awards, promotions, and selections
were numerous and overlapping.
Huàn received and introduced them,
with no guests lingering at his gate.
Furthermore, he possessed keen insight into people,
and was thoroughly conversant with all schools of thought.
All those he selected and promoted,
whether high officials or gentry,
were universally pleased and submissive.
His nature was upright and straightforward,
and he absolutely refused private requests.
Even the esteemed Crown Prince
or influential dukes and marquises,
who were driven by personal feelings to make requests,
could never make him yield.
When Shǐxīng Wáng Shūlíng was in Xiāngzhōu,
he repeatedly hinted to the relevant officials,
insistently seeking a position in the imperial court.
Huàn said:
"The office of Gǔnzhāng is primarily based on virtue,
not necessarily on imperial lineage."
He then spoke out strongly to Gāozōng.
Gāozōng said:
"Why is Shǐxīng suddenly aspiring to a high public office?
Moreover, if my son is to be a high public official,
he must be after Póyáng Wáng."
Huàn said:
"My view
is also as Your Majesty decrees."
The Later Emperor, while still the Crown Prince,
wished to appoint Jiāng Zǒng as Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
and had Guǎnjì Lù Yú convey this to Huàn.
Huàn said to Yú:
"Jiāng has the literary brilliance of Pān and Lù,
but lacks the solid substance of Yuán and Qǐ.
To assist and advise the Crown Prince,
I secretly find it difficult."
Yú reported this fully to the Later Emperor.
The Later Emperor deeply resented this,
and then spoke to Gāozōng himself.
When Gāozōng was about to agree,
Huàn then memorialized:
"Jiāng Zǒng is a man of literary talent.
The current Crown Prince's literary talent is no less,
so why would he need Zǒng?
In my humble opinion,
I wish to select a man of weighty character
to serve as his mentor."
The Emperor said:
"If it is as you say,
who should hold this position?"
Huàn said:
"Dūguān Shàngshū Wáng Kuò,
whose family has generations of excellent virtue,
and whose character is upright and keen,
can hold it."
The Later Emperor was also present at the time,
and said:
"Kuò is the son of Wáng Tài,
he cannot hold the position of Tàizǐ Zhānshì."
Huàn again memorialized:
"During the Sòng dynasty, Fàn Nàn, who was Fàn Tài's son,
also served as Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
Previous generations had no doubts about it."
The Later Emperor insisted on his objection,
and the Emperor ultimately appointed Zǒng as Zhānshì.
Because of this, Huàn went against the imperial will.
His principled uprightness was like this.
Initially,
the Later Emperor wanted to appoint his private favorites to office,
and brought this up with Huàn.
Huàn did not comply.
When Yòupúyè Lù Shàn was promoted,
Gāozōng wanted to appoint Huàn,
and the edict had already been drafted.
However, it was suppressed by the Later Emperor,
and thus not issued.
In the ninth year (577 CE),
he was promoted to Shìzhōng, Zhōngshū Lìng, concurrently leading Zuǒxiāoqí Jiāngjūn, and Dàzhōngzhèng of Yáng, Dōngyáng, and Fēng prefectures.
In the eleventh year (579 CE),
he was transferred to Tàicháng Qīng,
with Shìzhōng and Dàzhōngzhèng remaining as before.
In the fourteenth year (582 CE),
he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì, Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and concurrently leading Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
Before he was officially appointed,
he was reassigned to lead Hóngfàn Gōng Wèiwèi.
He died in Zhìdé first year (583 CE),
at the age of seventy.
He was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì,
with his original official position remaining as before.
He had a collection of fifteen juan,
and four juan of impeachment memorials.
His sons were Shào Xīn and Shào Zhōng.
Shào Zhōng, courtesy name Xiàoyáng,
also possessed talent and learning.
He rose to the office of Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ and Yítóng Póyáng Wáng Dōngcáo Yuàn.
Xiāo Yǔn, courtesy name Shúzǔ,
was a native of Lánlíng.
His great-grandfather, Sīhuà,
was Sòng Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Shàngshū Yòupúyè,
was Sànqí Chángshì, Tàifǔ Qīng, and Zuǒmín Shàngshū.
His father, Jiè,
was Liáng Shìzhōng and Dūguān Shàngshū.
Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) was well-known in his youth.
His demeanor was serene and profound,
and he was discerning and insightful.
His deportment was refined and reserved,
and his actions always conformed to propriety.
He began his career as the Judicatory Military Advisor (法曹參軍) to the Prince of Shàolíng (邵陵王).
He was then transferred to become the Chief Clerk (主簿) to the Prince of Xiāngdōng (湘東王),
and later promoted to太子洗馬 (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ).
When Hóu Jǐng (侯景) attacked and captured Táichéng (臺城),
the numerous officials scattered.
Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) alone sat in his palace quarters, neat in his attire,
and Hóu Jǐng’s (侯景) soldiers respected him and did not approach him.
Soon after, he left to reside in Jīngkǒu (京口).
At that time, bandits were rampant,
and the common people were terrified.
The gentry and aristocratic families
scattered in all directions,
but Xiāo Yǔn (蕭 yǔn) alone did not move.
When people asked him why,
Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) replied:
"The way of life and destiny
has its fixed course.
How can one escape it by fleeing?
Moreover, the birth of troubles
all originates from gain.
If one does not seek gain,
how can disaster arise?
Currently, the common people are vying to raise their arms and claim great merit,
becoming high ministers and chancellors with a single word.
What business do they have with a mere scholar like me?
I will not do what Zhuāng Zhōu (莊周) called 'fearing one's shadow and fleeing one's tracks'."
Thereupon, he closed his door and lived quietly,
eating once every two days,
and thus escaped harm.
After Hóu Jǐng (侯景) was pacified,
Gāozǔ (高祖) was stationed in Nánxúzhōu (南徐州).
He sent a letter to summon Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允),
but Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) again declined, citing illness.
In the Yǒngdìng (永定) era,
Hóu Āndū (侯安都) became the Governor (刺史) of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州).
He personally visited Xiāo Yǔn's (蕭允) dwelling
to show respect as a junior to an elder.
In the third year of Tiānjīa (天嘉) (45), he was summoned to be the Crown Prince's Household Administrator (太子庶子).
[一二] Three years later,
he was appointed General of Awe-Inspiring Might (稜威將軍) and Assistant to the Governor of Dānyáng Commandery (丹陽尹丞).
In the fifth year,
he concurrently served as Attendant (侍中)
and was dispatched as an envoy to Zhōu (周).
Upon his return, he was appointed Palace Secretary (中書侍郎) and Minister of Works (大匠卿).
When Gāozōng (高宗) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Palace Assistant Secretary (黃門侍郎).
In the fifth year,
he was dispatched as the Chief Clerk (長史) to the Prince of Jìn'ān (晉安王), then stationed as安前 (Ānqián).
In the sixth year,
when the Prince of Jìn'ān (晉安王) became the Governor of Nányùzhōu (南豫州),
Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) again served as his Chief Clerk (王長史).
At that time, the Prince was still young
and had not yet personally managed public affairs,
so he entrusted Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) with the administration of the prefecture and province.
He later entered the court as Minister of Ceremonies (光祿卿).
Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) was by nature earnest and steady,
and never harbored thoughts of glory or profit.
When the Prince of Jìn'ān (晉安) was sent to govern Xiāngzhōu (湘州),
he again insisted on taking Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) with him.
Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) had been friends with Cài Jǐnglì (蔡景歷) since youth.
Cài Jǐnglì's (蔡景歷) son, Cài Zhēng (蔡徵), out of respect for his father's old friend,
heard that Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) was about to leave.
He then went to Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) and said:
"Sir, your age and virtue are both exalted;
you are an elder statesman of the nation.
You could comfortably sit in a central position,
and in due course, you would certainly be appointed to a ministerial post.
Why bother to endure hardship out in the provinces again?"
Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) replied:
"I have already given my word to the Prince of Jìn'ān (晉安).
How can I break my promise?"
Such was his indifference to honor and power.
In the third year of Zhìdé (至德),
he was appointed Chief Clerk (長史) to the Prince of Yùzhāng (豫章王), who was then Grand Marshal (中衛).
He was successively promoted to Palace Counselor (通直散騎常侍), General of Brilliant Victory (光勝將軍), Chief Clerk (左長史) to the Grand Minister of Education (司徒), and Administrator of Āndé Palace (安德宮少府).
When the Prince of Póyáng (鄱陽王), then Commander-in-Chief (鎮衛), was sent to govern Kuàijī (會稽),
Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) again served as his Chief Clerk (長史)
and concurrently held the post of Assistant Administrator of Kuàijī Commandery (會稽郡丞).
Passing through Yánlíng (延陵), he visited the temple of Jìzǐ (季子).
He offered sacrificial plants and water,
metaphorically forming a bond across generations,
and composed a poem to express his feelings.
The verse and reasoning were clear and classic.
The Last Emperor (後主) once asked Cài Zhēng (蔡徵):
"Your family has been acquainted with Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) for generations.
What is this gentleman's ambition and character?"
Cài Zhēng (蔡徵) replied:
"His purity, detachment, and profound insight
are almost unfathomable.
As for his literary works,
I can speak of them."
He then recited Xiāo Yǔn's (蕭允) poem in reply,
and the Last Emperor (後主) praised it for a long time.
That year, he was appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies (光祿大夫).
When the Suí (隋) army crossed the Jiāng (江),
Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) was moved to Guānyòu (關右).
At this time, the court officials who arrived in Cháng'ān (長安)
were all, by precedent, granted official positions.
Only Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允) and Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射) Xiè Zhòu (謝伷) declined, citing old age and illness.
Emperor Wén (文帝) of Suí (隋) respected their integrity
and gave them both generous gifts of money and silk.
Soon after, he died of illness in Cháng'ān (長安),
at the age of eighty-four.
His younger brother, Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引).
Xiāo Yǐn's (蕭引) courtesy name was Shūxiū (叔休).
[一三] He was upright and possessed great capacity,
appearing solemn and dignified.
Even in casual situations,
he always adhered to proper conduct.
He was intelligent and quick-witted by nature,
extensively learned,
and skilled in writing.
He began his career as Assistant Compiler (著作佐郎)
and was then transferred to be the Chief Clerk (主簿) in the office of the Prince of Xīchāng (西昌侯).
During Hóu Jǐng’s (侯景) rebellion,
Emperor Yuán (元帝) of Liáng (梁) was the Governor (刺史) of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
and many court officials went to pledge allegiance to him.
Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引) said:
"The princes are fiercely contending, and calamities are just beginning.
Fleeing danger today
is not the time to choose a lord.
Our family has served as administrators of Shǐxīng (始興) Commandery for two generations,
and our benevolent legacy remains among the people.
It is simply right for me to go south to preserve our family's heritage."
Thereupon, he, along with his younger brother Xiāo Tóng (蕭彤) and over a hundred relatives, fled to Lǐngbiǎo (嶺表).
At that time, Ōuyáng Wèi (歐陽頠) of Shǐxīng (始興) was the Governor (刺史) of Héngzhōu (衡州),
and Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引) went to depend on him.
Ōuyáng Wèi (歐陽頠) later transferred to Guǎngzhōu (廣州)
and died of illness.
His son, Ōuyáng Hē (歐陽紇), took command of his troops.
Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引) always suspected Ōuyáng Hē (歐陽紇) of having ulterior motives
and tried to guide him toward rectitude on various occasions,
which gradually led to a cooling of their relationship and courtesy.
When Ōuyáng Hē (歐陽紇) raised an army and rebelled,
the capital's scholars, such as Cén Zhījìng (岑之敬) and Gōngsūn Tǐng (公孫挺), were all terrified.
Only Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引) remained composed
and said to Cén Zhījìng (岑之敬) and the others:
"Guǎn Yǒu'ān (管幼安) and Yuán Yàoyīng (袁曜卿) merely sat peacefully.
A gentleman rectifies himself to illuminate the Way
and straightens himself to practice righteousness.
What, then, is there to worry or fear?"
When Zhāng Zhāodá (章昭達) pacified Pānyú (番禺),
Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引) finally returned north.
Gāozōng (高宗) summoned Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引) and asked about affairs in Lǐngbiǎo (嶺表).
Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引) fully recounted the details from beginning to end,
and the Emperor was very pleased.
On that very day, he appointed him Ministry Secretary (金部侍郎).
Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引) was skilled in clerical script,
which was highly valued at the time.
Gāozōng (高宗) once reviewed a memorial
and pointed to Xiāo Yǐn's (蕭引) signature, saying:
"The brushstrokes of this character are graceful and flowing,
like a bird about to take flight."
Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引) bowed and replied:
"This is merely Your Majesty lending it wings."
The Emperor then said to Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引):
"Whenever I am angry,
seeing you always calms my mind.
Why is that?"
Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引) replied:
"This is simply Your Majesty not carrying over your anger;
what has this servant to do with such grace?"
In the seventh year of Tàijiàn (太建),
he was given the additional title of General of Illustrious Might (戎昭將軍).
In the ninth year,
he was appointed Advisor (諮議參軍) to the Prince of Shǐxīng (始興王), then Grand Marshal (中衛),
and concurrently Ministry Secretary (金部侍郎).
Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引) was by nature unyielding and straightforward,
and did not curry favor with the powerful.
He never sought favors from the Emperor's close attendants
or powerful ministers.
Although Gāozōng (高宗) often wished to promote him,
he was always blocked by those in power.
When the army was defeated at Lǚliáng (呂梁),
and military supplies became scarce,
Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引) was transferred to be Ministry Secretary (庫部侍郎),
in charge of manufacturing bows, crossbows, spears, and arrows.
Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引) served for one year,
and the weaponry was fully replenished.
He was frequently given additional titles as Palace Secretary (中書侍郎), General of Steadfast Awe (貞威將軍), and Palace Assistant Secretary (黃門郎).
In the twelfth year,
the position of Bureau Secretary (吏部侍郎) was vacant.
The department repeatedly recommended Wáng Kuān (王寬), Xiè Xiè (謝燮), and others,
but the Emperor did not use them.
Instead, he issued an imperial decree to appoint Xiāo Yǐn (蕭引).
At that time, the Prefect of Guǎngzhōu (廣州 Cìshǐ), Mǎ Jìng (馬靖), was very popular with the people of Língbiǎo (嶺表),
and his troops and armor were well-trained and refined.
Each year, he penetrated deep into the Lí Dòng (俚洞),
and had several military successes,
which caused considerable debate in the court and among the populace.
Gāozōng (高宗), knowing that Yǐn (引) was familiar with the conditions beyond the Líng (嶺),
sent Yǐn (引) to observe Jìng (靖),
to assess his actions,
and to subtly suggest he send hostages.
Yǐn (引) accepted the secret imperial order and traveled south,
ostensibly to collect and supervise tributary goods.
When he arrived in Pānyú (番禺),
Jìng (靖) immediately understood the intent
and sent all his sons and younger brothers to the capital as hostages.
On his return journey, when he reached Gànshuǐ (灨水),
Gāozōng (高宗) died.
The Later Emperor (Hòuzhǔ, 後主) ascended the throne,
and promoted Yǐn (引) to Zhōngshùzǐ (中庶子).
He left office due to illness.
The following year,
the capital was plagued by many bandits,
so he was recalled to serve as Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn (貞威將軍) and Jiànkāng Lìng (建康令).
At that time, Wú Jìn (吳璡), the Diànnèi Duìzhǔ (殿內隊主),
〔一四〕 along with the eunuchs Lǐ Shàndù (李善度) and Cài Tuō’ér (蔡脫兒), made many requests for favors.
Yǐn (引) refused them all.
Yǐn's (引) nephew, Mì (密), who was then Huángmén Láng (黃門郎),
admonished Yǐn (引), saying:
“Lǐ (李) and Cài’s (蔡) influence
is such that all officials fear and dread them;
you should also make some small plans for your own sake.”
Yǐn (引) replied:
“My conduct
has its own principles from beginning to end,
how can I change my behavior for Lǐ (李) and Cài (蔡)?
Even if things go badly,
it will be nothing more than being dismissed from office.”
Wú Jìn (吳璡) eventually wrote an anonymous defamatory letter,
and Lǐ (李) and Cài (蔡) confirmed it.
Yǐn (引) was dismissed from office
and died at home,
at the age of fifty-eight.
His son, Déyán (德言),
was the most famous.
Many of Yǐn’s (引) clan members and younger relatives
were renowned for their conduct and righteousness.
His younger brother, Tóng (彤),
was known for his tranquility and love of learning,
and rose to the positions of Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子) and Nánkāngwáng Zhǎngshǐ (南康王長史).
Mì (密), courtesy name Shìjī (士機),
was intelligent and astute in his youth,
with extensive learning and literary talent.
His grandfather, Chēn (琛),
was a Liáng Tèjìn (梁特進).
His father, Yóu (遊),
was Shǎofǔ Qīng (少府卿).
In the eighth year of Tàijiàn (太建), Mì (密)
concurrently held the position of Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍)
and was sent as an envoy to Qí (齊).
He successively served as Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎), Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子), and Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
The court historian (Shǐchén, 史臣) commented: Xiè (謝), Wáng (王), Zhāng (張), Xiāo (蕭),
all adopted purity and tranquility as their demeanor,
and their elegance spread their fame.
Although they encountered many difficulties,
they ultimately achieved renown.
Huàn (奐) was outspoken in public office,
and his heroic spirit shook up the customs.
Upon examining his actions,
he was indeed an enduring beloved figure from antiquity.
〔一五〕Gù (固) lived on simple vegetables and fruits, embracing Zen meditation,
〔一六〕 and thus was one who transcended worldly affairs.
Yet, he still encountered entanglements leading to demotion and dismissal,
and feared ruin.
From this, one knows that the power and influence of Shàngguān (上官) and Bólù (博陸),
and the tremors caused by Yán (閻), Dèng (鄧), Liáng (梁), Dòu (竇),
are truly formidable!
COLLATIONS
BIOGRAPHIES CHAPTER SIXTEEN Lù Zǐlóng (陸子隆) Qián Dàojí (錢道戢) Luò Yá (駱牙)
Lù Zǐlóng (陸子隆), courtesy name Xīngshì (興世),
was a native of Wú (吳) in Wújùn (吳郡).
His grandfather, Chǎngzhī (敞之), was the Liáng Jiāxīng Lìng (梁嘉興令).
His father, Qūn (悛),
was the Fēngshì Lìng (封氏令).
Zǐlóng (子隆) was high-spirited in his youth,
and ambitious for fame and achievement.
He began his career as Dōnggōng Zhíhòu (東宮直後).
During Hóu Jǐng’s (侯景) rebellion,
he gathered followers in his hometown.
At that time, Zhāng Biāo (張彪) was Wújùn Tàishǒu (吳郡太守),
and appointed Zǐlóng (子隆) as a general.
When Biāo (彪) moved his command to Kuàijī (會稽),
Zǐlóng (子隆) followed him.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) attacked Biāo (彪),
Biāo’s (彪) generals Shěn Tài (沈泰), Wú Bǎozhēn (吳寶真), Shēn Jìn (申縉), and others all surrendered,
but Zǐlóng (子隆) fought vigorously, suffering a defeat.
Shìzǔ (世祖) respected him
and reinstated him to command his troops,
appointing him Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (中兵參軍).
He successively served as the magistrate of Shǐfēng (始豐) and Yǒngxīng (永興) counties.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) succeeded to the throne,
Zǐlóng (子隆) led the armed guards.
Soon after, he followed Hóu Āndū (侯安都) to resist Wáng Lín (王琳) at Zhálkǒu (柵口).
After Wáng Lín (王琳) was pacified,
he was granted the title Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng (左中郎將).
In the first year of Tiānjiā (天嘉),
he was enfeoffed as the Earl (zǐ, 子) of Yìyáng Xiàn (益陽縣),
with an estate of three hundred households.
He was sent out to serve as Gāotángjùn Tàishǒu (高唐郡太守).
In the second year,
he was appointed Míngwēi Jiāngjūn (明威將軍) and Lúlíng Tàishǒu (廬陵太守).
At that time, Zhōu Dí (周迪) rebelled, occupying Línchuān (臨川),
and Xiū Xíngshī (脩行師), a man from Dōngchāng Xiàn (東昌縣), responded to him,
leading troops to attack Zǐlóng (子隆),
with great momentum.
Zǐlóng (子隆) set an ambush outside,
then closed the gates and concealed his weapons,
showing weakness.
When Xíngshī (行師) arrived,
Zǐlóng (子隆) attacked him from front and rear,
Xíngshī (行師) was utterly defeated
and then begged for surrender.
Zǐlóng (子隆) granted it
and sent him to the capital.
In the fourth year,
Zhōu Dí (周迪) with Chén Bǎo’yìng (陳寶應) again emerged from Línchuān (臨川).
Zǐlóng (子隆) followed Dūdū (都督) Zhāng Zhāodá (章昭達) to suppress Dí (迪).
Dí (迪) retreated,
and Zǐlóng (子隆) consequently followed Zhāodá (昭達) to cross the Dōngxīng Lǐng (東興嶺)
to attack Chén Bǎo’yìng (陳寶應).
When the army reached Jiàn’ān (建安),
Zǐlóng (子隆) was appointed supervisor of the commandery.
Bǎo’yìng (寶應) occupied the lakeside area of Jiàn’ān (建安) to resist the government forces.
Zǐlóng (子隆) and Zhāodá (昭達) each held a camp.
Zhāodá (昭達) first engaged the bandits
and was unsuccessful,
losing his drums and horns.
Zǐlóng (子隆) heard of this
and led his troops to the rescue,
greatly defeating the bandits
and recovering all the flags, insignias, armor, and weapons that Zhāodá (昭達) had lost.
After Jìn’ān (晉安) was pacified,
Zǐlóng’s (子隆) achievements were the greatest.
He was promoted to Jiǎjié (假節) and Dūdū Wǔzhōu Zhūjūnshì (都督武州諸軍事),
with his general title remaining as before.
Soon after, he was re-enfeoffed as the Earl (bó, 伯) of Cháoyáng Xiàn (朝陽縣),
with an estate of five hundred households.
When the deposed emperor (Fèidì, 廢帝) ascended the throne,
he was advanced to the title Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn (智武將軍),
and given the additional post of Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍),
the rest remaining as before.
When Huá Jiǎo (華皎) rebelled, occupying Xiāngzhōu (湘州),
he considered Zǐlóng (子隆) to be a vital impediment.
Jiǎo (皎) was deeply troubled by this,
and repeatedly sent envoys to entice him,
but Zǐlóng (子隆) did not comply.
Jiǎo (皎) then sent troops to attack him,
but again failed to overcome him.
When Jiǎo (皎) was defeated at Yǐngzhōu (郢州),
Zǐlóng (子隆) led his troops to attack his rear,
and then met up with the imperial army.
He was granted Chíjí (持節), Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍), and Dūdū Wǔzhōu Zhūjūnshì (都督武州諸軍事),
advanced in peerage to Marquis (hóu, 侯),
and his estate was increased to a total of seven hundred households, including the previous ones.
Soon after, he was transferred to Dūdū Jīngxìnyòu Sānzhōu Zhūjūnshì (都督荊信祐三州諸軍事), Xuānyì Jiāngjūn (宣毅將軍), and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史),
with the Chíjí (持節) and Chángshì (常侍) titles remaining as before.
At this time, Jīngzhōu (荊州) had been newly established,
governed from Gōng’ān (公安).
The city walls were not yet fortified.
Zǐlóng (子隆) rebuilt the city walls
and pacified and gathered both the indigenous and Huá (華) people,
earning great harmony among the populace.
He was considered competent at the time.
In the third year,
officials and commoners went to the capital to submit a memorial,
requesting to erect a monument to praise his achievements.
An imperial edict approved it.
In the first year of Tàijiàn (太建),
he was advanced to the title Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn (雲麾將軍).
He died in the second year,
at the age of forty-seven.
He was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
and given the posthumous name Wēi (威).
His son, Zhīwǔ (之武), succeeded him.
Zhīwǔ (之武), at sixteen years old,
commanded his father’s former troops,
and had achievements following Wú Míngchè (吳明徹) in the northern expedition.
He rose to the positions of Wángfǔ Zhǔbù (王府主簿) and Hóngnóng Tàishǒu (弘農太守),
still subordinate to Míngchè (明徹).
When Míngchè (明徹) was defeated at Lǚliáng (呂梁),
Zhīwǔ (之武) fled back
and was killed by someone,
at the age of twenty-two.
Lù Zǐlóng’s disciple, Cái,
also possessed talent and strategy.
He achieved merits by following Zǐlóng on campaigns,
was appointed Administrator of Nánpíng,
and enfeoffed as a Viscount of Shǐxīng County,
with an estate of three hundred households.
He followed Wú Míngchè on the Northern Expedition,
supervised Ānzhōu,
and was garrisoned at Sùyù.
He was appointed Counsellor-in-Attendance to the Prince of Shǐxīng in the Central Guard,
then promoted to Blazing Valor General and Prefect of Xìnzhōu.
He died in the thirteenth year of Tàijiàn
at the age of forty-two.
He was posthumously granted Supernumerary Palace Grandee of Scrutiny.
Qián Dàojí, courtesy name Zǐtāo,
was a native of Chángchéng, Wúxīng.
His father, Jǐngshēn,
was the Magistrate of Hànshòu during the Liáng dynasty.
When Dàojí was young, he was known for his filial conduct.
As he grew older,
he possessed considerable talent and strategy.
When Gāozǔ was still obscure,
he gave his younger paternal cousin to Dàojí in marriage.
He followed Lú Zǐlüè in pacifying Guǎngzhōu
and was appointed Magistrate of Bīnjiāng.
When Gāozǔ assumed regency,
he sent Dàojí to follow Shìzǔ in pacifying Zhāng Biāo in Kuàijī.
For his merits, he was appointed General of the Inner Apartments,
Supernumerary Palace Grandee of Scrutiny, Acting Imbued with Authority, and Prefect of Dōngxúzhōu,
enfeoffed as a Marquis of Yǒng'ān County,
with an estate of five hundred households.
He then led three thousand armored soldiers
and followed Hóu Āndū to garrison and defend Liángshān.
Soon after, he concurrently served as Magistrate of Qiántáng and Yúháng counties.
In the third year of Yǒngdìng,
he followed Shìzǔ to garrison at Nánwǎnkǒu.
In the first year of Tiānjiā,
he again served as Magistrate of Shàn,
garrisoned at Nányán of that county.
Soon after, he became Administrator of Línghǎi,
still garrisoned at Yán as before.
When Hóu Āndū attacked Liú Yì,
Dàojí led an army out of Sōngyáng to cut off his rear.
After Yì was pacified,

for his merits, he was appointed Imbued with Authority, Palace Grandee of Scrutiny with Straightforward Counsel, Light Chariot General, Area Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of the Two Héngzhōu provinces (East and West), and Prefect of Héngzhōu,
concurrently holding the post of Grand Administrator of Shǐxīng.
In the first year of Guāngdà,
his estate was increased to a total of seven hundred households.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
he summoned Ōuyáng Hè to court.
Hè, feeling suspicious and fearful,
raised an army and attacked Héngzhōu.
Dàojí fought with him
and repelled him.
When Area Commander-in-Chief Zhāng Zhāodá led troops to attack Hè,
Dàojí was made Commander of the Infantry
and cut off Hè’s rear by a secret path.
After Hè was pacified,
he was appointed General of the Left Guard.
In the second year of Tàijiàn,
he again followed Zhāodá to campaign against Xiāo Kuí in Jiānglíng.
Dàojí separately commanded the various armies with Lù Zǐlóng to burn the ships and boats at Qīngní,
then served as Zhāodá’s vanguard,
attacking Ānshǔ City
and capturing it.
For his merits, he was awarded Palace Grandee of Scrutiny and Benevolent Martial General,
and his estate was increased to a total of nine hundred households.
That same year,
he was promoted to Benevolent Authority General and Administrator of Wúxīng.
Before he could take up the post,
he was reassigned as Imbued with Authority, Area Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of the Three Provinces of Yǐng, Bā, and Wǔ, and Prefect of Yǐngzhōu.
When the imperial army campaigned north,
Dàojí and Grand Inspector Huáng Fǎqú besieged Lìyáng.
After Lìyáng City was pacified,
Dàojí was consequently garrisoned there.
For his merits, he was awarded Cloud-soaring General,
and his estate was increased to a total of one thousand five hundred households.
In the eleventh month of that year, he fell ill and died
at the age of sixty-three.
He was posthumously granted his original office
and given the posthumous name Sù.
His son, Miǎo, inherited his title.
Luò Yá, courtesy name Qímén,
was a native of Lín'ān, Wúxīng.
His grandfather, Mìdào,
was a Táncáo Staff Officer to the Prince of Ānchéng during the Liáng dynasty.
His father, Yù, was a Zhōngbīng Staff Officer to the Hereditary Prince of Póyáng.
When Yá was twelve,
a relative, who was skilled in physiognomy,
said,
“This young gentleman has an extraordinary appearance;
he will surely achieve greatness in the future.”
Towards the end of Tàiqīng of Liáng,
Shìzǔ once sought refuge in Lín'ān.
Yá's mother, Líng,
seeing Shìzǔ's dignified appearance,
knew he was no ordinary man,
and treated him very generously as a guest.
When Shìzǔ became Administrator of Wúxīng,
he appointed Yá as a military commander.
Consequently, Yá followed him in pacifying Dù Kān, Zhāng Biāo, and others.
In every battle, he would be the first to charge and break the enemy lines,
displaying courage that surpassed all other generals.
For his merits, he was appointed General of the Inner Apartments.
In the second year of Tàipíng,
he resigned his post due to mourning for his mother.
When Shìzǔ was garrisoned at Kuàijī,
he was reinstated as Magistrate of Shānyīn.
In the third year of Yǒngdìng,
he was appointed Zhōngbīng Staff Officer of the Āndōng Commandery,
and went out to garrison Yěchéng.
Soon after, he followed Shìzǔ in resisting Wáng Lín at Nánwǎn.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Acting Imbued with Authority, Terror-Subduing General, and Supernumerary Palace Grandee of Scrutiny,
enfeoffed as a Marquis of Cháng'ān County,
with an estate of five hundred households.
Soon after, he became Magistrate of Lín'ān,
then promoted to Prefect of Yuèzhōu,
with all other positions remaining as before.
Originally,
when Yá’s mother died,
it was a time of famine and war.
Only now was she finally buried.
An imperial edict posthumously granted Yá's mother the title of Grand Lady of Cháng'ān State,
with the posthumous name Gōng.
Yá was promoted to Chaste Authority General and Grand Administrator of Jìnlíng.
Three years later,
for his merits in pacifying Zhōu Dí,
he was promoted to Champion General and Grand Administrator of Línchuān.
In the third year of Tàijiàn,
he was appointed Pacifying Remote General and Grand Administrator of Héngyáng.
Before he could take up the post,
he was transferred to become Administrator of Guìyáng.
In the eighth year,
he returned to court
and was promoted to Palace Grandee of Scrutiny,
entering the palace to serve in the imperial secretariats.
In the tenth year,
he was appointed Prefect of Fēngzhōu,
with all other positions remaining as before.
He died in the second year of Zhìdé
at the age of fifty-seven.
He was posthumously granted Pacifying Remote General and Prefect of Guǎngzhōu.
His son, Yì, inherited his title.
The imperial historian says: Lù Zǐlóng and Qián Dàojí,
one joined with his whole family,
the other established meritorious deeds as an old retainer.
They possessed talent for command
and fulfilled the trust placed in them for military affairs.
As for their appointments to defend the provinces,
their achievements were all outstanding.
Excellent indeed!
Luò Yá recognized the true potential and served faithfully,
knowing Shìzǔ's heaven-granted virtue.
Was he not second only to Zhāng Liáng?
Yá's mother, with her profound and keen foresight,
matched the propriety of Bógǔ.
Can it be that a gentleman's discerning judgment is indeed far-reaching?
It is precisely in this!
