Biographies, Volume 17
Shěn Jūnlǐ, Wáng Yáng, Lù Shàn
Shěn Jūnlǐ, courtesy name Zhònglún,
was a native of Wúxīng.
His grandfather, Sēngcè,
was the Left Minister of the Ministry of Revenue during the Liáng dynasty.
His father, Xún,
was always on good terms with Gāozǔ.
During the Tàiqīng era of Liáng, he served as Administrator of Dōngyáng.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Emperor Yuán summoned him to be Minister of the Privy Treasury.
When Jīngzhōu fell,
Xiāo Chá appointed him Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple Seals.
Jūnlǐ had a beautiful demeanor,
was widely read in classics and history,
and possessed discernment.
He began his career as a Judicial Staff Officer to the Prince of Xiāngdōng.
When Gāozǔ was garrisoned at Nánxúzhōu,
Xún sent Jūnlǐ from Dōngyáng to pay his respects to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ appreciated his talent,
arranged for him to marry Princess Cháng of Kuàijī,
and appointed him Western Registrar of the Commandery.
He was gradually promoted to Central Guard, Aide-de-camp to the Prince of Yùzhāng,
and soon after was awarded Bright Authority General,
concurrently serving as Attendant Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel.
He was promoted to Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
and supervised Wújùn.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law,
and enfeoffed as a Marquis of Yǒng'ān Pavilion.
He went out to serve as Administrator of Wújùn.
At that time, military affairs were not yet settled,
and the common people were in distress.
Military and state expenditures
all relied on the eastern region.
Jūnlǐ recruited soldiers,
repaired weapons and equipment.
The people were pleased and attached to him,
and he was highly praised for his talent in administration.
When Shìzǔ succeeded to the throne,
Zhēng was appointed Shìzhōng.
He was promoted to Shǒu Zuǒmín Shàngshū.
Before he could assume the post,
he was appointed Míngwēi Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn.
In Tiānjiā third year (562),
he was again appointed Zuǒmín Shàngshū,
and concurrently Líng Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
Soon after, he was changed to Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the fourth year (563),
when Hóu Āndū was transferred to Zhènjiāng Jiāngzhōu,
he was made Jiān Nánxúzhōu with his original office.
In the sixth year (565),
he was dispatched as Rénwēi Jiāngjūn and Dōngyáng Tàishǒu.
In Tiānkāng first year (566),
he resigned due to a parent's mourning.
Jūnlǐ then requested to go to Jīngzhōu to escort the coffin back.
The court deliberated that as he was a high-ranking minister in office,
it would be difficult to allow him to leave the border.
So, his elder brother Jūnyán was sent instead.
When he returned,
and before the burial,
an imperial edict posthumously granted Xún the titles of Shìzhōng and Língjūn Jiāngjūn,
with the posthumous name Jìngzǐ.
That year, Jūnlǐ was recalled to office as Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
He was again recalled as Chíjíe, Dūdū Dōnghéng Héng Èrzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Rénwēi Jiāngjūn, and Dōnghéngzhōu Cìshǐ,
concurrently Líng Shǐxīng Nèishǐ.
He was again recalled as Míngwēi Jiāngjūn and Zhōngshū Lìng.
He was compelled to end mourning three times in total,
but he did not accept any of the appointments.
In Tàijiàn first year (569),
after the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
and acted as the head of the Eastern Palace affairs.
He was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū.
In the second year (570),
Gāozōng made Jūnlǐ's daughter the Empress Dowager Tàizǐfēi,
and bestowed upon him the title Wàngcài Xiànhóu,
with an estate of five hundred households.
In the fourth year (572),
he was granted the additional title of Shìzhōng.
In the fifth year (573),
he was promoted to Shàngshū Yòupúshè,
concurrently Líng Lìbù,
and Shìzhōng as before.
That year, he fell ill.
The Emperor personally visited him.
He passed away in the ninth month,
at the age of forty-nine.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him Shìzhōng and Tàizǐ Shàofù.
All necessities for the funeral
were to be provided from public funds.
He was again posthumously granted Yìzuǒ Jiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
with Shìzhōng as before.
His posthumous name was Zhēnxìan.
Jūnlǐ's son, Zūnjiǎn, had died young,
so his younger brother Jūngāo's son Zūnlǐ was made his heir.
Jūnlǐ's fifth uncle, Mài,
was also upright and capable.
He served Liáng as Shàngshū Jīnbù Láng.
During Yǒngdìng (557-559),
he was successively promoted to Zhōngshū Shìláng.
During Tiānjiā (560-566),
he successively held the posts of Tàipú and Tíngwèi.
He was dispatched as Zhèndōng Shǐxīngwáng Chángshǐ and Kuàijī Jùnjìng,
and acted as Dōngyángzhōu Shì.
In Guāngdà first year (567),
he was appointed Shàngshū Lìbù Láng.
In Tàijiàn first year (569),
he was promoted to Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
and attended the Eastern Palace.
He died in the second year (570),
at the age of fifty-two.
He was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì.
Jūnlǐ's sixth younger brother, Jūngāo,
courtesy name Jìgāo,
was famous in his youth,
had an upright and straightforward character,
and was capable in administration.
As a maternal relative of the imperial family,
he quickly attained high and prominent positions,
serving successively as Tàizǐ Shèrén, Xǐmǎ, Zhōngshèrén, Gāozōng Sīkōng Fǔ Cóngshì Zhōngláng, and Tíngwèi Qīng.
In Tàijiàn first year (569),
the eastern region suffered a great flood,
and the common people were starving and impoverished.
So, Jūngāo was appointed Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn and Wú Lìng.
Soon after, he was appointed Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ, Shàngshū Lìbù Láng, and Wèiwèi Qīng.
He was dispatched as Xuānyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Píngnán Chángshāwáng Chángshǐ, Nánhǎi Tàishǒu,
and acted as Guǎngzhōu Shì.
As his daughter was to become a royal consort,
he firmly declined the appointment and did not go.
He was reinstated as Wèiwèi Qīng.
In the eighth year (576),
an imperial edict appointed him Chíjíe, Dūdū Guǎng Děng Shíbāzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng, and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In Língnán, the Lǐ and Láopèi tribes were fighting each other.
Jūngāo was originally a civil official
without military capabilities.
He used sincerity to pacify and govern them,
and greatly achieved harmony among the people.
In the tenth year (578),
he died in office,
at the age of forty-seven.
He was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì,
with the posthumous name Qízǐ.
Wáng Yáng, courtesy name Zǐyú,
was the twelfth son of Sīkōng Chōng.
He was calm and composed, with a dignified demeanor.
He possessed a beautiful presence and graceful deportment.
His movements were refined and reserved.
During Liáng Dàtóng (535-546),
he began his career as Mìshū Láng,
and was promoted to Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ.
When Yuándì assumed imperial authority,
he was summoned as Zhōngshū Shìláng,
served directly in the palace,
and also managed the records of the Prime Minister's office.
He was dispatched as Dōnggōng Nèishǐ,
and promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
When he fell into mourning for his birth mother,
he returned to Dānyáng.
When Jiānglíng fell,
Liáng Jìngdì assumed imperial authority
and appointed him Rénwēi Jiāngjūn and Shàngshū Lìbù Lángzhōng.
When Zhēnyánghóu usurped the throne,
he made Jìngdì the crown prince,
and appointed Yáng Sànqí Chángshì,
to attend the Eastern Palace.
Soon after, he was promoted to Chángshǐ (兼侍中) and concurrent Shìzhōng.
When Gāozǔ entered to assist,
he was made Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ.
In Yǒngdìng first year (557),
he was promoted to Shǒu Wǔbīng Shàngshū.
When Shìzǔ succeeded to the throne,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
concurrently Líng Tàizǐ Shùzǐ,
and attended the Eastern Palace.
He was promoted to Líng Zuǒxiāoqí Jiāngjūn and Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
with Chángshì and Shìzhōng as before.
Yáng served as Shìzhōng for six years.
His father Chōng once asked Shìzǔ to relieve Yáng of the concurrent duty of Zhōngshùzǐ.
Shìzǔ looked at Chōng and said:
"The reason I have kept Yáng in Chénghuá for so long
is precisely because I want the Crown Prince to subtly adopt Yáng's demeanor and conduct."
When Fèidì succeeded to the throne,
Yáng was appointed Shìzhōng, concurrently Líng Zuǒxiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
In Guāngdà first year (567),
he resigned due to a parent's mourning.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
in Tàijiàn first year (569),
he was again appointed Shìzhōng,
concurrently Líng Zuǒxiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
He was promoted to Dùzhī Shàngshū,
concurrently Líng Yǔlín Jiān.
He was dispatched as Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn, Yúnhuī Shǐxīngwáng Chángshǐ,
and acted as the head of the provincial administration.
Before he could depart,
he was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng,
and soon after granted the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
He was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū,
with Chángshì as before.
Yáng was of a lenient and gentle nature.
When he held the selection office,
he strived for purity and tranquility,
meticulously adhered to documents and records,
and did not engage in favoritism or suppression.
Soon after, he was appointed Shàngshū Yòupúshè.
Before he could assume the post,
he was granted the additional title of Shìzhōng,
and promoted to Zuǒpúshè,
participating in the management of selection affairs,
with Shìzhōng as before.
Yáng had over thirty siblings.
At home, they were deeply harmonious.
Whenever there were seasonal gifts,
they were distributed to all close relatives.
He earnestly guided his younger brothers,
and they all abided by his rules and teachings.
He died in Tàijiàn eighth year (576),
at the age of fifty-four.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng, Tèjìn, and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
All necessities for the funeral were provided as needed.
His posthumous name was Guāngzǐ.
Yáng's thirteenth younger brother, Yú 瑜,
courtesy name Zǐguī 子珪,
was also well-known.
He had a beautiful appearance and bearing,
and early on experienced high and prominent positions.
At the age of thirty (corrected from "十" to "三"),
he reached the office of Shìzhōng 侍中.
In the first year of Yǒngdìng 永定 (557 CE),
he was sent as an envoy to Qí 齊.
He took Yuán Xiàn 袁憲 of Chénjùn 陳郡 as his deputy.
Because of Wáng Lín 王琳, Qí 齊
seized and imprisoned them.
When Emperor Wénxuān 文宣 of Qí 齊 went on an outing,
he would carry condemned prisoners with him.
The people of Qí 齊 called them
"gòngyù qiú" 供御囚 (imperial prisoners for disposal).
Whenever he had other anger,
he would summon and kill them
to satisfy his desires.
Yú 瑜 and Xiàn 憲 were both in mortal danger many times.
The Púshè 僕射 of Qí 齊, Yáng Zūnyàn 楊遵彥, pitied their innocence
and repeatedly protected them.
In the second year of Tiānjīa 天嘉 (561 CE), they returned to court.
An imperial edict reinstated Yú 瑜 as Shìzhōng 侍中.
Soon after, he died,
at the age of forty.
He was posthumously granted his original office
and given the posthumous title Zhēnzǐ 貞子.
Lù Shàn 陸繕, courtesy name Shìrú 士繻,
was a native of Wújùn 吳郡.
His grandfather, Huìxiǎo 惠曉,
was the Tàicháng Qīng 太常卿 of Qí 齊.
His father, Rèn 任 (corrected from "倕"),
was the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞 of Liáng 梁.
Shàn 繕 had aspirations and high moral standards from a young age,
and was known for his elegant correctness.
He began his career in Liáng 梁 as the Fǎcáo Cānjūn 法曹參軍 to the King of Xuānhuì Wǔlíng 宣惠武陵.
During the Chéngshèng 承聖 reign,
he was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng 中書侍郎
and managed the records of the Eastern Palace.
When Jiānglíng 江陵 fell,
Shàn 繕 escaped in civilian clothes and returned to the capital.
In the first year of Shàotài 紹泰 (555 CE),
he was appointed Sītú Yòu Zhǎngshǐ 司徒右長史
and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞.
However, because his father had held the latter office as his final position,
he firmly declined the appointment.
Gāozǔ 高祖 appointed Shàn 繕 as Sītú Sīmǎ 司徒司馬,
then promoted him to Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng 給事黃門侍郎, concurrently leading the Bùbīng Xiàowèi 步兵校尉 and Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì 通直散騎常侍,
and concurrently Shìzhōng 侍中.
In the first year of Yǒngdìng 永定 (557 CE),
he was promoted to Shìzhōng 侍中.
At that time, Liú Yì 留異 had taken control of Dōngyáng 東陽.
Xiàng Wénzhèng 向文政 of Xīn'ān 新安 allied with Yì 異
and consequently occupied his home commandery.
The imperial court appointed Shàn 繕 as Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn 貞威將軍 and Xīn'ān Tàishǒu 新安太守.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 succeeded to the throne,
he was summoned to be Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子,
leading the Bùbīng Xiàowèi 步兵校尉,
and managing the records of the Eastern Palace.
Shàn 繕 had an elegant and dignified appearance,
and his movements were refined and graceful.
Shìzǔ 世祖 made the Crown Prince and all the princes take him as a model.
Their walking and stepping
were all made to imitate Shàn's 繕 rules.
He was appointed Shàngshū Lìbù Lángzhōng 尚書吏部郎中,
with his position as Bùbīng 步兵 remaining as before,
and continued to serve in the Eastern Palace.
After Chén Bǎo Yìng 陳寶應 was pacified,
he was sent out as Zhēnyì Jiāngjūn 貞毅將軍 and Jiàn'ān Tàishǒu 建安太守.
After his term expired,
he became Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍 and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞.
Still, because this was his father's final office,
he firmly declined.
His request was not granted,
so he temporarily exchanged his official residence and moved.
In the early years of Tàijiàn 太建 (569 CE),
he was promoted to Dùzhī Shàngshū 度支尚書, Shìzhōng 侍中, Tàizǐ Zhànshì 太子詹事,
acting in charge of Eastern Palace affairs,
and concurrently leading Yángzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng 揚州大中正.
When the Crown Prince personally handled government affairs,
he was relieved of his acting duties,
given the additional title Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍,
and then again given the additional title Shìzhōng 侍中.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Yòu Púshè 尚書右僕射,
and soon after to Zuǒ Púshè 左僕射,
participating in the management of personnel selection,
with his Shìzhōng 侍中 position remaining as before.
He was again appointed Shàngshū Púshè 尚書僕射,
leading the Qián Jiāngjūn 前將軍.
He was again appointed Zuǒ Púshè 左僕射,
leading Yángzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng 揚州大中正,
and was separately commanded to participate in deliberating government affairs with Xú Líng 徐陵 and seven others.
He died in the twelfth year (580 CE),
at the age of sixty-three.
He was posthumously granted the titles Shìzhōng 侍中, Tèjìn 特進, and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū 金紫光祿大夫,
and given the posthumous title Ānzǐ 安子.
The Crown Prince, regarding Shàn 繕 as an old minister of the Eastern Palace,
specially bestowed a memorial offering.
Shàn's 繕 son, Biànhuì 辯惠,
was several years old.
An edict summoned him into the palace hall.
Biànhuì's 辯惠 responses and deportment showed his father's style.
Gāozōng 高宗 therefore bestowed upon him the name Biànhuì 辯惠,
and courtesy name Jìngrén 敬仁.
Shàn's 繕 elder brother's son, Jiànxián 見賢,
was also dignified and refined.
When Gāozōng 高宗 was Yángzhōu Mù 揚州牧,
he appointed Jiànxián 見賢 as Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ 治中從事史,
and he was deeply appreciated and trusted.
He successively held the positions of Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng 給事黃門侍郎,
Zhǎngshǐ 長史 for the two kings of Chángshā 長沙 and Póyáng 鄱陽,
concurrently Súnyáng Tàishǒu 尋陽太守,
and Shàofù Qīng 少府卿.
He died in the tenth year of Tàijiàn 太建 (578 CE),
at the age of fifty.
He was posthumously granted the title Tíngwèi Qīng 廷尉卿,
and given the posthumous title Píngzǐ 平子.
The court historian remarks: The elegant ways of the gentry
and the excellent counsels within the government
are truly based on sincere cultivation of conduct
and thorough rectitude of disposition.
The Classic says,
"Their demeanor can be observed,"
and the Odes say,
"Their deportment is without fault."
Those three individuals
indeed possessed this style.

Biographies, Volume 18: Zhōu Hóngzhèng 周弘正 (younger brother Hóngzhí 弘直, Hóngzhí's 弘直 son Què 確), Yuán Xiàn 袁憲
Zhōu Hóngzhèng 周弘正, courtesy name Sīxíng 思行,
was a native of Ānchéng 安城, Rǔnán 汝南.
He was the ninth-generation descendant of Yǐ 顗, the Guānglù Dàfū 光祿大夫 of Jìn 晉.
His grandfather, Yǒng 顒,
was the Zhōngshū Shìláng 中書侍郎 of Qí 齊,
and led the bureau of literary works.
His father, Bǎoshǐ 寶始,
was the Sītú Jìjiǔ 司徒祭酒 of Liáng 梁.
Hóngzhèng 弘正 was orphaned young.
He and his younger brothers Hóngràng 弘讓 and Hóngzhí 弘直
were all raised by their paternal uncle (corrected from "叔" to "伯"), Shìzhōng Hùjūn Shě 侍中護軍捨.
At the age of ten,
he was proficient in the Lǎozi 老子 and Zhōuyì 周易.
Shě 捨 often discussed these with him
and was always impressed by him,
saying:
"I observe your spirit and intelligence are keen and bright,
your thinking clear and incisive.
In later generations, your fame
will surely surpass mine."
Péi Zǐyě 裴子野 of Hédōng 河東 deeply admired and accepted him,
asking to give his daughter to him in marriage.
At fifteen,
he was summoned to be appointed a Guózǐshēng 國子生 (student of the Imperial College).
He then lectured on the Zhōuyì 周易 at the Guóxué 國學 (Imperial Academy),
and the students circulated and studied his interpretations.
He entered the academy in the last month of spring
and was due for examination in the first month of winter.
The academy officials, considering his short time there,
did not permit it.
The Bóshì 博士 Dào Qià 到洽 argued:
"Zhōu Láng 周郎 is not yet twenty,
yet he already lectures on a classic himself.
Although he is called a student,
he is truly worthy of being a teacher and model,
and does not need to be tested."
He began his career as Bóshì 博士 of Tàixué 太學 of Liáng 梁.
When the King of Jìn'ān 晉安 was Dānyáng Yǐn 丹陽尹,
he appointed Hóngzhèng 弘正 as his Zhǔbù 主簿.
He was sent out as Yè Lìng 鄴令,
but left office due to mourning for his mother.
After the mourning period,
he successively served as Qǔ'é 曲阿 and Ānjí Ānjí Lìng 令.
During the Pǔtōng 普通 reign,
the office of Sīwényì Láng 司文義郎 was first established,
who were on duty in the Shòuguāng Shěng 壽光省.
Hóngzhèng 弘正 was appointed Sīyì Shìláng 司義侍郎.
In the third year of Dàtōng 大通 (corrected from "中大通"),
Prince Zhāomíng 昭明 of Liáng 梁 died.
His heir, the Duke of Huáróng 華容, could not be established.
Therefore, the King of Jìn'ān 晉安 was made Crown Prince.
Hóngzhèng 弘正 then submitted a memorial, stating: "I have heard that the image of humility
originated from the divination hexagrams of Xī 羲 and Xuān 軒,
and the source of yielding and abdication
arose from the transfers of power by Yáo 堯 and Shùn 舜.
Its origins are ancient
and can be detailed
thus.
Indeed, the imperial court and the Fénshuǐ 汾水 (referring to the hermit Xu巢 and Xu許),
though different paths, lead to the same destination.
Jì 稷, Qì 契, Cháo 巢, and Xǔ 許,
though different names, are united in one principle.

외臣 (wàichén),
莫不內外相資 (mò bù nèiwài xiāngzī),
表𩹉成治 (biǎo lǐ chéng zhì),
斯蓋萬代同規 (sī gài wàndài tóng guī),

寖 (jìn)
以陵夷 (yǐ língyí),
各親其親 (gè qīn qí qīn),
各子其子 (gè zǐ qí zǐ).
乃至七國爭雄 (nǎizhì Qīguó zhēng xióng),
劉項競逐 (Liú-Xiàng jìng zhú),
皇漢扇其俗 (Huáng Hàn shàn qí sú),
有晉揚其波 (yǒu Jìn yáng qí bō),
謙 (qiān)
讓之道廢 (ràng zhī dào fèi),
多歷年所矣 (duō lì nián suǒ yǐ).
夫文質遞變 (fū wénzhì dì biàn),
澆淳相革 (jiāo chún xiāng gé),
還樸反古 (huán pǔ fǎn gǔ),
今也其時 (jīn yě qí shí).
伏惟明大王殿下 (fú wéi míng Dàwáng diànxià),
天挺將聖 (tiān tǐng jiāng shèng),
聰明神武 (cōngmíng shénwǔ),

詔答曰 (zhào dá yuē):
「設卦觀象 (shè guà guān xiàng),

沒 (mò),

梁丘擅琅邪之學 (Liángqiū shàn Lángyé zhī xué),
代郡范生 (Dàijùn Fàn Shēng),
山陽王氏 (Shānyáng Wángshì),
人藏荊山之寶 (rén cáng Jīngshān zhī bǎo),
各盡玄言之趣 (gè jìn xuányán zhī qù),
說或去取 (shuō huò qù qǔ),
意有詳略 (yì yǒu xiánglüè).
近搢紳之學 (jìn jìnshēn zhī xué),
咸有稽疑 (xián yǒu jīyí),
隨答所問 (suí dá suǒ wèn),
已具別解 (yǐ jù biéjiě).
知與張譏等三百一十二人須釋乾坤文言及二繫 (zhī yǔ Zhāng Jī děng sānbǎi yīshí'èr rén xū shì Qiánkūn wényán jí Èrxì),
萬機小暇 (wànjī xiǎo xiá),
Zhōu Hóngzhèng was learned and knowledgeable about celestial phenomena,
and skilled in prognostication.
At the end of Dàtóng,
he once said to his younger brother, Zhōu Hóngràng:
"The state is facing a difficult period;
in a few years, there will be military uprisings.
You and I do not know where we can escape to."
When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng accepted Hóu Jǐng,
Zhōu Hóngzhèng said to Zhōu Hóngràng:
"This is the beginning of the chaos."
When the capital city fell,
Zhōu Hóngzhí was the Interior Prefect of Héngyáng.
Emperor Yuán was in Jiānglíng,
and sent a letter to Zhōu Hóngzhí, saying:
"I have just received news from the capital.
My elder brother, the scholar, is safe.
However, among the gentry of the capital,
there is no one who has not sided with the rebels.
Wáng Kèjǐ has become a retainer,
and Lù Miǎn has been reduced to a common soldier.
Only Zhōu Shēng [Zhōu Hóngzhèng]
is firm and unyielding.
When I speak of the western army,
tears stream down my face.
He constantly thinks of my arrival,
as if longing for a whole year.
That the pine and cypress wither last,
he is the only one."
When Wáng Sēngbiàn was campaigning against Hóu Jǐng,
Zhōu Hóngzhèng and Zhōu Hóngràng extracted themselves and went to meet the army.
Wáng Sēngbiàn was greatly pleased to get them,
and immediately reported to Emperor Yuán that very day.
Emperor Yuán personally wrote to Zhōu Hóngzhèng, saying:
"The Xūn rebels have caused chaos,
and we have been separated by many seasons.
Among those I knew within the seas,
almost all have scattered and perished.
The wisdom of Hán Fēi
did not save him from the Qín prison.
The learning of Liú Xīn
still suffered in the collapse of the New Dynasty.
With no news of you,
I am always anxious.
I often wish to visit east of the mountains to seek Zǐyún,
and ask west of the passes for Bóqǐ.
Now that I have received this letter,
I strongly attach this message to inquire after you.
I await the arrival of your reply,
to comfort my prolonged longing."
Then he sent an envoy to welcome him,
and said to his court officials:
"When the Jìn dynasty pacified Wú,
they were delighted to obtain the two Lùs.
Now that I have defeated the rebels,
I have also obtained the two Zhōus.
Ancient and modern are alike at this moment,
it is truly a comparable event."
When Zhōu Hóngzhèng arrived,
the courtesies shown to him were extremely generous;
no other court official could compare.
He was appointed Huángmén Shìláng,
and served directly in the Shìzhōng Shěng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū,
and then additionally appointed Sànqí Chángshì.
Emperor Yuán once wrote Jīnlóu Zǐ,
saying:
"Among the monks, I highly esteem the Dharma Master Zhāotí Yǎn;
among recluses, I highly esteem Huáyáng Táo Zhēnbái;
and among scholar-officials, I highly esteem Rǔnán Zhōu Hóngzhèng.
Regarding his understanding of principles,
it is clear and inexhaustible.
He is indeed a renowned scholar of his time."
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Wáng Sēngbiàn requested that the imperial archives and books be sent,
and an imperial edict commanded Zhōu Hóngzhèng to collate and edit them.
At that time, the court deliberated moving the capital.
Court officials whose families were in Jīngzhōu
all did not wish to move.
Only Zhōu Hóngzhèng and Púyè Wáng Póu spoke to Emperor Yuán, saying:
"If all scholar-officials above the rank of 'bundle of dried meat' [referring to those who have attained some knowledge] who have even a slight understanding of ancient and modern times,
they know that the capital of emperors has no fixed location,
and there is no room for doubt.
As for the common people,
if they do not see the imperial carriage enter Jiànyè,
they will think you are merely one of the feudal lords,
and not yet call you Son of Heaven.
Now it is appropriate to follow the will of the people
and comply with the hopes of the four seas."
At that time, people from Jīng and Shǎn all said that Wáng and Zhōu were both Easterners,
and their desire to move east was
probably not a good plan.
Zhōu Hóngzhèng directly rebuked them, saying:
"If Easterners urging to move east is considered a bad plan,
then how can your desire as Westerners to stay west
be a good policy?"
Emperor Yuán then laughed heartily
and ultimately did not return the capital.
When Jiānglíng fell,
Zhōu Hóngzhèng escaped the siege
and returned to the capital.
Emperor Jìng appointed him Grand Administrator of Dà Sīmǎ Wáng Sēngbiàn,
and acting governor of Yángzhōu.
In the first year of Tàipíng,
he was appointed Shìzhōng,
and concurrently Jìjiǔ of the Guózǐ.
He was then promoted to Tàicháng Qīng and Dūguān Shàngshū.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Zhànshì.
In the first year of Tiānjiā,
he was promoted to Shìzhōng and Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
and went to Cháng'ān to welcome Gāozōng.
In the third year,
he returned from Zhōu,
and an imperial edict appointed him Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
with the additional honors of a golden seal and purple ribbon,
and concurrently Cíxùn Tàipú.
When the deposed emperor succeeded to the throne,
he concurrently held Dūguān Shàngshū,
and took overall charge of the five rituals.
He was then appointed Tàifù Chángshǐ,
and additionally Mingwēi Jiāngjūn.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Tèjìn,
again concurrently Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
Dàzhōngzhèng of Yùzhōu,
and given a walking stick.
In the fifth year of Tàijiàn,
he was appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púyè,
with his posts as Jìjiǔ and Dàzhōngzhèng remaining as before.
Soon after, he was commanded to attend the Eastern Palace
to lecture on the Lúnyǔ and Xiàojīng.
The Crown Prince, considering Zhōu Hóngzhèng an old minister of the court
with long-standing and heavy prestige,
humbled himself and lowered his status,
asking for more instruction with a book across his lap,
showing him the respect due to a teacher.
Zhōu Hóngzhèng was particularly skilled in xúanyán [metaphysical discourse],
and also understood Buddhist scriptures.
Even great scholars and renowned monks
would all come to ask him about their doubts and difficulties.
In the sixth year,
he died in office,
at the age of seventy-nine.
An imperial edict stated:
"Honoring the distant past and praising virtue
is a constant rule.
The late Shàngshū Yòu Púyè, concurrently Guózǐ Jìjiǔ, Dàzhōngzhèng of Yùzhōu, Zhōu Hóngzhèng,
had a profound and deep understanding,
and his accomplishments and scholarship were complete.
He was a forest of words and a treasury of principles,
an elder of the nation and a pillar of the people.
His Way illuminated the school gate,
his prestige was high in the ritual hall.
His sudden demise
has caused me sorrow.
He is hereby posthumously granted Shìzhōng and Zhōngshū Jiān.
Whatever is needed for his funeral arrangements
shall be generously provided."
The emperor then personally went to mourn and weep.
His posthumous name was Jiǎnzǐ.
His works included sixteen scrolls of lectures and commentaries on the Zhōuyì,
eleven scrolls of commentaries on the Lúnyǔ,
eight scrolls of commentaries on the Zhuāngzǐ,
five scrolls of commentaries on the Lǎozǐ,
two scrolls of commentaries on the Xiàojīng,
and a collection of twenty scrolls,
all circulated in the world.
His son, Zhōu Fén,
reached the official position of Lìbù Láng.
Zhōu Hóngzhèng had two younger brothers: Zhōu Hóngràng
and Zhōu Hóngzhí.
Zhōu Hóngràng was simple and unadorned by nature,
and broadly learned and versatile.
At the beginning of Tiānjiā,
as a commoner, he concurrently held Tàicháng Qīng and Guānglù Dàfū,
with the additional honors of a golden seal and purple ribbon.
Hóngzhí, courtesy name Sīfāng,
was intelligent and quick-witted from a young age.
Upon taking office, he was appointed a Bóshì of the Liáng Imperial Academy.
He was gradually promoted to Wàibīng Jìshì Cānjūn to the Xiāngdōng Wáng, who was the Xī Zhōngláng.
He served as a secretary alongside Bào Quán of Dōnghǎi, Zōng Lǐn of Nányáng, Liú Huǎn of Píngyuán, and Liú Jué of Pèijùn.
He then entered the court as Shàngshū Yícáo Láng.
When the Xiāngdōng Wáng was sent to govern Jiāng and Jīng prefectures,
he was repeatedly promoted to Lùshì Zīyì Cānjūn,
and concurrently held the posts of magistrate of Cáisāng and Dāngyáng counties.
When Emperor Yuán of Liáng assumed imperial authority,
he was granted the titles of Jiǎjié, Yīngguǒ Jiāngjūn, and Shìzǐ Zhǎngshǐ.
Soon after, he was appointed Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn and Héngyáng Nèishǐ.
He was promoted to Zhēnyì Jiāngjūn, Píngnán Zhǎngshǐ, and Chángshā Nèishǐ,
acting as the governor of Xiāngzhōu.
He was enfeoffed as Xiāngbīn Xiànhóu,
with six hundred households.
He successively served as the prefect of Shàolíng and Línglíng, Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn, and Chāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Wáng Lín raised an army,
Hóngzhí was in Xiāngzhōu.
After Lín was defeated,
he returned to the imperial court.
During the Tiānjiā era,
he successively held the posts of Guózǐ Bóshì, Lúlíng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ, Shàngshū Zuǒchéng, concurrently Yǔlín Jiān, Zhōngsàn Dàfū, and Mìshū Jiān,
and was in charge of the national history.
He was promoted to Tàicháng Qīng and Guānglù Dàfū,
and was awarded the golden seal and purple ribbon.
In the seventh year of Tàijiàn,
he fell ill and was about to die.
He left a memorial to his family, saying:
"This year, my
strength has declined;
one could say I am old,
yet the desire for life
I did not perceive myself.
I only pursued pleasure,
unaware that old age was approaching.
Now the current decree states that when
one is like the morning dew,
over seventy years,
it is quite sufficient.
To die intact
leaves no regrets.
After my last breath,
buy readily available materials in the market.
The materials must be small
to be easily carried.
Bury me in my daily clothes;
this was the common practice of the ancients.
However, when I meet my ancestors below,
it is necessary to be fully arrayed.
I can wear a simple skirt and shirt with old shoes.
Since I should attend to my parents,
it is appropriate to prepare a powder puff and towel.
If I meet good friends,
incense smoke will also be needed.
Inside the coffin, only place a white cloth handkerchief and a crude incense burner,
nothing else is needed outside."
He died at home
at the age of seventy-six.
He left a collection of twenty volumes.
His son was Què.
Què, courtesy name Shìqián,
had a beautiful appearance,
was generous, and had good conduct.
He extensively studied the classics and histories,
and was deeply fond of profound discourse.
His uncle, Hóngzhèng, especially cherished him.
Upon taking office in Liáng, he served as Bóshì of the Imperial Academy, Sītú Jìjiǔ, and Jìn'ān Wáng Zhǔbù.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he was appointed Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng.
He was successively promoted to Ānchéng Wáng Xiànnèi Jìshì.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Dōnggōng Tōngshì Shèrén.
He left office
due to his mother's mourning period.
After Ōuyáng Hē was pacified,
he was appointed Zhōngshū Shèrén.
He was ordered to comfort and entertain in Guǎngzhōu.
After the mourning period ended,
he became Tàicháng Qīng.
He successively served as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ, Shàngshū Zuǒchéng, and Tàizǐ Jiālìng.
He left office due to his father's mourning period.
Soon after, he was appointed Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn and Wú Líng,
but Què firmly declined the official post.
In the first year of Zhìdé,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Zuǒwèishuài and Zhōngshū Shèrén.
He was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì,
awarded Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn, and Xìnzhōu Nánpíng Wángfǔ Zhǎngshǐ,
acting as governor of Yángzhōu.
His governance was fair and just,
and he was praised as a good official.
He was promoted to Dūguān Shàngshū.
In the early Zhēnmíng era,
he fell ill
and died in office
at the age of fifty-nine.
An imperial edict posthumously awarded him Sànqí Chángshì and Tàicháng Qīng,
with the state providing for his funeral.
Yuán Xiàn, courtesy name Dézhāng,
was the younger brother of Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè Shū.
He was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
fond of learning,
and possessed a refined magnanimity.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng renovated and established schools,
opening five separate academies.
One of these academies was located west of Xiàn's residence.
Xiàn often invited students
to discuss with him.
Whenever he presented a new idea,
it would surprise everyone,
and his peers all admired and submitted to him.
In the eighth year of Dàtóng,
Emperor Wǔ compiled the *Kǒngzǐ Zhèngyán Zhāngjù*
and issued an edict to the Imperial Academy
to expound the imperial meaning.
Xiàn, then fourteen years old,
was summoned as a Guózǐ Zhèngyán Shēng.
He visited the Jìjiǔ, Dào Gài.
Gài looked at him and then saw him off,
admiring his spirit and demeanor.
After studying for a year,
Guózǐ Bóshì Zhōu Hóngzhèng said to Xiàn's father, Jūnzhèng:
"Would your worthy son like to take the examination this year?"
Jūnzhèng replied:
"His understanding of the classics is still shallow;
I dare not let him try."
A few days later,
Jūnzhèng sent his retainer, Cén Wénháo, with Xiàn to pay respects to Hóngzhèng.
It happened that Hóngzhèng was about to ascend the讲座,
and his disciples had all gathered.
He then invited Xiàn into the room,
handed him a deer-tail whisk,
and asked Xiàn to expound on a principle.
At that time, Xiè Qí and Hé Tuǒ were present.
Hóngzhèng said to them:
"Although you two wise men have delved into the profound and recondite,
do you not feel apprehensive about this young man?"
Hé and Xiè then successively raised points of argument,
delving deeply into the rationale.
Xiàn went back and forth with them several times,
responding calmly and skillfully.
Hóngzhèng said to Tuǒ:
"Ask whatever you wish;
do not treat him as a child."
At that time, the hall was full of students,
and spectators crowded around,
yet Xiàn remained composed,
debating with confidence.
Hóngzhèng asked him several difficult questions,
but he could not be stumped.
He then told Wénháo:
"When you return, consult Yuán Wúyùn.
This young man is already capable of serving as a Bóshì in our time."
At that time, students taking examinations
often offered bribes.
Wénháo asked to prepare a gift of cured meat (a token of tuition).
Jūnzhèng said:
"How can I buy an official position for my son with money?"
The academic officials resented this.
When Xiàn took the examination,
they competed to raise difficult questions.
Xiàn answered each question,
analyzing them fluently.
Dào Gài looked at Xiàn and said:
"Yuán Jūnzhèng indeed has an heir."
When Jūnzhèng was about to go to Wúyùn,
Gài hosted a farewell banquet for him at Zhēnglǔ Tíng,
and said to Jūnzhèng:
"Yesterday, the examinees Xiāo Mǐnsūn and Xú Xiàokè were not lacking in understanding,
but in terms of their demeanor and spirit,
they are far inferior to your worthy son."
Soon after, he was recommended as a Gāodì.
As a noble young master, he was chosen to marry Nánshā Gōngzhǔ,
who was the daughter of Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng.
In the first year of Dàtóng,
he was appointed Mìshū Láng.
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
Yuán Xiàn went east to Wújùn.
Soon after, he experienced the mourning for his father,
and his grief and debilitation exceeded the proper rites.
When Jìng Dì assumed power by decree,
he was summoned and appointed Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng.
When Gāozǔ became chancellor,
he was made Sītú Hùcáo.
In the first year of Yǒngdìng,
he was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng,
concurrently Sànqí Chángshì.
He was sent as an envoy to Qí with Huángmén Shìláng Wáng Yú,
and was not allowed to return for several years,
only coming back in the early years of Tiānjia.
In the fourth year,
an edict reinstated him as Zhōngshū Shìláng,
serving directly in the Shìzhōng Shěng.
In the first year of Tàijiàn,
he was made Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng,
and also took charge of the affairs of Tàicháng.
In the second year,
he was transferred to Shàngshū Lìbù Shìláng,
and soon after was appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
serving in the Eastern Palace.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and concurrently led the Yǔlín Jiān.
At that time, Yùzhāng Wáng Shúyīng did not abide by the laws and regulations,
and forcibly seized people's horses.
Yuán Xiàn impeached him based on the facts,
and Shúyīng was consequently dismissed.
From then on, both the court and the common people greatly respected and feared him.
Yuán Xiàn was thoroughly versed in court regulations,
and particularly skilled in judicial decision-making.
When cases were not fully investigated but the officials had already drawn up charges,
he would seize a moment of leisure
and often speak to the emperor about it,
and many people were vindicated by his efforts.
He once attended a banquet at Chéngxiāng Gé.
After the guests had retired,
Gāozōng kept Yuán Xiàn and Wèiwèi Fán Jùn, moving their mats to a mountain pavilion,
and they talked and feasted all day.
Gāozōng looked at Yuán Xiàn and said to Fán Jùn,
"The Yuán family truly has capable people,"
such was the esteem in which he was held.
In the fifth year,
he entered the court as Shìzhōng.
In the sixth year,
he was appointed Wújùn Tàishǒu,
but he firmly declined, citing his father's previous appointment.
He was instead appointed Míngwēi Jiāngjūn, Nánkāng Nèishǐ.
In the ninth year,
his term of office ended,
and he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
concurrently Lìbù Shàngshū,
and soon after became a full (Zhēn) incumbent.
Yuán Xiàn, having long held prominent and esteemed positions,
repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to be relieved of his duties.
Gāozōng said:
"Many officials in office
are frequently slandered.
You have handled many affairs,
and can be called pure and upright.
I will consider you for other appointments;
for now, do not resign."
In the thirteenth year,
he was promoted to Yòu Púyè,
participating in the selection of officials.
Previously, Yuán Xiàn's elder brother, Jiǎn Yìzǐ, was Zuǒ Púyè.
Now, Yuán Xiàn was Yòu Púyè.
Within the court and ministries, Jiǎn Yìzǐ was called Dà Púyè,
and Yuán Xiàn was called Xiǎo Púyè.
The court considered it an honor.
When Gāozōng fell ill,
Yuán Xiàn and Lìbù Shàngshū Máo Xǐ both received the dying injunction.
When Shǐxīng Wáng Shúlíng committed his outrageous act,
Yuán Xiàn directed and organized,
and played a significant part.
When Hòuzhǔ was critically wounded,
he held Yuán Xiàn's hand and said:
"My son is still young;
I entrust the future affairs to you."
Yuán Xiàn replied:
"The people earnestly hope
for Your Majesty's recovery;
I dare not accept
the decree concerning future affairs."
For his meritorious service, he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Jiàn'ān Xiàn,
with four hundred households,
and also held the title of Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
with all other positions remaining unchanged.
Soon after, he was appointed Shìzhōng, Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn, Tàizǐ Zhànshì.
In the first year of Zhìdé,
the Crown Prince came of age.
In the second year,
the Rì Shìdiàn ceremony was performed.
Yuán Xiàn then submitted a memorial requesting to resign,
but Hòuzhǔ refused,
granting him two attendants to assist him,
promoting him to Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn,
and providing him with subordinate officials.
The Crown Prince was somewhat undisciplined,
and Yuán Xiàn submitted a memorial containing ten points of remonstrance,
all citing ancient and modern examples,
with sincere and direct words.
Although the Crown Prince outwardly feigned acceptance,
his heart remained unrepentant.
Hòuzhǔ wished to establish his favorite concubine Zhāng Guìfēi's son, Shǐ'ān Wáng, as his heir,
and once spoke of it casually.
Lìbù Shàngshū Cài Zhēng agreed with the emperor and praised the idea.
Yuán Xiàn sternly rebuked him, saying:
"The Crown Prince is the heir to the nation,
on whom the hopes of the multitude rest.
Who are you,
to speak lightly of deposing and establishing an heir!"
In the summer,
the Crown Prince was eventually deposed as Wúxīng Wáng.
Hòuzhǔ, knowing of Yuán Xiàn's remonstrations,
sighed and said,
"Yuán Dézhāng is truly an upright and principled official."
On that very day, an edict appointed him Shàngshū Púyè.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng,
the Suí army invaded.
The Suí general Hèruò Bì advanced and burned the North Yèmén gate of the palace city.
The palace guards all scattered and fled,
and the court officials gradually left,
only Yuán Xiàn remained guarding the emperor's side.
Hòuzhǔ said to Yuán Xiàn:
"I have never treated you with preference over others,
but seeing you today,
it is truly a case of 'in the cold of winter, one knows that the pine and cypress wither last.'"
Hòuzhǔ, in a panic, was about to hide.
Yuán Xiàn, with a serious expression, said:
"When the northern troops enter,
they will certainly commit no offense.
With such a great matter at hand,
Your Majesty should remain calm.
I wish for Your Majesty to straighten your robes and crown,
and ascend the front hall,
following the example of Liáng Wǔ's meeting with Hóu Jǐng."
Hòuzhǔ did not comply,
but instead got off his couch and rushed away.
Yuán Xiàn followed him into Jǐngyáng Diàn in the rear hall.
Hòuzhǔ threw himself into a well.
Yuán Xiàn bowed and wept as he came out.
When the capital fell,
he entered the Suí dynasty.
The Suí appointed him Shǐchíjié, Chāngzhōu Zhūjūnsì, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Chāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the fourteenth year of Kāihuáng,
an edict appointed him Jìnwáng Fǔ Zhǎngshǐ.
He died in the eighteenth year,
at the age of seventy.
He was posthumously granted Dàjiāngjūn,
Ánchéngjùn Gōng,
with the posthumous name Jiǎn.
His eldest son, Chéngjiā,
served in the Suí dynasty as Mìshū Chéng and Guózǐ Sīyè.
The historian says: Emperor Yuán of Liáng called Rǔnán Zhōu Hóngzhèng a prominent figure among the gentry;
this statement is truly fitting!
Observing his elegant demeanor and outstanding character,
and his particular skill in metaphysical discourse,
he was truly a national preceptor of his generation.
Yuán Xiàn's style was rigorous and resolute,
and he upheld righteousness and trod the Dao.
Hán Zǐ praised officials who committed themselves,
whose hearts were undivided.
Yuán Xiàn remained steadfast from beginning to end,
which is truly commendable.
Textual notes
Biographies, Chapter 19: Péi Jì, Sūn Yáng
Péi Jì, courtesy name Wúwèi,
was a native of Wénxǐ, Hédōng.
His grandfather, Péi Máo,
was a Zhōngsàn Dàfū in the Liáng dynasty.
His father, Péi Zhīpíng,
was unconventional and possessed strategic talent.
He was summoned to serve as the chief commander of Wéndé.
During the Pǔtōng era of Liáng, when many armies campaigned northward,
Zhīpíng followed Grand Commandant Xiàhóu Dǎn to conquer and pacify Guō and Tóng.
For his accomplishments, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Fèixiàn.
At that time, the common people of Héngzhōu gathered and plundered.
An imperial edict appointed Zhīpíng as Jiǎjié, Chāowǔ Jiāngjūn, and Grand Commandant of all military affairs for the suppression of five commanderies in Héngzhōu.
When Zhīpíng arrived,
he immediately pacified and exterminated them all.
Liáng Wǔdì greatly praised and rewarded him.
During the Chéngshèng era of Yuándì,
he successively rose to Sànqí Chángshì, Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn, and Jìnlíng Tàishǒu.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Guānglù Dàfū
and Wèiwèi of the Cíxùn Palace.
He did not accept these positions,
but instead built mountains and dug ponds,
planting them with flowers and trees.
He resided there,
with the intention of spending his remaining years there.
He died in the first year of Tiānkāng,
and was posthumously granted Rénwēi Jiāngjūn and Guānglù Dàfū,
with the posthumous title Xīzǐ.
Jì was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
possessing foresight and judgment.
He was well-versed in historical records and biographies,
and was praised by his contemporaries.
He began his career as a Fǎcáo Cānjūn for the Prince of Yùzhāng of Liáng.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Jì gathered brave and strong men
and followed Gāozǔ in military campaigns,
accumulating merits to become Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn.
When Gāozǔ executed Wáng Sēngbiàn,
Sēngbiàn's younger brother Wáng Sēngzhì raised troops and occupied Wújun.
Gāozǔ dispatched Huáng Tā to lead troops to attack him.
Sēngzhì marched his troops out from Xīchāng Gate to resist,
and Tā was stalemated with him,
unable to overcome.
Gāozǔ said to Jì:
"The three Wú commanderies are a strategic region,
long known for their richness and fertility.
Although they have suffered from disaster and famine,
they are still prosperous.
But now, the bandits are gathering,
causing the world to waver.
Without you, it cannot be settled.
You should carefully consider your strategy."
Jì then marshaled his elite troops,
traveled lightly and doubled his pace,
heading directly from Qiántáng to Wújun.
He arrived at the city walls at night,
beating drums and shouting, pressing close.
Sēngzhì suspected a large army had arrived
and fled in light boats to Dù Kān.
Jì entered and occupied the commandery.
Gāozǔ praised him
and formally appointed him Wújun Tàishǒu.
When Gāozǔ accepted the abdication,
Jì was summoned to be Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
In the early Tiānjiā era,
he was sent out as Chíjié and Nánkāng Nèishǐ.
At that time, Zhāng Shàobīn, the Taishou of Yì'ān, rebelled by occupying his commandery.
Shìzǔ appointed Jì as Chíjié and Grand Commandant of all military affairs north of the Ridge,
leading troops to suppress and pacify him.
Upon his return, he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì and Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn and Wèiwèi Qīng,
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngxīng Xiàn,
with a stipend of six hundred households.
When Huá Jiǎo raised an army upriver,
Gāozōng was then acting as Lù Shàngshū Fǔzhèng,
and ordered all armies to go out and suppress the rebellion.
He entrusted Jì with overall command of all internal and external city defense military affairs.
When Jiǎo was pacified,
Gāozōng ascended the throne.
In the first year of Tàijiàn,
Jì was appointed Dōngyáng Tàishǒu,
and his enfeoffment was changed to the Marquis of Yuè'ān Xiàn,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
In the fourth year,
he entered the court as Tàifǔ Qīng.
In the fifth year,
he was transferred to Dūguān Shàngshū.
When Wú Míngchè led a large army on a northern expedition,
an imperial edict appointed Jì to supervise Míngchè's army in his current capacity.
After Huáinán was pacified,
he was appointed Jūnshī Jiāngjūn and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Jì was skilled at pacifying and comforting the people,
and greatly won their favor.
He was re-appointed Shǐ Chíjié, Grand Commandant of all military affairs of Qiáozhōu, and Qiáozhōu Cìshǐ.
Before he could take up his post,
Míngchè received an edict to advance and attack Péng and Biàn,
and Jì was appointed Grand Commandant
to advance alongside Míngchè, forming a pincer movement.
After the defeat at Lǚliáng,
he was captured by Zhōu.
Zhōu appointed him Shàng Kāifǔ.
He died in Cháng'ān in the fourteenth year of Kāihuáng of Suí,
at the age of seventy-three.
Sūn Yáng, courtesy name Délǐan,
was a native of Wú in Wújun.
His grandfather, Sūn Wénhuì,
was a Yuèqí Xiàowèi and Qīngyuǎn Tàishǒu in Qí.
His father, Sūn Xúndào,
was a Zhōngsàn Dàfū in Liáng,
known for his elegance and simplicity.
Yáng was unconventional in his youth,
fond of strategy,
widely read in classics and history,
and particularly skilled in writing.
He began his career as a Qīngchē Línchuān Sì Wáng Xíng Cānjūn in Liáng,
and successively rose to Ānxī Shàolíng Wáng Shuǐcáo Zhōngbīng Cānjūnshì.
When the Prince was stationed in Yǐngzhōu,
Yáng moved his entire family with the yamen
and was highly valued and treated well.
During the Tàiqīng calamity,
he was appointed Jiǎjié, Xuānměng Jiāngjūn, and Jūnzhǔ.
When Wáng Sēngbiàn campaigned against Hóu Jǐng,
Wáng Lín was the vanguard.
Lín and Yáng were from the same school,
so Lín recommended him for Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn and Yídū Tàishǒu,
and he then followed Sēngbiàn to rescue Xú Wénshèng at Wǔchāng.
When Yǐngzhōu fell,
he was left to garrison Bālíng with his troops,
preparing for defense and combat.
Soon after, Hóu Jǐng's troops arrived
and attacked day and night.
Yáng led his subordinate troops to resist with all their might,
and the bandit forces retreated.
Yáng followed the main army downstream.
After Guǒshú was captured,
Yáng distinguished himself in fierce battles,
and was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì,
enfeoffed as the Marquis of Fùyáng Xiàn,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
Soon after, he was appointed Jiǎjié, Xióngxìn Jiāngjūn, and Héngyáng Nèishǐ.
Before he could take up his post,
he was transferred to Héngzhōu Píngnán Fǔ Sīmǎ.
For his accomplishments in defeating the Huángdòng barbarian bandits,
he was appointed Dōngguǎn Tàishǒu,
acting as Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Soon after, he was appointed Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn,
supervising affairs in Xiāngzhōu.
When Jìngdì ascended the throne,
he was appointed Chíjié, Rénwēi Jiāngjūn, and Bāzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Gāozǔ accepted the abdication,
Wáng Lín enthroned Xiāo Zhuāng, the Prince of Yǒngjiā of Liáng, in Yǐngzhōu.
Yáng was summoned to be Tàifǔ Qīng,
and additionally granted Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì.
When Wáng Lín invaded,
Yáng was appointed Shǐ Chíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Grand Commandant of all military affairs of the five prefectures of Yǐng, Jīng, Bā, Wǔ, and Xiāng, Ānxī Jiāngjūn, and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ,
taking overall responsibility for the remaining yamen.
Zhōu dispatched its grand general Shǐ Níng to lead forty thousand troops,
who arrived suddenly and unexpectedly.
Yáng's assistant defender, Zhāng Shìguì, surrendered the outer city in response to them,
losing over three thousand soldiers, civilians, men, and women.
The Zhōu army then built earthen mounds and high ladders,
attacking day and night.
They also used the wind to set fire,
burning over fifty towers on the south side of the inner city.
At that time, Yáng's troops numbered less than a thousand.
He defended the city from the walls.
Yáng personally went on inspection tours,
distributing wine and food.
All the officers and soldiers were willing to fight to the death for him.
The Zhōu people suffered from their persistent attacks and could not conquer.
They then falsely appointed Yáng as Zhùguó and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ,
enfeoffing him as Wànhù Jùngōng.
Yáng feigned agreement to stall them,
but secretly repaired his military equipment.
The towers, battlements, and weapons were all rigorously prepared overnight,
which greatly deterred the Zhōu people.
When they heard that the main army had defeated Wáng Lín
and was advancing victoriously,
the Zhōu troops withdrew.
Yáng then took full control of the middle reaches of the river,
gathered his generals and soldiers, and said to them:
"I and Duke Wáng have exerted our strength and collaborated in righteousness
to jointly support the Liáng dynasty.
We have indeed toiled.
Now that the times are like this,
can Heaven be defied?"
Thereupon, he sent an envoy to present a memorial to the imperial court.
In the first year of Tiānjiā,
he was appointed Envoy with Staff, Palace Attendant, General of Annan, and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dìngxiāng County,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
Sūn Yáng harbored unease
and therefore firmly requested to return to the court.
He was summoned to serve as Palace Attendant and Central Leader of the Army.
Before he had taken up the post,
Emperor Shìzǔ casually said to Sūn Yáng,
"Jū Māichén once wished to serve his home county.
Do you perhaps have a similar intention?"
He was then reappointed as Envoy with Staff, General of Andong, and Grand Administrator of Wújùn,
and granted a set of drums and pipes.
When he was about to depart for his post,
the imperial carriage visited the nearby suburbs to see him off,
which brought honor to his hometown.
Upon completing his term,
he was summoned to be appointed Palace Attendant and Central Protector of the Army,
with the drums and pipes as before.
When Liú Yì rebelled in Dōngyáng,
an imperial edict commanded Sūn Yáng to oversee the naval forces and advance to suppress him.
After Liú Yì was pacified,
he was promoted to General of the Right to Guard the State,
with his Palace Attendant and drums and pipes remaining as before.
After a short while,
he was sent out as Envoy with Staff, General of Andong, and Grand Administrator of Jiàn'ān.
During the Guāngdà era,
he was dismissed for an official matter,
but soon reinstated as Palace Attendant with Free Access.
When Emperor Gāozōng ascended the throne,
recognizing Sūn Yáng's long-established achievements and reputation,
he placed great trust in him.
In the fourth year of Tàijiàn,
he was appointed Area Commander of the military affairs of Jīngzhōu and Xìnzhōu, General of Anxi, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
and sent to guard Gōng'ān.
Sūn Yáng further repaired the city walls,
and pacified and won over the border regions,
making him feared by neighboring territories.
After serving for six years,
he was again dismissed for an incident,
and again served as Palace Attendant with Free Access.
When Wú Míngchè's army was defeated at Lǚliáng,
he was appointed Envoy with Staff, Commander of all land and water forces along the river, and General who Guards the West,
and granted a set of drums and pipes.
Soon after, he was appointed Palace Attendant, Area Commander of the military affairs of Jīngzhōu, Yǐngzhōu, Bāzhōu, Wǔzhōu, and Xiāngzhōu, and Inspector of Yǐngzhōu,
with his staff, generalship, and drums and pipes remaining as before.
In the twelfth year,
he was convicted for border communication.
After the Last Emperor succeeded to the throne,
he was again appointed Palace Attendant with Free Access,
concurrently serving as Minister of the Bureau of Public Works.
Soon after, he was appointed Central Protector of the Army,
his title and fief restored,
and he entered the court as Minister of Revenue,
also overseeing the Colonel of Infantry.
Shortly after, he was granted the additional title of Palace Attendant,
and promoted to Court Attendant and Minister of Rites.
The Last Emperor frequently visited his residence,
and even composed poems and essays praising his achievements and virtue,
expressing the affection between sovereign and subject.
He also served as Minister of the Five Military Bureaus,
overseeing the General of the Right Army,
with his Court Attendant title remaining as before.
Due to old age, he repeatedly requested to retire,
but an imperial edict graciously refused.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng, he died in office,
at the age of seventy-two.
The Last Emperor personally wept for him with profound sorrow,
and granted him the posthumous title of General Protector of the Army,
with his Court Attendant title as before,
a set of drums and pipes,
a set of court robes,
a suit of clothes,
and additional funds for his funeral arrangements,
and he was posthumously granted the name Huánzi.
Sūn Yáng was known for his filial piety towards his parents,
and was deeply affectionate towards his younger brothers.
He had a magnanimous nature,
and distributed his wealth among relatives and friends.
However, his personal residence
was somewhat extravagant and luxurious.
His courtyards were excavated and built,
reaching the utmost beauty of forests and springs.
The singers, musicians, and dancing girls
were rarely paralleled in his time.
Guests filled his gate,
and carriages and sedan chairs were incessant.
When he was sent out to guard Yǐngzhōu,
he combined more than ten boats to form a large raft,
on which he erected pavilions and ponds,
and planted lotus and water caltrops.
Whenever there was a good day and beautiful scenery,
guests and officials would gather,
and they would drink wine while floating on the Yangtze River,
which was also a splendid pastime of that time.
He often set up a lecture hall in his mountain studio,
gathering scholars of Xuanxue and Confucianism,
providing for them throughout winter and summer,
and he was praised by scholars.
However, he was frank and easy-going in his conduct,
and did not use his rank to put on airs.
At that time, Master Lǎng of Xīnghuáng Temple was thoroughly versed in Buddhist scriptures.
Sūn Yáng often attended his lectures,
sometimes engaging in debates,
and all the Buddhist monks were captivated.
He also had extraordinary ingenuity.
As Minister of the Bureau of Public Works,
he invented many military and state implements.
He had good judgment,
and for the marriages of his sons and daughters,
he always chose those from noble families.
Upon his death,
Jiāng Zǒng, the Minister of the Department of State Affairs, wrote his epitaph.
The Last Emperor then inscribed forty characters after the epitaph,
and dispatched Cài Zhēng, Minister of the Bureau of Population, to convey the imperial edict and engrave it at his residence.
The inscription read:
"Autumn winds stir the bamboo,
Misty waters alarm the waves.
How many people on the woodcutter's path?
Where is the mountain bend?
Today's sun and moon,
Yesteryear's silken robes.
Heaven is long, the road far,
Earth is ancient, clouds numerous.
The meritorious minister not yet engraved,
What thought is this?"
Contemporary opinion considered it an honor.
Sūn Yáng had twenty-one sons,
all possessing their father's disposition.
His heir, Ràng,
died young.

he was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū
and concurrently held the position of Dà Zhùzuò.
Líng believed that since the end of Liáng,
appointments had often been misplaced.
Therefore, he took charge of the fundamental principles
and thoroughly examined names and realities.
At that time, there were those who aggressively sought advancement and office,
clamoring endlessly.
Líng then wrote a letter to declare and announce, saying:
"From ancient times, the Lìbù Shàngshū
evaluates human character,
selects their talents,
examines their family background,
and according to their prominence,
measures their official rank.
When Liáng Yuándì inherited the chaos and devastation left by Hóu Jǐng,
and Wáng Tàiwèi received the misfortune and defeat of Jīngzhōu,
at that time, due to the widespread disorder,
there were no proper regulations.
Thus, the official system
was reduced to this state of confusion.
During the Yǒngdìng period,
the sacred dynasty was founded,
but military conflicts had not ceased,
and there was no order either.
The treasuries were empty,
and rewards were severely lacking.
Silver was hard to come by,
and yellow diplomas were easily granted.
Temporarily, official ranks
were used as substitutes for money and silk.
The intention was to appease and accept,
without regard for quantity,
leading to countless Yuánwài and Chángshì
walking shoulder to shoulder on the roads,
and numerous Zīyì and Cānjūn
in the marketplaces.
How can this be the proper order of the court
that it should be like this?
Now, with proper attire, rituals, and music
flourishing day by day and year by year,
how can one still cling to old ideas
and harbor unreasonable hopes?
I see many gentlemen
exceeding their original station,
yet still complaining of great injustice
and not understanding noble aspirations.
If you ask about Zhū Lǐngjūn of the Liáng dynasty, who also became a high official,
did this not exceed his original station?
This was an appointment made by the Son of Heaven,
not related to selection or order.
Liáng Wǔdì said, 'People of the world say they discriminate based on appearance,
but I particularly do not discriminate based on the appearance of Fàn Tì.'
Sòng Wéndì also said, 'How can there be no fate in the human world?
Whenever there is a good official position vacant,
I immediately think of Yáng Xuánbǎo.'
These examples show that high-ranking and prominent positions
are not obtained through selection.
In Qín, Chēfǔ Lìng Zhào Gāo rose directly to Chéngxiàng.
In Hàn, Gāomiào Lìng Tián Qiānqiū also became Chéngxiàng.
Can these again be taken as examples?
Since I am entrusted with this selection process,
I must uphold the standards.
I hope all gentlemen
will deeply understand my humble intentions."
From then on, everyone was convinced,
and contemporary opinion compared him to Máo Jiè.
When Fèidì ascended the throne,
Gāozōng entered to assist him.
Planning to remove those with divergent views,
he invited Líng to participate in the deliberations.
When Gāozōng assumed the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Jiànchāng Xiàn Hóu,
with five hundred households.
In the first year of Tàijiàn,
he was appointed Shàngshū Yòupúyè.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè.
[一九]Líng submitted a memorial declining the post and recommending Zhōu Hóngzhèng and Wáng Mài, among others.
Gāozōng summoned Líng to the inner palace
and said:
"Why do you firmly decline this position and recommend others?"
Líng replied:
"Zhōu Hóngzhèng returned with Your Majesty from the west, having been an old藩chángshǐ.
Wáng Mài was the Chángshǐ of the prime minister's office in Tàipíng.
Zhāng Zhǒng is a virtuous relative from the imperial family.
If we select based on virtue and seniority,
your humble servant should be last."
He firmly declined for several days,
but Gāozōng strenuously urged him,
and Líng then accepted the imperial edict.
When the court deliberated on a northern expedition,
Gāozōng 曰 (said):
“My decision is made.
You may nominate a Grand Marshal.”
The assembly all agreed that Zhōngquán Jiāngjūn Chúnyú Liàng held a weighty position,
and jointly put forward his name.
Líng alone said:
“Not so.
Wú Míngchè's home is in Huaízuǒ,
he knows their customs thoroughly,
and as for military strategy and talent,
there is no one superior to him today.”
Thereupon, the debate lasted for several days without a decision.
Dūguān Shàngshū Péi Jì said:
“I agree with Xú Púshè.”
Líng responded instantly:
“Not only is Míngchè a good general,
but Péi Jì would also be a good deputy.”
On that day,
an imperial edict appointed Míngchè as Dà Dūdū,
and ordered Jì to oversee military affairs.
Consequently, they captured dozens of prefectures in Huaínán.
Gāozōng then hosted a banquet,
raised his cup and said to Líng:
“I reward you for your discernment of men.”
Líng rose from his mat and replied:
“The strategy was decided by Your Sacred Heart;
it is not due to my efforts.”
That year, he was promoted to Shìzhōng,
the rest remaining as before.
In the seventh year,
he assumed the concurrent post of Guózǐ Jìjiǔ and Nán Xúzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng.
He was dismissed from Shìzhōng and Púshè due to official matters.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Shìzhōng,
granted a sedan chair with bearers,
and also appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the eighth year,
he was promoted to Yì Yòu Jiāngjūn and Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
and given subordinate officials.
Shortly thereafter, he was transferred to Yòu Guānglù Dàfū,
the rest remaining as before.
In the tenth year,
he was again appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Soon after, he was transferred to Ān Yòu Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn.
In the thirteenth year,
he became Zhōngshū Jiān,
concurrently Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
granted a set of drum and wind instruments,
with his Shìzhōng, Jiāngjūn, Yòu Guānglù, and Zhōngzhèng titles remaining as before.
Líng, being old, repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement,
and Gāozōng also showed him favor,
ordering the construction of a grand fasting hall for him,
and allowing Líng to manage affairs from his residence.
When Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Tàizǐ Shàofù,
the rest remaining as before.
He died in Zhìdé first year,
at the age of seventy-seven.
An imperial edict stated:
“The ceremony for the conclusion of life has its precedents,
and this is indeed an ancient regulation.
Virtuous deeds can be distinguished,
and it is right to pursue them across generations.
Shìzhōng, Ān Yòu Jiāngjūn, Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, Tàizǐ Shàofù, Nán Xúzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng, Jiànchāng Xiàn Kāiguó Hóu Líng,
from a young age he pursued learning,
and showed outstanding brilliance when he entered court.
His achievements surpassed those of his contemporaries,
and his writing established a literary school.
When We recently inherited this brilliant position,
We particularly drew him close.
Although he often suffered from illness,
We still expected him to regain his vigor.
His sudden demise
fills Our heart with shock and grief.
He is posthumously granted Zhèn Yòu Jiāngjūn and Tèjìn.
His titles of Shìzhōng, Zuǒ Guānglù, drum and wind instruments, and Marquis remain as before.
Furthermore, officials are to express condolences,
and necessary funeral expenses
are to be supplied as appropriate.
His posthumous title is Zhāng.”
Líng had profound depth and breadth of mind,
and his bearing was admirable.
His nature was also pure and simple,
without any desire for accumulation.
He shared his salary and stipends with his relatives.
During Tàijiàn reign,
he received revenue from Jiànchāng Yì.
When the households of the邑 (fief) sent rice to the waterside,
Líng's relatives who were poor
were all allowed to take from it.
Within a few days, it was all gone,
and Líng's household soon found itself in want.
His subordinate officials were surprised and asked him the reason.
Líng said:
“I have chariots, oxen, and clothes that can be sold.
Do other households have anything to sell?”
Such was his generosity.
From a young age, he deeply believed in Buddhism,
and had a profound understanding of many sūtras and treatises.
When Hòuzhǔ was in the Eastern Palace,
he ordered Líng to lecture on the Dàpǐn Jīng.
Famous monks specializing in Buddhist teachings
gathered from afar.
Whenever there was a debate at the lecture,
none in the audience could contend with him.
He had blue pupils,
which people at the time considered a sign of intelligence and wisdom.
Since the establishment of the Chén dynasty,
military dispatches, official documents, and edicts for abdication or enthronement
were all authored by Líng,
with the Nine Bestowals being particularly exquisite.
He was the literary master of his generation,
yet he did not boast about this to others,
and never criticized other authors.
Towards those who came after him,
he was tireless in his guidance.
During the reigns of Shìzǔ and Gāozōng,
whenever the state needed a major literary work,
Líng drafted it.
His writing style largely transformed the old forms,
with ingenious and meticulous construction,
often featuring new ideas.
Whenever a piece of his writing was released,
enthusiasts would immediately copy and memorize it,
and it spread among both Chinese and barbarians,
with families preserving copies.
Later, due to wars and chaos,
many were lost,
with thirty volumes remaining.
He had four sons: Jiǎn,
Fèn,
Yí,
Zūn.
Jiǎn was also named Zhòng.
〔二０〕From a young age, he was upright and diligent,
studious and firm in character.
Zhōuhóngzhèng of Rǔnán respected him
and gave him his daughter in marriage.
At the beginning of Liáng Tàiqīng reign,
he began his career as Xíng Cānjūn in the household of Yùzhāng Wáng.
During the Hóu Jǐng rebellion,
Líng had not yet returned from his mission to Wèi,
and Jiǎn, then twenty-one years old,
carried his elderly relatives and children to take refuge in Jiānglíng.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng heard of his reputation
and summoned him to be Shàngshū Jīnbù Lángzhōng.
He once attended a banquet and composed a poem,
and Emperor Yuán exclaimed with admiration,
“The son of the Xú clan
is again a man of letters!”
When Jiānglíng fell,
he returned to the capital.
At the beginning of Yǒngdìng reign,
he became Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
then transferred to Zhèndōng Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
In Tiānjiā third year,
he was transferred to Zhōngshū Shìláng.
In the early Tài-Jiàn (太建) era,
Ōuyáng Hè (歐陽紇), the Governor (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Guǎng-Zhōu (廣州), raised an army in rebellion.
Gāo-Zōng (高宗) ordered Jiǎn (儉) to hold the imperial insignia and convey the imperial decree.
When Hè (紇) first met Jiǎn (儉),
he grandly displayed his guards and retinue,
and spoke with disrespect.
Jiǎn (儉) said:
"The affair of Lǚ Jiā (呂嘉)
is certainly a distant past,
but does Your Excellency not recall Zhōu Dí (周迪) and Chén Bǎo-Yìng (陳寶應)?
To turn misfortune into blessing
is not yet too late."
Hè (紇) remained silent, not answering.
Fearing that Jiǎn (儉) would demoralize his troops,
he did not permit him to enter the city.
He quartered Jiǎn (儉) at Gū-Yuán Temple (孤園寺)
and sent men to guard him,
so he could not return for several tens of days.
Hè (紇) once went out to see Jiǎn (儉).
Jiǎn (儉) said to him:
"Your Excellency has already raised an army.
I must return to report to the Son of Heaven.
Although my life is in Your Excellency's hands,
Your Excellency's success or failure does not depend on me.
I hope you will not detain me."
Hè (紇) then dispatched Jiǎn (儉) to rush back via a secluded path.
Gāo-Zōng (高宗) then ordered Zhāng Zhāo-Dá (章昭達) to lead troops to suppress Hè (紇).
As Jiǎn (儉) was thoroughly familiar with the situation,
an imperial edict ordered Jiǎn (儉) to supervise Zhāo-Dá's (昭達) army.
After Hè (紇) was pacified,
Gāo-Zōng (高宗) commended Jiǎn (儉),
bestowed upon him ten slaves,
and five hundred *hú* (斛) of rice.
He was appointed Counsellor (Zīyì Cānjūn 諮議參軍) to Zhèn-Běi Pó-Yáng-Wáng (鎮北鄱陽王),
and concurrently Secretariat Scholar (Zhōngshū Shèrén 中書舍人).
He was successively promoted to Grand Academician (Guózǐ Bóshì 國子博士) and Minister of Works (Dàjiàng Qīng 大匠卿),
the rest of his offices remaining as before.
Soon after, he was promoted to Palace Assistant Secretary (Huángmén Shìláng 黃門侍郎),
then transferred to Senior Secretariat Tutor (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子),
and additionally granted the title of Attendant Palace Censor (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì 通直散騎常侍),
concurrently Assistant Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒchéng 尚書左丞).
He was dismissed due to a public matter.
Soon after, he was reappointed as Special Counsellor (Xiàngwài Zīyì Cānjūn 限外諮議參軍) to Zhōng-Wèi Shǐ-Xīng-Wáng (中衛始興王),
and concurrently Secretariat Scholar (Zhōngshū Shèrén 中書舍人).
He again served as Senior Secretariat Tutor (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子),
and was promoted to General of Inspiring Awe (Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn 貞威將軍) and Colonel-Protector of the Left of the Crown Prince's Guard (Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ 太子左衛率),
his position as Secretariat Scholar remaining unchanged.
When the Last Emperor (Hòuzhǔ 後主) ascended the throne,
he was appointed General Who Harmonizes the Barbarians (Héróng Jiāngjūn 和戎將軍) and Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ 長史) to Xuān-Huì Jìn-Xī-Wáng (宣惠晉熙王),
and acted as Administrator of Dān-Yáng (丹陽) Commandery.
Soon after, he resigned due to his father's mourning.
He was soon reappointed as General Who Harmonizes the Barbarians (Héróng Jiāngjūn 和戎將軍),
and successively promoted to Grand Administrator (Nèishǐ 內史) of Xún-Yáng (尋陽).
His governance was strict and clear,
and banditry ceased.
He was promoted to Attendant Palace Censor (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍),
inherited the title of Marquis of Jiàn-Chāng (建昌),
and entered court as Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞).
Jiǎn's (儉) nature was fair and just,
without any partiality or subservience.
Jiāng Zǒng (江總), the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng 尚書令), whose prestige was great at the time,
was also impeached by Jiǎn (儉).
The Last Emperor (Hòuzhǔ 後主) deeply trusted and relied on him.
He also concurrently held the position of Commander of the Right Army (Yòujūn 右軍).
He died in the second year of Zhēn-Míng (禎明).
Fèn (份) showed his father's demeanor from a young age.
At nine *suì* (歲),
he composed a *fù* (賦) on a dream.
Líng (陵) saw it
and said to his close associates,
"Even I, when I was young and engaged in writing,
was not superior to this."
He began his career as Archivist (Mìshū Láng 祕書郎),
and was transferred to Palace Secretary to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人).
He was successively promoted to Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù 主簿) to Yù-Zhāng-Wáng (豫章王) and Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ 太子洗馬).
He was appointed Magistrate (Lìng 令) of Hǎi-Yán (海鹽),
where he achieved significant administrative success.
Upon completion of his term,
he returned to court as Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ 太子洗馬).
Fèn (份) was naturally filial and fraternal.
Líng (陵) once fell ill,
and was very critical.
Fèn (份) burned incense and wept,
kneeling and reciting the Classic of Filial Piety (Xiàojīng 孝經),
day and night without ceasing.
After three days of this,
Líng's (陵) illness suddenly recovered,
and all his relatives said it was due to Fèn's (份) filial devotion.
He died in the second year of Tài-Jiàn (太建),
at the age of twenty-two *suì* (歲).
Yí (儀) was intelligent and alert in his youth.
He passed the imperial examination with high honors based on the *Zhouyi* (周易) and became Archivist (Mìshū Láng 祕書郎).
He was appointed Magistrate (Lìng 令) of Wū-Shāng (烏傷).
In the early Zhēn-Míng (禎明) era,
he was promoted to Court Gentleman for Ceremonials (Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng 尚書殿中郎),
and soon concurrently served as Scholar of the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng Xuéshì 東宮學士).
After Chén (陳) fell, he entered Suí (隋).
In the ninth year of Kāi-Huáng (開皇),
he lived in seclusion on Zhě Mountain (赭山) in Qián-Táng (錢塘).
Yáng-Dì (煬帝) summoned him as a scholar,
and soon appointed him Director of the Imperial Library (Zhùzuò Láng 著作郎).
He died in the fourth year of Dà-Yè (大業).
Xiào-Kè (孝克)
was Líng's (陵) third younger brother.
In his youth, he studied the *Zhouyi* (周易),
was eloquent,
and skilled in discussing profound principles.
When he grew up,
he thoroughly understood the Five Classics,
read widely in historical records,
and was also good at writing,
though his writing did not match his meaning.
In the early Tài-Qīng (太清) era of Liáng (梁),
he began his career as Academician of the Imperial Academy (Tàixué Bóshì 太學博士).
He was extremely filial.
When his father passed away,
he almost could not bear the mourning.
He served his birth mother, Lady Chén (陳氏),
with utmost dedication.
Towards the end of Liáng (梁),
when Hóu Jǐng (侯景) caused rebellion,
the capital suffered a great famine,
and eighteen or nineteen out of ten died of starvation.
Xiào-Kè (孝克) supported his mother,
but could not even provide thin gruel.
His wife, Lady Zāng (臧氏) from Dōng-Guǎn (東莞),
was the daughter of Zāng Dùn (臧盾), the Commander of the Army (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn 領軍將軍).
She was very beautiful.
Xiào-Kè (孝克) then said to her:
"Now that the famine is so severe,
and our provisions are completely lacking,
I wish to marry you to a wealthy man,
hoping to save both of us.
What is your opinion?"
Lady Zāng (臧氏) did not agree.
At that time, there was a man named Kǒng Jǐng-Xíng (孔景行),
who was a general under Hóu Jǐng (侯景),
and very rich.
Xiào-Kè (孝克) secretly used a matchmaker to convey his intention.
Jǐng-Xíng (景行) brought many attendants,
and forced her to be taken away.
Zāng (臧) departed in tears.
The grain and silk he received
were all used to support his mother.
Xiào-Kè (孝克) also shaved his head and became a *shāmén* (沙門) (Buddhist monk),
changing his name to Fǎ-Zhěng (法整),
and begged for food to supplement their provisions.
Lady Zāng (臧氏) also deeply remembered their old affection,
and frequently sent private gifts of food,
so they did not lack supplies.
Later, Jǐng-Xíng (景行) died in battle.
Zāng (臧) waited for Xiào-Kè (孝克) on the road,
and after several days finally saw him.
She said to Xiào-Kè (孝克):
"What happened in the past
was not because I failed you.
Now that I am free,
I should return to serve and support you."
Xiào-Kè (孝克) remained silent, not answering.
Thereupon, he returned to secular life
and they became husband and wife again.
Later, he traveled east,
residing in Jiā-Yì-Lǐ (佳義里) in Qián-Táng (錢塘).
He discussed Buddhist scriptures with various monks,
and thus became proficient in the Three Treatises (Sānlùn 三論).
He lectured twice daily:
in the morning, he lectured on Buddhist scriptures,
and in the evening, on the Rites and Commentaries (Lǐzhuàn 禮傳).
Several hundred monks and laymen received instruction from him.
During the Tiān-Jiā (天嘉) era,
he was appointed Magistrate (Lìng 令) of Shàn (剡),
which was not to his liking,
and he soon resigned.
In the fourth year of Tài-Jiàn (太建),
he was summoned to be Secretariat Aide (Mìshū Chéng 祕書丞),
but he did not accept.
Instead, he ate only vegetables and maintained a long vegetarian fast,
observing the Bodhisattva precepts.
Day and night, he lectured on and recited the Lotus Sutra (Fǎhuá Jīng 法華經).
Gāo-Zōng (高宗) greatly admired his conduct.
Six years later,
he was appointed Guózǐ Bóshì.
He was promoted to Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
and concurrently served as Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
Soon after, he became the full-time incumbent.
Whenever Xiàokè attended a banquet,
he would not eat anything.
When the banquet dispersed,
the dishes in front of him would be diminished.
Gāozōng secretly noted this and asked the Zhōngshū Shèrén Guǎn Bīn about it.
Bīn could not answer.
From then on, Bīn observed him closely,
and saw Xiàokè take precious fruits and place them in his sash.
Bīn did not understand his intention at the time,
but later, after further inquiry,
he learned that Xiàokè took them back to give to his mother.
Bīn reported the truth,
and Gāozōng sighed in admiration for a long time.
He then ordered the relevant officials
that from now on at banquets,
the food in front of Xiàokè
should all be sent back
to feed his mother.
Contemporary opinion praised this.
During the Zhìdé reign,
the Crown Prince entered school for the Shìdiǎn ceremony.
All officials attended and stood in array.
Xiàokè delivered a lecture on the topic of the Xiàojīng.
The Hòuzhǔ then ordered the Crown Prince to face north and pay his respects.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng,
he entered the court as Dūguān Shàngshū.
Since the Jìn Dynasty,
the Shàngshū officials and their families all lived within the government compound.
The compound was located within the Táichéng city walls, near the Xiàshè Gate.
Inside, there was an elevated walkway
that spanned east to west across the road,
connecting to the imperial court.
The first building was the Dūguān's office,
its western side reaching the elevated walkway.
Due to its age,
it was haunted by many ghosts.
Every evening,
there would be unexplained sounds and lights,
or people wearing official robes and hats would be seen emerging from the well,
only to disappear again shortly after,
or doors would open and close by themselves.
Many who lived in the compound died.
The Shàngshū Zhōu Què died in this compound.
Xiàokè replaced Què
and immediately resided there.
After two years,
all the strange occurrences ceased.
People at the time all believed it was due to his upright and righteous character.
Xiàokè was pure and simple by nature, and fond of giving charity,
thus he could not avoid hunger and cold.
The Hòuzhǔ ordered that the taxes from Shítou jīn be given to him.
Xiàokè used it all to hold vegetarian feasts and copy scriptures,
spending whatever he received.
In the second year,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì
to serve in the Eastern Palace.
When Chén fell,
he entered Guānzhong as was customary.
His family was impoverished,
and his birth mother was ill,
wishing for rice porridge,
but he could not always provide it.
After his mother passed away,
Xiàokè always ate wheat.
When someone gave him rice,
Xiàokè would weep bitterly upon seeing it,
and never ate it again for the rest of his life.
In the tenth year of Kāihuáng,
Cháng'ān suffered from a plague.
Suí Wéndì, hearing of his reputation and conduct,
summoned him to lecture on the Jīngāng Bānruò Jīng in the Shàngshū Dūtáng.
Soon after, he was appointed Guózǐ Bóshì.
Later, he served in the Eastern Palace, lecturing on the Lǐ Zhuàn.
In the nineteenth year, he died of illness,
at the age of seventy-three.
At the time of his death,
he sat upright, chanting Buddha's name.
An extraordinary and unusual fragrance filled the room,
astonishing all the neighbors.
His son, Wànzài,
served as Jìn'ān Wáng Gōngcáo Shǐ and Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ.
The imperial historian says: Xú Xiàomù possessed the essence of the Five Elements,
and received the spiritual energy of heaven and earth.
He was exceptionally intelligent and perceptive,
encompassing both ancient and modern times.
When he established the rising dynasty
and encountered a period of great fortune,
his position as a high-ranking court official was prominent.
He offered counsel and advice,
and indeed, his integrity and rectitude were preserved.
Xiàokè disciplined himself and refined his conduct,
nurturing his parents beyond common禮.
He surely possessed the aspirations of Cān and Mǐn.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 21: Jiāng Zǒng, Yáo Chá
Jiāng Zǒng, courtesy name Zǒngchí,
was a native of Kǎochéng, Jìyáng.
He was the tenth-generation descendant of Jìn Sànqí Chángshì Tǒng.
His fifth-generation ancestor, Zhàn,
was Sòng Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and Zhōngjiǎn Gōng.
His grandfather, Qiàn,
was Liáng Guānglù Dàfū,
famous in his time.
His father, Fú,
was initially invited to be the principal clerk of his prefecture.
He suffered greatly during his father's mourning in his youth,
and died from it.
This is recorded in the Xiàoxíng Zhuàn of the Liángshū.
Zǒng was orphaned at seven,
and lived with his maternal relatives.
As a child, he was intelligent
and possessed true character.
His maternal uncle, Wú Píngguāng Hóu Xiāo Mài,
was highly respected at the time,
and particularly doted on him.
He once said to Zǒng:
"Your conduct is extraordinary,
