and your spirit is outstanding.
Your future fame
will surely surpass mine."
When he grew up,
he was diligent in study and eloquent in writing.
His family had been granted thousands of volumes of books,
and Zǒng read them day and night,
never ceasing.
At eighteen,
he began his official career as the Fǎcáo Cānjūn in the household of Xuānhuì Wǔlíng Wáng.
The Zhōngquán Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn Hé Jìngróng established his own administration,
appointing aides and scribes.
All were filled by nobles,
and Jìngróng's household principal clerk was appointed.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng.
When Liáng Wǔdì had just finished compiling the Zhèngyán,
he composed a poem expressing his feelings.
Zǒng participated in this composition.
The Emperor read Zǒng's poem
and greatly praised it.
He was then transferred to Shìláng.
Shàngshū Púyè Fànyáng Zhāng Zuǎn,
Dùzhī Shàngshū Lángyé Wáng Yún,
Dūguān Shàngshū Nányáng Liú Zhīlín,
were all highly talented and learned scholars.
Zǒng, though young at the time, was renowned,
and Zuǎn and others greatly admired him,
forming a friendship that transcended age.
Zhīlín once wrote a poem in response to Zǒng,
which roughly said:
"In a high position, residing in a place of solemn rites,
the temple and office are close.
I dread hearing the morning calls of the guards,
and always fear the rising morning light.
Our profound discussions are never exhausted,
and our appreciative meetings have no limit.
We seek out urgent matters and travel together,
forgetting to rest and eat during holidays.
How can we dispel vulgarity and avarice?
I humbly visit to see your countenance.
Discussing thousands of years,
we express our innermost thoughts."
Such was his admiration by accomplished individuals.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
and then went out to serve as Lín'ān Lìng.
He returned as Xiànnèi Lùshì Cānjūn in the household of Zhōngjūn Xuānchéng Wáng,
then transferred to Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén.
When diplomatic relations with the Wèi state were established,
an imperial edict appointed Zǒng and Xú Líng to act as officials and return the courtesies.
Zǒng did not go due to illness.
When Hóu Jǐng attacked the capital,
an edict appointed Zǒng to temporarily serve as Tàicháng Qīng,
guarding the small temple.
When Táichéng fell,
Zǒng sought refuge in perilous circumstances,
and after several years, reached Kuàijī Jùn,
resting at Lónghuá Sì.
He then composed the Xiūxīn Fù,
briefly narrating the events of the time.
Its text reads: In the seventh month of autumn in the fourth year of Tàiqīng,
I took refuge in Lónghuá Sì in Kuàijī.
This monastery
was constructed in the twenty-fourth year by my sixth-generation ancestor, Sòng Shàngshū Yòu Púyè Zhōulíng
Hóu Yuánjiā.
The Marquis's paternal grandfather, Jìn Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Bīn [虨],
once governed this region.
He chose to reside in Dūyáng Lǐ, Shānyīn,
intending for his descendants
to end their days there.
The monastery grounds are the old foundations of his residence,
with the Jiāng River to the left and a lake to the right,
facing mountains and backed by valleys,
spanning east and west,
north and south.
wandering circuitously,
I choose to share the daily life
with eminent monks of austere practice,
cultivating the Sūtras and precepts in the morning,
and perusing illustrations and books in the evening.
My dwelling place is amidst the wind and clouds,
my refuge rests upon the water and moon.
Unexpectedly, the distinction between
Hua and Rong became blurred,
and the imperial court and markets declined.
Such circumstances wounded my feelings,
and these feelings are surely understandable.
Though I write with tears,
how can I express my suppressed emotions?
I only hope that future gentlemen
will pity my lament here.
I praise the auspicious division of Nándǒu,
which initiated the spiritual mystery of Dōngyuè.
It displayed the 'Cypress Wind' in Hán's verses,
and recorded 'Zhenshān' in Zhōu's records.
It enshrined Dà Yǔ's golden book,
and carved
the stone inscriptions of the tyrannical Qín.
The grand historian came to explore its caves,
and Zhōnglí left to open its casket.
Indeed, bamboo arrows are precious,
but how rare it is for a common stone to be valued!
I offer grand sacrifices to the abundant virtue,
and reside in an ancient temple of tranquil meditation.
This was truly the old garden of Yùzhāng,
which became a splendid land of gold.
Thus, my secluded heart becomes silent,
as if in a mirror,
seeking from afar.
Facing the towering and distant Zengfù,
and close to the deep and boundless tranquil lake.
Mountain branches twist and turn,
water foliage spreads and invades.
Gibbons hang and descend in the morning,
hungry flying squirrels chant at night.
Fruit
thickets and medicinal gardens,
peach paths and orange groves,
touch the clouds and brush the sun,
forming shade and creating gloom.
I preserve the elegant taste of nature,
and disdain the wild clutter of human dwellings.
I gaze at the winding
islands,
and face the overlapping sources of the river.
The flowing moon drifts far into the night,
and the gleaming mist encircles at dawn.
Wind draws cicadas to hiss and buzz,
rain sounds in the forest, long and drawn out.
Birds gradually grow tame and know when to come,
clouds are devoid of emotion yet naturally converge.
Thereupon, a spiritual pagoda opened in the wilderness,
and a meditation dwelling was built on the land.
Joyful gardens stretched far,
and happy trees grew luxuriantly.
Walking meditation on the grass,
seated meditation by the stream.
Upholding precepts, rattling the staff,
measuring shadows to eat vegetables.
It can be likened to a forest of steadfastness,
and temporarily resembles a place of Nirvāṇa.
My sorrow arises not at the end of the music,
nor does it begin when leaves fall.
How could I humble my will and disgrace
myself,
or fail to reveal my talent and promote myself?
I am caught in the wind and rain as if it were perpetually dark,
and weary of the crowing of roosters that grates on my ears.
Fortunately, I seek refuge in a lofty dwelling,
relying on the teachings bequeathed by the Master of Taming.
I discern the subtle words of the [Buddhist] four analytical knowledge,
and comprehend the profound principles of the three vehicles.
I cast off the bonds of the ten [fetters],
and remove the dust and defilements of the five delusions.
For a long time, I have forsaken fame and fortune,
and hope to forget the burdens of
wife and children.
I feel emotion for past days,
and entrust my understanding to future generations.
Why should a distant traveler be sorrowful?
I know my self-pity will never cease.
In sum, my ninth maternal uncle, Xiāo Bó, first occupied Guǎngzhōu.
Zǒng then went from Kuàijī to rely on him.
When Emperor Yuán of Liáng pacified Hóu Jǐng,
he summoned Zǒng to be Mingwēi Jiāngjūn and Shǐxīng Nèishǐ.
He allocated eight hundred hú of rice from the commandery's emolument for Zǒng's travel expenses.
However, Jiānglíng fell,
so he did not depart.
From then on, Zǒng sojourned in Língnán for several years.
In the fourth year of Tiānjiā,
he was summoned back to court as Zhōngshū Shìláng,
serving directly in the Shìzhōng Shěng.
He was successively promoted to Sītú Yòu Chángshǐ,
in charge of the Dōnggōng guǎnjì,
then Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng,
and concurrently Nánxú Zhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng.
He was appointed Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ and Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
with his Dōnggōng and Zhōngzhèng positions remaining as before.
He was promoted to Zuǒmín Shàngshū,
then transferred to Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
with his Zhōngzhèng position remaining as before.
Because he engaged in lengthy night drinking with the Crown Prince,
adopted the Consort Chén as his daughter,
and the Crown Prince made incognito visits to Zǒng's residence,
the Emperor was angered and dismissed him.
Soon after, he was made Shìzhōng,
and concurrently Zǔo Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
He was again made Zuǒmín Shàngshū,
and concurrently Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn.
Before he could be formally installed,
he was again dismissed due to official matters.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Sànqí Chángshì, Míngliè Jiāngjūn, and Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ,
then promoted to Tàicháng Qīng.
When the Last Emperor ascended the throne,
he was appointed Cíbù Shàngshū,
and again concurrently Zuǒ Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
participating in the selection of officials.
He was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì and Lìbù Shàngshū.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shàngshū Púyè,
continuing to participate in selection matters as before.
In the fourth year of Zhìdé,
he was granted the title Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn,
and allowed to appoint a certain number of subordinate officials.
Soon after, he was appointed Shàngshū Lìng,
granted a set of drum and wind instruments,
and granted a walking aid,
with all other honors remaining as before.
The imperial edict stated:
"Alas!
The Minister of Personnel is the foundation of governance,
the manager who oversees the administration.
Wéi Biāo called it the pivot,
Lǐ Gù compared it to the Big Dipper.
Moreover, it comprehensively manages the five bureaus,
and harmonizes all the myriad affairs.
It shares the responsibilities of the Grand Minister,
and exclusively holds the duties of the imperial secretariat.
You, with your lofty conduct and deep
and profound insights,
your exemplary norms and pure rules,
are a standard for refined demeanor.
As a master of literature and a repository of learning,
you are a leader among officials.
Therefore, you are capable of serving as a teacher and elder to the six ministries,
receiving universal trust and filling the roles.
You are a brilliant official among the eight ministers,
your deportment and example extend far and wide.
It is my hope that you will
now take charge of the court's affairs.
Go, and be reverent!
Diligently establish your excellent strategies,
and brilliantly illuminate our state.
How can you not be cautious!"
In the second year of Zhēnmíng,
he was advanced to the title Zhōngquán Jiāngjūn.
When the capital fell,
he entered Suí,
and was made Shàng Kāifǔ.
In the fourteenth year of Kāihuáng,
he died in Jiāngdū,
at the age of seventy-six.
Zǒng once summarized his life, saying:
"I have successively risen to prominent positions,
filling various ranks in the imperial court.
I did not seek worldly gain,
nor did I involve myself with powerful favorites.
I often patted my body and sighed to the heavens, saying,
'Zhuāng Qīngzhái rose to the position of prime
minister,
but left no remarkable deeds to be recorded;
Zhào Yuánshū, as an accountant official,
shone in the biographies.'
Since serving as an official in Chén,
I have never fawned over anyone,
nor interfered in any matter.
Throughout the long
and dusty world,
many vulgar individuals
bore grudges and hatred towards me.
But whether glorious or withered, favored or disgraced,
I did not take it to heart.
During the reign of Tàijiàn,
power shifted to petty individuals,
and sycophants and the jealous wielded authority.
I was repeatedly suppressed and dismissed.
Alas, such was my fate.
The Last Emperor, while still the Crown Prince,
paid attention to literature and arts.
I had long been favored and promoted,
our bond of grace was deep.
On the day he ascended the throne,
the time
Jì Miùlóng,
his bearing was like a celestial mansion,
rectifying all affairs,
the eight laws and six canons,
there was nothing he did not control.
In the past, Jìn Wǔdì asked Xún Gōngzēng, saying,
"The Zhou dynasty's
Grand Tutor [zǒngzǎi]
is today's Shàngshū Lìng."
Moreover, his talent was not half of the ancients',
and he remained idle like this.
Jìn Tàiwèi Lù Wán said,
"If they make me one of the Sāngōng,
then I know there
are no capable people in the world."
High office is a transient thing,
how could it be something to seek out?
In his youth, he devoted himself to Buddhism,
at over twenty years old,
he entered Zhōngshān to receive the Bodhisattva precepts from Fǎshī at Língyào Temple.
In his twilight years, he served as an official in Chén,
and befriended Bù Shàngrén
of Shèshān,
deeply realizing suffering and emptiness,
he further refined his precepts,
cultivating goodness in his heart,
and practicing compassion towards others,
he was quite self-disciplined,
but unable to abstain from meat and fine foods,
still stained by
worldly defilements,
for this, he felt lifelong shame.
In summary, Zǒng,
people of his time called it a "true record."
Zǒng practiced righteousness diligently,
was tolerant, gentle, and magnanimous.
He loved learning
and was skilled in writing,
especially good at five-character and seven-character poems;
however, he suffered from being frivolous and ornate,
which is why he was favored by the Hòuzhǔ.
There are many side pieces (uncollected works),
which enthusiasts circulated and enjoyed,
and this continues to this day.
During the Hòuzhǔ's reign,
Zǒng held political power,
but did not manage government affairs,
instead spending his days feasting and playing with the Hòuzhǔ in the rear palace,
along with Chén Xuān, Kǒng Fàn, Wáng Cuō, and over ten others,
who were then called "intimate guests."
Because of this, state affairs daily declined,
and discipline was not upheld.
Those who spoke out
were immediately dismissed with accusations,
the ruler and ministers were confused and disorderly,
leading to the dynasty's demise.
He has a collection of thirty volumes,
all circulated in the world.
His eldest son, Yì,
courtesy name Shēnyuán,
was quite skilled in writing.
His nature was extravagant,
relying on influence to be arrogant towards others,
even close relatives and old friends
were not spared from his slander and deceit.
He successively served as Zuòzuò Zuǒláng, Tàizǐ Shèrén, Xǐmǎ, Zhōngshū Huángmén Shìláng, and Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
Upon entering Suí,
he became Qínwáng Wénxué.
His seventh son, Cuǐ,
was Fùmǎ Dūwèi, Mìshū Láng, Suí Gěishì Láng,
and Zhí Mìshūshěng Xuéshì.
Yáo Chá, courtesy name Bóshěn,
was a native of Wúxīng Wǔkāng.
His ninth-generation ancestor, Xìn,
was Wú Tàicháng Qīng,
renowned in the Jiāngzuǒ region.
Chá showed extreme filial piety from a young age,
and was known for his filial service to his parents.
At six years old,
he could recite over ten thousand words from books.
In his youth, he did not enjoy playing,
and never paid attention to games like chess or other diversions.
He diligently and assiduously studied,
continuing day and night.
At twelve,
he was already capable of writing prose.
His father, the former Kāifǔ Sēngyuán,
was famous during the Liáng Wǔdì era,
and received generous treatment from the two palaces.
Whenever he received offerings,
he would give them to Chá and his brothers
as funds for their studies.
Chá used them all to accumulate books and maps,
thus broadening his knowledge daily.
At thirteen,
Liáng Jiǎnwén Dì, then in the Eastern Palace,
was diligently cultivating literature and righteousness,
and immediately invited him to Xuānyóu Hall to listen to lectures and discussions,
and he was praised by scholars.
When Jiǎnwén succeeded to the throne,
he treated him with even greater courtesy.
He started his career as Nánhǎiwáng Guó Zuǒchángshì,
concurrently Sīwén Shìláng.
He was appointed Nánjùnwáng Xíngcānjūn,
concurrently Shàngshū Jiàbù Láng.
When the Liáng dynasty fell into chaos,
he returned to his hometown in Jīnlíng with his parents.
At that time, the eastern regions were ravaged by war,
people starved and resorted to cannibalism,
and there was no place to buy grain.
Chá's family was large,
and they all gathered wild vegetables to sustain themselves.
Chá often struggled through difficulties,
seeking and begging for provisions,
and they always managed to have a continuous supply of grain.
He also often reduced his own share to give to his younger siblings,
and even to old friends who were in dire need, sharing with them,
contenting himself with only wild herbs and coarse food.
During the period of chaos and separation,
he did not abandon his diligent studies.
Yuándì ascended the throne in Jīngzhōu,
and his father, following the example of court officials, went to the Western Terrace.
Yuándì appointed Chá as Yuánxiāng Lìng.
At that time, the district was desolate,
and the displaced people had not returned.
Chá lightened their taxes and labor,
and encouraged them to farm.
Consequently, the population prospered,
and the people praise him to this day.
Zhōngshū Shìláng and director of writings, Dù Zhīwěi, deeply admired Chá,
and submitted a memorial to appoint Chá as assistant in writing,
and to compile history.
In the early Yǒngdìng era,
he was appointed Shǐxīngwáng Fǔ Gōngcāo Cānjūn,
soon after he was made Jiādé Diàn Xuéshì,
then transferred to Zhōngwèi and Yítóng Shǐxīngwáng Fǔ Jìshì Cānjūn.
Lìbù Shàngshū Xú Líng, who was then director of writings,
again invited him to be a historical assistant.
When Líng submitted memorials requesting to resign and retire,
he asked Chá to draft them,
and Líng sighed in admiration, saying,
"I am not as capable!"
In the early Tàijiàn era,
he was made Xuānmíng Diàn Xuéshì,
and appointed Sànqí Shìláng and Zuǒ Tōngzhí.
Soon after, he concurrently served as Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
and was dispatched to Zhōu as an envoy.
The elderly scholars from Jiāngzuǒ who had previously been in Guān Yòu
all admired him.
Pèiguó Liú Zhēn secretly visited him at the official residence and inquired about over ten doubtful points in the Hàn Shū,
which he all analyzed and explained,
each with scriptural evidence.
Zhēn told his close associates,
"A renowned person is indeed not empty."
He wrote the Xīpìn Dàolǐ Jì,
which was very detailed.
Upon his return as envoy,
he was appointed Dōnggōng Xuéshì.
At that time, Jìyáng Jiāng Zǒng, Wúguó Gù Yěwáng, Lù Qióng, his cousin Yú, Hénán Chǔ Jiè, Běidì Fù Zài, and others,
all distinguished by their talent and learning,
entertained and served him day and night.
Whenever Chá spoke or wrote,
all the others respected him as their leader.
The crown prince showed him special courtesy,
and his affection surpassed that of other officials.
All the square-foot documents and handwritten notes required within the palace
were entrusted to Chá for drafting.
He was also frequently made to alternate with Yěwáng in questioning each other,
and always received praise and encouragement.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Cíbù Shìláng.
This office was responsible for sacrifices to heaven and earth and ancestral temples.
In the past, Wèi Wáng Sù proposed sacrifices to heaven and earth,
establishing palace music and suspended bells,
and the Eight-Row Dance,
and thereafter this practice was followed without change.
Liáng Wǔdì believed that while serving people required elaborate rites,
serving gods required simple rites,
and there was no ancient text mentioning palace music and suspended bells.
In the early Chén dynasty, this was adopted,
but no one proposed changes or additions.
Gāozōng wished to establish full musical performances,
and tasked the relevant officials to deliberate,
considering Liáng Wǔdì's view to be wrong.
At that time, prominent scholars, famous Confucians, and those in court positions,
all sought to align with the emperor's will,
and immediately agreed.
However, Chá extensively cited classics,
and alone disagreed with the consensus,
arguing that Liáng's music was correct.
Everyone was astonished at the time,
and all felt ashamed and convinced.
Púyè Xú Líng then changed his stance to agree with Chá's argument.
His refusal to conform to the times or follow popular customs
was always like this.
He was appointed as the Palace Affairs Recorder for Xuānhuì Yídū Wáng,
and concurrently served as an Erudite of the Eastern Palace.
He successively held the posts of Cínyì Cānjūn in the bureaus of Rénwēi Huáinán Wáng and Píngnán Jiàn'ān Wáng.
He resigned due to a mourning period for his mother.
Soon after, he was appointed as Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn,
and put in charge of compiling the history of the Liáng dynasty.
He firmly declined but was not excused.
When the Later Lord ascended the throne, he was commanded to concurrently serve as Tōngshì Shèrén of the Eastern Palace,
with his positions as Jiāngjūn and supervisor of history compilation remaining unchanged.
He was further commanded to exclusively manage the writing of eulogies, posthumous titles, and similar documents.
In the first year of Zhìdé,
he was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng,
then transferred to Tàizǐ Pú,
with all other positions remaining as before.
Initially,
when the Liáng dynasty fell,
his father, Yáo Tǎn (垣), entered Cháng'ān.
Yáo Chá subsisted on vegetarian food and wore plain clothes,
and did not listen to music.
At this time, the news of his father's death reached Jiāngnán through an envoy.
At that time, the mourning period for Chá's mother, Lady Wéi, had just concluded.
The Later Lord, seeing Chá's emaciated state,
feared that further grief would lead to collapse.
Thus, he secretly dispatched Zhōngshū Shèrén Sīmǎ Shēn to Chá's residence to express condolences,
and also ordered Shēn to specifically console and restrain him.
Afterwards, he again sent Shēn to convey an imperial decree and admonish him, saying:
"I know that your excessive grief has surpassed proper decorum,
and I am deeply concerned about this.
You are a solitary individual,
and the continuation of your lineage rests upon you.
To grieve to the point of destroying your health
is not permitted by the teachings of the sages.
You should slightly moderate your grief
to maintain ritual propriety.
Since your sorrow is so profound,
I have thus expressed this."
Soon after, he was appointed Zhongyì Jiāngjūn and concurrently Tōngshì Shèrén of the Eastern Palace.
Chá's ambition was to complete the mourning period,
and he repeatedly offered his resignation,
but these were all suppressed and disallowed.
He also submitted a memorial with a summary that read:
"My private household has suffered misfortune,
and I have endured calamity and punishment.
I have stolen a few moments of life,
hoping to express my filial piety and respect,
but illness has followed one after another,
my body is clad in coarse hemp,
I am no longer among ordinary people,
and I will soon end my days under a straw mat and on the earth.
How could I expect the imperial grace to extend to me so exceptionally,
bestowing upon me official attire?
Upon receiving this favor,
I feel even more ashamed and embarrassed.
Moreover, the palace is a secret and profound place,
and attending and reporting are frequent duties.
How can I, in this state of desolation and decay, presume to hold such a position?
I humbly wish that by Your Majesty's supreme virtue and filial rule,
you would pity my diminished state,
allowing my remaining soul to breathe
and fulfill the rest of my life."
The imperial edict replied:
"I have read your memorial and understand your feelings.
Your conduct is pure and profound,
and your reputation has long been well-known.
It is reasonable that you should uphold ritual propriety,
and not yet be burdened with official duties.
However, participating in the affairs of the Eastern Palace
is a sincere expectation placed upon you.
To genuinely suppress and refuse this
is something you cannot do."
Soon after, he was commanded to take charge of the affairs of Zhùzuò Láng.
When his mourning period ended,
he was appointed Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng,
and oversaw the compilation of writings.
As Chá had repeatedly been in mourning,
and had maintained a vegetarian diet for a long time,
after his release from mourning,
he developed a respiratory illness.
The Later Lord once summoned him for a private audience,
and seeing Chá's extreme emaciation,
he was moved.
He said to Chá:
"The court cherishes you,
and you should cherish yourself.
Since you have been on a sparse diet for years,
you may cease observing a prolonged vegetarian fast."
He also sent Dùzhī Shàngshū Wáng Yuàn to convey an imperial decree,
reiterating his comfort and persuasion,
and allowing him to eat an evening meal.
The handwritten edict said:
"You are so frail and emaciated,
and have maintained a sparse diet for many years.
It is not advisable to eat only one meal,
as it hinders your recovery.
If you follow what has been indicated,
it would be very good."
Although Chá received this edict,
he still adhered to his long-held vows.
He was again appointed Mìshū Jiān,
still overseeing the compilation of writings,
and he repeatedly declined,
but his refusals were graciously rejected.
While at the Mìshū Shěng, Chá made extensive revisions and corrections.
He also submitted a memorial proposing the compilation of the Zhōngshū Biǎojí.
He was appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
and soon after, Dùzhī Shàngshū.
Within a few months, he was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū,
still overseeing the compilation of writings as before.
Chá was extensively learned in ancient texts,
and particularly skilled in assessing people.
Regarding the origins of surnames,
the divisions of lineages,
official positions, marriages,
rise and fall, eminence and humbleness—
when he spoke of them,
nothing was missed.
Moreover, his ability to discern and assess
was long regarded by his contemporaries as that of a master craftsman.
When he was transferred to the Selection Department,
it perfectly aligned with the court's expectations.
Initially,
when Lìbù Shàngshū Cài Zhēng was transferred to Zhōngshū Lìng,
the Later Lord was selecting his replacement.
Shàngshū Lìng Jiāng Zǒng and others all recommended Chá.
The imperial edict replied:
"Yáo Chá is not only profoundly learned,
but also of pure and upright conduct.
A talent for administering selections is rare,
and now we have found him."
Then, the emperor personally drafted an edict
and read it to Chá.
Chá declined very earnestly.
On another day, he was summoned to discuss selection matters,
and Chá, shedding tears, bowed and pleaded:
"Your subject is of a humble clan from Dōnggāo,
and my talent is common and limited.
I have no ambition for distant achievements,
and my desire for a long career has ceased.
Recently, I have held positions unworthily,
knowing for a long time that I exceeded my station,
especially through my service to the Eastern Palace,
where I was unduly favored.
Today, my undeserved promotion
is not due to my talent.
Even if Your Majesty exceptionally elevates the unworthy and meager,
what about the established order of the court?
My ninth-generation ancestor, Yáo Xìn,
was renowned in past generations.
At that time, he merely held a position in the Selection Department,
and since then, few have followed in his footsteps.
Your subject, by chance of fortune, has been promoted,
bathed in imperial grace and favor,
repeatedly attaining undeserved positions,
always keenly aware of hindering worthy individuals.
Although I am ignorant,
I somewhat know myself.
In my words and actions,
I never sought glory or nobility.
How could I expect the weighty responsibility of selection
to be misguidedly entrusted to an untalented person?
Moreover, with Your Majesty's brilliant reign,
affairs surpass those of past eras.
With distinguished aristocratic families,
and renowned ministers in counsel,
if appointments are made appropriately,
then positions will be fitting.
Having been nurtured by moral teachings since childhood,
I certainly know this is not permissible."
The Later Lord said:
"The selection of officials
is where public opinion converges.
In the past, Máo Jiè had a refined and upright character,
Lú Yù was impartial and just,
Wáng Yùn made selections appropriately,
and Shān Tāo never lost talent in his recommendations.
Seeking these qualities in you,
you surely possess them all.
Although there is a ritual separation between us as sovereign and subject,
our relationship is extraordinary.
Your ability to discern human character
is a sincere hope I place in you.
Moreover, there is no shame in being prudent."
From the time Chá held prominent positions,
he was very diligent in maintaining integrity and purity,
and apart from his official salary,
he did not accept any other private dealings.
Once, a private student of his, not daring to offer a large gift,
only sent one bolt of Southern plain cloth
and one roll of patterned silk.
"My clothes are only made of hemp cloth and plain silk.
These items are useless to me.
If you wish to maintain contact,
please do not trouble yourself with such things."
The man humbly pleaded,
still hoping he would accept,
but Chá sternly ordered him out.
When the Chén dynasty was overthrown and incorporated into the Suí dynasty,
in the ninth year of the Kāihuáng reign,
an imperial edict appointed [Yáo] Chá as Mìshū Chéng.
He was separately ordered to compile the histories of the Liáng and Chén dynasties.
He was also ordered to attend court regularly at the Zhūhuá Gé.
Wén Dì observed Chá's modest lifestyle
and one day summoned him alone to the inner palace.
After bestowing upon him fruits and vegetables,
he pointed to Chá and said to his courtiers,
"I hear that Yáo Chá's scholarship and conduct are unmatched in this age.
In conquering Chén, I have gained only this one man."
In the thirteenth year,
he inherited the title of Běijiàng Jùngōng.
When Chá had previously been dispatched as an envoy to Zhōu,
he had been able to meet his father Sēng Yuán.
At the time of their parting,
Sēng Yuán had fainted and then revived.
Now, upon inheriting the title,
Chá's sorrow and emotion were intensified,
and all who witnessed it could not help but sigh in commiseration.
In his youth, Chá had once received the Bodhisattva precepts from Shàng Chánshī at Míngqìng Sì on Zhōngshān.
When he served as an official in Chén,
all his official salary and emoluments were donated to the temple for construction.
He also commissioned a stele to be erected for the Chánshī,
with a text that was very vigorous and beautiful.
At this time,
he happened to see a poem by Xiāo Ziyún, the Guózǐ Jìjiǔ of Liáng, written for the Chán retreat of this temple.
Reading it, he felt a surge of sadness,
and so he used Xiāo Ziyún's rhyme scheme to compose a poem expressing his feelings.
The words were again sorrowful and poignant,
and both clergy and laypeople praised him even more for it.
When his stepmother Dù Shì passed away,
he resigned from his post.
During his mourning period,
white doves nested above his door.
In the second year of Rénshòu,
an imperial edict stated:
"Former Mìshū Chéng and Kāiguó Gōng of Běijiàng Jùn, Yáo Chá,
is a diligent scholar awaiting questions,
extensively versed in all classics,
who cultivated his character and established his virtue,
remaining unwavering even in old age.
Although he is in a state of mourning,
it is fitting to set aside the mourning rites.
He is appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì,
and his enfeoffment remains as before."
He was also ordered to attend to Jìn Wáng Yáng Zhāo and read to him.
When Yáng Dì was initially the crown prince,
Chá was frequently summoned
to discuss literary works.
At the beginning of his reign,
an imperial edict appointed Chá as Tàizǐ Nèishèrén,
with all other positions remaining as before.
When the imperial carriage went on tours,
Chá always accompanied it.
When clothing and caps were changed,
and court rituals were revised and corrected,
Chá was the only one frequently consulted and interviewed
on these matters.
At the age of seventy-four,
in the second year of Dàyè,
he died in Dōngdū.
He left a will for a simple burial,
emphasizing frugality.
His instructions briefly stated:
"My family has always been composed of humble scholars,
with our own established customs.
My wish is to be clothed in monastic attire,
all of cloth,
with earth covering my body.
However, I fear you will not bear to do this.
If that is the case,
then a thin pine coffin,
just enough to enclose my body,
with earth covering only the coffin, will suffice.
On the day of the burial,
use only a simple cart
to transport the coffin directly to the north of the old family tomb.
In the Liáng era,
when I was fourteen,
I received the Bodhisattva precepts from Shàng Chánshī at Míngqìng Sì on Zhōngshān.
Since then, I have deeply understood suffering and emptiness,
and have somewhat known how to seek enlightenment.
I once lingered in the mountain temple,
and once I left, I forgot to return.
When I served in the Chén dynasty,
various prominent scholars then granted me reputation and esteem.
Combined with the emperor's favor,
my official career reached prominence.
Since entering court,
I have also received imperial grace.
However, being entangled in the human world,
my original aspirations were not fulfilled.
Moreover, I have practiced vegetarianism for over fifty years,
and as time passed,
I have maintained it without fail.
After I close my eyes,
there is no need to set up a spirit tablet.
Place a small bed,
offer clear water daily,
and on the six fast days, offer vegetarian food, fruits, and vegetables,
according to what the family has,
without needing special arrangements."
Initially,
Chá wished to read the complete Buddhist canon,
and he had already accomplished this.
As he was about to die,
he felt no pain or distress,
but merely sat facing west,
with clear mind,
saying,
"All is empty and tranquil."
Afterwards, his body remained soft,
and his complexion was as usual.
The two palaces mourned and felt regret,
sending very generous funeral gifts.
Chá was profoundly filial
and had an insightful understanding of human relationships.
He was modest and humble,
never boasting of his strengths.
He was serene all day long,
finding joy only in writing and records,
and there was no ancient text he had not read.
Whenever he composed something,
he often used novel and unique ideas,
unseen by others,
and everyone highly valued his rich erudition.
Moreover, he was dedicated to writing books,
unwearied even in old age,
personally copying and compiling,
without ever stopping for a moment.
He was especially fond of studying and verifying ancient and modern texts,
and correcting characters.
His work was brilliant and fluent,
and did not decline with age.
He was also familiar with Buddhist scriptures,
and the essays he composed about temples, pagodas, and monks
were particularly ornate and refined.
While in office, he often recommended others,
and if there was any good deed worthy of record,
he would invariably praise and promote it.
If anyone sought his assistance inappropriately,
he would dismiss them with reason.
He served his superiors with utmost devotion,
doing everything he knew how to do.
He handled confidential matters
without ever leaking them.
Although his appointments were already prominent,
and officials looked up to him,
he deeply cherished tranquility and retreat,
avoiding fame and power.
He maintained a clean and honest lifestyle,
his possessions were often meager,
and when some advised him to manage his livelihood,
he would smile without answering.
He was harmonious with his relatives
and devoted to old acquaintances.
The stipends and gifts he received
were all used for relief and assistance.
The compositions of the Later Emperor were numerous,
filling many scrolls.
He specifically copied a set and gave it to Chá,
ordering him to revise and correct any uncertainties.
Chá, too, sincerely served the emperor,
with nothing concealed.
The Later Emperor once casually said to his courtiers:
"Yáo Chá is learned and widely read,
his writing style is elegant and structured.
If one seeks his equal in antiquity,
〔一二〕it is still difficult to find a match.
In the present age,
he is truly a model teacher.
Moreover, his discussions and answers are very detailed and clear,
〔一三〕listening to him makes one forget fatigue."
Whenever Chá composed an essay,
the emperor would immediately request the original.
The emperor said:
"My enjoyment of Yáo Chá's writings
〔一四〕is not merely endless;
he is truly a master."
Xú Líng (徐陵) was famous in his generation.
Every time Zhá (察) made a literary composition,
he (Xú Líng) particularly admired and valued it.
He once said to Zǐjiǎn (子儉):
“Scholar Yáo (姚) has unparalleled virtue and learning;
you should take him as your teacher.”
Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Jiāng Zǒng (江總) was particularly close and friendly with Zhá (察).
Whenever he made a composition,
he would first show it to Zhá (察) for review,
and only then would he use it.
When Zǒng (總) was a Zhānshì (詹事),
he once composed a five-hundred-character poem titled “Dēng Gōngchéng (登宮城)”.
At that time, the crown prince and other famous worthies, including Xú Líng (徐陵), all wrote similar pieces.
Later, Xú Gōng (徐公) said to Jiāng (江):
“My fifty-rhyme harmonization is
sent to be included in your collection, my brother.”
When Jiāng (江) later compiled his writings,
he couldn't find Zhá's (察) harmonized version anymore.
He recounted Xú's (徐) intent
and said to Zhá (察):
“Your great talent and profound learning
would surely add splendor to my humble work.
Now I need your five-hundred-character harmonization
to match Lord Xú's (徐侯) chapter.”
Zhá (察), being modest, had not yet given it.
Jiāng (江) said:
“If I don't get your composition,
my poem will also have to be discarded,
which would also go against what Xú Gōng (徐公) entrusted to me.
How can I let both of us suffer such a loss?”
Zhá (察), having no choice,
then copied his original and gave it to him.
He was esteemed by cultivated people;
such instances were common.
His works included "Hànshū Xùnzǎn" (漢書訓纂) in thirty volumes,
"Shuō Lín" (說林) in ten volumes,
"Xī Pìn" (西聘), "Yù Xǐ" (玉璽), and "Jiànkāng Sān Zhōng" (建康三鍾) in one volume each,
all exhaustive and comprehensive.
Additionally, his collected works totaled twenty volumes,
all circulated in the world.
Although Zhá's (察) compilation of the histories of Liáng (梁) and Chén (陳) was not yet complete,
during the Kaihuáng (開皇) era of Suí Wéndì (隋文帝),
he sent the Nèishǐ Shèrén (內史舍人) Yú Shìjī (虞世基) to request the manuscript,
and it was presented to the emperor.
It is now in the imperial palace.
The originals of the two histories of Liáng (梁) and Chén (陳) were mostly compiled by Zhá (察).
As for the prefaces, treatises, annals, and biographies that were missing,
at the time of his death,
he still instructed his son Sīlián (思廉) on the principles and structure,
to widely seek out and continue the compilation.
Sīlián (思廉) tearfully complied.
Sīlián (思廉) served as Fǎcáo Cānjūn (法曹參軍) in the household of Héngyáng Wáng (衡陽王) in Chén (陳),
then transferred to Huìjī Wáng Zhǔbù (會稽王主簿).
Upon entering Suí (隋),
he was appointed Xíng Cānjūn (行參軍) in the household of Hàn Wáng (漢王),
managing the secretariat,
and soon after, he was made Sīfǎ (司法) of Héjiān Jùn (河間郡).
At the beginning of Dàyè (大業),
Nèishǐ Shìláng (內史侍郎) Yú Shìjī (虞世基) proposed that Sīlián (思廉) complete the histories of the Liáng (梁) and Chén (陳) dynasties.
From then on,
he gradually undertook the补续 (completion and continuation).
The imperial historian says: Jiāng Zǒng (江總) upheld a clear and noble standard,
enriched with eloquent prose,
and as a teacher and head of the six ministries,
he was graceful and enjoyed the respect of the court.
The imperial historian's former minister embodied this excellent virtue,
〔一五〕illuminating these hundred good deeds,
which could reform customs
and strengthen human relationships.
As for the books of the Nine Streams and Seven Epitomes,
the records of famous mountains and stone chambers,
the books of Jí Jùn (汲郡) and Kǒng Táng (孔堂),
and the texts on jade boxes and golden tablets,
he exhaustively researched their profound meanings
and thoroughly explored every hidden corner.
Therefore, his learning surpassed that of others,
and scholars regarded him as a standard.
Having held prominent positions,
the national decrees and court regulations,
as well as ancient and modern disputes,
the later ruler all relied on this former minister's judgments.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 22: Nine Kings of Shìzǔ (世祖), Twenty-nine Kings of Gāozōng (高宗), Eleven Sons of Hòuzhǔ (後主).
Shìzǔ (世祖) had thirteen sons: Shěn (沈) Empress gave birth to the deposed emperor and Shǐxīng Wáng Bómào (始興王伯茂).
Yán (嚴) Shúyuán (淑媛) gave birth to Póyáng Wáng Bóshān (鄱陽王伯山) and Jìn'ān Wáng Bógōng (晉安王伯恭).
Pān (潘) Rónghuá (容華) gave birth to Xīn'ān Wáng Bógù (新安王伯固).
Liú (劉) Zhāohuá (昭華) gave birth to Héngyáng Wáng Bóxìn (衡陽王伯信).
Wáng (王) Chōnghuá (充華) gave birth to Lúlíng Wáng Bórén (廬陵王伯仁).
Zhāng (張) Xiūróng (脩容) gave birth to Jiāngxià Wáng Bóyì (江夏王伯義).
Hán (韓) Xiūhuá (脩華) gave birth to Wǔlíng Wáng Bólǐ (武陵王伯禮).
Jiāng (江) Guìfēi (貴妃) gave birth to Yǒngyáng Wáng Bózhì (永陽王伯智).
Kǒng (孔) Guìfēi (貴妃) gave birth to Guìyáng Wáng Bómóu (桂陽王伯謀).
Bógù (伯固), who committed rebellion, has a separate biography.
Two sons died young,
their names are not recorded in this book.
Shǐxīng Wáng Bómào (始興王伯茂), courtesy name Yùzhī (鬱之),
was the second son of Shìzǔ (世祖).
Originally,
Gāozǔ's (高祖) elder brother, Shǐxīng Zhāoliè Wáng Dàotán (始興昭烈王道談), served in the Liáng (梁) dynasty,
as Dōnggōng Zhíhé Jiāngjūn (東宮直閤將軍).
During Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) rebellion,
he led two thousand archers to reinforce the capital,
and died in the city from a stray arrow.
(Shàotài (紹泰)) [Tàipíng (太平)] second year,
he was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng (侍中), Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dūdū Nán Yùnzhōu Zhū Jūnfù (都督南運州諸軍事), Nán Yùnzhōu Cìshǐ (南運州刺史),
and enfeoffed as (Yìxīng Jùngōng (義興郡公)) [Chángchéng Xiàngōng (長城縣公)],
with the posthumous title Zhāoliè (昭烈).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) received the abdication,
he was further posthumously granted Pàojì Dàjiāngjūn (驃騎大將軍), Tàifù (太傅),
Yángzhōu Mù (揚州牧),
and re-enfeoffed as Shǐxīng Jùnwáng (始興郡王),
with an estate of two thousand households.
The king gave birth to Shìzǔ (世祖) and Gāozōng (高宗).
Gāozōng (高宗) moved to Guān Yòu (關右) at the end of Liáng Chéngshèng (梁承聖) era.
At this point, Gāozǔ (高祖) remotely designated Gāozōng (高宗) to inherit the title of Shǐxīng Sìwáng (始興嗣王),
to offer sacrifices to Zhāoliè Wáng (昭烈王).
In the sixth month of Yǒngdìng (永定) third year,
Gāozǔ (高祖) passed away.
In the same month, Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the imperial throne.
At that time, Gāozōng (高宗) was in Zhōu (周) and had not yet returned.
Shìzǔ (世祖), finding the main lineage lacking a successor for sacrifices,
issued an edict in the tenth month of that year, stating:
“Recently, the imperial foundation was established,
and collateral relatives were enfeoffed.
I, being personally in this position,
specifically initiated a great state.
My younger brother Xū (頊) succeeded the ancestral sacrifices of the family.
Although his territory was established,
there was no way to offer sacrifices.
Furthermore, having experienced family misfortune
and early sorrow,
the crown prince is far away,
and his chariot has not returned.
I, a humble person,
have received this great destiny,
and follow the precedents of the imperial throne,
bearing profound sentiments like walking on thin ice.
Now that I have entered to serve the great lineage,
the feudal sacrifices are cut off.
The ancestral temple of Shǐxīng Guó (始興國) has no master for its seasonal sacrifices.
Looking at the frost and dew,
I am moved to extreme grief.
Therefore, Sìwáng Xū (嗣王頊) is to be re-enfeoffed as Ānchéng Wáng (安成王).
My second son, Bómào (伯茂), is to be enfeoffed as Shǐxīng Wáng (始興王),
to offer sacrifices to Zhāoliè Wáng (昭烈王).
Grant one rank of nobility to all who succeed their fathers in the realm.
May this express my boundless filial piety
and eternally secure the prosperity of the empire.”
According to the old system, kings who were enfeoffed
but not yet given military titles
were not assigned administrative staff.
Thereupon, the Bāzuò (八座) of the Shàngshū (尚書)奏 (memorialized), saying:
“Indeed, enhancing noble titles
and adorning carriages and attire
serve to illuminate their virtue
and influence the populace.
The second imperial son, the newly appointed Shǐxīng Wáng Bómào (始興王伯茂),
inherits supreme status,
with brilliant divine qualities.
His jade-like brilliance shines on his auspicious birth,
and his orchid-like fragrance graces his splendid youth.
His pure radiance and excellent reputation
grow daily and monthly.
His Way is as profound as Píng (平) and Hé (河),
and his fame surpasses Gǔn (袞) and Zhí (植).
The imperial heart, moved by affection,
and the emperor's profound nature,
seeing the main lineage lacking a successor,
appointed him to inherit the feudal lineage.
Although he has received the symbols of nobility,
he has not yet assumed military insignia.
How can this glorify his sagacious wisdom
and favor the imperial branch?
We, your ministers, have deliberated
and propose that he be granted the title of Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (寧遠將軍)
and assigned administrative staff.”
The edict said:
“Granted.”
Soon after, he was appointed Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dūdū Nán Lángyá Péngchéng Èr Jùn Zhū Jūnfù (都督南琅邪彭城二郡諸軍事), and Péngchéng Tàishǒu (彭城太守).
In Tiānjiā (天嘉) second year,
he was promoted to Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn (宣惠將軍) and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (揚州刺史).
Bómào (伯茂) was intelligent,
loved learning,
and was humble and respectful to scholars.
Also, being the crown prince's younger brother by the same mother, Shìzǔ (世祖) deeply loved and esteemed him.
At this time, soldiers from the Northern Expedition army in Dāntú (丹徒) illegally
excavated the tomb of Jìn Xī Tán (晉郗曇),
and obtained a large number of calligraphies by Jìn Yòujiāngjūn Wáng Xīzhī (晉右將軍王羲之) and other famous worthies.
When the matter was discovered,
the calligraphies were confiscated by the government
and stored in the imperial library.
Shìzǔ (世祖), knowing Bómào (伯茂) loved ancient things,
bestowed many of them upon him.
Because of this, Bómào (伯茂) became very skilled in cursive and clerical scripts,
and deeply mastered the style of Yòujūn (右軍).
In the third year,
he was appointed Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn (鎮東將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), and Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ (東揚州刺史).
When Fèi Dì ascended the throne,
Bó Mào was in the capital.
Liú Shīzhī and others forged an edict to send Gāo Zōng away,
and Bó Mào advised them to complete it.
After Shīzhī and others were executed,
Gāo Zōng feared that Bó Mào would stir up the court.
In the first year of Guāngdà,
he was promoted to Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn,
and ordered to reside in the forbidden palace,
spending his time exclusively with Fèi Dì.
At this time, the hopes of the four seas
all rested with Gāo Zōng.
Bó Mào was deeply displeased,
and was resentful day and night,
often uttering malicious words.
Gāo Zōng, considering him incompetent,
paid him no mind.
When Jiǎng Yù of Jiàn'ān and Hán Zǐgāo and others plotted rebellion,
Bó Mào also secretly participated in their scheme.
In the eleventh month of the second year,
the Empress Dowager issued an order to depose Fèi Dì as Línhǎi Wáng.
On that same day, another order was issued, saying:
"Bó Mào is frivolous;
from his tender age,
he has betrayed solemn teachings,
and increasingly indulged in wickedness and cunning.
He always believed that as the younger brother,
he ought to hold national power,
without regard for his years or virtue,
he became increasingly arrogant and reckless,
plotting to cause chaos and disorder,
inciting unrest in the inner palace,
seeking to attract dangerous elements,
and coveting high office.
The heir to the throne lost his way,
and this became the beginning of the chaos.
All these vicious individuals
acted as his masterminds.
It is right to remove him from his position
and punish this criminal.
Reflecting on the imperial lineage,
we still harbor sadness and regret.
He may be specially demoted to Wēnmá Hóu.
He should be placed under strict house arrest
and sent to his separate residence."
"That it should come to this
only increases our lamentation."
At that time, outside the six gates, there was a separate mansion
used for the coming-of-age ceremonies and weddings of the various princes,
named the Hūndì.
At this point, Bó Mào was ordered to reside there.
On the way, he encountered bandits
and died in his carriage
at the age of eighteen.
Póyáng Wáng Bóshān, courtesy name Jìngzhī,
was the third son of Shìzǔ.
He had a magnificent appearance
and elegant demeanor.
His joy or anger was not apparent on his face,
and Shìzǔ greatly admired him.
Initially, during Gāozǔ's time,
the empire was in its early stages,
and the protocols for the enfeoffment of princes were often incomplete.
When Bóshān was to be enfeoffed,
Shìzǔ wished to emphasize the importance of the event.
On the *bǐngchén* day of the seventh month in the first year of Tiānjiā,
the eight bureaus of the Shàngshū reported, saying:
"Your subjects have heard that when the main branch is upright and trustworthy,
the enterprise of Zōng Zhōu is expanded;
when the foundation is firmly established,
the base of Huáng Hàn endures for generations.
Thus, it could coordinate and proclaim the Five Phases,
and set the standard for a hundred kings,
firmly establish the spiritual roots,
and secure the predestined reign.
The third imperial son, Bóshān,
displayed sagacious virtue from his childhood,
and showed extraordinary talent from his youth.
He shines brightly in the inner court,
and illuminates the palace gates.
Yet his jade scepter has not been held,
nor his golden chariot driven.
How can this promote the proper order of the royal lineage
and establish the imperial relatives as bulwarks?
Your subjects have discussed this
and deem it appropriate to enfeoff him as Póyáng Jùnwáng."
An imperial edict said:
"Granted."
Then Xiāo Ruì, Sànqí Chángshì and Dùzhī Shàngshū, was sent with credentials, also serving as Tàizǎi, to announce it at the Tàimiào.
Wáng Zhì, Wǔbīng Shàngshū, was also sent with credentials, also serving as Tàizǎi, to announce it at the Tàishè.
In the tenth month of that year,
the Emperor, from the imperial veranda, issued the investiture edict, saying:
"Alas!
The establishment of feudal lords
to assist and protect the royal house
is a practice reverently followed from ancient precedents.
You, Bóshān,
have early on exhibited exceptional talent and virtue,
and possess innate knowledge of filial piety and reverence.
Your virtuous character and noble kinship
are universally acclaimed.
The establishment of a great state
is indeed for maintaining order.
Therefore, reverently following the people's aspirations,
we bestow upon you this jade regalia.
Go, and be diligent!
Strive to establish a good reputation and achievements,
and forever protect the imperial ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain.
How can one not be careful!"
After the ceremony,
an imperial order commanded all princes and dukes and those below them to feast at the prince's residence.
He was then appointed Dōng Zhōnglángjiāng and Wú Jùn Tàishǒu.
In the sixth year,
he was made Yuánjiāng Dūdū, Píngběi Jiāngjūn, and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the first year of Tiānkāng,
he was promoted to Zhènběi Jiāngjūn.
When Gāo Zōng was regent,
he did not wish Bóshān to be stationed on the frontier.
In the first year of Guāngdà,
he was transferred to Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn and Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the first year of Tàijiàn,
he was summoned to be Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn and Zhōnglǐngjūn.
In the sixth year,
he again became Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
Soon after, he was Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the eleventh year,
he entered the court as Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
with the added honorific Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and was also granted drum and pipe music and attendants.
When the Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zhōngquán Dàjiāngjūn.
In the fourth year of Zhìdé,
he was sent out as Chíjǐe, Dūdū Dōngyáng Fēng Èrzhōu Zhūjūnsì, and Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the added title of Shìzhōng,
while all other appointments remained as before.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng,
he mourned his birth mother
and resigned from office.
The following year,
he was reinstated as Zhènwèi Dàjiāngjūn,
Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and granted ten sword-bearing guards.
He passed away in the first month of the third year,
at the age of forty.
Bóshān was generous and kind-hearted,
and had a handsome demeanor.
Moreover, among the princes, he was the eldest,
and the Hòuzhǔ greatly respected and valued him.
Whenever there was a coming-of-age ceremony, wedding, or banquet at court,
Bóshān was always made the host.
When he mourned his birth mother,
he was known for his filial piety during the mourning period.
The Hòuzhǔ once visited the residence of Cài Zhēng, Shàngshū Púyè,
and then went to offer condolences to Bóshān.
Bóshān cried so much he almost fainted.
Consequently, he was reinstated as Zhènwèi Jiāngjūn.
The Hòuzhǔ then said to his officials:
"Póyáng Wáng's extreme filial piety is commendable.
Furthermore, he is the eldest of the 'Western Residences.'
Yùzhāng has already taken the position of Sīkōng;
he too should be promoted to Tàiwèi."
Before the edict could be issued, Bóshān passed away.
Soon after, the fall of the Chén dynasty occurred,
so he received no posthumous title or epithet.
His eldest son, Jūnfàn,
was appointed Póyáng Guó Shìzǐ during the Tàijiàn era.
Soon after, he became Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn and Jìnlíng Tàishǒu.
Before he could inherit the title, the Suí army arrived.
At this time, there were over a hundred royal princes and marquises in the capital.
The Hòuzhǔ feared they might cause trouble,
so he summoned them all
and ordered them to encamp in the imperial court hall,
making Yùzhāng Wáng Shúyīng their general commander,
and also secretly made preparations against them.
When the imperial army was defeated,
they collectively surrendered,
and subsequently followed the Hòuzhǔ into the pass.
Upon reaching Cháng'ān,
Suí Wéndì distributed them all to the various prefectures in Lǒngyòu and Héxī,
each given land and property to settle.
Initially,
Jūnfàn was on good terms with Jiāng Zǒng, Shàngshū Púyè.
At this time, Zǒng sent Jūnfàn a five-character poem,
expressing the sentiment of parting in a foreign land.
Its words were very poignant,
and literary men of the time all recited it.
In the second year of Dàyè,
Suí Yángdì took Hòuzhǔ's sixth daughter, Nǚ Zhōu, as a Guìrén.
She was extremely favored,
and consequently, he summoned all the sons and nephews of the Chén clan back to the capital,
employing them according to their talents.
Thus, they all became governors and magistrates,
spread throughout the empire.
In that year, Jūnfàn became Wēn Lìng.
Chén Bógōng 陳伯恭, Prince of Jìn'ān 晉安, courtesy name Sùzhī 肅之,
was Shìzǔ's 世祖 sixth son.
In Tiānjiā 天嘉 six (565 CE),
he was made Prince of Jìn'ān 晉安.
Soon after, he became General of Pacifying the East and Grand Administrator of Wú County,
with auxiliary officials appointed.
At that time, Bógōng 陳伯恭 was just over ten years old,
but he already paid close attention to government affairs,
and the official bureaus were well-managed.
In Tàijiàn 太建 one (569 CE),
he entered the court as General of Pacifying the Front and Protector of the Central Army,
then was promoted to Commander of the Central Army.
Soon after, he became General of the Central Guard and Inspector of Yáng Province,
but was dismissed due to official matters.
In Tàijiàn 太建 four (572 CE),
he was reinstated as General of Pacifying the Left,
and soon became General Who Guards the Right and Special Advanced Official,
granted an escort.
In Tàijiàn 太建 six (574 CE),
he was sent out as General Who Pacifies the South and Inspector of Nányù 南豫 Province.
In Tàijiàn 太建 nine (577 CE),
he returned to court as General of Pacifying the Front and Minister of Sacrifices.
In Tàijiàn 太建 eleven (579 CE),
he was promoted to General of the Army Adviser and Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs.
In Tàijiàn 太建 twelve (580 CE),
he was promoted to Assistant Director.
In Tàijiàn 太建 thirteen (581 CE),
he was promoted to Left Assistant Director,
and in Tàijiàn 太建 fourteen (582 CE),
he was sent out as General Who Pacifies the South and Inspector of Xiāng Province,
but had not yet taken up the post.
In Zhìdé 至德 one (583 CE),
he became Palace Attendant, General of the Central Guard, and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness,
but resigned due to mourning his birth mother.
In Zhēnmíng 禎明 one (587 CE),
he was reinstated as General of the Central Guard and Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness,
with auxiliary officials and escort as before.
In Zhēnmíng 禎明 three (589 CE), he entered Guānzhōng 關中.
In the early years of Suí Dàyè 隋大業 (605-618 CE),
he was Inspector of Chéng Province and Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
Chén Bóxìn 陳伯信, Prince of Héngyáng 衡陽, courtesy name Fúzhī 孚之,
was Shìzǔ's 世祖 seventh son.
In Tiānjiā 天嘉 one (560 CE),
Chāng 昌, the Prince Xiàn 獻 of Héngyáng 衡陽, returned to court from Zhōu 周,
but died on the way.
That same year, Shìzǔ 世祖 made Bóxìn 陳伯信 Prince of Héngyáng 衡陽,
to offer sacrifices to the Prince Xiàn 獻.
Soon after, he became General Who Proclaims Grace and Administrator of Dānyáng 丹陽,
with auxiliary officials appointed.
In Tàijiàn 太建 four (572 CE),
he became Protector of the Central Army.
In Tàijiàn 太建 six (574 CE),
he became General Who Declares Awe and Inspector of Yáng Province.
Soon after, he was granted the additional titles of Palace Attendant and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
In Tàijiàn 太建 eleven (579 CE),
he was promoted to General Who Guards the Front,
and Grand Mentor of the Crown Prince,
with all other titles remaining as before.
In Zhēnmíng 禎明 one (587 CE),
he was sent out as General Who Guards the South and Inspector of Xīhéng 西衡 Province.
In Zhēnmíng 禎明 three (589 CE),
the Suí 隋 army crossed the Jiāng 江 (Yangtze River),
and he, along with Fāngqìng 方慶, Marquis of Línrǔ 臨汝, were both killed by Wáng Yǒng 王勇, Inspector of Dōnghéng 東衡 Province.
The details are in Fāngqìng's 方慶 biography.
Chén Bórén 陳伯仁, Prince of Lúlíng 廬陵, courtesy name Shòuzhī 壽之,
was Shìzǔ's 世祖 eighth son.
In Tiānjiā 天嘉 six (565 CE),
he was made Prince of Lúlíng 廬陵.
In the early years of Tàijiàn 太建,
he became General of Light Chariots,
with auxiliary officials appointed.
In Tàijiàn 太建 seven (575 CE),
he was promoted to General of the Valiant Cavalry and Commander of the Central Army.
Soon after, he became General Who Pacifies the North and Inspector of Nánxú 南徐 Province.
In Tàijiàn 太建 twelve (580 CE),
he became General Who Assists the Left and Commander of the Central Army.
In Zhēnmíng 禎明 one (587 CE),
he was granted the additional title of Palace Attendant,
Libationer of the Directorate of Education,
and concurrently held the post of Chief Administrator to the Crown Prince.
In Zhēnmíng 禎明 three (589 CE), he entered Guānzhōng 關中,
and died in Cháng'ān 長安.
His eldest son, Fān 番,
was previously enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiāngbīn 湘濱.
During Suí Dàyè 隋大業,
he served as Magistrate of Zīyáng 資陽.
Chén Bóyì 陳伯義, Prince of Jiāngxià 江夏, courtesy name Jiānzhī 堅之,
was Shìzǔ's 世祖 ninth son.
In Tiānjiā 天嘉 six (565 CE),
he was made Prince of Jiāngxià 江夏.
In the early years of Tàijiàn 太建,
he became General Who Proclaims Grace and Inspector of Dōngyáng 東揚 Province,
with auxiliary officials appointed.

Soon after, he became General Who Declares Awe, Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs of Hé 合 and Huò 霍 two Prefectures, and Inspector of Hé 合 Prefecture.
[一０] In Tàijiàn 太建 fourteen (582 CE),
he was summoned to court as Palace Attendant, General of Loyalty and Valor, and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple.
In Zhēnmíng 禎明 three (589 CE), he entered Guānzhōng 關中,
was exiled to Guāzhōu 瓜州,
and died on the way.
His eldest son, Yuánjī 元基,
was previously enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiāngtán 湘潭.
During Suí Dàyè 隋大業, he served as Magistrate of Gǔshú 穀熟 County.
Chén Bólǐ 陳伯禮, Prince of Wǔlíng 武陵, courtesy name Yòngzhī 用之,
was Shìzǔ's 世祖 tenth son.
In Tiānjiā 天嘉 six (565 CE),
he was made Prince of Wǔlíng 武陵.
In the early years of Tàijiàn 太建,
he became General of Cloud Banners, Bearer of Imperial Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs of Wúxīng 吳興, and Grand Administrator of Wúxīng 吳興.
In the commandery, he acted wantonly, plundering violently,
forcibly conscripting commoners,
and seizing their wealth and goods.
The accumulated gains from these acts were vast,
causing suffering among the people.
In Tàijiàn 太建 nine (577 CE),
he was impeached by the appropriate authorities.
The emperor stated that the Prince was young,
and did not yet understand the ways of governance,
and that it was all due to his auxiliary officials' inability to admonish him.
He was specifically demoted in military rank,
but if he offended again,
he would certainly be dealt with according to the law.
The officials who failed to report it would share the same guilt.
In the spring of Tàijiàn 太建 eleven (579 CE),
he was recalled to be replaced,
but Bólǐ 陳伯禮 delayed his departure.
In the tenth month of that year,
Xú Jūnfū 徐君敷, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Palace Censor, submitted a memorial, saying: [一一]
"Your servant has heard that for carriages and shoes, one does not wait;
this is a common rule for imperial commands.
To be diligent day and night,
this is the constant principle for subjects.

I respectfully note that Bólǐ 陳伯禮, Prince of Wǔlíng 武陵, General of Cloud Banners, Bearer of Imperial Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs of Wúxīng 吳興, and Grand Administrator of Wúxīng 吳興,
has long displayed outstanding virtue,
[一二] and has long enjoyed a good reputation.
He was entrusted with important responsibilities,
and the people of his district looked to him.
Your Majesty cherishes the common people
and devotes your heart to the root of governance,
seeking to alleviate suffering together,
and promptly fulfilling the imperial will.
Yet, he has delayed his return journey,
taking advantage of the change of seasons,
postponing his departure,
needlessly wasting time on the road.
His virtuous discretion is not apparent,
his negligence is present.
It is proper to correct his faults and examine his conduct,
to serve as a warning.
Your servants have deliberated and propose that Bólǐ 陳伯禮 be dismissed from his current official posts for his present actions,
and return to his residence as a prince.
This memorial is respectfully submitted."
The imperial edict stated,
"Granted."
In Zhēnmíng 禎明 three (589 CE), he entered Guānzhōng 關中.
During Suí Dàyè 隋大業, he served as Cavalier Attendant and Grand Administrator of Líntáo 臨洮.
Chén Bózhì 陳伯智, Prince of Yǒngyáng 永陽, courtesy name Cèzhī 策之,
was Shìzǔ's 世祖 twelfth son.
In his youth, he was honest and sincere,
possessed great capacity,
and was widely read in the Classics and histories.
During Tàijiàn 太建,
he was made Prince of Yǒngyáng 永陽.
[一三] Soon after, he became Palace Attendant,
and was granted the additional title of General Who Manifests Awe,
with auxiliary officials appointed.
Soon after, he was granted the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and was repeatedly promoted to Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs.
[一四] He was sent out as Bearer of Imperial Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs of Dōngyáng 東揚 and Fēng 豐 two Prefectures, [一五] General of Pacifying the East,
and concurrently held the post of Administrator of Kuàijī 會稽.
In Zhìdé 至德 two (584 CE),
he returned to court as Palace Attendant and General Who Assists the Left,
and was granted the additional title of Special Advanced Official.
In Zhēnmíng 禎明 three (589 CE), he entered Guānzhōng 關中.
During Suí Dàyè 隋大業,
he served as Judicial Administrator of Qí 岐 Prefecture,
and was promoted to Vice Director of the Directorate of Education.
Chén Bómóu 陳伯謀, Prince of Guìyáng 桂陽,
courtesy name Shēnzhī 深之,
was Shìzǔ's 世祖 thirteenth son.
During Tàijiàn 太建,
he was made Prince of Guìyáng 桂陽.
[一六] In Tàijiàn 太建 seven (575 CE),
he became General Who Manifests Awe,
with auxiliary officials appointed.
Soon after, he became General Who Commands Awe and Administrator of Dānyáng 丹陽.
In Tàijiàn 太建 ten (578 CE),
he was granted the additional title of Palace Attendant.
He was sent out as Bearer of Imperial Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs of Wúxīng 吳興, East Central General, and Grand Administrator of Wúxīng 吳興.
In Tàijiàn 太建 eleven (579 CE),
he was granted the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
He died in Zhìdé 至德 one (583 CE).
His son, Fēng 酆, succeeded him.
During Dàyè 大業,
he served as Magistrate of Fānhé 番禾.
Gāozōng had forty-two sons: Empress Liǔ bore Hòuzhǔ;
Consort Péng Guìrén bore Prince Shǐxīng Shūlíng;
Consort Cáo Shúhuá bore Prince Yùzhāng Shūyīng;
Consort Hé Shúyí bore Prince Chángshā Shūjiān and Prince Yídū Shūmíng;
Consort Wèi Zhāoróng bore Prince Jiàn’ān Shūqīng;
〔一七〕Consort Qián Guìfēi bore Prince Hédōng Shūxiàn;
Consort Liú Zhāoyí bore Prince Xīncài Shūqí;
Consort Yuán Zhāoróng bore Prince Jìnxī Shūwén, Prince Yìyáng Shūdá, and Prince Xīnhuì Shūtǎn;
Lady Wáng Jī bore Prince Huáinán Shūbiāo and Prince Bāshān Shūxióng;
〔一八〕Lady Wú Jī bore Prince Shǐxīng Shūchóng;
Lady Xú Jī bore Prince Xúnyáng Shūyǎn;
Lady Chúnyú Jī bore Prince Yuèyáng Shūshèn;
Consort Wáng Xiūhuá bore Prince Wǔchāng Shūyú;
Consort Wéi Xiūróng bore Prince Xiāngdōng Shūpíng;
Lady Shī Jī bore Prince Línhè Shū’áo and Prince Yuánlíng Shūxīng;
Lady Zēng Jī bore Prince Yángshān Shūxuān;
Lady Yáng Jī bore Prince Xīyáng Shūmù;
Lady Shēn Jiéyú bore Prince Nán’ān Shūjiǎn, Prince Nánjùn Shūchéng, Prince Yuèshān Shūsháo, and Prince Tàiyuán Shūkuāng;
Lady Yuán Jī bore Prince Xīnxīng Shūchún;
Lady Wú Jī bore Prince Bādōng Shūmó;
Lady Liú Jī bore Prince Línjiāng Shūxiǎn;
〔一九〕Lady Qín Jī bore Prince Xīnníng Shūlóng and Prince Xīnchāng Shūróng.
His imperial sons Shūrùi, Shūzhōng, Shūhóng,
〔二０〕Shūyì, Shūxùn, Shūwǔ, Shūchǔ, and Shūfēng, a total of eight men,
Shūlíng committed treason,
and has a separate biography.
Three sons died young,
and are not named in this book.
Prince Yùzhāng Shūyīng, courtesy name Zǐliè,
was Gāozōng’s third son.
In his youth, he was generous, kind, and loving.
In the first year of Tiānjia (560 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Marquis Jiàn’ān.
In the first year of Tàijiàn (569 CE),
he was re-enfeoffed as Prince Yùzhāng,
and remained General Xuānhuì, Area Commander-in-Chief of Dōngyáng Prefecture, and Inspector of Dōngyáng Prefecture.
In the fifth year (573 CE),
he was promoted to General Píngběi and Inspector of Nányù Prefecture.
〔二一〕In the eleventh year (579 CE),
he became General Zhènqián and Inspector of Jiāng Prefecture.
〔二二〕When Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to General Zhēngnán.
Soon after, he was granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Central Guard Grand General,
with the rest of his titles remaining as before.
In the fourth year (582 CE),
he was promoted to Grand General Piàojì.
〔二三〕In the first year of Zhēnmíng (587 CE),
he was granted a set of drums and pipes,
and ten sword-bearers.
In that same year,
he was transferred to Sīkōng.
〔二四〕In the third year (589 CE),
when the Suí army crossed the Yangtze,
Shūyīng was in charge of the Shítóu army garrison affairs.
Soon after, he was ordered to encamp in the imperial court.
When the six armies were defeated,
he surrendered to the Suí general Hán Qínhǔ.
In that same year, he entered the pass.
During the Dàyè era of Suí, he served as Governor of Fúlíng.
His eldest son, Hóng,
in the first year of Zhìdé (583 CE),
was appointed Heir Apparent of the Principality of Yùzhāng.
Prince Chángshā Shūjiān, courtesy name Zǐchéng,
was Gāozōng’s fourth son.
His mother was originally a servant in a wine shop in Wúzhōng.
When Gāozōng was a commoner,
he once went there to drink,
and then had relations with her.
When he became noble,
he summoned and appointed her Shúyí.
Shūjiān was clever and astute in his youth,
but tyrannical and given to drunkenness.
He was especially fond of numerology, divination, incantations, and prohibitions,
and he mastered the intricacies of metal casting and jade carving.
During the Tiānjia era (560-566 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Marquis Fēngchéng.
In the first year of Tàijiàn (569 CE),
he was established as Prince Chángshā,
and remained General Dōngzhōngláng and Grand Administrator of Wújùn.
In the fourth year (572 CE),
he became General Xuānyì and Inspector of Jiāng Prefecture,
and was provided with staff officers.
In the seventh year (575 CE),
he was promoted to General Yúnhuī and Inspector of Yǐng Prefecture.
Before taking up the post,
he was transferred to General Píngyuè Zhōngláng and Inspector of Guǎng Prefecture.
Soon after, he became General Píngběi and Inspector of Hé Prefecture.
〔二五〕In the eighth year (576 CE),
he was again appointed General Píngxī and Inspector of Yǐng Prefecture.
In the eleventh year (579 CE),
he entered the court as General Yìzuǒ and Prefect of Dānyáng.
〔二六〕
Initially,
Shūjiān and Prince Shǐxīng Shūlíng both gathered retainers,
each contending for power and favor,
and were very displeased with each other.
Whenever there were court assemblies or ceremonial processions,
they would not concede precedence,
but would always take separate routes.
Their attendants sometimes fought over the right of way,
even resulting in deaths.
When Gāozōng fell ill,
Shūjiān, Shūlíng, and others all attended to him with Hòuzhǔ.
Shūlíng secretly harbored sinister intentions,
and ordered the imperial pharmacist, saying:
“The medicine-cutting knife is very dull;
it should be sharpened.”
When Gāozōng died,
in the urgency of the moment,
he again ordered his attendants to fetch a sword from outside.
The attendants did not understand,
and brought him the wooden sword worn with court attire.
Shūlíng was enraged.
Shūjiān, who was nearby, heard this,
suspected a plot,
and observed his actions.
The next day, during the minor dressing of the deceased,
Shūlíng, with the medicine-cutting knife hidden in his sleeve, rushed forward
and struck Hòuzhǔ,
hitting him in the neck.
Hòuzhǔ fainted to the ground.
The Empress Dowager and Hòuzhǔ’s wet nurse, Lady Lè’ān Wú Shì, both shielded him with their bodies,
and he narrowly escaped death.
Shūjiān grabbed Shūlíng from behind,
captured him,
and seized his knife.
He was about to kill him,
and asked Hòuzhǔ:
“Shall I finish him now,
or wait?”
Hòuzhǔ was unable to respond.
Shūlíng was historically very strong.
In a moment,
he struggled free,
exited the Yúnlóng Gate,
entered the Eastern City (Dōngfǔ Chéng),
summoned his attendants to cut off the Qīngxī Bridge road,
and released the prisoners in the East City to serve as soldiers.
He also sent people to Xīnlín
to recall his subordinate troops,
then personally put on armor,
wore a white cloth cap,
ascended the west gate of the city,
and recruited common people.
At this time, all the armies were defending along the river,
and the palace was empty.
Shūjiān then reported to the Empress Dowager, sending the太子舍人 Tàizǐ Shèrén Sīmǎ Shēn to summon Xiāo Móhē with Hòuzhǔ’s command,
ordering him to suppress the rebellion.
On the same day, they captured his generals Dài Wēn and Tán Qílín, etc.,
〔二七〕sent them to the palace,
beheaded them outside the Shàngshū Pavilion,
and displayed their heads throughout the East City.
Shūlíng was confused and did not know what to do.
He then killed all his wives and concubines,
and led several hundred attendants to flee towards Xīnlín.
Móhē pursued him,
beheaded him in Dānyáng Commandery,
and captured all his remaining followers.
In that same year,
for his merit, he was promoted to Grand General Piàojì, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Inspector of Yáng Prefecture.
Soon after, he was transferred to Sīkōng,
with his general and inspector titles remaining as before.
At this time, Hòuzhǔ suffered from a boil,
and could not attend to matters.
All affairs, great or small,
were entirely entrusted to Shújiān for decision.
Consequently, his influence overshadowed the imperial court.
Shújiān thereupon indulged in arrogance and extravagance,
and many of his actions were unlawful.
Hòuzhǔ, because of this, grew distant from him and became wary.
Kǒng Fàn, Guǎn Bīn, Shī Wénqìng and their ilk,
all former officials of the Eastern Palace,
陰持其短 (secretly held to his shortcomings) day and night.
In the first year of Zhìdé (583),
an imperial edict was issued, ordering him to use the "Three Offices" protocol with his original title,
and be sent out as the Cìshǐ of Jiāngzhōu.
Before he had departed,
another edict soon followed, appointing him as General of the Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn)
and reinstating him as Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
The real intention was to strip him of his power.
Shújiān did not feel secure,
and gradually became resentful.
He resorted to heterodox magic and enchantments to seek good fortune and aid,
carving wooden effigies,
dressing them in Daoist robes,
and installing mechanisms
so they could bow and kneel.
He performed libations day and night under the sun and moon,
and uttered curses over them.
In the winter of that year,
someone submitted a memorial accusing him of these deeds.
Investigations proved them all true.
Hòuzhǔ summoned Shújiān and imprisoned him in the Western Palace,
intending to kill him.
That night,
he ordered a close attendant to proclaim an imperial edict,
enumerating his crimes.
Shújiān replied,
“My original intention
was not for any other reason;
I merely wished to seek closeness and favor.
Since I have violated the heavenly laws,
my crime warrants ten thousand deaths.
On the day I die,
I will surely see Shúlíng.
I beg that you proclaim a clear edict,
and admonish him in the Underworld.”
Hòuzhǔ, moved by his past achievements,
then pardoned him,
specifically exempting him from his current office,
and allowing him to return to his residence as a prince.
Soon after, he was reappointed as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and General Who Guards the Left (Zhènzuǒ Jiāngjūn).
〔二八〕In the second year (584),
he was also granted drums and horns, and an oil-canopied carriage.
In the third year (585),
he was sent out as General Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn) and Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu.
In the fourth year (586),
he was promoted to Grand General of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Dàjiāngjūn) and Administrator with the Ceremonial Privilege of Opening a Government Office (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
In the second year of Zhēnmíng (588),
his term expired, and he returned to the capital.
In the third year (589), he entered the pass [to Súi territory],
and was relocated to Guāzhōu,
where his name was changed to Shúxián.
【叔】Xián was originally of noble birth,
〔二九〕and knew nothing of his family’s livelihood.
By this time, he and his consort, Shěn shì, brewed wine
and worked as hired laborers.
During the Dàyè era of the Súi dynasty,
he served as the Tàishǒu of Suìníng Commandery.
Chén Shúqīng, Prince of Jiàn'ān, whose courtesy name was Zǐbì,
was the fifth son of Gāozōng.
He was by nature straightforward and possessed talent and capacity,
with a very imposing appearance.
In the fourth year of Tàijiàn (572),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jiàn'ān,
and appointed General of the Central Guard (Dōng Zhōnglángjiāng) and Cìshǐ of Dōngyángzhōu.
In the seventh year (575),
he became General of the Cloud Banner (Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn) and Cìshǐ of Yǐngzhōu,
and was granted staff officers.
In the ninth year (577),
he was promoted to General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn) and Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu.
Upon Hòuzhǔ’s ascension,
he was promoted to General Who Guards the South (Ānnán Jiāngjūn).
He also served as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), General Who Guards the Right (Zhènyòu Jiāngjūn), and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshūlìng).
He was then transferred to Supervisor of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshūjiān).
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (589), he entered the pass [to Súi territory].
During the Dàyè era of the Súi dynasty,
he served as Director of the Bureau of Officials (Dūguānláng) and Grand Administrator of Shàngdǎng (Shàngdǎng Tōngshǒu).
Chén Shúmíng, Prince of Yídū, whose courtesy name was Zǐzhāo,
was the sixth son of Gāozōng.
He had a beautiful appearance
and gentle, delicate demeanor,
resembling a woman.
In the fifth year of Tàijiàn (573),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yídū,
and soon after appointed General Who Manifests Grace (Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn),
and granted staff officers.
In the seventh year (575),
he was appointed General of the Central Guard (Dōng Zhōnglángjiāng) and Cìshǐ of Dōngyángzhōu.
Soon after, he became General of Light Chariots (Qīngchē Jiāngjūn) and Grand Minister of the Imperial Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng).
In the thirteenth year (581),
he was sent out as Bearer of the Imperial Insignia (Shǐ Chíjié), General of the Cloud Banner (Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn), and Cìshǐ of Nánxúzhōu.
He also served as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and General Who Assists the Right (Yìyòu Jiāngjūn).
In the fourth year of Zhìdé (586),
he was promoted to General Who Guards the Right (Ānyòu Jiāngjūn).
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (589), he entered the pass [to Súi territory].
During the Dàyè era of the Súi dynasty, he served as Junior Minister of the Court of Diplomatic Receptions (Hónglú Shàolíng).
Chén Shúxiàn, Prince of Hédōng, whose courtesy name was Zǐgōng,
was the ninth son of Gāozōng.
He was by nature respectful and cautious,
intelligent, and fond of learning.
In the fifth year of Tàijiàn (573),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Hédōng.
In the seventh year (575),
he was appointed General Who Manifests Loyalty (Xuānyì Jiāngjūn),
and granted staff officers.

Soon after, he became Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì), General of the Military Adviser (Jūnshī Jiāngjūn), Regional Commander of All Military Affairs of Nánxúzhōu (Dūdū Nánxúzhōu Zhū Jūnshì), and Cìshǐ of Nánxúzhōu.
〔三０〕He died in the twelfth year (580),
at the age of thirteen.
He was posthumously granted Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), General of the Central Pacification (Zhōngfǔ Jiāngjūn), and Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
and given the posthumous title Kāngjiǎn.
His son, Xiàokuān, inherited his title.
Xiàokuān, in the first year of Zhìdé (583),
inherited the title of Prince of Hédōng.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (589), he entered the pass [to Súi territory].
During the Dàyè era of the Súi dynasty, he served as Magistrate of Wènchéng (Wènchéng Lìng).
Chén Shúqí, Prince of Xīncài, whose courtesy name was Zǐsù,
was the eleventh son of Gāozōng.
He had a bright and resourceful disposition,
was broadly versed in the classics and histories,
and excelled at writing essays.
In the seventh year of Tàijiàn (575),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xīncài,
and soon after became General Who Manifests Wisdom (Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn),
and granted staff officers.
He was sent out as General of the Central Guard (Dōng Zhōnglángjiāng) and Cìshǐ of Dōngyángzhōu.
In the second year of Zhìdé (584),
he entered the court as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng);
his General and staff officer positions remained as before.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng (587),
he was appointed Libationer of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ);
his Palace Attendant, General, and staff officer positions remained as before.
In the third year (589), he entered the pass [to Súi territory].
During the Dàyè era of the Súi dynasty, he served as Director of the Bureau of Guest Affairs (Shàngshū Zhǔkèláng).
Jìnxi Wáng Shūwén 晉熙王叔文, courtesy name Zǐcái 子才,
was Emperor Gāozōng 高宗’s twelfth son.
He was shallow and treacherous by nature,
fond of empty reputation,
and somewhat knowledgeable in books and history.
In the seventh year of Tàijiàn 太建 (575),
he was made Prince of Jìnxi.
Soon after, he became Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng 侍中), Mounted Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍), and General Xuānhuì (Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn 宣惠將軍),
and was given an administrative staff.
He was promoted to General Qīngchē (Qīngchē Jiāngjūn 輕車將軍) and Inspector of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Cìshǐ 揚州刺史).
In the first year of Zhìdé 至德 (583),

he was appointed Bearer of the Imperial Credentials (Chíjié 持節), Area Commander-in-chief of all military affairs in Jiāngzhōu (Dūdū Jiāngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì 都督江州諸軍事), and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ 江州刺史).
In the second year (584),

he was transferred to General Xìnwēi (Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn 信威將軍), Area Commander-in-chief of all military affairs in the four prefectures of Xiāngzhōu, Héngzhōu, Wǔzhōu, and Guìzhōu (Dūdū Xiāng Héng Wǔ Guì Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnshì 督湘衡武桂四州諸軍事), and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu (Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ 湘州刺史).
In the second year of Zhēnmíng 禎明 (588),
his term of office ended,
and he was summoned to be Attendant-in-ordinary and General Xuānyì (Xuānyì Jiāngjūn 宣毅將軍),
with his administrative staff remaining as before.
Before he could return,
the Suí 隋 army crossed the Yangtze River,
