broke through Táichéng 臺城, and
Qín Wáng 秦王, the Grand Marshal of the eastern division of Hàngdōng Hàngdōng Dào Xíngjūn Yuánshuài 漢東道行軍元帥, reached Hànkǒu 漢口.
At this time, Shūwén was returning to court from Xiāngzhōu.
When he reached Bāzhōu 巴州,
he, along with Bāzhōu Inspector Bì Bǎo 畢寶 and others, requested to surrender,
sending a letter to the Prince of Qín, saying:
"I humbly submit that there are no two suns in the sky,
and the order of day and night is never amiss.
There are no two kings in the land,
and the positions of superior and inferior are distinct.
Now that carriages and writings are united,
and gauges and tracks are universally the same,
I dare to reveal my sincere intentions,
and express my kneeling submission."
Upon receiving the letter, the Prince of Qín
dispatched Liǔ Zhuāng 柳莊 of the Field Army's Ministry of Personnel (Xíngjūn Lìbù 行軍吏部) and other officials from the Grand Marshal's office to Bāzhōu to welcome and comfort Shūwén.
Shūwén then, with Bì Bǎo and Jīngzhōu Inspector Chén Jì 陳紀, as well as civil and military officers, proceeded to Hànkǒu.
The Prince of Qín treated them all generously
and lodged them in the guesthouse.
In the third month of the ninth year of Suí Kāihuáng 隋開皇 (589),
when the armies returned triumphantly,
Emperor Wéndì 文帝 personally visited Wēntāng 溫湯 to commend them.
Shūwén, along with Chén Jì, Zhōu Luó 周羅, Xún Fǎshàng 荀法尚, and other surrendered individuals,
were presented along the road.
A few days later,
Shūwén, accompanying the Former Emperor (Hòuzhǔ 後主) and other princes, marquises, generals, and chancellors, as well as the imperial carriage, regalia, astronomical charts, and records,
were arranged in order,
and then surrounded by iron cavalry.
They followed the Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng 晉王) and the Prince of Qín, etc., entering in a triumphant procession,
and were arrayed in the ancestral temple courtyard.
The next day,
Suí Wéndì sat in the Guǎngyáng Mén Guān 廣陽門觀.
Shūwén again followed the Former Emperor to the south of the imperial hall.
Emperor Wéndì ordered Inner Secretariat Director Lǐ Délín 李德林 to declare his decree,
admonishing the Former Emperor and his ministers for their failure to support each other,
which led to their downfall.
The Former Emperor and his officials all knelt down in shame and fear,
unable to look up.
Shūwén alone was joyful and self-satisfied.
Sixteen days later,
he submitted a memorial, saying:
"Earlier, in Bāzhōu,
I had already sent my request for surrender.
I beg that this be acknowledged,
and hope to be treated exceptionally."
Although Emperor Wéndì disliked his disloyalty,
he was then intent on pacifying the Jiangbiǎo 江表 region.
So, he appointed him Kāifǔ 開府
and made him Inspector of Yízhōu (Yízhōu Cìshǐ 宜州刺史).
Huáinán Wáng Shūbiāo 淮南王叔彪, courtesy name Zǐhuá 子華,
was Emperor Gāozōng’s thirteenth son.
He was intelligent and wise in his youth,
and skilled at writing.
In the eighth year of Tàijiàn (576),
he was made Prince of Huáinán.
Soon after, he held the position of Attendant-in-ordinary and General Rénwēi (Rénwēi Jiāngjūn 仁威將軍),
and was given an administrative staff.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (589), he entered the Pass (Rù Guān 入關),
and died in Cháng'ān 長安.
Shǐxīng Wáng Shūzhòng 始興王叔重, courtesy name Zǐhòu 子厚,
was Emperor Gāozōng’s fourteenth son.
He was simple and unadorned by nature,
without special skills.
When Emperor Gāozōng died,
Shǐxīng Wáng Shūlíng 始興王叔陵 rebelled
and was executed. In the same year, Shūzhòng was made Prince of Shǐxīng,
to offer sacrifices to the posterity of Zhāoliè Wáng 昭烈王.
In the first year of Zhìdé (583),
he became General Rénwēi and Inspector of Yángzhōu,
and was given an administrative staff.
In the second year (584),
he was given the additional title of Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, Area Commander-in-chief of all military affairs in Jiāngzhōu, and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (589), he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè 大業 reign of the Suí dynasty, he was Taifù Shǎoqīng 太府少卿,
and then died.
Xúnyáng Wáng Shūyǎn 尋陽王叔儼, courtesy name Zǐsī 子思,
was Emperor Gāozōng’s fifteenth son.
He was composed and dignified by nature,
with proper demeanor.
When the Former Emperor ascended the throne,
he was made Prince of Xúnyáng.
In the first year of Zhìdé (583),
he became Attendant-in-ordinary and General Rénwǔ (Rénwǔ Jiāngjūn 仁武將軍),
and was given an administrative staff.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (589), he entered the Pass,
and soon died.
Yuèyáng Wáng Shūshèn 岳陽王叔慎, courtesy name Zǐjìng 子敬,
was Emperor Gāozōng’s sixteenth son.
He was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
able to compose essays at the age of ten.
In the fourteenth year of Tàijiàn (582),
he was made Prince of Yuèyáng,
at the age of eleven.
In the fourth year of Zhìdé (586),
he was appointed Attendant-in-ordinary, General Zhìwǔ (Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn 智武將軍), and Administrator of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn 丹陽尹).
At this time,
the Former Emperor particularly loved literature,
and Shūshèn, along with Héngyáng Wáng Bóxìn 衡陽王伯信 and Xīncài Wáng Shūqí 新蔡王叔齊, attended him day and night.
Whenever they were commanded to compose poems,
they were always praised and admired.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng (587),

he was sent out as Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, Area Commander-in-chief of all military affairs in the four prefectures of Xiāngzhōu, Héngzhōu, Guìzhōu, and Wǔzhōu, General Zhìwǔ, and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
In the third year (589),
the Suí army crossed the Yangtze River,
broke through Táichéng.
The former inspector, Prince of Jìnxi Shūwén, had returned to Bāzhōu,
and, along with Bāzhōu Inspector Bì Bǎo and Jīngzhōu Inspector Chén Jì, all surrendered.
Suí Field Army Grand Marshal, Duke of Qīnghé Yáng Sù 清河公楊素, led his troops down to Jīngmén 荊門.
He separately dispatched his general Páng Huī 龐暉 to lead troops to seize territory,
going south to Xiāngzhōu.
The officers and soldiers inside the city
had no firm resolve,
and set a date to surrender.
Shūshèn then hosted a banquet for his civil and military officials.
During the feast,
Shūshèn sighed, saying,
"Is the loyalty between sovereign and minister
to end here?"
Chief Clerk Xiè Jī 謝基 prostrated himself and wept.
Suìxīng Hóu Zhèng Lǐ 遂興侯正理, who was assisting in the defense of Xiāngzhōu, was present.
He stood up and said,
"If the lord is disgraced, his ministers die.
Are you gentlemen not ministers of the Chén 陳 state?
Now that the realm faces calamity,
this is truly the time to give our lives.
Even if we achieve nothing,
we will still demonstrate our loyalty as ministers.
Outside the Green Gate,
we would rather die than surrender.
This moment's opportunity
allows for no hesitation.
Those who hesitate will be beheaded!"
Everyone agreed,
and they sacrificed an animal and swore an oath.
They then sent someone to falsely present a letter of surrender to Páng Huī.
Huī believed it,
and entered on the appointed day.
Shūshèn lay in wait with armed men.
Huī ordered several hundred men to guard the city gate,
and personally led a few tens of his close followers into the hall.
Soon, the ambushing soldiers attacked,
captured Huī and paraded him,
seized all his party,
and beheaded them.
Shūshèn sat in the archery hall,
gathering soldiers and commoners.
Within a few days,
his army reached five thousand men.
Héngyáng Administrator Fán Tōng 樊通 and Wǔzhōu Inspector Wū Jūyè 鄔居業 all requested to join the resistance.
Before they arrived,
Suí dispatched Duke of Zhōngmóu Xuē Zhòu 中牟公薛冑 as Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
Hearing of Páng Huī's death,
he requested more troops.
Suí then dispatched Field Army Commander Líu Rén'ēn 劉仁恩 to reinforce him.
Before he arrived,
Xuē Zhòu's troops reached Éyángshān 鵝羊山.
Shūshèn sent Zhèng Lǐ and Fán Tōng, etc., to resist them.
A great battle ensued,
lasting from dawn until late afternoon.
The Suí army rested and fought in turns,
but Zhèng Lǐ's forces were outnumbered and no match.
Thus, they suffered a great defeat.
Zhòu pressed his advantage and entered the city,
capturing Shūshèn alive.
At this time,
Wū Jūyè led his troops from Wǔzhōu to reinforce.
He emerged from Héngqiáo Jiāng 橫橋江,
and hearing of Shūshèn's defeat,
he halted at Xīnkāngkǒu 新康口.
Suí Commander Líu Rén'ēn's troops also arrived at Héngqiáo,
set up camp by the water,
and held their ground for two nights.
They then engaged in battle,
and Jūyè was again defeated.
Rén'ēn captured Shūshèn, Zhèng Lǐ, Jūyè, and more than ten of their partisans.
The Prince of Qín beheaded them at Hànkǒu.
Shūshèn was eighteen years old at the time.
Yìyáng Wáng Shūdá (義陽王叔達), courtesy name Zǐcōng (子聰),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) seventeenth son.
In the fourteenth year of Tàijiàn (太建) (582 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yìyáng.
Soon after, he was appointed Rénwǔ Jiāngjūn (仁武將軍)
and given subordinate officials.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (587 CE),
he was made Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹).
In the third year (589 CE), he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he served as Nèishǐ (內史),
and later became Jìangjùn Tōngshǒu (絳郡通守).
Bāshān Wáng Shūxióng (巴山王叔雄), courtesy name Zǐměng (子猛),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) eighteenth son.
In the fourteenth year of Tàijiàn (太建) (582 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Bāshān.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass,
and died in Cháng'ān (長安).
Wǔchāng Wáng Shūyú (武昌王叔虞), courtesy name Zǐ'ān (子安),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) nineteenth son.
In the fourteenth year of Tàijiàn (太建) (582 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Wǔchāng.
Soon after, he was appointed Zhuàngwǔ Jiāngjūn (壯武將軍)
and given subordinate officials.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he served as Gāoyuàn Lìng (高苑令).
Xiāngdōng Wáng Shūpíng (湘東王叔平), courtesy name Zǐkāng (子康),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) twentieth son.
In the first year of Zhìdé (至德) (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xiāngdōng.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he served as Húsū Lìng (湖蘇令).
Línhè Wáng Shū'áo (臨賀王叔敖), courtesy name Zǐrén (子仁),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) twenty-first son.
In the first year of Zhìdé (至德) (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Línhè.
Soon after, he was appointed Rénwǔ Jiāngjūn (仁武將軍)
and given subordinate officials.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass.
At the beginning of the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he was appointed Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司).
Yángshān Wáng Shūxuān (陽山王叔宣), courtesy name Zǐtōng (子通),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) twenty-second son.
In the first year of Zhìdé (至德) (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yángshān.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he served as Jīngchéng Lìng (涇城令).
Xīyáng Wáng Shūmù (西陽王叔穆), courtesy name Zǐhé (子和),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) twenty-third son.
In the first year of Zhìdé (至德) (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xīyáng.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass,
and died in Cháng'ān (長安).
Nán'ān Wáng Shūjiǎn (南安王叔儉), courtesy name Zǐyuē (子約),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) twenty-fourth son.
In the first year of Zhìdé (至德) (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nán'ān.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass,
and died in Cháng'ān (長安).
Nánjùn Wáng Shūchéng (南郡王叔澄), courtesy name Zǐquán (子泉),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) twenty-fifth son.
In the first year of Zhìdé (至德) (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nánjùn.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he served as Língwǔ Lìng (靈武令).
Yuánlíng Wáng Shūxìng (沅陵王叔興), courtesy name Zǐtuī (子推),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) twenty-sixth son.
In the first year of Zhìdé (至德) (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yuánlíng.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he served as Jǐshì Láng (給事郎).
Yuèshān Wáng Shūsháo (岳山王叔韶), courtesy name Zǐqīn (子欽),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) twenty-seventh son.
In the first year of Zhìdé (至德) (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yuèshān.
Soon after, he was appointed Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn (智武將軍)
and given subordinate officials.
In the fourth year (586 CE),
he was made Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹).
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass,
and died in Cháng'ān (長安).
Xīnxīng Wáng Shūchún (新興王叔純), courtesy name Zǐgòng (子共),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) twenty-eighth son.
In the first year of Zhìdé (至德) (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xīnxīng.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he served as Héběi Lìng (河北令).
Bādōng Wáng Shūmó (巴東王叔謨), courtesy name Zǐguǐ (子軌),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) twenty-ninth son.
In the fourth year of Zhìdé (至德) (586 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Bādōng.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he served as Qiānyáng Lìng (岍陽令).
Línjiāng Wáng Shūxiǎn (臨江王叔顯), courtesy name Zǐmíng (子明),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) thirtieth son.
In the fourth year of Zhìdé (至德) (586 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Línjiāng.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he served as Qúnyú Lìng (鶉觚令).
Xīnhuì Wáng Shūtǎn (新會王叔坦), courtesy name Zǐkāi (子開),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) thirty-first son.
In the fourth year of Zhìdé (至德) (586 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xīnhuì.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he served as Shè Lìng (涉令).
Xīnníng Wáng Shūlóng (新寧王叔隆), courtesy name Zǐyuǎn (子遠),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) thirty-second son.
In the fourth year of Zhìdé (至德) (586 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xīnníng.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (589 CE), he entered the Pass,
and died in Cháng'ān (長安).
Xīnchāng Wáng Shūróng (新昌王叔榮), courtesy name Zǐchè (子徹),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) thirty-third son.
In the second year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (588 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xīnchāng.
In the third year (589 CE), he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he served as Nèihuáng Lìng (內黃令).
Tàiyuán Wáng Shūkuāng (太原王叔匡), courtesy name Zǐzuǒ (子佐),
was Gāozōng’s (高宗) thirty-fourth son.
In the second year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (588 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Tàiyuán.
In the third year (589 CE), he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he served as Shòuguāng Lìng (壽光令).
The Latter Lord had twenty-two sons: Zhang Guìfēi (張貴妃) gave birth to Crown Prince Shēn (深) and Kuàijī Wáng Zhuāng (會稽王莊);
Sun Jī (孫姬) gave birth to Wúxīng Wáng Yìn (吳興王胤);
Gāo Zhāoyí (高昭儀) gave birth to Nánpíng Wáng Yí (南平王嶷);
Lǚ Shúyuán (呂淑媛) gave birth to Yǒngjiā Wáng Yàn (永嘉王彥) and Shàolíng Wáng Jìng (邵陵王兢);
Gōng Guìpín (龔貴嬪) gave birth to Nánhǎi Wáng Qián (南海王虔) and Qiántáng Wáng Tián (錢塘王恬);
Zhāng Shúhuá (張淑華) gave birth to Xìnyì Wáng Zhī (信義王祗);
Xú Shúyí (徐淑儀) gave birth to Dōngyáng Wáng Quán (東陽王恮);
Kǒng Guìrén (孔貴人) gave birth to Wújùn Wáng Fān (吳郡王蕃).
His other imperial sons Zǒng (總), Guān (觀), Míng (明), Gāng (綱), Tǒng (統), Chōng (沖), Qià (洽), Tāo (縚), Chuò (綽), Wēi (威), and Biàn (辯), eleven in total,
were all not yet enfeoffed.
Crown Prince Shēn (深), courtesy name Chéngyuán (承源),
was the Latter Lord’s fourth son.
He was intelligent and wise in his youth,
with integrity and resolve.
His demeanor was solemn,
and even his close attendants
never saw him express joy or anger.
Because of his mother, Zhang Guìfēi (張貴妃),
he was especially beloved by the Latter Lord.
In the first year of Zhìdé (至德) (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Shǐ'ān (始安),
with an estate of two thousand households.
Soon after, he was appointed Jūnshī Jiāngjūn (軍師將軍) and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (揚州刺史),
and given subordinate officials.
In the second year of Zhēnmíng (禎明) (588 CE), when Crown Prince Yìn (胤) was deposed,
the Latter Lord then established Shēn (深) as Crown Prince.
In the third year (589 CE),
when the Suí (隋) army crossed the Jiāng (江) (Yangtze River),
and the six armies were defeated,
the Suí (隋) general Hán Qínhǔ (韓擒虎) entered through the southern gate.
The officials fled and dispersed.
At that time, Shēn (深) was over ten years old;
he closed his door and sat inside,
with Shèrén Kǒng Bóyú (舍人孔伯魚) attending him.
The Suí (隋) soldiers forced open the door and entered.
Shēn (深) ordered his messenger to greet them, saying:
“The army has been on the road;
are you not weary?”
The soldiers all respected him.
In that same year, he entered the Pass.
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty, he served as Fúhǎn Tàishǒu (枹罕太守).
Chén Yìn 陳胤, Prince of Wúxīng 吳興, courtesy name Chéngyè 承業,
was the eldest son of the Later Lord (Hòuzhǔ 後主).
In the second month, on the day Yǐchǒu 乙丑, of the fifth year of Tàijiàn 太建 (573 CE), he was born in the Eastern Palace.
His mother, Consort Sūn 孫姬, died in childbirth.
Empress Shěn 沈皇后 mourned her and adopted him,
raising him as her own son.
At that time, the Later Lord was still young [and]
had no heir.
Emperor Gāozōng 高宗 therefore commanded that he be made the imperial grandson.
On that day, an edict was issued saying:
"The imperial grandson has just been born,
and the national fortune is flourishing.
I wish to share this celebration with my officials.
All civil and military officials, both inside and outside the court, are to be granted silk, each according to their rank.
Those who have become fathers are to be granted one rank of nobility."
In the tenth year [of Tàijiàn 太建] (578 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Yǒngkāng 永康.
When the Later Lord ascended the throne,
he was established as the Imperial Crown Prince.
Yìn 胤 was intelligent and keen-witted,
fond of learning.
He diligently studied the classics,
tirelessly throughout the day.
He thoroughly understood the great principles [of governance and morality]
and was also skilled in literary composition.
In the third year of Zhìdé 至德 (585 CE),
he personally went to the Imperial Academy (Tàixué 太學) to lecture on the Classic of Filial Piety (Xiàojīng 孝經).
After the lecture,
he also performed a ritual offering to the Former Sages and Former Teachers.
On that day, music of bells and chimes was performed at the Imperial Academy,
and all princes, dukes, ministers, scholars, and students from the Imperial Academy attended the banquet.
At this time, Consort Zhāng 張貴妃 and Consort Kǒng 孔貴嬪 were both favored,
while Empress Shěn 沈皇后 was not.
The palace attendants frequently traveled between the Eastern Palace and [the Empress's residence],
and the Crown Prince also frequently sent people to the Empress.
The Later Lord suspected them of resentment and discontent,
and detested this greatly.
Furthermore, Consorts Zhāng 張 and Kǒng 孔 daily fabricated faults of the Empress and the Crown Prince.
Kǒng Fàn 孔範 and his ilk also conspired from outside to corroborate their stories.
In the second year of Zhēnmíng 禎明 (588 CE),
he was deposed as the Prince of Wúxīng 吳興,
and additionally appointed Grandee Remonstrant (Shìzhōng 侍中) and General of the Central Guard (Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn 中衛將軍).
In the third year [of Zhēnmíng 禎明] (589 CE), he entered the Pass [to go north]
and died in Cháng'ān 長安.
Chén Yí 陳嶷, Prince of Nánpíng 南平, courtesy name Chéngyuè 承嶽,
was the second son of the Later Lord.
He was upright and possessed a dignified bearing.
At several years old,
his demeanor and conduct
were like that of an adult.
In the first year of Zhìdé 至德 (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nánpíng 南平.
Shortly after, he was appointed General of Trustworthy Martiality (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn 信武將軍) and Administrator of the two commanderies of Nán Lángyá 南琅邪 and Péngchéng 彭城,
with auxiliary officials appointed.
He was promoted to Governor of Yángzhōu 揚州,
and granted the title of General Who Guards the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn 鎮南將軍).

Shortly after, he was made Bearer of Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe 使持節), Regional Commander of Military Affairs of Yǐng 郢, Jīng 荊, and Xiāng 湘 three prefectures (Dūdū Yǐng Jīng Xiāng Sānzhōu Zhū Jūnfēng 都督郢荊湘三州諸軍事), General Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn 征西將軍), and Governor of Yǐngzhōu 郢州.
Before he could take up his post, the Suí 隋 army crossed the Jiāng 江 River.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng 禎明 (589 CE), he entered the Pass [to go north]
and died in Cháng'ān 長安.
Chén Yán 陳彥, Prince of Yǒngjiā 永嘉, courtesy name Chéngyì 承懿,
was the third son of the Later Lord.
In the first year of Zhìdé 至德 (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yǒngjiā 永嘉.
Shortly after, he was made General of Loyal Martiality (Zhōngwǔ Jiāngjūn 忠武將軍),
Governor of Nánxúzhōu 南徐州,
and granted the title of General Who Pacifies the South (Ānnán Jiāngjūn 安南將軍).

[三五] He was appointed Palace Attendant with Rank of Scattered Cavalry (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍), Bearer of Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe 使持節), Regional Commander of Military Affairs of Jiāng 江, Bā 巴, Dōnghéng 東衡 three prefectures (Dūdū Jiāng Bā Dōnghéng Sānzhōu Zhū Jūnfēng 都督江巴東衡三州諸軍事), General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn 平南將軍), and Governor of Jiāngzhōu 江州.
[三六] Before he could take up his post,
the Suí 隋 army crossed the Jiāng 江 River.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng 禎明 (589 CE), he entered the Pass [to go north].
During the Dàyè 大業 reign (605-618 CE) of the Suí 隋, he served as Magistrate of Xiāngwǔ 襄武.
Chén Qián 陳虔, Prince of Nánhǎi 南海, courtesy name Chéngkè 承恪,
was the fifth son of the Later Lord.
In the first year of Zhìdé 至德 (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nánhǎi 南海.
Shortly after, he was made General of Martial Resolution (Wǔyì Jiāngjūn 武毅將軍),
with auxiliary officials appointed,
and granted the title of General of the Military Counselor (Jūnshī Jiāngjūn 軍師將軍).
In the second year of Zhēnmíng 禎明 (588 CE),
he was appointed General Who Pacifies the North (Píngběi Jiāngjūn 平北將軍) and Governor of Nánxúzhōu 南徐州.
[三七] In the third year [of Zhēnmíng 禎明] (589 CE), he entered the Pass [to go north].
During the Dàyè 大業 reign (605-618 CE) of the Suí 隋, he served as Magistrate of Zhuō 涿.
Chén Zhī 陳祗, Prince of Xìnyì 信義, courtesy name Chéngjìng 承敬,
was the sixth son of the Later Lord.
In the first year of Zhìdé 至德 (583 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xìnyì 信義.
Shortly after, he was made General of Robust Martiality (Zhuàngwǔ Jiāngjūn 壯武將軍),
with auxiliary officials appointed.

He was appointed Bearer of Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe 使持節), Regional Commander (Dūdū 都督), General of Wise Martiality (Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn 智武將軍), and Administrator of the two commanderies of Lángyá 琅邪 and Péngchéng 彭城.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng 禎明 (589 CE), he entered the Pass [to go north].
During the Dàyè 大業 reign (605-618 CE) of the Suí 隋, he served as Palace Gentleman for Discussion (Tōngyì Láng 通議郎).
Chén Jìng 陳兢, Prince of Shàolíng 邵陵, courtesy name Chéngjiǎn 承檢,
was the seventh son of the Later Lord.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng 禎明 (587 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Shàolíng 邵陵,
with an income of one thousand households.
Shortly after, he was made General of Benevolent Martiality (Rénwǔ Jiāngjūn 仁武將軍),
with auxiliary officials appointed.
In the third year [of Zhēnmíng 禎明] (589 CE), he entered the Pass [to go north].
During the Dàyè 大業 reign (605-618 CE) of the Suí 隋, he served as Vice Director of the Imperial Academy (Guózǐ Jiān Chéng 國子監丞).
Chén Zhuāng 陳莊, Prince of Kuàijī 會稽, courtesy name Chéngsù 承肅,
was the eighth son of the Later Lord.
His appearance was extremely ugly,
and his nature was cruel.
When he was several years old,
if his attendants failed to please him,
he would pierce and stab their faces,
or burn them.
Because his mother, Consort Zhāng 張貴妃, was favored,
the Later Lord loved him greatly.
In the fourth year of Zhìdé 至德 (586 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Kuàijī 會稽.
Shortly after, he was made General Who Assists the Vanguard (Yìqián Jiāngjūn 翊前將軍),
with auxiliary officials appointed.
He was appointed Bearer of Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe 使持節), Regional Commander of Military Affairs of Yángzhōu 揚州 (Dūdū Yángzhōu Zhū Jūnshì 都督揚州諸軍事), and Governor of Yángzhōu 揚州.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng 禎明 (589 CE), he entered the Pass [to go north].
During the Dàyè 大業 reign (605-618 CE) of the Suí 隋, he served as Magistrate of Huìlóng 會隆.
[三八]
Chén Quán 陳恮, Prince of Dōngyáng 東陽, courtesy name Chénghòu 承厚,
was the ninth son of the Later Lord.
In the second year of Zhēnmíng 禎明 (588 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Dōngyáng 東陽,
with an income of one thousand households.
Before he could take up his post,
in the third year [of Zhēnmíng 禎明] (589 CE), he entered the Pass [to go north].
During the Dàyè 大業 reign (605-618 CE) of the Suí 隋, he served as Palace Gentleman for Discussion (Tōngyì Láng 通議郎).
Chén Fān 陳蕃, Prince of Wújùn 吳郡, courtesy name Chéngguǎng 承廣,
was the tenth son of the Later Lord.
In the second year of Zhēnmíng 禎明 (588 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Wújùn 吳郡.
In the third year [of Zhēnmíng 禎明] (589 CE), he entered the Pass [to go north].
During the Dàyè 大業 reign (605-618 CE) of the Suí 隋, he served as Magistrate of Fúchéng 涪城.
Chén Tián 陳恬, Prince of Qiántáng 錢塘, courtesy name Chéngtán 承惔,
was the eleventh son of the Later Lord.
In the second year of Zhēnmíng 禎明 (588 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Qiántáng 錢塘,
with an income of one thousand households.
In the third year [of Zhēnmíng 禎明] (589 CE), he entered the Pass [to go north]
and died in Cháng'ān 長安.
In Jiāngzuǒ 江左, from the Western Jìn 西晉 dynasty onwards,
when princes were enfeoffed,
they were categorized into three grades – large, medium, and small – based on the number of households.
Large principalities were granted three generals: Upper, Middle, and Lower,
and one Marshal (Sīmǎ 司馬).
Medium principalities were granted two generals: Middle and Lower.
Small principalities were granted one general.
Other officials were also appointed according to this difference.
From the time Emperor Gāozǔ 高祖 received the mandate [of Heaven],
from Yǒngdìng 永定 to Zhēnmíng 禎明,
only Chén Chāng 陳昌, Prince of Héngyáng 衡陽, was specially favored
with up to five thousand households.
Apart from him, large principalities did not exceed two thousand households,
and small principalities were one thousand households.
However, the old histories are incomplete and fragmented,
so the exact number of households for each principality cannot be ascertained.
Therefore, the remaining accounts are appended here.
The Imperial Historian states: Emperors Shìzǔ 世祖, Gāozōng 高宗, and the Later Lord (Hòuzhǔ 後主) all established regional principalities
to strengthen their close relatives,
thereby solidifying the root and foundation,
and establishing a stable bedrock.
Chén Bóshān 陳伯山, Prince of Póyáng 鄱陽, had a dignified bearing and moral character,
and was indeed a model prince of his generation.
Chén Shúshèn 陳叔慎, Prince of Yuèyáng 岳陽, faced a time when the state was in peril,
grieved for his family and country,
exhausted his sincerity in confronting the enemy,
and had no intention of saving his own life.
Alas!
This is what is meant by the loyal and valiant in ancient times giving their lives.
Textual Notes
Biographies, Chapter 23: Zōng Yuánráo 宗元饒, Sīmǎ Shēn 司馬申, Máo Xǐ 毛喜, Cài Zhēng 蔡徵
Zōng Yuánráo 宗元饒
was a native of Jiānglíng 江陵, Nánjùn 南郡.
In his youth, he was fond of learning and known for his filial piety and respect.
During the Liáng 梁 dynasty,
he began his career as the Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù 主簿) of his home prefecture.
He was promoted to Acting Staff Officer of the General Who Conquers the South's (Zhēngnán Fǔ 征南府) headquarters,
and then transferred to Staff Officer for External Military Affairs (Wàibīng Cānjūn 外兵參軍).
When Grand Chancellor (Sītú 司徒) Wáng Sēngbiàn's 王僧辯 headquarters was first established,
Yuánráo 元饒 and Liú Shīzhī 劉師知 of Pèiguó 沛國 both served as Chief Clerks.
When Emperor Gāozǔ 高祖 received the abdication,
he was appointed Magistrate of Jìnlíng 晉陵.
He was then brought into the court as Director of Merits and Debates (Gōnglùn Láng 功論郎) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū 尚書).
After returning from an embassy to Qí 齊,
he served as Judicial Secretary (Tíngwèi Zhèng 廷尉正).
He was promoted to Grand Coachman (Tàipú Qīng 太僕卿),
concurrently serving as Great Arbiter of his home district (Běnyì Dà Zhōngzhèng 本邑大中正) and Palace Aide to the Imperial Secretary (Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén 中書通事舍人).
Shortly after, he was transferred to Imperial Justice (Tíngwèi Qīng 廷尉卿),
additionally appointed Palace Attendant with Rank of Through-going Scattered Cavalry (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì 通直散騎常侍),
and concurrently Assistant Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒchéng 尚書左丞).
At this time, Emperor Gāozōng 高宗 had just ascended the throne,
and military and state affairs were extensive.
Without regard to their importance,
he consulted him on all matters,
and the Imperial Secretariat and Department of State Affairs praised him as competent.
He was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng
and was in charge of the Five Rites.
At that time, Chén Póu, the Cìshǐ of Hézhōu, was notoriously corrupt,
sending envoys to collect fish from the sandbanks
and begging for rice from the six commanderies,
which greatly distressed the people.
Yuán Ráo impeached him, memorializing:
"Your servant has heard that setting up banners to seek out suffering
is truly entrusted to integrity and fairness,
and raising the curtain to care for the hidden
fundamentally relies on benevolence and clemency.
If, however, greed and corruption are rampant
and levies and taxes are insatiable,
though the net of Heaven is wide,
it will not let such escape.
We respectfully find that your servant Póu, the founding Marquis of Zhōnglíng County and Cìshǐ of Hézhōu,
by dint of much good fortune,
happened to be promoted,
his peerage bestowed by grace,
his office added by private means,
without virtue or merit,
idly enjoying honor and nobility.
The lands of Qiáo and Féi,
long fallen into improper hands,
were recovered by imperial might,
and the people looked up to benevolent rule.
A new state being taken lightly,
it all the more awaits magnanimity and kindness.
To be appointed as a shepherd over these,
the responsibility is particularly heavy.
Receiving special imperial favor,
he journeyed to Xuānshì,
personally receiving guidance and instruction,
the matter being as if spoken and uplifted.
Although he genuinely possessed no inherent integrity,
yet having received these severe admonitions,
he could have striven for refinement.
Instead, he arbitrarily imposed levies and taxes,
unscrupulously indulged in greedy exactions,
sought grain without satiety,
shaming Wáng Chén's distribution for relief,
and levied fish without limit,
unlike Yáng Xù's hanging of a dried fish.
To punish him with severe penalties
is truly a clear law.
Your servants have deliberated
and request, according to your decree, that Póu's official post, which should be revoked, be removed,
and that for those who should be permanently banished and later relegated from their original posts,
all should follow the law for removal from office."
The memorial was then approved.
Wǔlíng Wáng Bólǐ, the Tàishǒu of Wúxīng,
and Nánkāng Sìwáng Fāngtài, the Nèishǐ of Yùzhāng,
were both arrogant and unruly.
Yuán Ráo impeached them,
and they were all dismissed.
Yuán Ráo was fair-minded by nature,
skilled at upholding the law,
knowledgeable about precedents,
and adept at governance.
If officials violated the law,
if policies were inconvenient for the people, or if they were deficient in terms of moral principles,
he corrected them as appropriate,
providing much benefit.
He was promoted to Zhēn Wēi Jiāngjūn and Nánkāng Nèishǐ,
using over three thousand hú of his salary in rice to assist the people with their rent and taxes,
visiting and inquiring about the elderly,
and rescuing the destitute.
The people greatly relied on him.
Because his administration was rated excellent, he entered the court,
and an imperial edict added the titles Sǎnjì Chángshì and Jīng-Yōng-Xiāng-Bā-Wǔ Wǔzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng.
Soon after, he again concurrently held the post of Shàngshū Zuǒchéng in his original capacity.
He also served as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
He successively held the posts of Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū, Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn, and concurrently Qián Jiāngjūn,
and was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū.
He died in the thirteenth year of Tàijiàn,
at the age of sixty-four.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the titles Shìzhōng and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and the state provided for his funeral.
Sīmǎ Shēn, whose courtesy name was Jìhé,
was a native of Wēn in Hénèi.
His grandfather, Huìyuǎn,
was the Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě during the Liáng dynasty.
His father, Xuántōng,
was the Shàngshū Zuǒ Mín Láng during the Liáng dynasty.
Shēn showed an early spirit and character;
at fourteen, he was already skilled at chess.
He once accompanied his father to visit the Lìbù Shàngshū Dào Gài
At that time, Yīn Zǐchūn, the Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu, and Zhū Yì, the Lǐngjūn, were present.
Zǐchūn, who knew Shēn well, immediately called him over to play a game.
Shēn showed brilliant ideas in every move,
and Yì watched him with admiration,
subsequently inviting Shēn to associate with him.
When the Shàolíng Wáng of Liáng served as Dānyáng Yǐn,
he appointed Shēn as his Zhǔbù.
During the disturbances of Tàiqīng,
both his parents perished,
and because of this, he vowed
to eat only vegetables for the rest of his life.
When Emperor Yuán of Liáng assumed imperial authority,
he appointed Shēn as Kāiyuǎn Jiāngjūn,
and later promoted him to Zhèn Xī Wàibīng Jìshì Cānjūn.
When Hóu Jǐng attacked Yǐngzhōu,
Shēn followed Dūdū Wáng Sēngbiàn to defend Bālíng,
and every strategy he proposed
was adopted.
Sēngbiàn sighed, saying:
"This man may not be skilled in
wearing armor and spurring horses,
but if he were to manage troops and defend a city,
he would surely achieve extraordinary feats."
When Sēngbiàn was attacking Lù Nà,
Shēn was in the army.
At that time, the enemy suddenly arrived,
and those around him scattered.
Shēn personally shielded Sēngbiàn,
advancing with a shield.
Just then, Péi Zhīhéng arrived with reinforcements,
and the enemy retreated.
Sēngbiàn looked at Shēn and smiled, saying:
"A benevolent person must be brave—
how could that be empty talk!"
He was appointed Sǎnjì Shìláng.
In the early years of Shàotài,
he was promoted to Yítóng Hóu Āndū Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he was appointed Āndōng Línchuān Wáng Zīyì Cānjūn.
In the third year of Tiānjiā,
he was promoted to Zhēngběi Zīyì Cānjūn
and concurrently Tíngwèi Jiān.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Zhèndōng Zīyì Cānjūn
and concurrently Qǐbù Láng.
He was sent out as Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn and Jiāngchéng Lìng,
and achieved considerable administrative success.
He returned to serve as Shàngshū Jīnbù Láng.
He was promoted to Zuǒ Mín Láng,
but was dismissed due to official business.
In the early years of Tàijiàn,
he was appointed Zhēn Wēi Jiāngjūn and Zhēngnán Póyáng Wáng Zīyì Cānjūn.
In the ninth year,
he was appointed Mòlíng Lìng.
While in office, he was noted for his integrity and ability,
and white sparrows nested in the county court.
After his term expired,
a short while later,
he became a guest of the Eastern Palace
and soon concurrently held the post of Dōnggōng Tōngshì Shèrén.
He was promoted to Yuánwài Sǎnjì Chángshì,
while his position as Shèrén remained unchanged.
When Shūlíng committed treason,
and the plot failed,
he occupied the Eastern Mansion.
Shēn rushed to summon the Yòuwèi Xiāo Móhē, who led troops to arrive first,
pursued and beheaded him.
He then entered the city
and seized his treasury.
The Later Ruler greatly praised him.
For his achievements, he was appointed Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài,
enfeoffed as Wénzhāo Xiàn Bó,
with a fief of four hundred households,
and concurrently held the post of Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
Soon after, he was promoted to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn
and granted the additional title of Tōngzhí Sǎnjì Chángshì.
Due to illness, he returned home,
where he was granted the additional title of Sǎnjì Chángshì,
while his posts as Yòuwèi and Shèrén remained unchanged.
In the fourth year of Zhìdé, Shēn died.
The Later Emperor (Hòuzhǔ) sighed and grieved for a long time.
He issued an edict which stated:
“To attend to the end with care and honor the distant past,
reverently following old precedents,
determining the posthumous name upon the closing of the coffin,
is indeed a former tradition.
Shēn, the former Sànqí Chángshì, Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn, Kāngshāo Xiàn Kāiguó Bó,
was loyal and respectful in public service,
pure and upright in his self-conduct.
He managed complex affairs and adapted to humble circumstances,
sacrificing himself for righteousness.
My trust and affection for him were deep;
just as he was about to bring prosperity to various undertakings,
he suddenly passed away.
This causes me great sorrow.
He may be posthumously appointed Shìzhōng, Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
promoted to the rank of Hóu,
with his fiefdom increased by five hundred households,
and given the posthumous name Zhōng.
One set of court robes
and one suit of clothes shall be provided.
A day shall be set for mourning,
and all necessary funeral expenses
shall be supplied as needed.”
When Shēn was buried,
the Later Emperor himself composed the epitaph,
its words filled with deep sorrow.
The final lines read:
“Alas!
Heaven does not grant good fortune,
destroying my good minister.”
Such was the favor he enjoyed.
Shēn served three emperors,
managing secret affairs within the court.
Even during times of urgency,
in matters of great importance to the military and the state,
he directed and made decisions,
without any delay.
His son Xiù succeeded him,
and held the office of Tàizǐ Shèrén.
Máo Xǐ, courtesy name Bówǔ,
was a native of Yángwǔ, Xíngyáng.
His grandfather, Chēng,
was a Liáng Sànqí Shìláng.
His father, Qīzhōng,
was a Liáng Shàngshū Bǐbù Shìláng and Zhōngquán Sīmǎ.
Xǐ was fond of learning in his youth
and skilled in both cursive (cǎo) and clerical (lì) scripts.
He began his career in Liáng as an Xīchāng Hóu Xíngcānjūn under the Zhōngwèi,
and soon thereafter was promoted to Jìshì Cānjūn.
Gāozǔ had long known Xǐ,
and when he garrisoned Jīngkǒu,
he ordered Xǐ to go to Jiānglíng with Gāozōng.
He further instructed Gāozōng, saying:
“When you arrive at the Western Court (Xīcháo),
you may consult Máo Xǐ.”
Xǐ and Gāozōng together paid respects to Liáng Yuándì.
Immediately, Gāozōng was appointed Lǐngzhí,
and Xǐ was appointed Shàngshū Gōnglùn Shìláng.
When Jiānglíng fell,
Xǐ and Gāozōng were both moved to Guān Yòu.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Xǐ returned from Zhōu
and proposed a strategy for peace and harmony.
The court then dispatched Zhōu Hóngzhèng and others to exchange envoys.
When Gāozōng returned to the country,
Xǐ went to Yǐngzhōu to welcome him.
Xǐ was again sent to Guān
to request the return of the imperial family members.
The Zhōu prime minister (Zhǒngzǎi), Yǔwén Hù, held Xǐ’s hand and said:
“You are the one who can establish good relations between the two states.”
He then welcomed Empress Liǔ and the Later Emperor back.
They arrived at the capital (Jīngshī) in the third year of Tiānjiā.
Gāozōng was then the Piàojì Jiāngjūn,
and he appointed Xǐ as his Fǔ Zīyì Cānjūn
and concurrently Lǐng Zhōngjìshì.
All the literary works of the Fǔ and the court
were Xǐ’s compositions.
Shìzǔ once said to Gāozōng:
“All my sons have ‘bó’
in their names.
Your sons should use ‘shú’
as a prefix.”
Gāozōng consulted Xǐ about this,
and Xǐ immediately compiled a list of over twenty virtuous individuals from ancient times, such as Dù Shúyīng and Yú Shúqīng,
and presented it to Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ praised it as good.
When Shìzǔ died,
the deposed Emperor (Fèidì) was ignorant and muddled.
Gāozōng was appointed Lù Shàngshū to assist in governance.
Púyè Dào Zhòngjǔ and others, knowing that the court’s hopes rested with Gāozōng,
falsely issued an order from the Empress Dowager to send Gāozōng back to the Eastern Mansion (Dōngfǔ).
At that time, everyone was suspicious and fearful,
and no one dared to speak.
Xǐ immediately rushed in
and said to Gāozōng:
“The Chén dynasty has ruled the world for a short time,
and the realm (Hǎinèi) is not yet pacified.
Moreover, national calamities are striking together,
and all states are in peril.
The Empress Dowager deeply considers the paramount interest of the state (Shèjì),
and ordered the King to enter the palace.
You should be working together to bring prosperity to various undertakings,
emulating Yī and Zhōu.
Today’s words
surely do not represent the Empress Dowager’s true intention.
Considering the gravity of the imperial altars (Zōngshè),
I wish you would reconsider.
In my humble opinion,
it is necessary to inform the Empress Dowager again,
so that treacherous villains do not succeed in their plot.”
Ultimately, his plan was followed.
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Hán Zǐgāo had begun conspiring with Zhòngjǔ.
Before the matter was discovered,
Xǐ requested Gāozōng:
“It is advisable to select men and horses
and assign them to Zǐgāo,
and also bestow iron and charcoal upon him,
to allow him to repair his armor and weapons.”
Gāozōng was surprised and said:
“Zǐgāo is plotting rebellion,
and I am about to arrest him.
Why should I do this?”
Xǐ replied:
“The imperial tomb has just been completed,
and there are still many border bandits.
Although Zǐgāo was entrusted by the previous court,
and is ostensibly a supporter of righteousness,
he is very reckless and frivolous.
I fear he may not surrender in time;
if his execution is delayed,
it might contravene the king’s laws.
It is better to win his trust and reassure him,
so he does not become suspicious,
and then deal with him through the strength of a single brave warrior.”
Gāozōng deeply agreed with this,
and ultimately carried out his plan.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
he appointed Xǐ as Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng,
concurrently Zhōngshū Shèrén,
and placed him in charge of military and state secrets.
When Gāozōng was about to deliberate on a northern expedition,
he ordered Xǐ to draft military regulations.
There were thirteen articles in total;
they were promulgated throughout the realm by edict,
but due to their length, they are not recorded here.
Soon thereafter, he was promoted to Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
For his contributions to the succession plan (dìng cè gōng),
he was enfeoffed as Dōngchāng Xiàn Hóu,
with a fiefdom of five hundred households.
He also served concurrently as the administrator of the state affairs for the three princely mansions of Jiāngxià, Wǔlíng, and Guìyáng.
In the third year of Tàijiàn,
he resigned from office due to mourning for his mother.
An edict posthumously honored Xǐ’s mother, Lady Yǔ, as Dōngchāng Guó Tàifūrén,
bestowed five hundred bolts of cloth
and three hundred thousand coins,
and the government covered the funeral expenses.
He also sent Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì Dù Miǎn to survey and map his burial ground.
Gāozōng personally examined the map with Miǎn, pointing and marking locations.
Such was the esteem in which he was held.
Soon, he was recalled to serve as Míngwēi Jiāngjūn,
with his roles as Yòuwèi and Shèrén remaining unchanged.
He was then reassigned as Xuānyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Yìxīng Tàishǒu.
Soon after, with his original title, he entered the court as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
After the mourning period ended,
he was given the added title of Sànqí Chángshì and Wǔbīng Shàngshū,
and participated in selection affairs.
When the various armies launched the northern expedition
and captured the Huáinán territory,
Xǐ proposed strategies for pacifying the border regions.
Gāozōng adopted them
and implemented them on the very same day.
He then asked Xǐ:
“I intend to advance troops to Péng and Biàn;
what are your thoughts on this?”
Xǐ replied:
“Your subject is truly not a man of great wisdom;
how dare I predict what has not yet happened?
However, I secretly believe that Huáizuǒ has just been pacified,
and the border populace is not yet settled.
The Zhōu (Northern Zhōu) has just swallowed the Qí (Northern Qí) state,
making it difficult to contend with them.
How can we, with weary and exhausted troops,
again penetrate deeply?
Moreover, abandoning the advantages of boats and oars
to fight on chariot and cavalry terrain,
exchanging strengths for weaknesses,
is not advantageous for the people of Wú.
Your humble subject believes it would be better to pacify the people and secure our borders,
cease military action, and renew our alliance.
Then, we can widely recruit heroes
and act according to the opportune moment.
This is a strategy for long-term success.”
Gāozōng did not heed him.
Later, when Wú Míngchè was defeated by Zhōu,
Gāozōng said to Xǐ:
“What you said
has now been proven true.”
In the twelfth year,
he was promoted to Shìzhōng.
In the thirteenth year,
he was appointed Sǎnjì Chángshì and Dānyáng Yǐn.
He was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū,
with Chángshì as before.
When Gāozōng died,
and Shūlíng plotted rebellion,
he ordered Zhōngshùzǐ Lù Qióng to proclaim the imperial decree,
ordering all the northern and southern armies
to follow Móu Xǐ's commands.
After the rebels were pacified,
he was again promoted to Shìzhōng,
and his enfeoffment was increased to a total of nine hundred households.
In the first year of Zhìdé,
he was appointed Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn and Yǒngjiā Nèishǐ,
and his rank was increased to Zhōng'èrqiānshí.
Initially,
Gāozōng entrusted governance to Móu Xǐ,
and Xǐ also diligently offered loyal advice,
providing much correction and benefit.
He frequently offered remonstrances,
and his advice was always followed.
Because of this, for more than ten years,
though Jiāngdōng was small,
it achieved complete prosperity.
Only in the matter of seizing land north of the Huái River
did Gāozōng not adopt Xǐ's strategy,
and Wú Míngchè was ultimately defeated.
Gāozōng deeply regretted this,
and said to Yuán Xiàn:
"By not using Móu Xǐ's plan,
it led to this situation.
This is my fault."
As Xǐ became more favored,
he spoke without reservation.
However, the Crown Prince indulged in wine,
and frequently held long night banquets with his favored attendants.
Móu Xǐ once spoke about this,
and Gāozōng used it to admonish the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince secretly resented him for this,
and from then on, Xǐ gradually became estranged.
Initially,
the Later Lord was wounded by the Prince of Shǐxīng.
When his wound healed, he celebrated by himself,
setting up a banquet in the rear hall,
inviting Jiāng Zǒng and others,
to enjoy music and compose poetry.
While drunk, he summoned Móu Xǐ.
At that time, the imperial burial had just been completed,
and less than a year had passed.
Xǐ saw this and was displeased.
He wanted to remonstrate, but the Later Lord was already drunk.
Xǐ ascended the steps,
pretending to have a heart ailment,
and collapsed at the bottom of the steps.
He was moved out to the provincial office.
When the Later Lord sobered up,
he became suspicious of Xǐ,
and said to Jiāng Zǒng:
"I regret summoning Móu Xǐ.
I know he is not ill;
he merely wanted to obstruct my festive banquet.
This is not what I would do,
so he is being cunning and deceptive."
Then he conspired with Sīmǎ Shēn, saying:
"This man is arrogant.
I want to hand him over to the Póyáng brothers to let them seek revenge.
Is that permissible?"
He replied:
"He will ultimately be useless to Your Majesty.
I agree with your sacred intention."
Fù Zāi argued, saying:
"That is not right.
If you allow revenge,
where would you place the late Emperor?"
The Later Lord said:
"I shall grant him a small commandery,
so he will not be involved in human affairs."
Thus, Móu Xǐ was made Yǒngjiā Nèishǐ.
When Xǐ arrived in the commandery,
he refused his salary and emoluments.
His administration was upright and tranquil,
and the people and officials found it convenient.
When the Prefect of Fēngzhōu, Zhāng Dàbǎo, raised an army and rebelled,
the commandery bordered Fēngzhōu,
and was originally without defenses.
Móu Xǐ then repaired the city walls and moats,
and strictly embellished the weaponry.
He also dispatched Zhōu Pán, the Magistrate of Sōngyáng, under his command, to lead a thousand soldiers to reinforce Jiàn'ān.
After the rebels were pacified,
he was appointed Nán'ān Nèishǐ.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng,
he was summoned to be Guānglù Dàfū,
and concurrently Lǐng Zuǒxiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
Móu Xǐ had benevolent governance in the commanderies,
so he was summoned to court.
Those who accompanied him on the road extended for hundreds of li.
In that same year, he died of illness on the road,
at the age of seventy-two.
He had a collection of ten volumes.
His son Chǔchōng succeeded him,
and his official position reached Yítóng Cóngshì Zhōngláng and Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Cài Zhēng, courtesy name Xīxiáng,
was the son of Shìzhōng and Zhōngfǔjūn Jiāngjūn Jǐnglì.
From a young age, he was intelligent and sensitive,
with keen insight and a strong memory.
At the age of six,
he visited Liáng Lìbù Shàngshū Hénán Chǔ Xiáng.
Chǔ Xiáng, courtesy name Zhòngjǔ,
praised his outstanding intelligence.
At seven,
he mourned his mother,
observing mourning rites as an adult.
His stepmother, Lady Liú, was fierce and jealous,
and did not treat him properly.
Zhēng attended to her with even greater care,
showing no signs of resentment.
Zhēng's original name was Lǎn.
Jǐnglì believed he possessed the character of Wáng Xiáng,
and thus changed his name to Zhēng,
courtesy name Xīxiáng.
At the beginning of Chéngshèng of Liáng,
Gāozǔ was the Inspector of Nánxúzhōu.
He summoned Zhēng to be appointed Yíng Zhǔbù,
and soon after, he was appointed Tàixué Bóshì.
At the beginning of Tiānjiā,
he was promoted to Fǎcáo Xíngcānjūn of the Prince of Shǐxīng's Residence.
He successively held positions such as Wàibīng Cānjūnshì and Shàngshū Zhǔkèláng.
In all his posts, he was noted for his efficient administration.
At the beginning of Tàijiàn,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Shàofùchéng, Xīn'ān Wáng Zhǔbù, Tōngzhí Sǎnjì Shìláng, Jìn'ān Wáng Gōngcáoshǐ, and Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén,
concurrently Lǐngzhí of the Eastern Palace,
with Zhōngshèrén as before.
He left office to mourn his father.
After the mourning period ended,
he inherited the title of Marquis of Xīnfēng County,
and was appointed Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn and Zhènyòu Xīn'ān Wáng Zīyì Cānjūn.
In the second year of Zhìdé,
he was promoted to Tíngwèi Qīng,
and soon after became Lìbù Láng.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ and Zhōngshū Shèrén,
in charge of imperial edicts.
Soon after, he was appointed Zuǒmín Shàngshū,
and with Púshè Jiāng Zǒng, he oversaw the compilation of the Five Rites.
Soon after, he was granted Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn.
The Later Lord valued his talent and capability,
and increasingly relied on him.
He was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū and Ānyòu Jiāngjūn.
Every ten days, he would visit the Eastern Palace
to discuss with the Crown Prince the gains and losses of ancient and modern times, and current political affairs.
He was also ordered that in the prisons of the Tíngwèi Temple,
matters, regardless of their size,
were to be decided by Zhēng.
Shortly after, there was an imperial edict dispatching Zhēng to recruit soldiers,
to form his own units.
Zhēng was good at comforting and assisting them,
and won the hearts of the people.
Within a month,
his forces numbered nearly ten thousand.
As Zhēng's status and reputation became weighty,
and his prestige and influence grew formidable,
public opinion universally feared and respected him.
Soon, he was transferred to Zhōngshū Lìng,
with his general rank remaining as before.
The position of Zhōnglìng was clear and simple, with little to do.
Some said Zhēng had voiced complaints,
which reached the Later Lord.
The Later Lord was furious,
and confiscated his men and horses,
intending to execute him.
However, strong remonstrances saved him.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng,
the Suí army crossed the Yangtze River.
The Later Lord, seeing Zhēng's competence,
provisionally appointed him Zhōnglǐngjūn.
Zhēng worked diligently day and night,
devoting all his effort.
The Later Lord praised him,
saying:
"When this matter is settled, I will repay you."
When the decisive battle was fought at the southern ridge of Zhōngshān,
Zhēng was ordered to defend the main camp northwest of the palace city.
Soon after, he was ordered to oversee the conduct of all military operations.
When the city fell, he entered the pass as was customary.
Cài Zhēng was handsome and had a dignified appearance,
possessed eloquent speech,
and researched extensively.
Regarding scholars, officials,
imperial relatives,
the current dynasty's systems,
laws and protocols,
household registers and customs,
mountains, rivers, and land,
there was nothing he was asked about that he couldn't answer.
However, his nature was somewhat sycophantic and ambitious,
and he could not content himself with a simple, reclusive life.
When he was first appointed Lìbù Shàngshū,
he requested the Rear Master (Hòuzhǔ) to lend him military music (gǔchuī).
The Rear Master (Hòuzhǔ) said to the relevant department,
"Military music (gǔchuī) is granted for meritorious service.
Cài Zhēng does not know his place,
disrupting our court regulations.
However, since his father, Cài Jǐnglì, did have foundational achievements,
it is appropriate to temporarily grant his request,
but it must be recalled immediately after his appointment ceremony."
Zhēng did not maintain integrity and propriety;
these were all of this type.
When Emperor Wén of Suí heard of his quick wit and erudition,
he summoned him for counsel.
His words always hit the mark,
yet he was not promoted for many years.
After a long time,
he was appointed Tàicháng Chéng.
He successively served as Shàngshū Mínbù Yícáo Láng,
then transferred to Jǐshì [Láng].
He died
at the age of sixty-seven.
His son, Cài Yì,
studied the *Shàngshū*,
and his highest office was Sītú Shǔ and Déjiào Xuéshì.
Upon entering the Suí dynasty,
he became Dōnggōng Xuéshì.
The historian said: Zōng Yuán was diligent day and night,
benefitting affairs and his time.
Sīmǎ Shēn was pure and meticulous in court,
enduring hardships and establishing good conduct,
and moreover, he possessed loyalty and integrity.
Splendid!
Máo Xǐ deeply understood opportunities in affairs,
assisting and supporting the sovereign of his time.
Cài Zhēng was intelligent and talented,
but he usurped power and brought about his own downfall.
What a pity!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 24: Xiāo Jì, Lù Qióng (son Cóngdiǎn), Gù Yěwáng, Fù Zǎi (Zhāng Huá)
Xiāo Jì, courtesy name Xiàokāng,
was a native of Lánlíng, Dōnghǎi.
In his youth, he loved learning
and was well-versed in the classics and histories.
He consulted Emperor Wǔ of Liáng on over thirty difficult passages in the *Zuǒshì*.
Shàngshū Púyè Zhāng Zuǎn of Fányáng and Tàicháng Qīng Liú Zhīlín of Nányáng both discussed these with Jì,
but Zuǎn and the others could not refute him.
He began his career as Liáng Mìshū Láng,
and was promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén.
He participated in the campaign to suppress Hóu Jǐng,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Sōngyáng County,
with five hundred households.
When Gāozǔ became the governor of Xúfāng,
he appointed Jì as Míngwēi Jiāngjūn and Zhēngběi Chángshǐ.
In the second year of Chéngshèng,
he was summoned to be Zhōngshū Shìláng,
then transferred to Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì.
When Shìzǔ was Huìjī Tàishǒu,
he again appointed Jì as Xuānyìfǔ Chángshǐ,
and he was promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ.
Upon Shìzǔ's accession,
he was appointed Shìzhōng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Tàifǔ Qīng,
but he did not accept the appointment due to mourning his birth mother.
Jì assisted two emperors,
and his favor and treatment were exceedingly generous,
with rewards and gifts surpassing those of ordinary officials.
He successively governed the commanderies of Lánlíng, Yángxiàn, Línjīn, and Lín'ān,
wherever he went, he established a reputation for achievement.
At the beginning of Tàijiàn,
he entered the court as Wǔbīng Shàngshū,
and together with Zuǒ Púyè Xú Líng, Tèjìn Zhōu Hóngzhèng, Dùzhī Shàngshū Wáng Yáng,
and Sànqí Chángshì Yuán Xiàn, they all served the Eastern Palace.
He again became Sītú Chángshǐ.
Soon after, he was appointed Dùzhī Shàngshū,
and concurrently led the Yǔlín Jiān.
He was promoted to Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
still concurrently leading the Yǔlín.
He was granted the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and concurrently served as Āndé Gōng Wèiwèi.
Soon after, he was promoted to Rénwēi Jiāngjūn and Yángzhōu Chángshǐ.
Gāozōng once ordered the official documents from Yángzhōu to be brought,
and personally reviewed them.
Seeing that Jì's arrangements were detailed and meticulous,
and the writing was without flaws,
he turned to his attendants and said,
"I originally thought Xiāo Chángshǐ was skilled in classics and commentaries,
but I didn't expect him to be so proficient in complex administrative tasks,
to this extent."
He was promoted to Cíbù Shàngshū,
granted Jǐshìzhōng,
and again became Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
He died before taking up the appointment,
at the age of sixty-six.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him his original office,
and the state provided for his funeral.
Lù Qióng, courtesy name Bóyù,
was a native of Wú County, Wú Commandery.
His grandfather, Lù Wán,
was the commander of the two commanderies of Lángyá and Péngchéng in Liáng.
His father, Lù Yúngōng,
was Liáng Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng,
and was in charge of scholarly works.
Qióng was intelligent and discerning in his youth,
and at six years old, he composed five-character poems,
which were quite eloquent.
At the end of Dàtóng,
Yúngōng received an imperial edict from Emperor Wǔ of Liáng to collate and edit official ranks.
Dào Gài, Zhū Yì, and others were all gathered.
Qióng, then eight years old,
solved a chess problem in front of the guests.
Because of this, the capital called him a "divine child."
Yì spoke of him to Emperor Wǔ,
who issued an edict to summon him.
Qióng's demeanor was bright and alert,
and his movements were careful and deliberate.
The Emperor was greatly astonished by him.
At eleven,
he mourned his father,
and his extreme emaciation showed his profound filial piety.
His paternal uncle, Lù Xiāng, sighed,
"This child will surely uphold the family foundation;
he is truly 'one is not too few' (meaning one such child is enough)."
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
he took his mother to avoid the disaster in the western village of the county,
diligently studying
day and night without slackening.
Thus, he became widely learned
and skilled at writing.
During the Yǒngdìng era,
the prefecture recommended him as a Xiùcái.
In the first year of Tiānjiā,
he became Níngyuǎn Shǐxīngwáng Fǔ Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn.
Soon after, with his original office, he concurrently served as Shàngshū Wàibīng Láng.
Due to his literary talent, he was transferred to concurrently serve as Diànzhōng Láng,
and after a year, he became a regular appointee.
Qióng always had an excellent reputation
and was deeply admired by Shìzǔ.
When Shìzǔ campaigned against Zhōu Dí, Chén Bǎo'yìng, and others,
all the official documents and major writings
were entrusted to Qióng by imperial edict.
He was promoted to Xīn'ānwáng Wénxué,
and was in charge of the Dōnggōng guǎnjì.
When Gāozōng became Sītú,
he carefully selected his subordinates.
Lìbù Shàngshū Xú Líng recommended Qióng to Gāozōng, saying:
"Xīn'ānwáng Wénxué Lù Qióng
has superior insight and agility,
and his literary and historical knowledge is sufficient for use.
He has served in the Langshǔ for too long,
and years have passed.
The position of Zuǒxīyuàn is vacant,
and he is truly worthy of this selection.
His rank is slightly exceeded,
but his prolonged stagnation has accumulated."
So, he was appointed Sītú Zuǒxīyuàn.
Soon after, he concurrently served as Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
and was dispatched to Qí.
In the first year of Tàijiàn,
he again, with his original office, was in charge of the Dōnggōng guǎnjì.
He was appointed Tàizǐ Shùzǐ,
and concurrently served as Tōngshì Shèrén.
He was transferred to Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tàizǐ Jiālìng.
When Chángshāwáng became Jiāngzhōu Císhǐ,
he did not follow the laws and regulations.
Gāozōng, considering the king's youth,
appointed Qióng as Chángshǐ,
to oversee the affairs of Jiāngzhōu Fǔ,
and concurrently held the position of Xúnyáng Tàishǒu.
Qióng, considering his mother's old age,
did not wish to travel far,
and the Crown Prince also firmly requested him to stay,
so he did not go.
He was successively promoted to Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng,
and concurrently led the Yǔlín Jiān.
He was transferred to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
and concurrently led the Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
He also concurrently led the Dàzhùzuò,
and was responsible for compiling the national history.
When Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
he was assigned to the Zhōngshū Shěng,
in charge of imperial edicts.
Soon after, he was granted the position of Sànqí Chángshì,
concurrently Dùzhī Shàngshū,
and leader of Yángzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng.
In the first year of Zhìdé,
he was made Dùzhī Shàngshū,
and participated in managing imperial edicts,
while also presiding over the two prisons of Tíngwèi and Jiànkāng.
Initially,
Qióng's father, Gōng Yún, had been ordered by Liáng Wǔdì to compile the Jiāruìjì.
Qióng elaborated on its principles and continued it,
from Yǒngdìng until Zhìdé,
compiling it into a complete work.
He was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū,
with his role as Zhùzuò remaining unchanged.
Qióng was thoroughly conversant with genealogies and records,
and had an elegant discernment of human character.
Before this,
when Lìbù Shàngshū Zōng Yuánráo passed away,
Yòu Púshè Yuán Xiàn recommended Qióng,
but Gāozōng did not employ him.
Now, he occupied the position,
and was regarded as competent;
Hòuzhǔ greatly trusted and appointed him.
Qióng was humble and frugal by nature,
not seeking self-aggrandizement.
Although his position and prestige grew daily,
his resolve remained ever more modest.
His gardens, ponds, rooms, and houses
remained unaltered.
His carriages, horses, and clothes
were not adorned with fresh splendor.
His four seasons' emoluments
were all distributed among his clan,
leaving no surplus wealth in his home.
In his later years, he deeply harbored a sense of contentment and self-restraint,
desiring to avoid power and influence.
He constantly feigned illness and did not attend to affairs.
Soon, he experienced the mourning for his mother,
and resigned from his post.
Initially,
when Qióng served in the Dōnggōng,
his mother resided with him in the official residence,
and Hòuzhǔ bestowed generous rewards.
When her coffin was returned to their hometown for burial,
an imperial edict added to the funeral gifts,
and an attendant, Huáng Chángguì, was dispatched to offer sacrifices with an imperial decree.
Hòuzhǔ also personally composed the epitaph,
which was an honor to the court and the common people.
Qióng's sorrow and mourning were excessive, leading to his deterioration.
He died in the fourth year of Zhìdé,
at the age of fifty.
An imperial edict posthumously appointed him Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
and the state provided for his funeral.
A collection of his twenty volumes circulated in the world.
His eldest son, Cóngyí,
served as Wǔchāng Wáng Wénxué.
His third son, Cóngdiǎn,
courtesy name Yóuyí.
He was intelligent and quick-witted from a young age.
At eight,
he read Shěn Yuē's collection
and saw a palindromic inscription for an inkstone.
Cóngdiǎn immediately took up his brush to imitate it,
and it instantly possessed an exquisite quality.
At thirteen,
he composed "Liǔ Fù" (Ode to the Willow),
the language of which was exceedingly beautiful.
Qióng was then the Dōnggōng Guǎnjì,
and the palace officials were all outstanding talents of their time.
Qióng showed them this ode,
and they all marvelled at his extraordinary talent.
His paternal uncle, Yú, especially cherished and loved him.
When Yú was about to die,
he entrusted all the books and records in his household to Cóngdiǎn.
Cóngdiǎn then compiled Yú's writings into ten volumes,
and composed a preface to the collection,
the prose of which was very accomplished.
Cóngdiǎn was devoted to scholarship,
widely perusing many books,
with a particular interest in Bān Gù's history.
At fifteen,
he was recommended as Xiùcaí by his home prefecture.
He began his career as Zhùzuò Zuǒláng,
and was transferred to Tàizǐ Shèrén.
At that time, Hòuzhǔ bestowed poems upon Púshè Jiāng Zǒng and his father, Qióng.
Zǒng ordered Cóngdiǎn to draft a thank-you memorial,
which he completed in an instant.
Its literary grace and clear reasoning
greatly astonished Zǒng.
He was soon appointed Xìnyì Wáng Wénxué,
and transferred to Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ.
He was again promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Xīyuàn,
and concurrently Dōnggōng Xuéshì.
He resigned due to mourning for his father.
Soon after, he was appointed Déjiào Xuéshì,
but he firmly declined.
Hòuzhǔ decreed that one position be kept open,
to await Cóngdiǎn.
Shortly after, the fall of Jīnlíng occurred,
and he was moved to Guānyòu with others.
He served the Suí dynasty as Gěishìláng,
concurrently Dōnggōng Xuéshì.
He was also appointed Zhùzuò Zuǒláng.
Yòu Púshè Yáng Sù memorialized that Cóngdiǎn should continue Sīmǎ Qiān's Shǐjì up to the Suí dynasty,
but the book was not completed.
During the chaos and unrest at the end of the Suí dynasty,
he resided in Nányáng Jùn,
and died of illness,
at the age of fifty-seven.
Gù Yěwáng, courtesy name Xīféng,
was a native of Wú from Wújùn.
His grandfather, Zǐqiáo, was Liáng Dōng Zhōngláng Wǔlíng Wáng Fǔ Cānjūnshì.
His father, Xuǎn, was Xìnwēi Línhé Wáng Jìshì,
and concurrently Wǔguān Yuàn of his home commandery,
known for his Confucian scholarship.
Yěwáng was fond of learning from a young age.
At seven,
he read the Wǔjīng,
and generally understood their main ideas.
At nine, he could compose essays.
He once wrote "Rì Fù" (Ode to the Sun),
which Lǐngjūn Zhū Yì saw and marvelled at.
At twelve,
he followed his father to Jiàn'ān,
and compiled "Jiàn'ān Dìjì" in two fascicles.
As an adult, he extensively read classics and histories,
memorizing and silently learning.
He was conversant in astronomy, geography, divination with milfoil and tortoise shells, predictions, insect script, and strange characters,
leaving nothing he did not understand.
In the fourth year of Dàtóng of the Liáng dynasty,
he was appointed Tàixué Bóshì.
He was promoted to Zhōng Lǐngjūn Línhé Wáng Fǔ Jìshì Cānjūn.
When Xuānchéng Wáng was Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
Yěwáng and Lángyá Wáng Bāo were both his retainers,
and the King greatly admired their talent.
Yěwáng also loved painting,
and was skilled at depicting.
The King built a study in the eastern residence,
and ordered Yěwáng to paint ancient sages,
and commanded Wáng Bāo to write encomiums,
which people at the time called "the two perfections."
During the Hou Jǐng Rebellion,
Yěwáng went into mourning for his father,
and returned to his home commandery.
He then recruited several hundred villagers
to join the righteous army and assist the capital.
Yěwáng was naturally frail and thin,
barely six feet tall.
Moreover, his mourning led to excessive deterioration,
to the point where he could barely bear his clothes.
Yet, when he wielded a spear and wore armor,
he expounded on the righteousness of ruler and subject,
and the principles of rebellion and obedience,
speaking with strong words and a resolute expression.
Those who saw him were all inspired.
When the capital fell,
Yěwáng fled to Kuàijī,
then went to Dōngyáng,
where he joined forces with Liú Guīyì to hold the city and resist the rebels.
After Hou Jǐng was pacified,
Tàiwèi Wáng Sēngbiàn greatly commended him,
and made him Supervisor of Hǎiyán Xiàn.
When Gāozǔ served as prime minister,
he was appointed as General Wēi of Jīn and Rènjìshì Cānjūn of the Prince of Āndōng-Línchuān's manor.
Soon after, he was transferred to Cānmóu Cānjūn of the manor.
In the first year of Tiānjiā (560),
he was ordered to be appointed as a Xuǎnshǐ Xuéshì,
and soon thereafter was promoted to Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn.
In the first year of Guāngdà (567),
he was appointed Zhèndōng-Póyángwáng Cānmóu Cānjūn.
In the second year of Tàijiàn (570),
he was promoted to Guózǐ Bóshì.
When the Latter Lord was in the Eastern Palace (as Crown Prince),
Yěwáng concurrently served as Guǎnjì of the Eastern Palace,
while retaining his original post.
In the sixth year (574),
he was appointed Tàizǐ Shuàigēnglìng,
and soon after was given the concurrent post of Dà Zhùzuò,
in charge of the National Histories,
overseeing affairs related to the History of Liáng,
and concurrently served as Tōngshì Shèrén of the Eastern Palace.
At that time, among the officials in the palace were Jiāng Zǒng of Jìyáng,
Lù Qióng of Wúguó,
Fù Zài of Běidì,
and Yáo Chá of Wúxīng.
All were renowned for their talent and scholarship,
and commentators held them in high esteem.
He was promoted to Huángmén Shìláng,
then Guānglù Qīng,
and was in charge of the Five Rites,
while retaining his other posts.
He died in the thirteenth year (581),
at the age of sixty-three.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Mìshū Jiān.
In the second year of Zhìdé (584),
he was further posthumously granted the title of Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
Yěwáng was known from a young age for his diligent scholarship and innate integrity.
He never spoke excessively or lost his composure in any situation.
Observing his demeanor,
he seemed to be a man of few words,
yet in his earnest efforts and actions,
he surpassed all others.
His third younger brother, Chōngguó, died early,
and Yěwáng raised the orphans,
showing profound kindness and righteousness.
His compiled works include the Yùpiān in thirty volumes,
Yúdì Zhì in thirty volumes,
Fúruì Tú in ten volumes,
Gù Shì Pǔzhuàn in ten volumes,
Fēnyě Shūyào in one volume,
Xù Dòngmíng Jì in one volume,
and Xuánxiàng Biǎo in one volume,
all of which circulated in the world.
He also compiled the Tōngshǐ Yàolüè in one hundred volumes
and Guóshǐ Jìzhuàn in two hundred volumes,
but died before completing them.
He left behind a collection of essays in twenty volumes.
Fù Zài, courtesy name Yíshì,
was a native of Língzhōu, Běidì.
His father, Yí,
was the Magistrate of Línyí during the Liáng dynasty.
Zài was intelligent from a young age,
and by the age of seven, he could recite over ten myriad words of ancient poetry and rhapsodies.
As he grew older, he was fond of learning
and skilled at writing.
Towards the end of Tàiqīng of Liáng (547-549),
he took his mother south to flee from chaos.
Soon after, his mother passed away,
and amidst the turmoil of war,
he observed the mourning rites fully,
his grief and emaciation rendering him bone-thin.
Scholars and friends praised him for this.
Later, he relied on Xiāo Xún, the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
Xún was quite fond of scholars
and extensively collected books.
Zài indulged his passion in reading them,
thereby becoming widely knowledgeable in various texts.
Wáng Lín heard of his reputation
and invited him to be his Fǔ Jìshì.
When Lín was defeated,
Zài returned to the capital with Sūn Yáng, Lín's general.
At that time, Shìzǔ sent Yán Huàng to bestow various items upon Yáng.
Yáng entrusted Zài with drafting the memorial of thanks,
and the wording and reasoning were so elegant and appropriate
that not a single character needed revision.
Huàng reported this to Shìzǔ upon his return,
and Zài was soon summoned to serve as Xuǎnshǐ Xuéshì.
He was appointed Sīkōng Fǔ Jìshì Cānjūn,
then promoted to Piàojì-Ānchéngwáng Zhōng Jìshì,
while continuing his work as a historian.
Zài was a devout believer in Buddhism.
He studied the Three Treatises under the Dharma Master Xīnghuáng Huìlǎng
and thoroughly mastered their teachings.
At that time, the Dharma Master Dàxīn Gǎo wrote the Wúzhēng Lùn to criticize them.
Zài then composed the Míngdào Lùn
to refute these difficulties.
Its summary states: The Wúzhēng Lùn says: Recently, there are those who propagate the Three Treatises,
thoughtlessly condemning and criticizing,
arbitrarily enumerating faults,
repeatedly slandering various masters,
and rejecting all other schools of thought.
They discuss the Middle Way yet cling to
partial views,
speak of forgetting the mind yet contend for sole supremacy.
By studying several treatises,
they become enemies.
Once enmity is formed,
strife and contention greatly arise.
With such a mind,
they create negative
karma.
If negative karma does not cease,
will it not greatly increase birth and death,
and amass great suffering?
The reply states: The rise of the Three Treatises
has been for a long time.
Nāgārjuna initiated their source,
removing
the partial views of internal studies;
Deva propagated their essence,
dispelling the erroneous attachments of external paths.
The aim is to make the great transformation flow unhindered,
and the profound doctrine flourish without decline.
Its words are
vast,
its meaning profound,
its path broad,
its current deep.
This is indeed like the soaring of dragons and elephants,
the circling flight of the Kūn and Pèng birds.
How can
a disabled
bird with broken wings expect to reach such heights?
In recent times, the age is shallow and dissolute,
and there are no magnanimous scholars.
If one merely practices minor studies
to enlighten a naive mind,
gradually this permeates and becomes custom,
thereby losing the right path.
They only compete to bore
holes,
each indulging in their own constructions.
The branches and leaves become overly lush,
while the root source daily darkens.
One master's explanation
differs from another's,
changing old traditions
and establishing new ideas.
Among fellow students,
their
understandings again diverge.
Thus, in this ongoing progression,
additions and confusions multiply.
If one uses them all,
the mind has no clear standard;
if one selects and acts,
which is the correct one?
Is it
not like Huàndùn injuring its orifices,
or a beautiful tree losing its sprouts?
Even if people say it is not a horse,
and families hold a spirit,
with an inappropriate goblet,
it is like drawing a cake on the ground.
Is it
not fitting that they
stray from the Dao?
The teachings of Shèshān,
however, are not like this.
They preserve unity and adhere to the source,
without the fault of arbitrary alterations;
they elaborate meaning concisely,
and prevent the
tendency for subjective judgment.
Their words are not pre-conceived,
their principles not pre-arranged.
They respond only when circumstances arise,
and act only when confronted by an opponent.
They move horizontally and vertically, interweaving,
suddenly vast and obscure.
Sometimes they encompass
without end,
sometimes they dissolve into nothingness.
They shine with literary brilliance,
yet leave no discernible trace;
they are profoundly immeasurable,
yet directly relevant to affairs, not distant.
Whenever they engage in
dialogue,
they meticulously examine the principles.
What jealousy or deceit is there
to offend various masters?
Moreover, are the teachings of the masters
to be condemned,
or not to be condemned?
If they can be condemned,
destroying the old leads to decline;
if it cannot be destroyed,
destruction will not reach it.
Why does the Fǎshī alone shield and protect, not permitting destruction?
Moreover, teachings have greater and lesser scopes,
fully elaborated in the holy
edicts.
The texts of Mahāyāna
point out and criticize the lesser path.
Now, promoting the Great Dharma,
how can one not speak the meaning of Mahāyāna?
This involves praise and blame,
derived from extensive
learning;
words of acceptance and rejection
are based on scriptural discussion.
How can one believe and assent upon seeing the Buddha's words,
yet defy and rebel against my words?
Is this what is meant by a mind of non-contention and equality?
Furthermore, anger and vexation
are constant characteristics of ordinary beings;
those who lose reason
are mostly afflicted by these.
How can one, because of three unsatisfactory cultivations
or the resentment of the six teachers,
hide the subtle Dharma of Nirvāṇa,
never to proclaim it?
One merely hopes that once their anger reaches its peak,
a calm awakening will naturally come to be.
Human faces differ,
and their minds are also different.
Some have
contradictory words and intentions,
while others have minds and mouths in accord.
How can one necessarily say that others speak the Middle Way but are inwardly prejudiced,
while one's own conduct is non-contending,
outwardly compliant and inwardly
equal?
Enmity, strife, and lawsuits
are not my concern;
the accumulation of sins and karma
is what those who contend fear.
The Wúzhēng Lùn says: "The Great Master Shèshān's persuasive guidance
was not like this;
he truly practiced non-contention."
The virtue of enlightenment has passed,
and the pure
and unified style has become diluted.
The heart of competition
and the melody of criticism
are rampant now.
I wish to cease contention to attain the Way,
and yield superiority to forget virtue.
Why must one exclude
and oppose other schools,
arousing their anger?
If one acts with a Middle Way mind in relation to Chéngshí,
one can also be non-contending;
if one speaks of the Middle
Treatise with a prejudiced mind,
one can also have contention.
Thus, one knows that contention or non-contention
depends solely on a single factor.
Answer: The Great Master Shèshān was indeed non-contending,
but what the Fǎshī appreciates
does not
fully capture his integrity.
He quietly dwelt in a secluded valley,
serene and non-active.
All his instructions and encouragements
were given to like-minded individuals.
He spoke and remained silent at ease,
and no one found fault.
Therefore, although his intentions were
profound,
his words were very concise.
The current situation for exposition
is not like that.
Dwelling in a corner of the royal city,
within a settlement,
amidst guests who breathe and gaze,
and scholars who debate
eloquently,
they sharpen their wits,
brandish their wings,
open their eyes wide and are bold,
wearing armor and gripping sharp weapons.
They challenge other schools,
display different understandings,
spy for weaknesses,
and seek opportunities for
strengths and weaknesses.
When engaging in debate with them,
and weighing their merits,
how can one remain silent,
simply assenting to commands?
One must pick out commonalities and differences,
expose flaws and defects,
forget oneself to
promote the Way,
and offend the mundane to spread the teaching.
To consider this a fault
only shows a lack of understanding.
If the Great Master were in this situation,
why would he necessarily remain silent,
and be esteemed by the Fǎshī
for it?
The Fǎshī also said:
“I wish to cease contention to attain the Way,
and yield superiority to forget virtue.”
Matters of virtue
are not limited to contention or non-contention,
or yielding
or not yielding.
These words are simply highly valued among people;
the Fǎshī, admiring them, speaks them,
but ultimately does not know how superiority can be yielded.
If others' Way is superior,
then they are naturally superior, and there is no need to yield;
if others' Way is inferior,
then yielding is fruitless.
Are words of wishing to yield
not merely empty pronouncements?
The mind of the Middle Way
is
applicable everywhere.
What causes disagreement between Chéngshí and the Sānlùn?
One only needs to abandon the understanding of "guarding the stump"
and eliminate the intention of "gluing the pegs of the zither,"
and then
all matters will be in the middle.
Your letter states
“contention or non-contention
depends solely on a single factor.”
Why then do you exclusively praise non-contention?
Is this not a contradiction?
The Wúzhēng Lùn says: "Right and wrong, gain and loss,
victory and defeat, truth and falsehood,
must arise from the mind;
it does not mean that the spoken Dharma
has a fixed nature that determines superiority or inferiority."
If one criticizes different opinions as right or wrong,
taking attachment as a wrong statement,
and sees neither right nor wrong,
thereby dissolving their gains and losses,
and considers this treatise superior and excellent,
beyond other treatises,
this too
is a fault.
Why?
Whatever the mind refutes,
how can the mind that refutes be without mind?
