Then the mind of victory and defeat is not forgotten;
how can it not contain the victor?
This means
one considers oneself correct,
and dismisses others' faults,
thus having acceptance and rejection,
generating great right and wrong,
which is an increase in contention.
Answer: Words are used by the mind,
and the mind is explained by words;
when roots and objects
harmonize,
and winds and breaths are stirred,
then speech is formed.
Matters must arise from the mind,
just as the Tathāgata said.
As for the mind creating falsehoods to direct the mouth,
and the mouth acting deceptively to respond to
the mind,
outwardly harmonious but inwardly treacherous,
words compliant but intentions rebellious,
seeking profit and support,
attracting fame and reputation—
among those who have entered the path
and lay practitioners,
such people are not few.
That is why the Sages
elaborately set forth teachings and admonishments,
and deeply established safeguards,
speaking of present calamities and misfortunes,
and future troubles and harms.
These texts are clear,
brighter than the sun and moon,
yet there are still those who forget
their beloved bodies,
defy strict regulations,
tread through boiling water and burning coals,
and endure bitterness,
insisting on action without regard.
How can they be pleased by works of non-contention
and turn back to change their ways?
If
Those who propagate the Dào,
and scholars who spread transformation,
when their hearts know something is superior,
their mouths say it is superior;
when their hearts know something is inferior,
their mouths say it is inferior.
They conceal nothing,
nor do they
have any reservations.
They simply act with an upright heart.
Even if another Dào is inferior,
it is still the teaching of the sages.
Even if one's own virtue is superior,
it is also the teaching of the sages.
If I am superior, then
the sages are superior;
if others are inferior, then the sages are inferior.
The superiority or inferiority of the sages
is simply what suits the root-conditions.
With regard to this or that,
how can there be favoritism?
Even if one
spends the whole day pressing a sword
and the whole night striking a watchman's clapper,
staring with eyes wide in contention over gain and loss,
or stirring up anger to seek victory and defeat,
whose side is it on?
To have a mind or not to have a mind,
is merely to
wish to differentiate empty space.
Why should I not be allowed to discuss and speak,
and instead be made to be humble and retreat?
This is like a jiāo péng [蚉] that has already soared into the vast firmament,
while the hunter
still peers into the dense thickets to seek it.
Alas!
A true man should spread this Dào!
Wúzhēng Lùnyán (無諍論言) says: The Dào of Wúzhēng (無諍)
permeates both internal and external.
What you say, that one must contend,
is to use the branches to save the root,
losing the root while cultivating the branches.
Now, I will explain it to you.
Why?
If we follow the external scriptures,
and look back to before the invention of writing,
to the era of ultimate simplicity,
when hearts were pure and unadorned,
and the teaching was enacted without words,
at that time,
the people
would live to old age and death without interacting,
each finding their proper place.
What contention could there have been?
Thus, it is known that the root [末] is without contention,
this is the
truth of things.
The reply is: Contention and non-contention
cannot be adhered to unilaterally.
As for root and branch,
how can one truly know?
If it has always been non-contention,
how do we know it's not the branch?
If it is contention now,
what evidence is there that it is not the root?
Indeed,
standing behind and looking forward
is called "front";
standing in front and looking backward
is called "back".
And the affairs of front and back are just like that
— this and that.
That calls this "that,"
and this calls that "that."
The names of "this" and "that"
where do they truly reside?
From this,
all matters can be understood.
Root and branch, front
and back,
right and wrong, good and evil—
can they be constantly maintained?
How can one confidently trust one's own intelligence
and disregard the ears and eyes of others?
Indeed, water bubbles arise and perish,
fire wheels revolve.
Entering deep pits,
being bound by fetters,
giving rise to worries and fears,
and generating afflictions—
what is the cause of this loss?
It is not aligning with the Dào,
and instead giving rise to various views.
Those who align are not so.
They are
non-active (wúwéi),
yet there is nothing they do not do.
Good and evil cannot coexist,
yet they are never separate from good and evil.
Life and death cannot reach them,
yet they are forever within life and death.
Therefore, they attain eternal liberation
and act freely.
This is why the sages contemplate the difficulty of escaping the binds of shackles,
and pity the hardship of being freed from sticky glue.
Thus, they diligently teach and instruct,
providing various skillful means.
For those who aspire
to it,
who seek and have affinity,
though qílín (驎) horns are hard to form,
and elephant shapes are easy to lose,
how can they not dimly perceive the distant path
and strive with their short mornings?
One should instead reflect on the good
and evil of one's own body,
and not fathom other things.
To wish to differentiate,
and say "I am intelligent,"
"I have insight,"
"I calculate,"
"I ponder"—
to speak in this manner
is also to be superficial.
Other people are truly hard to fathom.
They might truly be ordinary mortals,
or they might be sages who condescend to appear ordinary.
What appears suitable to the current customs,
what is seen as appropriate by karmic retribution.
How can one give full
vent to one's feelings,
and indulge in one's nature,
and then give rise to ridicule?
One should indeed empty oneself and wander through the world,
bowing and rising in the midst of lightning and dew.
When the bright moon is in the sky,
all waters
see it.
When the clear wind reaches the forest,
all sounds resonate.
How can I oppose things?
I do not enter a place of stinking fish,
nor do I crave a rotten rat.
How can I be the same as things?
Who can
know me,
and travel this path together?
How vast!
How majestic!
How can one still see contention as wrong,
and non-contention as right?
This means that those who contend, contend on their own;
those who are
non-contending, are non-contending on their own.
I embrace and utilize both.
Why should Fǎshī Níng (寧法師) labor,
dotting pens and paper,
only to expound on non-contention;
or disciples exhaust their lips and tongues,
wasting
time,
only to argue about the clear Dào?
What a trivial discussion!
What dregs!
If one truly wishes to examine truth and falsehood,
and temporarily observe gain and loss,
there is nothing better than relying on the words of the worthy and sages,
and examining
the principles of action and concealment.
Researching from beginning to end,
synthesizing and scrutinizing extensively,
will render superficial rhetoric useless,
and deceitful Dào will naturally disappear.
Please wait for the later banquet,
to observe its wonder.
Subsequently, he was appointed to his original official post concurrently as Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng (通直散騎侍郎), dispatched to Qí (齊).
Upon his return, he was appointed Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎) and Cānjūn (參軍) to Zhènnán Shǐxīngwáng (鎮南始興王)'s advisory,
concurrently serving as Dōnggōng Guǎnjì (東宮管記).
He successively held the posts of Tàizǐ Shùzǐ (太子庶子) and Pú (僕),
with the concurrent post of Guǎnjì (管記) as before.
When the Hòuzhǔ (後主) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Mìshūjiān (祕書監) and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (右衞將軍),
concurrently serving as Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén (中書通事舍人),
responsible for imperial edicts.
Fù Zài's writing was elegant and
his nature was also keen and swift.
Even for matters of military and state,
he would put pen to paper and finish them instantly,
never needing to draft.
Even those who pondered deeply could not surpass him,
and he was greatly esteemed by the Latter Lord.
However, his nature was stubborn
and he did not maintain proper conduct.
He was arrogant due to his talent and prone to temper,
insulting and belittling people.
Many court officials resented him.
At this time, Shī Wénqìng and Shěn Kèqīng, through flattery, gained favor
and controlled the levers of power,
while Fù Zài became increasingly estranged.
Wénqìng and others then jointly slandered Fù Zài, accusing him of accepting gold from an envoy of Gāolì.
The Latter Lord had Fù Zài arrested and imprisoned.
Fù Zài, being naturally upright,
became indignant
and wrote a memorial from prison, saying:
"A ruler
should respectfully serve the Heavenly Emperor,
love the common people as his children,
curtail his desires,
keep flatterers and sycophants at a distance,
don his clothes before dawn,
and forget food until dusk.
Thus, his beneficence will cover the realm
and blessings will flow to his descendants.
Your Majesty, recently, has indulged excessively in wine and women,
not sincerely worshipping the gods of the suburban temples,
but solely fawning over lewd and confused spirits.
Petty men are by your side,
eunuchs wield power,
they detest the loyal and upright as if they were enemies,
and view the common people as grass and mustard seeds.
The imperial harem wears elaborate silks,
while the stables have surplus grains.
The people are displaced and scattered,
and corpses cover the fields.
Bribery is rampant,
and the national treasury is depleted.
God is angry, and the people resentful;
the multitude rebels, and relatives abandon.
I fear that the imperial aura of the Southeast
will from this point onwards be completely extinguished."
When the memorial was presented,
the Latter Lord was greatly enraged.
After a while,
his anger somewhat subsided,
and he sent an envoy to Fù Zài, saying:
"I wish to pardon you.
Can you change your ways?"
Fù Zài replied:
"My heart is like my face.
If my face can be changed,
then my heart can be changed."
The Latter Lord then became even more furious,
and ordered the eunuch Lǐ Shànqìng to thoroughly investigate the matter.
He was subsequently granted death in prison,
at the age of fifty-five.
His collected works in ten volumes circulated in the world.
At that time, there was Zhāng Huá of Wúxīng,
courtesy name Zhòngzōng.
His family had been farmers for generations,
but Huá alone was fond of learning.
He associated with gentlemen,
read extensively in classics and histories,
and was skilled at writing.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
he traveled to Lǐngnán,
residing in a temple on Mount Luófú,
devoting himself to diligent study.
Ouyáng Wěi, when he was the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu,
appointed him as the Administrator of Nánhǎi.
When Ouyáng Hè was defeated,
he returned to the capital.
During the TàiJiàn era,
Gāozōng sent Xiāo Yǐn, the Attendant Censor of the Ministry of Personnel, to admonish Mǎ Jìng, the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu,
ordering him to send his son as a hostage.
Yǐn memorialized that Huá should accompany him.
Upon their return,
Gāozōng had passed away.
When the Latter Lord ascended the throne,
court officials, seeing that Huá had no military accomplishments,
competed to discredit him.
He was appointed Magistrate of the Great Market.
As this was not to his liking,
he resigned on account of illness,
feeling frustrated and discontent.
In the early Zhēnmíng era,
he submitted a memorial strongly remonstrating,
its general purport being:
"In the past, Gāozǔ pacified the hundred Yuè in the south
and executed the rebellious barbarians in the north.
Shìzǔ settled Wú-Huì in the east
and defeated Wáng Lín in the west.
Gāozōng recovered Huáinán
and expanded territory for a thousand li.
The achievements of the three ancestors were indeed arduous.
Your Majesty has been on the throne
for five years now,
yet you do not contemplate the hardships of the former emperors,
nor do you know the awe-inspiring nature of Heaven's mandate.
You are steeped in favorites,
bewitched by wine and women.
You do not leave to sacrifice at the Seven Ancestral Temples,
but attend to concubines by facing the imperial pavilion.
Veteran ministers and seasoned generals
are abandoned in the wilderness,
while sycophants and treacherous villains
are promoted to the court.
Now the borders shrink daily,
and Suí armies press upon our territory.
If Your Majesty does not change his ways,
your servant foresees deer once again roaming the Gūsū Terrace."
When the memorial was presented,
the Latter Lord was greatly enraged,
and immediately ordered his execution.
The Grand Historian comments: Xiāo Jì and Lù Qióng
were both distinguished by their talent and learning.
Gù Yěwáng was widely learned in all classics,
and Fù Zài was intelligent and exceptionally discerning.
They were all outstanding talents of their generation.
However, Fù Zài failed to advance and retreat according to the Dao,
and thus ended up caught in the extreme net of the law.
What a tragedy!
Collations
Biographies, Chapter 25: Xiāo Móhē, Rèn Zhōng, Fán Yì (younger brother Měng), Lǔ Guǎngdá
Xiāo Móhē, courtesy name Yuán Yìn,
was from Lánlíng.
His grandfather, Jìng,
was a Right General of Liáng.
His father, Liàng,
was the Assistant Administrator of Shǐxīng Commandery during Liáng.
Móhē followed his father to the commandery.
When he was several years old, his father died.
His aunt's husband, Cài Lùyǎng, was then in Nánkāng,
so he took him in and raised him.
As he grew up, he was resolute and possessed great strength.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Gāozǔ went to relieve the capital.
Lùyǎng raised an army to resist Gāozǔ.
Móhē, then thirteen years old,
rode out alone to battle,
and no one in the army could stand against him.
When Lùyǎng was defeated,
Móhē submitted to Hóu Āndū.
Āndū treated him very well,
and from then on, he always served Āndū in campaigns.
When Rèn Yuē and Xú Sìhuī led Qí troops to invade,
Gāozǔ sent Āndū north to resist the Qí army at Zhōngshān Lóngwěi and the Northern Altar.
Āndū said to Móhē:
"You are renowned for your bravery and valor.
A thousand hearings are not as good as one seeing."
Móhē replied:
"Today, the Duke will see."
When they battled,
Āndū fell from his horse and was surrounded.
Móhē, on horseback alone, shouted loudly,
and charged directly into the Qí army.
The Qí army was routed,
and thus gradually dispersed,
and Āndū was then saved.
In the early Tiānjīa era,
he was appointed Magistrate of his home county.
For his accomplishments in pacifying Liú Yì and Ouyáng Hè,
he was successively promoted to Administrator of Bāshān.
In the fifth year of Tàijiàn,
the assembled armies launched a northern expedition.
Móhē followed Commander-in-Chief Wú Míngchè across the Jiāng to attack Qínjùn.
At that time, Qí sent its great general Yù Pòhú and others to lead a force of 100,000 to reinforce them.
Their vanguard included
"Cāngtóu",
"Xījiǎo",
and
"Dàlì"
units,
all of whom were eight chí tall
and possessed extraordinary strength.
Their vanguard was extremely sharp.
There were also Hú from the Western Regions,
who were skilled with the bow and arrow;
not a single shot missed its mark.
The assembled armies particularly feared them.
When it was time for battle,
Míngchè said to Móhē,
"If we can kill this Hú,
then their army will lose its morale.
You have the fame of Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi;
you can slay Yán Liáng!"
Móhē said,
"Please show me his appearance,
and I will get him for you."
Míngchè then summoned a surrendered man who recognized the Hú.
He said the Hú wore a crimson robe,
had a birch-bark-wrapped bow,
and bone nocks at both ends.
Míngchè sent someone to scout,
and upon learning the Hú was in the formation,
he personally poured wine for Móhē to drink.
After Móhē finished drinking,
he galloped his horse and charged the Qí army.
The Hú broke out of the formation by more than ten paces.
Before he could draw his bow and shoot,
Móhē hurled a sharp javelin from a distance,
hitting him squarely in the forehead.
He fell immediately.
More than ten
"Dàlì"
soldiers of the Qí army came out to fight,
and Móhē cut them down as well.
Thereupon, the Qí army retreated.
For his meritorious service, he was awarded the title of Míngyì Jiāngjūn and Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì,
and enfeoffed as the Earl of Liánpíng Xiàn,
with an estate of five hundred households.
Soon after, his noble rank was advanced to Hóu,
and he was transferred to Tàipú Qīng,
with the rest of his appointments remaining as before.
In the seventh year,
he again followed Míngchè to advance and besiege Sùyù,
defeating and driving off the Qí general Wáng Kāngdé.
For this merit, he was appointed Jìnxī Tàishǒu.
In the ninth year,
Míngchè advanced his army to Lǚliáng
and engaged in a great battle with the Qí people.
Móhē led seven cavalrymen in first,
personally seizing the great banner of the Qí army,
causing the Qí multitude to collapse.
For this merit, he was granted the title of Chíjí, Wǔyì Jiāngjūn, and Qiáozhōu Cìshǐ.
When Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu destroyed Qí,
he sent his general Yǔwén Xīn to lead a force to contest Lǚliáng,
and they fought at Lónghuì.
At that time, Xīn had several thousand elite cavalry.
Móhē led twelve cavalrymen deep into the Zhōu army,
fighting fiercely and widely,
and slaying many.
When Zhōu sent its great general Wáng Guǐ to assist,
he constructed a long dike of piled stones (Zhà) in the lower reaches of Lǚliáng,
cutting off the main army's return route.
Móhē said to Míngchè,
"I hear Wáng Guǐ has just started constructing the dike in the lower reaches.
He is building fortresses at both ends,
but they are not yet complete.
If Your Excellency sends me to attack them,
they will certainly not dare to resist.
The waterway is not yet cut,
and the enemy's position is not yet firm.
If those fortresses are completed,
then we will all be captured."
Míngchè then bristled his beard and said,
"Seizing banners and breaking formations
is the general's business;
long-term calculations and distant strategies
are this old man's business."
Móhē turned pale and withdrew.
Within ten days,
the Zhōu forces increased.
Móhē again pleaded with Míngchè,
"Now we cannot seek battle,
and there is no way to advance or retreat.
If we secretly break out with the army,
it would not be a disgrace.
I wish Your Excellency would lead the infantry,
traveling slowly in a horse-drawn litter,
while Móhē leads several thousand armored cavalry,
riding back and forth,
and will surely ensure Your Excellency reaches the capital."
Míngchè said,
"Your plan, my brother,
is indeed a good one.
However, this old man received the sacrificial meat and was specifically entrusted with this campaign;
I could not win battles or take cities.
Now, being surrounded and pressed,
I am ashamed and have nowhere to hide.
Moreover, since the infantry is numerous,
and I am the commander-in-chief,
I must personally remain at the rear,
leading them to advance together.
Your cavalry should be in the front,
without delay."
Móhē then led the cavalry and departed by night.
Previously,
after the Zhōu army's long siege had closed,
they also laid several layers of ambushes at key routes.
Móhē selected eighty elite cavalry,
led them in the initial charge,
and the rest of the cavalry followed.
By dawn, they reached Huáinán.
Gāozōng issued an imperial edict recalling him,
and appointed him Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
In the eleventh year,
Zhōu forces attacked Shòuyáng.
Móhē and Fán Yì, along with other armies, went to reinforce them,
but returned without success.
In the fourteenth year,
Gāozōng passed away.
Shǐxīng Wáng Shūlíng personally attacked the Later Lord with a dagger inside the palace,
wounding him but not killing him.
Shūlíng fled to Dōngfǔ Chéng.
At that time, the hearts of the people were still hesitant,
and no one moved to suppress the rebel.
Sīmǎ Shēn, a Shèrén of the Eastern Palace, reported to the Later Lord,
and swiftly summoned Móhē.
He entered, received the imperial command,
and then led several hundred cavalry and infantry,
first rushing to the west gate of Dōngfǔ Chéng to encamp.
Shūlíng, in a panic,
exited through the south gate of the city.
Móhē led his troops in pursuit and beheaded him.
For this merit, he was granted Sànqí Chángshì and Chējì Dàjiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Suíjiàn Jùn,
with an estate of three thousand households.
Shūlíng had long accumulated vast amounts of gold and silk,
all of which the Later Lord bestowed upon him.
Soon after, he was reappointed Shìzhōng and Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn,
and given the additional title of Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū.
According to old regulations, only the Sāngōng could have chīwěi ornaments on the yellow gates of their offices.
The Later Lord specially granted Móhē permission to open yellow gates,
set up horse barriers at the entrance,
and have chīwěi ornaments in both his office and sleeping chamber.
Furthermore, his daughter was made the Imperial Crown Prince's Consort.
At that time, the Suí general manager Hèruò Bì (賀若弼) was garrisoned in Guǎnglíng (廣陵),
eyeing the territory south of the Jiāng (江).
Hòuzhǔ (後主) entrusted Móhē (摩訶) with the responsibility of defense,
appointing him as the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州),
with all other positions remaining as before.
In the first month of the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明), during the New Year's assembly,
Móhē was summoned back to the capital.
Hèruò Bì (賀若弼) took advantage of the emptiness to cross the Jiāng (江),
attacking Jīngkǒu (京口).
Móhē requested troops for a counterattack,
but Hòuzhǔ (後主) refused.
When Bì (弼) advanced his army to Zhōngshān (鍾山),
Móhē again requested, saying:
"Hèruò Bì (賀若弼)'s army is deep in our territory,
his support is still far away.
Moreover, his fortifications are not yet strong,
and his men are fearful.
If we send out troops to ambush them,
we will surely achieve a great victory."
Hòuzhǔ (後主) again refused.
When the Suí army arrived in great force,
they prepared to go out and fight.
Hòuzhǔ (後主) said to Móhē (摩訶):
"You can decide this for me."
Móhē (摩訶) said:
"Previously in battle,
I fought for the state and for myself.
Today's matter
is also for my wife and children."
Hòuzhǔ (後主) gave out a large amount of gold and silk,
distributing awards to all the armies.
He ordered the Zhōnglǐngjūn (中領軍) Lǔ Guǎngdá (魯廣達) to deploy his troops on Báitǔgǎng (白土崗),
positioned on the southern flank of the main forces.
Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn (鎮東大將軍) Rèn Zhōng (任忠) was next,
Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (護軍將軍) Fán Yì (樊毅) and Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書) Kǒng Fàn (孔範) were next.
Móhē (摩訶)'s army was positioned furthest north.
The various armies stretched twenty *lǐ* (里) from north to south,
their head and tail advancing and retreating,
each unaware of the others.
Hèruò Bì (賀若弼) initially thought there would be no battle,
and led light cavalry
to ascend the mountain and observe the terrain.
When he saw the various armies,
he immediately galloped down to set up his formation.
Guǎngdá (廣達) first led his division forward to engage,
and Bì (弼)'s army repeatedly retreated,
but soon rallied.
He then divided his army to attack the northern generals.
Kǒng Fàn (孔範) came out to fight,
engaged the enemy, and then fled.
The various generals were scattered,
their formation not yet cohesive.
The cavalry and infantry dispersed in disarray,
and could not be stopped.
Móhē (摩訶) could not exert his strength,
and was captured by the Suí army.
When the capital fell,
Hèruò Bì (賀若弼) placed Hòuzhǔ (後主) in Déjiào Diàn (德教殿),
ordering soldiers to guard him.
Móhē (摩訶) requested Bì (弼), saying:
"Now as a prisoner,
my life is momentary.
I wish to see my former lord once more;
then I will have no regrets even in death."
Bì (弼) pitied him and allowed it.
Móhē (摩訶) entered to see Hòuzhǔ (後主),
prostrated himself and wailed,
then went to the old kitchen to get food and offered it to him.
He bid farewell and left.
The guards were all unable to look up.
That year, he entered Suí (隋) territory and
was granted the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
Soon after, he followed Hànwáng (漢王) Liàng (諒) to Bìngzhōu (幷州),
joined Liàng (諒) in rebellion,
and was executed.
He was seventy-three years old at the time.
Móhē (摩訶) was slow of speech,
a humble and virtuous elder.
However, when facing the enemy in battle,
his spirit would surge,
and he was irresistible.
Before he reached adulthood,
he followed Hóu Āndū (侯安都) in Jīngkǒu (京口).
He was fond of hunting
and did not miss a day without going out to the field.
When Āndū (安都) campaigned east and west,
winning battles and taking cities,
Móhē (摩訶)'s contributions were truly significant.
His son, Shìlián (世廉),
was intelligent and handsome in his youth,
brave and possessing his father's demeanor.
He was extremely filial.
When Móhē (摩訶) met a tragic end,
after the period of mourning,
his grief and longing intensified.
If old acquaintances of his father happened to mention him,
Shìlián (世廉) would respond
with uncontrollable sorrow and weeping,
causing those who spoke to sigh in sympathy.
He never held a sword or axe again in his life;
people of his time praised this.
Móhē (摩訶) had a cavalry officer named Chén Zhìshēn (陳智深),
whose bravery and strength surpassed others.
For his merit in subduing Shūlíng (叔陵),
he was made Bālíng Nèishǐ (巴陵內史).
When Móhē (摩訶) was executed,
his wife and children had already been confiscated.
Zhìshēn (智深) collected Móhē (摩訶)'s body,
personally prepared it for burial,
causing passersby to be moved to sorrow.
Gentlemen considered this righteous.
Chén Yǔ (陳禹) of Yǐngchuān (潁川)
also followed Móhē (摩訶) on campaigns.
He was intelligent, insightful, and broad-minded.
He studied classics and histories,
understood *fēngjiǎo* (風角) and military treatises,
and was quite skilled in writing.
He was good at horsemanship and archery.
His official position reached Wángfǔ Zīyì (王府諮議).
Rèn Zhōng (任忠), courtesy name Fèngchéng (奉誠),
childhood name Mánnú (蠻奴),
was from Rǔyīn (汝陰).
Orphaned and humble in his youth,
he was not respected by his local community.
As he grew older,
he became cunning and resourceful,
with extraordinary physical strength,
and was especially skilled in horsemanship and archery.
Young men in his prefecture all attached themselves to him.
Xiāo Fàn (蕭範), King of Póyáng (鄱陽) of Liáng (梁), was the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Hézhōu (合州).
Hearing of his reputation,
he brought him close to him.
During Hóu Jǐng (侯景)'s rebellion,
Zhōng (忠) led several hundred of his local community
to follow Jìnxī Tàishǒu (晉熙太守) Méi Bólóng (梅伯龍) in attacking Jǐng (景)'s general Wáng Guìxiǎn (王貴顯) in Shòuchūn (壽春),
repelling the enemy in every battle.
At that time, the local Hú Tōng (胡通) gathered a mob to plunder.
Fàn (範) ordered Zhōng (忠) and his chief commander Méi Sīlì (梅思立) to join forces and suppress them.
He then followed Fàn (範)'s heir apparent Sì (嗣) in leading troops to provide aid.
By the time the capital fell,
he had returned to garrison Jìnxī (晉熙).
After Hóu Jǐng (侯景) was pacified,
he was appointed Dàngkòu Jiāngjūn (蕩寇將軍).
Wáng Lín (王琳) established Xiāo Zhuāng (蕭莊),
appointing Zhōng (忠) as Bālíng Tàishǒu (巴陵太守).
After Lín (琳)'s defeat, he returned to the court.
He was promoted to Míngyì Jiāngjūn (明毅將軍) and Ānxiāng Tàishǒu (安湘太守),
and then followed Hóu Tián (侯瑱) to campaign against Bā (巴) and Xiāng (湘).
He was successively promoted to Yùníng Tàishǒu (豫寧太守) and Héngyáng Nèishǐ (衡陽內史).
When Huá Jiǎo (華皎) raised an army,
Zhōng (忠) was involved in his planning.
After Jiǎo (皎) was pacified,
Gāozōng (高宗), because Zhōng (忠) had earlier secretly informed the imperial court,
released him without questioning.
In the early years of Tàijiàn (太建),
he followed Zhāng Zhāodá (章昭達) to attack Ōuyáng Hè (歐陽紇) in Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
For his merit, he was granted Zhíhé Jiāngjūn (直閤將軍).
He was promoted to Wǔyì Jiāngjūn (武毅將軍) and Lúlíng Nèishǐ (廬陵內史).
After his term was full,
he entered the court as Yòujūn Jiāngjūn (右軍將軍).
In the fifth year,
when the armies campaigned north,
Zhōng (忠) led troops out on the western route,
defeating Qí (齊)'s Lìyángwáng (歷陽王) Gāo Jǐng'ān (高景安) at Dàxiàn (大峴),
and pursued them to Dōngguān (東關).
He then captured their two cities, east and west.
He advanced to Qí (蘄) and Qiáo (譙),
and took them both.
He directly attacked Héféi (合肥),
entering its outer wall.
He then captured Huòzhōu (霍州).
For his merits, he was granted Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍),
enfeoffed as Ānfù Xiànhóu (安復縣侯),
with an estate of five hundred households.
When the army was defeated at Lǚliáng (呂梁),
Zhōng (忠) returned with his entire army intact.
Soon after, an imperial edict ordered Zhōng (忠) to oversee the various armies along the Huái (淮) River in Shòuyáng (壽陽), Xīncài (新蔡), and Huòzhōu (霍州).
He was promoted to Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (寧遠將軍) and Huòzhōu Cìshǐ (霍州刺史).
He entered the court as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍).
In the eleventh year,
he was given additional responsibility as Běitǎo Qiánjūnshì (北討前軍事) and
promoted to Píngběi Jiāngjūn (平北將軍),
leading infantry and cavalry towards Qínjùn (秦郡).
In the twelfth year,
he was promoted to Shǐchíjíe (使持節), Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), Dūdū Nányùzhōu Zhūjūnshì (都督南豫州諸軍事), Píngnán Jiāngjūn (平南將軍), and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ (南豫州刺史).
His estate was increased to a total of one thousand five hundred households.
He then led infantry and cavalry towards Lìyáng (歷陽).
Zhōu (周) dispatched Wáng Yánguì (王延貴) to lead troops as reinforcements.
Zhōng (忠) greatly defeated them
and captured Yánguì (延貴) alive.
After Hòuzhǔ (後主) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zhènnán Jiāngjūn (鎮南將軍)
and given a set of drums and pipes.
He entered the court as Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍),
was given the additional title of Shìzhōng (侍中),
and enfeoffed as Liángxìn Jùngōng (梁信郡公)
with an estate of three thousand households.
He was sent out as Wúxīng Nèishǐ (吳興內史),
with an additional salary of two thousand *dàn* (石).
When the Sui army crossed the Changjiāng,
Zhōng, from Wúxīng, came to assist,
and garrisoned his troops at the Zhūquè Gate.
Hòuzhǔ summoned Xiāo Móhē and others to the inner palace to deliberate,
and Zhōng argued, saying:
"Military strategists say that guest and host forces have different advantages;
the guest values swift battle,
while the host values holding fast.
It is advisable to reinforce and steadfastly defend the imperial city,
and dispatch the navy to separate directions, towards Nányùzhōu and Jīngkǒu,
to cut off the enemy's grain supply.
Wait for the spring floods to rise,
and the armies of Zhōu Luó and others from the upper Changjiāng,
will certainly come downriver to reinforce us.
This is an excellent plan."
The opinions of the others differed,
and so they went out to battle.
After the defeat,
Zhōng rushed into the palace to see Hòuzhǔ,
reported the state of the defeat,
and said:
"Your Majesty should only prepare boats and oars,
and go to the armies upstream;
I will protect you with my life."
Hòuzhǔ believed him,
and ordered Zhōng to go out and make arrangements.
Zhōng excused himself, saying:
"After I have made the arrangements,
I will come to escort you."
Hòuzhǔ ordered his palace women to get ready to await Zhōng,
but after a long wait, he did not arrive.
The Sui general Hán Qínhǔ advanced from Xīnlín,
and Zhōng then led a few cavalrymen to Shízǐgǎng and surrendered to him,
and then led Qínhǔ's army to enter the Nányèmén together.
When Táichéng fell,
that year he entered Cháng'ān,
and the Sui granted him the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
He died
at the age of seventy-seven.
His son, Yòuwǔ,
reached the official position of Yítóng Sānsī.
At that time, there was a man named Shěn Kèqīng,
a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
He was by nature cunning, greedy, cruel, and merciless.
As Zhōngshū Shèrén,
he always proposed unusual schemes,
only taking the oppression and exploitation of the common people as his business,
thereby advancing himself.
There was also a man named Shī Wénqìng,
a native of Wūchéng, Wúxīng.
He rose from humble beginnings
and was skilled in administration.
Hòuzhǔ promoted him to Zhǔshū,
then transferred him to Zhōngshū Shèrén,
and soon after promoted him to Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Before he could take up his post,
the Sui army came to attack.
Reports from various prefectures and garrisons across the four directions
arrived one after another.
Wénqìng and Kèqīng were both in charge of secret affairs.
All external memorials and reports
were presented by them.
Wénqìng was pleased with the important position of Xiāngzhōu,
and hoped to depart early,
so he and Kèqīng jointly suppressed the memorials,
and did not report them.
Hòuzhǔ was unaware of this,
and thus, being unprepared,
led to the downfall of the state.
This was truly the fault of these two men.
Once the Sui army entered,
both were executed in front of the palace gate.
Fán Yì, courtesy name Zhìliè,
was a native of Húyáng, Nányáng.
His grandfather, Fāngxīng,
was Liáng Sànqí Chángshì, Rénwēi Jiāngjūn, Sīzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Earl of Yúfù County.
His father, Wénchì,
was Liáng Sànqí Chángshì, Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, Yìzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Earl of Xīncài County.
Yì came from a family of generals for generations,
and learned martial arts and archery in his youth.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Yì led his troops and followers to accompany his uncle, Wénjiǎo, to reinforce Táichéng.
Wénjiǎo died in battle at Qīngxī.
Yì led his clan and younger relatives to Jiānglíng,
and was then subordinate to Wáng Sēngbiàn,
campaigning against the King of Hédōng, Xiāo Yù.
For his merits, he was appointed Jiǎjié, Wēiróng Jiāngjūn, and Yòuzhōnglángjiāng.
He succeeded his elder brother, Jùn, as Tàishǒu of Liángxīng,
and commanded the mobile armies of three prefectures,
accompanying the Marquis of Yífēng, Xiāo Xún, to attack Lù Nà in Xiāngzhōu.
When the army reached Bālíng,
before the camp was fully established,
Nà secretly arrived with his army at night,
approaching the camp with a great clamor.
The officers and soldiers in the camp were all alarmed and disturbed.
Yì, with only a few tens of men from his retinue,
fought bravely at the camp gate,
beheading more than ten enemies,
and beating the drums to issue commands,
whereupon the troops calmed down.
For his merits, he was granted Chíjié, Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as Earl of Yídào County,
with an income of three hundred households.
Soon after, he was appointed Tiānmén Tàishǒu,
his peerage was advanced to Marquis,
and his income increased to a total of one thousand households.
When Western Wèi besieged Jiānglíng,
Yì led troops to reinforce it.
When Jiānglíng fell,
he was captured by the King of Yuèyáng.
After a long time, he escaped and returned.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
Yì and his younger brother, Měng, raised troops to support Wáng Lín.
When Lín was defeated and fled to Qí,
Tàiwèi Hóu Diàn sent an envoy to summon Yì.
Yì led his sons, younger relatives, and followers back to court.
In Tiānjiā year two,
he was granted Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
and then accompanied Hóu Diàn to campaign against Bā and Xiāng.
He was successively promoted to Wǔzhōu Cìshǐ.
In early Tàijiàn,
he was transferred to Fēngzhōu Cìshǐ,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāochāng County,
with an income of one thousand households.
He entered the court as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
In year five,
when all armies launched a northern expedition,
Yì led his troops to attack Chǔzǐ City in Guǎnglín,
capturing it,
and routed the Qí army at Yǐngkǒu.
The Qí reinforcements at Cānglíng
were also defeated by him.
In year seven,
he advanced and captured six cities including Tóngzhōu, Xiàpī, and Gāozhá.
When the army suffered a defeat at Lǚliáng,
an imperial edict appointed Yì as Dàdūdū,
promoted his title to Píngběi Jiāngjūn,
and ordered him to lead his troops across the Huái River,
build a city facing Qīngkǒu,
and resist the Zhōu people.
Due to continuous rain, the city was damaged,
but Yì extricated his entire army.
Soon after, he was transferred to Zhōnglǐngjūn.
In year eleven,
when the Zhōu general Liáng Shìyàn led troops to besiege Shòuyáng,
an imperial edict appointed Yì as Dūdū Běitǎo Qiánjūn Shì,
and ordered him to lead the navy into Jiāohú.
Soon after, he was granted Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn and Dūdū Jīng Yǐng Bā Wǔ Sìzhōu Shuǐlù Zhūjūn Shì.
In year twelve,
he was promoted to Dūdū Miǎnhàn Zhūjūn Shì,
but was dismissed for official matters.
In year thirteen,
he was summoned and appointed Zhōnghùjūn.
Soon after, he was transferred to Hùjūn Jiāngjūn and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
After Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zhēng Xī Jiāngjūn,
and his enfeoffment was changed to Marquis of Xiāoyáo Commandery,
with an income of three thousand households,
the rest remaining as before.
He entered the court as Shìzhōng and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
When the Sui army crossed the Changjiāng,
Yì said to Púshè Yuán Xiàn:
"Jīngkǒu and Cǎishí
are both crucial locations.
Each requires several thousand elite troops
and two hundred 'golden-winged' vessels.
These should be stationed in the river up and down from the capital,
to defend it from all sides.
If not,
the great affair will be lost."
All the generals agreed with his proposal.
However, Shī Wénqìng and others suppressed the news of the Sui army,
so Yì's plan was not implemented.
When the imperial capital fell,
he entered Guān according to regulations,
and died shortly thereafter.
Méng's [courtesy] name was Zhìwǔ,
and he was Yì's younger brother.
From a young age, he was unconventional and unrestrained,
possessing strategy and leadership.
Once he reached adulthood,
he became skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and his courage surpassed that of others.
In the Battle of Qīngxī,
Méng, from dawn to dusk,
engaged in close-quarters combat with the enemy,
inflicting numerous casualties.
When Táichéng fell,
he followed his elder brother Yì westward to Jīng,
and for his accumulated military achievements, he was made Wēiróng Jiāngjūn.
Liáng (Ān) Nán Hóu Xiāo Fāngjǔ served as the Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu.
At that time, Wǔlíng Wáng Xiāo Jì raised an army and moved eastward down the Hànjiāng.
Fāngjǔ dispatched Méng to lead the troops from Xiāng and Yǐng,
and, accompanying Dūdū Lù Fǎhé, advanced to resist him.
By then, Jì had already descended,
his tower ships and warships occupying Bājiāng,
contending for the Xiákǒu.
They were in a stalemate for a long time,
unable to break through.
Fǎhé surmised that Jì's army was weary and demoralized.
He then ordered Méng to lead three thousand brave and elite soldiers,
and over a hundred light boats,
to charge upstream directly,
taking them by surprise,
beating drums and shouting to assail them.
Jì's troops were caught off guard and panicked,
unable to form ranks.
They all abandoned their ships and climbed ashore,
with thousands drowning.
At that time, several hundred of Jì's confidants
were still by his side.
Méng, with over thirty of his subordinates,
holding shields and cross-wielding halberds,
directly boarded Jì's boat.
With wide eyes, he roared loudly,
causing Jì's attendants to scatter and fall back,
piling up against each other, not daring to move.
Méng personally captured Jì and his two sons,
executing them in the Zīzhong,
and seized all their ships, vehicles, and equipment.
For his achievement, he was appointed Yóuqí Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as the Bó of Ānshān Xiàn,
with a thousand households.
He then advanced his army to pacify and settle Liáng and Yì,
and the entire territory of Shǔ was pacified.
When the army returned,
he was promoted to Chíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Qīngchē Jiāngjūn, and Sīzhōu Cìshǐ,
his noble rank was advanced to Hóu,
and his households were increased to a total of two thousand.
In the first year of Yǒngdìng,
Zhōu Wényù and others were defeated at Dùnkǒu
and captured by Wáng Lín.
Lín, capitalizing on his victory, was about to conquer the southern prefectures.
He sent Méng and Lǐ Xiàqīn and others to lead troops to attack Yùzhāng,
then pressed towards Zhōu Dí.
His army was defeated
and he was captured by Dí.
Soon after, he escaped and returned to Wáng Lín.
After Wáng Lín's defeat,
he returned to court.
In the second year of Tiānjiā,
he was appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì and Yǒngyáng Tàishǒu.
He was promoted to Ānchéng Wáng Fǔ Sīmǎ.
In the first year of Guāngdà,
he was appointed Zhuàngwǔ Jiāngjūn and Lúlíng Nèishǐ.
In early Tàijiàn,
he was promoted to Wǔyì Jiāngjūn and Shǐxīng Píngnán Fǔ Chángshǐ,
concurrently serving as Chángshā Nèishǐ.
Soon after, he was subordinate to Zhāng Zhāodá in the western campaign against Jiānglíng.
He secretly led his army into the gorges
and burned the Zhōu army's ships.
For this achievement, he was enfeoffed as the Hóu of Fùchuān Xiàn,
with five hundred households.
He successively served as Sànqí Chángshì,
then was promoted to Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū Jīng Xìn Èrzhōu Zhū Jūnshì, Xuānyuǎn Jiāngjūn, and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He entered the court as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
When the Latter Lord ascended the throne,
his households were increased to a total of one thousand,
with all other positions remaining as before.
In the fourth year of Zhìdé,
he was appointed Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū Nányùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì, Zhōngwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Suí general Hán Qínhǔ crossed the Jiāng,
Méng was in the capital.
His sixth son, Xún, temporarily managed the affairs of the prefecture.
Qínhǔ advanced his army and captured it.
Xún and his family were all captured.
At that time, Méng and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Jiǎng Yuánsùn led eighty qīnglóng ships as a naval force,
patrolling at Báixià
to defend against Suí troops from Liùhé.
The Latter Lord knew that Méng's wife and children were in the Suí army
and feared he might harbor disloyal intentions,
wishing to replace him with Rèn Zhōng.
However, he also worried about hurting Méng's feelings,
and thus refrained.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng, he entered Suí.
Lǔ Guǎngdá's [courtesy] name was Biànlǎn,
and he was the younger brother of Cìshǐ Sīdá of Wúzhōu.
From a young age, he was generous and uninhibited,
determined to achieve fame and merit.
He humbly cherished scholars,
and guests would sometimes come from afar.
At that time, the generals and commanders south of the Jiāng
each led their own troops,
often numbering in the thousands,
but the Lǔ clan had a particularly large number.
Upon entering officialdom, he was appointed Liáng Shàolíng Wáng Guó Zuǒchángshì,
and then promoted to Píngnán Dāngyáng Gōng Fǔ Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
he and his elder brother Sīdá gathered a multitude and held Xīncài.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng, acting by imperial authority,
appointed him Jiǎjié, Zhuàngwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Jìnzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Wáng Sēngbiàn campaigned against Hóu Jǐng,
Guǎngdá went out of the border to meet and receive him,
providing military provisions.
Sēngbiàn said to Shěn Jiǒng:
"Lǔ Jìnzhōu is also the host for our eastern route army."
He then led his troops to follow Sēngbiàn.
After Jǐng was pacified,
he was given the additional title of Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì,
with other positions remaining as before.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he was appointed Zhēngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu.
Soon after, he was transferred to Guìyáng Tàishǒu,
but he firmly declined the appointment.
He entered the court as Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì.
He was appointed Jiǎjié, Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Xīncài Tàishǒu.
He accompanied Wú Míngchè in campaigning against Zhōu Dí at Línchuān,
consistently achieving the most merit in every battle.
He then succeeded his elder brother Sīdá as Wúzhōu Cìshǐ,
and was enfeoffed as the Hóu of Zhōngsù Xiàn,
with five hundred households.
In the first year of Guāng (Lù) Dà (Fū),
When Huá Jiǎo raised an army upriver,
an imperial edict ordered Sīkōng Chúnyú Liàng to lead the various armies to campaign against him.
When the army reached Xiàkǒu,
Jiǎo's naval force was strong,
and no one dared to advance.
Guǎngdá was the first to lead his brave and elite soldiers
to directly charge the enemy army.
Once the warships engaged,
Guǎngdá, filled with righteous anger, shouted loudly,
climbed onto the ship's tower,
and encouraged his soldiers.
The wind was fierce and the ships turned,
causing the tower to sway.
Guǎngdá lost his footing and fell into the water,
submerged for a long time.
He was eventually rescued and escaped.
After Jiǎo was pacified,
he was appointed Chíjié, Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn, Dūdū Bāzhōu Zhū Jūnshì, and Bāzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the early years of the Tài-Jiàn reign (569-582 CE),
he, along with Yí-Tóng Zhāng Zhāo-Dá, entered the Qia-Kǒu,
and extended and secured various prefectures and garrisons such as Ān-Shǔ.
At that time, the Zhōu family planned to attack the jiāng-zuǒ (Jiangdong region),
and built many ships and boats in Shǔ,
and also transported grain to Qīng-Ní.
Guǎng-Dá, along with Qián Dào-Jí and others, led troops to ambush them,
and set fire to them.
For this achievement, he was granted an additional fief, making a total of two thousand households,
and then returned to his original garrison.
As an administrator, Guǎng-Dá was concise and to the point,
sincerely trusting and employing his subordinates.
Officials and common people found him convenient.
When his term of office expired,
all went to the imperial court to submit a petition,
whereupon an imperial edict ordered him to remain for two more years.
In the fifth year (573 CE),
the various armies marched north,
seizing the former territory of Huái-Nán.
Guǎng-Dá met the Qí army at Dà-Xiàn,
and thoroughly defeated them,
beheading their Fū-Chéng-Wáng Zhāng Yuán-Fàn,
〔一二〕and capturing countless prisoners and spoils.
He then advanced and conquered Běi-Xú-Zhōu,
and was appointed Dū-Dū of all military affairs in Běi-Xú-Zhōu and Cì-Shǐ of Běi-Xú-Zhōu.
〔一三〕Soon after, he was given the additional title of Sǎn-Qí-Cháng-Shì,
and entered the court as Yòu-Wèi-Jiāng-Jūn.
In the eighth year (576 CE),
he was sent out as Cì-Shǐ of Běi-Yǔn-Zhōu,
and later transferred to Cì-Shǐ of Jìn-Zhōu.
In the tenth year (578 CE),
he was appointed Shǐ-Chí-Jié, Dū-Dū of all military affairs in Hé and Huò Prefectures,
and promoted to the title of Rén-Wēi-Jiāng-Jūn and Cì-Shǐ of Hé-Zhōu.
In the eleventh year (579 CE),
the Zhōu general Liáng Shì-Yàn led troops to besiege Shòu-Chūn.
An imperial edict ordered Zhōng-Lǐng-Jūn Fán Yì and Zuǒ-Wèi-Jiāng-Jūn Rèn Zhōng and others to lead their divisions towards Yáng-Píng and Qín-Jùn respectively.
Guǎng-Dá led his troops into the Huái River,
forming a pincer movement to attack them.
The Zhōu army captured Yù and Huò Prefectures,
while the southern and northern Yǔn, Jìn, and others each withdrew.
〔一四〕All the generals achieved nothing,
and lost all the land south of the Huái River.
Guǎng-Dá was consequently dismissed from office,
and returned to his residence as a Hóu (Marquis).
In the twelfth year (580 CE),
he, along with Yù-Zhōu-Cì-Shǐ Fán Yì, led troops on a northern expedition,
〔一五〕and captured Guō-Mò-Chéng.
Soon after, he was appointed Shǐ-Chí-Jié, Píng-Xī-Jiāng-Jūn, Dū-Dū of the military affairs of the ten prefectures above Yǐng-Zhōu,
〔一六〕and led a fleet of forty thousand soldiers,
stationed in Jiāng-Xià.
Yuán Jǐng, the Zǒng-Guǎn of Ān-Zhōu of the Zhōu dynasty, led troops to invade the area outside the Jiāng River.
〔一七〕Guǎng-Dá ordered a detachment to attack and repel them.
After the Hòu-Zhǔ (Last Emperor) ascended the throne,
he entered the court as Ān-Zuǒ-Jiāng-Jūn.
Soon after, he was appointed Píng-Nán-Jiāng-Jūn and Nán-Yù-Zhōu-Cì-Shǐ.
In the second year of Zhì-Dé (584 CE),
he was appointed Ān-Nán-Jiāng-Jūn,
summoned to be appointed Shì-Zhōng,
and again became Ān-Zuǒ-Jiāng-Jūn.
He was redesignated as Suí-Yuè-Jùn-Gōng,
with his fief remaining as before.
Soon after, he became Zhōng-Lǐng-Jūn.
When Hè-Ruò Bì advanced his army to Zhōng-Shān,
Guǎng-Dá led his troops to set up a formation south of Bái-Tǔ-Gǎng,
facing Bì's flags and drums.
Guǎng-Dá personally donned armor and helmet,
held a drumstick in his hand,
and encouraged the daredevils,
advancing through blades.
The Suí army retreated,
and Guǎng-Dá pursued them to their camp,
killing and wounding many,
doing this several times.
When Bì defeated the various generals,
and, riding on his victory, reached the imperial city,
burning the North Yè-Mén,
Guǎng-Dá still commanded his remaining troops,
fighting fiercely without ceasing,
killing and capturing hundreds.
As night fell,
he disarmed,
bowed twice towards the platform (palace) and wept bitterly,
saying to his troops:
“I cannot save the nation with my own body,
my sin is deep.”
The officers and soldiers all shed tears and sighed,
and then he was captured.
In the third year of Zhēn-Míng (589 CE),
he entered Suí territory as per custom.
Guǎng-Dá was grieved by the fall of his former dynasty,
contracted an illness that could not be cured,
and soon died of indignation,
at the age of fifty-nine.
Shàng-Shū-Lìng Jiāng Zǒng mourned over his coffin and wept bitterly,
then took a brush and inscribed on the head of his coffin,
composing a poem which read:
“Though the Yellow Springs hold regret,
His name shines brightly in the sun.
I mourn his death for righteousness,
Not living to betray grace.”
Zǒng also composed an epitaph for Guǎng-Dá's tomb,
which briefly stated:
“Calamity spread through Huái-Hǎi,
The impregnable defenses were lost.
The times were difficult, destiny exhausted,
The dynasty changed, Heaven fell.
Claws and teeth (generals) betrayed righteousness,
Armored warriors were disloyal.
Only he stood out for loyalty and bravery,
Leading and commanding with skill.
His sincerity pierced the bright sun,
His spirit stirred the severe frost.
Grateful for kindness, mindful of回报,
How could he forget his duties?”
Initially,
when the Suí general Hán Qín-Hǔ crossed the Jiāng River,
Guǎng-Dá's eldest son, Shì-Zhēn, was in Xīn-Cài.
He, along with his younger brother Shì-Xióng and their subordinates, defected to Qín-Hǔ.
Qín-Hǔ sent an envoy with a letter,
〔一八〕to persuade Guǎng-Dá.
Guǎng-Dá, then stationed with troops in the capital,
〔一九〕then impeached himself before the Tíng-Wèi (Ministry of Justice) to confess his guilt.
The Hòu-Zhǔ said to him:
“Although Shì-Zhēn took a different path, you are a prominent minister of the state,
on whom I rely.
How can you consider yourself under suspicion?”
He was further bestowed with gold,
and returned to his camp that very day.
Guǎng-Dá had a platoon leader, Yáng Xiào-Biàn,
who was with Guǎng-Dá in the army at the time.
He fought bravely, breaking through enemy lines.
His son also followed Xiào-Biàn,
wielding a blade and killing more than ten Suí soldiers.
When his strength was exhausted,
both father and son died.
The historian says: Xiāo Mó-Hē's spirit surpassed all three armies,
he was a fine general of his time.
Although lacking in wisdom and strategy,
he was nonetheless a peerless brave man of his generation.
However, he was slow of speech but firm of heart,
perhaps a follower of Lǐ Guǎng in his cautious manner.
Although Rèn Zhōng was brave, decisive, and resolute,
he was double-minded and fickle,
deceiving his sovereign.
He stumbled into his own evil,
how contemptible!
As for Lǔ Guǎng-Dá, he maintained loyalty and upheld the Way,
sacrificing himself for righteousness.
He was truly a fine minister of the Chén dynasty.

Biographies Chapter 26: Filial Piety Yīn Bù-Hài (younger brother Bù-Nìng), Xiè Zhēn, Sī-Mǎ Gǎo, Zhāng Zhāo.
Confucius said:
“What virtue of a sage
can surpass filial piety?”
Filial piety is the root of all actions,
the ultimate of human relations.
All beings with sensibility,
how can they not follow this?
If one serves parents with utmost care in life,
and mourns with utmost sorrow after death,
or weeps blood for three years,
or abstains from liquids for seven days,
their longing for the *Liáo-É* (a classic poem expressing sorrow for parents) is intense,
their remembrance of parental kindness is deep.
Or their virtue moves Heaven and Earth,
their sincerity penetrates the visible and invisible.
Throughout history,
such people have existed.
The Chén dynasty inherited the chaos and decline of the Liáng dynasty,
its customs were corrupted, its influence weak.
When traces (of filial piety) became hidden among the common people,
unheard and unseen,
what is now collected and compiled
is to make up for what is lacking.
Yīn Bù-Hài, courtesy name Cháng-Qīng,
was a native of Cháng-Píng, Chén-Jùn.
His grandfather, Rèn,
was an acting staff officer for the Prince of Yù-Zhāng of Qí.
His father, Gāo-Míng,
was Shàng-Shū Zhōng-Bīng-Láng of Liáng.
Bù-Hài was extremely filial by nature.
During his father's mourning, he exceeded customary rites,
and thus became famous in his youth.
His family was habitually frugal,
and lived in great poverty.
He had five younger brothers,
all young and weak.
Bù-Hài served his old mother,
raised his young brothers,
and worked diligently at everything, leaving nothing undone.
The literati praised him for his strong moral conduct.
When he was seventeen,
Yīn Bùhài served as the Court Judge (Tíngwèi Píng) in the Liáng court.
Bùhài excelled in governance,
and was also adorned with Confucian learning.
Whenever he found legal principles (míngfǎ) to be unbalanced or inconvenient,
he would immediately submit a memorial discussing them,
and many of his suggestions were adopted.
In the fifth year of Dàtóng (539 CE),
he was promoted to Record Keeper (Jìshì Cānjūn) of the Zhenxī Mansion.
Soon after, he concurrently served as Attendant Reporter (Tōngshì Shèrén) of the Eastern Palace in his original capacity.
At this time, many of the court's political affairs were entrusted to the Eastern Palace.
Bùhài and Attendant Reporter Yú Jiānwú were on duty, presenting memorials.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng once said to Jiānwú:
"You are a man of letters;
clerical matters are not your forte.
Why not have Yīn Bùhài come instead?"
Such was the extent of his recognition.
Jiǎnwén also saw that Bùhài was good at serving his parents,
and bestowed upon his mother, Lady Cài, brocade skirts, jackets, felt mats, and bedding,
both unlined and padded, all complete.
In the seventh year (541 CE),
he was appointed Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi) of the Eastern Palace.
In the early Tàiqīng era (547 CE),
he was promoted to Counselor-in-Attendance (Zīyì Cānjūn) of the Píngběi Mansion,
while retaining his position as Attendant Reporter.
During Hóu Jǐng's Rebellion,
Bùhài followed Jiǎnwén into the palace.
When the imperial city fell,
Jiǎnwén was in the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng).
Hóu Jǐng, leading armed troops, entered to have an audience (bìjiàn) in the imperial court.
He passed by to pay his respects to Jiǎnwén.
Hóu Jǐng's soldiers were all mixed-race Qiāng and Hú,
and they jostled around,
acting very disrespectfully.
The guards were not startled or pushed back in fear;
only Bùhài and the Household Supervisor (Zhōngshùzǐ) Xú Chī stood motionless at his side.
When Jiǎnwén was imprisoned by Hóu Jǐng,
he sent someone to request Bùhài to be with him in his residence.
Hóu Jǐng permitted it,
and Bùhài served him with even greater diligence.
One night, Jiǎnwén dreamt he swallowed a clod of earth,
which made him very unhappy.
He told Bùhài about it.
Bùhài said:
"In the past, when Duke Wén of Jìn fled,
a countryman offered him a clod of earth,
and he eventually returned to Jìn.
Your Majesty's dream,
does it not portend this?"
Jiǎnwén said:
"If there is a heavenly omen,
I hope these words are not vain."
When Emperor Yuán of Liáng ascended the throne,
he appointed Bùhài as Palace Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng),
and concurrently as Court Judge (Tíngwèi Qīng).
Consequently, Bùhài moved his family westward.
When Jiānglíng fell,
Bùhài was first supervising the battle in another location,
and lost track of his mother.
At that time, it was extremely cold,
with ice and snow falling continuously.
The old and weak who froze to death filled the ditches. Bùhài walked and wept along the roads,
searching far and wide,
leaving no place untouched.
Whenever he saw a dead person in a ditch or water,
he would immediately jump in,
supporting and examining the body.
His entire body became frozen and wet.
He took no food or drink,
and his wailing and crying never ceased.
This continued for seven days
before he finally found his mother's corpse.
Bùhài leaned on the corpse and wept,
each time he raised his voice, he would almost faint.
Passersby all shed tears for him.
He temporarily interred his mother in Jiānglíng,
and then, along with Wáng Póu and Yú Xìn, entered Cháng'ān.
From then on, he ate vegetarian food and wore coarse clothes,
becoming emaciated and skeletal.
All who saw him felt sorrow.
In the seventh year of Tàijiàn (575 CE),
he returned to the court from Zhōu.
That year, an imperial edict appointed him Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng Qīng).
Soon after, he was promoted to Grand Master of Brilliant Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū).
In the eighth year (576 CE),
he was given the additional titles of General of Manifest Might (Míngwēi Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator of Jìnlíng (Jìnlíng Tàishǒu).
While in the commandery, he fell ill.
An edict recalled him as Grand Master of Brilliant Happiness to recuperate.
When the Last Lord ascended the throne,
he was given the additional title of Attendant Palace Censor (Jǐshì Zhōng).
Initially,
when Bùhài returned, Zhōu kept his eldest son, Sēngshǒu,
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (589 CE),
when the capital fell,
Sēngshǒu came to welcome him.
Bùhài fell ill and died on the way,
who consequently resided in Guānzhōng.
Yīn Bùníng, courtesy name Jìqīng,
was Bùhài's younger brother.
From a young age, he established a reputation for integrity.
During his father's mourning period, he was known for his extreme filial piety.
He loved reading,
and was particularly skilled in official duties.
He began his career in Liáng as a Central Army Bureau Director (Zhōngbīng Láng) in the Department of State Affairs,
and was highly praised for his competence.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng, acting by imperial command,
appointed him General of Martial Enlightenment (Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn) and Counselor-in-Attendance (Zīyì Cānjūn) to the Prince of Wǔlíng.
In the early Chéngshèng era (552 CE),
he was promoted to Magistrate of Wǔkāng.
At that time, there was war and famine,
and the common people were displaced.
Bùníng toured, comforted, and rallied them,
and thousands came, carrying their children on their backs.
Coincidentally, Jiānglíng fell,
and his mother died.
The roads were cut off,
and he could not rush to her for a long time.
For four years,
he wept day and night,
and in his daily life and diet,
he always observed the rites of mourning.
When Emperor Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he was appointed General of Martial Enlightenment (Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn)
and Magistrate of Lóu.
At this point,
his fourth elder brother, Yīn Bùqí, finally went to Jiānglíng
to retrieve their mother's coffin for reburial.
Bùníng observed the mourning rites
as if he had just heard the news,
and this continued for another three years.
He personally carried earth
and planted pines and cypresses by hand.
During the seasonal festivals of Fú and Là each year,
he would invariably fast for three days.
When Emperor Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Director of the Left Bureau of Civil Affairs (Zuǒmín Láng) in the Department of State Affairs.
He did not take up the post.
Later, he became Counselor-in-Attendance (Zīyì Cānjūn) to the Prince of Shǐxīng,
and concurrently Assistant Director (Yòuchéng) in the Department of State Affairs,
then promoted to Attendant Reporter (Tōngshì Shèrén) of the Eastern Palace.
When Emperor Shìzǔ died,
the Deposed Emperor succeeded him.
Emperor Gāozōng became Grand Mentor (Tàifù),
and oversaw the Department of State Affairs, assisting in governance.
He was greatly respected by the court.
Bùníng had always established himself with a reputation for integrity,
and was also entrusted with duties in the Eastern Palace.

So he, along with the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Púshè) Dào Zhòngjǔ, Palace Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén) Liú Shīzhī, Assistant Director (Yòuchéng) of the Department of State Affairs Wáng Xiān, and others,
conspired to forge an imperial edict to remove Gāozōng.
The others hesitated,
not daring to make the first move.
Bùníng then rushed to the Prime Minister's residence,
and personally declared the imperial order (chì),
commanding the Prince (Xiàng Wáng) to return to his mansion.
When the plot was discovered,
Zhòngjǔ and the others were all executed.
Gāozōng deeply esteemed Bùníng,
and specially pardoned him,
only dismissing him from office.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
he appointed Bùníng as Counselor-in-Attendance (Zīyì Cānjūn) to the Prince of Shǐxīng, the Army Supervisor (Jūnshī),
and added the title General for Enlisting the Distant (Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn).
Soon after, he was appointed Grand Architect (Dàjiàng Qīng).
Before he could accept the appointment,
he was given the additional title of Attendant-in-Ordinary with the Title of Cavalier-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì),
and concurrently Assistant Director (Yòuchéng) in the Department of State Affairs.
Shortly, he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì),
retaining his position as Assistant Director.
He died in the fifth year of Tàijiàn (573 CE),
at the age of fifty-six.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Supervisor of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān).
His third elder brother, Yīn Bùyí,
followed by Bùzhān,
and then Bùqí,
all died young.
Bùníng was the youngest.
He served his second sister-in-law, Lady Zhāng, with great devotion,
and never kept any of his official salary or emoluments for himself.
His eldest son, Fàntóng,
rose to the office of Director of the Bureau of Metal Affairs (Jīnbù Láng) in the Department of State Affairs.
Xiè Zhēn, courtesy name Yuánzhèng,
was from Yángxià, Chén Commandery.
He was the ninth-generation descendant of Grand Mentor (Tàifù) Ān of Jìn.
His grandfather, Suī,
was an Assistant Scriptor (Zhùzuò Zuǒláng) and Eastern Palace Attendant (Tàizǐ Shèrén) during the Liáng dynasty.
His father, Lín,
was an Attendant-in-Ordinary with the Title of Cavalier-in-Ordinary (Zhèng Yuánwài Láng)
and concurrently a Cavalier-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
Xiè Zhēn was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
possessing an utmost filial nature.
His paternal grandmother, Ruan Shì, had previously suffered from dizzy spells.
Whenever they occurred, she would be unable to eat or drink for a day or two.
Zhēn was seven years old at the time.
When his grandmother did not eat,
Zhēn also did not eat.
This happened often,
and his relatives were all amazed by it.
His mother, Wáng Shì,
taught Zhēn the Lúnyǔ and Xiàojīng.
He would recite them as soon as he finished reading.
At the age of eight,
he once composed a five-character poem titled "Spring Day Idle Dwelling."
His maternal uncle, Shàngshū Wáng Jūn, found its charm remarkable,
and said to his close acquaintances:
“This child is capable of great achievements.
Phrases like 'The wind has settled, yet flowers still fall,'
are already on par with Huìlián.”
From then on, he became known among famous personages.
At thirteen,
he had a general understanding of the main principles of the Wǔjīng,
and was particularly skilled in the Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn.
He was adept at cursive, clerical, insect, and seal scripts.
At fourteen,
when his father died,
he wailed and collapsed to the ground,
reviving after several fainting spells.
Initially,
his father Lín, when mourning his mother Ruan Shì,
had died from not eating and crying blood.
His family and guests feared that Zhēn would do the same.
His paternal cousin Qià and clan brother Gǎo then went together to the Huáyán Sì,
and asked Chan Master Chángzhǎo to expound the Dharma to Zhēn.
They also said to Zhēn:
“A filial son has no brothers;
you must take utmost care of yourself.
If you destroy your health through grief,
who will support your mother?”
After that, he gradually started to eat gruel.
During the chaos of Tàiqīng,
his relatives scattered and perished.
Zhēn was trapped in Jiānglíng,
while Gǎo fled to Pānyú.
Zhēn's mother became a nun at Xuānmíng Sì.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Gǎo returned to his hometown
and supported Zhēn's mother
for nearly twenty years.
In the fifth year of Tàijiàn (573 CE),
Zhēn returned to court
and was appointed Wàibīng Cānjūnshì of the Zhìwǔ Fǔ.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shàngshū Jiàbù Lángzhōng,
and then to Shìláng.
When Shǐxīngwáng Shūlíng became Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
he appointed Cíbù Shìláng Ruǎn Zhuó as his Jìshì,
and invited Zhēn to be his Zhǔbó.
Zhēn had no choice but to go.
Soon after, he was promoted to Fǔ Lùshì Cānjūn,
also holding the post of Dānyáng Céng.
Zhēn realized that Shūlíng harbored rebellious intentions,
and so he and Zhuó distanced themselves from the prince.
Whenever there was a feast or outing,
they would always excuse themselves due to illness,
never participating.
Shūlíng deeply respected them
and did not blame them.
Shortly thereafter, when Gāozōng died,
Shūlíng committed treason.
Many of the prince's officials were implicated,
but only Zhēn and Zhuó were not charged.
Hòuzhǔ then ordered Zhēn to manage the notes and records of the Zhōnggōng,
and promoted him to Nánpíngwáng Yǒu,
with the added title of Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn,
managing the Jìshì affairs.
The Fǔ Chángshǐ Rǔnán Zhōu Què, newly appointed Dūguān Shàngshū,
asked Zhēn to draft a table of resignation for him.
Hòuzhǔ read it and found it extraordinary.
Once, at a banquet, he asked Què:
“Did you compose your memorial yourself?”
Què replied:
“My memorial of thanks was written by Xiè Zhēn.”
Hòuzhǔ then ordered Shèrén Shī Wénqìng, saying:
“Xiè Zhēn, while serving the prince,
has no official emolument yet.
He should be granted a hundred shí of rice.”
In the third year of Zhìdé (585 CE),
he resigned from his post due to mourning his mother.
After a short while,
an imperial edict ordered him to return to his post,
and he was again given the title of Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn,
managing the Jìshì.
Zhēn repeatedly petitioned to firmly decline,
and the imperial edict replied:
“Your petition expressing your feelings has been noted.
Although we know you are in a state of sorrow and mourning,
the court needs talented officials,
and etiquette allows for expedient exceptions.
You may, therefore, return to your post despite your illness.”
Zhēn, overcome by grief and emaciated,
ultimately could not return to the official residence.
At that time, Shàngshū Yòuchéng Xú Zuò and Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Shěn Kèqīng both came to visit Zhēn.
Seeing his skeletal figure,
Zuò and the others sighed sorrowfully.
Xú then gently advised him:
“My dear brother, you are already old and frail.
Etiquette has its constant rules,
but it is advisable to restrain your grief a little to preserve yourself.”
Zhēn then felt even more heartbroken and wept,
losing consciousness for a long time.
The two men, weeping,
could not control themselves,
and left in compassionate silence.
Zuò said to Kèqīng:
“Indeed,
a filial son comes from a filial family.”
Kèqīng said:
“The Xiè family is renowned for its utmost filial piety,
which no scholar-official does not admire and emulate.
I fear he may not recover.
What is to be done?”
Lìbù Shàngshū Wúxìng Yáo Chá, who was a close friend of Zhēn,
visited him when Zhēn's illness became critical.
He asked about his final arrangements.
Zhēn said:
“This orphaned son, burdened with misfortune,
will soon turn to dust.
My clan nephew Kǎi and others have somewhat established themselves,
and I have already entrusted them with a letter.
This is certainly not enough to fully repay your great kindness.
Today, I struggle with labored breathing;
my time cannot be postponed.
This will be our eternal farewell.
My young son, only six years old,
named Jìng,
courtesy name Yīrén,
is a burden I cannot forget.
I dare to entrust him to you.”
He died that night.
An imperial edict bestowed one hundred hú of rice
and thirty bolts of cloth for his funeral.
Hòuzhǔ asked Chá:
“What relatives does Xiè Zhēn have?”
Chá then replied:
“Zhēn has a son who is six years old.”
An imperial edict was immediately issued to provide him with clothing and provisions indefinitely.
Earlier,
when Zhēn was critically ill,
he left a memorial to his clan nephew Kǎi, saying:
“I suffered severe hardships in my youth.
At fourteen, I lost my external support,
and at sixteen, I endured the calamity of Tàiqīng,
wandering and separated in distant lands
for over twenty years.
Crying out to heaven and treading the earth,
I was moved by compassion,
and able to return and serve [my mother]
and guard the ancestral tombs.
For my lot, this is sufficient.
I did not expect the court to pick me up from obscurity,
and repeatedly promote me to high ranks.
Even if I die now,
I have nothing to repay.
Now, in the midst of mourning,
my time is running out.
I will fold my hands and return [to dust].
What more is there to worry about?
After my last breath,
if I could be simply abandoned in the wilderness,
following the Buddhist monastic practice of leaving bodies in a charnel ground,
that would be my wish.
I only fear it would be too unconventional.
You may use thin boards to enclose my body,
place it on a funeral cart,
cover it with a reed mat,
and bury it by digging into a hill.
Furthermore, I have few brothers
and no other sons or grandsons.
Jìng is too young,
not yet familiar with worldly affairs.
You only need to set up a small bed for three months,
and place perfumed water,
to show your sincere affection as brothers.
Then remove it.
Do not engage in useless practices.”
Initially,
Shěn Zhēn 沈貞, when in Zhōu 周, once served King Zhào 趙 as a tutor for his reading.
The King was the beloved younger brother of Emperor Wǔ 武 of Zhōu 周,
and treated him with great courtesy.
The King once heard his attendants say that whenever Zhēn 貞 was alone, he would weep day and night.
He privately sent someone to inquire,
and learned that Zhēn’s 貞 mother was old
and far away in Jiāngnán 江南.
So he said to Zhēn 貞:
"If this King were to reside in a fiefdom,
I would send the tutor back home to provide for his mother."
Several years later,
the King indeed left.
He then sought an audience,
and directly memorialized, saying:
"Xiè Zhēn 謝貞 is extremely filial, and his mother is old.
Your servant requests that he be allowed to return home."
The Emperor admired the King's benevolence and permitted it,
so Zhēn 貞 returned to his homeland with the envoy Dù Zǐhuī 杜子暉.
His collected writings
were mostly lost due to military disturbances.
Sīmǎ Gǎo 司馬暠, whose courtesy name was Wénshēng 文昇,
was a native of Wēn 温, Hénèi 河內.
His great-great-grandfather was Sīmǎ Róuzhī 司馬柔之, who was a Jìn 晉 Grand Master of Imperial Sacrifices and Minister of the Household,
a descendant of Prince Nándùn 南頓 Shào 紹, and of King Wénxiàn 文獻 Yōu 攸 of Qí 齊.
His father was Zǐchǎn 子產,
who was a Liáng 梁 Minister of the Ministry of Public Works, Water Bureau Vice-Director, and Grand Administrator of Yuèyáng 岳陽,
and was the maternal cousin of Emperor Wǔ 武 of Liáng 梁.
Gǎo 暠 was intelligent and discerning in his youth,
and possessed utmost filial piety.
At the age of twelve,
he suffered the internal bereavement (of his mother),
and his grief exceeded propriety.
He did not take in water or gruel
for almost ten days.
Every time he wailed,
he would become faint,
and his relatives, both inside and outside the family,
all feared that he would not survive the mourning.
His father, Zǐchǎn 子產, would often reason with him,
and force him to eat congee and gruel,
but he still became emaciated and skeletal.
After the mourning period ended,
as a relative by marriage,
he was permitted to enter and pay respects.
Emperor Wǔ 武 of Liáng 梁 saw Gǎo 暠's thinness,
sighed for a long time,
and said to his father Zǐchǎn 子產:
"Yesterday I saw Luó’ér 羅兒, his face was haggard
and it made me feel sorrow.
This is truly not disgracing the family tradition;
you have a son indeed."
Luó’ér 羅兒
was Gǎo 暠's childhood name.
He was appointed Erudite of the Imperial Academy,
and successively promoted to Gentleman-in-Waiting.
When his father died,
his grief and self-mutilation were even more severe.
He built a hut by the side of the tomb,
and consumed only one pint of thin wheat porridge per day.
The tomb was in Xīnlín 新林,
connected to hills and mounds,
and historically had many fierce beasts.
Gǎo 暠 lived in the hut for several years,
and jackals and wolves disappeared from the area.
There were often two doves nesting and roosting by his hut,
unusually tame and familiar.
This story is still told in Xīnlín 新林 today.
During the Chéngshèng 承聖 era,
he was appointed Crown Prince's Household Administrator.
When Jiānglíng 江陵 fell,
he was moved into the pass with the others as per regulation.
However, the Liáng 梁 imperial family had massacred the Crown Prince,
and his burial place was lost.
Gǎo 暠, as an imperial official,
submitted a memorial to the Zhōu 周 court,
requesting to return to Jiānglíng 江陵 to rebury him.
His words were very poignant.
The Zhōu 周 court replied with a gracious edict, saying:
"In the past, when Zhǔfù 主父 was executed,
Kǒng Chē 孔車 showed the demeanor of a noble man.
When Péng Yuè 彭越 was punished,
Luán Bù 欒布 received the etiquette due to a loyal minister.
The Household Administrator's hometown has changed,
yet he still harbors the sentiment of accompanying the deceased.
This truly demonstrates his loyalty and integrity,
and only now do we understand the way of a minister.
Therefore, an order is issued to Jīngzhōu 荊州
to inter him with proper rites."
In the eighth year of Tàijiàn 太建 (576 CE),
he returned to court from Zhōu 周.
Gāozōng 高宗 particularly bestowed special rites
and generous rewards upon him.
He was appointed Adjutant to the Prince of Yídū 宜都,
then transferred to Grand Administrator of the Āndé 安德 Palace, Director of the Cavalier Attendants, Grand Master of the Central Palace, and Grand Central Justiciar of Sīzhōu 司州.
He died in office.
He had ten volumes of collected works.
His son, Yányì 延義,
whose courtesy name was Xīzhōng 希忠,
was quiet, intelligent, and fond of learning in his youth.
When Jiānglíng 江陵 fell,
he followed his father into the pass.
Upon his mother's death,
his mourning exceeded propriety.
When Gǎo 暠 returned to the capital,
Yányì 延義 personally carried the spiritual coffin on his back,
hiding by day and traveling by night,
braving ice and frost.
His hands and feet were all chapped and frostbitten.
When he arrived at the capital,
he suffered from a cold wind (stroke),
which led to paralysis and disability.
It took several years for him to recover.
He was gradually promoted to Adjutant to the Prince of Póyáng 鄱陽, Friend of the Prince of Yuánlíng 沅陵, and Supervising Secretary of the Minister of Works.
Zhāng Zhāo 張昭, whose courtesy name was Démíng 德明,
was a native of Wú 吳 in Wújùn 吳郡.
In his youth, he was filial
and diligently cared for his parents,
never acting contrary to ritual.
His father, Gàn 熯,
often suffered from diabetes (thirst-wasting disease)
and had a craving for fresh fish.
Zhāo 昭 personally wove nets to catch fish
to supply him morning and evening.
His younger brother, Gān 乾,
whose courtesy name was Xuánmíng 玄明,
was intelligent and learned,
and also possessed utmost filial piety.
When their father died,
both brothers wore no cotton or silk
and ate no salt or vinegar,
only one pint of wheat flour porridge a day.
Every time they were overcome with grief,
they would vomit blood.
When their neighbors heard their cries,
they all wept for them.
Before their father's mourning period ended,
their mother, Lady Lù 陸氏, also passed away.
The brothers then grieved and emaciated themselves for six years,
becoming skeletal in appearance.
Their relatives and friends who saw them no longer recognized them.
Their family was poor
and they could not afford a grand funeral,
so they wore coarse clothes and ate vegetables
for over ten years,
shutting their doors and staying indoors,
completely isolating themselves from social interactions.
At that time, Prince Héngyáng 衡陽 Bóxìn 伯信 was administering the commandery.
He nominated Gān 乾 as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate,
but Gān 乾 firmly declined.
Both brothers fell ill due to their self-mutilation during mourning.
Zhāo 昭 lost one eye,
and Gān 乾 also suffered from a cold affliction and severe disability.
Both died at home before the age of fifty,
and both lines of descent ended.
During the reign of Gāozōng 高宗, there was a Wáng Zhīxuán 王知玄 from Tàiyuán 太原
who resided as an immigrant in Shàn 剡 County, Kuàijī 會稽.
He was known for his filial piety at home.
Upon his father's death,
he grieved himself to death.
Gāozōng 高宗 praised him
and issued an edict to change the name of his residence, Qīngkǔ Lǐ 清苦里 (Pure Hardship Lane), to Xiàojīa Lǐ 孝家里 (Filial Family Lane).
The historian says:
Among human virtues,
none is greater than filial piety.
Therefore, it is about repaying one's origins and returning to the beginning,
exhausting one's nature and delving into the spiritual.
Oh, filial piety,
one must not fail to strive for it!
Thus, the record says,
"It fills heaven and earth!"
How grand it is!

The old laws of the Liáng dynasty,

Therefore, under heavy shackles,

Morning and evening, two periods,

and only one confessed.
I foolishly believe that for prisoners tainted by crime,
prison officials should clearly differentiate and analyze,
exhaustively examining the facts.
If the crime is doubtful,
it is appropriate to request review and separate judgment,
hopefully avoiding abusive interrogation.
If there is clear evidence of the crime,
then it is permissible to request review and interrogation.
This way, right and wrong will be distinguished,
and punishment and clemency will be rational.
Fàn Quán now cites the Hàn laws,
saying: 'For capital crimes and those incurring removal from office,
when the evidence is clear,
and torture has been applied,
but the accused conceals and does not confess,
the case should be reported for disposition.'
Dù Yù's annotation says: 'Disposition refers to
the clear state of evidence,
listing the intent of concealment.'
I secretly observed that the old system was severe,
with only one in a hundred not confessing.
The new system is lenient and generous,
with nine in ten not confessing.
Comparing the two texts,
lenience and severity are truly different.
The disposition and reporting
have not been changed.
I foolishly believe it should be handed over to the legal authorities
to further review the text regarding 'disposition and reporting'."
Zhū deliberated, saying:
"Interrogation at night
is easily deceptive due to varying urgency and relaxation.
Using day-time water clocks as well
is appropriate for the matter.
However, the length of the water clock kè
differs between ancient and modern times.
The 'Treatise on Pitch-pipes and the Calendar' in the Hàn Shū,
and the water clock records of Hé Chéngtiān, Zǔ Chōngzhī, and Zǔ Gēng's father and son,
all state that from the 'guān gǔ' to the 'xià gǔ',
and from the 'bū gǔ' to the 'guān gǔ',
are all thirteen kè,
without difference in the four seasons of winter and summer.
If the days vary in length,
the division is before and after midday.
Now, using the water clock revised at the end of Liáng,
after the 'xià gǔ',
the variations in length are divided.
On the summer solstice,
each period is seventeen kè;
on the winter solstice,
each period is twelve kè.
I humbly received the imperial decree
that the kè should be consistent with the legal commands.
Upon inspection, the total kè of a day is the same,
but the usage varies across the four seasons.
The Tíngwèi now reports
that due to the short duration of the kè,
criminals do not confess.
My humble opinion is to eliminate the ambiguity of night interrogation,
and follow the clarity of the day-time water clock.
By weighing the ancient and modern,
and integrating the meaning of the two water clocks,
we should abandon the fewer kè of autumn and winter,
and follow the longer daylight of summer.
Regardless of hot or cold,
all should follow the present summer solstice.
Morning and evening interrogations,
each should be seventeen kè.
Compared to the ancient water clock,
this is four kè more per interrogation than in the past.
If using the current water clock,
it is five kè more than on the winter solstice.
Although during the winter solstice,
a few kè encroach upon the night,
it is precisely a shorter day,
so there is no doubt in the matter.
