Hopefully, criminals will not use the short clock as a defense,
and prisoners will not be falsely accused at night.
In my humble opinion,
I secretly believe this is appropriate and reasonable."
The assembly deliberated and believed it was appropriate to follow Fàn Quán's previous system.
Gāozōng said:
"Zhǎngshǐ Shěn's deliberation is moderate;
it is appropriate to discuss it more broadly."
Zuǒchéng Zōng Yuánráo deliberated, saying:
"I secretly observed that Shěn's deliberation is not completely different from Fàn's.
It precisely aims to equalize the number of kè across the four seasons,
and also to weigh its advantages
to balance severity and leniency.
It is the same as requesting to send it back to the Shāndìng Cáo for detailed revision of the previous system."
Gāozōng acted accordingly.
Zhū died in the first year of Tàijiàn,
at the age of fifty-two.
Qī Gǔn, courtesy name Gōngwén,
was a native of Yángguān, Wú Jùn.
His grandfather, Xiǎn,
was Qí Jǐshìzhōng.
His father, Bà,
was Liáng Línhè Wáng Fǔ Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
Zhāng Jī was intelligent and outstanding in his youth,
possessing profound thought.
At the age of fourteen,
he had mastered the Xiàojīng and Lúnyǔ.
He was deeply fond of Xuánxué discourse
and studied under Zhōu Hóngzhèng of Rǔnán.
Whenever he had a new insight,
he was highly praised and respected by his elders.
During the Dàtóng era of the Liáng dynasty,
he was summoned to serve as a Guózǐ Zhèngyán Shēng.
Liáng Wǔdì once lectured on the Xuányán of Qián and Kūn in Wéndé Diàn.
Zhāng Jī, Yuán Xiàn of Chénjùn, and others were present.
An imperial edict commanded Zhāng Jī to discuss it.
No other scholar dared to speak first.
Zhāng Jī then composed himself and stepped forward,
engaging in circular and thorough consultation,
his rhetoric being gentle and elegant.
Liáng Wǔdì was very impressed by him,
bestowing upon him a skirt, tunic, silk, etc.,
and further stated,
"This demonstrates your power of studying antiquity, my lord."
Zhāng Jī lost his mother in his youth.
He possessed a embroidered silk scarf,
which was a memento left by his mother.
As he grew older and became aware,
his family informed him fully about it.
Every year, at festive times, he would face the scarf and choke with sobs,
unable to control himself.
When his father passed away,
he observed mourning beyond the prescribed rites.
After the period of mourning ended,
he was summoned to serve as Zuǒ Chángshì for the prince of Xiāngdōng,
then transferred to Tiáncáo Cānjūn,
and promoted to Shìlín Guǎn Xuéshì.
When Jiǎnwén was in the Eastern Palace,
he issued a topic for the Xiàojīng at the Shìlín Guǎn.
Zhāng Jī's arguments and counter-arguments
were greatly admired and praised.
From then on, whenever there was a lecture or gathering,
an envoy would surely be sent to summon Zhāng Jī.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
even amidst the siege,
Zhāng Jī still attended Ái Tàizǐ in the Wǔdé Hòu Diàn to lecture on Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi.
When Liángtái fell,
Zhāng Jī struggled to avoid the disaster,
and ultimately did not serve Hóu Jǐng.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
he successively held the post of Lín'ān Lìng.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he was appointed Tàicháng Chéng,
and then transferred to Xíngyù Cānjūn for the prince of Shǐxīng.
During the Tiānjiā era,
he was promoted to Guózǐ Zhùjiào.
At this time, Zhōu Hóngzhèng was in the Guóxué,
lecturing on a topic from the Zhōuyì.
Hóngzhèng's fourth younger brother, Hóngzhí, was also present at the lecture.
Zhāng Jī debated with Hóngzhèng,
and Hóngzhèng was defeated.
Hóngzhí sat upright and spoke sternly,
assisting his brother in presenting his case.
Zhāng Jī then sternly said to Hóngzhí:
"Today's gathering is to
clarify the correct principles.
Although I know you are in distress, my brother,
Master Four is not permitted to assist."
Hóngzhí said:
"I am assisting my teacher.
Why is it not allowed?"
The entire assembly burst into laughter.
Hóngzhèng once said to people:
"Whenever I ascend the platform,
seeing Zhāng Jī in the audience
makes me feel awe-struck."
During Gāozōng's reign,
he successively served as Jìshì Cānjūn for the prince of Jiàn'ān,
concurrently Xuéshì of the Eastern Palace,
then transferred to Xiànnèi Jìshì for the prince of Wǔlíng,
his position as Xuéshì remaining as before.
When Hòuzhǔ was in the Eastern Palace,
he gathered officials for a banquet.
A new jade-handled duster had just been completed.
Hòuzhǔ personally held it,
saying:
"Although there are many talented people like a forest today,
as for someone truly capable of holding this,
it is only Zhāng Jī."
He then handed it to Zhāng Jī.
He also ordered him to lecture on Zhuāngzi and Lǎozi in Wēnwén Diàn.
Gāozōng visited the palace to listen,
bestowing upon him a set of clothes he had worn.
After Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
Zhāng Jī held the concurrent posts of Zīyì Cānjūn for the prince of Nánpíng and Xuéshì of the Eastern Palace.
Soon after, he was promoted to Guózǐ Bóshì,
his position as Xuéshì remaining as before.
Hòuzhǔ once visited Zhōngshān Kāishàn Sì, summoning his attendants to sit under the pine forest southwest of the temple.
He commanded Zhāng Jī to deliver a lecture.
At that time, the duster had not yet arrived.
Hòuzhǔ ordered a pine branch to be brought,
personally handed it to Zhāng Jī,
saying,
"This can substitute for the duster."
He then looked at his courtiers and said,
"This will be a future anecdote about Zhāng Jī."
In the third year of Zhēnmíng, he entered Suí.
He died in Cháng'ān
at the age of seventy-six.
Zhāng Jī was tranquil by nature,
not seeking glory or profit.
He always admired leisure and ease.
In his residence, he built a garden with a pond,
planted flowers and fruits,
and lectured on the Zhōuyì, Lǎozi, and Zhuāngzi, teaching there.
Lù Yuánlǎng of Wújùn, Zhū Mèngbó, the Buddhist monk Fǎcái of Yīchéng Sì, the Buddhist monk Huìxiū of Fǎyún Sì,
and the Daoist Yáo Suí of Zhìzhēn Guān,
Zhāng Jī authored Zhōuyì Yì in thirty scrolls,
Shàngshū Yì in fifteen scrolls,
Máoshī Yì in twenty scrolls,
Xiàojīng Yì in eight scrolls,
Lúnyǔ Yì in twenty scrolls,
Lǎozǐ Yì in eleven scrolls,
Zhuāngzi Nèipiān Yì in twelve scrolls,
Wàipiān Yì in twenty scrolls,
Zápīan Yì in ten scrolls,
Xuánbù Tōngyì in twelve scrolls.
He also compiled Yóu Xuán Guìlín in twenty-four scrolls.
Hòuzhǔ once ordered people to copy these from his home into the Mìgé.
His son, Xiàozé,
reached the official position of Shǐ'ān Wáng Jìshì Cānjūn.
Gù Yuè, courtesy name Sīnán,
was a native of Yánguān, Wújùn.
His residence, Xīnpō Huánggāng,
had a family school for generations,
thus many of the Gù clan were Confucian scholars.
Gù Yuè was orphaned in his youth,
and established himself through diligence and hardship.
He was intelligent and eloquent,
expounding on the Máoshì Shī,
and also conversant with various interpretations.
Zhōu Shě, Grand Tutor to the Liáng Crown Prince, greatly admired him.
He was appointed to Yángzhōu Yìcáo Shǐ,
concurrently Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài Chéng.
Gù Yuè was precise and clear in his understanding of principles,
excelling particularly in argumentation.
He and Hé Wénfā of Kuàijī were both highly esteemed by Wěi, the prince of Nánpíng during the Liáng dynasty,
who invited them as guests.
Soon after, he was appointed Wǔjīng Bóshì.
In the first year of Shàotài,
he was promoted to Guózǐ Bóshì.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Zīyì Cānjūn for the prince of Shǐxīng,
and attended the Eastern Palace for reading.
Shìzǔ, considering Gù Yuè to be elderly,
treated him generously,
appointing him Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng,
and also concurrently Guózǐ Bóshì,
continuing his service as attendant for reading.
When Fèidì succeeded to the throne,
he was appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì and Zhōngshū Shèrén.
When Huá Jiǎo staged his rebellion,
Gù Yuè was in Dōngyáng.
Someone slandered him to Gāozōng,
saying he had rebellious intentions.
An imperial edict ordered his imprisonment,
and consequently, he was dismissed from office.
In the first year of Tàijiàn, he died at home
at the age of seventy-eight.
At that time, there was Gōng Mèngshū from Dōngyáng,
who also studied the Máoshì Shī
and was skilled in discussing philosophical principles.
During Liáng Wǔdì's era,
he rose to the position of Xúnyáng Jùnchéng.
When Yuándì was in Jiāngzhōu,
he treated him with great respect,
personally serving him as a teacher.
During the Chéngshèng era,
he concurrently held the post of Zhōngshū Shèrén.
In early Tiānjiā,
he was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì,
concurrently Guózǐ Zhùjiào and Tàizhōng Dàfū.
He died during the Tàijiàn era.
Shěn Bùhài, courtesy name Xiàohé,
was a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
His grandfather, Zǒng,
was Qí Shàngshū Cíbù Láng.
His father, Yì,
was Liáng Shàolíng Wáng Cānjūn.
Bù Hài (不害) did not harm the young and orphaned,
but cultivated good learning.
At fourteen,
he was summoned to be appointed a Guózǐshēng (國子生) and
passed the Míngjīng (明經) examination.
He was successively promoted to Bóshì (博士) of the Liáng Tàixué (梁太學),
then transferred to Xíngyù Cānjūn (刑獄參軍) in the palace of Lúlíng Wáng (廬陵王),
Zīyì (諮議) in the palace of Chángshā Wáng (長沙王),
and concurrently served as Rǔnán Lìng (汝南令).
At the beginning of Tiānjiā (天嘉) era,
he was appointed Zhōngjìshì Cānjūn (中記室參軍) in the palace of Héngyáng Wáng (衡陽王),
and concurrently Xuéshì (學士) of Jiādé Diàn (嘉德殿).
From the end of the Liáng (梁) dynasty's chaos and disorder,
until this time, the Guóxué (國學) had not yet been established.
Bù Hài (不害) submitted a memorial, saying: "I have heard that in establishing a person and founding a state,
nothing is more esteemed than honoring the literati.
To shape customs and transform the people,
it is essential to promote teaching and learning.
Thus, the Dōngjiāo (東膠) and Xīxù (西序) [schools]
flourished greatly in the Three Dynasties,
and the Huánlín (環林) and Bìshuǐ (璧水) [academies]
saw their enterprises prosper in the Two Capitals.
Since the pure source has become distant,
and the turbulent waves have spread,
the things that move people are inexhaustible,
and people's pursuit of desires is without restraint.
Therefore,
establishing instructions and setting standards,
guides and illuminates the mind.
It is likened to dyeing indigo,
and similar to carving jade,
after which human relations become harmonious,
and the low and high have their proper order.
When the principles of loyalty and filial piety are clear,
the way of ruler and subject is thus solidified.
Adhering to rites as a foundation,
is why the Duke of Lǔ (魯) was hard to insult.
When songs and music were coarse,
the Earl of Zhèng (鄭) perished first.
When shields and axes were danced, the Miáo (苗) [people]
came,
and when the Pàngōng (泮宮) was completed, the Huáiyí (淮夷) submitted.
One longs for the customs of Zhū (洙) and Sì (泗) [rivers],
and recalls the prosperity of Yān (淹) and Jì (稷).
Whether possessing a state or a family,
none fail to value these.
In the final years of Dàiqīng (太清) era of Liáng (梁),
it frequently encountered misfortune and decline.
Barbarians invaded from outside,
and traitors stirred trouble within.
In the morning, the sound of drums and gongs was heard,
and in the evening, beacon fires illuminated the sky.
Great scholars and profound academics
were
scattered worse than those buried alive,
and the Five Canons and Nine Hills [writings]
were annihilated more than if covered by curtains.
Chéngjūn (成均) thus lost its enterprise,
and Gǔzōng (瞽宗) was not thereafter repaired.
The sacrifices to Bāochéng (褒成) were not
displayed with libations,
and the rite of 'scattering vegetables' had no mention of *fǔ* (簠) and *dòu* (豆) [ritual vessels].
The sounds of odes were silent,
and this continued for over twelve years.
Later generations, though eager to learn,
did not see the ceremonies of *hán zhàng* (函杖) [receiving the ceremonial staff],
and late learners, though they studied
and looked up,
only deepened their sighs of longing for those who sat on mats [to teach].
Your Majesty has succeeded to the throne,
holding the mirror and overseeing the world.
Your Way permeates the realm,
and your prestige extends everywhere.
The muddy currents have been clarified,
and the heavy haze has been dispersed.
All living beings are prosperous and thriving,
and the multitudes are all flourishing.
It is fitting to greatly revive rites and music,
and establish schools and academies.
Following ancient precedents,
Your Majesty should grace the Confucian palace with your presence,
and select the sons of high officials,
all to enter the school.
Assistive
teaching *bóshì* (博士) [academicians] [should]
lecture and practice morning and evening,
so that those carrying baskets and bearing satchels [for books]
may gracefully join their robes,
with square collars and measured steps,
forming a multitude like a forest.
Like cutting and filing,
they hear poetry and hear
rites,
and in one year, their achievements can be doubled,
and three winters are thus sufficient.
Thus they can excel in prominent regions,
and be displayed in the court, observing the state.
Upon entering officialdom and ascending to court,
they will rely on their excellent learning to
assist themselves.
When taking up office and governing,
they will have their classical studies to cultivate themselves,
their carriages will line the court,
and purple and green [robes] will be picked up from the ground [i.e., officials will be numerous].
In ancient times, though the crown prince was noble,
he still ranked with the *guózǐ* (國子).
Down to the Hàn (漢) heirs,
this rite did not fall into disuse.
And by the Two Jìn (晉) dynasties,
this matter became even more grand,
which shows
that the teacher is strict and the Way is revered.
The Crown Prince, born with innate knowledge,
needs no careful instruction.
Yet, he should still conceal his eminence and conform,
specialize in classics and request instruction,
offer wine to his former teachers,
solemnly adhering to the old norms.
In the past, the hall of Quēlǐ (闕里),
though overgrown with weeds, was opened up.
Within the old residence,
string and wind instruments sounded.
The enduring legacy of the former sages
is a profound and clear warning.
Moreover,
with no worries east of the Jiāng (江) river,
and the lands beyond the sea unified,
how can we not expand great policies
and propagate the ultimate Way?
How can we allow the profound teachings and Confucian traditions
not to flourish in a sagely era,
and great virtues
and grand undertakings
to be hidden away in a time like Yáo's (堯)?
I am a student of meager learning,
and my words are not worth counting.
I humbly offer my humble opinions,
and am filled with trepidation."
The imperial edict replied:
"I have read and heard your memorial.
Since the old regulations fell into disuse,
and subtle words were about to cease,
I have succeeded to the imperial enterprise,
with the thought of restoring and clarifying.
However, as warfare has not yet ceased,
and the military and state are in their initial stages,
I constantly fear that the excellent norms of former kings
will one day be obliterated.
Your talent and thought are excellent and comprehensive,
and your writing and reasoning are commendable.
You care deeply about the overall structure,
and are diligent in the teachings of proper conduct.
Submit this to the outside for detailed discussion,
and implement it according to the matter."
He also submitted a memorial to revise the musical chapters.
An edict ordered him to compose eight songs for the music of the three courts,
totaling twenty-eight pieces,
which were performed in the imperial music bureau.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Gǎn Lìng (灨令).
He entered service as Shàngshū Yícáo Láng (尚書儀曹郎),
was promoted to Guózǐ Bóshì (國子博士),
took charge of Yǔlín Jiān (羽林監),
was ordered to manage the Five Rites,
and presided over eulogies and posthumous title discussions.
During the Tàijiàn (太建) era,
he was appointed Chángshǐ (長史) of Rénwǔ Nánkāng Sìwáng (仁武南康嗣王) palace,
and concurrently managed the affairs of Dānyáng (丹陽) Commandery.
He was then transferred to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍) and Guānglù Qīng (光祿卿).
Soon after, he became Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn (戎昭將軍) and Míngwēi Wǔlíng Wáng (明威武陵王) Chángshǐ (長史),
and concurrently managed the affairs of Wúxīng (吳興) Commandery.
Shortly thereafter, he entered service as Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍),
and concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞).
He died in the twelfth year,
at the age of sixty-three.
Bù Hài (不害) was skilled in classical studies
and good at writing essays.
Although he was broadly versed in ancient texts,
his home had no scrolls.
Whenever he composed an essay,
he would take up his brush and finish it immediately,
without ever needing to look up references.
The Púyè (僕射) of Rǔnán (汝南), Zhōu Hóngzhèng (周弘正), often praised him, saying:
"Shěn (沈) can be called a mind of a sage!"
He authored *Zhì Wǔ Lǐ Yí* (治五禮儀) in one hundred scrolls,
and a collected works in fourteen scrolls.
His son, Zhìdào (志道),
courtesy name Chóngjī (崇基),
was renowned in his youth.
He began his career as Yángzhōu (揚州) Zhǔbù (主簿),
soon concurrently serving as Wénlín Zhùshì (文林著士),
and successively as Āndōng Xīncài Wáng (安東新蔡王) Jìshì Cānjūn (記室參軍).
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明), he entered Suí (隋).
Wáng Yuánguī (王元規), courtesy name Zhèngfàn (正範),
was a native of Jìnyáng (晉陽) in Tàiyuán (太原).
His grandfather, Dàobǎo (道寶),
was Qí (齊) Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍) and Jìn'ān Jùnshǒu (晉安郡守).
His father, Wěi (瑋),
was Jìshì Cānjūn (記室參軍) in the palace of Liáng Wǔlíng Wáng (梁武陵王).
Yuán-Guī (元規) became an orphan at the age of eight.
He and his two brothers,
with their mother, went to live with their maternal uncle in Lín-Hǎi (臨海) Commandery.
At that time, he was twelve years old.
A local magnate of the commandery, Liú Tián (劉瑱),
possessed immense wealth
and offered his daughter to Yuán-Guī (元規) in marriage.
Yuán-Guī's (元規) mother, seeing that her sons were young and weak,
wished to form a powerful alliance.
Yuán-Guī (元規) wept and pleaded, saying:
"Maintaining kinship in marriage
[二一] was valued by the ancients.
How can we seek temporary peace in a foreign land
and hastily marry into a dissimilar family!"
His mother was moved by his words and ceased the arrangement.
Yuán-Guī (元規) was by nature filial,
serving his mother with utmost diligence,
never leaving her side from dawn till dusk.
During the Liáng (梁) dynasty, there was a violent flood in Shān-Yīn (山陰) County,
which swept away homes.
Yuán-Guī (元規) only had a small boat.
In haste, he brought his mother, sister, and orphaned niece into the boat.
[二二] Yuán-Guī (元規) himself took up the oar and left,
leaving his three children (two sons and one daughter)
stranded in a treetop.
When the water receded, they were all saved.
People at the time all praised his utmost virtue.
Yuán-Guī (元規) was fond of learning in his youth.
He studied under Shěn Wén-Ē (沈文阿) of Wú-Xīng (吳興).
At eighteen,
he mastered the Chūn-Qiū Zuǒ-Shì (春秋左氏), Xiào-Jīng (孝經), Lún-Yǔ (論語), and Sāng-Fú (喪服).
In the first year of Zhōng-Dà-Tōng (中大通) of the Liáng (梁) dynasty,
an imperial decree ordered a policy on the Chūn-Qiū (春秋).
He was ranked as a high scholar,
and contemporary famous Confucians all praised him.
He started his career as Zuǒ Cháng-Shì (左常侍) in the state of Xiāng-Dōng Wáng (湘東王),
then transferred to Yuán-Wài Sǎn-Qí Shì-Láng (員外散騎侍郎).
When Jiǎn-Wén (簡文) was still the crown prince,
he was invited as a guest scholar,
frequently asked to lecture and debate,
and was treated with great courtesy.
He was appointed Jì-Shì Cān-Jūn (記室參軍) in the Middle Army's Xuān-Chéng Wáng (宣城王) Household.
When Hóu Jǐng (侯景) caused rebellion and chaos,
he took his family back to Kuài-Jī (會稽).
During the Tiān-Jiā (天嘉) era,
he was appointed Gōng-Cáo Cān-Jūn (功曹參軍) in the Shǐ-Xīng Wáng (始興王) Household,
concurrently serving as Guó-Zǐ Zhù-Jiào (國子助教).
He then transferred to Jì-Shì Cān-Jūn (記室參軍) in the Zhèn-Dōng Pó-Yáng Wáng (鎮東鄱陽王) Household,
retaining his position as Zhù-Jiào (助教).
When the Later Lord was still the crown prince,
he was invited as an academician
and personally taught the meaning of the Lǐ-Jì (禮記), Zuǒ-Zhuàn (左傳), Sāng-Fú (喪服), etc.
He received generous rewards.
He was promoted to Guó-Zǐ Jì-Jiǔ (國子祭酒).
Xīn-Ān Wáng (新安王) Bó-Gù (伯固) once happened to enter the palace just as Yuán-Guī (元規) was about to lecture,
and requested permission to hold the classic text.
This was considered an honor at the time.
Soon after, he was appointed Shàng-Shū Cí-Bù Láng (尚書祠部郎).
Since the Liáng (梁) dynasty, scholars who passed down the study of the Zuǒ-Shì (左氏)
all used the interpretations of Jiǎ Kuí (賈逵) and Fú Qián (服虔) to challenge Dù Yù (杜預),
totaling 180 articles.
Yuán-Guī (元規) cited and analyzed them thoroughly,
leaving no further doubts or ambiguities.
Whenever the state deliberated on auspicious or inauspicious grand ceremonies,
he always participated.
He resigned from his post due to his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Lù-Shì Cān-Jūn (錄事參軍) in the Pó-Yáng Wáng (鄱陽王) Household.
Soon after, he was transferred to Sǎn-Qí Shì-Láng (散騎侍郎),
then promoted to Xiàn-Nèi Cān-Jūn (限內參軍) in the Nán-Píng Wáng (南平王) Household.
When the King became the Governor of Jiāng-Zhōu (江州),
Yuán-Guī (元規) followed the household to the garrison.
Students from all directions,
traveling a thousand lǐ (里) or more, came to seek his teachings,
often numbering dozens or hundreds.
In the third year of Zhēn-Míng (禎明), he entered the Suí (隋) dynasty
and became Dōng-Gé Jì-Jiǔ (東閤祭酒) in the Qín Wáng (秦王) Household.
At seventy-four,
he died in Guǎng-Líng (廣陵).
Yuán-Guī (元規) authored eleven volumes of Chūn-Qiū Fā-Tí-Cí Jí Yì-Jì (春秋發題辭及義記),
[二三] fourteen volumes of Xù Jīng-Diǎn Dà-Yì (續經典大義),
two volumes of Xiào-Jīng Yì-Jì (孝經義記),
three volumes of Zuǒ-Zhuàn Yīn (左傳音),
and two volumes of Lǐ-Jì Yīn (禮記音).
His son, Dà-Yè (大業),
was known for his intelligence and quick wit.
At that time, there was Lù Qìng (陸慶) from Wú-Jùn (吳郡),
who was fond of learning in his youth,
thoroughly understanding the Five Classics,
and particularly clear on the Chūn-Qiū Zuǒ-Shì-Zhuàn (春秋左氏傳).
His integrity was very high.
He was first appointed Yòu Cháng-Shì (右常侍) in the state of Liáng Wǔ-Líng Wáng (梁武陵王),
served as Mò-Cáo Xíng Cān-Jūn (墨曹行參軍) in the Zhēng-Xī Fǔ (征西府),
and was appointed Magistrate of Lóu (婁).
Amidst the chaos and decline of the Liáng (梁) dynasty,
he devoted himself to Buddhist scriptures,
thoroughly studying all sūtras and treatises.
In the early Tiān-Jiā (天嘉) era,
he was summoned as Tōng-Zhí Sǎn-Qí Shì-Láng (通直散騎侍郎),
but did not accept.
When Yǒng-Yáng Wáng (永陽王) was the Grand Administrator of Wú-Jùn (吳郡),
he heard of Lù Qìng's (陸慶) reputation
and wished to meet him,
but Qìng (慶) firmly declined, citing illness.
At that time, a kinsman, Lù Róng (陸榮), was the Wǔ-Guān Yuán (五官掾) of the commandery.
Qìng (慶) once visited him.
The King then went to Róng's (榮) residence in plain clothes
and peered through a hole in the wall to observe him.
The King said to Róng (榮):
"Observing Lù Qìng's (陸慶) dignified and imposing demeanor,
he is almost unfathomable.
How could Yán Jūn-Píng (嚴君平) or Zhèng Zǐ-Zhēn (鄭子真) surpass him?"
Pó-Yáng (鄱陽) and Jìn-Ān Wáng (晉安王) both summoned him as Jì-Shì (記室),
but he declined both.
He then built a secluded house
and dedicated himself to Zen meditation and chanting.
Consequently, those who received his teachings became rare.
The historian says: To cultivate oneself and refine one's conduct
must first involve classical learning.
To establish a state and elevate a family
largely follows this path.
Therefore, royal governance achieves supreme order through it,
and human relations attain proper sequence through it.
Scholars like Shěn Wén-Ē (沈文阿),
each specializing in and teaching classics,
were indeed great Confucians of their era.
Wén-Ē (文阿) further initiated the drafting of rituals;
he was indeed a successor to Shú-Sūn Tōng (叔孫通).

Textual Notes: Biographies, Chapter 28, Literature: Dù Zhī-Wěi (杜之偉), Yán Huǎng (顏晃), Jiāng Dé-Zǎo (江德藻), Yǔ Chí (庾持), Xǔ Hēng (許亨), Chǔ Jiè (褚玠), Cén Zhī-Jìng (岑之敬), Lù Yǎn (陸琰) (younger brother Yú (瑜)), Hé Zhī-Yuán (何之元), Xú Bó-Yáng (徐伯陽), Zhāng Zhèng-Jiàn (張正見), Cài Níng (蔡凝), Ruǎn Zhuó (阮卓).
The Yì (易) says:
"Observe the culture of humanity to transform and perfect the world."
Kǒng-Zǐ (孔子) said:
"How splendid are its elegant patterns!"
From the Chǔ (楚) and Hàn (漢) dynasties onward,
literary figures emerged continuously.
In Luò-Ruì (洛汭) and Jiāng-Zuǒ (江左),
their influence spread even more widely.
All sought to rival creation,
and shine alongside the sun and moon.
Greatly, they emulated the canons and counsels,
assisting and supporting the royal way.
Minimally, their writings were clear and upright,
expressing their innate spirit.
As for ordering rites and music,
comprehending human relations,
understanding past and present,
and describing beauty and ugliness,
nothing surpasses this.
After the Later Lord succeeded to the throne,
he greatly admired literary compositions
and widely sought out scholars and artists,
who gathered in brilliance.
Whenever his officials presented memorials or offered odes and eulogies,
he personally reviewed them.
If the composition was skillful,
he would praise and encourage it with his divine brush,
and increase the author's rank and position.
Thus, all the literati
knew to exert themselves.
If literary figures like Huǎng (晃) were of high repute,
their achievements would be discussed separately.
Now, Dù Zhī-Wěi (杜之偉) and others, whose learning also encompassed literature,
are included in this chapter.
Dù Zhī-Wěi (杜之偉), courtesy name Zǐ-Dà (子大),
was a native of Qián-Táng (錢塘) in Wú-Jùn (吳郡).
His family had generations of Confucian scholarship,
specializing in the Three Rites.
His father, Guī (規),
served as Fèng-Cháo-Qǐng (奉朝請) during the Liáng (梁) dynasty
and was a close friend of Guāng-Lù Dà-Fū (光祿大夫) Jiāng Gé (江革) of Jì-Yáng (濟陽) and Dū-Guān Shàng-Shū (都官尚書) Kǒng Xiū-Yuán (孔休源) of Kuài-Jī (會稽).
Zhī Wěi was intelligent and sensitive in his youth,
possessing exceptional talent.
At seven years old,
he received the *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents),
and gradually studied the *Shī* (Book of Odes) and *Lǐ* (Book of Rites),
gaining a general understanding of their teachings.
At fifteen,
he had read extensively in history and literature, as well as ceremonial texts and historical anecdotes.
His contemporaries praised him for his early maturity.
The *Púshè* (Director of the Imperial Secretariat) Xú Miǎn once saw his writings,
and greatly valued his writing skill.
In the first year of Zhōngdà (later called Dàtōng)
of Liáng Wǔdì's reign, the Emperor visited Tóngtài Sì to renounce the world and become a monk.
He ordered Xú Miǎn to compile and finalize the ceremonial procedures.
Xú Miǎn, noting that the imperial court had no prior precedent for this ritual,
summoned Zhī Wěi to draft the arrangements.
Subsequently, he was appointed *Dōnggōng Xuéshì* (Scholar of the Eastern Palace),
and with scholars like Liú Zhì, he copied and compiled various books,
each contributing to specific topics.
Of the two essays compiled, "Fùjiào" (Enriching Teachings) and "Zhèngdào" (Way of Governance),
Zhī Wěi wrote the prefaces for both.
When Xiāngyīn Hóu Xiāo Áng became the *Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ* (Prefect of Jiāngzhōu),
he appointed Zhī Wěi to manage his secretariat.
After Xiāo Áng's death,
Lúlíng Wáng Xù succeeded him,
and personally extended an invitation to Zhī Wěi.
Zhī Wěi firmly declined the offer,
and instead escorted Xiāo Áng's coffin back to the capital.
He then served Línchéng Gōng (formerly Línchéng Gōng) as a reader.
Soon after, he was appointed *Yángzhōu Yìcáo Cóngshì* (Advisor in the Deliberation Office of Yángzhōu) and *Nánkāng Sì Wáng Mòcáo Cānjūn* (Consultant in the Taxation Office for the Heir of Nánkāng),
concurrently serving as *Tàixué Xiànnèi Bóshì* (Imperial Academy Doctor within the Quota).
In the seventh year of Dàtóng,
the Liáng Crown Prince performed the *Shìdiàn* (Sacrificial Ceremony) at the National Academy.
At the time, the Music Bureau had no songs for Confucius or Yánzǐ to be sung.
The *Shàngshū Cānyì Lìng* (Director of Consultation in the Department of State Affairs) ordered Zhī Wěi to compose the lyrics.
The performers learned and practiced them,
and they became part of the official repertoire.
He was then transferred to *Ānqián Shàolíng Wáng Tiáncáo Cānjūn* (Consultant in the Agricultural Office for Prince Shàolíng of Ānqián),
and then to *Xíngyù Cānjūn* (Consultant in the Judicial Office).
Zhī Wěi's rank and position were quite low,
but specifically because of his strong memory and outstanding talent,
he had a considerable reputation in his time.
The *Lìbù Shàngshū* (Minister of Personnel) Zhāng Zuǎn knew him deeply,
considering him a vessel for the highest offices.
When Hóu Jǐng revolted,
Zhī Wěi fled and hid in the mountains and marshes.
When Gāozǔ became *Chéngxiàng* (Chancellor),
having long heard of his reputation,
he summoned him to be appointed *Jìshì Cānjūn* (Consultant in the Secretariat).
He was promoted to *Zhōngshū Shìláng* (Gentleman of the Central Secretariat),
and concurrently held the position of *Dà Zhùzuò* (Grand Historian).
When Gāozǔ accepted the abdication,
he was appointed *Hónglú Qīng* (Minister of the Court of Diplomatic Reception),
with other duties remaining as before.
Zhī Wěi petitioned to resign from the position of *Zhùzuò*,
saying:
"Since the first year of Shàotài,
I have unworthily served as *Zhōngshū Shìláng*,
managing the national history,
for four years now.
I am by nature humble and common,
yet have been mistakenly recognized and favored.
Wishing to repay this kindness and encouragement,
I dared not abandon my post.
Now that the imperial calendar is renewed,
and the Emperor drives the chariot of Xuan and Hao,
the task of recording words and deeds
is not one whose incumbent can be easily changed.
For the talent of a *Zhùzuò*,
it is even more appropriate to select from many.

*Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng* (Palace Censor) Shěn Jiǒng, *Shàngshū Zuǒchéng* (Assistant Minister of the Left) Xú Líng, the former Liáng *Jiān Dà Zhùzuò* (concurrent Grand Historian) Yú Lì, and the former Liáng *Huángmén Shìláng* (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate) Kǒng Huàn,
are either brilliant writers with ample skill, or possess strong memories and are well-versed in ancient history.
The responsibility of a Qiān or Dǒng [i.e., Sīmǎ Qiān and Dǒng Hú]
is truly suited for such a group of talents.
It is not fitting for me to suddenly change the capital [referring to leaving the capital for provincial office],
and again obstruct the path of worthy individuals.
The humility of Yáo's court
is indeed beyond reach,
but to exert my strength and take my place
is perhaps to know how to avoid fault."
A gracious imperial decree disallowed his resignation.
Soon after, he was transferred to *Dàjiàng Qīng* (Minister of the Grand Architect),
then promoted to *Tàizhōng Dàfū* (Grand Master of the Palace),
and was further ordered to compile the history of the Liáng dynasty.
He died in the third year of Yǒngdì,
at the age of fifty-two.
Gāozǔ greatly lamented and cherished him.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of *Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì* (Regular Attendant, Grand Master of Remonstrance),
bestowed five thousand *qián*,
fifty bolts of cloth,
and one coffin,
and set a date for mourning.
Zhī Wěi's writing
did not pursue superficial showiness,
but was warm, elegant, and extensive.
Most of his works have been lost;
seventeen volumes survive.
Yán Huàng, courtesy name Yuánmíng,
was a native of Línyí, Lángyá.
Orphaned and poor in his youth,
he loved learning
and possessed literary talent.
He began his career as *Liáng Shàolíng Wáng Jiān Jìshì Cānjūn* (Concurrent Consultant in the Secretariat for Prince Shàolíng of Liáng).
At that time, Yǔ Xìn, a scholar of the Eastern Palace, once visited the prince's residence.
The prince had Yán Huàng receive him.
Yǔ Xìn, slighting his youth,
asked:
"How many concurrent consultants in the secretariat does this residence have?"
Yán Huàng replied:
"Probably fewer than the scholars in the imperial palace."
At the time, this was considered a clever retort.
During the Hóu Jǐng rebellion,
he fled west to Jīngzhōu.
At the beginning of Chéngshèng,
he was appointed *Zhōngshū Shìláng*.
At that time, Dù Kān was *Wúxīng Tàishǒu* (Governor of Wúxīng),
and was exclusively fond of bravery and strength.
His subordinates were mostly rash and dangerous youths.
Yuándì was troubled by this,
so he made Yán Huàng manage his correspondence.
He also ordered Dù Kān, saying:
"You are still young,
and it is not too late to study.
Yán Huàng is a man of literature,
and will assist you.
In moments of haste,
you must consult him."
After Dù Kān was executed,
Yán Huàng returned to Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ entrusted him with secretarial duties
and treated him with great intimacy.
He was appointed *Xuānyì Fǔ Zhōng Lùshì* (Registrar in the Xuānyì Commandery)
and concurrently *Jìshì Cānjūn*.
In the second year of Yǒngdì,
Gāozǔ visited Dàzhuāngyán Sì,
and sweet dew descended there.
Yán Huàng presented an "Ode to Sweet Dew,"
whose words and meaning were comprehensive and classical.
Gāozǔ greatly admired it.
At the beginning of Tiānjīa,
he was promoted to *Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì* (Supernumerary Grand Master of Remonstrance)
and concurrently *Zhōngshū Shèrén* (Secretariat Drafter),
managing imperial edicts.
He died in the third year,
at the age of fifty-three.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of *Sīnóng Qīng* (Minister of Agriculture),
with the posthumous name Zhēnzǐ,
and also granted him burial land.
Yán Huàng's family had always been of humble status,
with no influential relatives,
yet he maintained himself with integrity
and was known by his contemporaries.
When he drafted memorials, decrees, and edicts,
he would complete them instantly,
capturing the essence of the matter,
and his style was elegant and refined.
He compiled twenty volumes of his works.
Jiāng Dézǎo (formerly Jiāng Dé cāo), courtesy name Dézǎo,
was a native of Kǎochéng, Jìyáng.
His grandfather, Róuzhī,
was *Qí Shàngshū Cāngbù Lángzhōng* (Director of the Granary Section, Department of State Affairs, during Qí).
His father, Gé,
was *Liáng Dùzhī Shàngshū* (Minister of Finance during Liáng) and *Guānglù Dàfū* (Grand Master of Remonstrance).
Jiāng Dézǎo loved learning
and was skilled at composing essays.
He had a handsome appearance
and was seven *chǐ* four *cùn* tall.
He was extremely filial by nature
and served his parents with utmost decorum.
He lived with his half-siblings,
showing them great kindness and generosity.
He began his career as *Liáng Nán Zhōngláng Wǔlíng Wáng Xíng Cānjūn* (Acting Consultant for Prince Wǔlíng, Grand Administrator of the South during Liáng).
The *Dà Sīmǎ* (Grand Marshal) Nánpíng Wáng Xiāo Wěi, hearing of his talent,
summoned him to be *Dōnggé Jìjiǔ* (Libationer of the Eastern Pavilion).
He was promoted to *Ānxī Xiāngdōng Wáng Fǔ Wàibīng Cānjūn* (Consultant in the Outer Military Office for Prince Xiāngdōng, General Who Pacifies the West),
and soon after was appointed *Shàngshū Bǐbù Láng* (Director of the Personnel Section, Department of State Affairs).
He left his post due to his father's mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
his appearance was emaciated and haggard,
as if still in mourning.
He was appointed *Ānxī Wǔlíng Wáng Jìshì* (Secretary to Prince Wǔlíng, General Who Pacifies the West),
but did not accept.
After a long time,
he was granted the position of *Lúlíng Wáng Jìshì Cānjūn*.
He was appointed *Tíngwèi Zhèng* (Judge of the Court of Judicial Review),
and soon after was dispatched to serve as *Nán Xùnzhōu Zhìzhōng* (Administrator of Nán Xùnzhōu).
When Gāozǔ became *Sīkōng* (Minister of Works) and *Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn* (General Who Conquers the North),
he enlisted Jiāng Dézǎo as *Fǔ Zīyì* (Adviser in the Commandery).
He was transferred to *Zhōngshū Shìláng*,
and promoted to *Yúnhuī Línhǎi Wáng Chángshǐ* (Chief Clerk for Prince Línhǎi, General of the Cloud Banners).
When the Chén dynasty was established,
he was appointed *Shàngshū Lìbù Shìláng* (Assistant Minister of Personnel).
Gāozǔ received the abdication.
He was appointed Secretary-General of the Palace Library (mìshūjiān),
and concurrently Assistant Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū zuǒchéng).
Soon after, he concurrently held the post of Palace Secretary (zhōngshū shèrén) with his original office.
In the fourth year of Tiānjiā,
he concurrently served as Cavalier-in-Ordinary (sànqí chángshì).
He was sent as an envoy to Qí with Palace Secretary Liú Shīzhī.
He authored "Record of the Northern Campaign Principles" (Běizhēng Dàolǐ Jì) in three volumes.
Upon his return, he was appointed Palace Mid-Secretary to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ zhōngshùzǐ),
and concurrently Commandant of Infantry (bùbīng xiàowèi).
After a short while, he was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief (yùshǐ zhōngchéng),
but was dismissed due to a public affair.
Soon after, he was appointed General Who Shakes the Distant (zhènyuǎn jiāngjūn) and Palace Attendant and Cavalier-in-Ordinary (tōngzhí sànqí chángshì).
He requested to govern a county himself,
and was sent out to serve as the Magistrate of Xīnyù.
His administration favored kindness and benevolence,
and he achieved considerable remarkable results.
In the sixth year,
he died in office
at the age of fifty-seven.
Shìzǔ greatly mourned and regretted his passing,
and issued an edict posthumously appointing him Cavalier-in-Ordinary (sànqí chángshì).
His collected writings totaled fifteen volumes.
His son, Chūn,
was also skilled in writing,
and successively held the posts of Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ shùzǐ) and Assistant Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū zuǒchéng).
Yǔ Chí, courtesy name Yǔndé,
was a native of Yānlíng, Yǐngchuān.
His grandfather, Pèiyù,
was the Grand Administrator of Chángshā during the Sòng dynasty.
His father, Shāmí,
[一０]was the Magistrate of Chángchéng during the Liáng dynasty.
Chí was orphaned young
and was extremely filial by nature.
During his father's mourning period, he exceeded the prescribed rites.
He was devoted to learning
and particularly skilled in calligraphy and official documents,
gaining fame for his talent and skill.
He first served as Left Palace Attendant of the Kingdom of Nánpíng, Liáng dynasty, and Acting Staff Officer of the Prince of Hédōng's Manor, with the rank of Light Chariot General (qīngchē).
He concurrently served as a Palace Secretary (shàngshūláng),
and soon after was formally appointed to that position.
He was sent out to be the Magistrate of Ānjí,
then promoted to Recorder (jìshì) beyond the establishment in the Prince of Shàolíng's Manor, General Who Guards the East (zhèndōng),
and concurrently Magistrate of Jiànkāng.
In the early Tiānjiān period,
Shìzǔ had an old acquaintance with Chí.
[一一]When Shìzǔ became the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng,
he appointed Chí as the Prefectural Aide (jùnchéng),
concurrently in charge of literary affairs.
From then on, he always relied on Wéndì.
When Wéndì defeated Zhāng Biāo
and was stationed in Kuàijī,
he again ordered Chí to oversee Línhǎi Commandery.
Because of his greed and indulgence, he lost the people's harmony
and was abducted by mountain bandits.
He was held captive for ten days.
Shìzǔ sent Liú Chéng to quell the bandits,
and Chí was then released.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he was appointed Advisory Counselor in the Manor of the Prince of Línchuān, General Who Pacifies the East (āndōng).
In the early Tiānjiā period,
he was promoted to Assistant Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū zuǒchéng).
For his participation in the campaign at Chángchéng,
he was enfeoffed as a Viscount of Chóngdé County,
with an income of three hundred households.
On the day he was enfeoffed,
he invited the clerks as guests
and accepted their gifts and provisions.
Shìzǔ was angry at this,
and consequently he was dismissed.
Soon after, he became Advisory Counselor in the Manor of the Prince of Shǐxīng, General Who Spreads Benevolence (xuānhuì).
He was appointed Magistrate of Lín'ān,
but was stripped of his enfeoffment for having flogged a county resident to death.
[一二](He was transferred) [一三]He returned to serve as Attendant at the Yellow Gate (gěishì huángmén shìláng).
He was appointed General of Martial Prowess (léngwēi jiāngjūn) and Magistrate of Yánguān.
In the first year of Guāngdà,
he was promoted to Secretary-General of the Palace Library (mìshūjiān),
and concurrently oversaw national historical affairs.
He also served as Minister of the Privy Treasury (shàofù qīng),
and concurrently Supervisor of the Feathered Forest Guard (yǔlín jiān).
He was promoted to Grand Master of the Palace (tàizhōng dàfū),
and concurrently Commandant of Infantry (bùbīng xiàowèi).
He died in the first year of Tàijiàn
at the age of sixty-two.
An edict posthumously appointed him Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (guānglù dàfū).
Chí was skilled in calligraphy.
Whenever he composed prose,
he liked to use unusual characters,
which literary scholars also criticized him for.
He had a collection of ten volumes.
Xǔ Hēng, courtesy name Hēngdào,
was a native of Xīnchéng, Gāoyáng.
He was the sixth-generation descendant of Jìn Recluse Xún.
His great-grandfather, Guī,
successively served as Attendant (gěishìzhōng),
and was entrusted with the post of Grand Administrator of Guìyáng.
He held lofty aspirations
and resided in Jìu Mountain in Yǒngxīng,
which was where Xún had lived in reclusion.
His grandfather, Yǒnghuì,
was the Household Manager to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ jiālìng) and Junior Minister of the Guards (róngcóng púshè) during the Qí dynasty.
His father, Mào,
was the Administrator of the Two Commanderies of Shǐpíng and Tiānmén during the Liáng dynasty, Palace Mid-Secretary to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ zhōngshùzǐ), and Cavalier-in-Ordinary (sànqí chángshì).
He was known for his scholarship and artistic skill.
He compiled "Explanations of the Comparisons and Analogies in the 'Airs' and 'Odes' of the Classic of Poetry" (Máoshī Fēngyǎ Bǐxìng Yìlèi) in fifteen volumes,
and "Record of Expeditions" (Shù Xíng Jì) in four volumes.
Hēng inherited the family scholarship in his youth,
being solitary, firm, and upholding moral principles.
He was extensively read in all books
and knew many old stories from previous generations.
His peers all praised him,
and he was highly esteemed by Liú Zhīlín of Nányáng,
who often spoke highly of him.
He first served as Acting Staff Officer to the Prince of Āndōng, Liáng dynasty,
[一四]and concurrently Academician of the Imperial University (tàixué bóshì).
Soon after, he was appointed Recorder and Staff Officer to the General Who Pacifies the West (píngxī fǔ jìshì cānjūn).
In the early Tàiqīng period,
he served as Central Recorder to the General Who Conquers the West (zhēngxī zhōng jìshì),
and concurrently Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (tàicháng chéng).
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
he sought refuge in Yǐngzhōu.
When the Prince of Shàolíng of Liáng arrived from the eastern route,
he was invited to be Advisory Counselor.
When Wáng Sēngbiàn attacked Yǐngzhōu,
he had long heard of Hēng's reputation
and summoned him to be Ceremonial Aide-de-camp (yítóng cóngshì zhōngláng).
He was promoted to Aide-de-camp to the Grand Commandant (tàiwèi cóngshì zhōngláng),
and with Shěn Jiǒng of Wúxīng, jointly managed official documents.
All administrative affairs of the princely court
were entrusted to them.
When the Prince of Jìn'ān acted as regent,
Hēng was appointed Attendant at the Yellow Gate (gěishì huángmén shìláng).
Hēng submitted a memorial to the princely manor to decline,
to which Sēngbiàn replied:
"I have perused your message,
and learn of your appointment by the court,
which is indeed a virtuous promotion.
Your conduct is earnest and profound,
and your literary and artistic skills are comprehensive.
Your learning excels, and your official position
has naturally led you to high office.
Moreover, you have been constrained for a long time like a swift steed,
and are about to achieve a momentous career,
assisting and guiding me in my confusion,
with a truly deep expectation.
I am pleased with your association,
and forget my toil and humility,
but an oriole nesting in a thorny bush
always causes me to sigh with increasing admiration.
Although the selection of an evening attendant
is considered clear and prominent,
your position has risen with your talent,
and you are not at all ashamed.
And yet, you just said you know your destiny
and are about to gallop on a broad road;
you have not yet experienced the weariness of holding a halberd,
but already express the lament of traveling late at night.
Reviewing your recent letter,
I am truly perplexed.
Ancient people, when they longed for each other,
would travel a thousand *lǐ* to meet.
A sincere heart is not obscured,
how can it be limited by city walls?
My profound regard for you
causes me endless shame for my unworthiness."
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
Hēng was appointed Grand Master (zhōngsàn dàfū),
and concurrently Supervisor of the Feathered Forest Guard (yǔlín jiān).
He was promoted to Grand Master of the Palace (tàizhōng dàfū),
and concurrently Grand Compiler of History (dà zhùzuò),
overseeing the compilation of the History of Liáng.
Previously,
when Sēngbiàn was executed,
the officials collected Sēngbiàn's and his son Wěi's [一五]corpses,
and buried them in the same pit on Fāng Shān.
Until then, no one dared to speak of it.
As a former subordinate, Hēng
submitted a memorial requesting their burial.
He then, with former colleagues Xú Líng, Zhāng Zhǒng, Kǒng Huàn, and others,
jointly used their family wealth to arrange the burial.
[一六]All seven coffins were re-interred.
In the early Guāngdà period,
when Gāozōng became regent,
he greatly admired and respected Hēng for his integrity and uprightness, possessing the character of ancient people.
He always treated him with the respect due to a teacher.
When Dào Zhòngjǔ plotted to remove Gāozōng,
Máo Xǐ knew of his deceit.
Gāozōng asked Hēng,
and Hēng advised him not to obey the edict.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
he appointed Hēng Minister of the Imperial Guards (wèiwèi qīng).
He died in the second year of Tàijiàn
at the age of fifty-four.
He initially compiled "History of Qí" (Qí Shū) including fifty chapters of treatises,
but these were lost during the chaos.
Later, he compiled "History of Liáng" (Liáng Shǐ),
of which fifty-eight volumes were completed.
His collected writings produced after the Tàiqīng period of Liáng totaled six volumes.
Zǐ Shànxīn,
became famous early,
and rose to the official position of Shàngshū Dùzhī Shìláng.
Chǔ Jiè, courtesy name Wēnlǐ,
was a native of Yángzhái, Hénán.
His great-grandfather, Xuàn,
in the early Shēngmíng era of the Sòng dynasty, along with Xiè Fěi, Jiāng Xiáo, and Liú Yǔ, entered to serve in the palace,
and they were called the Four Friends.
He rose to the official positions of Shìzhōng and Lìbù Shàngshū,
and was posthumously granted the title Zhēnzǐ.
His grandfather, Yún,
was the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng of the Liáng dynasty.
His father, Méng,
was a Tàizǐ Shèrén.
Jiè was orphaned at the age of nine
and was raised by his uncle, Piàojì Cóngshì Zhōngláng Suí.
He had an early reputation for excellence,
and many prominent figures recognized his talent and ability.
When he grew up,
he had a beautiful demeanor,
was skilled in conversation,
was widely learned, and capable of writing literary compositions.
His words and meanings were classic and substantial,
and he disliked the ornate and frivolous.
He began his career as a Wángfǔ Fǎcáo,
and successively transferred to Wàibīng Jìshì.
During the Tiānjiā era,
he concurrently served as Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
was dispatched to Qí,
and upon his return, became Guìyáng Wáng Yǒu.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Shùzǐ and Zhōngshū Shìláng.
During the Tàijiàn era,
Shānyīn County had many powerful and unruly individuals.
Previous magistrates had all been dismissed due to corruption.
Gāozōng was concerned about this
and said to Zhōngshū Shèrén Cài Jǐnglì:
“Jīyīn is a large district
that has long lacked a good administrator.
Among the literati,
try to think of such a person.”
Jǐnglì stepped forward and said:
“Chǔ Jiè is incorruptible, frugal, and capable.
I wonder if he is suitable for this selection?”
Gāozōng said:
“Excellent.
Your words are consistent with my own thoughts.”
So, he was appointed Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn and Shānyīn Lìng.
The county residents Zhāng Cìdì, Wáng Xiūdá, and others colluded and committed bribery with various corrupt officials,
and many full-grown households
were found to be concealed.
Jiè then apprehended Cìdì and others,
and reported the full details to the court.
Gāozōng personally issued an edict to commend him
and also sent envoys to assist Jiè in searching and uncovering
more than eight hundred military and civilian households.
At that time, Shèrén Cáo Yìdá was favored by Gāozōng.
A county resident named Chén Xìn, whose family was rich,
flattered and served Yìdá.
Xìn’s father, Xiǎnwén, relied on his influence to act tyrannically.
Jiè then sent an envoy to apprehend Xiǎnwén
and flogged him one hundred times.
Thereupon, officials and commoners trembled with fear,
and no one dared to offend.
Later, Xìn, through Yìdá, slandered Jiè,
and he was eventually dismissed from office.
Jiè was in office for over a year,
merely living on his salary.
On the day he left office,
he could not afford to return to the capital on his own
and therefore remained in the county,
growing vegetables to support himself.
Some mocked Jiè, saying he lacked the talent to govern a hundred-li district.
Jiè replied:
“My tax collection and performance were excellent,
not inferior to other prefectures.
I eradicated the cruel and removed the violent,
and corrupt officials walked on eggshells.
If you say I could not enrich myself,
then so be it.
But to say I am unskilled in governance,
I am not convinced.”
People at the time thought this was true.
The Crown Prince, knowing Jiè had no funds for his return journey,
personally wrote a letter and bestowed upon him two hundred *hú* of grain and rice.
Thus, he returned to the capital.
The Crown Prince admired Jiè’s literary style
and ordered him to serve directly in the palace secretariat.
In the tenth year,
he was appointed Diànwēi Jiāngjūn and Rénwēi Huáinán Wáng Zhǎngshǐ.
Soon after,
he concurrently managed the Đônggông Guǎnjì with his original post.
In the twelfth year,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng
and died in office,
at the age of fifty-two.
Jiè was resolute and courageous,
and also skilled in archery and horsemanship.
He once accompanied Sīkōng Hóu Āndū on a hunt in Xúzhōu,
and encountered a ferocious beast.
〔一七〕Jiè drew his bow and shot it.
Both arrows struck its mouth and penetrated its belly.
Soon after, the beast died.
When he became Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
he gained a great reputation for impartiality.
Since the chaos at the end of the Liáng dynasty,
court regulations had fallen into disuse,
and the Censorate had followed old ways,
maintaining them without reform.
Jiè intended to make changes,
drafting extensive regulations,
and generally outlining the framework.
However, the compilation was not completed,
so it is not listed hereafter.
Upon his death,
the Crown Prince personally composed an epitaph
to express his remembrance.
In the second year of Zhìdé,
he was posthumously appointed Mìshū Jiān.
He authored over two hundred memorials, reports, and miscellaneous writings,
all of which were pertinent to affairs,
and thus he was highly regarded at the time.
His son, Liàng,
had talent and learning,
and rose to the official position of Shàngshū Diànzhōng Shìláng.
Cén Zhījìng, courtesy name Sīlǐ,
was a native of Jíyáng, Nányáng.
His father, Shànyú,
was known in the Liáng era for his classical learning,
and rose to the official positions of Wúníng Lìng and Sīyì Láng.
When Zhījìng was five years old,
he read the *Xiàojīng*.
Every time he burned incense and sat upright,
his relatives all marveled at him.
At the age of sixteen,
he submitted essays on the principles of *Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn* and the meaning of *Xiàojīng*,
and was selected as a *Gāodì*.
The censor reported:
“Among the numerous scholars of our Imperial Dynasty,
the norm is only to be clear on the classics.
Only individuals like Yán and Mǐn
should be designated *Gāodì*.”
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng reviewed his essays and said:
“What's to prevent me from having another Yán or Mǐn?”
Consequently, he summoned Zhījìng for a personal interview
and ordered him to ascend the lecture platform.
He commanded Zhōngshū Shèrén Zhū Yì to hold the *Xiàojīng*
and chant the “Shì” chapter,
while Emperor Wǔ himself debated with him.
Zhījìng expounded and analyzed freely,
responding like an echo.
Those around him were all filled with admiration.
He was then appointed Tóngzǐ Fèngchēláng
and generously rewarded.
At eighteen,
he attended the Fǎhuì at Chóngyúndiàn.
At that time, Emperor Wǔ personally offered incense
and looked closely at Zhījìng, saying:
“Not long ago, I saw him,
and suddenly he wears a cap!”
On that very day, he was appointed Tàixué Xiànnèi Bóshì.
Soon after, he became Shòuguāng Xuéshì and Sīyì Láng,
and was also appointed Wǔlíng Wáng Ānxī Fǔ Xíngyù Cānjūnshì.
In the first year of Tàiqīng,
he submitted a memorial requesting to be tested for office
and was appointed Nánshā Lìng.
During Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion,
Zhījìng led his subordinates
to reinforce the capital.
Upon reaching the county border,
he heard that Táichéng had fallen.
So, he bid farewell to his men
and returned to his hometown.
In the second year of Chéngshèng,
he was appointed Jìn’ān Wáng Xuānhuì Fǔzhōng Jìshì Cānjūn.
At this time, Xiāo Bó occupied Lǐngbiǎo.
Zhījìng was ordered to convey a comforting imperial decree.
When Jiānglíng fell,
he remained in Guǎngzhōu.
In the early Tàijiàn era,
he returned to court
and was granted the position of Đônggông Yìshěng Xuéshì.
The Crown Prince had long heard of his reputation
and particularly bestowed favors upon him.
He was successively promoted to Póyáng Wáng Zhōngwèifǔ Jìshì, Zhènběifǔ Lùshì Cānjūn, Nántái Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ, and Zhēngnánfǔ Zīyì Cānjūn.
Zhī Jìng began his career by advancing through the classics,
and extensively studied literature and history.
He possessed refined literary talent,
not being merely a pure Confucian scholar.
His nature was humble and cautious;
he never boasted of his talent and learning to others.
When guiding junior scholars,
he was always gentle and unassuming.
On every death anniversary, he would arrange a vegetarian feast,
and personally clean and sweep,
weeping all day.
Gentlemen praised him for his earnest conduct.
In the eleventh year, he passed away,
at the age of sixty-one.
The Crown Prince lamented his passing,
and bestowed a very generous funeral gift.
A collection of his works in ten volumes circulated in the world.
His son, Dé Rùn,
inherited his father's style,
and rose to the position of Record Keeper for the Prince of Wúxīng in the Central Army.
Lù Yǎn, courtesy name Wēn Yù,
was the paternal cousin of Qióng, the Minister of Personnel.
His father, Lìng Gōng,
was the Record Keeper and Adjutant for the Prince of Xuānchéng in the Liáng Central Army.
Yǎn was orphaned young but loved learning,
and possessed firm principles.
The province nominated him as Xiùcái.
He received his first official appointment as an Acting Adjutant for the Prince of Shǐxīng in the Xuānhuì Commandery,
and successively moved up to Adjutant of the Judicial Bureau and External Military Adjutant,
serving directly as a scholar in the Jiā Dé Palace.
During his leisure from listening to and reviewing affairs,
Emperor Shìzǔ paid considerable attention to historical records.
Because Yǎn was well-read
and skilled in divination and recitation,
he was summoned to attend the Emperor's side.
Once, the Emperor ordered him to compose an inscription for a sword.
Yǎn took up his brush and completed it instantly,
without any revisions or corrections.
Emperor Shìzǔ greatly admired and praised him for a long time,
and bestowed upon him a set of robes.
Soon after, he concurrently served as a Palace Attendant and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and accompanied Prince of Lángxié, Hòu, on an important diplomatic mission to Qí.
Upon arriving in Yèxià, Hòu fell ill and died,
so Yǎn became the chief envoy himself.
At that time, he was only twenty-something years old;
his demeanor was bright and elegant,
and his responses were calm and quick-witted.
The scholars and officials of Qí were greatly impressed by him.
Upon returning, he became the Chief Clerk for the Prince of Xīn'ān in the Yúnhuī Commandery,
and was promoted to Chief Clerk for the Prince of Ānchéng,
In the early years of Tàijiàn,
he became the Personnel Officer for the Prince of Wǔlíng in the Míngwēi Prefecture,
and concurrently the Record Keeper for the Eastern Palace.
He resigned from office to observe mourning for his mother.
In the fifth year, he passed away,
at the age of thirty-four.
The Crown Prince deeply grieved his death,
personally ordered a period of mourning,
increased his funeral gifts,
and also personally composed his epitaph.
In the second year of Zhìdé,
he was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Agriculture.
Yǎn had few desires
and rarely competed,
his mind was devoted to classical studies,
and he was always at peace.
Many of his literary compositions did not survive in their original form.
The Later Sovereign sought out his remaining writings
and compiled them into two volumes.
He had a younger brother named Yú.
Yú, courtesy name Gàn Yù.
From a young age, he was devoted to learning
and had excellent literary talent.
The province nominated him as Xiùcái.
He received his first official appointment as an Acting Adjutant for the Prince of Ānchéng in the Piàojí Commandery,
then transferred to External Military Adjutant for the Prince of Jìn'ān in the Jūnshī Commandery, and Scholar of the Eastern Palace.
His elder brother Yǎn was then serving as Record Keeper,
and both, with their talent and learning, served to entertain the Emperor.
People at the time compared them to the "Two Yìngs."
In the second year of Tàijiàn,
the Crown Prince offered sacrifices to Confucius at the Imperial Academy,
and all palace officials composed poems.
Yú was ordered to write the preface,
which was extremely rich and beautiful.
He was promoted to Director of the Ministry of Rites,
and resigned from his post to observe mourning for his mother.
After the mourning period,
he became the Personnel Officer for the Prince of Guìyáng in the Míngwēi General's office,
and concurrently the Record Keeper for the Eastern Palace.
He successively rose to Literary Attendant for the Prince of Yǒngyáng, Palace Usher, and Palace Attendant.
Yú studied extensively from childhood,
day and night without ceasing.
He was intelligent and had a strong memory;
once he read something, he never forgot it.
He once studied Zhuāng and Lǎo from Zhōu Hóngzhèng of Rǔnán,
and learned the Chengshi Lun from Dharma Master Sēng Tāo;
he mastered the main principles of both.
At that time, the Crown Prince was fond of learning
and wished to read widely.
Due to the vast number of philosophical works,
he ordered Yú to compile and edit them.
He died before completing the task,
at the age of forty-four.
The Crown Prince wept for him,
personally ordered a period of mourning,
had the government cover the funeral expenses,
and also personally composed a funeral eulogy,
sending an envoy to offer condolences and sacrifices.
"The Record Keeper Lù Yú
suddenly passed away.
My sorrow and lamentation,
how can these feelings ever cease?
My lifelong affections,
as you all know,
are for learning and refinement.
Though I do not reach the ancients,
my admiration for the virtuous and fondness for scholars
are particularly strong.
During the chaos and turmoil of the Liáng dynasty,
when the world was in turmoil,
historical records were incomplete,
and rites and music collapsed,
later generations and students
were not without their blind spots.
One who truly stood out from the crowd
was this man alone.
Although my scope of understanding is limited,
I have never relied on others' opinions for my judgments.
As for even minor virtues or small talents,
I especially commend them.
How much more so for a person of vast intellect and extraordinary talent?
This is indeed a place where words fail.
Speaking of his extensive knowledge of various philosophical schools and historical works,
his thorough understanding of Confucianism and Mohism,
nothing escaped his ears,
and whatever he saw, he could recite.
A praise or a criticism,
an incitement or an exaltation,
discoursing on profound theories, analyzing principles,
sifting through texts and extracting sentences—
never failed to make listeners submit in their hearts
and smile in understanding,
their intentions meeting in harmony.
I considered this a reward for a commoner.
During my leisure from supervision
and my free time,
I often used lively conversations and laughter to entertain myself,
and occasionally played the zither or drank wine.
Refined poems and beautiful verses
would emerge in succession.
Whenever a clear breeze blew and the moon shone bright,
or on beautiful scenes and auspicious days,
facing the towering, uneven mountains,
gazing at the vast, shimmering waves,
or admiring new flowers,
sometimes watching falling leaves,
having listened to spring birds,
and then hearing autumn geese—
I never failed to sit close, raise a cup,
share feelings and express elegant words,
exchanging insights
and interspersing them with banter,
delighting both ears and eyes,
and engaging all our emotions.
I used to say that a hundred years pass quickly,
and morning dew is lamentable.
How could I have known that a jade would break and an orchid wither,
so suddenly succumbing to a short life?
My sorrow and regret,
what more can be said?
His遗迹 (relics) and remaining writings
bring fresh tears to my eyes at every sight.
Breaking the zither strings and laying down the brush,
I constantly feel a bitter sorrow.
I just express this thought;
tears flow endlessly,
and words cannot fully convey my feelings."
His high regard was thus.
In the second year of Zhìdé,
he was posthumously granted the title of Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
He had a collection of ten volumes.
Yú had a paternal cousin named Jiè
and a paternal younger brother named Chēn.
Jiè, courtesy name Rùnyù,
was the son of Liáng Grand Minister Yàn.
〔二一〕He was elegant and discerning,
fond of learning,
and skilled at writing.
He was recommended as a Xiùcái,
and his policy proposals earned him a high ranking.
Yuan Shū, the Minister of Personnel, recommended him to Shìzǔ,
who exceptionally appointed him as Literary Director to the Prince of Héngyáng,
and concurrently an Academician of the Tiānbǎo Palace.
In the early years of Tàijiàn,
he was transferred to be a Friend of the Prince of Chángshā,
and concurrently Registrar.
When Hòuzhǔ was in the Eastern Palace,
he heard of Jiè’s great reputation
and summoned him to be his Scribe.
Subsequently, he was appointed Zhongshèrén,
with his duties as Scribe remaining unchanged,
and he was greatly favored and trusted.
Soon after, he lost his sight due to illness,
and was about to return to his hometown.
The Crown Prince took off his own clothes and gave them to Jiè,
shedding tears for him.
He died in the eighth year,
at the age of thirty-seven.
There was an imperial order to hold mourning for him,
and to provide further burial gifts.
In the second year of Zhìdé,
he was posthumously awarded the title of Shàofù Qīng.
He had a collection of ten volumes.
Chēn, courtesy name Jiéyù,
was the son of Qiū Gōng, Xuan Yí Línchuān Wáng Zhǎngshǐ.
He was intelligent and outstanding in his youth,
and was known for his filial piety towards his stepmother.
When Shìzǔ was the Administrator of Kuàijī,
Chēn, at the age of eighteen,
presented a eulogy on good governance,
which was very eloquent.
From this, he became well-known
and was recommended as a Xiùcái.
He started his career as Chief Clerk to the Prince of Héngyáng,
concurrently serving as Scribe in the Eastern Palace.
He successively held the positions of Literary Director to the Prince of Yùzhāng,
concurrently Registrar,
Chief Clerk to the Sītú,
and Academician of the Xuānmíng Palace.
Soon after, he was transferred to be Shangshū Sāngōng Shìláng,
concurrently Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
and was sent on an embassy to Qí.
Upon his return, he became Zuǒ Xīyuán to the Sītú.
He again took charge of the Eastern Palace’s Scribe duties,
and the Crown Prince admired Chēn’s talent and eloquence,
treating him with deep respect.
After Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
Chēn was transferred to be Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng and Zhōngshū Shèrén,
participating in managing confidential affairs.
Chēn was rather careless by nature,
and was implicated for leaking imperial secrets.
An imperial edict ordered him to commit suicide,
at the age of forty-two.
Hé Zhīyuán was a native of Qián, Lújiāng.
His grandfather, Sēngdá,
was Qí’s Nántái Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ.
His father, Fǎshèng,
was known for his conduct and scholarship.
Zhīyuán was fond of learning in his youth,
and possessed talent and intellect.
His mourning for his parents exceeded the customary rites,
and he was highly esteemed by Liáng Sīkōng Yuán Áng.
At the end of Tiānjiān,
Áng recommended him in a memorial,
and he was thus summoned for an audience.
He began his career as Liáng Tàiwèi Línchuān Wáng Yángzhōu Yìcáo Cóngshìshǐ,
and soon after was transferred to Chief Clerk.
When Áng became the Administrator of Dānyáng,
he appointed Zhīyuán as Dānyáng Wǔguān Yuán,
managing household affairs.
Soon after, he was appointed Magistrate of Xìnyì.
Zhīyuán’s kinsman, Jìngróng,
held a prominent and influential position,
and frequently visited him.
However, Zhīyuán never returned his visits.
Someone asked him the reason,
and Zhīyuán said:
“In the past, the people of Chǔ gained favor with Guānqǐ,
and those who owned horses all fled.
If one’s virtue is shallow but their position is high,
they are bound to face downfall.
I fear I would not gain from it but instead invite disaster.”
Discerning individuals praised him for this.
At that time, Ānxī Wǔlíng Wáng was the Inspector of Yìzhōu,
and appointed Zhīyuán as Ānxī Xíngyù Cānjūn.
During the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng,
Wǔlíng Wáng, acting as Tàiwèi under imperial authorization,
appointed him Nánliáng Zhōu Cìshǐ and
When Wǔlíng Wáng raised troops in Chéngdū and marched eastward,
Zhīyuán and the common people of Shǔ opposed it in a memorial, urging him not to proceed.
The King considered this to be discouraging to the troops,
and imprisoned Zhīyuán on a warship.
After Wǔlíng’s army was defeated,
Zhīyuán accompanied Shàolíng Tàishǒu Liú Gōng to his commandery.
〔二三〕Soon after, Jiānglíng fell,
and Liú Gōng died.
Wáng Lín summoned Zhīyuán to be his Jìshì Cānjūn.
When Liáng Jìngdì appointed Lín as Sīkōng,
Zhīyuán was appointed Sīkōng Fǔ Zīyì Cānjūn,
concurrently Registrar.
When Wáng Lín established Xiāo Zhuāng,
Zhīyuán was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng.
When Qí Wénxuān Dì died,
Zhīyuán was ordered to go to mourn.
Upon his return to Shòuchūn,
Wáng Lín was defeated.
The Qí ruler then appointed him Yángzhōu Biéjià,
the jurisdiction of which was Shòuchūn.
When the combined armies marched north
and gained control of Huáinán,
Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Shǐxīng Wáng Shūlíng sent his Gōngcáo Shǐ Liǔ Xián with a letter to summon Zhīyuán.
Zhīyuán initially had a disagreement with the imperial court,
and when the letter arrived,
he was greatly alarmed.
He read the letter to the part
“Kǒng Zhāng is innocent,
and Zuǒ Chē is employed.”
Zhīyuán looked up and sighed, saying:
“If the words and meaning are like this,
how could they deceive me?”
Thus, he followed Xián to Xiāngzhōu.
In the eighth year of Tàijiàn,
he was appointed Zhōngwèifǔ Gōngcáo Cānjūnshì,
and soon after was transferred to Zīyì Cānjūn.
After Shūlíng was executed,
Zhīyuán withdrew from social life
and diligently focused on writing.
He believed that the Liáng dynasty, which began with Wǔ Huáng
and ended with Jìng Dì,
its rise and fall,
and its periods of prosperity and decline,
were sufficient to serve as a warning
and to establish praise and censure.
Tracing its beginning to end,
starting from the first year of Qí Yǒngyuán
until Wáng Lín’s capture,
seventy-five years of events,
he drafted thirty volumes,
titled them *Liáng Diǎn*.
Its preface says: The histories that record events
are not uniform in their styles.
Among chronological works,
〔二四〕none is like the *Chūnqiū*,
which is a record of the state of Lǔ, not a register of emperors.
Upon examination, the records of the Three Sovereigns are the *Sān Fén*,
and the strategies of the Five Emperors are the *Wǔ Diǎn*.
This is the origin of the meaning of *diǎn*.
Furthermore, the *Shàngshū* describes the Tang Emperor as *Yáo Diǎn*
and the Yu Emperor as
*Shùn Diǎn*.
This is also clearly documented in the classics.
Therefore, the meaning of *diǎn* has existed for a long time.
As for the histories of Mǎ [Qiān] and Bān [Gù],
they narrate emperors and call them annals (jì).
From then on,
successive generations followed this practice.
However, the work compiled by Chén Shòu
was named *Zhì*,
encompassing the Three Kingdoms,
each taking its own path.
Only Hé Fǎshèng’s *Jìn Shū*
changed the imperial annals to *Dì Diǎn*.
Since he claimed to follow the ancients,
this is logically superior.
Therefore, the current work
is titled *Liáng Diǎn*.
The Liáng dynasty ruled the world.
Before Dàtóng,
the region was peaceful and tranquil.
After Tàiqīng,
bandits invaded repeatedly.
Considering the beginning and the end,
it was not entirely beautiful.
Therefore, this book is divided into six sections.
As Gāozǔ established the foundation
following the end of Qí,
to trace the origin,
it starts from Yǒngyuán.
The preceding volumes
are designated as a retrospective account.
Gāozǔ was born a commoner
and grew up amidst common customs,
knowing the good and bad of social conduct
and discerning the true and false among the people.
Upon ascending the throne,
he propagated these policies.
These
methods, within four eras,
are truly said to be prosperous.
Now, a certain number of volumes are designated as the period of Great Peace.
The world is not always peaceful,
and times do not have constant order.
It was not after us
that there was
a rampant flood of chaos.
Now, a certain number of volumes are designated as the period of disorder.
At the year of Gāo Zǔ's (高祖) passing,
and the year of Tài Zōng's (太宗) humiliation,
the songs of praise and prison petitions
faced west towards Shǎnxī (陝西), not east towards the
capital.
The rebellious people
and the fleeing scholars,
as for expeditions, punishments, rites, and music,
returned to Shì Zǔ (世祖), not Tài Zōng (太宗).
Bringing order out of chaos and restoring what is right,
his merit lies therein.
Order was established and achievements
made,
his distinguished service is attributable.
Now, a certain number of volumes are designated as Shì Zǔ (世祖).
As for the four seas being in distress and poverty,
and the Five Virtues rising and falling,
then Jìng Huáng (敬皇) was enthroned,
and subsequently abdicated to
Chén (陳).
Now, a certain number of volumes are designated as Jìng Dì (敬帝).
Piáo Qí (驃騎) Wáng Lín (王琳)
enthroned a successor.
Although he did not fully grasp the mandate of Heaven,
it was nonetheless his loyalty and integrity.
Now, a certain number of volumes
are designated as the successor ruler.
As for Tài Zōng (太宗),
although he was given a beautiful posthumous title,
the title of 'Great Treasure'
was not followed by the world,
presumably because he was constrained by the rebel Jǐng (景).
The Chéng Shèng (承聖) era
chronicles,
beginning from the time of Dà Qīng (太清),
divine imperial edicts and decrees,
were changed whenever inappropriate.
This will be detailed in a later discussion;
there is indeed a reason for it.
Indeed, events have beginnings and ends,
and people have careers and actions.
Between the principal and the subordinate,
it is quite appropriate to differentiate.
Zāng Róngxù (臧榮緒) stated that historical records without judgment
are merely like the 'Records of Daily Life and Activity'.
From this,
it can be said
that thoroughness is truly essential.
Also, for arranging events chronologically and citing the year sequence,
this is to ensure clarity and ease of searching.
As for the Xiǎnyǔn (獫狁) becoming extremely rampant,
obstructing our Central Plains,
starting from one ruler
and ending with two rulers,
the events are intertwined,
and the narratives become confused.
Now, the period before the division is designated as Běi Wèi (北魏),
the part supported by the Gāo (高) clan after the division is Dōng Wèi (東魏),
and the part held by the Yǔwén (宇文) clan is Xī Wèi (西魏).
This is how they are distinguished.
Moreover, to display distinct styles
and variations in length,
there are quite a few general principles for additions and deletions within them.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (禎明),
the capital fell,
so he moved to Jìnlíng (晉陵) County in Chángzhōu (常州).
In the thirteenth year of Kǎihuáng (開皇) of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
he died at home.
Xú Bóyáng (徐伯陽), courtesy name Yǐnrěn (隱忍),
was a native of Dōnghǎi (東海).
His grandfather, Dùzhī (度之),
was the Secretariat Registrar in charge of Deliberations for Nán Xúzhōu (南徐州) during the Qí (齊) dynasty.
His father, Sēngquán (僧權),
was a Secretariat Attendant of the Eastern Palace during the Liáng (梁) dynasty,
and concurrently served as Secretary of the Imperial Library,
known for his excellent calligraphy.
Bóyáng (伯陽) was intelligent and fond of learning,
skilled in supporting his parents,
and had dignified comportment.
At the age of fifteen,
he was known for his literary talent and writing.
He studied the Spring and Autumn Annals and Zuǒ Commentary.
His family owned historical texts,
and he read nearly three thousand volumes.
He scored highly in the imperial examinations,

and the Department of State Affairs appointed him Right Regular Attendant of Hédōng (河東) Princely State, Scholar of the Eastern Palace, and Staff Officer in charge of Records for the Prince of Línchuān (臨川) Successor's Residence during the Liáng (梁) dynasty.
During the Dàtóng (大同) period,
he was appointed Magistrate of Hòuguān (侯官),
and was highly successful in bringing harmony to the people.
During Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) rebellion,
Bóyáng (伯陽) sailed south to Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
taking refuge with Xiāo Bó (蕭勃).
After Bó (勃) was pacified and returned to court,
he brought his family to Wújùn (吳郡).
In the second year of Tiānjiā (天嘉),
he was ordered to attend upon the Prince of Jìn'ān (晉安) for studies.
Soon after, he was appointed Staff Officer for Records to Sīkōng (司空) Hóu Āndū (侯安都).
Āndū (安都) had long heard of his reputation,
and upon seeing him,
descended from his seat as a sign of respect.
When sweet dew fell in the Lèyóu (樂遊) Garden,
an imperial edict bestowed it upon Āndū (安都),
and Bóyáng (伯陽) was ordered to draft a memorial of thanks.
Shì Zǔ (世祖) read it and marveled at it.
In the early years of Tàijiàn (太建),

the Middle Secretariat Lǐ Shuǎng (李爽), Secretariat Zhāng Zhèngjiàn (張正見), Left Ministry Official Hé Chè (賀徹), Scholar Ruǎn Zhuó (阮卓), Palace Attendant Xiāo Quán (蕭詮), Three Dukes Official Wáng Yóulǐ (王由禮), Recluse Mǎ Shū (馬樞), Secretariat Zǔ Sūndēng (祖孫登), Censorate Official Hé Xún (賀循), and Chief Clerk Liú Shān (劉刪) became friends of a literary society.
Later, Cài Níng (蔡凝), Liú Zhù (劉助), Chén Xuān (陳暄), and Kǒng Fàn (孔範) also joined,
all prominent scholars of their time.
They held gatherings and composed poems,
which were compiled into volumes.
Bóyáng (伯陽) wrote the preface for their collection,
which became widely circulated throughout the world.
When the Prince of Xīn'ān (新安) became the Inspector of Nán Xúzhōu (南徐州),
he was appointed Secretariat Staff Officer for the Prince of Xīn'ān (新安) Residence, Zhenběi (鎮北) Command,
concurrently serving as Deputy Governor of Nán Xúzhōu (南徐州),
and holding the post of Commandant of Dōnghǎi (東海) Commandery.
When the Prince of Póyáng (鄱陽) became the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
Bóyáng (伯陽) once went there on an imperial mission.
The Prince, with his officials, ascended Mount Kuāng (匡嶺) with Bóyáng (伯陽),
held a banquet,
and when the wine flowed freely,
ordered them to compose twenty poems with difficult rhymes.
Bóyáng (伯陽) and Zǔ Sūndēng (祖孫登) finished first,
and the Prince rewarded them with servants and miscellaneous items.
When the Prince of Xīn'ān (新安) returned to the capital,
he was appointed Consulting Staff Officer of the Prince of Lín Hǎi (臨海) Successor's Residence, outside the regular quota.
In the spring of the eleventh year,
the Crown Prince visited the Imperial Academy.
An imperial edict ordered the Prince of Xīn'ān (新安) to initiate a discussion on the Analects at Bìyōng (辟雍),
and further commanded Bóyáng (伯陽) to compose a eulogy for Bìyōng (辟雍),
which was highly praised.
〔二五〕 He was appointed Consulting Staff Officer for the Prince of Xīn'ān (新安) Residence, Zhènyòu (鎮右) Command.
In the thirteenth year,
upon hearing of his sister's death,
he fell ill and died,
at the age of sixty-six.
Zhāng Zhèngjiàn (張正見), courtesy name Jiànzé (見賾),
was a native of Dōngwǔchéng (東武城) in Qīnghé (清河).
His grandfather, Gàizhī (蓋之),
was a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Governor of Bóhǎi (勃海) and Chánglè (長樂) Commanderies during the Wèi (魏) dynasty.
His father, Xiūlǐ (脩禮),
was a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary during the Wèi (魏) dynasty,
returned to Liáng (梁),
and was reappointed to his original post,
then promoted to Governor of Huáifāng (懷方).
Zhèngjiàn (正見) was fond of learning from a young age
and possessed refined talent.
When Liáng Jiǎnwén Dì (梁簡文帝) was in the Eastern Palace,
Zhèngjiàn (正見), then thirteen years old,
presented a eulogy,
and Jiǎnwén (簡文) deeply praised and appreciated it.
Jiǎnwén (簡文) was elegantly devoted to scholarship,
and whenever he personally ascended the platform to expound on scriptures,
Zhèngjiàn (正見) often attended the lectures,
asking to resolve difficult points.
His articulation was harmonious and smooth,
and his demeanor composed and elegant.
Everyone present paid close attention to him.
In the early Tàiqīng (太清) period,
he achieved a high rank in the imperial examinations
and was appointed Left Regular Attendant of Shàolíng (邵陵) Princely State.
When Emperor Yuán of Liáng (梁元帝) was enthroned,
he was appointed Director of Communications and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
then promoted to Magistrate of Péngzé (彭澤).
During the chaos and disorder of the late Liáng (梁) dynasty,
he sought refuge in Kuāngsú (匡俗) Mountain.
At that time, Jiāo Sēngdù (焦僧度) gathered followers for self-preservation
and sent an envoy to request an alliance.
Zhèngjiàn (正見) feared him,
but offered humble words to extend the invitation.
However, he held himself with propriety and law,
and Sēngdù (僧度) also respected and feared him greatly.
When Gāo Zǔ (高祖) received the abdication,
he ordered Zhèngjiàn (正見) to return to the capital
and appointed him Staff Officer of Records for the Prince of Póyáng (鄱陽) Residence, Zhèndōng (鎮東) Command,
concurrently serving as Chief Clerk for the Prince of Héngyáng (衡陽) Residence.
He successively served as Secretariat Official for the Prince of Yídū (宜都), outside the regular quota, Compiler of History,
and concurrently Commandant of Xúnyáng (尋陽) Commandery.
He was repeatedly promoted to Official of the Department of State Affairs for Finance and Revenue, and Director of Communications and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
retaining his post as Compiler of History.
He died during the Tàijiàn (太建) period,
at the age of forty-nine.
He had a collection of fourteen volumes,
his five-character poems being particularly excellent
and widely circulated throughout the world.
Cài Níng
had the courtesy name Zǐjū and was a native of Kǎochéng, Jìyáng.
His grandfather, Zǔn,
