was a Grand Master of Imperial Counsel with Gold and Purple and Minister of Personnel during the Liáng dynasty.
His father, Yàngāo,
was a Palace Attendant in the Liáng dynasty.
Níng was intelligent and perceptive in his youth,
and had a handsome appearance and demeanor.
When he grew up,
he extensively studied classics and histories,
and was skilled in literary composition,
especially in cursive and clerical scripts.
In the fourth year of Tiānjiā (563 CE),
he received his first official appointment as a Secretary in the Imperial Library,
and later became a Literary Scholar to the Prince of Lúlín.
In the first year of Guāngdà (567 CE),
he was appointed as an Equerry to the Crown Prince and a Registrar in the Ministry of the Grand Minister over the Masses.
In the first year of Tàijiàn (569 CE),
he was promoted to Central Attendant to the Crown Prince.
As a son of a renowned family, he was chosen to marry Princess Xìnyì,
and was appointed as Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-law and Vice Minister of the Central Secretariat.
He was then promoted to Administrator of Jìnlíng Commandery.
When he was about to depart for the commandery,
he ordered his attendants to repair and tidy up the office of the Central Secretariat,
saying to his guests and friends:
"Would it not be good if those who come later would not have to exert themselves?"
Soon after, he was granted the title General Who Guards the Distant and concurrently served as Vice Minister of Personnel.
Though Níng's age and rank were not yet high,
his talent and background were highly esteemed by the people of his time.
He often sat upright in his western study;
unless they were people of noble birth or distinguished reputation,
he rarely socialized with others.
Many who sought worldly advantages mocked him for this.
Gāozōng once said to Níng:
"I want to appoint Qián Sù, the son-in-law of Princess Yìxīng, as a Palace Attendant.
What do you think?"
Níng replied with a serious expression:
"If he is an old relative from the imperial capital,
and the favor comes from your sacred will,
then there is nothing more to ask.
However, if we are to judge him by general consensus,
for the position of Palace Attendant,
one must indeed possess both personal and family virtues.
Your Majesty should decide."
Gāozōng remained silent and dropped the matter.
Sù heard of this and bore a grudge.
He had Princess Yìxīng frequently slander Níng to Gāozōng,
and soon Níng was dismissed from office
and exiled to Jiāozhǐ.
After a while,
he was recalled.
After Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
Níng was appointed Consultant and Adjutant to the Prince of Jìn'ān,
and later transferred to Palace Attendant.
Hòuzhǔ once held a banquet,
and the officials were extremely joyful.
He intended to move the feast to Hóngfàn Palace.
Everyone followed,
except for Níng and Yuán Xiàn.
Hòuzhǔ asked:
"What are you doing?"
Níng replied:
"Chánglè Palace is solemn and dignified;
it is not a place for revelry after drinking.
Your servant dares not obey the decree."
Everyone present changed color.
Hòuzhǔ said:
"You are drunk!"
And immediately ordered him to be led out.
On another day,
Hòuzhǔ said to Cài Zhēng, Minister of Personnel:
"Cài Níng is conceited about his background and talent;
he is of no use."
Soon after, he was transferred to serve as Chief Clerk of the household of the Prince of Jìnxī, General Xìnwēi.
He was depressed and dissatisfied with his lot,
and sighed deeply, saying:
"The Way of Heaven has its rise and fall.
Confucius said, 'He who delights in Heaven knows his fate.'
This principle can perhaps be understood."
Consequently, he composed the "Fu on the Small Chamber" to express his aspirations,
which was rich in literary and philosophical content.
When the Chén dynasty fell and entered the Suí,
he died of illness on the road,
at the age of forty-seven.
His son, Jūnzhī, was quite famous.
Ruǎn Zhuó
was from Wèishì, Chénliú.
His grandfather, Quán,
was a Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary during the Liáng dynasty.
His father, Wèndào,
was a Recorder and Adjutant in the household of the Prince of Yuèyáng, General Níngyuǎn, during the Liáng dynasty.
Zhuó was intelligent and perceptive in his youth,
devoted himself to classics,
was skilled in discourse,
and particularly adept at five-character-line poetry.
He was extremely filial.
When his father followed the Prince of Yuèyáng to garrison Jiāngzhōu,
he fell ill and died.
Zhuó, then fifteen years old,
rushed from the capital,
not touching food or drink for several days.
During the chaos of Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
the roads were blocked,
but Zhuó braved the dangers
and transported his father's coffin back to the capital.
He encountered bandits on the way.
Zhuó, looking emaciated and distraught,
cried and explained his situation.
The bandits, taking pity, did not kill him,
and even escorted him out of their territory.
When crossing Lake Pénglǐ,
a sudden strong wind struck in the middle of the lake,
and the boat nearly capsized several times.
Zhuó looked up to the sky and cried out in sorrow.
Soon after, the wind subsided.
Everyone believed this was due to his extreme filial piety.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Zhuó was appointed External Military Adjutant in the household of the Prince of Póyáng, Light Chariot General.
In the first year of Tiānkāng (566 CE),
he was transferred to Recorder and Adjutant in the household of the Prince of Xīn'ān, General of Cloud-like Cavalry,
and then continued as Recorder of the Household of the Right Flank,
concurrently serving as a historian and scholar.
He was promoted to Clerk in the Central Guard Office of the Prince of Póyáng,
then transferred to Recorder in the household of the Prince of Jìn'ān,
still holding the scholar position.
After Ōuyáng Hè's rebellion was quelled,
the Yi and Liao tribes in Jiāozhǐ often gathered to raid and plunder.
Zhuó was sent on a mission to pacify and appease them.
Jiāozhǐ connected with Rìnán and Xiàngjùn,
and produced many precious and rare goods like gold, kingfisher feathers, pearls, and shells.
All previous envoys had brought back such items,
but only Zhuó returned empty-handed,
his attire showing no change.
Contemporary opinion unanimously praised his integrity.
He was promoted to Central Clerk and Adjutant in the household of the Prince of Héngyáng.
He entered the court as an Official in the Ministry of Rites.
He was promoted to Recorder and Adjutant in the Central Guard Office of the Prince of Shǐxīng.
When Shúlíng was executed,
Hòuzhǔ said to his court officials:
"Ruǎn Zhuó has never associated with traitors,
so he should be specially honored."
In the first year of Zhìdé (583 CE),
he entered the court as an academician in the Déjiào Palace.
Soon after, he concurrently served as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and accompanied Wáng Huà as deputy envoy to the Suí.
The Suí emperor had long heard of Zhuó's reputation,
and dispatched Xuē Dàohéng from Hédōng and Yán Zhītuī from Lángyá, among others,
to converse, feast, and compose poetry with Zhuó,
and bestowed gifts upon him with extra courtesy.
Upon his return, he was appointed General Who Recruits the Distant and Consultant and Adjutant in the household of the Prince of Nánhǎi.
Due to an eye ailment, he did not take up the official post.
He retired to his village residence,
rebuilt his pavilions and halls,
cultivated his mountain pond and plants,
and invited guests and friends,
finding joy in literature and wine.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (589 CE), he entered the Suí.
When he reached Jiāngzhōu,
he was overcome with emotion remembering where his father had died,
and consequently fell ill and passed away,
at the age of fifty-nine.
At that time, there was also Yīn Kēng
from Wǔwēi,
who had the courtesy name Zǐjiān and was the son of Zǐchūn, the General of the Left Guard during the Liáng dynasty.
He was intelligent and astute in his youth;
at five years old, he could recite poetry and prose,
a thousand words a day.
When he grew up,
he extensively studied historical records,
and was particularly skilled in five-character-line poetry,
which was highly valued at the time.
He received his first official appointment as Judicial Adjutant to the Prince of Xiāngdōng during the Liáng dynasty.
During cold weather,
Kēng once feasted and drank with his guests and friends.
Seeing the person serving wine,
he turned and offered wine and roasted meat to him.
All those seated laughed,
but Kēng said:
"We drink merrily all day long,
but the person holding the wine cup does not know its taste.
This is not humane."
During the chaos of Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Kēng was once captured by bandits.
Someone rescued him and he escaped.
Kēng asked why,
and it turned out to be the person he had previously offered wine to.
During the Tiānjiā period (560-566 CE),
he served as Central Clerk and Adjutant in the household of the Prince of Shǐxīng.
Shìzǔ once held a banquet for his officials to compose poetry.
Xú Líng spoke of Kēng to Shìzǔ,
who immediately summoned Kēng to attend the banquet that day
and had him compose a poem about the newly completed Ānlè Palace.
Kēng took up his brush and finished it immediately.
Shìzǔ greatly praised and admired him.
He was successively promoted to General Who Recruits the Distant, Administrator of Jìnlíng Commandery, and Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and passed away shortly thereafter.
His collected works in three volumes circulated in the world.
The imperial historian says: Literature and scholarship
are perhaps the foundation of human relations.
Therefore, a gentleman differs from the common folk.
In the past, when Zhòngní discussed the four subjects,
he began with moral conduct
and concluded with literature and scholarship.
This shows that even the sage valued them.
As for Dù zhī Wěi and his ilk,
they encountered a fortunate era,
each displaying their talents;
Zhī Wěi was particularly distinguished.
"Jiāng Décāo, courtesy name Dézǎo"
or in some versions
"Jiāng Dézǎo, courtesy name Dézǎo" ,
doubtful.

Biographies, Chapter 29: Xióng Tánlǎng, Zhōu Dí, Liú Yì, Chén Bǎoyìng
Xióng Tánlǎng
was a native of Nánchāng, Yùzhāng.
His family had for generations been a prominent clan in the commandery.
Tánlǎng was unruly and unrestrained,
possessed great physical strength,
and a very imposing appearance.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
he gradually gathered young men,
occupied Fēngchéng County, building a stockade,
and many cunning brigands attached themselves to him.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng appointed him as the Administrator of Bāshān.
When Jīngzhōu fell,
Tánlǎng's military strength gradually grew.
He plundered neighboring counties,
bound and sold the inhabitants,
and in the valleys,
he became the greatest scourge.
When Hóu Tián garrisoned Yùzhāng,
Tánlǎng outwardly feigned submission,
but secretly plotted against Tián.
When Hóu Fāng'ér rebelled against Tián,
Tánlǎng acted as his chief strategist.
When Tián was defeated,
Tánlǎng acquired many of Tián's horses, weapons, sons, and daughters.
When Xiāo Bó crossed the mountains,
Ōuyáng Wěi served as his vanguard.
Tánlǎng deceived Wěi into going together to Bāshān to raid Huáng Fǎlì,
and also informed Fǎlì that they would collectively defeat Wěi,
promising,
"If the matter succeeds, give me horses and weapons."
When the army set out,
he advanced with Wěi, feigning a pincer movement.
He then deceived Wěi again, saying,
"Yú Xiàokǐng intends to ambush us.
We need to leave behind a division of crack troops.
Since our armor and weapons are few,
I fear we cannot succeed."
Wěi then sent three hundred suits of armor to assist him.
Upon arriving at the city walls,
and just before battle,
Tánlǎng feigned retreat to the north.
Fǎlì seized the opportunity and attacked,
leaving Wěi without support.
Wěi retreated in disarray and defeat.
Tánlǎng took his horses and weapons and returned.
At that time, Chén Dìng of Bāshān also commanded troops and established a stronghold.
Tánlǎng falsely offered his daughter in marriage to Dìng's son.
He also told Dìng,
"Zhōu Dí and Yú Xiàokǐng both disapprove of this marriage.
You must come with strong forces to escort her."
Dìng then dispatched three hundred elite armored soldiers along with twenty local magnates to escort her.
Upon their arrival,
Tánlǎng seized them,
confiscated their horses and weapons,
and demanded a ransom for their release.
In the second year of Shàotài (558 CE),
Tánlǎng, as a powerful chieftain from Nánchuān,
was appointed General of Light Cavalry according to custom.
Soon after, he was granted the titles of Bearer of the Imperial Insignia, General of Soaring Valor, and Inspector of Guìzhōu,
and concurrently served as Magistrate of Fēngchéng.
He successively held the posts of Administrator of Yíxīn and Yùzhāng commanderies.
When Wáng Lín sent Lǐ Xiàojīn and others to follow Yú Xiàokǐng in attacking Zhōu Dí in Línchuān,
Tánlǎng led his forces to reinforce them.
In the same year,
for his accomplishments, he was appointed Bearer of the Imperial Insignia, Palace Aide to the Censorate, General Who Pacifies the Distant,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒnghuà County,
with one thousand households,
and granted a set of ceremonial drums and horns.
For his achievement in resisting Wáng Lín,
he was appointed General Who Pacifies the West, and given the honors of Minister with Powers Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers,
with all other titles remaining as before.
When Zhōu Wényù attacked Yú Xiàomài in Yùzhāng,
Tánlǎng led his troops to join him.
When Wényù suffered a defeat,
Tánlǎng then killed Wényù
to curry favor with Wáng Lín;
the details are in Wényù's biography.
Thereupon, he seized all the generals under Wényù's command,
occupied Xīngàn County,
and built a city along the river.
When Wáng Lín marched east,
Emperor Shìzǔ summoned troops from Nánchuān.
Zhōu Dí, the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, and Huáng Fǎlì, the Inspector of Gāozhōu, wished to descend the river to answer the call.
Tánlǎng then occupied the city and deployed warships to block them.
Dí and Fǎlì then led troops from Nánzhōng to build a city and besiege him,
cutting off his communications with Lín.
When Wáng Lín was defeated and fled,
Tánlǎng's partisans lost heart.
Dí attacked and captured his city,
taking more than ten thousand men and women as captives.
Tánlǎng fled into a village,
where the villagers killed him,
and sent his head to the capital,
where it was hung from the Zhūquè Gate Tower.
Then all his clan members were rounded up,
and both young and old were executed in the marketplace.
Zhōu Dí
was a native of Nánchéng, Línchuān.
In his youth, he lived in the valleys,
possessed great physical strength,
and could draw a powerful crossbow.
He made a living by hunting.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Dí's clansman Zhōu Xù raised an army in Línchuān.
Xiāo Yì, Prince of Shǐxīng of Liáng, ceded the commandery to Xù.
Dí recruited local people to follow Xù,
and in every battle, he always displayed the greatest courage among all the armies.
The chieftains under Xù's command
were all powerful local families in the commandery.
They gradually became arrogant and overbearing,
and Xù somewhat restrained them.
The chieftains and others all resented him,
and so they banded together to kill Xù.
They then acclaimed Dí as their leader,
and Dí consequently occupied the territory of Línchuān,
building a city at Gōngtáng.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng appointed Dí Bearer of the Imperial Insignia, Palace Aide to the Censorate, General of Spirited Might, and Inspector of Gāozhōu,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Línrǔ County,
with five hundred households.
In the second year of Shàotài (558 CE),
he was appointed Administrator of Línchuān.
Soon after, he was granted the titles of Commissioner with Imperial Insignia, Palace Aide to the Censorate, General Who Manifests Awe, and Inspector of Héngzhōu,
and concurrently Administrator of Línchuān.
When Zhōu Wényù campaigned against Xiāo Bó,
Dí kept his armor on and protected his borders,
observing the outcome.
Wényù sent his Chief Clerk Lù Shāncái to persuade Dí.
Dí then sent out a large amount of grain and provisions
to supply Wényù.
After Bó was pacified,
for his merit, he was promoted to General Who Manifests the Distant,
and transferred to Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
When Emperor Gāozǔ received the abdication,
and Wáng Lín marched east,
Dí wished to establish himself independently in Nánchuān.
He then summoned all the administrators and magistrates of the eight commanderies under his command to form an alliance,
ostensibly to answer the imperial summons.
The imperial court feared that he might revolt,
and so greatly appeased and consoled him.
When Lín arrived at Pénchéng,
Yú Xiàokǐng, the chieftain of the caves of Xīnwú, raised an army in support of Lín.
Lín believed that the various commanderies of Nánchuān could be pacified by a mere proclamation,
and so dispatched his generals Lǐ Xiàojīn, Fán Měng, and others to levy provisions in the south.
Měng and others joined forces with Yú Xiàokǐng,
their forces reaching nearly twenty thousand,
and advanced towards Gōngtáng,
connecting eight strongholds to pressure Dí.
Dí sent Zhōu Fū to lead his forces to encamp at the old Línchuān commandery,
cutting off the river mouth.
He then went out to battle them,
and utterly defeated them.
He destroyed their eight strongholds,
captured Lǐ Xiàojīn, Fán Měng, and Yú Xiàokǐng alive and sent them to the capital,
and confiscated their military supplies.
Weapons were piled up like mountains,
and he also captured their men and horses,
all of which Dí appropriated for himself.
In the second year of Yǒngdìng (558 CE),
for his accomplishments, he was promoted to General Who Pacifies the South, and given the honors of Minister with Powers Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers,
his granted households increased by one thousand five hundred,
and granted a set of ceremonial drums and horns.
When Shìzǔ succeeded to the throne,
Dí was promoted to the title of Grand General of Ānnán.
When Xióng Tánlǎng rebelled,
Dí, along with Zhōu Fū and Huáng Fǎlì, led troops to jointly besiege Tánlǎng.
They massacred him
and took possession of all his followers.
After Wáng Lín's defeat,
Shìzǔ summoned Dí to garrison Pénchéng,
and also summoned his son to enter the court.
Dí hesitated and looked on,
and neither arrived.
Zhōu Fū, the Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng, had originally belonged to Dí,
but by this time, he and Huáng Fǎlì led their respective units to the imperial court.
Shìzǔ recognized their achievement in defeating Xióng Tánlǎng,
and awarded them with official posts and rewards.
When Dí heard of this,
he was greatly displeased,
and secretly allied himself with Liú Yì.
When the imperial army attacked Yì,
Dí became suspicious and uneasy,
and so he sent his younger brother, Fāngxīng, to lead troops to assault Zhōu Fū.
Fū engaged them in battle
and defeated them.
Dí also separately sent troops to attack Huá Jiǎo at Pénchéng,
but the plot was discovered,
and all were captured by Jiǎo.
In the spring of the third year of Tiānjiā [562 CE],
Shìzǔ issued an edict pardoning the gentry and commoners of Nánchuān who had been misled by Dí,
and ordered Wú Míngchè, the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, to command all armies
along with Huáng Fǎlì, the Inspector of Gāozhōu, and Zhōu Fū, the Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng, to suppress Dí.
Thereupon, the Department of the Grand Secretariat issued a proclamation stating: "To the gentry and commoners of Línchuān Commandery: In the past, when the Western Capital flourished,
Xìn and Yuè were rebellious;
when the Eastern Capital experienced a revival,
Méng and Chǒng were disobedient.
Thus, falcons and sparrowhawks competed for spoils,
and rebels were utterly annihilated—
this has been so since ancient times,
and has a long history.
The rebel Zhōu Dí
originally came from a humble background.
During the chaos of the Liáng dynasty,
he plundered the mountains and valleys.
Our Gāozǔ personally led the Bǎiyuè,
his army reaching Jiǔchuān,
washing away their mud
and sand,
granting them feathers,
cutting off parts of their ceremonial robes,
and then bestowing military tallies.
His benevolent protection
cannot be compared to anything else.
When the imperial fortune was first established,
he demonstrated considerable sincerity and loyalty.
When the nation's
progress was difficult,
he ultimately showed little effort.
With dragon banners and embroidered robes,
he used his princely rank to command his inferiors;
with bear banners and armored plates,
he relied on strategic terrain to disrespect his superiors.
Earlier, Wáng Lín first
turned traitor,
and Xiāo Bó was not yet pacified.
He allied with Sānxiāng in the west,
and communicated with Wǔlǐng in the south.
After Héng and Guǎng were pacified,
and the wavering elements were settled,
Jiāng and Yǐng became tumultuous,
and he again fostered disloyalty.
He occupied
a single commandery,
and was full of disingenuous intentions,
his words and actions constantly contradicting each other.
His statements did not match his conduct.
It was particularly because Xīnwú was not yet pacified,
and his territory was distant and his army strong,
that they mutually annexed each other,
forming their own
power.
He confiscated weapons and equipment,
and captured gentry and commoners,
claiming all as private property,
never once reporting victories.
When an envoy was occasionally sent,
he consistently played both sides.
The imperial court, being immensely broad
and magnanimous,
accepted and highly favored him,
so that his position was equal to that of the Three Councillors,
and his responsibilities were on par with the Four Sacred Mountains.
His wealth and honor were gloriously prominent,
surpassing all meritorious ministers.
Moreover, when the army crossed the岭,
to remotely provide
assistance,
he halted his troops and severed the Jiāng,
suddenly becoming suspicious and resistant.
Thus, the late Sīkōng, Duke Mǐn,
who was bound by kinship,
and felt like family,
had contiguous cities and
was in a relationship like lips and teeth,
but Dí watched the disaster of Péng's
demise
and the ensuing difficulties,
using this pretext
to form his faction and allies.
At that time, the northern bandits invaded,
and the western rebels pressed aggressively.
Shoes, provisions, and food
were all supplied
to the bandits.
His titles and military appearance
were entirely in line with the pseudo-faction.
When the imperial army triumphantly advanced
and stabilized the realm,
the vast net of heaven was generous,
casting him outside its bounds.
Imperial edicts and decrees
offered
reassurance and warm consideration,
and official caps and sashes
were repeatedly bestowed upon him.
As for the annihilation of Xióng Tánlǎng
and the pacification of Fēngchéng,
this was due to the great merit of Yítóng Fǎlì
and the efforts of Ānxī Zhōu Fū.
The Ministry of Personnel had its regulations,
and rewards were bestowed as before.
However, he hated the upright and despised the righteous,
making enemies of them.
His perverse rites and treacherous schemes
thereupon intensified.
Summoned to
Pénchéng,
he failed to arrive for years.
Asked to send a hostage son,
he did not appear at court for a long time.
Externally, he enticed fugitives
and gathered malcontents.
Internally, he agitated the capital,
plotting extraordinary things.
He arbitrarily
collected taxes,
seldom remitting them to the nine treasuries.
He obstructed merchants,
harming the common people.
He secretly allied with the rebel Yì,
forming a joint defense,
like-minded in their evil,
secretly providing support.
He believed that our six armies were stretched thin,
and Sānyuè was not yet settled.
He massacred and destroyed Shùchéng,
capturing wives and children.
He separately attacked Pénzhèn,
and raised an army in Líbāng,
coercing local magnates,
and besieging
cities and towns.
Fortunately, the state was prepared,
and they were immediately repelled and annihilated.
Huá Jiǎo, Acting Commissioner, Regular Mounted Attendant with Special Powers, General Who Manifests Martial Prowess, Grand Administrator of Xúnyáng, and Earl of Huáirén County;
Lù Zǐlóng, General Who Manifests Awe, Grand Administrator of Lúlíng,
and Viscount of Yìyáng County;
both defeated the bandits
and secured their respective commanderies.
Zhōu Fū, Bearer of Credentials, Regular Mounted Attendant, General Who Pacifies the West, Inspector of Dìngzhōu,
and concurrently
Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng and Marquis of Xīfēng County,
personally defended the fortifications,
enduring arrows and stones,
leading righteous volunteers,
and with a smaller force, crushed a larger one,
slaying tens of thousands
and capturing
thousands.
Dí, collecting the remaining remnants,
returned to reinforce his city walls.
Fǎlì, Bearer of Credentials, General Who Pacifies the South, Minister Overseeing Affairs, Inspector of Gāozhōu, and Marquis of Xīnjiàn County,
whose heroic achievements were declared early,
and whose loyalty was long established,
even before receiving the king's command,
previously led righteous troops,
not only assisting Fū and others,
but also securing Zǐlóng.
With provisions packed and armor donned,
he then pursued
fly and run,
the armies that smash through bears,
galloping faster than lightning.
The forces that demonstrate military might
can roar and move mountains.
With these to pursue the fleeing,
there is no reason for any to be left behind.
Even if a decaying tree is to be uprooted,
it does not await a regular axe;
if falling leaves are about to perish,
they do not need a fierce wind.
However, to eradicate grass at its root
is best done before it spreads.
To quench a fire and stop a
blaze
is crucial for its swift extinction.
Dividing orders among generals
truly relies on brave and resolute individuals.
Now, We dispatch Zhèn Nán Yí Tóng Sī Mǎ, Xiāng Dōng Gōng Xiàng Liú Guǎngdé,
concurrently Píng Xī Sī
Mǎ Sūn Xiǎo,
Běi Xīn Cài Tàishǒu Lǔ Guǎngdá,
Chí Jié, Ān Nán Jiāng Jūn, Wú Zhōu Cì Shǐ Péngzé Xiàn Hóu Lǔ Xīdá,
with ten thousand armed soldiers,
to march out from Xīngkǒu.
We also dispatch former Wú Xīng Tàishǒu Hú Shuò,
Shù Gōng Jiāng Jūn, former Xuān Chéng Tàishǒu Qián Fǎchéng,
Tiān Mén and Yì Yáng two commanderies’ Tàishǒu
Fán Yì,
Yún Huī Jiāng Jūn, Hé Zhōu Cì Shǐ Nán Gù Xiàn Hóu Jiāo Sēngdù,
Yán Wǔ Jiāng Jūn, Jiàn Zhōu Cì Shǐ Chén Xiàn Zǐ Zhāng Zhìdá,
Chí Jié,
Dūdū Jiāng Wú Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūn Shì, Ān Nán Jiāng Jūn, Jiāng Zhōu Cì Shǐ Ān Wú Xiàn Hóu Wú Míngchè,
with warships, cavalry, and infantry,
to advance directly on Línchuān.
Former
Ān Chéng Nèi Shǐ Liú Shìjīng,
Bā Shān Tàishǒu Cài Sēngguì,
Nán Kāng Nèi Shǐ Liú Fēng,
Lú Líng Tàishǒu Lù Zǐlóng,
Ān Chéng Nèi Shǐ Quē Shèn,
all shall receive orders from Yí Tóng Fǎ Dù,
and gather in their former commandery.
We also order Xún Yáng Tàishǒu Huá Jiǎo,
Guāng Liè Jiāng Jūn, Bā Zhōu Cì Shǐ Pān Chún,
Píng Xī
Jiāng Jūn, Yǐng Zhōu Cì Shǐ Xīnlè Xiàn Hóu Zhāng Zhāodá,
all to lead their fierce troops
and proceed directly to the bandit city.
Shǐ Chí Jié, Sàn Qí Cháng Shì, Zhèn Nán Jiāng Jūn,
Kāi Fǔ Yí Tóng Sān Sī, Xiāng Zhōu Cì Shǐ Xiāng Dōng Jùn Gōng Dù,
shall dispatch his subordinate generals
to follow one another on the road.
Warships will cover the waters, and mounted archers will fill the mountains.
Furthermore,
We
decree Zhèn Nán Jiāng Jūn, Kāi Fǔ Yí Tóng Sān Sī Ōuyáng Wěi,
to lead his sons and younger brothers, Jiāo Zhōu Cì Shǐ Shèng, the newly appointed Tàizǐ Yòu Shuài Suì, Héng Zhōu Cì Shǐ
Hóu Xiǎo and others,
with the elite troops of Yuè,
to cross the mountains and march north.
A thousand li converge on the same day,
a hundred routes gather simultaneously.
If We delay even a little longer,
and tarry for another ten days,
Sī
Kōng and Dà Dūdū Ān Dū will already have pacified the bandit Dì,
and his triumphant return will not be long.
When the ceremony of drinking upon return is complete,
he will press on with his victory,
to eliminate the wicked and ugly,
as easily as burning hair.
There is already
a clear imperial edict:
the crime is limited to Dì himself;
what crime have the common people committed?
All shall be pardoned.
Those who seize the opportunity to establish merit
will be rewarded according to a separate scale;
those who remain stubbornly deluded and do not change
will be punished without
pardon.
When Wú Míngchè reached Línchuān,
he ordered all armies to construct continuous fortifications to attack Dì.
They held each other at bay and could not overcome him.
Shìzǔ then sent Gāo Zōng to supervise the attack on him.
Dì’s forces collapsed,
and his wife and children were all captured.
He himself escaped across the mountains to Jìn’ān,
and sought refuge with Chén Bǎoyìng.
Bǎoyìng provided Dì with troops,
and Liú Yì also sent his second son, Zhōngchén, to accompany him.
The following year in autumn,
he again crossed the Dōngxīng Ridge.
The people of Dōngxīng, Nánchéng, and Yǒngchéng counties
were all Dì’s old acquaintances,
and again rallied in support of him.
Shìzǔ sent Dūdū Zhāng Zhāodá to campaign against Dì.
Dì again dispersed into the mountains and valleys.
Initially,
during Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion,
the common people all abandoned their regular occupations
and gathered to become bandits.
Only Dì’s department
did not harass or invade.
Instead, he distributed fields,
and supervised their cultivation.
The people were able to pursue their occupations freely,
each having surplus savings.
His governance and teachings were strict and clear,
and his levies were always collected.
Other commanderies that suffered shortages
all looked to him for supplies.
Dì’s nature was simple and plain,
he did not bother with elaborate ceremonies.
In winter, he wore a short coarse cloth robe;
in summer, a purple gauze vest.
He usually went barefoot.
Although there were guards stationed outside,
and female entertainers inside,
he would twist ropes and split bamboo strips,
as if no one else were present.
However, he was light with wealth and fond of giving.
Whatever he provided for,
even the smallest amount was strictly equal.
He was slow of speech,
but his heart was sincere and honest.
The people of Línchuān all admired him for his virtue.
At this time, they all hid him together.
Even if punishments were applied,
no one was willing to speak.
Zhāodá then crossed the mountains,
and encamped at Jiàn’ān,
contending with Chén Bǎoyìng.
Dì again gathered his forces and emerged at Dōngxīng.
At that time, Xuān Chéng Tàishǒu Qián Sù garrisoned Dōngxīng,
and surrendered the city to Dì.
Wú Zhōu Cì Shǐ Chén Xiáng
led his army to attack Dì.
Xiáng’s army was utterly defeated.
Qián Huà Hóu Chén Chuài and Chén Liú Tàishǒu Zhāng Suì both died in battle.
Thereupon, Dì’s forces revived.
Shìzǔ sent Dūdū Chéng Língxǐ to attack and defeat him.
Dì again fled with more than ten people into a mountain cave.
As days and months passed,
those who accompanied him also gradually suffered.
Later, he sent someone to secretly go out to the market in Línchuān Commandery to buy fish.
His feet hurt,
so he stayed at a villager’s house.
The villager reported him to Línchuān Tàishǒu Luò Yá.
Yá seized him
and ordered him to capture Dì himself to prove his loyalty.
Consequently, he sent trusted brave warriors to follow him into the mountains,
lured Dì out to hunt,
and ambushed him by the roadside.
They beheaded him
and sent his head to the capital,
where it was displayed at the Zhūquè Guān for three days.
Liú Yì was
a native of Dōngyáng Chángshān.
His family had been a prominent surname in the commandery for generations.
Yì was skilled at managing himself,
and his speech was reserved and refined,
making him a local strongman.
He gathered many unruly youths
who bullied the poor and humble.
Governors and magistrates all found him troublesome.
During the Liáng dynasty, he served as the commander of Xièpǔ Garrison,
and successively as magistrate of Jìn’ān and Āngù counties.
During Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion,
he returned to his hometown
and recruited soldiers.
The Dōngyáng Commandery Assistant Administrator, who had a grudge against Yì,
led troops to punish him,
and his wife and children.
Tàishǒu Shěn Xún aided the court
and yielded the commandery to Yì.
Yì made his nephew, Chāo, supervise the affairs of the commandery,
and led troops to follow Xún out to the capital.
When the capital fell,
Yì followed the Duke of Línchéng, Xiāo Dàlián.
Dàlián made Yì a Sīmǎ,
entrusting him with military affairs.
Yì was cruel and tyrannical by nature,
lacking foresight.
He harshly controlled Dàlián's military commanders and privately exercised power and influence over his subordinates,
which caused everyone much distress.
At that time, General Jǐng, Sòng Zǐxiān, crossed the Zhèjiāng River,
and Yì fled back to his hometown.
Soon after, he led his followers to surrender to Zǐxiān.
At this time, Dàlián also headed to Xìn'ān Lǐng in Dōngyáng,
intending to go to Póyáng.
Yì then acted as a guide for Zǐxiān,
leading him to capture Dàlián.
Hóu Jǐng appointed Yì as the Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng,
and took his wife and children as hostages.
Hóu Jǐng's Xíngtái, Liú Shénmào, raised an army to resist Hóu Jǐng.
Outwardly, Yì allied with Shénmào,
but secretly colluded with Hóu Jǐng.
When Shénmào was defeated
and executed by Hóu Jǐng,
Yì alone escaped punishment.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Wáng Sēngbiàn sent Yì to console Dōngyáng,
and then to gather his fellow villagers
and hold strategic strongholds.
His followers became very numerous,
and the prefectures and commanderies feared him.
Emperor Yuán appointed him as the Magistrate of Xìn'ān.
When Jīngzhōu fell,
Wáng Sēngbiàn made Yì the Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng.
When Emperor Shìzǔ pacified Kuàijī,
although Yì transported grain and provisions,
he monopolized an entire commandery,
wielding all power and influence himself.
In the second year of Shàotài (553 CE),
for his efforts in receiving and assisting,
he was appointed Chíjǐe, Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Cǐshǐ of Jìnzhōu,
concurrently serving as Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒngxīng County,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
In the same year, he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì and Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn,
with an additional three hundred households,
the rest remaining as before.
Furthermore, Emperor Shìzǔ's eldest daughter, Princess Fēng'ān, was married to Yì's third son, Zhēnchén.
In the second year of Yǒngdìng (558 CE),
Yì was summoned to serve as Shǐchíjǐe, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū of the Military Affairs of Nánxúzhōu, Píngběi Jiāngjūn, and Cǐshǐ of Nánxúzhōu.
Yì procrastinated and did not take up the post.
When Emperor Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was reassigned as Dūdū of the Military Affairs of Jìnzhōu, Ānnán Jiāngjūn, and Cǐshǐ of Jìnzhōu,
concurrently serving as Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng.
Yì frequently sent his Registrar, Wáng Sī, as an envoy to the court.
Sī often spoke of the court's weakness,
and Yì believed him.
Although he outwardly displayed loyalty as a subject,
he constantly harbored two intentions,
and secretly exchanged communications with Wáng Lín from Xìn'ān Lǐng in Póyáng.
Wáng Lín also sent envoys to Dōngyáng,
appointing magistrates and prefects.
When Lín was defeated,
Emperor Shìzǔ sent the Left Guard General, Shěn Kè, to replace Yì as the commander of the commandery,
effectively attacking him with troops.
Yì led his forces to Xiàhuái to resist.
Kè engaged him in battle
and was defeated,
retreating to Qiántáng.
Yì then submitted a memorial expressing apology and submission.
At this time, the armies were engaged in Shāngzhōu and Yǐngzhōu,
so an imperial edict was issued to console and appease him,
and also to restrain him.
Yì also knew that the court would eventually punish him,
so he dispatched troops to garrison Xiàhuái and Jiàndé
to guard the river route.
When Shāngzhōu was pacified,
Emperor Shìzǔ issued an edict which stated: "In ancient times, the Four Criminals were beyond reform,
and Dàguī granted no pardon.
When the Jiǔlí caused disorder in virtue,
Shàohào inevitably executed them.
From ancient times, emperors and kings
did not covet military conquests.
But
when scoundrels plagued the age,
such actions became unavoidable.
The rebel Liú Yì,
who deserves to perish countless times,
has been building up his forces for many years.
When advancing, he feigned humility like the gathering dragons,
only to leap thousands of miles for himself.
When retreating, he was indecisive like a timid mouse,
always
harboring a hundred minds.
In middle age, he secretly colluded with Pānyú,
yet we extended the heavenly net,
bestowing upon him titles,
and solidifying ties with national marriage.
We hoped that he would embrace our grace
and still be able to change his ways.
Wáng
Lín secretly seized the middle reaches of the river,
and Yì reciprocated the connection,
further opening the mountain path of Nánchuān,
and acting as the sole host of the eastern route.
He allied with the villainous leader,
only delighting in disaster and chaos.
Now that
the evil aura has been swept away and settled,
his spirits are low and his heart isolated,
like a wounded bird startled by a bowstring,
or a cornered beast plotting attack.
Although he sent his family as hostages,
his attitude remained increasingly like that of Zǐyáng;
and though his son returned to court as an attendant,
his ambition remained as fierce as that of Kuí Xiāo.
Our intention was to support and nurture him,
disregarding his flaws and misdeeds,
opening our heart and engaging in earnest
and solicitous persuasion.
Yet his 'wasp eyes' became more apparent,
and his 'owl voice' remained unchanged.
He then positioned troops at the river mouth
and heavily garrisoned Xiàhuái,
plainly rebelling,
and is beyond toleration.
Moreover, the fertile Jìn region
and the vast expanse south of Kuàijī
have long been severed from royal tribute
and kept the common people from the state.
The excellent timber of bamboo and arrows
is cut off from the capital,
and small bandits from the reeds and cattails
collectively indulge in greed and cruelty.
We think of those remaining commoners
and share their sighs.
The Western barbarians have bent the knee,
submitting themselves at the critical passes.
Qín
has yielded to our influence,
and all borderlands have submitted their territories.
The three frontiers are already settled,
and the four directions are all peaceful.
Only this petty demon
ought to be completely eradicated.
Therefore, Shǐchíjǐe, Dūdū of the Military Affairs of Nánxúzhōu,
Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn, Sīkōng, and Cǐshǐ of Nánxúzhōu, the Founding Duke of Guìyáng Commandery, Ān Dū, is hereby dispatched to capture and execute him.
The punishment shall be limited to Yì himself;
the rest
shall not be questioned."
Yì had originally thought that the imperial army would come up from the Qiántáng River,
but Ān Dū instead attacked him via the land route through Kuàijī and Zhūjì.
When Yì heard that troops had arrived,
he was greatly alarmed,
abandoned the commandery, and fled to Táozhī Lǐng,
where he erected a stockade at the mouth of the ridge to secure himself.
The following spring,
Ān Dū decisively broke his stockade.
Yì and his second son, Zhōngchén, fled to Chén Bǎo Yìng,
and thus thousands of his remaining followers, men and women, were captured.
In the fifth year of Tiānjiā (564 CE),
Chén Bǎo Yìng was pacified,
and Yì was captured and sent to the capital,
where he was beheaded in Jiànkāng market.
His sons, nephews, and accomplices, regardless of age, were all executed,
except for his third son, Zhēnchén, who was spared because he was married to a princess.
Chén Bǎo Yìng was
a native of Hòuguān in Jìn'ān.
His family had been one of the four prominent clans in Mǐnzhōng for generations.
His father, Yǔ, was capable
and a powerful local figure in the commandery.
Bǎo Yìng was by nature fickle
and full of deceit.
During the Liáng dynasty, Jìn'ān frequently rebelled,
repeatedly killing the commandery administrators.
Yǔ initially instigated and facilitated these incidents,
but later acted as a guide for the imperial army to defeat them.
As a result, all military authority in the commandery came from him.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Xiāo Yún, the Grand Administrator of Jìn'ān and Marquis of Bīnhuà, yielded the commandery to Yǔ.
Yǔ was old,
so he only managed commandery affairs,
and let Bǎo Yìng command the troops.
At this time, there was a famine in the eastern region,
especially severe in Kuàijī,
where seven or eight out of ten people died.
Common people, men and women,
all sold themselves.
Only Jìn'ān was abundant and fertile.
Bǎo Yìng plundered Lín'ān, Yǒngjiā, Kuàijī, Yúyáo, and Zhūjì by sea.
He also transported rice and millet to trade with them,
acquiring many valuables like jade, silk, and young women.
Those who could provide boats
also flocked to him.
Thus, he amassed great wealth
and his army became strong.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Emperor Yuán then made Yǔ the Grand Administrator of Jìn'ān.
When Gāozǔ assisted in governance,
Yǔ requested to retire,
and sought to transfer the commandery to Bǎoyìng.
Gāozǔ granted his request.
In the first year of Shàotài (555 CE),
he was appointed Zhuàngwǔ Jiāngjūn (General of Vigorous Martiality) and Jìn'ān Tàishǒu (Administrator of Jìn'ān Commandery),
and soon after, promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (Supernumerary Palace Attendant).
In the second year (556 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Hòuguān Xiàn Hóu (Marquis of Hòuguān County),
with an estate of five hundred households.
At this time, the roads over the eastern and western mountain ranges
were blocked by bandits and rebels,
so Bǎoyìng traveled by sea to Kuàijī for tribute.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he was appointed Chíjié (bearer of Imperial credentials), Sànqí Chángshì (Palace Attendant), Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn (General of Martial Trust), and Mínzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Mínzhōu),
also holding the post of Kuàijī Tàishǒu (Administrator of Kuàijī).
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Xuānyì Jiāngjūn (General who Manifests Righteousness),
and his father was also elevated to Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Glorious Happiness).
Furthermore, the Zōngzhèng (Court of Imperial Clan Affairs) was ordered to record his lineage
and enroll him as a member of the imperial clan,
and an envoy was dispatched to list his children,
all of whom, regardless of age, were granted titles and ranks.
Bǎoyìng married Liú Yì’s daughter as his wife.
When Hóu Āndū was campaigning against Yì,
Bǎoyìng sent troops to assist him.
He also supplied Zhōu Dí with provisions
and raided Línchuān.
After Dūdū (Commander-in-chief) Zhāng Zhāodá defeated Dí at Dōngxīng and Nánchéng,
Shìzǔ then ordered Zhāodá to command all forces,
to cross the mountains via the southern route from Jiàn'ān,

and also ordered Yìzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yìzhōu), also holding Xìnyì Tàishǒu (Administrator of Xìnyì Commandery), Yú Xiàoqǐng, to command the forces from Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Línhǎi, and Yǒngjiā from the eastern route to join him,
in order to suppress Bǎoyìng,
and also decreed that the Zōngzhèng (Court of Imperial Clan Affairs) should sever his lineage from the imperial clan register.
Thereupon, the Shàngshū (Minister of the Secretariat) issued a declaration saying: To the gentry and commoners of Jìn'ān: In ancient times, when Lǒngxī resisted,
the Hàn did not delay in punishing them;
when Liáodōng rebelled and changed allegiance,
the Wèi declared its grand strategy.
As for Wúzhū, who earned merit for the Hàn,
or Yǒuhù, who shared a surname with the Xià,
when it came to harboring Wú Bì's son,
it led to an army across the sea;
disobeying Sǐ Qǐ's command
resulted in the punitive expedition of Gān Shì.
How much more so now, when a clan is not connected
to the imperial alliance,
and its name is not recorded in the registers of merit,
yet conspicuously commits three acts of rebellion,
and its wickedness deepens into four major crimes?
We find that the Mín rebels Chén Bǎoyìng and his son,
barbarian offshoots,
were fundamentally ignorant of reverence and respect.
During the chaos and disorder of the late Liáng dynasty,
the Mín region was isolated.
His father, being a local strongman,
incited
the barbarian tribes,
wearing topknots and sitting cross-legged,
establishing himself as a chieftain,
unfamiliar with instruction and righteousness,
relying on deceit and flattery.
He then indulged in savagery like wasps and jackals,
and soon renounced his official seal.
When the fiery element (referring to the Liáng dynasty) was waning,
the net
allowed a leviathan to escape,
and as days and months passed,
he was beyond its reach.
Since the auspicious aura of royalty manifested in the southeast,
it truly signified the foundation of a sage (emperor).
The gathering of stars in Dǒuniú (constellations)
truly corresponded to the signs of royalty.
Though he claimed sincerity by climbing mountains and navigating
seas,
his tribute was meager despite his self-appropriation of rare treasures.
He still appropriated rare treasures,
and his tribute was ultimately insignificant.
The imperial court, upholding nurturing and magnanimity,
showered him with immense favor and prestige,
appointing him to govern a commandery from a humble origin,
bestowing upon him the
honor of a splendid official.
He was granted territory to establish a prefecture,
endowed with the grandeur of a regional governor's banner.
He was immediately enfeoffed with a household,
and given a town in Yuèyáng.
Ten men rode in splendid carriages,
while countless others in humble dwellings held high official rank.
Furthermore,
following the example of the great Hàn dynasty,
which extended grace to Lóu Jìng,
and the grand Zhou court,
which appointed the Marquis of Téng as its head,
thus, purple edicts and green documents
conveyed distant imperial benevolence,
and official sashes were distributed
even to infants
in the villages.
Having risen from a humble valley to a towering tree,
who could possibly compare?
Yet, he concealed virulent poison,
and dared to act with wolfish cruelty.
He allied with Liú Yì,
and openly supported Zhōu Dí,
forming blood oaths and marital ties,
making
themselves interdependent like lips and teeth,
entrenching themselves in the mountains and valleys,
delaying for years.
When our cavalry defended the mountains,
securing the western part of Qínwàng,
and our war boats descended the rapids,
conquering the southern
rivers of Huìzé,
he then dared to raise his axe,
assisting the evil rebels.
None failed to be shattered by the bowstring,
and all the ugly hordes were annihilated.
We always considered the crime to lie with the chieftains,
pitying those who were forced and coerced.
The captives
and heads taken
were all ordered to be released with clemency.
Still, imperial envoys were dispatched,
and imperial edicts were issued,
the vast imperial net
still permitted a change of heart.
However, Yì had already fled to danger,
and Dí had escaped punishment,
deceiving and insulting
the imperial emissaries,
making them their cover.
Thus, Yuán Xī requested a mat,
longing for a journey (a distant position),
and Mǎ Yuán observed the frogs,
still content at the bottom of the well.
Furthermore, he withheld the nine taxes,
plundering
the four classes of people,
confiscating all wealth within the borders,
and seizing entire households.
All the common people,
were all oppressed.
Thieves and bandits incited each other,
conspiring and colluding,
even crossing the sea,
raiding Jiámiǎo,
and attacking Jiákǒu,
invading the mountains,
and assaulting Shùchéng,
binding and plundering officials and commoners,
and burning government offices.
If such acts can be tolerated,
what cannot be forgiven?
Now we dispatch Shāzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Shāzhōu) Yú Wénjiǒng,
Míngwēi Jiāngjūn (General of Illustrious Might) Chéng Wénjì,
Jiǎjié (acting Imperial credential bearer), Xuānměng Jiāngjūn (General who Manifests Ferocity), Chéngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Chéngzhōu) Gān Tā,
Jiǎjié (acting Imperial credential bearer), Yún
qí Jiāngjūn (General of Cloud Banner) Tán Zhèn,
Jiǎjié (acting Imperial credential bearer), Xuānměng Jiāngjūn (General who Manifests Ferocity), former Jiān Línhǎi Jùn (Inspector of Línhǎi Commandery) Chén Sīqìng,
Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Vanguard) Xú Zhìyuǎn,
Míngyì Jiāngjūn (General of Illustrious Resolution), Yíhuáng Xiàn
Kāiguó Hóu (Marquis of the Founding of Yíhuáng County) Huì Jì,
Kāiyuǎn Jiāngjūn (General who Extends Distances), newly appointed Jìn'ān Tàishǒu (Administrator of Jìn'ān Commandery) Zhào Duàn,
Chíjié (bearer of Imperial credentials), Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (Palace Attendant who Penetrates Rectitude), Zhuàngwǔ Jiāngjūn (General of Vigorous Martiality), Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Dìngzhōu)
Kānglè Xiàn Kāiguó Hóu (Marquis of the Founding of Kānglè County) Lín Féng,

Jiǎjié (acting Imperial credential bearer), Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn (General of Trustworthy Might), Dūdū Dōngtǎo Zhū Jūnshì (Commander-in-chief of all forces for the Eastern Expedition), Yìzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yìzhōu) Yú Xiàoqǐng,
leading two myriad of imperial guards,
with shielded assault boats covering the sea,
crossing the vast waves,
to sweep clean their nests and lairs.
These are all men who understand shame and are trained for battle,
who have marshaled armies at Rúxū,
who have repeatedly followed Yáng Pú,
and frequently routed Sūn Ēn,
who can slay dragons in midstream,
and command Fēng Yí to beat drums,
with turtles and alligators as their chariots,
and large fish erecting banners at Fānghú.
Yì'ān Tàishǒu (Administrator of Yì'ān Commandery) Zhāng Shàobīn,
whose loyalty and sincerity are fully manifest,
has repeatedly requested troops.
Nánkāng Nèishǐ (Prefect of Nánkāng) Péi Jì,
newly appointed Qīngchē Jiāngjūn (General of Light Chariots) Liú Fēng,
Dōnghéng
zhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Dōnghéngzhōu) Qián Dàojí,
will all immediately dispatch their armed men
to travel with Shàobīn.
The late Sīkōng (Minister of Works) Ōuyáng Gōng,
who in the past submitted memorials,
requesting a punitive expedition,
his distant thoughts align with ours,
like Fúbō's discussion of military tactics.
Though long departed, his sincerity remains,
like Zǐ Yán.
them not to be pardoned.
When the General who Conquers the South passed away,
the Emperor's strategy was not forgotten.
The lingering regrets of Zhōu Nán
were not disgraced by his successor.
Ōuyáng Hé, the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu,
upheld his family's reputation,
and
followed a broad strategy.
His naval and infantry forces,
totaling twenty thousand, advanced in separate routes.
They blocked the "long whales" (enemy ships) by water,
and trapped the "sealed boars" (enemy land forces) by land.
He commanded the armies of Héng and Guǎng prefectures,
to meet our six armies.
Lǐ Zhā (李[⿰月者]), the Inspector of Tóngzhōu,
Dài Huàng, the Inspector of Míngzhōu,
Ōu Báishòu, the Inspector of Xīnzhōu,
〔一０〕Xiū Xíngshī, the General of Dauntless Might,
Zhāng Suí, the Administrator of Chénliú,
Quē Shèn, former Grand Administrator of Ānchéng,
Lù Zǐlóng, former Grand Administrator of Lúlíng,
Rèn Mánnú, former Grand Administrator of Yùníng,
〔一一〕Huáng Fǎcí, the Administrator of Bāshān,
Xú Jìngchéng, General of Martial Brilliance and heir apparent of the Duke of Xiāngdōng,
Lǔ Guǎngdá, the Inspector of Wúzhōu,
Xiáng, former Inspector of Wúzhōu and founding marquis of Suìxīng County,
Shāo Dá,
who held the imperial insignia, was Commander-in-chief of all expeditionary forces, Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary, and General of the Household Guard,
led five thousand elite cavalry
and twenty thousand armored troops.
They crossed directly to Shàowǔ,
and then
stationed themselves at Jìn'ān.
They controlled their reins and hoisted their banners,
leveling mountains and filling valleys.
They aimed to attack from all sides at the appointed time,
to control the "flying and running" (enemy movements).
Qián Sù, former Administrator of Xuānchéng,
〔一二〕Luò Yá, the Administrator of Línchuān,
Sūn Xǔ, the Left Guard Commander of the Crown Prince,
Mò Jǐnglóng, the Administrator of Xúnyáng,
Liú Guǎngdé,
the Administrator of Yùzhāng,
all responded to the situation by suppressing and blocking,
continuously on the road.

Fǎ Mǎ (法☴), who held the imperial insignia, was Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary, General who Guards the South, Governor with the Honors of the Three Ducal Ministers, Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, and founding marquis of Xīnjiàn County,
prepared for battle
in the middle of the river,
to serve as the rear guard.
Wherever the axes and battle-axes reached,
only the chief culprits and the father and son of Liú Yì were to be punished.
As for the main leaders of his faction,
even if they requested to surrender at Hángǔ Pass
or turned their backs on Huáinán,
if they could suddenly
change their plans
and achieve merits based on the opportunity,
they would not only be pardoned,
but also rewarded and promoted.
〔一三〕As for the common people of Jiàn and Jìn who
had long been coerced,
the grand army would clearly
pacify and comfort them.
Each would peacefully enjoy their livelihood,
and those who had been displaced and lost their homes
would immediately return to their native land.
As for others who performed meritorious service,
the rewards are already specified.
If they persist in their delusion and do not change,
and hesitate
in their wickedness,
once the axes and battle-axes arrive,
there will be no one left to pardon.
After Shāo Dá defeated Zhōu Dí,
he crossed the Dōngxīng Ridge
and stationed his forces at Jiàn'ān.
Yú Xiàoqǐng then attacked Jìn'ān from the sea route of Línhaí.
Chén Bǎo Yīng occupied the lakeside of Jiàn'ān,
and resisted the imperial army,
building stockades by water and land.
Shāo Dá dug deep trenches and built high ramparts,
not engaging in battle,
but only ordering his soldiers to cut wood to make rafts.
Soon, the water level rose,
and he released the rafts with the current,
breaking through their water stockades.
Then, he attacked them by both water and land.
Bǎo Yīng's forces collapsed,
and he fled into the mountains and grasslands.
Cornered, he was captured,
and along with his twenty sons and younger brothers, he was sent to the capital
and executed in Jiànkāng market.
The historian remarks: During the calamities of the late Liáng dynasty,
many villains rose in contention.
The chiefs of prefectures and remote areas,
and the powerful figures of villages and fortified strongholds,
gained strength through plunder
and grew powerful through insolence.
Gāozǔ (Emperor Gāo) responded to the times by quelling chaos,
and pacified and settled the realm.
Although Xióng Tánlǎng, Zhōu Dí, Liú Yì, and Chén Bǎo Yīng lived in an era of rising fortune,
their ambition was still to disrupt the established order.
Tánlǎng's treachery and duplicity
led to his eradication, which was fortunate.
As for Bǎo Yīng and Yì,
Shìzǔ (Emperor Shì) either bound them by marriage
or settled them among their relatives.
It was not that he could not overawe and control them,
but rather that he sought to win them over with virtue.
Yet, they betrayed his kindness and abandoned righteousness,
each pursuing different ambitions.
Despite their land not being Huáinán,
they harbored aspirations of becoming emperor.
Despite their power not being that of Yōng or Shǔ,
they initiated the heart of a king (aspired to kingship).
Alas,
since this was due to their delusion and ignorance,
the slaughter and extermination of their five clans
was fitting!
(In the Biography of Chén Bǎo Yīng,
"These all illustrate shame and teach warfare,
mobilizing troops at Rúxū,"
this may be an error.
(For "Lǐ Zhā (李[⿰月者]), the Inspector of Tóngzhōu,"
some versions write
"Jì Là (季腊),"
or
"Lǐ Dǔ (李睹),"
doubtful.
)Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 30: Shǐxīng Wáng Shúlíng, Xīn'ān Wáng Bógù
Shǐxīng Wáng Shúlíng, courtesy name Zǐsōng,
was the second son of Gāozōng (Emperor Gāo).
During the Tiānchéng reign of Liáng,
Gāozōng was a General of the Imperial Guard in Jiānglíng,
and Shúlíng was born there.
When Jiānglíng fell,
Gāozōng was moved to Guānyòu,
while Shúlíng remained in Rángchéng.
When Gāozōng returned,
he offered the Later Lord and Shúlíng as hostages.
In the third year of Tiānjia (562 CE),
he returned to court with the Later Lord,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Kānglè,
with an estate of five hundred households.
Shūlíng 叔陵, when young, was quick-witted in debate,
sought after fame,
and was strong-willed, never yielding.
In the first year of Guāngdà 光大 (567),
he was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng 中書侍郎 (Palace Gentleman of the Secretariat).
In the second year (568),

he was dispatched as Chíjīe 持節 (bearer of credentials), Dūdū Jiāngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì 都督江州諸軍事 (Area Commander of all military affairs in Jiāngzhōu), Nánzhōnglángjiàng 南中郎將 (General of the Southern Palace Guard), and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ 江州刺史 (Governor of Jiāngzhōu).
In the first year of Tàijiàn 太建 (569),
he was enfeoffed as Shǐxīng Jùnwáng 始興郡王 (Prince of Shǐxīng Commandery),
to maintain the sacrifices to Zhāoliè Wáng 昭烈王.

He was promoted to Shǐchíjīe 使持節 (Imperial Envoy with credentials), Dūdū Jiāng Yǐng Jìn Sānzhōu Zhū Jūnshì 都督江郢晉三州諸軍事 (Area Commander of all military affairs in the three prefectures of Jiāng, Yǐng, and Jìn), and Jūnshī Jiāngjūn 軍師將軍 (General of the Army Advisor),
with his post as Cìshǐ 刺史 (Governor) remaining unchanged.
Shūlíng 叔陵 was sixteen at the time,
and all government affairs originated from him;
his subordinates had no part in them.
His nature was severe and harsh,
and his subordinates were awed and feared him.
All the princely sons, nephews, and retired county magistrates
were compelled to serve him.
Qián Fǎchéng 錢法成, the Yùzhāng Nèishǐ 豫章內史 (Administrator of Yùzhāng), went to Shūlíng’s 叔陵’s residence to pay respects,
and was immediately ordered to assign his son Jìqīng 季卿 to lead cavalry guards.
Jìqīng 季卿 felt ashamed,
and did not arrive in time.
Shūlíng 叔陵 was furious,
and insulted Fǎchéng 法成.
Fǎchéng 法成, in resentment, hanged himself.
Even for prefectures and counties not within his jurisdiction,
he would summon and interrogate their officials.
If any court noble or lower official displeased him,
he would falsely accuse them of crimes,
entrapping them with severe penalties.
Soon after, he was advanced to the title of Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn 雲麾將軍 (General of the Cloud-flying Banners)
and additionally appointed Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍 (Palace Attendant).
In the third year (571),
he was additionally appointed Shìzhōng 侍中 (Palace Attendant).
In the fourth year (572),

he was transferred to Dūdū Xiāng Héng Guì Wǔ Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnshì 都督湘衡桂武四州諸軍事 (Area Commander of all military affairs in the four prefectures of Xiāng, Héng, Guì, and Wǔ), Píngnán Jiāngjūn 平南將軍 (General Quelling the South), and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ 湘州刺史 (Governor of Xiāngzhōu),
with his posts as Shìzhōng 侍中 and Shǐchíjīe 使持節 remaining unchanged.
When the various prefectural garrisons heard of his arrival,
they all trembled with fear.
Shūlíng 叔陵 became increasingly tyrannical and violent.
When he campaigned against the Yíliáo 夷獠 (barbarians),
all spoils he acquired went to himself;
not a thread or a fraction was given as reward.
His demands for taxes and labor
had no limit.
At night, he often did not sleep,
burning candles until dawn,
summoning guests,
discussing trivial matters among the common people,
and engaging in all sorts of frivolous jokes.
By nature, he did not drink wine,
but he would place many dishes of meat and fish,
and merely eat them day and night.
From dawn until midday,
he would then begin to sleep.
Documents from his offices
could not be presented without his summons.
Those who were flogged and punished were all imprisoned,
often for several years without being examined.
South of Xiāo 瀟 and Xiāng 湘,
all people were forced to serve as his attendants;
scarcely any remained in the hundreds of lí 里.
If any of them managed to escape,
he would immediately kill their wives and children.
No prefecture or county dared to report this,
and Gāozōng 高宗 was unaware of it.
Soon after, he was advanced to the title of Zhènnán Jiāngjūn 鎮南將軍 (General Guarding the South),
granted a set of drums and pipes,
and transferred to Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn 中衛將軍 (General of the Central Guard).
In the ninth year (577),

he was appointed Shǐchíjīe 使持節 (Imperial Envoy with credentials), Dūdū Yáng Xú Dōngyáng Nányù Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnshì 都督揚徐東揚南豫四州諸軍事 (Area Commander of all military affairs in the four prefectures of Yáng, Xú, Dōngyáng, and Nányù), and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ 揚州刺史 (Governor of Yángzhōu),
with his posts as Shìzhōng 侍中, Jiāngjūn 將軍 (General), and the drums and pipes remaining unchanged.
In the tenth year (578),
he arrived at the capital,
was granted a staff,
and provided with an oil-canopy carriage.
Shūlíng’s 叔陵’s administration was located in the Eastern Palace (Dōngfǔ 東府).
Many affairs concerned the provincial secretariats.
The officials in charge,
if they followed his wishes and complied with his directives,
he would hint for them to be promoted and used.
If they showed even slight disobedience,
they would surely be charged with a major crime,
with serious cases leading to execution.
Rumors spread widely on the roads,
all saying that he harbored extraordinary ambitions.
Shūlíng 叔陵 cultivated a false reputation;
whenever he entered court,
he would always hold a scroll and read in his carriage or on horseback,
reciting loudly and at length,
appearing calm and composed.
When he returned and sat in his study,
he might wield an axe himself to perform "macaque acrobatics" (mùhóu bǎixì 沐猴百戲).
He also liked to roam among tombs,
and whenever he encountered tomb markers with identifiable names,
he would order his attendants to excavate them,
taking the stone epitaphs and ancient artifacts,
along with the skulls and limb bones,
to play with them and admire them,
storing them in his treasury.
Among the common people within his jurisdiction, if there were any unmarried women or young girls
with a slight beauty,
he would immediately force them into his concubinage.
In the eleventh year (579),
he left his post due to mourning for his birth mother, Lady Péng 彭氏.
After a short while,
he was reinstated as Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn 中衛將軍 (General of the Central Guard),
with his posts as Shǐchíjīe 使持節, Dūdū 都督 (Area Commander), and Cìshǐ 刺史 (Governor) remaining unchanged.
During the Jìn 晉 dynasty, many princes, dukes, and nobles
were buried on Méilǐng 梅嶺.
When Lady Péng 彭 died,
Shūlíng 叔陵 petitioned to bury her on Méilǐng 梅嶺.
He then excavated the old tomb of the former Tàifù 太傅 (Grand Tutor) Xiè Ān 謝安,
discarded Xiè Ān’s 謝安’s coffin,
and buried his mother there.
On the day of the initial mourning,
he feigned great grief and sorrow,
claiming to have pricked his blood to copy the Nirvāṇa Sūtra.
Less than ten days later,
he ordered the cooks to prepare fresh food,
serving delicious meals daily.
He also secretly summoned the wives and daughters of his attendants,
and committed adultery with them.
His actions became increasingly lawless,
and news of this gradually reached the emperor.
Gāozōng 高宗 reprimanded Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞 (Censor-in-Chief) Wáng Zhèng 王政,
dismissing Zhèng 王政 from office for failing to impeach Shūlíng 叔陵,
and also removed his Diǎnqiān Qīnshì 典籤親事 (supervising clerks and personal attendants),
and additionally had them flogged.
Gāozōng 高宗 had always loved Shūlíng 叔陵,
and did not punish him according to the law,
but merely reproached him.
When the mourning period ended,
he again became Shìzhōng 侍中 (Palace Attendant) and Zhōngjūn Dàjiāngjūn 中軍大將軍 (Grand General of the Central Army).
When Gāozōng 高宗 fell ill,
the Crown Prince and other princes all entered to attend him.
Gāozōng 高宗 died in the Xuānfú Diàn 宣福殿.
The next morning,
Hòuzhǔ 後主 (the future Last Emperor) was grief-stricken and prostrated.
Shūlíng 叔陵 used a medicine-chopping knife to strike Hòuzhǔ 後主 on the back of his neck.
The Empress Dowager rushed to save him,
and Shūlíng 叔陵 struck the Empress Dowager several times.
Hòuzhǔ’s 後主’s wet nurse, Lady Wú 吳氏,
who was then beside the Empress Dowager,
pulled Shūlíng’s 叔陵’s elbow from behind.
Hòuzhǔ 後主 was thus able to get up.
Shūlíng 叔陵 still held Hòuzhǔ’s 後主’s clothes,
but Hòuzhǔ 後主 struggled free.
Chángshā Wáng Shūjiān 長沙王叔堅 grabbed Shūlíng 叔陵 by the throat,
took away his knife,
then dragged him to a pillar,
and bound him with his robe sleeves.
At this time, Lady Wú 吳氏 had already helped Hòuzhǔ 後主 escape the assassin.
Shūjiān 叔堅 sought Hòuzhǔ’s 後主’s whereabouts,
intending to receive orders.
Shūlíng 叔陵 then struggled free from the sleeves,
rushed out through the Yúnlóng Mén 雲龍門,
galloped his carriage back to the Eastern Palace,
summoned his armored soldiers,
scattered gold and silver as rewards,
and externally summoned the various princes and generals.
None responded,
except Xīn’ān Wáng Bógù 新安王伯固 who heard and came.
Shūlíng 叔陵 gathered barely a thousand soldiers.
Initially, he intended to hold the city and defend,
but soon after, Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn 右衛將軍 (General of the Right Guard) Xiāo Móhē 蕭摩訶 arrived with troops at the western gate of the residence.
Shūlíng 叔陵, in urgent panic,
dispatched Jìshì Wéi Liàng 記室韋諒 to send his drums and pipes to Móhē 摩訶,
and then said to him:
"If the matter succeeds,
I will surely make you a grand minister."
Móhē 摩訶 falsely replied,
saying,
"I must have a trusted general from the Prince himself come,
then I would dare to obey the order."
Shūlíng 叔陵 immediately sent Dài Wēn 戴溫 and Tán Qíyín 譚騏驎 to Móhē 摩訶’s location.
Móhē 摩訶 seized them and sent them to the imperial court,
where they were beheaded beneath the corridor.
Shūlíng 叔陵, knowing he would not succeed,
then went inside and drowned his consort Lady Zhāng 張氏 and seven beloved concubines in a well.
Shūlíng 叔陵 had some subordinate soldiers already in Xīnlín 新林.
Therefore, he led several hundred men and horses,
crossed a small ferry,
intending to rush to Xīnlín 新林,
and then enter the north by boat.
As they traveled to Báiyáng Lù 白楊路,
they were intercepted by the imperial army.
Bógù 伯固, seeing the soldiers arrive,
immediately hid in an alley.
Shūlíng 叔陵 galloped his horse, drawing his blade, and pursued him.
Bógù 伯Gù 伯固 returned.
Many of Shūlíng’s 叔陵’s subordinates
abandoned their armor and scattered.
Móhē’s 摩訶’s cavalryman Chén Zhìshēn 陳智深 rode forward and stabbed Shūlíng 叔陵,
who fell dead to the ground.
The eunuch Wáng Fēiqín 王飛禽 drew a knife and chopped him more than ten times,
and the cavalryman Chén Zhònghuá 陳仲華 then beheaded him,
sending it to the imperial court.
The matter was settled from Yín (3-5 AM) to Sì (9-11 AM).
The Eight Bureaus of the Shàngshū reported:
“The rebel bandit, the former Shìzhōng, Zhōngjūn Dàjiàngjūn, Shǐxīngwáng Shūlíng,
was cruel and perverse in youth,
and indulged in avarice and tyranny in adulthood.
When he governed Xiāngnán,
and then garrisoned Jiǔshuǐ,
the common people of both regions
were completely devastated.
With wasp-like eyes and jackal-like voice,
he befriended frivolous individuals,
was unfilial and inhumane,
relied on military power and was callously cruel,
unmannered and unjust,
and only known for massacres.
During his partial mourning,
he indulged in debauchery and pleasure,
fathered children within his residence,
with one after another.
He hid by day and roamed by night,
constantly engaging in villainous schemes,
plundering residents,
and repeatedly excavating graves.
Xiè Tàifù, who assisted in establishing the Jìn dynasty,
founded the state south of the river,
yet Shūlíng hacked open his coffin and exposed his remains,
a deed shocking to hear and see.
Since the great departed Emperor fell ill,
and did not recover the next day,
Shūlíng, from his noble position,
participated in attending to his medicine.
Outwardly, he showed no sorrow,
but inwardly harbored rebellious and regicidal intentions.
After the Emperor's condition became critical,
and the Sacred Body cried out in agony,
he then used the opportunity of crawling close
to lay hands on the imperial carriage.
When the Empress Dowager came to attend,
he further threatened her with blades,
his wickedness and rebellion were extreme,
unparalleled throughout history.
Fortunately, Chángshāwáng Shūjiān, with his sincere filial piety and earnestness,
bravely exerted himself,
personally struck him down,
and shielded the Sacred Body.
Shūlíng then fled to Dōngchéng,
gathered his wicked followers,
his remaining venom still raging,
and even killed his own wife and children.
Although he was promptly executed and his head displayed,
it still does not assuage the indignation.
We, your ministers, have deliberated
and request to follow the precedent of the Sòng dynasty,
to cast his corpse into the middle of the river,
to defile and inundate his residence,
and also to destroy the tomb and temple of his mother, the Péng clan,
and return the Xiè clan's burial ground.”
The imperial edict stated:
“The villainous and rebellious owl-like creature
turned to attack the palace.
Thanks to the spiritual power of the ancestral temples,
he was destroyed in due course.
Considering the circumstances,
I am filled with both sorrow and indignation.
Since the court has made its proposal,
it should be followed as submitted.”
Shūlíng’s sons
were all immediately granted death.
The former Héngyáng Nèishǐ Péng Gǎo, Cīyì Cānjūn concurrently Jìshì Zhèng Xìn, Zhōng Lùshì Cānjūn concurrently Jìshì Wéi Liàng, and Diǎnqiān Yú Gōngxǐ
were all executed.
Gǎo
was Shūlíng’s maternal uncle.
He initially followed Gāozōng in Guānzhōng,
and had some meritorious service.
He then, relying on Shūlíng, served as commander of the two commanderies of Lìyáng and Héngyáng.
Xìn was favored
for his skill in writing documents,
and participated in all his schemes.
Liàng,
a native of Jīngzhào,
was the son of Liáng Shìzhōng and Hùjūn Jiàngjūn Càn.
He was drawn to Shūlíng for his scholarship.
Chén Zhìshēn, for his merit in executing Shūlíng, was appointed Bālíng Nèishǐ
and ennobled as Yóu'ānxiànzǐ.
Chén Zhònghuá was appointed Xiàcuì Tàishǒu
and ennobled as Xīnyíxiànzǐ.
Wáng Fēiqín was appointed Fúbō Jiàngjūn.
Gold was bestowed upon them in varying amounts.
Xīn'ānwáng Bógù, courtesy name Láozhī,
was the fifth son of Shìzǔ.
He was born with a turtle-like chest,
his eyes showed the whites all around the pupils,
and his physique was small,
but he was intelligent and eloquent.
In the sixth year of Tiānjiā,
he was enfeoffed as Xīn'ānjùnwáng,
with an estate of two thousand households.
Upon the ascension of the dethroned emperor,
he was made Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Nán Lángyá Péngchéng Dōnghǎi Sānjùn Zhūjūnshì, Yúnhuī Jiàngjūn, and Péngchéng Lángyá Èrjùn Tàishǒu.
Soon after, he was appointed Dānyáng Yǐn,
with his general title remaining as before.
In the first year of Tàijiàn,
he was promoted to the title Zhìwǔ Jiàngjūn,
his Yin title remaining as before.
Upon completion of his term,
he was promoted to the title Yìyòu Jiàngjūn.
Soon after, he was appointed Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Wúxīng Zhūjūnshì, Píngdōng Jiàngjūn, and Wúxīng Tàishǒu.
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Shìzhōng, Yìqián Jiàngjūn,
then transferred to Ānqián Jiàngjūn, Zhōnglǐngjūn.
In the seventh year,
he was appointed Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Nánsú Nányù Nánběi Yǔn Sìzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Zhènběi Jiàngjūn, and Nánsúzhōu Cìshǐ.
Bógù was fond of wine,
but not keen on accumulating wealth.
His salary and emoluments
were spent without restraint.
After getting drunk,
he would often beg for things.
Among the various princes,
he was the poorest.
Gāozōng always pitied him
and bestowed special rewards upon him.
Bógù's nature was usually light-hearted,
and he was fond of whipping and beating.
While in his province, he paid no attention to governance,
spending his days hunting.
Sometimes he would ride a sleeping carriage to the fields,
and would summon commoners to join him in his outings,
which often lasted for ten days.
The deer and elk he caught
were mostly kept alive.
Gāozōng was quite aware of this,
and repeatedly sent envoys to reprimand him.
In the tenth year,
he came to court,
and was again appointed Shìzhōng, Zhènyòu Jiàngjūn,
and soon after, Hùjūn Jiàngjūn.
In the same year,
he was appointed Guózǐ Jìjiǔ
and concurrently Lǐng Zuǒxiāoqí Jiàngjūn,
with Shìzhōng and Zhènyòu remaining as before.
Bógù had some knowledge of profound principles,
but was lazy in his studies and did not thoroughly understand anything.
However, when it came to dissecting sentences and posing difficult questions,
he often had unique insights.
His governance was strict and harsh.
For those in the national academy who were lazy, playful, and did not study,
he severely punished them with rods,
making the students fearful.
As a result, their academic progress improved considerably.
In the twelfth year,
he concurrently served as Zōngzhèng Qīng.
In the thirteenth year,
he was appointed Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Yáng Nánsú Dōngyáng Nányù Sìzhōu Zhūjūnshì, and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
with Shìzhōng and his general title remaining as before.
When Hòuzhǔ was initially in the Eastern Palace,
he and Bó Gù were very intimate.
Bó Gù was also good at playful banter,
so Gāozōng would often invite him
whenever he held banquets.
When Shūlíng was in Jiāngzhōu,
he resented Bó Gù's favor
and secretly sought out flaws
to prosecute him by law.
When Shūlíng entered the court,
Bó Gù, fearing punishment,
fawned to gain his favor.
Thereupon, they together slandered and disparaged court worthies,
criticizing all civil and military officials.
Even those of advanced age and high rank
were directly rebuked to their faces,
without any fear or taboo.
Bó Gù was fond of shooting pheasants,
and Shūlíng was fond of opening up tombs.
Whenever they went out to the fields,
they would always go together.
Thus, their sentiments were greatly aligned,
and they consequently plotted rebellion.
Bó Gù, attending in the forbidden palace,
would report
any secret conversation to Shūlíng.
When Shūlíng fled to the Eastern Palace,
he sent a messenger to inform Bó Gù.
Bó Gù rode a single horse and galloped to him,
assisting Shūlíng in giving commands.
Knowing the plot would not succeed,
he intended to escape.
As the four gates were already closed, he could not get out,
so he headed together towards the Bái Yáng Dao.
The imperial horse cavalry
arrived and killed him,
his body lying by the gate of Dōngchāng Guǎn.
He was twenty-eight years old at the time.
An imperial edict stated:
"Bó Gù shared in this rebellious act,
and died on the road.
Now, based on external discussion,
I still cannot bear it.
He may be specially permitted to be buried with the rites of a commoner."
Another imperial edict stated:
"Bó Gù participated in a great rebellion,
cutting himself off from Heaven,
ensuring no offspring would be left behind,
which is a constant rule.
However, as the young children are ignorant
and also connected by distant kinship,
to treat them as commoners
is truly out of compassion.
As for Bó Gù's birth mother, Lady Wáng,
she may also be specially pardoned as a commoner."
His domain was abolished.
The historian says: Confucius stated,
"Wealth and honor
are what people desire,
but if obtained by improper means,
one should not dwell in them."
From emperors
down to the common people,
there is no one for whom there is not a difference between legitimate and illegitimate,
and an order between elder and younger.
Shūlíng was treacherous, restless, and ambitious,
and thus committed acts of rebellion.
Having his body torn apart and quartered
did not fully exhaust his crime;
having his residence polluted and flooded
was not enough to make his transgressions manifest.
Alas!
(The biography of Shǐxīng Wáng states,
"Wáng Fēiqín was appointed Fúbō Jiāngjūn,"
or some versions have
"Zhànghòu Jiāngjūn."
Doubtful.)
